Li and Zhou (2016) and independently Ketover (2016) proved that the min‑max value is achieved by a stationary integral varifold V with free boundary on ∂M, and that V is a smooth embedded minimal hypersurface away from a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most n−7. Moreover, the Morse index of the resulting hypersurface is bounded above by the number of parameters in the sweepout (the “genus” of the min‑max family). This index bound is crucial for applications to the Steklov eigenvalue problem: Fraser and Schoen (2016) showed that the first non‑zero Steklov eigenvalue of a domain in Euclidean space is maximised by a free boundary minimal surface in the unit ball, and the min‑max construction provides the existence of such extremal surfaces. Regularity up to the boundary follows from the work of Grüter and Jost (1986) on the regularity of stationary varifolds with free boundary, combined with the Allard boundary regularity theorem. The construction also yields multiplicity‑one results for generic metrics, a fact proved by Zhou (2020) using a perturbation argument analogous to the one used by Marques and Neves for the closed case. These techniques have been further extended to produce free boundary minimal submanifolds of higher codimension and to study the topology of the space of such submanifolds.

Worked Example: Computing the Width of a Simple Sweepout
Let M be the unit ball B3 ⊂ ℝ3 with the Euclidean metric. Consider the sweepout Φ(t) = ∂Bt where Bt is the concentric ball of radius t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Compute the width of this sweepout and identify the min‑max minimal surface.
The mass of Φ(t) is the area of the sphere of radius t, i.e. 4πt2. The maximum over t ∈ [0,1] occurs at t = 1 and equals 4π. Hence the width of this particular sweepout is 4π. By the min‑max theorem, there exists a free boundary minimal surface in B3 with area ≤ 4π. The equatorial disk D2 = {x3 = 0} ∩ B3 is a free boundary minimal surface with area π, which is strictly less than the width. The min‑max construction applied to the full homotopy class of sweepouts yields the critical surface of least area among all non‑trivial sweepouts; in the ball this is the equatorial disk, and its area π is the true min‑max value (the width of the optimal sweepout). The example illustrates that a naïve sweepout may overestimate the width; the min‑max procedure searches over all sweepouts to find the true critical value.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the existence of a free boundary minimal surface, first identify the ambient manifold and its boundary. Recall that the Almgren–Pitts min‑max theory requires a non‑trivial homotopy class of relative cycles; the width is the min‑max of the maximal slice area. The resulting surface is smooth up to the boundary except for a singular set of codimension ≥ 7, and its Morse index is bounded by the number of parameters. Mention the index bound and the regularity theorem (Allard boundary regularity) to gain full credit.

The Entropy Functional and Convergence of the Calabi Flow

The Calabi flow is the gradient flow of the Calabi energy ∫M R2 dV on the space of Kähler metrics in a fixed Kähler class. Written in terms of the Kähler potential φ, the flow reads ∂tφ = ΔR + R − r̄, where R is the scalar curvature and r̄ its average. Chen and He (2012) introduced an entropy functional W(g, f, τ) = ∫M [τ(|∇f|2 + R) + f − n] (4πτ)−n/2 e−f dV, directly analogous to Perelman’s W‑entropy for the Ricci flow. They proved that W is monotone non‑decreasing along the Calabi flow when τ evolves by ∂tτ = −1 and f satisfies the conjugate heat equation. This monotonicity yields a no‑local‑collapsing theorem: if the Calabi energy is initially bounded, then the flow cannot collapse regions of high curvature too quickly. Using this entropy, Chen and He established long‑time existence and convergence of the Calabi flow on compact Kähler manifolds with non‑positive first Chern class (c1 ≤ 0). In this setting the flow exists for all time and converges smoothly to a constant scalar curvature Kähler (cscK) metric, which is the unique minimiser of the Calabi energy in the Kähler class. For Fano manifolds (c1 > 0) the situation is more delicate; Streets and Tian (2017) showed that if the initial metric has positive bisectional curvature, the Calabi flow converges to a Kähler–Ricci soliton. The entropy functional also plays a role in the stability analysis of cscK metrics: the second variation of W at a critical point is precisely the Lichnerowicz operator acting on the space of Hamiltonian functions, linking the Calabi flow to the Futaki invariant and the Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture. Recent work by Darvas and Rubinstein (2020) uses the entropy to construct a metric completion of the space of Kähler potentials, providing a variational framework for the Calabi flow analogous to the one developed by Perelman for Ricci flow.

The Prescribed Ricci Curvature Problem: Obstructions and Existence Results

Given a smooth symmetric 2‑tensor ρ on a compact manifold Mn, the prescribed Ricci problem asks for a metric g such that Ric(g) = ρ. The problem is not variational in general because the Ricci tensor is not the Euler–Lagrange operator of a diffeomorphism‑invariant functional. Nevertheless, the DeTurck trick linearises the Ricci operator: fixing a background metric g0, one considers the modified Ricci tensor RicW(g) = Ric(g) + ½(∇W + ∇WT) where W is the DeTurck vector field. The equation RicW(g) = ρ becomes a strictly elliptic system for g when W is expressed in terms of g and g0. Short‑time existence for the associated parabolic flow (the Ricci–DeTurck flow with source ρ) follows from standard parabolic theory, yielding local existence for the elliptic problem via the implicit function theorem. However, global obstructions are severe. The contracted Bianchi identity div Ric = ½ dR forces div ρ = ½ d(trgρ), a differential constraint that ρ must satisfy for any solution. In dimension two, the Gauss–Bonnet theorem gives the topological obstruction ∫M trgρ dV = 2π χ(M). For n ≥ 3, Lohkamp (1994) proved that every smooth manifold admits a metric with negative Ricci curvature, and later that any negative definite ρ can be realised as the Ricci tensor of some metric. For positive Ricci curvature the problem is rigid: the only known examples are Einstein metrics (ρ = λg) and certain warped product constructions. Cao and Chen (2005) showed that on a compact manifold with boundary, the Dirichlet problem for prescribed Ricci curvature is solvable for ρ sufficiently close to the Ricci tensor of a background metric, provided the Lopatinskii–Shapiro condition holds. Recent progress by Gursky and Viaclovsky (2021) uses the continuity method combined with a priori estimates derived from the maximum principle for the modified system, establishing existence for a broader class of ρ on manifolds with positive Yamabe invariant.

Ricci Flow on Noncompact Manifolds with Bounded Curvature

Shi (1989) proved that the Ricci flow has a short‑time solution on any complete noncompact Riemannian manifold (M, g0) with bounded curvature |Rm| ≤ K. The proof uses a heat kernel parametrix on the manifold and a contraction mapping in the space of tensors with the sup norm weighted by a suitable time‑dependent factor. The solution satisfies the same curvature bound for a short time and is unique among solutions with bounded curvature. Long‑time existence is more subtle: if the curvature remains bounded on a maximal time interval [0, T), the flow can be extended past T. Perelman’s non‑collapsing theorem extends to the noncompact setting under the additional assumption of a uniform lower bound on the volume of unit balls; the reduced volume monotonicity still holds because the reduced distance is defined via L‑geodesics that stay within the region where curvature is controlled. Hamilton’s compactness theorem for Ricci flow also has a noncompact version: a sequence of pointed Ricci flows (Mi, gi(t), pi) with uniform curvature bounds on compact time intervals subconverges to a smooth pointed Ricci flow (M∞, g∞(t), p∞). This compactness is the key tool in the classification of ancient κ‑solutions in higher dimensions. Bamler (2020) used it to prove that any non‑collapsed ancient solution with bounded curvature in dimension four is either a shrinking cylinder, a Bryant soliton, or a quotient thereof. The theory also underpins the study of the Ricci flow on asymptotically flat or asymptotically conical manifolds, where the curvature decays at infinity and the flow preserves the asymptotic geometry. In the Kähler setting, the Kähler–Ricci flow on noncompact manifolds with bounded curvature has been analysed by Song and Tian (2012), who proved long‑time existence and convergence to a Kähler–Ricci soliton under appropriate assumptions on the initial metric.

  • Confusing the Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions for Ricci flow; they lead to different Lopatinskii–Shapiro requirements and are not interchangeable.
  • Assuming the min‑max width for free boundary minimal surfaces equals the area of a single explicit sweepout; the true width is the infimum over all sweepouts.
  • Neglecting the role of the entropy monotonicity in proving non‑collapsing for the Calabi flow; without it one cannot control the formation of singularities.
  • Overlooking the Bianchi identity constraint div ρ = ½ d(tr ρ) when attempting to prescribe a Ricci tensor; this differential condition is necessary for any solution.
  • Believing that Shi’s short‑time existence theorem for noncompact manifolds requires a positive injectivity radius; bounded curvature alone suffices.
  • Forgetting that the Morse index bound in the free boundary min‑max construction depends on the number of parameters in the sweepout, not on the topology of the ambient manifold.

Self‑Shrinkers and the Fine Classification of Mean Curvature Flow Singularities

Self‑shrinkers are complete immersed hypersurfaces Σ in Euclidean space satisfying H = ⟨x, ν⟩/2, where H is the mean curvature, ν the unit normal, and x the position vector. They arise as blow‑up limits of Type‑I singularities in mean curvature flow and as critical points of the Gaussian area functional F(Σ) = (4π)-n/2 ∫_Σ e-|x|2/4 dμ. The classification programme, initiated by Huisken and developed by Colding‑Minicozzi, distinguishes between generic and non‑generic singularities. Generic singularities are modeled on the round sphere S^n, the generalized cylinders S^k × ℝn‑k (1 ≤ k ≤ n‑1), and the translating bowl soliton in dimension two. Non‑generic singularities correspond to higher‑index self‑shrinkers such as the Angenent torus in ℝ3 and the infinite family of rotationally symmetric self‑shrinkers constructed by Kapouleas‑Yang. The Łojasiewicz‑Simon gradient inequality for the F‑functional, proved by Colding‑Minicozzi, yields uniqueness of the tangent flow for generic singularities and provides a quantitative rate of convergence to the limiting self‑shrinker. In higher dimensions, the work of Bernstein‑Wang and others shows that any self‑shrinker with polynomial volume growth and entropy close to that of the cylinder must be a cylinder itself, a rigidity result that underpins the surgery programme of Huisken‑Sinestrari. The entropy functional λ(Σ) = supx₀,t₀>0 (4π t₀)-n/2 ∫_Σ e-|x‑x₀|2/(4t₀) dμ, introduced by Colding‑Ilmanen‑Minicozzi, gives a monotone quantity along the flow and a compactness criterion for sequences of self‑shrinkers. Recent advances by Hershkovits‑White establish that the space of self‑shrinkers with bounded entropy and genus is compact in the smooth topology, enabling a finite‑dimensional Morse‑theoretic description of the singular set. These tools together give a fine stratification of the singular set: the regular part consists of points modeled on cylinders, while the singular part has Hausdorff dimension at most n‑2 and is rectifiable, a result that extends the earlier partial regularity theory of Brakke and White.

The Prescribed Q‑Curvature Problem on Four‑Manifolds

The Q‑curvature, introduced by Branson, is a fourth‑order conformal invariant on a Riemannian four‑manifold (M,g) defined by Q_g = -1/12 Δ_g R_g + 1/16 R_g2 - 1/8 |Ric_g|2, where R_g is the scalar curvature and Ric_g the Ricci tensor. Under a conformal change g̃ = e2w g, the Q‑curvature transforms according to P_g w + 2 Q_g = 2 Qg̃ e4w, where P_g = Δ_g2 + δ( (2/3) R_g g - 2 Ric_g ) d is the Paneitz operator, a conformally covariant fourth‑order elliptic operator. The prescribed Q‑curvature problem asks: given a smooth function K on M, does there exist a conformal metric g̃ with Qg̃ = K? This is the fourth‑order analogue of the Yamabe problem. The variational structure is given by the functional I(w) = ∫_M ( w P_g w + 4 Q_g w ) dV_g - ∫_M K e4w dV_g, whose Euler‑Lagrange equation is precisely the transformation law. The main analytical difficulty is the lack of a maximum principle for fourth‑order operators and the presence of a critical Sobolev exponent (the embedding W2,2 L^∞ fails in dimension four). Chang‑Yang (1995) proved existence when the total Q‑curvature ∫_M Q_g dV_g is less than 8π2 and K is positive, using a blow‑up analysis and a concentration‑compactness principle adapted to the Paneitz operator. Later, Malchiodi (2006) removed the sign condition on K by employing a min‑max scheme based on the topology of the sublevel sets of I, showing that a solution exists for any K provided the Paneitz operator is non‑negative and the kernel consists only of constants. The case of a negative Paneitz operator is more subtle; Gursky‑Malchiodi (2015) established existence under a generic non‑degeneracy assumption on the linearized operator, using a Lyapunov‑Schmidt reduction and a careful analysis of the bubbling profiles, which are given by the standard bubbles on S4 with Q‑curvature 6. The prescribed Q‑curvature problem is intimately linked to the conformal geometry of four‑manifolds: the total Q‑curvature ∫_M Q_g dV_g equals 4π2 χ(M) - 1/2 ∫_M |W_g|2 dV_g, where χ is the Euler characteristic and W_g the Weyl tensor, so the problem encodes topological information through the Gauss‑Bonnet‑Chern formula.

Worked Example: Verifying the Conformal Transformation of Q‑Curvature
Let (M,g) be a closed four‑manifold and g̃ = e2w g. Show that the Q‑curvature transforms as P_g w + 2 Q_g = 2 Qg̃ e4w. Outline the main steps, indicating where the Paneitz operator appears.
Start from the transformation laws for the scalar curvature and Ricci tensor under a conformal change: Rg̃ = e-2w( R_g - 6 Δ_g w - 6 |∇w|2 ) and Ricg̃ = Ric_g - 2 ∇2 w - 2 dw ⊗ dw + ( 2 |∇w|2 - Δ_g w ) g. Compute the Laplacian of Rg̃ and the squared norm |Ricg̃|2, keeping terms up to fourth order in w. After a lengthy but systematic expansion, the combination -1/12 Δg̃ Rg̃ + 1/16 Rg̃2 - 1/8 |Ricg̃|2 simplifies to e-4w( -1/12 Δ_g2 w - 1/6 Δ_g (R_g w) + 1/8 R_g Δ_g w + 1/8 R_g2 w - 1/4 ⟨Ric_g, ∇2 w⟩ + lower‑order terms ). Recognising the fourth‑order part as the Paneitz operator P_g w = Δ_g2 w + δ( (2/3) R_g g - 2 Ric_g ) d w, one obtains P_g w + 2 Q_g = 2 Qg̃ e4w. The key point is that all third‑order derivative terms cancel because of the Bianchi identities, leaving a conformally covariant operator.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the transformation law of a higher‑order curvature invariant, write down the known transformation formulas for the metric, scalar curvature, and Ricci tensor first. Then compute the variation of the invariant term by term, grouping derivatives of the conformal factor w. The highest‑order terms will always assemble into a conformally covariant operator (Paneitz, GJMS, etc.). Identify that operator by its principal symbol and lower‑order coefficients; this avoids memorising the full expanded formula.

Ricci Flow on Manifolds with Positive Isotropic Curvature

Positive isotropic curvature (PIC) is a curvature condition on a Riemannian manifold (M^n,g) requiring that for every orthonormal four‑frame {e₁,e₂,e₃,e₄} the isotropic curvature R(e₁,e₃,e₁,e₃) + R(e₁,e₄,e₁,e₄) + R(e₂,e₃,e₂,e₃) + R(e₂,e₄,e₂,e₄) - 2 R(e₁,e₂,e₃,e₄) is strictly positive. Introduced by Micallef‑Moore (1988) in the context of minimal surface stability, PIC is preserved by the Ricci flow in all dimensions, a result proved by Hamilton (1997) using his tensor maximum principle for systems. The preservation of PIC is a cornerstone of the differentiable sphere theorem: Brendle‑Schoen (2009) showed that any compact manifold with PIC is diffeomorphic to a spherical space form S^n/Γ. The proof proceeds by evolving the metric by Ricci flow, establishing that PIC implies a pinching estimate that forces the curvature operator to become positive, after which Hamilton’s convergence theorem yields a round metric. In dimension four, PIC is equivalent to the positivity of the self‑dual and anti‑self‑dual Weyl curvatures combined with a scalar curvature bound, and the flow can be analysed via the decomposition of the curvature operator into irreducible components under SO(4). The maximum principle for the curvature operator on the cone of PIC operators, developed by Brendle (2008), shows that the cone is invariant under the ODE dR/dt = R² + R^#, where R^# is the quadratic term from the Bianchi identity. This ODE‑PDE method also yields a classification of ancient solutions with PIC: any non‑compact ancient κ‑solution with PIC in dimension four is either a shrinking cylinder S³ × ℝ or a Bryant‑type steady soliton. The PIC condition is strictly weaker than positive sectional curvature but stronger than positive scalar curvature; it sits naturally between the two and provides a robust framework for topological classification via Ricci flow.

Ricci Flow on Asymptotically Conical Manifolds

An asymptotically conical (AC) Riemannian manifold (M^n,g) is a complete non‑compact manifold that outside a compact set is diffeomorphic to (R,∞) × Σ with metric dr² + r² g_Σ + o(r²), where (Σ,g_Σ) is a compact link. The Ricci flow on AC manifolds was first studied by Deruelle (2010) and later by Schulze‑Simon (2013), who proved short‑time existence for initial data with bounded curvature and a suitable decay rate. The key analytic tool is a weighted Hölder space Ck,α_δ with weight δ ∈ (2‑n,0) that captures the conical geometry; the linearised Ricci‑DeTurck operator is then an isomorphism between appropriate weighted spaces, allowing a contraction‑mapping argument. Long‑time behaviour is governed by the existence of expanding Ricci solitons asymptotic to the same cone. If the link Σ admits a Sasaki‑Einstein metric, the cone is Ricci‑flat and the flow exists for all time, converging to the cone at a polynomial rate. When the cone is not Ricci‑flat, the flow typically develops a Type‑I singularity at finite time, and a blow‑up analysis yields a gradient expanding soliton as the tangent flow. The work of Bamler‑Cabezas‑Rivas‑Wilking (2021) extends the Hamilton‑Perelman compactness theorem to the AC setting, showing that a sequence of pointed AC Ricci flows with uniform curvature bounds on compact time intervals subconverges to a smooth AC Ricci flow. This compactness underpins the classification of ancient AC solutions and the study of the moduli space of AC Ricci expanders. An important application is the construction of Ricci‑flat metrics on crepant resolutions of conical singularities via the Ricci flow, a programme initiated by Hein‑Sun (2015) and completed for Calabi‑Yau cones by Chen‑Wang (2020). The AC framework also provides a natural setting for the study of the Ricci flow on orbifolds with isolated conical singularities, where the flow smooths out the singularity instantaneously if the link has positive Ricci curvature.

Min‑Max Theory for Free Boundary Minimal Hypersurfaces

Free boundary minimal hypersurfaces are properly embedded hypersurfaces Σ in a manifold with boundary (M,∂M) that meet ∂M orthogonally and have zero mean curvature. The min‑max construction, pioneered by Almgren‑Pitts for closed manifolds, was adapted to the free boundary setting by Li‑Zhou (2018) and independently by Ketover‑Marques‑Neves (2019). One considers sweepouts {Σ_t}t∈[0,1] of M by hypersurfaces with free boundary, i.e. each Σ_t is a relative cycle in (M,∂M) with ∂Σ_t ⊂ ∂M. The width ω = infsweepouts sup_t Area(Σ_t) is a min‑max value. The main regularity theorem states that for a generic metric on M, there exists a smooth, properly embedded, free boundary minimal hypersurface Σ (possibly with multiplicity) whose area equals ω, and whose Morse index is bounded by the number of parameters in the sweepout. The proof uses the Almgren‑Pitts combinatorial argument to produce a stationary varifold with free boundary, then applies the regularity theory of Grüter‑Jost and the free boundary Allard theorem of Edelen‑Li to upgrade regularity. A crucial new ingredient is the free boundary version of the Simon‑Łojasiewicz inequality, which guarantees uniqueness of the tangent cone at singular points and yields a discrete set of singularities of codimension at least seven. The multiplicity one conjecture, proved by Zhou (2020) for three‑manifolds, asserts that the min‑max hypersurface appears with multiplicity one for a bumpy metric. Applications include the existence of infinitely many distinct free boundary minimal hypersurfaces in any compact manifold with boundary of dimension three, and a Weyl law for the volume spectrum: the k‑th width ω_k grows like C k1/(n+1). The theory also connects to the Steklov eigenvalue problem: the first non‑zero Steklov eigenvalue σ₁ satisfies σ₁ ≤ C ω1-1/(n-1), linking spectral geometry to the min‑max widths.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the Paneitz operator with the conformal Laplacian; the former is fourth order and appears in the Q‑curvature transformation, the latter is second order and governs the Yamabe problem.
  • Assuming that positive isotropic curvature is preserved by any geometric flow; it is preserved by Ricci flow but not by mean curvature flow or Yamabe flow.
  • Neglecting the weight parameter δ in weighted Hölder spaces when working on asymptotically conical manifolds; the isomorphism property of the linearised operator fails if δ lies outside the indicial interval.
  • Believing that the min‑max width for free boundary hypersurfaces equals the area of a single explicit sweepout; the width is the infimum over all admissible sweepouts.
  • Overlooking the role of the entropy functional λ in the classification of self‑shrinkers; without entropy monotonicity one cannot rule out exotic non‑generic singularities.
  • Thinking that the prescribed Q‑curvature problem always has a solution when the total Q‑curvature is positive; the sign of the Paneitz operator and the topology of the manifold impose further constraints.
  • Forgetting that the Morse index bound in the free boundary min‑max construction depends on the number of parameters in the sweepout, not on the topology of the ambient manifold.

Ricci Flow on Manifolds with Boundary: Short‑Time Existence and Boundary Conditions

The extension of Hamilton's Ricci flow to manifolds with boundary requires a careful treatment of the boundary data because the flow equation ∂tg = −2Ric(g) is only elliptic in the interior after the DeTurck modification. The first short‑time existence result for smooth compact manifolds with boundary was obtained by Shen (1995) using a double‑manifold reflection technique combined with the DeTurck trick. Later, Simon (2002) gave a direct proof by constructing a strictly parabolic system on the manifold with boundary and imposing either Dirichlet (fixed induced metric) or Neumann (fixed second fundamental form) boundary conditions. The mixed boundary condition, where the tangential‑tangential components of the metric are fixed while the normal‑normal component evolves freely, was introduced by Chen‑Wang (2015) to preserve the mean curvature of the boundary. A key technical point is that the linearised operator with these boundary conditions satisfies the Lopatinskii‑Shapiro condition, which guarantees maximal regularity in Hölder or Sobolev spaces. Applications include the construction of metrics with positive scalar curvature on manifolds with boundary via the Ricci flow with surgery (Böhm‑Wilking 2008) and the study of the Yamabe problem on manifolds with boundary (Escobar 1992) where the flow provides a parabolic approach to the prescribed scalar curvature equation. Recent work by Li‑Zhang (2021) shows that if the initial metric has nonnegative Ricci curvature and the boundary is totally geodesic, the flow exists for all time and converges to a product metric on the double.

The Hamilton Harnack Inequality for Mean Curvature Flow and Ancient Solutions

Hamilton's differential Harnack inequality for the mean curvature flow (1993) states that for a convex solution Mt of the flow in ℝn+1 the quantity Z = ∂tH + ∇H·X + H/(2t) is nonnegative, where H is the mean curvature and X is the position vector. This inequality is the parabolic analogue of Li‑Yau's gradient estimate for the heat equation and implies that the mean curvature is pointwise nondecreasing along the flow. The Harnack estimate was extended by Andrews (1994) to fully nonlinear curvature flows and by Haslhofer‑Hershkovits (2015) to ancient solutions that are not necessarily convex. In the ancient setting, the inequality forces the solution to be a translating soliton or a shrinking sphere when equality holds. The classification of ancient low‑entropy solutions in ℝ3 by Choi‑Haslhofer‑Hershkovits‑White (2018) relies crucially on the Harnack inequality to rule out exotic non‑generic singularities. Moreover, the inequality yields a monotonicity formula for the Gaussian density, which is used in the proof of the multiplicity‑one conjecture for mean curvature flow. The Harnack inequality also plays a central role in the construction of the mean curvature flow with surgery by Huisken‑Sinestrari (1999), where it provides the curvature pinching needed to perform the surgery at neck regions.

Worked Example: Applying the Harnack Inequality to an Ancient Solution
Let Mt be an ancient solution of mean curvature flow in ℝ3 with bounded entropy. Show that if the Harnack quantity Z vanishes at some point, then Mt is a shrinking sphere.
The Harnack inequality gives Z ≥ 0 everywhere. If Z = 0 at (x₀,t₀), the strong maximum principle for the parabolic equation satisfied by Z implies Z ≡ 0 on Mt for all t ≤ t₀. The equality case of Hamilton's Harnack inequality characterises solutions for which the vector field X = ∇H/H + x/(2t) is a conformal Killing field. In ℝ3 this forces the solution to be a family of concentric spheres shrinking to a point at time T, i.e. Mt = √(2n(T−t)) S2. The bounded entropy condition excludes the translating bowl soliton, which has infinite entropy. Hence the only ancient solution with Z ≡ 0 and bounded entropy is the shrinking sphere.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the classification of ancient solutions, first recall the entropy bound and the Harnack inequality. Write down the Harnack quantity, state the equality case, and then invoke the known classification theorems (Choi‑Haslhofer‑Hershkovits‑White). This structured approach earns full marks even if you cannot reproduce the full proof.

The Almgren Big Regularity Theorem for Area‑Minimizing Currents in Higher Codimension

Almgren's monumental 2000 monograph proved that an area‑minimizing integral current of dimension m in a Riemannian manifold of dimension n has a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most m−2. This result, known as the big regularity theorem, holds for arbitrary codimension and is the culmination of a programme that began with Federer‑Fleming's compactness theorem (1960) and the partial regularity theory of De Giorgi (1961) for codimension one. Almgren's proof introduces the concept of multiple‑valued functions to approximate the current near singular points and develops a sophisticated frequency function (the Almgren frequency) to control the branching of these approximations. The theorem was later streamlined by De Lellis‑Spadaro (2014‑2016) using a more accessible blow‑up analysis and a refined version of the frequency function. Their work also yields quantitative estimates: the singular set is (m−2)‑rectifiable and its (m−2)‑dimensional Minkowski content is bounded by a constant depending only on the mass of the current. Applications include the regularity of minimizers in the calculus of variations (e.g. harmonic maps into spheres) and the structure of stationary varifolds with bounded first variation. The big regularity theorem is also a key ingredient in the Almgren‑Pitts min‑max construction of minimal hypersurfaces, where the min‑max limit is an integral varifold that is almost minimizing in small annuli and therefore regular away from a set of codimension ≥7.

Shi's Local Derivative Estimates and Long‑Time Existence for Ricci Flow on Complete Noncompact Manifolds

Shi (1989) established local derivative estimates for solutions of the Ricci flow on complete noncompact manifolds with bounded curvature. The estimates state that for any k ≥ 0 there exists a constant Ck depending only on k and the dimension such that |∇kRm| ≤ Ck t−k/2 on any time interval where the curvature is bounded by K. The proof uses a clever induction on k together with the maximum principle applied to a suitably chosen cutoff function. These estimates imply that if a complete noncompact manifold has uniformly bounded curvature on a time interval [0,T), then the flow can be extended past T provided the curvature remains bounded. Consequently, Shi's theorem gives a criterion for long‑time existence: a solution exists for all time if and only if the curvature stays bounded on every finite time interval. This result was extended by Chen‑Zhu (2006) to the Kähler‑Ricci flow and by Bamler (2018) to the Ricci flow with surgery. In the noncompact setting, the estimates are also essential for the construction of ancient solutions via blow‑up limits, because they guarantee that the rescaled flows converge smoothly on compact subsets. A notable application is the proof of the Hamilton‑Perelman compactness theorem for noncompact Ricci flows, which underpins the classification of κ‑solutions in three dimensions.

The Perelman W‑Entropy, Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality, and Gaussian Log‑Sobolev Inequality

Perelman introduced the W‑entropy functional W(g,f,τ) = ∫M [τ(|∇f|² + R) + f − n] (4πτ)−n/2 e−f dV, where τ > 0 and ∫ (4πτ)−n/2 e−f dV = 1. Its monotonicity along the coupled system ∂tg = −2Ric, ∂tf = −Δf + |∇f|² − R + n/(2τ), ∂tτ = −1 is the cornerstone of the noncollapsing theorem. When τ is fixed and the metric is Euclidean, the W‑entropy reduces to the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality: ∫ f² log(f²/∫ f²) dγ ≤ 2∫ |∇f|² dγ for the standard Gaussian measure γ. This inequality, due to Gross (1975), is equivalent to the hypercontractivity of the Ornstein‑Uhlenbeck semigroup and plays a central role in probability theory. Perelman's insight was to recognise that the W‑entropy is a geometric deformation of the Gaussian log‑Sobolev inequality, with the scalar curvature R acting as a potential term. The monotonicity of W implies that the Gaussian log‑Sobolev constant is nondecreasing along the Ricci flow, which in turn yields a lower bound on the volume of geodesic balls (the no‑local‑collapsing theorem). Subsequent work by Ni (2005) and Cao‑Hamilton‑Ilmanen (2004) clarified the relationship between the W‑entropy, the reduced volume, and the classical log‑Sobolev inequality on manifolds with Ricci curvature bounded below. The Gaussian log‑Sobolev inequality also appears in the study of the entropy of self‑shrinkers for mean curvature flow, where it characterises the Gaussian density of the shrinker.

  • Confusing the boundary conditions for Ricci flow: Dirichlet fixes the induced metric, Neumann fixes the second fundamental form, and mixed conditions are not interchangeable.
  • Assuming the Hamilton Harnack inequality holds for all mean curvature flows; it requires convexity or an entropy bound.
  • Overlooking the role of the Almgren frequency function in the big regularity theorem; it controls the branching of multiple‑valued approximations.
  • Neglecting the cutoff function in Shi's derivative estimates; the estimates are local and the constants depend on the choice of cutoff.
  • Treating the W‑entropy as a purely analytic object without its geometric coupling to the Ricci flow; the monotonicity relies on the coupled evolution of f and τ.
  • Believing that the Gaussian log‑Sobolev inequality implies the Euclidean log‑Sobolev inequality directly; they differ by a scaling factor and the presence of the Gaussian measure.
  • Forgetting that the singular set in Almgren's theorem has dimension at most m−2, not m−1, even in higher codimension.

These advanced topics illustrate the deep interplay between parabolic PDE, geometric measure theory, and functional inequalities that defines modern geometric analysis.

The Classification of Self‑Shrinkers for Mean Curvature Flow

Self‑shrinkers are hypersurfaces Σⁿ ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹ satisfying H = ⟨x, ν⟩/2, where H is the mean curvature, ν the outward unit normal, and x the position vector. They arise as blow‑up limits of Type‑I singularities in mean curvature flow and correspond to critical points of the Gaussian area functional F(Σ) = (4π)⁻ⁿ/² ∫_Σ e‑|x|²/4 dμ. Huisken (1990) proved the monotonicity formula ∂ₜ ∫_Σ e‑|x|²/4t dμ ≤ 0, which forces any Type‑I blow‑up to be a self‑shrinker. The classification problem asks for all complete, properly embedded self‑shrinkers. In dimension n = 1 the only complete embedded examples are the line, the circle, and the Abresch‑Langer curves. For n ≥ 2 the known embedded self‑shrinkers include the hyperplanes, the round cylinders Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ (1 ≤ k ≤ n), and the rotationally symmetric “bowl” soliton constructed by Altschuler‑Wu (1994) and later shown to be unique among non‑flat, convex, entire graphical shrinkers by Colding‑Minicozzi (2012). Brendle (2016) proved that any embedded self‑shrinker with polynomial volume growth and genus zero in ℝ³ must be a plane, a cylinder, or the bowl. The Colding‑Minicozzi generic mean curvature flow program uses the Łojasiewicz‑Simon inequality for the F‑functional to show that the only stable self‑shrinkers are the hyperplanes and the cylinders Sⁿ⁻¹ × ℝ, while the bowl is unstable with Morse index one. Recent work by Bernstein‑Wang (2020) extended the classification to self‑shrinkers with bounded entropy, proving that any such shrinker in ℝ³ is one of the above three. The entropy λ(Σ) = supx₀,t₀ (4πt₀)⁻ⁿ/² ∫_Σ e‑|x‑x₀|²/4t₀ dμ, introduced by Colding‑Ilmanen‑Minicozzi‑White (2013), provides a quantitative measure of complexity; the plane has entropy 1, the cylinder S¹ × ℝ has entropy ≈ 1.52, and the bowl has entropy ≈ 1.38. These values are crucial for the multiplicity‑one conjecture and for ruling out exotic singularities in generic flows.

The Geometric Analysis of the Ricci Flow on Manifolds with Boundary

Extending Hamilton’s Ricci flow ∂ₜ g = –2 Ric to compact manifolds with boundary requires prescribing boundary conditions that are both geometrically natural and analytically well‑posed. The most studied are the Dirichlet condition (fixing the induced metric g|_∂M) and the Neumann condition (fixing the second fundamental form Π|_∂M). Shen (1998) established short‑time existence for the Dirichlet problem using the DeTurck trick combined with a reflection argument, showing that the flow exists on a maximal time interval [0,T) and that the boundary metric evolves by a parabolic equation coupled to the interior. For the Neumann problem, the boundary condition is overdetermined for the standard Ricci flow; a compatible condition is the “free boundary” condition where the boundary remains totally geodesic (Π = 0) and the flow preserves this property. Recent work by Chen‑Wang (2021) proved short‑time existence for the Neumann problem on manifolds with convex boundary by reducing to a system of quasilinear parabolic equations with oblique derivative boundary conditions and applying the theory of maximal regularity. Long‑time behavior is governed by the evolution of the boundary scalar curvature and the mean curvature of ∂M. Under the Dirichlet condition, if the initial metric has positive scalar curvature and the boundary is mean‑convex, the flow develops a Type‑I singularity in finite time unless the manifold is a spherical space form. For the Neumann condition, the preservation of the totally geodesic boundary forces the interior to evolve by a Ricci flow with a Neumann‑type boundary condition on the Ricci tensor; this setting appears naturally in the study of the Einstein constraint equations on manifolds with boundary. The Hamilton‑Ivey pinching estimate does not directly extend to the boundary case; instead one uses a boundary maximum principle for the curvature tensor (see Brendle‑Choi‑Daskalopoulos 2020) to obtain curvature bounds up to the boundary. These results are essential for the geometric applications of Ricci flow to the positive mass theorem with boundary and to the classification of manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature and convex boundary.

Worked Example: Entropy Monotonicity for a Cylindrical Self‑Shrinker
Consider the cylinder Σ = S¹(√2) × ℝ ⊂ ℝ³, which satisfies H = ⟨x, ν⟩/2. Compute its Gaussian entropy λ(Σ) and verify that the Huisken monotonicity formula yields a non‑increasing quantity along the mean curvature flow starting from Σ.
The cylinder has radius √2, so its mean curvature H = 1/√2. The position vector on Σ is x = (√2 cos θ, √2 sin θ, z). The outward unit normal is ν = (cos θ, sin θ, 0). Then ⟨x, ν⟩ = √2, and indeed H = ⟨x, ν⟩/2 = √2/2 = 1/√2. The Gaussian area functional is F(Σ) = (4π)⁻¹ ∫_Σ e‑|x|²/4 dμ. Using cylindrical coordinates, |x|² = 2 + z², dμ = √2 dθ dz. Hence F = (4π)⁻¹ ∫‑∞∞ ∫₀2π √2 e‑(2+z²)/4 dθ dz = (4π)⁻¹ (2π√2) e‑1/2 ∫‑∞∞ e‑z²/4 dz = (√2/2) e‑1/2 √(4π) = √(2π) e‑1/2. The entropy λ(Σ) is the supremum of the Gaussian density over all centers and scales; for a self‑shrinker the supremum is attained at the origin with scale 1, so λ(Σ) = F(Σ) ≈ 1.52. Huisken’s monotonicity formula states that for any mean curvature flow Σₜ, the quantity Θ(x₀,t₀) = (4π(t₀‑t))⁻¹ ∫Σₜ e‑|x‑x₀|²/4(t₀‑t) dμ is non‑increasing in t. Since Σ is a self‑shrinker, the flow Σₜ = √(1‑t) Σ is a homothetic shrinking solution. Substituting this family into Θ shows Θ is constant in time, confirming monotonicity (non‑increase) and that the cylinder is a critical point of the entropy functional.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the entropy of a self‑shrinker, first identify whether the surface is a plane, cylinder, or bowl. Recall the exact entropy values: plane = 1, cylinder S¹×ℝ ≈ 1.52, bowl ≈ 1.38. For Ricci flow with boundary, distinguish Dirichlet (fixed induced metric) from Neumann (fixed second fundamental form) and note which short‑time existence theorem applies. Write the boundary condition explicitly in the answer; examiners award marks for stating “totally geodesic boundary preserved” for the Neumann case.

The Role of the Entropy Functional in the Long‑Time Behavior of Mean Curvature Flow

The entropy functional λ(Σ) = supx₀∈ℝⁿ⁺¹, t₀>0 (4πt₀)⁻ⁿ/² ∫_Σ e‑|x‑x₀|²/4t₀ dμ, introduced by Colding‑Ilmanen‑Minicozzi‑White (2013), is a scale‑invariant measure of the complexity of a hypersurface. It is monotone non‑increasing along mean curvature flow and strictly decreasing unless the flow is a self‑shrinker. This property makes λ a Lyapunov function for the flow. For a smooth, closed initial hypersurface Σ₀, the entropy satisfies λ(Σ₀) ≥ 1, with equality only for hyperplanes. If λ(Σ₀) < λ(S¹×ℝ) ≈ 1.52, then by the work of Bernstein‑Wang (2020) the flow cannot develop a cylindrical singularity; the only possible singular models are planes, which are smooth, so the flow exists for all time and converges smoothly to a round sphere after appropriate rescaling. This yields a sharp entropy threshold for long‑time existence and convergence in the class of mean‑convex hypersurfaces. For non‑mean‑convex initial data, the entropy still controls the formation of singularities: any sequence of parabolic rescalings about a singular point produces a limit flow whose entropy is bounded above by λ(Σ₀). The classification of low‑entropy shrinkers (plane, cylinder, bowl) then restricts the possible singularity models. In the context of the multiplicity‑one conjecture, the entropy gap between the cylinder and the bowl (≈ 0.14) is used to rule out multiple sheets forming at a singularity. Recent advances by Hershkovits‑White (2022) show that if the entropy of the initial hypersurface is below the entropy of the Clifford torus in S³ (≈ 1.86), then the flow cannot develop a singularity modeled on the Clifford torus, which is relevant for the Willmore flow. The entropy also appears in the level‑set formulation of mean curvature flow, where the viscosity solution’s fattening phenomenon is characterized by a jump in entropy. Thus λ serves as a bridge between geometric measure theory, PDE regularity theory, and the variational structure of the flow.

The Theory of Ancient Solutions to the Ricci Flow in Dimensions Four and Higher

An ancient solution to the Ricci flow is a complete solution defined on (‑∞, T] for some T ≤ ∞. In three dimensions, Perelman’s classification of κ‑solutions (ancient, κ‑noncollapsed, non‑flat, with nonnegative curvature operator) yields only the shrinking round sphere S³, the shrinking round cylinder S²×ℝ, and their quotients. In dimensions n ≥ 4 the landscape is far richer. Hamilton (1995) constructed the Bryant soliton, a rotationally symmetric, steady gradient Ricci soliton on ℝⁿ with positive curvature operator, which is an ancient solution. Brendle (2013) proved that any rotationally symmetric, steady gradient Ricci soliton on ℝⁿ with positive curvature operator is isometric to the Bryant soliton, establishing uniqueness in that class. For ancient solutions with nonnegative curvature operator, the work of Brendle‑Choi‑Daskalopoulos (2020) shows that any non‑compact ancient solution with positive curvature operator and bounded curvature is either a gradient shrinking soliton (hence a quotient of Sⁿ or Sⁿ⁻¹×ℝ) or a steady soliton asymptotic to a cylinder. The classification of ancient solutions with nonnegative isotropic curvature (NIC) is open in general, but recent progress by Brendle‑Huisken‑Sinestrari (2022) shows that any ancient solution with NIC and bounded entropy must be a shrinking soliton. The entropy here is Perelman’s λ‑entropy λ(g) = inff ∫_M (R + |∇f|²) e‑f dV, which is monotone along the flow. The Hamilton‑Ivey pinching estimate does not hold in higher dimensions; instead one uses the algebraic curvature tensor pinching of Böhm‑Wilking (2008) to show that positive isotropic curvature is preserved and improves under the flow. This allows the construction of ancient solutions via blow‑up limits at Type‑II singularities. The existence of non‑gradient ancient solutions (so‑called “eternal” solutions) is a major open problem; the only known examples are the translating solitons for mean curvature flow, not for Ricci flow. The study of ancient solutions is crucial for the surgery program in higher dimensions, because the canonical neighborhoods in the singularity model are modeled on ancient κ‑solutions. Understanding their topology (e.g., whether they are diffeomorphic to ℝⁿ or to a line bundle over a lower‑dimensional manifold) informs the topological classification of manifolds admitting metrics with positive isotropic curvature.

The Geometric Analysis of the Willmore Flow and Its Critical Points

The Willmore functional W(Σ) = ∫_Σ H² dμ, where H is the mean curvature of an immersed surface Σ ⊂ ℝ³, is conformally invariant in three dimensions. Its L²‑gradient flow, the Willmore flow ∂ₜ x = –Δ_Σ H – 2H(H²‑K) ν (with K the Gauss curvature), is a fourth‑order quasilinear parabolic equation. Kuwert‑Schätzle (2001, 2004) proved short‑time existence for smooth initial immersions and established a monotonicity formula for the Willmore energy analogous to Huisken’s formula for mean curvature flow. They also showed that if the initial Willmore energy is below 8π, the flow exists for all time and converges smoothly to a round sphere (the unique minimizer of W among spheres). The threshold 8π is sharp: the Clifford torus in S³, stereographically projected to ℝ³, has Willmore energy 2π² ≈ 19.74 > 8π and is a critical point of W. The Willmore conjecture, proved by Marques‑Neves (2014) using Almgren‑Pitts min‑max theory, states that the Clifford torus minimizes W among all tori in ℝ³ (or S³). For higher genus, the infimum of W is not known explicitly, but the existence of minimizers for each genus was established by Simon (1993) using geometric measure theory. The flow can develop singularities in finite time; the blow‑up analysis by Rivière (2008) and later by Bernard‑Rivière (2015) shows that any singularity model is a complete Willmore surface in ℝ³ with finite total curvature, which by the classification of Bryant (1984) must be a plane, a sphere, or a member of the Bryant family of Willmore surfaces with ends asymptotic to planes. The Łojasiewicz‑Simon gradient inequality for the Willmore functional, proved by Kuwert‑Schätzle (2004), guarantees convergence of the flow to a critical point when the energy is below a certain threshold and the flow stays in a small neighborhood of a non‑degenerate critical point. Recent work by Michelat‑Rivière (2021) extends the regularity theory to the Willmore flow of surfaces with boundary, where the natural boundary conditions are the Navier conditions (fixed boundary curve, free normal derivative). These results connect the Willmore flow to the theory of elastic surfaces, conformal geometry, and the min‑max construction of minimal surfaces in S³.

  • Confusing the entropy λ of a self‑shrinker with Perelman’s λ‑entropy for Ricci flow; they are different functionals with distinct monotonicity properties.
  • Assuming the Dirichlet boundary condition for Ricci flow preserves the mean curvature of the boundary; it fixes the induced metric, not the second fundamental form.
  • Believing that any ancient solution to Ricci flow in dimension four must be a gradient soliton; non‑gradient ancient solutions are not ruled out.
  • Overlooking the role of the 8π energy threshold in the Willmore flow; above this value finite‑time singularities can occur.
  • Treating the Bryant soliton as a shrinking soliton; it is a steady (translation‑invariant) gradient Ricci soliton.
  • Neglecting the distinction between Type‑I and Type‑II singularities when applying the entropy monotonicity; the entropy bound only controls Type‑I blow‑ups directly.
  • Forgetting that the Clifford torus has Willmore energy 2π², not 8π, and that the Willmore conjecture concerns the minimizer among tori, not spheres.

The advanced topics above illustrate how entropy, boundary conditions, ancient solutions, and higher‑order flows intertwine to shape the modern landscape of geometric analysis.

The Gromov–Hausdorff Convergence and the Structure of Ricci Limit Spaces

The Gromov–Hausdorff topology provides a framework for studying limits of sequences of Riemannian manifolds when the metrics themselves degenerate or collapse. A sequence of compact metric spaces (X_i, d_i) converges in the Gromov–Hausdorff sense to a compact metric space (X, d) if there exist ε_i → 0 and ε_i-isometries f_i : X_i → X. When the manifolds satisfy a uniform lower Ricci curvature bound Ric ≥ (n−1)K and a uniform upper diameter bound, Gromov's compactness theorem guarantees that a subsequence converges to a compact metric length space, called a Ricci limit space. The Cheeger–Colding theory (1996–2000) established that such limit spaces are rectifiable as metric measure spaces: they admit a decomposition into a regular set ℛ of full measure, where the space is locally bi-Hölder to Euclidean space, and a singular set 𝒮 of Hausdorff dimension at most n−2. The regular set carries a natural Riemannian metric tensor in the sense of L² convergence of harmonic coordinates, and the limit measure is the n-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Colding–Naber (2012) proved that the singular set is (n−2)-rectifiable and that the tangent cones at almost every singular point are metric cones splitting off an ℝn−2 factor. This stratification theory was refined by Cheeger–Jiang–Naber (2015) using quantitative differentiation, yielding effective Minkowski estimates for the singular strata. The Gromov–Hausdorff framework is essential for the compactification of moduli spaces of Einstein metrics, the study of collapsing with bounded curvature (Fukaya, Yamaguchi), and the analysis of non-collapsed limits in the Ricci flow surgery program. In the collapsed case, the limit space has lower Hausdorff dimension, and the fibers are almost nilmanifolds; the structure theory involves the nilpotent Killing structure and the theory of F-structures. The stability of the Perelman entropy functionals under Gromov–Hausdorff convergence (Colding, 1997) links the analytic monotonicity to the geometric compactness.

The Ricci Flow on Surfaces: Hamilton's Uniformization Theorem and the Chow–Gulliver Theorem

On a closed surface M², the Ricci flow ∂ₜg = −2Kg reduces to a scalar equation for the conformal factor. Writing g(t) = e2u(t)g₀, the flow becomes ∂ₜu = Δg₀u − K₀, where K₀ is the Gauss curvature of g₀. Hamilton (1988) proved that for any initial metric on S², the normalized flow ∂ₜg = (r − 2K)g, where r = ∫ K dA / Area is the average curvature, exists for all time and converges exponentially fast in C^∞ to a constant curvature metric. This provides a nonlinear parabolic proof of the uniformization theorem for S². For surfaces of genus ≥ 1, the unnormalized flow ∂ₜg = −2Kg exists for all time and converges to a flat metric (genus 1) or a hyperbolic metric (genus ≥ 2) after suitable rescaling. The key estimate is the Harnack inequality for the heat equation on evolving metrics, which Hamilton derived using the maximum principle for the quantity Q = Δ log K + K. Chow (1991) extended the result to all initial metrics on S² without the positive curvature assumption, using an entropy functional E(g) = ∫ (|∇K|²/K + K²) dA and a clever blow-up argument to rule out finite-time singularities. The convergence rate is exponential in the normalized flow. For noncompact surfaces, the Ricci flow was studied by Shi (1989) and Chen–Yin (2014); on ℝ², the flow converges to the flat metric if the initial curvature is nonnegative and decays sufficiently fast. The Ricci flow on surfaces with boundary was analyzed by Hamilton (1991) and later by Brendle (2002), who proved convergence to a constant curvature metric with geodesic boundary under the Neumann boundary condition for the conformal factor. The surface case is the only dimension where the Ricci flow is a scalar equation, making it a crucial testing ground for techniques—maximum principle, entropy monotonicity, blow-up analysis—that generalize to higher dimensions. The Chow–Gulliver theorem (1997) gives a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a metric of constant curvature in a given conformal class on a surface with boundary, using the Ricci flow with Dirichlet boundary conditions.

Worked Example: Normalized Ricci Flow on the 2-Sphere
Consider the normalized Ricci flow ∂ₜg = (r − 2K)g on S² with initial metric g₀ of total area 4π. Show that the flow exists for all time and that the curvature K(t) converges uniformly to 1. Outline the role of the entropy functional E(g) = ∫S² (|∇K|²/K + K²) dA in Chow's proof.
The normalized flow preserves total area. Hamilton's Harnack estimate for the heat equation on evolving metrics gives ∂ₜK = ΔK + 2K(K − r). The maximum principle implies that if K > 0 initially, it remains positive. The entropy E(g) satisfies dE/dt = −2∫ (ΔK + K(K−r))²/K dA ≤ 0. Chow's key insight: if a singularity formed at finite time T, then E would blow up, but the monotonicity and the logarithmic Sobolev inequality bound E from below. A blow-up argument around a hypothetical singularity produces an ancient solution on ℝ² with nonnegative curvature, which by Hamilton's classification must be the cigar soliton—but the cigar has infinite area, contradicting the fixed area 4π. Hence no finite-time singularity exists. Long-time existence plus entropy decay forces K → r = 1 uniformly, with exponential rate by linearization around the round metric.
Exam Strategy: Distinguishing Normalized vs. Unnormalized Flow
In surface Ricci flow questions, check whether the flow is normalized (preserves area/volume) or unnormalized (area evolves by dA/dt = −∫ 2K dA = −4πχ(M) by Gauss–Bonnet). For S², unnormalized flow shrinks to a point in finite time; normalized flow exists forever and converges to round metric. For genus ≥ 1, unnormalized flow expands forever; normalized flow converges to flat/hyperbolic metric. The sign of χ(M) dictates the behavior.

The Mean Curvature Flow with Free Boundary Conditions

The mean curvature flow (MCF) with free boundary conditions asks for a family of hypersurfaces Σ_t in a manifold with boundary (M, ∂M) such that each Σ_t meets ∂M orthogonally and evolves by ∂ₜx = Hν. This models the motion of capillary surfaces and grain boundaries in materials science. The orthogonal intersection condition is ∂Σ_t ⊂ ∂M and ν_Σ ⊥ ν_∂M along ∂Σ_t. Stahl (1996) proved short-time existence and uniqueness for smooth initial hypersurfaces meeting ∂M orthogonally, assuming ∂M is strictly mean-convex (H_∂M > 0). The evolution of the second fundamental form satisfies a parabolic system with Neumann-type boundary conditions for the tangential derivatives. A key monotonicity formula was established by Huisken (1990) for MCF without boundary; for free boundary MCF, the monotonicity holds with a boundary term involving the second fundamental form of ∂M. If ∂M is convex, the boundary term has a good sign. The Huisken–Ilmanen inverse mean curvature flow (IMCF) was adapted to free boundary by Brendle–Hung–Wang (2016) to prove a Riemannian Penrose inequality for manifolds with boundary. Singularity analysis for free boundary MCF was developed by Edelen (2020) and Hershkovits–White (2019): Type-I singularities are modeled on self-shrinkers with free boundary on a half-space, which are classified as half-spheres, half-cylinders, and the translating bowl soliton with boundary. The multiplicity-one conjecture for free boundary MCF was proved by Colding–Minicozzi (2021) using the frequency function method. For the Clifford torus in the unit ball B⁴ ⊂ ℝ⁴ meeting ∂B⁴ orthogonally, the free boundary MCF converges to an equatorial disk. The regularity theory for the free boundary minimal surface problem (the stationary case) was established by Grüter–Jost (1986) and later refined by Schygulla (2012) using Allard-type boundary regularity. The free boundary Yamabe problem (Escobar, 1992) and the free boundary minimal surface problem are linked via the first variation of the area functional with the boundary term ∫∂Σ H_∂M dσ.

The Yamabe Invariant (Sigma Invariant) and the Classification of Manifolds by Sign of Yamabe Invariant

The Yamabe invariant σ(M) of a smooth closed manifold Mⁿ (n ≥ 3) is defined as the supremum over all conformal classes [g] of the Yamabe constant Y(M, [g]) = infg̃∈[g] (∫ Rg̃ dVg̃) / (Volg̃(M))(n−2)/n. Equivalently, σ(M) = sup[g] Y(M, [g]). It is a diffeomorphism invariant that measures the extent to which M admits metrics of positive scalar curvature. The sign of σ(M) classifies manifolds into three types: σ(M) > 0 (positive type), σ(M) = 0 (zero type), σ(M) < 0 (negative type). For n = 3, Perelman's Ricci flow with surgery implies that σ(M) > 0 iff M is a connected sum of spherical space forms and copies of S²×S¹; σ(M) = 0 iff M admits a geometric structure modeled on ℝ³, Nil, or Sol; σ(M) < 0 otherwise. In dimension 4, the classification is incomplete. LeBrun (1999) computed σ(ℂℙ²) = 12√2 π and σ(ℂℙ²#ℂℙ²) = 0, showing that the Yamabe invariant is not additive under connected sum. For Kähler surfaces, the Seiberg–Witten invariants give constraints: if M has a Kähler metric with c₁² > 0, then σ(M) ≤ 32π²c₁²/χ_h. The Yamabe invariant of Sⁿ is n(n−1)ω_n2/n, achieved by the round metric. For S¹×Sn−1, σ = 0. The invariant is related to the Gromov–Lawson–Rosenberg conjecture on positive scalar curvature: if M is spin and σ(M) > 0, then the α-invariant vanishes. The computation of σ(M) for specific manifolds often uses the conformal Laplacian L_g = −4(n−1)/(n−2)Δ_g + R_g and the sharp Sobolev inequality. The Aubin–Schoen theorem gives Y(M, [g]) ≤ Y(Sⁿ, [g_round]) with equality iff (M, g) is conformally equivalent to the round sphere. The Yamabe invariant is also the critical value for the existence of solutions to the prescribed scalar curvature problem: if the prescribed function f changes sign and ∫ f dV < σ(M) Vol(n−2)/n, then a solution exists (Kazdan–Warner type results).

The Theory of Metric Measure Spaces and the RCD Condition

The theory of metric measure spaces (X, d, m) generalizes Riemannian manifolds by replacing the smooth structure with a metric and a reference measure. The curvature-dimension condition CD(K, N) of Lott–Villani and Sturm (2006) defines lower Ricci curvature bounds via convexity of the relative entropy functional Ent_m(ρ) = ∫ ρ log ρ dm along Wasserstein geodesics in the space of probability measures. The Riemannian curvature-dimension condition RCD(K, N) adds the requirement that the Cheeger energy Ch(f) = (1/2)∫ |∇f|² dm is a quadratic form, which is equivalent to the infinitesimal Hilbertianity of the space. For Riemannian manifolds, RCD(K, N) is equivalent to Ric ≥ Kg and dim ≤ N. The RCD condition is stable under measured Gromov–Hausdorff convergence (Gigli–Mondino–Savaré, 2015), making it the natural framework for compactness of spaces with Ricci ≥ K and dimension ≤ N. On RCD(K, N) spaces, a first-order calculus exists: the tangent module L²(TX) carries a pointwise norm, and the heat flow generates a Markov semigroup with Gaussian heat kernel bounds (Jiang–Li–Zhang, 2016). The splitting theorem (Gigli, 2013) states that if an RCD(0, N) space contains a line, it splits isometrically as a product Y×ℝ. The structure theory of singular sets was developed by Mondino–Naber (2019): the singular set has Hausdorff dimension at most N−2, and the regular set is a C¹,α Riemannian manifold. The RCD framework encompasses Ricci limit spaces, Alexandrov spaces (with curvature bounded below), and finite-dimensional Alexandrov spaces. It also includes non-collapsed limits of manifolds with Ric ≥ K and vol ≥ v > 0. The Perelman entropy functionals extend to RCD spaces, and the Ricci flow can be defined as a gradient flow of the entropy in the Wasserstein space (Gigli–Mantegazza, 2018). The theory provides a synthetic approach to geometric analysis where PDE methods are replaced by optimal transport and functional inequalities.

  • Confusing the Yamabe invariant σ(M) with the Yamabe constant Y(M, [g]); the former is a supremum over conformal classes, the latter an infimum within a fixed class.
  • Assuming the normalized Ricci flow on surfaces preserves the conformal class without checking the boundary conditions; Neumann conditions for the conformal factor are required for free boundary problems.
  • Overlooking that the Gromov–Hausdorff limit of manifolds with Ric ≥ K may have Hausdorff dimension strictly less than n (collapsing), in which case the limit is not an RCD(K, N) space for the same N.
  • Treating the free boundary condition for MCF as a Dirichlet condition for the position vector; it is a Neumann-type condition on the angle of intersection.
  • Believing that the RCD condition implies a smooth structure; RCD spaces can be singular (e.g., cones), and the regular set is only C¹,α.
  • Neglecting the role of the entropy functional E(g) in Chow's proof for S²; the blow-up argument relies on the fact that E is scale-invariant and bounded below.
  • Confusing the sigma invariant with the Yamabe constant of the round sphere; σ(Sⁿ) = Y(Sⁿ, [g_round]) but for other manifolds σ(M) can be strictly less than the Yamabe constant of any conformal class.

The Uhlenbeck Compactness Theorem and the Geometric Analysis of Yang‑Mills Connections

The Uhlenbeck compactness theorem (1982) is the foundational compactness result for connections on principal bundles with bounded Yang‑Mills energy. Let P → M be a principal G-bundle over a closed Riemannian manifold M of dimension n ≥ 4, where G is a compact Lie group. A connection A has curvature FA ∈ Ω²(M, ad P). The Yang‑Mills functional is YM(A) = ∫M |FA|² dvol. Uhlenbeck proved that if a sequence of connections Ai satisfies YM(Ai) ≤ Λ and the L2 norm of the curvature is uniformly bounded, then after passing to a subsequence and applying suitable gauge transformations ui ∈ 𝒢(P), the transformed connections ui·Ai converge weakly in W1,2 and strongly in Lp for p < 2* to a limiting connection A∞ on a possibly different bundle P∞. The limiting bundle may have a different topological type; the difference is measured by the energy concentration set, a closed subset of Hausdorff dimension at most n−4. In dimension 4, the energy identity YM(Ai) → YM(A∞) + ∑k 8π²|c2(Pk)| holds, where the sum runs over the bubbles Pk → S⁴ formed at the concentration points. This bubbling analysis is the gauge‑theoretic analogue of the concentration‑compactness principle for harmonic maps and the Yamabe problem. The theorem requires the small‑energy regularity estimate: if ∫Br(x) |FA|² < ε0 (a universal constant depending only on G and n), then in a suitable Coulomb gauge the connection satisfies |∇A| ≤ C r⁻¹ (∫B2r |FA|²)1/2. The proof uses the Uhlenbeck lemma: on a ball with small curvature, there exists a gauge transformation putting the connection in Coulomb gauge (d*A = 0) with W1,2 bounds. The compactness theorem underpins the construction of the Yang‑Mills moduli space, the proof of the Donaldson invariants for smooth four‑manifolds, and the Uhlenbeck‑Yau correspondence between stable holomorphic bundles and Hermitian‑Yang‑Mills connections on Kähler manifolds. In the context of geometric analysis, the theorem is often combined with the monotonicity formula for the Yang‑Mills energy (Price, 1983) to analyse the singular set of limiting connections. The singular set has Hausdorff dimension at most n−4 and is rectifiable (Tian, 2000). For n = 4, the singular set is a finite set of points, and the limiting connection extends smoothly across them after removing the bubbles. The Uhlenbeck compactness theorem also plays a central role in the proof of the Atiyah‑Singer index theorem via the heat kernel method, where the adiabatic limit of the Yang‑Mills functional on a family of metrics collapsing the fibres of a fibration leads to the Chern‑Weil forms representing characteristic classes.

The Cheeger‑Gromov Theory of Collapsing and F‑Structures on Collapsed Manifolds

While the Cheeger‑Colding theory describes non‑collapsed limits of manifolds with a lower Ricci curvature bound (vol ≥ v > 0), the Cheeger‑Gromov theory (1986–1991) addresses the complementary case where the volume collapses to zero. Let Mi be a sequence of closed Riemannian n-manifolds with |sec| ≤ 1 and diam ≤ 1, but vol(Mi) → 0. The Gromov‑Hausdorff limit X is a compact metric space of Hausdorff dimension k < n. Cheeger and Gromov proved that for sufficiently large i, Mi admits an F-structure of positive rank: a sheaf of local torus actions Tr → Diff(Mi) of rank r ≥ n−k that are compatible on overlaps. An F-structure is a generalization of a torus action; it is defined by a covering of M by open sets Uα with effective torus actions Trα on Uα that commute on intersections. The rank of the F-structure is the minimum of the rα. The existence of an F-structure of positive rank implies strong topological restrictions: the Euler characteristic χ(Mi) = 0, and the fundamental group π₁(Mi) contains a nilpotent subgroup of finite index (by the Gromov almost‑flat manifold theorem). The collapsed limit X carries a natural stratified structure: the regular stratum Xreg is a smooth manifold of dimension k, and the singular strata correspond to orbits of the F-structure with non‑trivial isotropy. The metric on Mi can be described as a Riemannian submersion with fibres that are almost flat tori (or more generally, infranilmanifolds) over Xreg, with the fibres collapsing to points. The curvature bound |sec| ≤ 1 implies that the second fundamental form of the fibres is uniformly bounded, and the horizontal distribution converges to a connection on the torus bundle. The theory was extended by Fukaya (1987) to the case of a lower Ricci curvature bound Ric ≥ −(n−1) without a sectional curvature bound, using the notion of a nilpotent Killing structure. In this setting, the limit space X is an Alexandrov space with curvature ≥ −(k−1), and the fibres are almost flat infranilmanifolds. The Cheeger‑Gromov‑Fukaya theory is essential for understanding the boundary of the moduli space of Einstein metrics, the degeneration of Kähler‑Einstein metrics (Tian, 1990), and the compactness of the space of manifolds with Ric ≥ −(n−1) and diam ≤ 1 in the Gromov‑Hausdorff topology. It also underlies the construction of the Cheeger‑Gromov universal cover and the proof of the Margulis lemma for manifolds with bounded curvature. In the context of Ricci flow, the collapsing theory describes the behaviour of Type III singularities and the formation of cusp regions in the thick‑thin decomposition of 3‑manifolds (Perelman, 2003). The F-structure provides a canonical way to perform surgery on collapsed regions by cutting along the torus fibres and capping off with solid tori, preserving the lower curvature bound in the sense of Alexandrov geometry.

Worked Example: Energy Identity for Yang‑Mills Bubbling
Let Ai be a sequence of SU(2) connections on a principal bundle P → S⁴ with YM(Ai) ≤ 8π² and Ai converging weakly to a flat connection A∞ away from a single point x₀. Suppose the energy concentration at x₀ is exactly 8π². Show that the bubbling limit is an instanton on S⁴ with instanton number 1, and compute the limiting energy identity.
By Uhlenbeck's compactness theorem, after gauge transformations the sequence Ai converges to a limiting connection A∞ on a bundle P∞ over S⁴ {x₀}. Since A∞ is flat and S⁴ {x₀} is simply connected, A∞ is gauge equivalent to the trivial connection on the trivial bundle. The energy concentration at x₀ is 8π². Rescale around x₀ by λi → 0 such that the rescaled connections Ãi on ℝ⁴ have curvature concentrated in a fixed ball. By the removable singularities theorem (Uhlenbeck, 1982), the limiting connection Ã∞ on ℝ⁴ extends to a smooth connection on S⁴ = ℝ⁴ ∪ {∞}. The Yang‑Mills energy of Ã∞ is exactly the concentrated energy 8π². For SU(2) bundles over S⁴, the Yang‑Mills energy satisfies YM(A) = 8π²|c₂(P)|, where c₂ is the second Chern class (instanton number). Since the energy is 8π², we have |c₂| = 1. The connection Ã∞ is therefore an instanton (self‑dual or anti‑self‑dual) with instanton number ±1. The energy identity is YM(Ai) → YM(A∞) + YM(Ã∞) = 0 + 8π² = 8π². The limiting bundle P∞ is trivial, while the bubble bundle over S⁴ has c₂ = ±1. The topological charge of the original bundle P is the sum of the charges of the limit and the bubbles: c₂(P) = c₂(P∞) + ∑ c₂(bubble) = 0 + 1 = 1.
Exam Strategy: Distinguishing Collapsed vs Non‑Collapsed Limits
When a question asks about the limit of a sequence of manifolds with Ric ≥ −(n−1) and diam ≤ 1, first check whether a positive volume lower bound vol ≥ v > 0 is given. If yes, invoke Cheeger‑Colding theory: the limit is an RCD(K, N) space with the same dimension n, regular set is C¹,α, singular set has dimension ≤ n−2. If no volume bound is given (or vol → 0), invoke Cheeger‑Gromov‑Fukaya theory: the limit has dimension k < n, the manifolds admit F-structures of rank ≥ n−k, fibres are almost flat infranilmanifolds, and the limit is an Alexandrov space. A common trap is to apply the non‑collapsed regularity theory (e.g., C¹,α regularity of the regular set) to a collapsed limit where the regular set is only a topological manifold with a C¹,α structure coming from the nilpotent Killing structure. Always state which compactness theorem you are using and verify its hypotheses.

The Theory of Ricci Flow on Manifolds with Boundary and the Hamilton‑DeTurck Boundary Value Problem

The Ricci flow on manifolds with boundary was initiated by Hamilton (1993) and developed extensively by Shen, Simon, and others. Let (M, g(t)) be a smooth one‑parameter family of metrics on a compact manifold M with boundary ∂M ≠ ∅. The Ricci flow equation ∂tg = −2 Ric(g) is a weakly parabolic system. To obtain a well‑posed initial‑boundary value problem, one must impose boundary conditions that are compatible with the diffeomorphism invariance of the flow. The natural geometric boundary conditions are: (i) Dirichlet condition: g(t)|∂M = h fixed; (ii) Neumann‑type condition: the second fundamental form Π(t)|∂M = Π₀ fixed; (iii) Conformal Dirichlet: the conformal class [g(t)|∂M] is fixed. Hamilton and DeTurck (1983) introduced the DeTurck trick to break diffeomorphism invariance by adding a Lie derivative term: ∂tg = −2 Ric(g) + £W(g,ḡ)g, where W(g,ḡ) is the vector field whose components are gij(Γkij(g) − Γkij(ḡ)) and ḡ is a fixed background metric. This modified flow is strictly parabolic. For manifolds with boundary, one must also modify the boundary conditions to make the system strictly parabolic in the sense of Agmon‑Douglis‑Nirenberg. The correct boundary condition for the DeTurck flow is the oblique derivative condition: on ∂M, the vector field W is required to be tangent to the boundary, and the metric satisfies a condition relating the normal derivative of the tangential components to the second fundamental form. Shen (2007) proved short‑time existence and uniqueness for the Ricci flow with Dirichlet boundary condition g|∂M = h and the condition that the mean curvature of the boundary is prescribed. The proof uses the Nash‑Moser implicit function theorem or the method of maximal regularity for parabolic systems with boundary. The long‑time behaviour of Ricci flow on manifolds with boundary is closely related to the geometry of the boundary. If the boundary is totally geodesic (Π = 0) and the initial metric has positive Ricci curvature, the flow exists for all time and converges to a metric of constant positive curvature (a spherical space form) with totally geodesic boundary. If the boundary is convex (Π ≥ 0), the flow may develop singularities at the boundary. The boundary singularity analysis uses the reflection method: double the manifold across the boundary and extend the metric by even reflection. The doubled metric has a Lipschitz singularity along the boundary, and the Ricci flow on the double is studied using the theory of Ricci flow on singular spaces (Simon, 2012). An important application is the proof of the uniformization theorem for surfaces with boundary: the Ricci flow with Dirichlet boundary condition converges to a metric of constant curvature with geodesic boundary. For higher dimensions, the flow is used to construct Einstein metrics with prescribed boundary data (Anderson, 2005). The Hamilton‑DeTurck boundary value problem is also essential for the gluing construction of Ricci flow solutions: given two Ricci flow solutions on manifolds with boundary, one can glue them along their boundaries to obtain a global solution, provided the boundary metrics and second fundamental forms match to high order. This gluing technique underlies the construction of ancient solutions and the proof of the Hamilton‑Tian conjecture in higher dimensions.

The Anderson‑Cheeger Theory of Einstein Metrics and the Compactness of Moduli Spaces

The moduli space of Einstein metrics on a fixed smooth manifold M is the set of Einstein metrics modulo diffeomorphisms and scaling. Anderson (1989) and Cheeger (1991) developed a comprehensive compactness theory for this moduli space under the assumptions |Ric| ≤ (n−1) and vol ≥ v > 0 (or equivalently, a lower bound on the injectivity radius). The key result is that the space of Einstein metrics satisfying these bounds is precompact in the C¹,α topology (and in fact in C∞ topology by elliptic regularity). The proof uses the harmonic radius rh(x), defined as the supremum of radii r such that there exists a harmonic coordinate chart on Br(x) with metric components satisfying C¹,α bounds. For Einstein metrics, the harmonic radius is equivalent to the injectivity radius and the Ln/2 norm of the curvature (Anderson, 1990). The lower volume bound and the Einstein condition imply a positive lower bound on the harmonic radius, which yields C¹,α precompactness. The limit of a sequence of Einstein metrics is an Einstein metric on a possibly singular space: an Einstein orbifold with singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most n−4. In dimension 4, the singular set is a finite set of points, and the limit is an Einstein orbifold with isolated singularities modeled on ℝ⁴/Γ for finite subgroups Γ ⊂ SO(4). The energy identity for the L² norm of the curvature holds: ∫ |Rm|² = ∫ |Rm∞|² + ∑ 8π²|c₂(Pk)|, where the bubbles are gravitational instantons (ALE Ricci‑flat metrics). The compactness theorem has profound consequences for the topology of 4‑manifolds. The moduli space of Einstein metrics on a 4‑manifold with positive scalar curvature is compact up to bubbling, and the bubbling corresponds to connected sums with CP² or CP²̅. This leads to the Anderson‑Cheeger‑Gromov classification of 4‑manifolds admitting Einstein metrics: a simply connected 4‑manifold admits an Einstein metric iff it is homeomorphic to S⁴, CP², or a connected sum of copies of CP² and CP²̅ (LeBrun, 1999). In higher dimensions, the compactness theory is used to study the Einstein moduli space on manifolds with positive Ricci curvature. The Einstein condition implies the Bochner formula Δ|∇f|² = 2|Hess f|² + 2 Ric(∇f, ∇f) for any function f. For an Einstein metric with Ric = λg, λ > 0, this gives a spectral gap for the Laplacian on functions: the first non‑zero eigenvalue λ₁ ≥ 2λ (Lichnerowicz). The compactness of the moduli space implies that the spectrum of the Laplacian varies continuously, and the space of Einstein metrics is a finite‑dimensional real analytic variety (Koiso, 1980). The Anderson‑Cheeger theory also provides the foundation for the Cheeger‑Colding theory of Ricci limit spaces: the non‑collapsed limit of Einstein manifolds is a smooth Einstein manifold, while the collapsed limit is described by the F-structure theory. The interplay between the two theories gives a complete picture of the compactification of the Einstein moduli space.

The Theory of Minimal Hypersurfaces in Spheres and the Classification of Isoparametric Hypersurfaces

Minimal hypersurfaces in the unit sphere Sⁿ⁺¹ are critical points of the area functional. They are closely related to isoparametric hypersurfaces, which are level sets of isoparametric functions f : Sⁿ⁺¹ → ℝ satisfying |∇f|² = b(f) and Δf = a(f) for smooth functions a, b. Cartan (1938–1940) classified isoparametric hypersurfaces with g = 1, 2, 3 distinct principal curvatures. For g = 1, the hypersurfaces are totally umbilic (geodesic spheres). For g = 2, they are Clifford tori Sp(√(p/n)) × Sq(√(q/n)) with p+q = n. For g = 3, the multiplicities of the principal curvatures are equal (m₁ = m₂ = m₃ = m), and m ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8} corresponding to the division algebras ℝ, ℂ, ℍ, 𝕆. The classification for g = 4 was completed by Münzner (1980), who showed that the multiplicities come in pairs (m₁, m₂) and the isoparametric hypersurfaces are tubes of constant radius around the Veronese embeddings of the projective planes ℝℙ², ℂℙ², ℍℙ², 𝕆ℙ². For g = 6, the only possibility is the homogeneous hypersurface in S¹⁷ associated with the exceptional Lie group G₂. Minimal hypersurfaces in Sⁿ⁺¹ are exactly the isoparametric hypersurfaces with g = 1, 2, 3 (and some with g = 4, 6). The Clifford tori are minimal and have index 1 for p = q = 1 (the minimal Clifford torus in S³) and higher index otherwise. The stability of minimal hypersurfaces in spheres is governed by the Simons inequality: for a minimal hypersurface Σ ⊂ Sⁿ⁺¹, the second fundamental form A satisfies Δ|A|² ≥ 2|A|²(|A|² − n). If |A|² ≤ n, then Σ is stable. The equality case |A|² = n characterizes the Clifford tori Sp × Sq with p = q = n/2 (when n is even). The Lawson correspondence (1970) relates minimal hypersurfaces in Sⁿ⁺¹ to minimal hypersurfaces in ℝⁿ⁺¹ and ℍⁿ⁺¹ via the spherical, Euclidean, and hyperbolic Gauss maps. This correspondence preserves the second fundamental form and the principal curvatures. The classification of minimal hypersurfaces in spheres with low index or low Morse index is a major open problem. The Willmore conjecture (proved by Marques‑Neves, 2012) states that the Willmore energy ∫Σ H² dA ≥ 2π² for any torus in S³, with equality for the Clifford torus. This is equivalent to the statement that the Clifford torus minimizes the Willmore energy among all tori in S³. The proof uses the min‑max theory for minimal surfaces in S³ and the Almgren‑Pitts construction. The theory of minimal hypersurfaces in spheres is also connected to the theory of harmonic maps: a minimal hypersurface in Sⁿ⁺¹ corresponds to a harmonic map from the hypersurface to Sⁿ with constant energy density. The classification of isoparametric hypersurfaces has applications to the theory of focal sets, the topology of level sets of isoparametric functions, and the construction of Einstein metrics on spheres via the Hopf fibration.

  • Confusing the Uhlenbeck compactness theorem for Yang‑Mills connections with the Uhlenbeck compactness for minimal surfaces; the former deals with connections on bundles and energy concentration in codimension 4, the latter with varifolds and codimension 1.
  • Assuming that the Cheeger‑Gromov collapsed limit is an RCD(K, N) space with the same dimension N; collapsed limits have strictly lower Hausdorff dimension and are Alexandrov spaces, not RCD spaces for the original N.
  • Neglecting the oblique derivative boundary condition in the Hamilton‑DeTurck flow on manifolds with boundary; the standard Dirichlet condition for the metric is not sufficient to make the DeTurck‑modified flow strictly parabolic up to the boundary.
  • Believing that the Anderson‑Cheeger compactness theorem for Einstein metrics requires a lower bound on the injectivity radius; the volume bound vol ≥ v > 0 together with the Einstein condition is sufficient (via the harmonic radius estimate).
  • Confusing isoparametric hypersurfaces with minimal hypersurfaces in spheres; all isoparametric hypersurfaces are minimal, but not all minimal hypersurfaces are isoparametric (e.g., minimal hypersurfaces constructed by min‑max methods).
  • Overlooking that the energy identity for Yang‑Mills bubbling involves the second Chern class c₂ of the bubble bundle, while for harmonic maps it involves the homotopy class of the bubble map πn(N).
  • Assuming that the F-structure on a collapsed manifold is a global torus action; it is only a sheaf of local torus actions that may not integrate to a global action.

The Entropy Functional and the Classification of Ancient Solutions to Ricci Flow

Perelman introduced two monotone quantities along the Ricci flow: the W‑entropy and the reduced volume. The W‑entropy is defined for a metric g and a positive function f with ∫ e−f dV = 1 by
