The theory has profound applications to the min-max construction of minimal hypersurfaces: the min-max widths ω_p(M) produce minimal hypersurfaces with index ≤ p, and the compactness theorem allows one to study the limit of min-max sequences as the metric varies, leading to the Weyl law for the volume spectrum proved by Liokumovich, Marques, and Neves (2018). A key technical tool is the replacement lemma of Colding-Minicozzi, which allows one to replace a minimal hypersurface with a nearby one that has better regularity while preserving the index bound. This lemma fails in higher codimension, explaining why the theory is most developed for hypersurfaces. The classification of minimal surfaces in ℝ³ with finite index and finite total curvature remains a guiding problem: besides the plane and catenoid, the only known examples are the Costa-Hoffman-Meeks surfaces (genus 1, index 5) and their higher-genus generalizations. Whether there are finitely many such surfaces for each fixed index is an open question.

The Regularity Theory for the Singular Set of Self-Shrinkers and Translating Solitons of Mean Curvature Flow

Self-shrinkers and translating solitons are the fundamental building blocks of singularity formation in mean curvature flow (MCF). A self-shrinker is a hypersurface Σ ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹ satisfying H = ⟨x, ν⟩/2, where H is the mean curvature, x is the position vector, and ν is the unit normal. It evolves by homothetic shrinking: Σ_t = √(-t) Σ for t < 0. A translating soliton satisfies H = ⟨V, ν⟩ for a fixed vector V, and evolves by translation: Σ_t = Σ + tV. Both are critical points of the Gaussian area functional F(Σ) = ∫_Σ e-|x|²/4 dℋⁿ and the weighted area functional ∫_Σ e-⟨V, x⟩ dℋⁿ, respectively. The regularity theory for these objects parallels that of minimal surfaces but with crucial differences due to the drift terms. Colding and Minicozzi (2012) developed a comprehensive regularity theory for self-shrinkers, proving that the singular set of an n-dimensional self-shrinker has Hausdorff dimension at most n-7, matching the minimal surface bound. The proof adapts the Federer dimension reduction argument to the Gaussian setting, using the monotonicity formula for the Gaussian density Θ_G(Σ, x, r) = (4π)-n/2 ∫Σ∩B(x,r) e-|y-x|²/4r dℋⁿ(y). The key observation is that tangent cones at singular points are self-shrinkers in ℝⁿ⁺¹ that are cones, hence minimal cones in the Euclidean sense. The classification of low-dimensional self-shrinkers is complete: in ℝ³, the only smooth, embedded, complete self-shrinkers with polynomial volume growth are the plane, the cylinder S¹ × ℝ, and the sphere S² (Huisken 1990; Colding-Minicozzi 2012). The cylinder is the only non-flat example with entropy less than that of the sphere, making it the generic blow-up limit at singularities of MCF in ℝ³. For translating solitons, the regularity theory was developed by Haslhofer (2015) and Wang (2014). The singular set of an n-dimensional translating soliton also has dimension at most n-7. The classification in ℝ³ is richer: besides the plane and the bowl soliton (a rotationally symmetric translating graph over a plane), there are the grim reaper cylinder (the product of the grim reaper curve with ℝ) and the wing-like translators discovered by Xuan Hien Nguyen (2009). The grim reaper cylinder is the only non-flat, complete, embedded translating soliton in ℝ³ with entropy less than the bowl soliton. The entropy functional λ(Σ) = supx₀,t₀ (4π t₀)-n/2 ∫_Σ e-|x-x₀|²/4t₀ dℋⁿ, introduced by Colding-Minicozzi, plays the role of area in the Gaussian setting. A fundamental result is that the entropy of a self-shrinker is lower semicontinuous under smooth convergence, and any sequence of self-shrinkers with bounded entropy has a subsequence converging smoothly away from a singular set of dimension ≤ n-7. This compactness theorem is essential for the min-max construction of self-shrinkers by Ketover (2016) and the proof of the multiplicity-one conjecture for MCF by Colding-Minicozzi (2015). The regularity theory extends to ancient solutions of MCF: an ancient solution is a solution defined for all t < 0. If it is non-collapsed (i.e., satisfies an interior ball condition), then it is either a self-shrinker, a translating soliton, or a compact ancient solution like the Angenent oval (in ℝ²) or the ancient oval (in ℝ³, constructed by Angenent-Daskalopoulos-Sesum 2018). The singular set of a non-collapsed ancient solution has the same dimension bound. A common exam trap is to confuse the Gaussian density with the Euclidean density: the Gaussian density of a plane through the origin is 1, but the Euclidean density is infinite. Another trap is to assume that all self-shrinkers are minimal cones; only tangent cones at singularities are minimal cones, while the self-shrinker itself satisfies H = ⟨x, ν⟩/2, which is not the minimal surface equation unless x is tangent to Σ.

Worked Example: Entropy of the Cylinder vs Sphere
Compute the entropy of the cylinder S¹(√2) × ℝ ⊂ ℝ³ and the sphere S²(2) ⊂ ℝ³ as self-shrinkers, and explain why the cylinder is the generic blow-up limit for MCF in ℝ³.
The entropy of a self-shrinker Σ is λ(Σ) = F(Σ) = (4π)-n/2 ∫_Σ e-|x|²/4 dℋⁿ. For the cylinder Σ = S¹(√2) × ℝ, parametrize by (θ, z) with x = (√2 cos θ, √2 sin θ, z). Then |x|² = 2 + z², dℋ² = √2 dθ dz. The Gaussian integral factorizes: ∫_ℝ e-z²/4 dz = 2√π, and ∫S¹ e-2/4 √2 dθ = 2π√2 e-1/2. Thus F(Σ) = (4π)-1 · 2√π · 2π√2 e-1/2 = √(2/e) ≈ 0.8578. For the sphere Σ = S²(2), |x|² = 4, dℋ² = 4 sin φ dφ dθ, area = 16π. F(Σ) = (4π)-1 · 16π · e-1 = 4/e ≈ 1.4715. Since √(2/e) < 4/e, the cylinder has lower entropy. By the Colding-Minicozzi generic regularity theorem, the blow-up limit at a generic singularity of MCF in ℝ³ is the self-shrinker with the lowest entropy among non-flat self-shrinkers, which is the cylinder. The sphere has higher entropy and appears only at special singularities (e.g., neckpinches with symmetry).
Exam Strategy: Distinguishing Self-Shrinkers from Translators
When a question asks about singularity models for MCF, first identify whether the singularity is Type I (curvature blows up like 1/√(T-t)) or Type II (faster blow-up). Type I singularities yield self-shrinkers after parabolic rescaling; Type II singularities yield translating solitons or ancient solutions after appropriate rescaling. Memorize the entropy values: plane = 1, cylinder = √(2/e) ≈ 0.858, sphere = 4/e ≈ 1.472, grim reaper cylinder = √(π/2) ≈ 1.253, bowl soliton ≈ 1.38. The cylinder has the lowest entropy among non-flat self-shrinkers in ℝ³, making it the generic Type I blow-up. The grim reaper cylinder has the lowest entropy among non-flat translators in ℝ³. For exam proofs, always state the monotonicity formula you are using: Huisken's monotonicity for self-shrinkers (backward heat kernel) vs the translating soliton monotonicity (weighted by e-⟨V,x⟩). Confusing these two is a major mark-loser.

The Theory of Minimal Submanifolds in Spheres and the Lawson Correspondence

The study of minimal submanifolds in the unit sphere Sⁿ⁺¹ is a classical subject with deep connections to harmonic maps, isoparametric hypersurfaces, and the construction of minimal submanifolds in Euclidean space via the cone construction. A submanifold Σⁿ ⊂ Sⁿ⁺¹ is minimal if its mean curvature vector vanishes identically. The cone C(Σ) = {t x : t > 0, x ∈ Σ} ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺² is then a minimal cone (away from the vertex) if and only if Σ is minimal in Sⁿ⁺¹. This correspondence, exploited by Simons (1968), reduces the classification of minimal cones in ℝⁿ⁺² to the classification of minimal hypersurfaces in Sⁿ⁺¹. Lawson (1970) discovered a profound duality: there is a one-to-one correspondence between minimal submanifolds in Sⁿ⁺¹ and minimal submanifolds in ℝⁿ⁺¹, known as the Lawson correspondence. Specifically, if Σ ⊂ Sⁿ⁺¹ is a minimal submanifold, then its stereographic projection to ℝⁿ⁺¹ is a minimal submanifold with respect to a conformally flat metric, and conversely. More precisely, if Σ ⊂ Sⁿ⁺¹ is minimal, then its image under stereographic projection is a minimal submanifold in ℝⁿ⁺¹ with the metric g = (1+|x|²)⁻² δ_ij. This correspondence preserves the index and the Morse index of the Jacobi operator. Using this, Lawson constructed infinitely many compact minimal surfaces in S³ of arbitrary genus, generalizing the Clifford torus S¹(1/√2) × S¹(1/√2). The Clifford torus is the unique embedded minimal torus in S³ (Brendle 2012), and it minimizes area in its homology class. The classification of minimal hypersurfaces in S⁴ is complete: they are the equatorial S³, the Clifford torus S¹(1/√2) × S²(1/√2), and the homogeneous hypersurfaces of cohomogeneity one classified by Hsiang and Lawson (1971). In higher dimensions, the classification is open, but the theory of isoparametric hypersurfaces provides a rich class of examples. An isoparametric hypersurface in Sⁿ⁺¹ is a hypersurface with constant principal curvatures. Cartan (1938-1940) classified isoparametric hypersurfaces with g ≤ 3 distinct principal curvatures. For g = 4, the classification was completed by Münzner (1980) and Cecil-Ryan (1981), showing that the multiplicities (m₁, m₂) must satisfy m₁ = m₂ or (m₁, m₂) = (2,2), (4,5), (6,9), or (8,16) — the famous FKM construction related to Clifford algebras. For g = 6, the only known examples are the homogeneous ones with multiplicities (1,1) or (2,2). The regularity theory for minimal submanifolds in spheres parallels the Euclidean theory: the singular set of an area-minimizing integral current in Sⁿ⁺¹ has dimension at most n-7 (Almgren 2000). The monotonicity formula holds with the spherical distance, and tangent cones at singular points are minimal cones in the tangent space, which is Euclidean. The Simons cone C(S² × S²) ⊂ ℝ⁸ is area-minimizing (Lawson-Osserman 1977), and its link S²(1/√2) × S²(1/√2) ⊂ S⁷ is a minimal isoparametric hypersurface with g = 2. The stability of minimal submanifolds in spheres is governed by the Jacobi operator L = Δ_Σ + |A|² + n, where the +n term comes from the positive curvature of the sphere. This makes stability more restrictive than in Euclidean space: the first eigenvalue of L on a minimal hypersurface in Sⁿ⁺¹ is at most -n (Simons 1968). The Clifford torus in S³ is stable (index 0), but the minimal surfaces of higher genus constructed by Lawson have index growing with genus. The min-max theory in spheres, developed by Marques and Neves (2012), produces minimal hypersurfaces with controlled index, and the Weyl law for the volume spectrum holds with the same leading coefficient as in Euclidean space. A common exam question is to derive the condition for a hypersurface in Sⁿ⁺¹ to be minimal in terms of its principal curvatures κ_i: Σ is minimal iff ∑ κ_i = 0. For a hypersurface given as a graph of a function u over an equatorial Sⁿ, the minimal surface equation becomes div(∇u/√(1+|∇u|²)) + n u/√(1+|∇u|²) = 0. The Lawson correspondence maps this to the minimal surface equation in ℝⁿ with a conformal factor.

The Regularity Theory for the Singular Set of the Allen-Cahn Equation and the Modica-Mortola Convergence

The Allen-Cahn equation Δu = (1/ε²) W'(u) with a double-well potential W(u) = (1-u²)²/4 is the prototypical phase-field model for interface motion. As ε → 0, the transition layers {u ≈ 0} converge to minimal hypersurfaces, a phenomenon rigorously established by Modica and Mortola (1977) for the energy functional E_ε(u) = ∫ (ε/2)|∇u|² + (1/ε)W(u) dx. The Γ-convergence of E_ε to the perimeter functional (up to a constant c₀ = ∫-11 √(2W(s)) ds = 2√2/3) implies that minimizers of E_ε converge to minimizers of perimeter. The regularity theory for the singular set of the limiting minimal hypersurface is a cornerstone of geometric measure theory. Hutchinson and Tonegawa (2000) proved that if u_ε are minimizers of E_ε in a domain Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹ with uniformly bounded energy, then as ε → 0, the measures μ_ε = (ε/2)|∇u_ε|² + (1/ε)W(u_ε) dx converge weakly to c₀ ℋⁿ ⌞ Σ, where Σ is an integral varifold with bounded first variation. Moreover, Σ is a minimal hypersurface outside a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most n-7. The proof uses the monotonicity formula for the Allen-Cahn energy: for any x₀ ∈ Ω, the quantity Φ_ε(x₀, r) = r-n ∫B(x₀,r) [(ε/2)|∇u_ε|² + (1/ε)W(u_ε)] dx is monotone non-decreasing in r up to an error of order ε/r. Passing to the limit yields the standard monotonicity formula for the limiting varifold. The dimension bound n-7 follows from Federer's dimension reduction argument applied to the limiting minimal hypersurface. The regularity theory extends to critical points of E_ε with bounded Morse index. Gaspar and Guaraco (2018) showed that if u_ε are critical points with index ≤ I, then the limiting varifold has index ≤ I and the convergence is smooth away from at most I points. This is the Allen-Cahn analogue of the Colding-Minicozzi compactness theorem for minimal hypersurfaces with bounded index. The Modica-Mortola convergence also holds for the parabolic Allen-Cahn equation ∂_t u = Δu - (1/ε²)W'(u). Ilmanen (1993) proved that the zero level sets of solutions converge to the Brakke flow of mean curvature, with the same singular set dimension bound. The key technical tool is the equipartition of energy: for minimizers, ∫ (ε/2)|∇u_ε|² dx ≈ ∫ (1/ε)W(u_ε) dx, which implies that the energy density concentrates on the interface. The convergence rate of the energy density to the limit measure is quantified by the Modica estimate: |∇u_ε| ≤ (1/ε)√(2W(u_ε)). This gradient bound is essential for the compactness argument. A major open problem is the regularity of the singular set for the Allen-Cahn equation in higher codimension (vector-valued u). The Γ-convergence to the area functional for maps u: Ω → ℝ^m with a potential W vanishing on a submanifold N ⊂ ℝ^m was studied by Jerrard and Soner (1998), but the singular set dimension bound remains unknown for m > 1. In the scalar case, the sharp regularity theory for the singular set of the limiting minimal hypersurface is complete: the singular set is (n-7)-rectifiable and has finite (n-7)-dimensional Hausdorff measure (Naber-Valtorta 2017). The stratification of the singular set by the dimension of the spine of tangent cones yields the same quantitative Minkowski bounds as for stationary varifolds. A common exam trap is to confuse the Modica-Mortola constant c₀ with the surface tension of the limiting interface: c₀ = ∫-11 √(2W(s)) ds, and the limiting perimeter functional is c₀ Per(Σ). Another trap is to assume that the convergence of u_ε to the characteristic function of the phase is strong in L¹; it is only weak-* in BV. The energy measures μ_ε converge weakly as measures, but the gradient measures ε|∇u_ε|² dx may not converge without additional assumptions. The equipartition property holds for minimizers but not for general critical points.

The Theory of Minimal Hypersurfaces in Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature and the Schoen-Yau Theory

The interplay between minimal hypersurfaces and scalar curvature is one of the most powerful tools in geometric topology. Schoen and Yau (1979) revolutionized the field by using stable minimal hypersurfaces to prove the positive mass theorem and the non-existence of metrics with positive scalar curvature on certain manifolds. The key observation is the stability inequality for a two-sided minimal hypersurface Σⁿ in a Riemannian manifold (Mⁿ⁺¹, g): for any compactly supported function f on Σ, ∫_Σ (|∇f|² - (Ric(ν,ν) + |A|²)f²) dℋⁿ ≥ 0. Using the Gauss equation, Ric(ν,ν) = (R - R_Σ)/2 + (|A|² - H²)/2, where R is the scalar curvature of M, R_Σ is the scalar curvature of Σ, and H = 0 for minimal Σ. For a stable minimal hypersurface, this yields ∫_Σ (|∇f|² - (R/2 + R_Σ/2)f²) dℋⁿ ≥ 0. If R > 0 on M, then choosing f = 1 gives ∫_Σ R_Σ dℋⁿ < 0, which forces Σ to have negative scalar curvature somewhere. In dimension n = 2, this means Σ cannot be a torus (which has R_Σ = 0) or a sphere (which has R_Σ > 0); it must have genus ≥ 1. Schoen and Yau used this to prove that if a 3-manifold M admits a metric with R > 0, then every stable minimal surface in M must be a sphere. This leads to the topological restriction that π₂(M) = 0 for such M, and ultimately to the classification of 3-manifolds with positive scalar curvature: they are connected sums of spherical space forms and S² × S¹. In higher dimensions, the Schoen-Yau theory uses induction on dimension: if Mⁿ⁺¹ has R > 0, then any stable minimal hypersurface Σⁿ also admits a metric with positive scalar curvature (by the Gauss equation and the stability inequality). This allows one to propagate topological restrictions from low dimensions to high dimensions. The positive mass theorem states that an asymptotically flat manifold with R ≥ 0 has non-negative ADM mass, with equality iff it is Euclidean space. The proof constructs a stable minimal hypersurface asymptotic to a coordinate plane at infinity and uses the stability inequality to derive a contradiction if the mass were negative. The regularity theory for the singular set of area-minimizing hypersurfaces in manifolds with positive scalar curvature is the same as in Euclidean space: the singular set has dimension at most n-7. However, the positive scalar curvature condition imposes strong constraints on the topology of the regular part. Gromov and Lawson (1980) extended the Schoen-Yau theory using the Dirac operator and spin geometry, proving that a spin manifold with positive scalar curvature has vanishing Â-genus. The minimal hypersurface approach was refined by Schoen and Yau (2017) to prove the positive mass theorem in all dimensions without spin assumption, using the regularity theory of minimal hypersurfaces with singularities (the singular set has dimension ≤ n-7, so the induction works for n+1 ≤ 7; for higher dimensions, they use the Almgren-Pitts min-max theory to produce minimal hypersurfaces with controlled singularities). The recent work of Chodosh and Li (2021) on the topology of stable minimal hypersurfaces in manifolds with positive scalar curvature shows that if Σⁿ is a closed, stable minimal hypersurface in Mⁿ⁺¹ with R > 0, then Σ cannot be a torus, and its fundamental group has no abelian subgroup of rank n. This generalizes the 3-dimensional result that stable minimal surfaces in positive scalar curvature 3-manifolds are spheres. The regularity theory for the singular set of stable minimal hypersurfaces in positive scalar curvature manifolds is an active area: the singular set is still of dimension ≤ n-7, but the stability inequality holds in a weak sense across the singular set (using the varifold first variation). A common exam question is to derive the stability inequality from the second variation of area: δ²A(f) = ∫_Σ (|∇f|² - (Ric(ν,ν) + |A|²)f²) dℋⁿ. Then use the Gauss equation to replace Ric(ν,ν) with (R - R_Σ)/2 + |A|²/2, yielding δ²A(f) = ∫_Σ (|∇f|² - (R/2 + R_Σ/2)f²) dℋⁿ. For a stable minimal hypersurface, δ²A(f) ≥ 0 for all f. If R > 0, then taking f = 1 gives ∫_Σ R_Σ dℋⁿ < 0. In dimension 2, R_Σ = 2K, so ∫_Σ K dℋ² < 0, which by Gauss-Bonnet implies genus(Σ) ≥ 1. The trap is to forget the factor of 1/2 in the Gauss equation or to confuse the scalar curvature of M with the scalar curvature of Σ.

  • Confusing the Morse index of a minimal hypersurface with the number of negative eigenvalues of the Jacobi operator on the whole manifold; the index is defined for normal variations only.
  • Assuming the entropy of a self-shrinker is the same as its Gaussian area; entropy is the supremum of Gaussian areas over all centers and scales.
  • Applying the Lawson correspondence without checking the conformal factor; the stereographic projection maps minimal submanifolds in Sⁿ⁺¹ to minimal submanifolds in ℝⁿ⁺¹ with a specific conformal metric, not the Euclidean metric.
  • Forgetting the Modica-Mortola constant c₀ when stating the Γ-convergence of the Allen-Cahn energy to the perimeter functional; the limit is c₀ Per(Σ), not Per(Σ).
  • Using the stability inequality for minimal hypersurfaces in positive scalar curvature manifolds without the Gauss equation correction term; the correct inequality involves R/2 + R_Σ/2, not just R.
  • Assuming the singular set dimension bound n-7 holds for all critical points of the Allen-Cahn energy; it holds for minimizers and bounded-index critical points, but not for general critical points without index bounds.
  • Confusing the blow-up limits for Type I and Type II singularities in MCF; Type I yields self-shrinkers, Type II yields translating solitons or ancient solutions.
The advanced regularity theories for minimal hypersurfaces, self-shrinkers, and phase-field models form a unified framework where monotonicity formulas, dimension reduction, and compactness theorems interact to control singular sets across diverse geometric settings.

The Capillary Problem and the Regularity of the Contact Line

The capillary problem asks for the equilibrium shape of a liquid drop resting on a solid container under the influence of surface tension and gravity. Mathematically, it is a free boundary problem for a hypersurface Σ of prescribed mean curvature H = κ (constant, proportional to the pressure difference) meeting the container wall ∂Ω at a prescribed contact angle θ ∈ (0, π) determined by Young's law: cos θ = (σ_sv − σ_sl)/σ, where σ, σ_sv, σ_sl are the liquid-vapor, solid-vapor, and solid-liquid surface tensions. The energy functional is E(Σ) = ℋⁿ(Σ) − cos θ ℋⁿ(Σ ∩ ∂Ω) + κ Vol(Σ), minimized among sets of finite perimeter. The Euler-Lagrange equation yields the constant mean curvature equation div(ν) = κ in Ω and the boundary condition ν · μ = cos θ on ∂Ω, where ν is the unit normal to Σ and μ is the inward co-normal to ∂Ω. Regularity theory divides into interior regularity (Σ is analytic away from the contact line by elliptic regularity for the minimal surface equation with forcing) and boundary regularity at the contact line Γ = ∂Σ ∩ ∂Ω. The foundational results are due to Gerhardt (1976) and Simon (1987): if ∂Ω is C²,α and θ ∈ (0, π), then Γ is a C¹,α hypersurface in ∂Ω, and Σ is C¹,α up to Γ. Higher regularity (C^k,α or analytic) follows if ∂Ω and θ are smoother, by Schauder estimates for the oblique derivative problem. The singular set of the contact line is empty for n ≤ 7; for n ≥ 8, singularities can occur where the contact line touches the boundary of the container in a non-transversal way, but the dimension of the singular set is at most n−8 by the Federer dimension reduction principle applied to the blow-up limits, which are minimal cones in half-spaces meeting the boundary at angle θ. A key technical tool is the reflection method: extending Σ across ∂Ω by odd reflection of the graph function reduces the oblique derivative problem to a transmission problem for a minimal surface equation with a jump in the gradient, allowing the use of Allard's boundary regularity theorem for varifolds with free boundary. The capillary problem in a convex container has a unique solution for each volume when θ ∈ (0, π/2] (Concus-Finn, 1974); for θ > π/2, multiple solutions can exist, and the global minimizer may have a disconnected contact line. The regularity of the contact line for the capillary problem with gravity (κ ≠ 0) is the same as for κ = 0, since the forcing term is lower order.

The Regularity Theory for the Isoperimetric Problem in Riemannian Manifolds

The isoperimetric problem in a Riemannian manifold (Mⁿ⁺¹, g) seeks regions Ω ⊂ M of given volume V that minimize perimeter P(Ω) = ℋⁿ(∂*Ω). Existence of isoperimetric regions for all volumes in complete manifolds with non-negative Ricci curvature was proved by Morgan and Johnson (2000) using the concentration-compactness principle; in general complete manifolds, existence holds for small volumes (Morgan, 2003) or under asymptotic volume ratio conditions. The regularity of isoperimetric regions follows from the fact that they are (Λ, r₀)-perimeter minimizers: there exist Λ, r₀ > 0 such that P(Ω) ≤ P(F) + Λ|Vol(Ω) − Vol(F)| for all competitors F coinciding with Ω outside a ball of radius r₀. By the De Giorgi structure theorem, the reduced boundary ∂*Ω is a C¹,α hypersurface, and the singular set Σ = ∂Ω ∂*Ω has Hausdorff dimension at most n−7 (n−8 for n+1 ≥ 8) by the Federer-Almgren dimension reduction. The proof uses the monotonicity formula for the density Θ(x) = limr→0 P(Ω ∩ B_r(x)) / ω_n rⁿ and the fact that blow-up limits at singular points are area-minimizing cones in ℝⁿ⁺¹. In manifolds with positive Ricci curvature, the isoperimetric profile I(V) = inf{P(Ω) : Vol(Ω) = V} is strictly concave (Morgan-Johnson), and isoperimetric regions are unique for small volumes (Morgan, 2003). For manifolds with non-negative Ricci curvature, the Cheeger-Gromoll splitting theorem implies that if an isoperimetric region has a Euclidean blow-up limit, then M splits isometrically as ℝ × N. The regularity theory for the singular set of isoperimetric regions in Riemannian manifolds is identical to the Euclidean case up to dimension 7; for higher dimensions, the singular set is (n−7)-rectifiable and has finite ℋⁿ⁻⁷ measure by the Naber-Valtorta quantitative stratification. A major open problem is the regularity of the singular set for isoperimetric regions in sub-Riemannian manifolds (e.g., the Heisenberg group), where the blow-up limits are not cones but homogeneous sets with respect to the Carnot-Carathéodory dilation; the best known result is that the singular set has dimension at most n−2 (Monti-Rickly, 2004).

Worked Example: Contact Angle Regularity
Let Ω ⊂ ℝ³ be a bounded domain with C² boundary, and let Σ be a capillary surface in Ω with constant mean curvature H = 1 meeting ∂Ω at a constant contact angle θ = π/3. Suppose Σ is given as a graph u(x,y) over a domain D ⊂ ℝ² near a point p ∈ ∂Σ ∩ ∂Ω. Write the oblique derivative boundary condition for u and explain why the reflection method yields C¹,α regularity up to the boundary.
The capillary surface Σ = graph(u) satisfies the prescribed mean curvature equation div(Du/√(1+|Du|²)) = 1 in D. On ∂D, the contact angle condition ν · μ = cos θ becomes (Du/√(1+|Du|²)) · ν_∂D = cos(π/3) = 1/2, where ν_∂D is the outward unit normal to ∂D in ℝ². This is an oblique derivative condition because the directional derivative of u in the direction of the conormal is prescribed. To apply the reflection method, extend u across ∂D by defining ũ(x) = u(x) for x ∈ D and ũ(x) = 2φ(x) − u(R(x)) for x ∉ D, where R is the reflection across ∂D and φ is a C² function chosen so that the extended graph has a jump in the normal derivative matching the contact angle condition. The extended function ũ satisfies a minimal surface equation with a discontinuous coefficient (a transmission problem). By Allard's boundary regularity theorem for integral varifolds with free boundary (or by the C¹,α estimates for transmission problems of Kinderlehrer-Nirenberg), ũ is C¹,α across ∂D, which implies u is C¹,α up to ∂D. The key is that the contact angle θ ∈ (0, π) ensures the obliqueness condition (the conormal is not tangent to ∂D), which is necessary for the Schauder estimates to hold.
Exam Strategy: Capillary vs. Free Boundary
Distinguish the capillary problem (prescribed contact angle θ ∈ (0, π), constant mean curvature) from the free boundary minimal surface problem (θ = π/2, H = 0). The capillary problem has a forcing term (κ ≠ 0) and a non-orthogonal contact angle; the free boundary problem is a special case. In exams, check whether the contact angle is given as a constant ≠ π/2 — if so, the reflection method requires a non-trivial extension (odd reflection with a shift), not simple odd/even reflection. The regularity theory (C¹,α up to the boundary) is the same for both, but the blow-up limits at the contact line differ: for capillary, they are minimal cones in a half-space meeting the boundary at angle θ; for free boundary, they are minimal cones meeting the boundary orthogonally (θ = π/2).

The Regularity Theory for the Singular Set of the Volume-Preserving Mean Curvature Flow

The volume-preserving mean curvature flow (VPMCF) evolves a hypersurface Σ_t by the normal velocity V = H − h(t), where h(t) = (∫Σ_t H dℋⁿ) / ℋⁿ(Σ_t) is the average mean curvature, chosen so that the enclosed volume Vol(Σ_t) remains constant. This flow arises as the L²-gradient flow of the area functional under a volume constraint. Short-time existence and uniqueness for smooth initial data follow from the theory of quasilinear parabolic equations with a non-local term (Huisken, 1987). The long-time behavior and singularity formation are more subtle than for standard MCF. For convex initial data in ℝⁿ⁺¹, Huisken (1987) proved that the flow exists for all time and converges exponentially to a round sphere. For non-convex data, singularities can form in finite time. The singular set analysis uses the monotonicity formula for the Gaussian density adapted to the volume-preserving flow: Θ(x,t) = limr→0 (4πr²)-n/2 ∫Σt−r² e-|y−x|²/4r² dℋⁿ(y). The key difference from standard MCF is that the non-local term h(t) is bounded by the maximum principle (|h(t)| ≤ maxΣ_t |H|), so the flow is a bounded perturbation of MCF. Blow-up limits at singular points are self-shrinkers of the standard MCF (since h(t) scales to zero under parabolic rescaling), so the singular set has the same structure: it is (n−1)-rectifiable and has dimension at most n−1, with the same stratification by Gaussian density. However, the non-local term affects the Type II singularity analysis: translating solitons and ancient solutions of VPMCF satisfy H − h = ⟨ν, v⟩ for some constant vector v, where h is the average of H over the soliton. The regularity of the singular set for VPMCF in higher codimension or in Riemannian manifolds is less developed; in manifolds with bounded geometry, the short-time existence holds (Escher-Simonett, 1998), but the singular set dimension bound n−1 is conjectured to hold under the same conditions as for MCF. A major open problem is the existence of a Brakke-type weak formulation for VPMCF that preserves volume and satisfies a monotonicity formula; the current weak formulations (Mugnai-Seis, 2016; Kim-Tonegawa, 2017) use a time-discrete minimizing movement scheme with a volume constraint, and the singular set regularity for these weak solutions is an active area of research.

The Regularity Theory for the Singular Set of the Anisotropic and Crystalline Mean Curvature Flows

Anisotropic mean curvature flow generalizes MCF by replacing the isotropic surface energy ℋⁿ(Σ) with an anisotropic energy F(Σ) = ∫_Σ γ(ν) dℋⁿ, where γ : Sⁿ → (0, ∞) is a smooth, uniformly convex norm (the surface tension). The first variation gives the anisotropic mean curvature H_γ = div_Σ(∇γ(ν)), and the flow is V = H_γ. The Wulff shape W_γ = {x : x·ν ≤ γ(ν) for all ν} is the unique (up to translation and scaling) minimizer of F under a volume constraint, and it is the asymptotic profile for the flow. Regularity theory for smooth γ follows from the uniform parabolicity of the equation: the linearized operator is uniformly elliptic, so the flow is a quasilinear parabolic system, and the singular set has the same structure as for isotropic MCF (White, 2000; Bellettini-Novaga, 2007). The crystalline case corresponds to γ being a convex, piecewise linear norm (e.g., γ(ν) = ∑i=1^N |ν·e_i| for a polyhedral Wulff shape). The energy is not differentiable, and the flow is defined via the subdifferential of the total variation functional in the space of functions of bounded variation (Almgren-Taylor-Wang, 1993; Giga-Giga, 1998). Facets (flat regions where ν is constant) evolve by a system of ODEs coupled with the curved regions; the normal velocity on a facet is the crystalline mean curvature, a constant determined by the geometry of the adjacent facets. Singularities in crystalline flow include facet breaking (a facet splits into two), facet bending (a curved region becomes flat), and facet disappearance. The regularity theory for crystalline flow is much less complete: the flow is not unique in general (multiple weak solutions can exist), and the singular set can have positive measure in time. However, for convex initial data in ℝ², the flow is unique and the singular set consists of isolated points in space-time (Giga-Giga-Pozar, 2016). In higher dimensions, the singular set of the crystalline flow is conjectured to be (n−1)-rectifiable, but this is open. The anisotropic flow with a smooth but non-convex γ (e.g., γ with negative curvature) can develop singularities where the surface becomes non-graphical; the regularity theory in this case is related to the theory of minimal surfaces with non-convex integrands (Fonseca-Müller, 1993).

The Theory of the Regularity of the Singular Set for the Minimal Surface Equation with a Volume Constraint

The minimal surface equation with a volume constraint seeks hypersurfaces Σ of constant mean curvature H = λ (a Lagrange multiplier) that enclose a prescribed volume V. This is the Euler-Lagrange equation for the isoperimetric problem: minimize area subject to Vol(Σ) = V. The regularity theory is a special case of the regularity theory for (Λ, r₀)-perimeter minimizers, where Λ = |λ|. By the De Giorgi structure theorem, the reduced boundary ∂*Σ is a C¹,α hypersurface, and the singular set Σ = ∂Σ ∂*Σ has Hausdorff dimension at most n−7 (n−8 for n+1 ≥ 8). The proof follows the same dimension reduction argument as for area-minimizing currents: blow-up limits at singular points are area-minimizing cones in ℝⁿ⁺¹ (the volume constraint scales away in the limit). The constant mean curvature condition H = λ implies that the second variation of area is δ²A(f) = ∫_Σ (|∇f|² − |A|²f²) dℋⁿ − λ ∫_Σ H f² dℋⁿ, and stability (δ²A(f) ≥ 0 for all f with ∫_Σ f dℋⁿ = 0) gives a spectral gap for the Jacobi operator. For isoperimetric regions in ℝⁿ⁺¹, the only stable constant mean curvature hypersurfaces are round spheres (Barbosa-do Carmo, 1984), and the singular set is empty for n ≤ 7. In Riemannian manifolds, the singular set dimension bound holds, but the classification of stable CMC hypersurfaces is more complex. The regularity of the singular set for CMC hypersurfaces with a volume constraint in sub-Riemannian manifolds (e.g., the Heisenberg group) is an open problem; the blow-up limits are not cones but homogeneous sets with respect to the Carnot-Carathéodory dilation, and the singular set dimension is conjectured to be at most n−2. A related problem is the regularity of the singular set for the capillary problem with a volume constraint (the sessile drop problem), where the contact angle is prescribed and the volume is fixed; the regularity theory combines the oblique derivative boundary regularity with the interior regularity for (Λ, r₀)-minimizers.

  • Confusing the capillary problem with the free boundary minimal surface problem: the capillary problem has a prescribed contact angle θ ≠ π/2 and often a non-zero mean curvature (κ ≠ 0); the free boundary problem has θ = π/2 and H = 0. The reflection method differs: capillary requires a shifted odd reflection, free boundary uses standard odd/even reflection.
  • Assuming the singular set dimension bound n−7 holds for isoperimetric regions in all Riemannian manifolds: it holds for n+1 ≤ 7; for higher dimensions, the bound is n−8 for the singular set of the reduced boundary, but the full singular set can have dimension n−7. The Federer dimension reduction gives dim Σ ≤ n−7, but the improved bound n−8 for area-minimizing hypersurfaces uses the Simons cone argument which requires the minimizer to be a cone — isoperimetric regions are only (Λ, r₀)-minimizers, so the n−7 bound is sharp in general.
  • Thinking the volume-preserving MCF has the same singularities as standard MCF: the blow-up limits are the same (self-shrinkers), but the non-local term h(t) affects the Type II analysis and the construction of weak solutions. The Brakke flow formulation does not directly preserve volume; discrete minimizing movement schemes are used instead.
  • Believing crystalline MCF has a unique solution for all initial data: uniqueness fails in general for crystalline flow in dimensions n ≥ 2; multiple weak solutions can exist due to the non-strict convexity of the energy. Uniqueness holds for convex initial data in ℝ² (Giga-Giga-Pozar) but is open in higher dimensions.
  • Confusing the Lagrange multiplier λ in the volume-constrained minimal surface equation with the mean curvature H: the equation is H = λ, where λ is a constant determined by the volume constraint. λ is not the mean curvature of the unconstrained minimizer; it is the mean curvature of the constrained minimizer. For a given volume, λ is unique, but different volumes give different λ.
  • Assuming the regularity theory for CMC hypersurfaces with volume constraint in sub-Riemannian manifolds is the same as in Riemannian manifolds: the blow-up limits are homogeneous with respect to the Carnot-Carathéodory dilation, not Euclidean dilation, so the singular set dimension can be larger (conjectured n−2 vs n−7). The monotonicity formula and dimension reduction arguments fail without a Euclidean cone structure.
  • Overlooking the role of the Wulff shape in anisotropic MCF: the Wulff shape is the unique (up to scaling) self-similar solution and the asymptotic profile for the flow. Its regularity (strict convexity, smoothness) depends on the smoothness and uniform convexity of γ. For crystalline γ, the Wulff shape is a polyhedron, and the flow develops facets that evolve by a system of ODEs.

The Isoperimetric Inequality in Metric Measure Spaces and the Lévy–Gromov Theorem

The classical Euclidean isoperimetric inequality states that among all sets of given volume the ball minimizes perimeter. In the setting of metric measure spaces (X, d, μ) satisfying a curvature‑dimension condition CD(K, N) with K > 0 and N ∈ [1, ∞), the Lévy–Gromov theorem provides a sharp comparison: the isoperimetric profile of X is bounded below by the isoperimetric profile of the N‑dimensional model space of constant curvature K (the sphere of radius 1/√K when K > 0). The proof uses the localization technique of Klartag and the needle decomposition of the space into one‑dimensional geodesics along which the measure has a log‑concave density. On each needle the one‑dimensional isoperimetric inequality is explicit, and integrating over the family of needles yields the global bound. Equality forces the space to be a spherical suspension, which in the smooth Riemannian case implies that X is isometric to the round sphere. The theorem has been extended to non‑smooth RCD(K, N) spaces by Cavalletti–Mondino, where the reduced boundary of a set of finite perimeter is defined via the De Giorgi structure theorem in the metric setting. Applications include concentration of measure estimates, spectral gap lower bounds for the Laplacian, and rigidity results for manifolds with Ricci curvature bounded below. In particular, the Lévy–Gromov inequality implies the sharp Lichnerowicz eigenvalue estimate λ₁ ≥ K N/(N − 1) for the first non‑zero eigenvalue of the Neumann Laplacian on convex domains.

A key technical point is the definition of perimeter in a metric measure space: for a Borel set E ⊂ X the perimeter P(E) is the total variation of the characteristic function χ_E in the sense of BV functions on metric spaces (Ambrosio–Di Marino). The reduced boundary ∂*E is the set of points where the measure‑theoretic normal exists, and the De Giorgi structure theorem guarantees that P(E) = ℋN‑1(∂*E) for RCD(K, N) spaces. The isoperimetric profile I_X(v) = inf{P(E) : μ(E) = v} is then compared with the model profile IM_K^N(v). The localization argument reduces the problem to a family of one‑dimensional weighted intervals (needles) whose densities satisfy the curvature‑dimension condition in the sense of Bakry–Émery. On each needle the isoperimetric problem is solved by intervals, and the Brunn–Minkowski inequality on the needle yields the desired comparison after integration. The rigidity part uses the fact that equality in the Brunn–Minkowski inequality forces the density to be a power of the sine function, which characterizes the spherical suspension.

The Theory of Minimal Submanifolds in Symmetric Spaces and Calibrated Geometry

Symmetric spaces G/K provide a rich source of examples where calibrated geometry yields explicit minimal submanifolds. A calibration on a Riemannian manifold (M, g) is a closed differential form φ of degree p such that φ|_ξ ≤ vol_ξ for every oriented p‑plane ξ, with equality exactly on a distinguished set of planes. If a p‑dimensional submanifold Σ satisfies φ|_TΣ = vol_Σ, then Σ is absolutely area‑minimizing in its homology class. In symmetric spaces the existence of parallel forms (invariant under the isotropy group) gives rise to calibrations. For instance, on the complex projective space ℂP^n with the Fubini–Study metric the Kähler form ω calibrates complex submanifolds, and the real part of the holomorphic volume form calibrates special Lagrangian submanifolds in Calabi–Yau manifolds. In the quaternionic projective space ℍP^n the Kraines form calibrates quaternionic submanifolds. The classification of calibrated submanifolds in symmetric spaces often reduces to the representation theory of the isotropy group: the calibrated planes correspond to orbits of the isotropy representation on the Grassmannian of p‑planes. Harvey and Lawson showed that in the round sphere S2n+1 the standard contact form calibrates Legendrian submanifolds, and in the sphere S4n+3 the 3‑Sasakian structure yields calibrated 3‑dimensional submanifolds. The second variation formula for a calibrated submanifold simplifies because the Jacobi operator is non‑negative on normal variations preserving the calibration condition; this yields stability without computing eigenvalues explicitly. Moreover, the moduli space of calibrated submanifolds in a symmetric space can be studied via moment map techniques: the calibration condition is equivalent to the vanishing of a moment map for the action of the isometry group on the space of submanifolds. This links minimal submanifold theory to Hamiltonian geometry and provides a framework for constructing new examples by symplectic reduction. Recent work by Lotay and others has extended these ideas to nearly Kähler and G₂ manifolds, where the associative and co‑associative calibrations produce minimal submanifolds of dimensions three and four respectively. The regularity theory for calibrated submanifolds follows from the general Allard regularity theorem once one knows that the submanifold is a stationary integral varifold; the calibration gives a pointwise bound on the density, which forces the tangent cones to be calibrated planes, hence smooth.

Worked Example: Calibration on ℂP²
Show that a complex line ℂP¹ ⊂ ℂP² is calibrated by the Kähler form ω and deduce that it minimizes area in its homology class.
The Fubini–Study metric on ℂP² has Kähler form ω satisfying dω = 0. For any complex line L ≅ ℂP¹ the tangent space at each point is a complex line in ℂ², and ω restricts to the area form on L because ω(v, Jv) = g(v, v) for any tangent vector v. Hence ω|_L = vol_L. Since ω is closed, Stokes’ theorem gives ∫_L ω = ∫_Σ ω for any other 2‑cycle Σ homologous to L. But ω|_Σ ≤ vol_Σ pointwise, so ∫_L ω ≤ Area(Σ). Equality forces ω|_Σ = vol_Σ, which implies Σ is also a complex submanifold. Therefore L is absolutely area‑minimizing in its homology class.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for a calibration argument, first identify a closed form that bounds the volume form on all p‑planes. Verify the pointwise inequality on the tangent planes of the candidate submanifold. Then invoke homology invariance of the integral of the closed form to compare areas. Remember that calibrations give absolute minimizers, not just local ones.

The Sub‑Riemannian Isoperimetric Problem in the Heisenberg Group and the Pansu Conjecture

The Heisenberg group ℍ¹ is the simplest non‑trivial Carnot group: it is ℝ³ with coordinates (x, y, t) and group law (x, y, t)·(x', y', t') = (x + x', y + y', t + t' + ½(xy' − yx')). The horizontal distribution is spanned by the left‑invariant vector fields X = ∂_x − ½y∂_t and Y = ∂_y + ½x∂_t. The Carnot–Carathéodory distance d_cc induces a homogeneous dimension Q = 4. The sub‑Riemannian perimeter of a set E ⊂ ℍ¹ is the total variation of χ_E with respect to the horizontal gradient ∇_H = (X, Y). Pansu conjectured in 1984 that the isoperimetric sets in ℍ¹ are precisely the translations and dilations of the Korányi balls (the unit balls of the Korányi gauge N(x, y, t) = ((x² + y²)² + 16t²)1/4). The conjecture remains open in full generality, but significant progress has been made. Monti and Rickly proved that any isoperimetric set has a boundary which is a C¹,α hypersurface except for a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most 2. The blow‑up analysis at a regular point shows that the tangent cone is a vertical plane, while at a singular point the tangent cone is a homogeneous set invariant under the group dilations δ_λ(x, y, t) = (λx, λy, λ²t). The classification of such homogeneous cones is a key step: the only stable cones are the vertical planes and the Korányi spheres. The first variation formula for the horizontal perimeter yields the sub‑Riemannian mean curvature H_H = div_H(ν_H), where ν_H is the horizontal unit normal. For a Korányi sphere H_H is constant, confirming that it is a critical point. The second variation involves the horizontal Hessian and the Reeb vector field T = ∂_t. Stability requires the quadratic form Q(f) = ∫∂E (|∇_H f|² − (|A_H|² + Ric_H(ν_H, ν_H))f²) dℋ³ to be non‑negative for all f with ∫ f = 0. Recent work by Figalli, Maggi, and Pratelli established the isoperimetric inequality with a sharp constant for sets of finite perimeter in ℍ¹, but the characterization of equality cases (the Pansu conjecture) is still open. The problem is closely related to the regularity of the sub‑Riemannian minimal surface equation, which is a degenerate elliptic PDE. Techniques from geometric measure theory in metric spaces (Cheeger differentiation, Poincaré inequalities) and the theory of BV functions on Carnot groups are essential tools.

The Theory of the Allen–Cahn Equation as a Diffuse Interface Approximation to Minimal Surfaces

The Allen–Cahn equation ε²Δu − W'(u) = 0 on a Riemannian manifold (M, g) with a double‑well potential W(u) = ¼(1 − u²)² provides a phase‑field approximation of minimal hypersurfaces. As ε → 0 the energy functional E_ε(u) = ∫_M (ε|∇u|²/2 + W(u)/ε) dvol Γ‑converges to the perimeter functional (up to a constant factor c₀ = ∫‑11 √(2W(s)) ds). The zero level set {u_ε = 0} converges in the sense of varifolds to a minimal hypersurface Σ. The Modica–Mortola theorem establishes the Γ‑convergence in the Euclidean setting; the extension to Riemannian manifolds uses the fact that the leading order term of the energy is local and the curvature of M appears only at higher order. The regularity of the limit interface follows from the uniform energy bounds and the monotonicity formula for the Allen–Cahn energy: the quantity Φ_ε(x, r) = r1‑n∫B_r(x) (ε|∇u_ε|²/2 + W(u_ε)/ε) dvol is monotone non‑decreasing in r. This monotonicity is a diffuse analogue of the classical monotonicity formula for minimal surfaces and yields density bounds for the limiting varifold. The linearized Allen–Cahn operator L_ε = ε²Δ − W''(u_ε) has a spectral gap that controls the stability of the transition layer. In the limit ε → 0 the first eigenvalue of L_ε converges to the first eigenvalue of the Jacobi operator on Σ, linking the stability of the phase‑field solution to the stability of the minimal hypersurface. The work of Hutchinson–Tonegawa and later of Gaspar–Guaraco shows that any sequence of solutions with uniformly bounded energy has a subsequence converging to an integral varifold with bounded first variation, and the limit is stationary. If the solutions are stable (second variation non‑negative), the limit varifold is a stable minimal hypersurface, and the regularity theory of Schoen–Simon applies, giving smoothness away from a singular set of dimension at most n − 7. The Allen–Cahn approximation is also used numerically (the diffuse interface method) because it avoids explicit tracking of the interface. The convergence rate of the zero level set to the minimal surface in Hausdorff distance is O(ε|log ε|) under non‑degeneracy assumptions.

The Theory of the Cahn–Hilliard Equation and Its Geometric Measure Theoretic Limit

The Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂_t u = Δ(ε²Δu − W'(u)) models phase separation with conserved order parameter. The associated energy is the same Allen–Cahn functional E_ε(u). As ε → 0 the dynamics formally converge to motion by mean curvature with a volume constraint: the interface evolves by normal velocity V = H − λ(t), where λ(t) is a Lagrange multiplier enforcing conservation of the total mass ∫ u dx. In the sharp‑interface limit the mass constraint translates into preservation of the enclosed volume. The rigorous derivation of this limit uses the method of matched asymptotic expansions combined with varifold compactness. The key analytical tool is the energy‑dissipation inequality d/dt E_ε(u_ε) = −∫ |∇μ_ε|² dx, where μ_ε = ε²Δu_ε − W'(u_ε) is the chemical potential. Uniform bounds on the dissipation yield compactness of the diffuse interfaces in the space of integral varifolds. The limit varifold V_t satisfies Brakke’s inequality with an additional forcing term coming from the Lagrange multiplier. The multiplier λ(t) is determined by the condition d/dt μ(V_t) = 0, where μ(V_t) is the mass of the varifold (the volume enclosed). The regularity of the limiting flow follows from the regularity theory for Brakke flows with forcing, provided the forcing term is sufficiently regular. In the work of Otto and Reznikoff, the Γ‑convergence of the gradient flow structure is established in the sense of De Giorgi’s minimizing movements: the Cahn–Hilliard flow is the gradient flow of E_ε in the H-1 metric, and the limit is the gradient flow of the perimeter in the same metric, which coincides with volume‑preserving mean curvature flow. The singular set of the limit flow has parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n − 2, a result proved by extending the partial regularity theory of Brakke to the forced setting. The Cahn–Hilliard equation also admits a thin‑interface limit where the interface thickness scales like ε and the mobility scales like ε-1; this leads to the same geometric motion but with a different kinetic coefficient. The analysis of the Cahn–Hilliard equation on Riemannian manifolds requires the Bochner formula for the Laplacian on forms and the curvature terms appear in the dissipation estimate, but the Γ‑convergence result remains valid under bounded geometry assumptions.

  • Confusing the Lévy–Gromov isoperimetric profile with the Euclidean one: the model space is a sphere of constant curvature, not a Euclidean ball.
  • Assuming every calibrated submanifold is automatically stable without checking the Jacobi operator on normal variations preserving the calibration.
  • Treating the Heisenberg group isoperimetric problem as Euclidean: the homogeneous dimension is 4, not 3, and the dilations are anisotropic.
  • Believing the Allen–Cahn zero level set converges to a minimal surface without the uniform energy bound and monotonicity formula.
  • Neglecting the volume‑preserving Lagrange multiplier in the Cahn–Hilliard sharp‑interface limit; the limit motion is not pure mean curvature flow but mean curvature flow with a global forcing term.
  • Thinking the singular set dimension for the Cahn–Hilliard limit flow is the same as for standard Brakke flow; the forcing term can increase the parabolic dimension of the singular set.
  • Remember to review these traps before the exam.

The Theory of Minimal Submanifolds in Manifolds with Density and the Gaussian Isoperimetric Problem

A manifold with density is a Riemannian manifold equipped with a positive weight function e-f that modifies both volume and area. The weighted area of a hypersurface Σ becomes ∫Σ e-f dHn-1 and the weighted volume of a region Ω is ∫Ω e-f dHn. The first variation formula acquires an extra term ∫Σ ⟨ ∇ f,nu⟩ e-f dHn-1, so stationary hypersurfaces satisfy H = ⟨ ∇ f,nu⟩ where H is the classical mean curvature. This framework unifies many classical problems: the Gaussian space Rn with density e-|x|2/2 corresponds to the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator, and its isoperimetric problem asks for sets of given Gaussian measure minimizing Gaussian perimeter.

The Gaussian isoperimetric inequality, proved independently by Borell and by Sudakov–Tsirelson in the 1970s, states that half‑spaces are the unique minimizers of Gaussian perimeter for a prescribed Gaussian measure. The proof uses the Ehrhard symmetrization, a rearrangement that preserves Gaussian measure while decreasing perimeter. In the language of manifolds with density, the Gaussian space is a model space with Bakry–Émery Ricci curvature operatorname{Ric}f = operatorname{Ric} + ∇2f = I, which satisfies the curvature‑dimension condition CD(1,n). This curvature bound allows the use of the Lévy–Gromov isoperimetric comparison, yielding the same half‑space conclusion.

Regularity theory for weighted minimal hypersurfaces follows the classical Allard regularity theorem after a conformal change of metric. If the density e-f is smooth and strictly positive, the weighted area functional is an elliptic functional of the same structure as the classical area. The work of Morgan and later of Cañete–Rosales shows that the singular set of a weighted area‑minimizing hypersurface has Hausdorff dimension at most n-8, exactly as in the unweighted case. The key point is that the Euler–Lagrange equation remains uniformly elliptic because the weight only appears as a bounded multiplicative factor in the coefficients.

Applications extend to probability and statistical mechanics. The Gaussian isoperimetric inequality implies the Gaussian concentration of measure phenomenon: any set of measure at least 1/2 has its r-neighbourhood of measure at least Φ(Φ-1(1/2)+r), where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. This concentration underlies many results in high‑dimensional geometry, such as Dvoretzky’s theorem on almost Euclidean sections of convex bodies. In the calculus of variations, the weighted setting provides a natural framework for the study of self‑shrinkers of mean curvature flow, which are critical points of the Gaussian area functional.

Recent developments include the extension of the isoperimetric profile to manifolds with density satisfying a lower bound on the Bakry–Émery Ricci curvature. The work of Milman and others shows that the model spaces for such inequalities are either Gaussian spaces or spheres with appropriate densities, depending on the sign of the curvature bound. The classification of isoperimetric regions in these model spaces remains an active area, with connections to the stability of the Gaussian inequality and to the spectral gap of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator.

The Theory of the Monge–Ampère Equation and its Geometric Measure Theoretic Solutions

The Monge–Ampère equation det D2u = f arises naturally in optimal transport, where u is a convex potential pushing forward a source measure μ to a target measure nu via the map ∇ u. In the geometric measure theory language, the graph of ∇ u is an n-dimensional rectifiable current in RntimesRn calibrated by the symplectic form, and the equation expresses the Jacobian determinant of the transport map. Alexandrov introduced a weak notion of solution: a convex function u satisfies det D2u ≥ f in the sense of measures if for every Borel set E, the Monge–Ampère measure μu(E) = |∂ u(E)| dominates ∫E f. This measure is precisely the push‑forward of Lebesgue measure by the subgradient mapping ∂ u.

Caffarelli’s regularity theory, developed in the 1990s, shows that if f is bounded away from zero and infinity and the domains are convex, then any Alexandrov solution is strictly convex and C1,α for some α>0. The proof uses a geometric measure theoretic blow‑up argument: at a point where the solution is not strictly convex, the rescaled functions converge to a quadratic polynomial, and the Monge–Ampère measure converges to a constant multiple of Lebesgue measure. The strict convexity then follows from a Harnack inequality for the linearized Monge–Ampère operator. Further regularity (C2,α and smoothness) requires additional smoothness of f and the boundary data, and is obtained by the Evans–Krylov theorem applied to the linearized equation.

The connection with optimal transport is made precise by Brenier’s theorem: for absolutely continuous measures μ,nu on Rn with μ having a density, there exists a unique (up to additive constant) convex function u solving the Monge–Ampère equation in the Alexandrov sense such that ∇ u#μ = nu. The graph of ∇ u is a calibrated current, and the optimal transport cost equals the integral of the quadratic cost against the transport plan. This variational formulation allows the use of GMT compactness theorems (Federer–Fleming compactness for integral currents) to prove existence of optimal maps under very weak assumptions on the measures.

In the setting of metric measure spaces, the Monge–Ampère equation can be formulated via the theory of c-concave functions and the c-subdifferential. The work of Figalli and others extends Caffarelli’s regularity to the Riemannian setting, where the cost function is the squared distance. The geometric measure theoretic tools — rectifiable currents, tangent measures, and the constancy theorem — are essential for defining the Monge–Ampère measure on a manifold and for proving that the optimal transport map is given by the exponential of the gradient of a c-convex potential.

Recent advances include the study of the Monge–Ampère equation on singular spaces such as Alexandrov spaces with curvature bounded below, where the notion of convexity and the Monge–Ampère measure are defined via the theory of DC functions. The regularity theory in this context uses the GMT structure of the space of directions and the existence of tangent cones. Another direction is the quantitative stability of the Monge–Ampère equation: if two right‑hand sides are close in Wasserstein distance, the corresponding potentials are close in C1,α norm, with explicit estimates depending on the dimension and the bounds on the densities.

Worked Example: Gaussian Isoperimetric Profile
Let γn be the standard Gaussian measure on Rn. Show that for any Borel set A with γn(A)=1/2, the Gaussian perimeter Pγ(A) satisfies Pγ(A)≥ (1)/(√(2π)). Identify the equality case.
The Gaussian isoperimetric inequality states that half‑spaces minimize Gaussian perimeter for a given measure. For a half‑space H={x1≤ 0}, γn(H)=1/2 and its Gaussian perimeter equals the Gaussian density at the boundary: Pγ(H)=(1)/(√(2π))e-02/2=(1)/(√(2π)). By the Borell–Sudakov–Tsirelson theorem, any set A with γn(A)=1/2 satisfies Pγ(A)≥ Pγ(H)=(1)/(√(2π)). Equality holds iff A is a half‑space (up to a null set). The proof uses Ehrhard symmetrization, which preserves Gaussian measure and does not increase perimeter, reducing the problem to the one‑dimensional case where the inequality is elementary.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the isoperimetric profile in a weighted manifold, first identify the model space (Gaussian, sphere, or Euclidean) by checking the Bakry–Émery Ricci curvature lower bound. Then recall the explicit minimizers: half‑spaces for Gaussian, geodesic balls for sphere, and balls for Euclidean. Write the profile function I(v) using the appropriate cumulative distribution function (Gaussian Φ or spherical area). This avoids re‑deriving the inequality from scratch.

The Theory of the Sub‑Riemannian Isoperimetric Problem in Carnot Groups

Carnot groups are simply connected nilpotent Lie groups whose Lie algebra admits a stratification g=V1⊕⋯⊕ Vs with [V1,Vj]=Vj+1. The horizontal distribution V1 defines a sub‑Riemannian structure: only horizontal curves are admissible, and their length is measured by a fixed inner product on V1. The homogeneous dimension is Q=Σj=1s jdim Vj, which replaces the topological dimension in scaling arguments. The Heisenberg group H1 (dimension 3, Q=4) is the simplest non‑trivial example.

The sub‑Riemannian isoperimetric problem asks for sets of given Haar measure minimizing the horizontal perimeter PH(E)=sup{∫Eoperatorname{div}Hφ : φ∈ C1c(G,V1), |φ|≤ 1}. Pansu proved in 1982 that in the Heisenberg group the isoperimetric sets are not Euclidean balls but rather “Pansu bubbles” — sets bounded by surfaces of revolution around the vertical axis with a specific profile determined by an ODE. The proof uses the blow‑up technique: at a point of the reduced boundary, the rescaled sets converge to a vertical half‑space, which is a tangent cone. The classification of tangent cones then forces the global shape to be a Pansu bubble.

In higher step Carnot groups, the isoperimetric problem is largely open. The existence of minimizers follows from the compactness theorem for sets of finite horizontal perimeter (the De Giorgi structure theorem holds in this setting). Regularity of the reduced boundary is known: it is a C1,α hypersurface in the horizontal directions, and the horizontal normal exists HQ-1-a.e. The work of Capogna–Danielli–Garofalo and later of Montefalcone establishes a first variation formula and a monotonicity formula for horizontal perimeter, which are the main tools for blow‑up analysis.

A major difficulty is the lack of a Euclidean‑type symmetrization that preserves horizontal perimeter. The spherical symmetrization used in the Heisenberg group relies on the group’s rotational symmetry around the vertical axis, which is absent in general Carnot groups. Recent progress by Figalli–Maggi–Pratelli uses the mass transport method: they construct a map pushing forward the Haar measure to a candidate minimizer and estimate the change in horizontal perimeter via the Jacobian of the map. This approach yields quantitative stability estimates but not a full classification.

The isoperimetric profile I(v) in the Heisenberg group is known explicitly only in terms of the solution of the ODE for Pansu bubbles. Asymptotically, for small volumes v→ 0, the profile behaves like c v(Q-1)/Q with the same constant as in the Euclidean space of dimension Q, reflecting the fact that at small scales the geometry looks like the tangent cone (a vertical half‑space). For large volumes, the profile is linear in v because the isoperimetric sets become essentially cylinders over the vertical direction. Understanding the transition between these regimes is an active research area.

The Solution of the Plateau Problem for Integral Currents in Metric Spaces by Ambrosio and Kirchheim

The classical Plateau problem asks for a surface of minimal area spanning a given boundary. In Euclidean space, the solution by Douglas and Radó uses parametric methods, while the later solution by Federer and Fleming uses integral currents. Ambrosio and Kirchheim (2000) extended the Federer–Fleming theory to complete metric spaces, defining metric currents as multilinear functionals on tuples of Lipschitz functions satisfying suitable continuity and locality axioms. An integral current is a metric current with finite mass and finite mass of its boundary, both representable by integer‑multiplicity rectifiable sets.

The key compactness theorem states that a sequence of integral currents with uniformly bounded masses and boundary masses has a subsequence converging in the flat norm to an integral current. The proof adapts the Federer–Fleming deformation theorem to the metric setting: one constructs a Lipschitz retraction onto a finite‑dimensional simplicial complex approximating the space, then uses the Euclidean deformation theorem on the complex. The flat norm convergence implies convergence of the associated varifolds, so the limit is an area‑minimizing integral current.

Existence of a solution to the Plateau problem for a given integral current boundary T follows by taking a minimizing sequence of integral currents Sk with ∂ Sk=T and M(Sk)→ inf{M(S):∂ S=T}. Compactness yields a limit S with ∂ S=T and M(S)=inf. The regularity theory for area‑minimizing integral currents in metric spaces is much less developed than in Euclidean space; however, if the ambient space is a Riemannian manifold, the classical Almgren regularity theorem applies after an isometric embedding into a Euclidean space.

The Ambrosio–Kirchheim theory also provides a notion of push‑forward of currents under Lipschitz maps, which is essential for the formulation of the Plateau problem in metric spaces that are not linearly embedded. The mass of a current is lower semicontinuous with respect to flat convergence, and the boundary operator is continuous. These properties mirror the Euclidean theory and allow the use of the direct method of the calculus of variations.

Applications include the existence of area‑minimizing surfaces in sub‑Riemannian manifolds (viewed as metric spaces with the Carnot–Carathéodory distance) and in spaces with singularities such as Alexandrov spaces. The theory also underpins the recent work on the Plateau problem for curves in metric spaces, where the boundary is a 1‑dimensional integral current (a Lipschitz curve) and the solution is a 2‑dimensional integral current. The flat norm topology is crucial because it is metrizable and compatible with the weak convergence of measures, making it suitable for variational problems.

The Regularity Theory for the Singular Set of the Cahn–Hilliard Equation and Volume‑Preserving Mean Curvature Flow

The Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂tu = Δ(varepsilon2Δ u - W'(u)) models phase separation with a conserved order parameter. The associated energy is the Allen–Cahn functional Evarepsilon(u)=∫ (varepsilon)/(2)|∇ u|2 + (1)/(varepsilon)W(u). As varepsilon→ 0, the diffuse interfaces converge to a sharp interface moving by volume‑preserving mean curvature flow: the normal velocity satisfies V = H - λ(t), where λ(t) is a Lagrange multiplier chosen so that the enclosed volume remains constant. The rigorous derivation uses the energy‑dissipation inequality (d)/(dt)Evarepsilon(uvarepsilon) = -∫ |∇ μvarepsilon|2 with chemical potential μvarepsilon=varepsilon2Δ uvarepsilon-W'(uvarepsilon).

Uniform bounds on the dissipation yield compactness of the diffuse interfaces in the space of integral varifolds. The limit varifold Vt satisfies Brakke’s inequality with an additional forcing term -λ(t)1. The multiplier λ(t) is determined by the condition (d)/(dt)μ(Vt)=0, where μ(Vt) is the mass of the varifold (the volume enclosed). The work of Otto and Reznikoff establishes the Γ-convergence of the gradient flow structure in the sense of De Giorgi’s minimizing movements: the Cahn–Hilliard flow is the gradient flow of Evarepsilon in the H-1 metric, and the limit is the gradient flow of the perimeter in the same metric, which coincides with volume‑preserving mean curvature flow.

Regularity of the limiting flow follows from the partial regularity theory for Brakke flows with forcing. The singular set of a Brakke flow has parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n-2. For the forced flow, the same dimension bound holds provided the forcing term is bounded in L∞. In the Cahn–Hilliard limit, λ(t) is bounded because the volume constraint forces the average mean curvature to stay bounded. The proof adapts the stratification argument of White: at a singular point, one performs a parabolic blow‑up; the limit is a stationary varifold with a forcing term, which must be a cone. The dimension reduction then proceeds as in the unforced case.

Quantitative estimates on the singular set have been obtained by extending the Naber–Valtorta quantitative stratification to the forced setting. One defines the k-th quantitative stratum Sketa,r as the set of points where no eta-approximate symmetry of order k exists at scale r. The Minkowski content of these strata is controlled by the Gaussian density and the forcing term. This yields effective bounds on the size of the singular set at positive times, which are useful for numerical analysis of the diffuse interface method.

An important open problem is the regularity of the singular set at the initial time when the initial data is only assumed to have bounded energy. The Allen–Cahn approximation provides a selection principle: the limit flow is the “viscosity solution” of the volume‑preserving mean curvature flow in the sense of the level‑set method. The uniqueness of this limit is known for convex initial data, but for general data the selection may depend on the subsequence. Understanding the structure of the singular set at time zero remains a central challenge linking the Cahn–Hilliard equation to the geometric measure theory of mean curvature flow.

  • Confusing the Gaussian isoperimetric profile with the Euclidean one: the minimizers are half‑spaces, not balls, and the profile involves the Gaussian error function Φ.
  • Assuming every solution of the Monge–Ampère equation is smooth without checking the boundedness and positivity of the right‑hand side f and the convexity of the domains.
  • Treating the sub‑Riemannian isoperimetric problem in a general Carnot group as if the Heisenberg group symmetrization works; the rotational symmetry is special to the Heisenberg group.
  • Believing the Ambrosio–Kirchheim compactness theorem holds for arbitrary metric spaces without the completeness and local compactness assumptions required for the deformation theorem.
  • Neglecting the volume‑preserving Lagrange multiplier λ(t) in the Cahn–Hilliard sharp‑interface limit; the limit motion is not pure mean curvature flow but mean curvature flow with a global forcing term.
  • Thinking the singular set dimension for the forced Brakke flow is larger than n-2; the forcing term is bounded and does not increase the parabolic dimension of the singular set.
  • Assuming the Cahn–Hilliard limit flow is unique for all initial data; uniqueness holds only under additional convexity or symmetry assumptions.

Forced Brakke Flows and the Cahn–Hilliard Sharp‑Interface Limit

A forced Brakke flow is a family of integral varifolds Vt satisfying Brakke’s inequality with an additional bounded forcing term f(x,t). For a test function φ ≥ 0 the inequality reads

d/dt ∫ φ dμVt ≤ ∫ (−φ|H|2 + ∇φ·H + φf) dμVt.

The forcing term arises naturally in the sharp‑interface limit of the Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂tu = Δ(ε2Δu − W′(u)). The diffuse interface energy Eε(u) = ∫ (ε/2)|∇u|2 + (1/ε)W(u) Γ‑converges to the perimeter functional. The gradient flow structure in the H−1 metric (Otto–Reznikoff) passes to the limit: the limiting varifold evolves by volume‑preserving mean curvature flow, i.e. normal velocity V = H − λ(t) where λ(t) is a Lagrange multiplier chosen so that the enclosed volume stays constant. In the varifold formulation this is exactly a forced Brakke flow with f = −λ(t).

Regularity theory for forced flows mirrors the unforced case. White’s stratification argument adapts because the forcing term is bounded in L∞; at a singular point a parabolic blow‑up yields a stationary varifold with a constant forcing term, which must be a cone. Consequently the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of the singular set remains at most n−2. Quantitative stratification (Naber–Valtorta) has been extended to the forced setting: one defines the k‑th quantitative stratum Skη,r as points where no η‑approximate symmetry of order k exists at scale r. The Minkowski content of these strata is controlled by the Gaussian density and the L∞ norm of the forcing. This yields effective bounds on the size of the singular set at positive times, which are valuable for numerical analysis of the diffuse interface method.

An important open problem is the regularity of the singular set at the initial time when the initial data only has bounded energy. The Allen–Cahn approximation provides a selection principle: the limit flow coincides with the viscosity solution of the volume‑preserving mean curvature flow in the level‑set sense. Uniqueness of this limit is known for convex initial data, but for general data the limit may depend on the subsequence. Understanding the structure of the singular set at time zero remains a central challenge linking the Cahn–Hilliard equation to the geometric measure theory of mean curvature flow.

Classification of Ancient Solutions and Self‑Shrinkers in Mean Curvature Flow

An ancient solution of mean curvature flow is a smooth family of hypersurfaces Mt defined for all t < 0. Self‑shrinkers are a distinguished subclass: they satisfy H = −x⊥/2 and evolve by homothetic shrinking Mt = √(−t) M−1. They arise as Type I blow‑up limits at singularities. In low dimensions the classification is nearly complete. For curves in the plane the only embedded self‑shrinkers are the line, the circle, and the Angenent oval (a closed convex curve). In ℝ3 the embedded self‑shrinkers with polynomial volume growth are the plane, the sphere, the cylinder S1×ℝ, and a family of rotationally symmetric caps (the “bowl” solitons are translating, not shrinking). Brendle proved that any embedded self‑shrinker in ℝ3 with genus zero and polynomial volume growth is one of these. In higher dimensions the classification is open, but Colding–Minicozzi showed that generic singularities are modeled on spheres, cylinders, or planes. The entropy functional λ(M) = supx0,t0 (4πt0)−n/2 ∫M exp(−|x−x0|2/4t0) is monotone along the flow and attains its minimum on the plane. Self‑shrinkers are critical points of entropy. The work of Bernstein–Wang and others has extended the classification to self‑shrinkers with low entropy, showing that the only embedded self‑shrinkers in ℝ4 with entropy below that of the cylinder are the plane and the sphere.

Ancient solutions that are not self‑shrinkers include translating solitons (which move by constant speed) and more exotic examples such as the ancient ovals constructed by Angenent and the ancient asymptotically cylindrical flows of Brendle–Choi. The classification of ancient solutions with bounded entropy is a major theme: in ℝ2 the only embedded ancient solutions are the shrinking circle, the translating grim reaper, and the stationary line. In higher dimensions the picture is richer; the existence of ancient non‑collapsed flows (Andrews–Bryan) and the recent classification of ancient low‑entropy flows by Choi–Haslhofer–Hershkovits have advanced the program. These results rely on the monotonicity of the Gaussian density, the Huisken monotonicity formula, and the ε‑regularity theorem for ancient solutions.

Identifying Singularity Type via Blow‑Up
A mean curvature flow in ℝ3 develops a singularity at time T. At a singular point p the Gaussian density Θ(p,T) = 1.5. Explain why a parabolic blow‑up at (p,T) yields a self‑shrinker, and why the limit cannot be a translating soliton.
The Gaussian density Θ(p,T) = limr→0 ∫MT−r2 (4πr2)−1 exp(−|x−p|2/4r2) dμ. If Θ = 1.5, the singularity is Type I because the density is strictly between 1 (plane) and the cylinder density ≈ 1.57. For Type I singularities the rescaled flows Mλ(s) = λ(MT+s/λ2 − p) converge as λ→∞ to a self‑shrinker by Huisken’s monotonicity formula. Translating solitons arise as blow‑up limits of Type II singularities where the curvature blows up faster than (T−t)−1/2; their Gaussian density is 1 (they are asymptotic to a cylinder at infinity). Since the given density is 1.5 > 1, the blow‑up limit must be a self‑shrinker (the cylinder or a sphere), not a translating soliton.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the singularity model, first compute or recall the Gaussian density. Density = 1 → plane (regular). Density between 1 and the cylinder density → Type I, expect self‑shrinkers (sphere, cylinder). Density = 1 with curvature blow‑up rate > (T−t)−1/2 → Type II, expect translating solitons or other ancient solutions. Always mention Huisken’s monotonicity and the ε‑regularity theorem to justify the convergence of the blow‑up sequence.

Translating Solitons and Their Role in Singularity Formation

A translating soliton is a hypersurface M that moves by translation with constant velocity v, i.e. Mt = M + tv. The equation is H = v⊥. In the plane the grim reaper curve y = −log cos x (|x| < π/2) translates upward with speed 1. It is the unique embedded translating soliton in ℝ2 up to rigid motions. In higher dimensions the bowl soliton is a rotationally symmetric, strictly convex translating soliton in ℝn+1 that is asymptotic to a paraboloid. Its existence and uniqueness were proved by Altschuler–Wu (for n=2) and by Wang (for all n). Translating solitons appear as Type II blow‑up limits at singularities where the curvature blows up faster than the Type I rate. For example, a neckpinch in a rotationally symmetric mean curvature flow can be modeled by a translating soliton after a suitable parabolic rescaling that is not the standard Type I scaling. The work of Angenent–Velázquez and later of Merle–Zaag constructed solutions that develop Type II singularities modeled on the grim reaper or the bowl soliton.

The classification of translating solitons is an active area. In ℝ3 the only embedded, strictly convex translating solitons are the bowl soliton and the plane. Non‑convex examples include the “wing” translators and the “grim reaper cylinder” Γ×ℝ. The method of moving planes (used by Wang) and the maximum principle are key tools. Translating solitons also play a role in the surgery program for mean curvature flow: Huisken–Sinestrari’s surgery removes necks that are modeled on cylinders, but in the presence of Type II singularities one must understand the translating soliton models to continue the flow past singularities. Recent work by Bamler–Kleiner on the structure of singularities uses the entropy functional to show that any ancient solution with low entropy is either a self‑shrinker, a translating soliton, or a plane.

The Regularity Theory for the Anisotropic Mean Curvature Flow

The anisotropic mean curvature flow is the gradient flow of the anisotropic perimeter Pφ(E) = ∫∂E φ(ν) dℋn, where φ is a norm on ℝn+1 (the surface tension). The Wulff shape Wφ = {x : x·y ≤ φ(y) ∀y} is the unit ball of the dual norm and minimizes the anisotropic perimeter for given volume. The anisotropic mean curvature is Hφ = div∂E ∇φ(ν). The flow equation is V = Hφ. Bellettini, Novaga, and Paolini developed a regularity theory for this flow using the theory of φ‑regular sets. They proved that if the initial set is φ‑regular (i.e. its boundary is a C1,α graph with respect to the anisotropic metric), then the flow remains φ‑regular for a short time. The singular set of a general anisotropic flow has parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n−2, provided φ is uniformly elliptic (i.e. the Hessian of φ2 is positive definite). The proof adapts Allard’s regularity theorem to anisotropic varifolds: one defines the φ‑mass of a varifold and shows that the monotonicity formula holds with the anisotropic density. The ε‑regularity theorem then gives that points with density close to 1 are regular. The anisotropic monotonicity formula involves the anisotropic heat kernel, and the blow‑up limits are cones that are stationary for the anisotropic perimeter. The regularity of the Wulff shape itself is a classical result: if φ is smooth and uniformly convex, then Wφ is smooth and strictly convex. For crystalline φ (non‑smooth) the Wulff shape is a polytope, leading to the crystalline flow discussed next.
