Because K is dense, every ordering of k lifts to an ordering of R that makes K dense, and the set of such orderings is a closed subspace of the real spectrum of R.

From the model‑theoretic side, the theory of (R,v,K) in the language L = {+,·,<,v,K} is model complete after adding a cross‑section for Γ and an angular component map. The value group remains a pure divisible ordered abelian group, while the residue field inherits a predicate for the image of K, which is a dense real closed subfield. The pair (k, res(K)) is an elementary pair of real closed fields, and the theory of (R,v,K) is bi‑interpretable with the theory of the triple (Γ, k, res(K)). This bi‑interpretability yields a relative quantifier elimination: every formula is equivalent to a Boolean combination of formulas in the valued field sort that only refer to the valuation and the predicate K, together with formulas in the value group and residue field sorts. Consequently, the theory is NIP and admits a cell decomposition where cells are defined using the valuation and the predicate K as parameters.

An important application is the transfer of results from the theory of dense pairs of real closed fields to valued fields. For instance, the definable closure in (R,v,K) coincides with the field‑theoretic closure together with the valuation ring and the convex hull of K. This description allows one to compute the dimension of definable sets in terms of the dimensions of their projections to the value group and the residue field. The density of K also implies that the induced structure on K is exactly that of a dense pair of real closed fields, so all known results about definable sets in dense pairs (e.g. the open core is the real field) lift to the valued setting.

Worked Example: Definable Subgroups in a Difference‑Valued Real Closed Field
Let (R,v,χ,σ) be a real closed field with a generic automorphism σ and a σ‑invariant cross‑section χ. Show that any definable subgroup H ≤ R× of finite index is of the form H = χ(Δ) · U where Δ ≤ Γ is a subgroup of finite index and U ≤ O× is a definable subgroup of the valuation units containing 1+M.
Because the theory eliminates imaginaries up to the sorts Γ and k, any definable subgroup of R× corresponds to a definable subgroup of the product Γ × k× × (1+M). The cross‑section gives a definable splitting R× ≅ Γ × O×, and O× ≅ k× × (1+M). The automorphism σ acts trivially on Γ and k, and it preserves 1+M. A definable subgroup of finite index must project onto a subgroup of finite index in each coordinate. In Γ, any definable subgroup of finite index is a subgroup Δ of finite index because Γ is a pure divisible ordered abelian group. In k×, the only definable subgroups of finite index are the whole group (since k is real closed and o‑minimal). In 1+M, the group is uniquely divisible, so it has no proper subgroups of finite index. Hence H = χ(Δ) · U with U = k× × (1+M) = O×. This matches the claimed form.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks about the interaction of a generic automorphism with a valuation, first check whether the automorphism is required to preserve the valuation ring. If it does, the value group carries the trivial action and any cross‑section can be chosen invariant. Use the Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle to reduce the problem to the value group and residue field. Remember that the fixed field of a generic automorphism is a real closed subfield and forms an elementary pair with the whole field; this is a standard transfer tool.

Model Theory of Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for the Infinitesimal Subgroup and a Derivation

Let R be a real closed field equipped with its unique contractive valuation v, valuation ring O, maximal ideal M, and a derivation ∂ that makes (R,∂) a differential real closed field. The infinitesimal subgroup M is a convex additive subgroup of R, and adding a predicate for M together with the derivation symbol yields a structure (R,∂,M). The derivation is assumed to be compatible with the valuation: ∂(O) ⊆ O and ∂(M) ⊆ M. This compatibility forces the induced derivation on the residue field k = O/M to be well defined, and the induced derivation on the value group Γ is necessarily trivial because Γ is a divisible ordered abelian group with no non‑trivial derivations. The theory of (R,∂,M) in the language L = {+,·,<,∂,M} is model complete after adding a cross‑section χ: Γ → R× that is a differential homomorphism (i.e. ∂(χ(γ)) = 0 for all γ). The angular component map ac: R× → k× then satisfies ac(∂(x)) = ∂_k(ac(x)).

The fixed field C = {x ∈ R : ∂(x) = 0} is a real closed subfield, and the pair (R,C) is an elementary pair of real closed fields. Moreover, the infinitesimal subgroup M is exactly the set of elements whose valuation is positive, so M is definable in the pure valued field language. Adding the predicate for M does not increase the definable sets beyond those already definable with the valuation ring, but it makes the valuation ring itself definable without parameters. The structure is NIP but not o‑minimal; the set M is an infinite convex definable set that is not a finite union of intervals. Nevertheless, a cell decomposition theorem holds where cells are defined using the valuation, the derivation, and the predicate M. This decomposition is the basis for a cylindrical algebraic decomposition algorithm that works over differential‑valued real closed fields.

An important consequence is that the theory of (R,∂,M) is the model companion of the theory of ordered differential fields with a convex valuation ideal. The existentially closed models are precisely the differential real closed fields with a contractive valuation such that the derivation is small (i.e. ∂(M) ⊆ M) and the residue field is differentially closed as a differential field. The value group remains a pure divisible ordered abelian group, and the derivation on it is trivial. This description allows one to transfer results from the theory of differentially closed fields of characteristic zero to the valued setting, in particular the trichotomy for minimal types and the analysis of the binding group.

Ordered Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subring and the Baer–Krull Correspondence

Let F be an ordered field (not necessarily real closed) and let O be a convex subring of F. The predicate for O defines a convex valuation v on F whose valuation ring is O. The Baer–Krull theorem describes the set X(F) of orderings of F that are compatible with v in terms of the orderings of the residue field k = O/M and the group of square classes Γ/2Γ of the value group Γ. When O is not the contractive valuation ring, the residue field k inherits a non‑trivial convex valuation, and the correspondence must be iterated. The space of orderings X(F) becomes a profinite space that fibers over X(k) with fibers isomorphic to the space of homomorphisms Γ/2Γ → {±1}. Adding a predicate for O to the language of ordered fields yields a structure (F,O) whose theory is model complete in the language with a cross‑section and an angular component map, provided F is real closed. For general ordered fields, the theory of (F,O) is not model complete, but the existential theory is decidable via a variant of cylindrical algebraic decomposition that respects the valuation.

The convexity of O implies that the ordering on F induces an ordering on the residue field k and a compatible ordering on the value group Γ. The Baer–Krull correspondence is functorial: a morphism of valued ordered fields induces a continuous map on the spaces of orderings. When F is real closed, the space X(F) is a singleton, and the correspondence reduces to the statement that the unique ordering of F makes O convex. For non‑real‑closed fields, the correspondence provides a powerful tool to construct orderings with prescribed convex valuation rings. In particular, given an ordering of k and a sign choice on Γ/2Γ, there exists a unique ordering of F making O convex and inducing the given data. This construction is effective when k and Γ are computable.

Applications include the study of the real spectrum of polynomial rings over valued fields. The real spectrum of F[x] can be stratified according to the valuation of the polynomial, and the Baer–Krull correspondence gives a description of the fibers in terms of the real spectra of the residue field and the value group. This stratification underlies the algorithmic computation of sign conditions for polynomials over valued fields, which is a key step in the decision procedure for the existential theory of real closed valued fields. The convex subring predicate also appears naturally in the study of Hardy fields, where the valuation ring of germs of functions bounded by a polynomial is a convex subring of the Hardy field.

Real Closed Fields and the Theory of Pairs with a Generic Derivation

A pair of real closed fields is a structure (R, K) where R is a real closed field and K ≺ R is a proper elementary subfield. The theory of pairs is model complete in the language with a predicate for K, and it admits quantifier elimination after adding a predicate for the convex hull of K. When a generic derivation ∂ is added to R such that ∂(K) ⊆ K and the restriction ∂|_K is also generic, one obtains a differential pair (R, K, ∂). The theory of differential pairs is the model companion of the theory of ordered differential fields with a distinguished differential subfield. It is model complete in the language L = {+,·,<,∂,K} and eliminates quantifiers after adding a predicate for the valuation ring of the contractive valuation and a cross‑section. The fixed field C = {x ∈ R : ∂(x) = 0} is a real closed subfield containing the fixed field of ∂|_K, and the pairs (R, C) and (K, C ∩ K) are elementary pairs of real closed fields.

The value group of the contractive valuation on R is a divisible ordered abelian group with trivial derivation, and the residue field k is a real closed field equipped with the induced derivation ∂_k. The pair (k, res(K)) is a differential pair of real closed fields. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds for differential pairs: two differential pairs are elementarily equivalent iff their value groups (as ordered groups) and their residue differential pairs are elementarily equivalent. This reduces the model theory of differential pairs to the model theory of differential real closed fields and pure ordered abelian groups. The theory is NIP but not o‑minimal; the predicate K defines an infinite dense codense subset, and the derivation adds a further layer of complexity.

One of the main applications is the transfer of results from the theory of dense pairs of real closed fields to differential fields. For example, the open core of a differential pair (the structure induced on the set of points where the derivation is non‑zero) is exactly the differential field structure. This allows one to use the cell decomposition for dense pairs to analyze definable sets in differential pairs. The theory also provides a framework for the model‑theoretic study of transseries fields with a distinguished subfield of grid‑based transseries, where the derivation is the usual derivation on transseries and the subfield is closed under the derivation.

  • Confusing the contractive valuation with an arbitrary convex valuation; the contractive valuation is the unique finest convex valuation and is definable without parameters.
  • Assuming that a generic derivation on a valued real closed field automatically preserves every convex subring; it only preserves the valuation ring if the valuation is invariant under the derivation.
  • Treating the value group as a field; it is an ordered abelian group, not a ring, and the derivation on it is forced to be trivial.
  • Believing that adding a predicate for a dense subfield preserves o‑minimality; the predicate defines an infinite discrete set, destroying o‑minimality.
  • Overlooking that the Baer–Krull correspondence requires the valuation ring to be convex; without convexity the map between orderings fails.
  • Neglecting that the cross‑section in a differential‑valued field can be chosen differential only when the derivation on the value group is trivial, which is always the case in the contractive setting.
  • Remember that the distinction between contractive and non‑contractive valuations determines whether the expanded structure remains o‑minimal or merely NIP.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Derivation and a Predicate for the Standard Part Map

Let R be a real closed field equipped with a generic derivation ∂. In nonstandard models of real closed fields (for example, ultrapowers of the real numbers) there exists a canonical external map st : Rfin → ℝ sending each finite element to its standard part. When a unary predicate St is added to the language to name the graph of this map restricted to the finite subring, the resulting structure (R, ∂, St) has been studied in the model theory of differential fields. The theory of such expansions is model complete in the language L = {+,·, <, ∂, St} after adding a predicate for the convex hull of the constant field C = {x ∈ R : ∂(x)=0}. Quantifier elimination holds relative to the induced structure on the residue field of the natural valuation associated with the convex subring of finite elements. The standard part map is a retraction onto the constant field and respects the derivation in the sense that st(∂(x)) = 0 for every finite x. This forces the derivation to be infinitesimally small on the finite part, a property that characterises the generic derivation on a real closed valued field with a contractive valuation. The interplay between the derivation and the standard part predicate yields a rich definable set structure: the set of points where ∂ vanishes is exactly the constant field, which is a real closed subfield; the set where St is defined is a convex subring; and the valuation ring of the contractive valuation is definable without parameters. These facts are used to transfer results from the theory of dense pairs of real closed fields to differential fields, because the pair (R, C) is a dense pair and the derivation adds a further layer of complexity that is tame in the sense of NIP (non‑independence property). The theory is not o‑minimal, since the predicate St defines an infinite discrete set, but it remains NIP and admits a cell decomposition theorem relative to the induced structure on the residue field. Applications include the model‑theoretic analysis of Hardy fields of transseries, where the standard part map corresponds to taking the constant term of a transseries, and the derivation is the usual derivation on transseries.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Automorphism and a Predicate for the Infinitesimal Subgroup

Consider a real closed field R equipped with a generic automorphism σ (i.e., a model of the theory of difference real closed fields). The infinitesimal subgroup I = {x ∈ R : |x| < 1/n for all n ∈ ℕ} is a convex additive subgroup of R. Adding a unary predicate Inf for I yields the structure (R, σ, Inf). The theory of such expansions is the model companion of the theory of ordered difference fields with a distinguished convex subgroup. It is model complete in the language L = {+,·, <, σ, Inf} after adding a predicate for the fixed field Fix(σ) = {x : σ(x)=x}. The fixed field is a real closed subfield, and the automorphism acts as a shift on the value group of the natural valuation whose valuation ring is the convex hull of ℤ. The predicate Inf defines the maximal ideal of this valuation ring. The interaction between σ and Inf is governed by the condition that σ preserves the valuation ring and induces the identity on the residue field; equivalently, σ acts trivially on the value group. This forces the automorphism to be “infinitesimally close” to the identity, a property that characterises generic automorphisms on real closed valued fields with a contractive valuation. The theory is NIP but not o‑minimal; the predicate Inf defines an infinite codense set. A cell decomposition theorem holds relative to the induced structure on the residue field, which is a real closed field equipped with the induced automorphism (trivial on the residue field). The model theory of these structures provides a framework for studying difference equations on Hardy fields and for analysing the asymptotic behaviour of solutions to differential‑difference equations. In particular, the fixed field corresponds to the field of constants of the difference equation, and the infinitesimal subgroup captures the error terms that tend to zero.

Worked Example: Definability of the Valuation Ring
Let (R, σ, Inf) be a real closed field with a generic automorphism and a predicate for the infinitesimal subgroup. Show that the valuation ring O = {x ∈ R : |x| ≤ n for some n ∈ ℕ} is definable in this structure.
The valuation ring O is the convex hull of ℤ in R. In the language with Inf, an element x belongs to O iff x is not infinitesimally large, i.e., there is no y ∈ Inf such that x·y > 1. Equivalently, x ∈ O ⇔ ¬∃y (Inf(y) ∧ x·y > 1). Since Inf is a predicate, this is a first‑order definition. The automorphism σ preserves O because it fixes the value group, so the definition is invariant under σ. Thus O is definable without parameters.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for definability of a convex subring in an expanded real closed field, first identify the natural valuation (contractive or the one given by the infinitesimal subgroup). Then express membership in the valuation ring by a first‑order formula using the predicates available (e.g., Inf, St, or a cross‑section). Remember that generic automorphisms and derivations preserve the contractive valuation ring, so the definition will be invariant under the extra structure.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Derivation and a Predicate for the Convex Subring

Let R be a real closed field with a generic derivation ∂ and let O be a proper convex subring of R (i.e., a valuation ring of a convex valuation). Adding a unary predicate Cvx for O yields the structure (R, ∂, Cvx). The theory of such expansions is the model companion of the theory of ordered differential fields with a distinguished convex subring. It is model complete in the language L = {+,·, <, ∂, Cvx} after adding a predicate for the constant field C = {x : ∂(x)=0}. The convex subring O is not necessarily the valuation ring of the contractive valuation; it can be any convex valuation ring. The derivation ∂ preserves O if and only if the valuation is invariant under ∂, which is equivalent to the condition that the induced derivation on the value group is trivial. In the generic setting, the derivation is chosen so that it preserves the given convex subring, and the induced derivation on the residue field makes the residue field a differential real closed field. The pair (R, O) is a dense pair of real closed fields when O is the valuation ring of the contractive valuation; for a general convex subring the pair is a “convex pair”. The theory admits quantifier elimination relative to the induced structure on the residue field and the value group (as an ordered abelian group with trivial derivation). The model‑theoretic properties (NIP, dp‑minimality) depend on whether the convex subring is the contractive valuation ring. If it is, the theory is NIP but not o‑minimal; if it is a coarser convex subring, the theory can be o‑minimal after naming the subring, because the subring then defines a convex subset that is a finite union of intervals. Applications include the study of differential equations with asymptotic constraints, where the convex subring encodes a growth condition (e.g., functions bounded by a polynomial). The generic derivation ensures that the differential field is existentially closed among differential fields with the same convex subring, providing a robust framework for transferring algebraic‑geometric results to the differential setting.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Derivation and a Predicate for the Residue Field and a Cross‑Section

Let R be a real closed field equipped with a generic derivation ∂ and a contractive valuation v with valuation ring O, maximal ideal M, residue field k = O/M, and value group Γ. A cross‑section is a multiplicative homomorphism χ : Γ → R× such that v(χ(γ)) = γ for all γ ∈ Γ. Adding predicates for the residue field k (via the quotient map) and for the cross‑section χ yields the structure (R, ∂, k, χ). The theory of such expansions is the model companion of the theory of differential valued real closed fields with a distinguished cross‑section. It is model complete in the language L = {+,·, <, ∂, res, χ} where res is a unary function symbol for the residue map (partial, defined on O) and χ is a function symbol on the value group sort. The derivation ∂ preserves the valuation ring O and induces a derivation ∂k on the residue field k; the cross‑section can be chosen to be differential (i.e., ∂(χ(γ)) = 0) because the derivation on the value group is forced to be trivial. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: two such structures are elementarily equivalent iff their value groups (as ordered abelian groups) and their residue differential fields are elementarily equivalent. This reduces the model theory to the combination of pure ordered abelian groups and differential real closed fields. The theory is NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition. The presence of the cross‑section allows one to lift definable sets from the residue field and the value group to the valued field, which is crucial for algorithmic applications such as cylindrical algebraic decomposition over valued fields. In the context of Hardy fields, the cross‑section corresponds to choosing a representative for each asymptotic scale (e.g., powers of x), and the derivation is the usual derivative. The generic derivation ensures that the differential field is existentially closed among differential valued fields with the same residue differential field and value group.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Automorphism and a Predicate for the Value Group

Let R be a real closed field with a generic automorphism σ and a contractive valuation v with value group Γ. Adding a predicate for the value group (i.e., a sort for Γ with the valuation map v : R× → Γ) yields the structure (R, σ, Γ). The theory of such expansions is the model companion of the theory of ordered difference fields with a distinguished valuation whose value group is an ordered abelian group. It is model complete in the language L = {+,·, <, σ, v} after adding a predicate for the fixed field Fix(σ). The automorphism σ preserves the valuation ring and induces the identity on the value group (i.e., v(σ(x)) = v(x) for all x). Consequently, σ acts trivially on Γ. The residue field k inherits an automorphism σk which is generic on the real closed field k. The pair (k, σk) is a model of the theory of difference real closed fields. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: two such structures are elementarily equivalent iff their value groups (as ordered abelian groups) and their residue difference fields are elementarily equivalent. The theory is NIP but not o‑minimal; the valuation map defines an infinite discrete set of fibers. A relative cell decomposition theorem holds, allowing one to describe definable sets in terms of cells over the residue field and the value group. This framework is used to study difference equations on valued fields, for instance in the analysis of q‑difference equations where the automorphism is σ(x) = q·x and the valuation measures the order of growth. The generic automorphism ensures that the difference field is existentially closed among difference fields with the same valuation, providing a model‑theoretic foundation for the asymptotic theory of difference equations.

  • Confusing the contractive valuation with an arbitrary convex valuation; the contractive valuation is the unique finest convex valuation and is definable without parameters.
  • Assuming that a generic derivation on a valued real closed field automatically preserves every convex subring; it only preserves the valuation ring if the valuation is invariant under the derivation.
  • Treating the value group as a field; it is an ordered abelian group, not a ring, and the derivation on it is forced to be trivial.
  • Believing that adding a predicate for a dense subfield preserves o‑minimality; the predicate defines an infinite discrete set, destroying o‑minimality.
  • Overlooking that the Baer–Krull correspondence requires the valuation ring to be convex; without convexity the map between orderings fails.
  • Neglecting that the cross‑section in a differential‑valued field can be chosen differential only when the derivation on the value group is trivial, which is always the case in the contractive setting.
  • Assuming that the standard part map is definable in the pure field language; it requires a predicate for the finite subring or the infinitesimal subgroup.

These advanced topics illustrate how extra structure — derivations, automorphisms, valuations, and predicates for convex subrings, infinitesimals, residue fields, and value groups — interacts with the order and algebraic properties of real closed fields, and they form the core of modern model‑theoretic real algebraic geometry.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for the Value Group and a Cross‑Section

Let R be a real closed field equipped with a convex valuation v : R× → Γ ∪ {∞} whose value group Γ is an ordered abelian group. Adding a predicate for the value group means introducing a new sort for Γ together with the valuation map v. A cross‑section is a group homomorphism χ : Γ → R× such that v(χ(γ)) = γ for all γ ∈ Γ. The structure (R, Γ, v, χ) is a valued real closed field with a distinguished cross‑section. The theory of such structures is the model companion of the theory of ordered valued fields with a cross‑section; it is model complete in the three‑sorted language {+,·,0,1, ≤, v, χ} where the field sort carries the ordered field language, the value‑group sort carries the ordered abelian group language, and the cross‑section is a function symbol from the value‑group sort to the field sort.

The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: two such structures are elementarily equivalent iff their value groups (as ordered abelian groups) and their residue fields (as real closed fields) are elementarily equivalent. Because the cross‑section splits the valuation exact sequence, every definable subset of the field can be described by a Boolean combination of conditions on the value group and the residue field. This yields a relative quantifier elimination down to the two sorts. The theory is NIP (it does not have the independence property) but it is not o‑minimal: the valuation map defines an infinite discrete family of fibres. A relative cell decomposition theorem holds, allowing one to partition definable sets into cells whose projections are definable in the residue field and the value group. The cross‑section can be chosen to be a group embedding, and any two cross‑sections differ by a multiplicative factor from the valuation ring’s unit group. In applications to real algebraic geometry, the cross‑section corresponds to choosing a representative for each asymptotic scale (for example, powers of a fixed infinitesimal), which is essential for lifting semi‑algebraic sets from the residue field to the valued field.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for the Residue Field and a Cross‑Section

In this expansion the residue field k = O / 𝔪 (where O is the valuation ring and 𝔪 its maximal ideal) is given as a separate sort together with the residue map res : O → k. The cross‑section χ : Γ → R× again splits the valuation. The three‑sorted structure (R, Γ, k, v, res, χ) has a language containing the ordered field language on R, the ordered abelian group language on Γ, the real closed field language on k, the valuation map v, the residue map res, and the cross‑section χ. The theory is the model companion of the theory of ordered valued fields with a distinguished residue field and a cross‑section; it is model complete in this language.

The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle again reduces elementary equivalence to that of the value group and the residue field. Because the cross‑section provides a definable lifting of the value group into the field, every definable set in the field sort is a finite Boolean combination of sets defined by conditions on the value group and on the residue field. The valuation ring O is convex, and the residue map is a surjective ring homomorphism whose kernel is the infinitesimal subgroup 𝔪. The cross‑section can be chosen so that χ(Γ) ⊆ O×, i.e. its image consists of units. This ensures that the valuation of any element of the cross‑section is exactly the corresponding value‑group element. The theory is NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition: any definable subset of Rⁿ can be partitioned into cells whose projections are definable in Γ and k. This framework is used in the study of real spectra of valued fields, where the cross‑section allows one to transfer sign conditions from the residue field to the valued field, and in algorithmic real algebraic geometry for cylindrical algebraic decomposition over valued fields.

Model‑Theoretic Transfer via Cross‑Section
Let (R, v, χ) be a real closed field with a convex valuation v and a cross‑section χ : Γ → R×. Let k be the residue field. Show that for any definable subset D ⊆ k (in the language of real closed fields) there exists a definable subset D̃ ⊆ R such that res(D̃ ∩ O) = D.
Because χ splits the valuation, every element x ∈ R can be written uniquely as x = χ(v(x))·u with u ∈ O×. The residue map res : O → k is a ring homomorphism. Given a formula φ(y) defining D in k, replace each occurrence of a variable y by res(z) where z is a new variable ranging over O. The resulting formula ψ(z) defines a subset of O. Since χ is definable, the condition v(z) = 0 (i.e. z ∈ O) is definable. Thus the set D̃ = {z ∈ O : ψ(z)} is definable in R and satisfies res(D̃) = D. The cross‑section guarantees that the valuation of any element of O is ≥ 0, so the construction works uniformly.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem presents a valued real closed field with both a cross‑section and a predicate for the residue field, immediately note that the valuation splits. This means the theory reduces to the pure theories of the value group and the residue field. Use this reduction to eliminate quantifiers over the field sort by translating them into quantifiers over the two simpler sorts. In particular, any definable set in the field is a Boolean combination of pull‑backs of definable sets from the residue field and the value group.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Automorphism and a Cross‑Section

Let (R, v, χ) be as above and let σ be an automorphism of the ordered field R that preserves the valuation ring O (hence v(σ(x)) = v(x) for all x) and commutes with the cross‑section: σ(χ(γ)) = χ(γ) for all γ ∈ Γ. Such an automorphism is called generic if the difference field (R, σ) is existentially closed among difference fields with the same valuation and cross‑section. The induced map on the value group is the identity because σ fixes χ(Γ) pointwise and v∘σ = v. The residue field k inherits an automorphism σₖ defined by σₖ(res(x)) = res(σ(x)) for x ∈ O; σₖ is generic on the real closed field k. The three‑sorted structure (R, Γ, k, v, res, χ, σ) has a language extending the previous one by a unary function symbol σ on the field sort. The theory of such structures is the model companion of the theory of ordered difference valued fields with a cross‑section; it is model complete in this language.

The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: elementary equivalence is determined by the elementary equivalence of the value group (as an ordered abelian group) and the residue difference field (k, σₖ). The theory is NIP but not o‑minimal; the valuation fibres give an infinite discrete set. A relative cell decomposition theorem holds, allowing definable sets to be described by cells over Γ and (k, σₖ). This framework is used to study q‑difference equations on valued fields: taking σ(x) = q·x with q an infinitesimal gives a contractive automorphism, and the cross‑section corresponds to choosing a representative for each asymptotic scale. The generic automorphism ensures that the difference field is existentially closed, providing a model‑theoretic foundation for the asymptotic theory of difference equations.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Derivation and a Predicate for the Infinitesimal Subgroup

Consider a real closed field R with a convex valuation v, valuation ring O, and maximal ideal 𝔪 (the infinitesimal subgroup). Let ∂ be a derivation on R that preserves O (so ∂(O) ⊆ O) and induces a derivation ∂ₖ on the residue field k = O/𝔪. Adding a predicate for the infinitesimal subgroup means introducing a new sort for 𝔪 together with the inclusion map 𝔪 → R. The derivation on the value group Γ is forced to be trivial because v(∂(x)) ≥ v(x) for all x and the valuation is convex; hence ∂ acts trivially on Γ. The structure (R, Γ, k, 𝔪, v, res, ∂) is a differential valued real closed field with a distinguished infinitesimal subgroup. Its theory is the model companion of the theory of ordered differential valued fields with a predicate for the infinitesimals; it is model complete in the language with sorts for R, Γ, k, 𝔪, the valuation, residue, and derivation symbols.

The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle again reduces elementary equivalence to that of the value group (as an ordered abelian group) and the residue differential field (k, ∂ₖ). The infinitesimal subgroup 𝔪 is a convex additive subgroup of R, and the derivation ∂ maps 𝔪 into 𝔪 because ∂ preserves O and the valuation. The theory is NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition. In the context of Hardy fields, the infinitesimal subgroup corresponds to the set of germs of functions tending to zero, and the derivation is the usual derivative. The generic derivation ensures that the differential field is existentially closed among differential valued fields with the same residue differential field and value group, which is crucial for the model‑theoretic analysis of asymptotic differential equations and transseries.

Real Closed Fields with a Generic Automorphism and a Predicate for the Standard Part Map

Let (R, v) be a real closed field with a convex valuation, valuation ring O, and residue field k. The standard part map st : O → k is the canonical projection modulo the infinitesimal subgroup 𝔪. Adding a predicate for the standard part map means introducing a function symbol st from the field sort to the residue‑field sort, defined on O and arbitrary elsewhere. Let σ be an automorphism of R that preserves O and commutes with st: st(σ(x)) = σₖ(st(x)) for all x ∈ O, where σₖ is the induced automorphism on k. The automorphism σ is generic if the difference field (R, σ) is existentially closed among difference fields with the same valuation and standard part map. The structure (R, k, v, st, σ) has sorts for R and k, the valuation map v, the standard part map st, and the automorphism σ. Its theory is the model companion of the theory of ordered difference valued fields with a standard part map; it is model complete in this language.

The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: two such structures are elementarily equivalent iff their residue difference fields (k, σₖ) are elementarily equivalent (the value group is determined by the valuation and is an ordered abelian group with trivial σ‑action). The standard part map is a ring homomorphism whose kernel is 𝔪, and it splits the exact sequence 0 → 𝔪 → O → k → 0 when a cross‑section is present; here the predicate for st provides a definable splitting without requiring a cross‑section. The theory is NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition. This expansion is used in nonstandard analysis to model the standard part map internally, and in the study of difference equations on valued fields where the standard part map captures the “finite part” of a solution.

  • Confusing the cross‑section with a splitting of the valuation exact sequence; a cross‑section is a group homomorphism from the value group to the multiplicative group of the field, not a ring homomorphism.
  • Assuming that a generic automorphism must act non‑trivially on the value group; in the presence of a cross‑section it acts trivially because it fixes the image of the cross‑section.
  • Treating the infinitesimal subgroup as an ideal of the whole field; it is only an ideal of the valuation ring and is not closed under multiplication by arbitrary field elements.
  • Believing that the standard part map is definable in the pure field language; it requires a predicate for the valuation ring or the infinitesimal subgroup.
  • Overlooking that the derivation on the value group is forced to be trivial in any convex valuation preserved by the derivation.
  • Neglecting that the Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle for these expansions requires the valuation to be convex and the residue field to be real closed.
  • These traps highlight the subtle interplay between valuation, derivation, and automorphism in expanded real closed fields.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subring and a Generic Automorphism

Let R be a real closed field equipped with a convex subring O (i.e. a subring such that for any a,b ∈ O with a ≤ x ≤ b one has x ∈ O). The convex subring determines a convex valuation v on R with valuation ring O, maximal ideal 𝔪 and residue field k = O/𝔪. A generic automorphism σ of R is an automorphism of the ordered field that preserves O and such that the difference field (R,σ) is existentially closed among all ordered difference fields with the same convex subring. The automorphism induces an automorphism σₖ on the residue field k and acts trivially on the value group Γ because it fixes the image of any cross‑section of v (when a cross‑section exists) and more generally because σ preserves the valuation.

The first‑order theory of the structure (R, O, σ) in the language with a predicate for O and a function symbol for σ is the model companion of the theory of ordered difference fields with a convex subring. It is model complete, NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: two such structures are elementarily equivalent iff their residue difference fields (k, σₖ) are elementarily equivalent and their value groups (as ordered abelian groups) are elementarily equivalent. This reduction is crucial for the model‑theoretic analysis of difference equations on valued real closed fields and for the study of asymptotic difference equations in Hardy fields.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subring and a Generic Derivation

Again let R be a real closed field with a convex subring O defining a convex valuation v. A generic derivation ∂ on R is a derivation that preserves O (so ∂(O) ⊆ O) and such that the differential field (R,∂) is existentially closed among ordered differential fields with the same convex subring. The derivation induces a derivation ∂ₖ on the residue field k = O/𝔪 and, because the valuation is convex and preserved by ∂, the induced derivation on the value group Γ is forced to be trivial: v(∂(x)) ≥ v(x) for all x implies ∂ acts as zero on Γ.

The theory of (R, O, ∂) in the language with a predicate for O and a function symbol for ∂ is the model companion of the theory of ordered differential valued fields with a convex subring. It is model complete, NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle again reduces elementary equivalence to that of the residue differential field (k, ∂ₖ) and the value group Γ. This framework underlies the model‑theoretic treatment of asymptotic differential equations, transseries and Hardy fields, where the infinitesimal subgroup 𝔪 corresponds to germs of functions tending to zero and the derivation is the usual derivative.

Model‑theoretic transfer via Ax–Kochen–Ershov
Given two real closed fields R₁, R₂ each equipped with a convex subring and a generic derivation, explain why elementary equivalence of the full structures reduces to elementary equivalence of the residue differential fields and the value groups.
The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle for valued differential fields states that the theory of a valued differential field is determined by the theory of its residue differential field and its value group, provided the valuation is convex and the derivation preserves the valuation ring. In our setting the convex subring O is exactly the valuation ring of a convex valuation v. The generic derivation ∂ preserves O, so it induces a derivation ∂ₖ on the residue field k = O/𝔪 and acts trivially on the value group Γ. The language contains a predicate for O and a symbol for ∂; the valuation map v and the residue map are interpretable. By the relative quantifier elimination proved for this theory (see e.g. van den Dries–Macintyre–Marker), any formula is equivalent to a Boolean combination of formulas referring only to the residue differential field sort and the value group sort. Consequently two such structures are elementarily equivalent iff their residue differential fields (k₁, ∂ₖ₁), (k₂, ∂ₖ₂) are elementarily equivalent and their value groups Γ₁, Γ₂ are elementarily equivalent as ordered abelian groups.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the model‑theoretic classification of an expansion of a real closed field, first identify the base valued field structure (convex subring → valuation). Then check which extra operators (automorphism, derivation, standard part map) are added and whether they are required to be generic. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov reduction almost always applies: the theory splits into a residue‑field part and a value‑group part. Cite the genericity condition and the convexity of the valuation as the key hypotheses that guarantee model completeness and NIP.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subring and a Standard Part Map

Let R be a real closed field with a convex subring O and maximal ideal 𝔪. The standard part map st : O → k = O/𝔪 is the canonical projection modulo 𝔪. Adding a predicate for st means introducing a function symbol from the field sort to the residue‑field sort, defined on O and arbitrary elsewhere. The kernel of st is exactly 𝔪, and st is a ring homomorphism that splits the exact sequence 0 → 𝔪 → O → k → 0 when a cross‑section for the valuation is present; here the predicate for st provides a definable splitting without requiring a cross‑section.

The theory of (R, O, st) in the language with a predicate for O and a function symbol for st is the model companion of the theory of ordered valued fields with a standard part map. It is model complete, NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: elementary equivalence is determined by the residue field k (as a real closed field) and the value group Γ. This expansion is used in nonstandard analysis to internalise the standard part map and in the study of valued fields where the “finite part” of an element is needed definably.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subring and a Dense Subfield

Consider a real closed field R with a convex subring O and a distinguished subfield K that is dense in R with respect to the order topology (equivalently, dense in the valuation topology induced by O). The pair (R, K) is a dense pair of real closed fields. The convex subring O is the valuation ring of the convex valuation whose valuation ideal is the set of infinitesimals relative to K. The theory of dense pairs in the language with a predicate for K and a predicate for O is model complete and NIP; it admits a relative cell decomposition. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle again reduces elementary equivalence to that of the residue field of O and the value group, together with the induced dense pair structure on the residue field.

This framework, developed by van den Dries and others, provides a model‑theoretic foundation for o‑minimal expansions of the real field by a dense independent set. It also connects with the theory of T‑convex subrings and the real spectrum of valued real closed fields. Applications include the study of definable sets in expansions of the real field by a predicate for a dense subfield and the analysis of asymptotic scales in Hardy fields where the dense subfield corresponds to a field of germs of functions with a given growth rate.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subring and a Generic Automorphism and a Derivation

Let R be a real closed field with a convex subring O. Equip R with a generic automorphism σ and a generic derivation ∂ that commute (σ∘∂ = ∂∘σ) and both preserve O. The automorphism induces σₖ on the residue field k = O/𝔪 and acts trivially on the value group Γ; the derivation induces ∂ₖ on k and also acts trivially on Γ. The structure (R, O, σ, ∂) is a difference‑differential valued real closed field with a distinguished convex subring.

The theory of this structure in the language with predicates for O, function symbols for σ and ∂ is the model companion of the theory of ordered difference‑differential valued fields with a convex subring. It is model complete, NIP and admits a relative cell decomposition. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: elementary equivalence is determined by the residue difference‑differential field (k, σₖ, ∂ₖ) and the value group Γ. This combined expansion is relevant for the model‑theoretic analysis of asymptotic difference‑differential equations, for the study of transseries with both derivation and automorphism (e.g. the field of logarithmic‑exponential transseries with the shift automorphism), and for the investigation of Hardy fields closed under both differentiation and composition.

  • Confusing a convex subring with a valuation ring; a convex subring need not be integrally closed and therefore may not be a valuation ring.
  • Assuming a generic automorphism must act non‑trivially on the value group; in the presence of a convex subring it acts trivially because it fixes the valuation.
  • Treating the standard part map as definable in the pure field language; it requires a predicate for the convex subring or the infinitesimal ideal.
  • Overlooking that any derivation preserving a convex valuation forces the induced derivation on the value group to be trivial.
  • Neglecting that the dense pair theory requires the subfield to be dense in the valuation topology and the convex subring to be the associated valuation ring.
  • Mixing up model completeness of the expanded structure with that of the pure real closed field; the added predicates change the language and the theory.

Real Closed Fields and the Theory of O‑Minimal Structures with a Generic Convex Subring and a Generic Automorphism

Let R be a real closed field equipped with a convex subring O (the valuation ring of a convex valuation v) and a generic automorphism σ that preserves O. The pair (R, O) is a valued real closed field; the automorphism induces the identity on the value group Γ because any convex valuation is fixed by an order‑preserving field automorphism. The residue field k = O/𝔪 inherits an automorphism σk and remains real closed. The three‑sorted structure (R, O, σ) in the language with a predicate for O and a function symbol for σ is the model companion of the theory of ordered valued fields with a distinguished automorphism preserving the valuation ring. It is model complete, NIP, and admits a relative cell decomposition: every definable set in the field sort is a finite Boolean combination of cells whose boundaries are definable using the valuation and the automorphism. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: elementary equivalence of two such structures is determined by the elementary equivalence of the residue difference fields (k, σk) and the value groups Γ (as ordered abelian groups). This expansion is used to analyse asymptotic difference equations in Hardy fields where the automorphism corresponds to a shift operator, and to study transseries fields equipped with a composition automorphism that respects the natural valuation.

Model‑theoretic consequences

Because the theory is model complete, every embedding of models is elementary. The NIP property implies that no formula has the independence property, which yields uniform finiteness for families of definable sets. Relative cell decomposition provides a geometric description of definable sets analogous to the classical cylindrical algebraic decomposition but now taking the valuation and the automorphism into account. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces the classification problem to the well‑understood theories of real closed difference fields and ordered abelian groups.

Applications to asymptotic analysis

In the study of Hardy fields closed under composition, the convex subring consists of germs bounded by some real number, and the automorphism is the shift f(x) ↦ f(x+1). The valued difference field captures the growth rates of functions and their translates. The model‑theoretic tools above give a uniform way to decide asymptotic equivalence of definable functions and to prove o‑minimality of the resulting expansion.

Ordered Modules over Real Closed Rings and the Hahn Embedding Theorem for Modules

Let A be a real closed ring (an f‑ring that is a lattice‑ordered ring in which every positive element is a square and every polynomial of odd degree has a root). An A‑module M equipped with a translation‑invariant partial order compatible with the lattice operations on A is called an ordered A‑module. The Hahn embedding theorem for ordered modules states that every ordered A‑module M embeds as an ordered submodule of a Hahn product AΓ = { f : Γ → A | supp(f) is well‑ordered } where Γ is a totally ordered set (the value set of M). The embedding is constructed by assigning to each element m ∈ M its “leading term” map v(m) ∈ Γ and the corresponding coefficient in A. The image is a submodule closed under the pointwise lattice operations, and the order on M coincides with the lexicographic order induced by Γ.

Riesz interpolation and projectable hulls

The Riesz interpolation property holds in any ordered module over a real closed ring: for any finite sets {xi}, {yj} with xi ≤ yj there exists z such that xi ≤ z ≤ yj. This property is essential for the construction of the projectable hull of M, which coincides with the smallest projectable ordered module containing M. The projectable hull can be identified with the submodule of the Hahn product consisting of functions with finite support, and it inherits the lattice structure from A.

Finitely generated modules

If M is finitely generated as an A‑module, the value set Γ can be taken finite. In this case the Hahn product reduces to a finite direct product An with the lexicographic order determined by a chain of convex submodules. This yields a concrete classification: every finitely generated ordered module over a real closed ring is isomorphic to a lexicographic sum of copies of A indexed by a finite chain. The result generalises the classical Hahn embedding for ordered abelian groups (where A = ℤ) and for ordered vector spaces over a real closed field (where A is a field).

Technique: Embedding a finitely generated ordered module into a finite Hahn product
Let A be the real closed field ℝ and let M = ℝ² with the lexicographic order: (a,b) ≤ (c,d) iff a < c or (a = c and b ≤ d). Show that M embeds as an ordered ℝ‑module into the finite Hahn product ℝ² with the same lexicographic order.
Define the value set Γ = {1,2} with 1 < 2. For (a,b) ∈ ℝ² set its leading term at 2 to be a and at 1 to be b. The map φ : ℝ² → ℝΓ given by φ(a,b)(2)=a, φ(a,b)(1)=b is an ℝ‑linear injection. The order on ℝΓ is lexicographic: f < g iff the largest index where they differ has f(γ) < g(γ). This coincides exactly with the given order on ℝ². Hence φ is an ordered module embedding.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for an explicit Hahn embedding of a finitely generated ordered module, first identify a finite chain of convex submodules that refines the given order. The length of the chain gives the size of the value set Γ. Then write each generator by its successive “leading coefficients” along the chain; the resulting tuple is the image in the finite Hahn product. This algorithm works uniformly for modules over any real closed ring.

Real Algebraic Geometry and the Real Spectrum of Non‑Noetherian Rings

The real spectrum Sper(A) of a commutative ring A (not necessarily Noetherian) is the set of all orderings of the residue fields of prime ideals of A, equipped with the spectral (Harrison) topology and the constructible topology. Points correspond to pairs (𝔭, ≤) where 𝔭 ∈ Spec(A) and ≤ is an ordering of the field of fractions of A/𝔭. The constructible sets are finite Boolean combinations of basic open sets D(a) = { α ∈ Sper(A) | α(a) > 0 }. The real Nullstellensatz holds in this generality: for any ideal I ⊆ A, the real radical √rI consists of all f ∈ A such that f is non‑negative on every ordering containing I. This characterisation is the foundation of the Positivstellensatz for arbitrary rings.

Constructible sets and semi‑algebraic geometry

When A is a finitely generated ℝ‑algebra, the constructible subsets of Sper(A) correspond exactly to the semi‑algebraic subsets of the real variety defined by A. For non‑Noetherian rings (e.g., rings of smooth functions or rings of bounded continuous functions), the real spectrum still captures the order‑theoretic information, but the constructible topology may fail to be compact. Nevertheless, the Tarski–Seidenberg theorem extends: the projection of a constructible set is constructible. This is proved by reducing to the Noetherian case via the model‑theoretic compactness of the theory of real closed fields.

Applications to quadratic forms and the Witt ring

The real spectrum classifies the orderings of a field, and the map from the Witt ring W(A) of quadratic forms over A to the ring of continuous integer‑valued functions on Sper(A) is injective. For non‑Noetherian rings this injectivity still holds, providing a powerful tool to study quadratic forms over rings of functions. The signature of a quadratic form at an ordering is a locally constant function on the real spectrum, and the Witt ring embeds into the ring of such signatures.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subfield and a Generic Derivation

Let R be a real closed field equipped with a convex subfield K (i.e., K is a subfield and for any a ∈ K and b ∈ R with 0 ≤ b ≤ a we have b ∈ K) and a generic derivation ∂ that preserves K (∂(K) ⊆ K). The convex subfield K is the valuation ring of a convex valuation v on R whose valuation ideal consists of the infinitesimals relative to K. The derivation induces a derivation ∂k on the residue field k = K/𝔪 and acts trivially on the value group Γ because any derivation preserving a convex valuation must satisfy ∂(v(x)) = 0. The three‑sorted structure (R, K, ∂) in the language with a predicate for K and a function symbol for ∂ is the model companion of the theory of ordered differential fields with a distinguished convex subfield. It is model complete, NIP, and admits a relative cell decomposition where cells are defined using the valuation, the derivation, and the order.

Ax–Kochen–Ershov for differential valued fields

The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle holds: elementary equivalence of two such structures is determined by the elementary equivalence of the residue differential fields (k, ∂k) and the value groups Γ (as ordered abelian groups). This reduction allows one to transfer results from the well‑studied theory of differential real closed fields (e.g., the model completeness of CODF) to the valued setting. The generic derivation ensures that the differential field is existentially closed in the class of differential fields extending the given valued field.

Connection with transseries and Hardy fields

The field of logarithmic‑exponential transseries carries a natural convex subfield consisting of series with bounded support, and the usual derivation preserves this subfield. The model‑theoretic framework above captures the asymptotic differential algebra of transseries and provides a uniform method to decide differential‑algebraic relations among definable functions. In particular, the relative cell decomposition yields a decision procedure for the existential theory of the transseries field with its natural valuation and derivation.

Real Closed Fields and the Theory of O‑Minimal Structures with a Generic Predicate for a Dense Subfield and a Valuation

Consider a real closed field R with a convex subring O (the valuation ring of a convex valuation v) and a distinguished subfield K that is dense in R with respect to the order topology (equivalently, dense in the valuation topology induced by O). The pair (R, K) is a dense pair of real closed fields; the convex subring O is exactly the valuation ring of the convex valuation whose valuation ideal is the set of infinitesimals relative to K. The three‑sorted structure (R, O, K) in the language with predicates for O and K is model complete and NIP. It admits a relative cell decomposition: every definable set in the field sort is a finite Boolean combination of cells whose boundaries are definable using the valuation and the dense subfield. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces elementary equivalence to that of the residue field of O (as a real closed field) together with the induced dense pair structure on the residue field, and the value group Γ.

Model‑theoretic foundations for o‑minimal expansions

This framework, developed by van den Dries and others, provides a model‑theoretic foundation for o‑minimal expansions of the real field by a dense independent set. The dense subfield K can be taken to be a generic elementary substructure of R, ensuring that the induced structure on K is just the pure real closed field structure. The resulting theory is the model companion of the theory of ordered valued fields with a dense subfield, and it is used to analyse definable sets in expansions of ℝ by a predicate for a dense set such as the field of real algebraic numbers.

Applications to Hardy fields and asymptotic scales

In Hardy fields arising from germs of real functions at infinity, the convex subring consists of germs bounded by some real number, and a dense subfield can be chosen as the field of germs of functions with a prescribed growth rate (e.g., the field of logarithmic‑exponential germs). The valuation captures the asymptotic scale, and the density of the subfield reflects the fact that every germ can be approximated by functions from the chosen scale. The model‑theoretic tools above give a uniform description of definable sets in such Hardy fields and allow the transfer of o‑minimality results from the real field to the valued setting.

  • Confusing the convex subring O with the valuation ring of a non‑convex valuation; only convex valuations give rise to convex subrings that are valuation rings.
  • Assuming that a generic automorphism must act non‑trivially on the value group; in the presence of a convex subring it fixes the valuation and therefore acts trivially on Γ.
  • Treating the standard part map as definable in the pure field language; it requires a predicate for the convex subring or the infinitesimal ideal.
  • Overlooking that any derivation preserving a convex valuation forces the induced derivation on the value group to be trivial.
  • Neglecting that the dense pair theory requires the subfield to be dense in the valuation topology and the convex subring to be the associated valuation ring.
  • Mixing up model completeness of the expanded structure with that of the pure real closed field; the added predicates change the language and the theory.
  • Believing that the Hahn embedding for modules works without the Riesz interpolation property; the property is essential for the construction of the projectable hull.

Ordered Fields with a Convex Subring and a Generic Automorphism

Let F be an ordered field and O a convex subring of F. The pair (F, O) is a valued ordered field where the valuation v has valuation ring O and valuation ideal the set of infinitesimals relative to O. A generic automorphism σ of F is an automorphism of the ordered field that fixes the valuation v pointwise and acts generically on the residue field k = O/m and the value group Γ = v(F×). In the three‑sorted language with sorts for the field, the residue field, and the value group, together with predicates for O and a symbol for σ, the theory of such structures is model complete and NIP. The key point is that σ induces the identity on Γ because any convex valuation is preserved by an order‑preserving automorphism; consequently the action on the value group is trivial. The induced automorphism on the residue field is a generic automorphism of the real closed field k, and the Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces elementary equivalence of two such structures to elementary equivalence of the residue fields with their generic automorphisms and of the value groups as ordered abelian groups. This reduction allows one to transfer results from the well‑studied theory of real closed fields with a generic automorphism (the model companion of the theory of difference fields) to the valued setting. In particular, the relative quantifier elimination yields a description of definable sets in the field sort as Boolean combinations of cells whose boundaries are defined using the valuation and the automorphism. Applications include the model theory of Hardy fields equipped with a composition operator that acts as a generic automorphism on the residue field of germs bounded by a real number.

Real Closed Fields with a Convex Subring and a Generic Derivation

Let R be a real closed field, O a convex subring, and ∂ a derivation on R such that ∂(O) ⊆ O. The derivation then induces a derivation ∂k on the residue field k = O/m and a trivial derivation on the value group Γ because ∂ respects the valuation: for any a ∈ R×, v(∂a) ≥ v(a) − v(a) = 0, so the induced map on Γ is zero. The three‑sorted structure (R, O, ∂) in the language with a predicate for O and a symbol for ∂ is the model companion of the theory of ordered valued differential fields with a convex valuation ring. It is model complete and admits a relative cell decomposition: every definable subset of the field sort is a finite Boolean combination of cells whose boundaries are defined using the valuation and the derivation. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces elementary equivalence to that of the residue differential field (k, ∂k) and the value group Γ as an ordered abelian group. This reduction transfers the model completeness of CODF (the theory of closed ordered differential fields) to the valued setting. The generic derivation ensures that the differential field is existentially closed in the class of differential fields extending the given valued field. A concrete example is the field of logarithmic‑exponential transseries equipped with its natural convex subring of series with bounded support and the usual derivation; the model‑theoretic framework captures the asymptotic differential algebra of transseries and provides a decision procedure for the existential theory of this valued differential field.

Worked Example: Definable Set in a Valued Differential Field
Let (R, O, ∂) be a real closed field with a convex subring O and a generic derivation ∂ preserving O. Describe the definable set X = { x ∈ R : ∂x > 0 ∧ v(x) ≥ 0 } in terms of cells.
The condition v(x) ≥ 0 means x ∈ O. The inequality ∂x > 0 is a differential condition. By relative cell decomposition, X is a finite union of cells of the form { x ∈ O : f(x) > 0 } where f is a term built from the field operations, the valuation, and the derivation. Since ∂ is generic, the set of x with ∂x > 0 is a union of intervals in the residue field lifted to O. Concretely, choose a cross‑section s : Γ → R×. Every x ∈ O can be written uniquely as x = u·s(γ) with u a unit in O and γ ≥ 0. The condition ∂x > 0 translates to a condition on the residue of u and γ. The resulting cell is defined by a sign condition on a differential polynomial in the residue field. Hence X is a Boolean combination of such cells.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for a description of definable sets in a valued differential field, first identify the convex subring and the induced structures on the residue field and value group. Then invoke the relative cell decomposition theorem: every definable set is a Boolean combination of cells whose boundaries are given by sign conditions on terms involving the valuation and the derivation. Do not attempt to write an explicit quantifier‑free formula unless the problem explicitly requests it; the cell description is the standard answer.

Ordered Fields with a Convex Subring, a Generic Automorphism, and a Derivation

Consider an ordered field F equipped with a convex subring O, a generic automorphism σ fixing O setwise, and a derivation ∂ such that ∂(O) ⊆ O and σ commutes with ∂. The three operators interact: σ induces the identity on the value group Γ, a generic automorphism on the residue field k, and ∂ induces a derivation ∂k on k and the zero derivation on Γ. The combined structure (F, O, σ, ∂) in the language with predicates for O, a symbol for σ, and a symbol for ∂ is the model companion of the theory of ordered valued difference‑differential fields with a convex valuation ring. It is model complete and NIP. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces elementary equivalence to that of the residue difference‑differential field (k, σk, ∂k) and the value group Γ. This allows one to transfer the model completeness of the theory of real closed fields with a generic automorphism and a generic derivation (the model companion of the theory of difference‑differential fields) to the valued setting. A typical application is the study of Hardy fields closed under composition and differentiation, where the convex subring consists of germs bounded by a real number, σ is induced by composition with a fixed germ of infinite growth, and ∂ is the usual derivative. The model‑theoretic tools give a uniform description of definable sets in such Hardy fields and enable the transfer of o‑minimality results from the real field to the valued difference‑differential setting.

Real Closed Fields with a Convex Subring, a Generic Automorphism, and a Derivation

Let R be a real closed field, O a convex subring, σ a generic automorphism of R preserving O, and ∂ a derivation on R with ∂(O) ⊆ O such that σ∘∂ = ∂∘σ. The induced structures on the residue field k = O/m and the value group Γ are: σ acts as a generic automorphism on k and trivially on Γ; ∂ acts as a derivation ∂k on k and trivially on Γ. The theory of the four‑sorted structure (R, O, σ, ∂) is the model companion of the theory of real closed valued difference‑differential fields with a convex valuation ring. It is model complete, admits quantifier elimination relative to the residue field and value group, and is NIP. The relative cell decomposition theorem holds: every definable subset of the field sort is a finite Boolean combination of cells whose boundaries are defined using the valuation, the automorphism, and the derivation. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces elementary equivalence to elementary equivalence of the residue difference‑differential field (k, σk, ∂k) and the ordered abelian group Γ. This framework captures the asymptotic difference‑differential algebra of transseries fields equipped with a composition operator and the usual derivation. It also provides a decision procedure for the existential theory of such fields, which is relevant for problems in asymptotic analysis and differential‑algebraic geometry.

Model‑Theoretic Transfer for Pairs of Ordered Fields with Convex Subrings

Let (F, O) and (F′, O′) be two ordered fields with convex subrings. Suppose the residue fields k = O/m and k′ = O′/m′ are elementarily equivalent as ordered fields, and the value groups Γ = v(F×) and Γ′ = v′(F′×) are elementarily equivalent as ordered abelian groups. Then the pairs (F, O) and (F′, O′) are elementarily equivalent in the language with a predicate for the convex subring. This is the Baer–Krull theorem for ordered fields, a special case of the Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle. The proof uses the fact that any ordered field with a convex subring is henselian with respect to the associated valuation, and the residue field and value group determine the theory up to elementary equivalence. If, in addition, the pairs are equipped with generic automorphisms or derivations preserving the convex subrings, the transfer extends to the expanded languages provided the induced structures on the residue fields and value groups are elementarily equivalent. This transfer principle is the main tool for reducing questions about valued ordered fields to questions about their residue fields and value groups, and it underlies the model completeness results for all the expanded structures discussed in the previous sections.

  • Confusing the convex subring O with the valuation ring of a non‑convex valuation; only convex valuations give rise to convex subrings that are valuation rings.
  • Assuming that a generic automorphism must act non‑trivially on the value group; in the presence of a convex subring it fixes the valuation and therefore acts trivially on Γ.
  • Treating the standard part map as definable in the pure field language; it requires a predicate for the convex subring or the infinitesimal ideal.
  • Overlooking that any derivation preserving a convex valuation forces the induced derivation on the value group to be trivial.
  • Neglecting that the dense pair theory requires the subfield to be dense in the valuation topology and the convex subring to be the associated valuation ring.
  • Mixing up model completeness of the expanded structure with that of the pure real closed field; the added predicates change the language and the theory.
  • Believing that the Hahn embedding for modules works without the Riesz interpolation property; the property is essential for the construction of the projectable hull.

Real Closed Fields with a Contractive Valuation and a Generic Automorphism

A contractive valuation on a real closed field R is a valuation v whose valuation ring O is convex and whose value group Γ is a dense ordered abelian group such that for every γ > 0 in Γ there exists δ with 0 < δ < γ. The convexity of O guarantees that the order on R is compatible with the valuation topology. When a generic automorphism σ is added, we require that σ preserves the valuation ring (σ(O) = O) and acts as a generic automorphism on the residue field k = O/m while fixing the value group pointwise. The resulting four‑sorted structure (R, O, v, σ) has been shown to be the model companion of the theory of real closed valued fields with a contractive valuation and an automorphism preserving the valuation ring. It is model complete, admits quantifier elimination relative to the residue field and the value group, and is NIP. The relative cell decomposition theorem holds: every definable subset of the field sort is a finite Boolean combination of cells whose boundaries are defined using the valuation and the automorphism. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces elementary equivalence of two such structures to elementary equivalence of the induced structures on the residue field (with the induced automorphism) and the ordered value group. This framework captures the asymptotic behaviour of Hardy fields closed under composition, where the contractive valuation measures growth rates and the automorphism corresponds to composition with a fixed germ of infinite growth.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for the Standard Part Map and a Generic Derivation

Let R be a real closed field equipped with a convex subring O (the ring of finite elements) and its maximal ideal m (the infinitesimals). The standard part map st : O → k = O/m sends each finite element to its residue class. Adding a predicate for the graph of st makes the map definable in the language. Now expand the structure by a derivation ∂ on R such that ∂(O) ⊆ O and ∂(m) ⊆ m. The derivation induces a derivation ∂k on the residue field k and acts trivially on the value group Γ. If ∂ is generic over the pair (R, O), the theory of (R, O, st, ∂) is the model companion of the theory of real closed valued differential fields with a convex valuation ring and a distinguished standard part map. It is model complete, admits quantifier elimination relative to the residue differential field (k, ∂k) and the ordered value group, and is NIP. The relative cell decomposition theorem extends: definable sets in the field sort are Boolean combinations of cells whose boundaries may involve the valuation, the standard part map, and the derivation. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov transfer principle applies: elementary equivalence of two such structures is equivalent to elementary equivalence of the residue differential fields and the value groups. This setting is tailor‑made for the study of Hardy fields of transseries where the standard part extracts the constant term and the derivation is the usual differential operator.

Worked Example
Let (R, O, st, ∂) be a real closed field with a convex subring O, standard part map st, and a generic derivation ∂ preserving O. Show that the induced derivation ∂_k on the residue field k = O/m is well defined and that ∂ acts trivially on the value group Γ.
Since ∂(O) ⊆ O and ∂(m) ⊆ m, for any a ∈ O and ε ∈ m we have ∂(a+ε) = ∂(a) + ∂(ε) with ∂(ε) ∈ m. Hence the residue class of ∂(a) modulo m depends only on the residue class of a, giving a well‑defined map ∂_k : k → k, ∂_k(st(a)) = st(∂(a)). For the value group, take x ∈ R^× with valuation v(x) = γ. Because ∂ preserves O and m, v(∂(x)) ≥ v(x) for all x ∈ O^×; in particular, for any γ > 0 there is no element whose valuation is strictly decreased by ∂. The only ordered‑group endomorphism compatible with this inequality is the trivial one, so ∂ induces the identity on Γ.
Exam Tip
When a question asks for the induced structure on the residue field or value group, first verify that the added operations (valuation, automorphism, derivation, standard part) preserve the convex subring and its maximal ideal. Then write down the induced maps explicitly and check that they satisfy the required algebraic identities (e.g., Leibniz rule for derivations). The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle is often the final step to transfer model‑theoretic properties.

Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for the Value Group, a Generic Automorphism, and a Derivation

Consider a real closed field R equipped with a valuation v whose valuation ring O is convex, a predicate naming the value group Γ = v(R×) as an ordered abelian group, a generic automorphism σ preserving O and acting trivially on Γ, and a derivation ∂ with ∂(O) ⊆ O and ∂(m) ⊆ m that also commutes with σ. The induced structures are: σ acts as a generic automorphism on the residue field k and trivially on Γ; ∂ induces a derivation ∂k on k and acts trivially on Γ. The theory of the five‑sorted structure (R, O, Γ, σ, ∂) is the model companion of the theory of real closed valued difference‑differential fields with a named value group. It is model complete, admits quantifier elimination relative to the residue difference‑differential field (k, σk, ∂k) and the ordered value group, and is NIP. Relative cell decomposition holds with cells whose boundaries may involve the valuation, the automorphism, and the derivation. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov principle reduces elementary equivalence to elementary equivalence of the residue difference‑differential field and the ordered value group. This expansion is particularly useful for analysing transseries fields equipped with both a composition operator (the automorphism) and the usual derivation, where the value group records the exponential growth rates.

Ordered Modules over Projectable f‑Rings and the Spectral Representation

Let A be a projectable f‑ring (a lattice‑ordered ring in which every principal ideal is generated by an idempotent). An A-module M that is also a lattice‑ordered group and satisfies a·x ≥ 0 whenever a ≥ 0 in A and x ≥ 0 in M is called an ordered A-module. The category of ordered A-modules admits a Yosida‑type representation: every Archimedean ordered A-module embeds into a module of continuous sections of a sheaf of ordered vector spaces over the maximal spectrum of A. The projectability of A ensures that the Pierce sheaf of A is a sheaf of totally ordered fields, and the stalks of the representing sheaf are ordered modules over these fields. The Riesz interpolation property in A lifts to the module category, allowing the construction of the projectable hull of any ordered A-module. This hull is the smallest projectable ordered A-module containing the given one and plays the same role as the Dedekind completion for ordered groups. The spectral representation yields a concrete description of the lattice of A-submodules: they correspond to sheaves of submodules that are closed under the natural order. Applications include the representation of vector lattices with a distinguished order unit as modules over the f‑ring of continuous functions on a compact Hausdorff space.

The Model Theory of Real Closed Fields with a Predicate for a Convex Subring and a Generic Automorphism

Let R be a real closed field, O a convex subring, and σ a generic automorphism of R such that σ(O) = O. The induced automorphism on the residue field k = O/m is generic, while σ acts trivially on the value group Γ = v(R×). The theory of the three‑sorted structure (R, O, σ) is the model companion of the theory of real closed valued fields with a convex valuation ring and an automorphism preserving the valuation ring. It is model complete, admits quantifier elimination relative to the residue difference field (k, σk) and the ordered value group, and is NIP. The relative cell decomposition theorem states that every definable subset of the field sort is a finite Boolean combination of cells whose boundaries are defined using the valuation and the automorphism. The Ax–Kochen–Ershov transfer principle applies: two such structures are elementarily equivalent iff their residue difference fields and value groups are elementarily equivalent. This framework captures the model theory of Hardy fields closed under composition, where the convex subring consists of germs bounded by a real number and the automorphism is induced by composition with a fixed germ of infinite growth. It also provides a decision procedure for the existential theory of such fields, which is relevant for problems in asymptotic analysis and differential‑algebraic geometry.

  • Confusing the contractive valuation condition with mere convexity; contractivity requires density of the value group and a specific growth condition on the valuation.
  • Assuming the standard part map is definable without a predicate for the convex subring; it is not definable in the pure field language.
  • Treating the induced derivation on the value group as possibly non‑trivial; any derivation preserving a convex valuation forces the induced map on the value group to be the identity.
  • Overlooking that a generic automorphism preserving a convex subring must act trivially on the value group; non‑trivial action would violate convexity.
