SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with Entanglement Entropy and the Replica Trick

The entanglement entropy of a quantum critical system in two dimensions is computed via the replica trick: one evaluates the partition function Zn on an n-sheeted Riemann surface obtained by gluing n copies of the original domain along a cut, then takes the limit S = −∂n log Zn|n=1. In the SLE framework the cut is replaced by an SLEκ curve, and the n-sheeted surface is uniformized by a conformal map that solves a Loewner equation with n force points. The partition function Zn becomes an SLEκ partition function with n boundary condition changing operators inserted at the endpoints of the cut. For a single interval of length L in an infinite system at central charge c, the CFT prediction is S = (c/3) log(L/a) where a is a UV cutoff. The SLE derivation reproduces this by identifying the scaling dimension of the twist operator that implements the cyclic permutation of replicas: hn = (c/24)(n − 1/n). The SLEκ martingale observable for the n-replica problem satisfies a level-n null-vector equation, and its asymptotic behavior as the curve approaches the boundary yields the twist operator dimension. For κ = 6 (percolation, c = 0) the entanglement entropy vanishes, consistent with the fact that percolation clusters are not quantum entangled. For κ = 3 (Ising, c = 1/2) one obtains S = (1/6) log(L/a). The replica trick also gives access to the Rényi entropies Sn = (1/(1−n)) log(Zn/Z1n), which in SLE language are ratios of partition functions with different numbers of force points. The analytic continuation n → 1 is subtle because the SLEκ partition function for non-integer n requires a Coulomb gas representation with screening charges; the correct continuation is achieved by fixing the background charge to maintain conformal invariance. This SLE-based replica approach has been used to compute entanglement entropy in the quantum dimer model, the quantum loop model, and the critical FK-percolation model, where the SLE parameter κ = 16/3 gives c = 1 and S = (1/3) log(L/a).

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with Boundary States and the Cardy Condition

In boundary conformal field theory a conformally invariant boundary condition is encoded in a boundary state |B⟩ in the closed-string Hilbert space. The Cardy condition requires that the open-string partition function on a strip, computed as ⟨B1|qHclosed|B2⟩, admits an expansion in characters of the chiral algebra with non-negative integer coefficients — these are the multiplicities of boundary condition changing operators. In SLE the boundary condition is specified by the initial data of the Loewner equation: a pure boundary condition corresponds to a deterministic driving function, while a mixed boundary condition introduces force points with weights ρi. The SLEκ partition function Z(ρ1, …, ρm) is precisely the open-string partition function between the boundary states associated with the force points. For minimal models M(p, q) with κ = 4p/q, the boundary states are labeled by Kac table entries (r, s) with 1 ≤ r ≤ p−1, 1 ≤ s ≤ q−1. The Cardy condition translates into the requirement that the SLEκ partition functions form a representation of the fusion algebra of the corresponding modular tensor category. For the Ising model (κ = 3, M(4,3)) there are three boundary states: free (1,1), fixed up (1,2), fixed down (2,1). The SLE(3,ρ) partition functions with ρ = 0, 1, 2 realize the fusion rules σ × σ = 1 + ψ, σ × ψ = σ, ψ × ψ = 1. The boundary entropy g = ⟨0|B⟩ is computed from the SLE partition function on the upper half-plane with a single force point: g = limt→∞ Z(ρ)/√t. For κ = 3 one finds gfree = 1, gfixed = 1/√2, reproducing Affleck and Ludwig's result. The Cardy condition also constrains the allowed values of ρ in SLE(κ,ρ): they must correspond to boundary operators in the Kac table, i.e., ρ = 2hr,s = ((pr − qs)2 − (p − q)2)/(2pq). This quantization of ρ explains why SLE(κ,ρ) processes with generic ρ do not arise as scaling limits of local lattice models.

Worked Example: Entanglement Entropy from SLE Partition Function
Consider critical percolation (κ = 6, c = 0) on the upper half-plane. An SLE6 curve grows from 0 to ∞. Compute the second Rényi entropy S2 for an interval [−L, L] on the real line using the replica trick with n = 2. The twist operator dimension is h2 = (c/24)(2 − 1/2) = 0. The SLE6 partition function with two force points at ±L is Z2 = ⟨exp(−2∫0∞ (1/t) dWt)⟩ where Wt is the driving function. Show that S2 = 0.
For κ = 6 the central charge c = 0, so the twist operator dimension h2 = 0. The SLE6 partition function with two force points of weight ρ = 2h2 = 0 is simply Z2 = 1 (no drift term). The single-replica partition function Z1 = 1. The second Rényi entropy is S2 = (1/(1−2)) log(Z2/Z12) = −log(1) = 0. This matches the CFT prediction S = (c/3) log(L/a) = 0 for c = 0. The vanishing entanglement entropy reflects the fact that critical percolation is a classical statistical mechanics model without quantum entanglement; the SLE6 curve describes a geometric cluster boundary, not a quantum entanglement cut.
Exam Strategy: Replica Trick and SLE
When a question asks for entanglement entropy in an SLE context, first identify κ and the corresponding central charge c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ). The twist operator dimension is hn = (c/24)(n − 1/n). The Rényi entropy Sn = (1/(1−n)) log(Zn/Z1n) where Zn is the SLE partition function with n force points of weight ρ = 2hn. For integer n, Zn satisfies a level-n null-vector equation. The analytic continuation n → 1 gives the von Neumann entropy S = (c/3) log(L/a). Memorize the formula c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ) and the values for key models: κ=2 (c=−2), κ=3 (c=1/2), κ=4 (c=1), κ=6 (c=0), κ=8 (c=−2).

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with Topological Recursion and Matrix Models

The Eynard-Orantin topological recursion computes all-genus correlation functions of a matrix model from a spectral curve. In CFT, the spectral curve is the Riemann surface on which the theory is defined, and the recursion generates the expansion of correlation functions in the genus parameter. For SLE, the Loewner equation defines a family of conformal maps whose coefficients are random variables; their moments are the SLE partition functions. These partition functions satisfy a set of PDEs (the BPZ equations) that can be recast as a topological recursion on the moduli space of Riemann surfaces with boundary. The spectral curve for SLEκ is the x-y curve defined by the algebraic equation y2 = x(x − 1)(x − t) for the four-point function on the sphere, where t is the cross-ratio. The topological recursion kernel is K(z1, z2) = (1/2) ∫z2z̄2 B(z1, ·)/(y(·) − y(z̄2)) where B is the Bergman kernel. The recursion produces the genus expansion of the SLE partition function: log Z = Σg≥0 ħ2g−2 Fg. For κ = 6 (percolation) the genus-zero free energy F0 reproduces the crossing probability formula of Cardy. For κ = 4 (GFF) the recursion generates the moments of the Gaussian multiplicative chaos measure. The matrix model dual to SLEκ is the Hermitian matrix model with potential V(M) = (1/2)M2 + (κ/4) log M for κ > 0; the eigenvalue density gives the SLE hull capacity. The loop equations of this matrix model are equivalent to the Virasoro constraints on the SLE partition function. This connection has been used to compute the all-genus expansion of the SLEκ partition function on the torus and to prove the modular invariance of the genus-one partition function for κ = 3, 4, 6.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with Modular Differential Equations and Virasoro Characters

The characters of irreducible highest-weight representations of the Virasoro algebra satisfy modular differential equations (MDEs) of order equal to the number of characters in the theory. For a rational CFT with central charge c and a finite set of primary fields, the vector of characters χi(τ) transforms under the modular group SL(2,ℤ) by a representation ρ. Zhu's theorem states that the characters satisfy an MDE of the form [Dn + Σk=1n φk(τ) Dn−k] χ = 0 where D = (1/2πi) d/dτ − (k/12) E2(τ) is the Serre derivative and φk are modular forms of weight 2k. In SLE, the partition function on the annulus or torus is a linear combination of Virasoro characters with coefficients given by the multiplicities of boundary condition changing operators. For minimal models M(p, q) the MDE has order (p−1)(q−1)/2. For the Ising model (κ = 3, M(4,3)) there are three characters: χ0, χ1/2, χ1/16. They satisfy a third-order MDE with φ1 = 0, φ2 = −(1/12)E4, φ3 = (1/216)E6. The SLE3 partition function on the annulus with free/fixed boundary conditions is Z = χ1/16; with fixed/fixed it is χ0 + χ1/2. The MDE implies that these partition functions are vector-valued modular forms of weight zero. For non-rational CFTs like Liouville theory (κ ∈ (0,4) ∪ (4,8)), the spectrum is continuous and the MDE is replaced by a modular integral equation. The SLEκ partition function on the torus for generic κ is given by the DOZZ formula integrated over the continuous spectrum, and it satisfies the modular bootstrap equations. The connection between SLE and MDEs provides a powerful tool for computing SLE partition functions on higher-genus surfaces and for proving their modular properties without relying on Coulomb gas integrals.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with Integrable Boundary Conditions and Reflection Matrices

Integrable boundary conditions in a lattice model are those that preserve the Yang-Baxter integrability of the bulk. They are classified by solutions of the boundary Yang-Baxter equation (BYBE) for the reflection matrix K(u), where u is the spectral parameter. In the scaling limit, integrable boundary conditions correspond to conformally invariant boundary states in CFT. For SLE, the boundary condition is encoded in the drift term of the driving function: dWt = √κ dBt + Σi (ρi/t) dt for force points at the boundary. The parameters ρi are determined by the boundary operator dimensions. For the O(N) loop model with κ = 4π/arccos(−N/2), the integrable boundary conditions are labeled by the boundary weights a, b, c satisfying the BYBE. The reflection matrix K(u) is a 2×2 matrix for the six-vertex model (κ = 4) and a higher-rank matrix for the RSOS models. The eigenvalues of K(u) give the boundary scaling dimensions via the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz (TBA). For the critical FK-percolation model (κ = 16/3, N = 1) the integrable boundary conditions are free, wired, and mixed. The mixed boundary condition corresponds to a non-diagonal reflection matrix with off-diagonal entries that implement the boundary condition changing operator. The SLE(16/3,ρ) partition function with ρ = 2/3 (mixed) satisfies the BYBE at the level of the CFT: the monodromy of the four-point function of boundary condition changing operators reproduces the R-matrix of the quantum group Uq(sl2) with q = eiπ/κ. The boundary entropy g is computed from the ground state eigenvalue of the transfer matrix with the integrable boundary condition, and it matches the SLE partition function on the half-plane. This integrable boundary framework explains why the ρ-parameters in SLE(κ,ρ) are quantized: they correspond to the discrete set of solutions of the BYBE for a given bulk integrable model.

  • Confusing the replica trick for entanglement entropy with the replica trick for disorder averaging; the former uses cyclic permutation of replicas, the latter uses n → 0 limit of Zn.
  • Assuming the Cardy condition applies to all boundary conditions; it only applies to conformally invariant boundary states, not to arbitrary boundary perturbations.
  • Treating the topological recursion as a perturbative expansion in κ; it is an expansion in the genus parameter ħ = 1, with κ fixed.
  • Misidentifying the order of the modular differential equation; it equals the number of primary fields in the rational CFT, not the number of boundary conditions.
  • Confusing the reflection matrix K(u) of the boundary Yang-Baxter equation with the bulk R-matrix; K acts on a single boundary space, R acts on the tensor product of two bulk spaces.
  • Assuming all SLE(κ,ρ) processes correspond to integrable boundary conditions; only those ρ that solve the BYBE for the corresponding lattice model are integrable.
  • Neglecting the distinction between diagonal and non-diagonal boundary conditions; non-diagonal ones have off-diagonal K-matrices and correspond to boundary condition changing operators with non-zero ρ.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Natural Parametrization of SLE Curves and the Minkowski Content

The standard Loewner parametrization of SLEκ uses half-plane capacity, which is convenient for the Loewner equation but does not correspond to a geometric length along the curve. For κ ≤ 4, the SLE trace is a simple curve with Hausdorff dimension d = 1 + κ/8, and it admits a natural parametrization by its d-dimensional Minkowski content. This parametrization, constructed by Lawler and Sheffield (2011) for κ < 8 and extended by Gwynne and Miller (2017) for all κ, assigns to each initial segment of the curve its d-dimensional Minkowski content, defined as the limit limε→0 ε2−d Area(Nε(γ[0,t])), where Nε is the ε-neighborhood. The existence of this limit almost surely and its equivalence to the d-dimensional Hausdorff measure on the trace is a deep result relying on the multifractal spectrum of SLE and the KPZ relation. For κ ∈ (4,8), the curve is non-simple and self-intersecting; the natural parametrization still exists but the Minkowski content must be defined via the occupation measure of the curve. For κ ≥ 8, the curve is space-filling and the natural parametrization coincides with the Lebesgue measure on the domain. The natural parametrization is conformally covariant: if φ is a conformal map, the Minkowski content of φ(γ) is the pushforward of the Minkowski content of γ weighted by |φ'|d. This property is essential for defining the quantum length of SLE curves in Liouville quantum gravity, where the LQG metric is constructed so that the quantum length of an SLE curve matches its natural parametrization. The construction uses the Gaussian multiplicative chaos measure associated with the GFF and the KPZ formula to relate Euclidean and quantum dimensions. The natural parametrization also plays a key role in the mating-of-trees framework, where the space-filling SLEκ' for κ' = 16/κ is parametrized by its quantum area, and the left/right boundary lengths evolve as a correlated Brownian motion.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Tip Regularity and the Hölder Exponent of SLE Traces

The local regularity of the SLE trace at its tip is characterized by the optimal Hölder exponent, which depends on κ. For κ ∈ (0,4], the trace is a simple curve and the tip is almost surely Hölder continuous with exponent 1/2 − ε for any ε > 0, but not with exponent 1/2. This was proved by Lind, Marshall, and Rohde (2010) using the Loewner equation and the fact that the driving function is √κ times Brownian motion, which is almost surely Hölder-1/2−ε. The conformal map gt from the slit domain to the upper half-plane extends continuously to the tip, and its derivative at the tip behaves like (t−s)−1/2 as s t. For κ ∈ (4,8), the trace is non-simple and the tip regularity is more subtle: the curve has double points and the tip is not a well-defined point in the same sense. However, the forward and backward tips (when parametrized by capacity) still exhibit Hölder regularity with exponent 1/2 − ε. For κ ≥ 8, the curve is space-filling and the concept of a tip is replaced by the boundary of the explored region. The optimal Hölder exponent for the inverse map gt−1 at the tip is related to the multifractal spectrum of the harmonic measure. Specifically, the integral means spectrum β(q) of the derivative of the conformal map governs the moments of the derivative near the tip. For SLEκ, β(q) = (κ/4)q2 + (1 − κ/4)q for q ≥ 1/2, and the tip regularity is connected to the value β(1/2) = 1/2 − κ/16. The precise modulus of continuity of the SLE trace was established by Rohde and Schramm (2005) for κ ≠ 8, showing that the trace is almost surely Hölder-1/2−ε. For κ = 8, the trace is space-filling and the regularity is logarithmic. These regularity results are crucial for numerical algorithms such as the zipper algorithm and the Marshall-Rohde method, where the convergence rate depends on the Hölder regularity of the driving function and the trace.

Worked Problem: Hölder Regularity of SLEκ Trace
Let γ be an SLEκ trace in the upper half-plane ℍ from 0 to ∞, driven by Wt = √κ Bt. Show that for any ε > 0, the trace γ is almost surely locally Hölder continuous with exponent 1/2 − ε, but not with exponent 1/2. Use the fact that Brownian motion is almost surely Hölder-1/2−ε but not Hölder-1/2.
The Loewner equation ∂t gt(z) = 2/(gt(z) − Wt) with g0(z) = z generates the conformal maps gt from ℍ γ[0,t] to ℍ. The trace γ(t) = limy0 gt−1(Wt + iy). Rohde and Schramm (2005) proved that the map t ↦ γ(t) is almost surely Hölder continuous with exponent 1/2 − ε for any ε > 0. The proof uses the estimate |gt−1(Wt + iy) − gs−1(Ws + iy)| ≤ C |t−s|1/2−ε for y small, which follows from the Hölder regularity of the driving function Wt = √κ Bt. Since Brownian motion Bt is almost surely Hölder-1/2−ε but not Hölder-1/2 (by the law of iterated logarithm, limsuph→0 |Bt+h−Bt|/√(2h log log 1/h) = 1), the same holds for Wt. The Loewner equation preserves this regularity: if W is α-Hölder, then γ is α-Hölder for α < 1/2. For α = 1/2, the law of iterated logarithm for Brownian motion implies that the driving function has oscillations of order √(h log log 1/h), which translate into oscillations of the trace of the same order, preventing 1/2-Hölder continuity. Thus γ is almost surely locally Hölder-1/2−ε but not Hölder-1/2.
Exam Strategy: SLE Regularity and Numerical Methods
When asked about convergence of SLE simulation algorithms (zipper, Marshall-Rohde), recall that the error depends on the Hölder regularity of the driving function. The zipper algorithm converges with rate O(n−1/2+ε) for κ < 8 because the driving function is Hölder-1/2−ε. For κ = 8, the convergence is slower due to space-filling nature. The natural parametrization by Minkowski content is the correct geometric time for SLE in LQG; capacity parametrization is a computational tool, not a physical one. Memorize the Hausdorff dimension d = 1 + κ/8 for κ ≤ 8 and d = 2 for κ ≥ 8.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Large Deviations Principle for SLE and the Loewner Energy as a Rate Function

The large deviations principle (LDP) for SLEκ as κ → 0 describes the probability that the SLE trace deviates from the deterministic curve that minimizes the Loewner energy. The Loewner energy of a curve γ in a simply connected domain D from a to b is defined as ID(γ) = (1/2) ∫0T |W't|2 dt, where Wt is the driving function of γ under the Loewner equation parametrized by capacity. For a chordal curve in ℍ from 0 to ∞, this equals (1/2) ∫ |W'|2. The Loewner energy is finite if and only if the driving function is in the Dirichlet space H1. Rohde and Wang (2013) proved that the family of SLEκ measures satisfies an LDP on the space of curves with the uniform topology, with speed κ and rate function I(γ)/2. Specifically, for any measurable set A of curves, limκ→0 κ log Pκ(γ ∈ A) = − infγ∈A I(γ)/2. The minimizer of the Loewner energy among curves connecting two boundary points is the hyperbolic geodesic, which has zero Loewner energy. The Loewner energy is conformally invariant: ID(γ) = Iφ(D)(φ(γ)) for any conformal map φ. It also satisfies a domain monotonicity property: ID(γ) ≥ ID'(γ) for D' ⊂ D. The Loewner energy is closely related to the Weil-Petersson metric on the universal Teichmüller space: the Weil-Petersson class of quasicircles is exactly the set of curves with finite Loewner energy. The LDP for SLEκ as κ → ∞ (after rescaling) is also known: the curve converges to a straight line, and the fluctuations are governed by a Gaussian process. The Loewner energy appears in the asymptotic expansion of the SLE partition function and in the semiclassical limit of the Virasoro conformal blocks. In the context of Liouville quantum gravity, the Loewner energy is the rate function for the LDP of the SLE curve coupled with the GFF, and it is related to the Liouville action via the KPZ formula.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the SLE(κ) for κ > 8 and the Space-Filling Exploration of the Gaussian Free Field

For κ > 8, the SLEκ trace is a space-filling curve that visits every point in the domain. This regime is dual to κ' = 16/κ ∈ (0,2) via the relation κκ' = 16. The space-filling SLEκ for κ > 8 can be constructed as the exploration path of the Gaussian free field (GFF) with appropriate boundary conditions, as shown by Miller and Sheffield (2016) in their imaginary geometry framework. Specifically, a space-filling SLEκ for κ > 8 is the flow line of the GFF with angle θ = π/2, or equivalently, the level line of the GFF with height gap λ' = π/√κ. The curve is parametrized by the quantum area (Lebesgue measure) of the explored region, which coincides with the natural parametrization by Minkowski content. The left and right boundary lengths of the explored region, measured in the quantum length induced by the GFF, evolve as a correlated two-dimensional Brownian motion with correlation −cos(4π/κ). This is the mating-of-trees construction: the space-filling SLEκ encodes a pair of continuum random trees (CRTs) that are glued together to form a sphere or disk decorated by a GFF. The space-filling SLEκ for κ > 8 is also the scaling limit of the Peano curve of the uniform spanning tree on a random planar map (the mated-CRT map). The duality κ 16/κ exchanges the roles of the curve and the dual curve: the outer boundary of an SLEκ for κ > 8 is an SLE16/κ curve. The conformal welding of two independent quantum disks along their boundaries produces a quantum sphere decorated by a space-filling SLEκ. The partition function of space-filling SLE on the sphere is given by the DOZZ formula for Liouville CFT. The central charge of the corresponding CFT is c = 1 − 6(4−κ)2/κ, which for κ > 8 is less than 1. The space-filling SLEκ is reversible in the sense of Zhan: the time-reversal of a space-filling SLEκ from a to b is a space-filling SLEκ from b to a, with the same law. This reversibility is a consequence of the symmetry of the GFF under time-reversal of the exploration.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Malliavin Differentiability of the SLE Trace and the Absolute Continuity of SLE Laws

The Malliavin calculus provides a powerful framework for studying the regularity of the law of the SLE trace as a random variable in the space of curves. The SLE trace γ is a functional of the driving Brownian motion Bt. The Malliavin derivative Dsγ(t) measures the sensitivity of the trace at time t to a perturbation of the Brownian path at time s. For κ < 8, the trace γ(t) is Malliavin differentiable for each fixed t, and its Malliavin derivative satisfies a linearized Loewner equation. The Malliavin covariance matrix of the trace at a finite set of times is almost surely invertible, which implies by the Bouleau-Hirsch criterion that the law of the trace has a smooth density with respect to the Lebesgue measure on the appropriate finite-dimensional projection. This absolute continuity result was established by Lind and Marshall (2016) for chordal SLEκ with κ < 8. For κ ≥ 8, the trace is space-filling and the Malliavin differentiability is more delicate; the trace as a curve parametrized by capacity is not differentiable at the times when it hits the boundary. However, the natural parametrization by Minkowski content restores regularity. The Malliavin calculus approach also yields quantitative estimates on the density of the SLE trace, such as the small-ball probabilities P(supt∈[0,1] |γ(t) − γ0(t)| < ε) for a deterministic curve γ0. These probabilities are related to the Loewner energy via the large deviations principle. The Malliavin derivative of the SLE trace can be expressed in terms of the derivative of the conformal map gt with respect to the driving function. Specifically, if Wt = √κ Bt, then DsWt = √κ 1s≤t, and the chain rule gives Dsgt(z) = −2 ∫st (g'u(z))/(gu(z)−Wu)2 DsWu du. This leads to a representation of the Malliavin derivative of the trace as a stochastic integral involving the derivative of the inverse map. The absolute continuity of SLE laws is crucial for statistical inference problems, such as estimating κ from a single realization of the trace, and for proving that the SLE measure is mutually absolutely continuous with respect to the law of a smooth curve perturbed by noise.

  • Assuming the SLE trace is Hölder-1/2 for κ < 8; it is almost surely Hölder-1/2−ε for any ε > 0 but not Hölder-1/2, as shown by the law of iterated logarithm for the driving Brownian motion.
  • Misapplying the large deviations principle for SLEκ as κ → 0; the rate function is the Loewner energy I(γ)/2, not the Dirichlet energy of the curve itself, and the speed is κ, not 1/κ.
  • Treating space-filling SLEκ for κ > 8 as a simple curve; it is space-filling, has Hausdorff dimension 2, and its outer boundary is an SLE16/κ curve, not an SLEκ curve.
  • Neglecting the duality κ 16/κ; the space-filling SLEκ for κ > 8 is dual to the non-space-filling SLE16/κ for 16/κ < 2, and this duality exchanges the curve with its outer boundary.
  • Assuming Malliavin differentiability holds for all κ; for κ ≥ 8 the capacity-parametrized trace is not Malliavin differentiable at boundary hitting times, though the naturally parametrized trace is regular.
  • Confusing the Loewner energy with the Dirichlet energy of the driving function; the Loewner energy is (1/2)∫|W'|2dt, which is the Dirichlet energy of the driving function, but it is a functional of the curve, not the parametrization.

Malliavin Calculus and Absolute Continuity for SLE Traces

The driving function of chordal SLE is Wt=√κ Bt, where Bt is a standard one‑dimensional Brownian motion. Malliavin calculus studies the differentiability of functionals of stochastic processes with respect to the underlying noise. For SLE, the trace γ(t) can be written as a functional 𝔉 of the driving Brownian path: γ(t)=𝔉(B[0,t]). The Malliavin derivative Dsγ(t) quantifies how an infinitesimal perturbation of B at time s (≤ t) changes the location of the tip at time t.

Using the chain rule for stochastic flows, one obtains

 Dsgt(z)=−2∫st (g′u(z))/(gu(z)−Wu)² DsWu du,  where DsWu=√κ 1{s≤u}.

Evaluating at the tip z=γ(t) and using gt(γ(t))=Wt, the derivative simplifies to a stochastic integral that depends only on the Loewner kernel. This representation shows that for κ<8 the trace is Malliavin differentiable on any interval that does not contain a boundary‑touching time. When κ≥8, the capacity‑parametrized trace hits the boundary with positive probability, and the derivative ceases to exist at those hitting times; however, the naturally parametrized trace (by Minkowski content) retains differentiability almost surely.

Absolute continuity between SLE laws follows from the Cameron‑Martin theorem. If two driving functions differ by an H¹‑function h(t), the corresponding SLE measures are mutually absolutely continuous, with Radon‑Nikodym derivative

 exp {(1/√κ)∫₀^T h′(t) dBt − (1/2κ)∫₀^T |h′(t)|² dt}.

This formula is the basis for statistical inference: given a single observed trace, one can construct a likelihood for κ by comparing the observed driving function (obtained via the inverse Loewner map) with a Brownian motion perturbed by a deterministic drift. The Malliavin derivative also yields a Clark‑Ocone representation of functionals of the trace, which is useful for variance reduction in Monte‑Carlo simulations of SLE‑related observables.

Large Deviation Principles and Loewner Energy in the Small‑κ Regime

When κ→0, SLE paths become increasingly deterministic and converge to the straight line segment joining the boundary points. The quantitative description of this convergence is provided by a large deviation principle (LDP). For a fixed time horizon T, the family {γκ}κ>0 satisfies an LDP with speed κ and good rate function I(γ)=½ ∫₀^T |W′(t)|² dt, where W is the driving function that generates γ via the Loewner equation. Because W(t)=√κ Bt, the rate function coincides with the Loewner energy of the curve, a conformally invariant functional introduced by Wang and later studied by Yilin Wang and others.

The Loewner energy I(γ) can be expressed purely in geometric terms: if γ is a simple curve from 0 to ∞ in the upper half‑plane, then

 I(γ)= (1/π) ∫ℍ\γ |∇ log |f′(z)||² dA(z),

where f is the conformal map from ℍ\γ onto ℍ normalised at infinity, and dA denotes planar Lebesgue measure. This Dirichlet integral measures how far the curve deviates from a geodesic in the Weil‑Petersson metric on the space of Jordan curves.

Consequences of the LDP are twofold. First, the most likely deviation from the straight line under a small κ perturbation is the minimiser of I(γ) subject to prescribed endpoint constraints; this minimiser is precisely the hyperbolic geodesic in ℍ, i.e. a circular arc orthogonal to the real axis. Second, the LDP yields exponential tail estimates for events such as “the SLE trace stays within distance ε of a given deterministic curve”. Explicitly, for any ε>0,

 P( sup₀≤t≤T dist(γκ(t), Γ(t)) ≥ ε ) ≤ exp(−c ε²/κ),

where Γ is the geodesic and c>0 depends only on the geometry of the domain. These estimates are indispensable when proving convergence of discrete models to SLE, because they control the probability of large “wiggles” that would otherwise spoil tightness.

Conformal Restriction Measures via SLE(κ,ρ) on Multiply Connected Domains

Restriction properties were first identified for chordal SLE with κ=8/3, where the law of the curve conditioned to avoid a fixed hull A is identical to the original law after conformal mapping by ϕA. This one‑sided restriction extends to SLE(κ,ρ) processes, where the driving function satisfies

 dWt=√κ dBt + ∑j=1ⁿ ρj / (Wt−Vj(t)) dt,

with auxiliary points Vj(t) that evolve according to the Loewner flow. The parameters ρj encode the strength of repulsion from marked boundary points. When the underlying domain is multiply connected—e.g., an annulus—the Loewner equation must be replaced by the Komatu‑Loewner equation, which incorporates the harmonic measure of each boundary component.

In an annulus A(r)= {z: r<|z|<1}, the driving function lives on the universal cover and the Loewner vector field contains a term proportional to the logarithmic derivative of the annular Green’s function. The restriction exponent α for a chordal SLE(κ,ρ) in A(r) is given by

 α = (6−κ−2∑ρj)/2κ,

provided the ρ’s satisfy the balance condition ∑ρj=κ−6. This formula reduces to the classical α= (8−3κ)/2κ for κ=8/3 and ρ=0. The restriction measure can be constructed by weighting ordinary SLE(κ) with a martingale Mt=∏j(g′t(xj))βj, where βj= (ρj(ρj+4−κ))/4κ. The martingale property follows from Itô’s formula applied to the Loewner map in the annular setting.

These restriction measures are instrumental in deriving exact crossing probabilities for critical models on cylinders or toroidal lattices, where the presence of non‑trivial homology classes forces the interface to wind around the domain. The exponent α determines the power‑law decay of the probability that the interface avoids a prescribed annular obstacle, a result that can be verified numerically via loop‑erased random walk simulations on periodic lattices.

Exam‑style question
Consider chordal SLE(κ,ρ) in the upper half‑plane with a single marked boundary point at x>0. Derive the martingale that implements the one‑sided restriction property, and compute the corresponding restriction exponent α in terms of κ and ρ.

Let gt be the Loewner map and Vt=gt(x) the image of the marked point. The driving function satisfies dWt=√κ dBt+ρ/(Wt−Vt) dt, while Vt evolves by dVt=2/(Vt−Wt) dt.

Define Mt=(g′t(x))β with β to be chosen. Using Itô’s formula,

 dMt=Mt β (g′′t(x)/g′t(x)) dVt + (1/2)Mt β(β−1) (g′′t(x)/g′t(x))² (dVt)².

Substituting dVt and simplifying using the Loewner equation yields the drift term

 Mt [ β(ρ+2)−β(β−1)κ/2 ] / (g′t(x)(Wt−Vt)²) dt.

For Mt to be a local martingale the drift must vanish, giving the quadratic equation

 β(β−1)κ/2 = β(ρ+2) ⇒ β = 2(ρ+2)/κ.

Hence the martingale is Mt=(g′t(x))2(ρ+2)/κ.

The restriction exponent α is defined by P[γ∩A=∅]=ϕ′A(0)^α for a hull A avoiding the origin. Comparing with the martingale scaling gives α=β/2 = (ρ+2)/κ.

Therefore, the one‑sided restriction exponent for SLE(κ,ρ) with a single marked point is α = (ρ+2)/κ.

Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for a restriction exponent, write down the martingale ansatz Mt=(g′t(x))β first. Apply Itô’s formula carefully, keep track of the drift and diffusion terms, and solve the resulting linear equation for β. Remember that α=β/2 for one‑sided restriction; this shortcut avoids a full derivation of the conformal map ϕA.

Quantum Zipper and Welding of Multiple Quantum Surfaces

The quantum zipper, introduced by Sheffield, describes how to glue together two independent Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surfaces along a common SLE interface while preserving the quantum length measure. For a single pair of quantum disks, the welding is encoded by a pair of correlated Brownian motions (Lt,Rt) with covariance −cos(4π/κ). The natural generalisation to m surfaces involves an m‑dimensional Brownian motion with a covariance matrix Σ whose off‑diagonal entries are determined by the pairwise angles θij = 4π/κ · δij (δij being the Kronecker delta). The joint law of the boundary lengths (ℓ₁,…,ℓ_m) evolves according to the stochastic differential system

 dℓ_i = √κ dB_i + ∑j≠i cot(θij) dB_j,  i=1,…,m,

where (B₁,…,B_m) is a standard m‑dimensional Brownian motion. This system ensures that the total quantum length ℓ₁+…+ℓ_m is a martingale, reflecting the conformal invariance of the total boundary.

In the mating‑of‑trees picture, each quantum surface corresponds to a continuum random tree (CRT) encoded by a Brownian excursion. The multi‑surface zipper glues the CRTs together along a common “spine” that is itself a space‑filling SLE_κ curve. The resulting quantum surface is a sphere with m marked boundary arcs, each carrying its own quantum length. The law of the glued surface is invariant under cyclic permutations of the arcs, a manifestation of the underlying modular symmetry of LQG.

Applications include the construction of higher‑genus LQG surfaces by iteratively welding disks along multiple SLE interfaces, and the derivation of exact formulas for the joint distribution of quantum areas of the constituent pieces. For κ=6 (critical percolation), the quantum zipper reproduces the Cardy‑type crossing probabilities on random triangulations, confirming the universality of the percolation scaling limit beyond deterministic lattices.

Time‑Reversal Symmetry Beyond Simple SLE: Zhan’s Generalized Reversibility

Zhan proved that chordal SLE_κ is reversible for all κ∈(0,8]; that is, the time‑reversed trace has the same law as an SLE_κ run from the opposite endpoint. The proof relies on coupling the forward and backward Loewner chains via a common Brownian motion and exploiting the conformal Markov property. For SLE(κ,ρ) with multiple force points, reversibility holds only under a balance condition ∑ρ_j = κ−6, which guarantees that the forward and backward driving functions have the same drift structure after a Möbius transformation that swaps the start and target points.

In the space‑filling regime κ>8, reversibility is more subtle. The forward curve fills the domain, while the backward curve traces the same space‑filling path in reverse order. Miller and Sheffield showed that the pair (γ, γ̃), where γ̃ is the time‑reversal, can be coupled with a single GFF such that γ is a flow line of angle θ and γ̃ is the flow line of angle θ+π. This coupling yields a deterministic relationship between the forward and backward parametrizations: the quantum area explored up to time t in the forward direction equals the quantum area remaining after time T−t in the reverse direction.

For SLE on multiply connected domains, Zhan’s method extends by using the Komatu‑Loewner equation. The reversibility condition now involves the harmonic measure of each boundary component; the driving function acquires an additional term reflecting the logarithmic capacity of the inner holes. When the domain is an annulus, the reversed SLE is again an SLE(κ,ρ) with the same κ but with the force points reflected across the radial line connecting the two boundary circles.

These reversibility results have concrete consequences for statistical mechanics models. In the critical Ising model, the interface between + and − spins is an SLE₃ curve; reversibility implies that the distribution of the interface is symmetric under swapping the spin boundary conditions. For the FK‑percolation model at q=2 (κ=16/3), the cluster exploration process is reversible only after conditioning on the outer boundary, a nuance that appears in rigorous proofs of conformal invariance for the random‑cluster model.

Multifractal Formalism for SLE Harmonic Measure and Exact Spectra

The harmonic measure ω on an SLE trace quantifies the probability that a Brownian motion started far away first hits the curve at a given point. Near a typical point z on the trace, ω scales like rα(z) where r is the Euclidean distance to z and α(z) is the local Hölder exponent. The multifractal spectrum f(α) gives the Hausdorff dimension of the set of points with a prescribed exponent α.

For chordal SLE_κ, the exact spectrum was derived by Duplantier using Coulomb‑gas techniques and later confirmed by rigorous probabilistic arguments. The result is

 f(α)= 2 + ( (4−κ)² / (8κ) ) − ( (α−1)² κ / 8 ),  α∈[1−2/κ, 1+2/κ].

The spectrum is symmetric about α=1, reflecting the duality between interior and exterior harmonic measure. The maximal dimension f(α_max)=2 occurs at α=1, corresponding to points where the harmonic measure behaves like the Lebesgue measure. The left endpoint α_min=1−2/κ yields f(α_min)=1−(4/κ), which matches the Hausdorff dimension of the set of cut points on the SLE trace.

These formulas extend to SLE(κ,ρ) by replacing κ with an effective parameter κ_eff = κ · (1+∑ρ_j/κ)², which accounts for the additional drift induced by the force points. In the space‑filling case κ>8, the harmonic measure becomes trivial (α=2 everywhere) because the curve visits every point, and the multifractal spectrum collapses to a single point (f(2)=2).

From an exam perspective, knowing the explicit f(α) allows one to answer questions about the dimension of exceptional subsets of the trace, such as double points, cut points, or the set of points where the curve approaches the boundary at a prescribed angle. The spectrum also provides a quick check for consistency: any claimed dimension must lie on the parabola defined above.

  • Confusing the Malliavin derivative of the capacity‑parametrized trace with that of the natural parametrization; the former fails at boundary hits for κ≥8.
  • Omitting the balance condition ∑ρ_j = κ−6 when asserting reversibility of SLE(κ,ρ); without it the time‑reversed law acquires a different drift.
  • Using the simple restriction exponent α = (6−κ)/2κ for SLE(κ,ρ) without adjusting for the ρ‑terms; the correct formula is α = (ρ+2)/κ for a single marked point.
  • Assuming the Loewner energy I(γ) equals the Euclidean length of γ; it is a conformally invariant Dirichlet integral of the logarithmic derivative of the uniformizing map.
  • Applying the multifractal spectrum outside its validity interval; for α outside [1−2/κ, 1+2/κ] the spectrum is −∞, indicating an empty set.
  • Treating the quantum zipper covariance as always −cos(4π/κ); in the multi‑surface case the covariance matrix involves pairwise angles and is not simply a scalar.
  • Neglecting the effect of multiply connected domains on the Komatu‑Loewner drift term, which leads to incorrect reversal formulas for annular SLE.

SLE and the Stress‑Energy Tensor: Virasoro Ward Identities and Martingale Observables

The stress‑energy tensor T(z) generates conformal transformations in a boundary conformal field theory. Its holomorphic component satisfies the Virasoro algebra with central charge c. For chordal SLEκ the central charge is c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ). The null‑vector condition at level two for a primary field of weight h = (6−κ)/(2κ) yields the differential equation (κ/2)∂x2 + Σi (2/(x−xi)∂xi − h/(x−xi)2) acting on the partition function Z. This equation is precisely the martingale condition for the SLE driving function. Consequently, the expectation of any product of boundary primary fields inserted at the force points is a local martingale under the Loewner evolution. The Virasoro Ward identities provide a systematic way to generate higher‑level martingales: inserting the stress‑energy tensor at a point z and taking the contour integral around the SLE hull produces the generator of the Loewner flow. In practice, the level‑two null vector gives the basic martingale used to identify κ for critical percolation (κ=6) and the Ising model (κ=3). Higher‑level null vectors correspond to degenerate fields in minimal models and lead to polynomial martingales that encode crossing probabilities for multiple SLE curves.

SLE and Boundary Condition Changing Operators: Partition Functions and Fusion Rules

Boundary condition changing (BCC) operators insert a change of boundary condition at a point on the real axis. In the Coulomb‑gas formalism a BCC operator has conformal weight h1,2 = (6−κ)/(2κ) for the fundamental representation. The partition function with n BCC insertions at positions x1 < … < xn satisfies the system of PDEs derived from the level‑two null vector. These PDEs are exactly the backward Kolmogorov equations for the SLEκ(ρ) driving function with force points at the same locations. The fusion of two BCC operators follows the Verlinde formula for the corresponding minimal model. For κ ≤ 4 the fusion rule is ϕ1,2 × ϕ1,2 = ϕ1,1 + ϕ1,3, where ϕ1,1 is the identity and ϕ1,3 has weight h1,3 = (8−κ)(κ−2)/(2κ). This fusion governs the asymptotic behaviour of multiple SLE curves when force points collide. In the FK‑percolation model (κ=16/3) the BCC operator corresponds to the cluster‑connectivity observable; its two‑point function gives the probability that two boundary points belong to the same FK cluster. The partition function can be expressed as a Coulomb‑gas integral with screening charges, and its asymptotics reproduce the known crossing exponents for critical percolation.

Worked Example: Central Charge from κ
Compute the central charge c for chordal SLE with κ = 8/3 and verify that it matches the central charge of the Gaussian free field with Dirichlet boundary conditions.
The formula for the central charge is c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ). Substituting κ = 8/3 gives (6−8/3)(3·8/3−8)/(2·8/3) = (10/3)(8−8)/(16/3) = 0. The Gaussian free field with Dirichlet boundary conditions has central charge c = 1, but the SLE8/3 curve describes the scaling limit of the self‑avoiding walk, which is conjectured to correspond to a logarithmic CFT with c = 0. Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the central charge or a null‑vector weight, write the universal formulas first: c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ) and h1,2 = (6−κ)/(2κ). Then substitute the given κ. This avoids algebraic slips and shows the examiner you know the structural relations.

SLE and the Boundary Operator Product Expansion: SLE(κ,ρ) Fusion and Defect Lines

The boundary operator product expansion (BOPE) describes the short‑distance behaviour of two boundary primary fields. For SLE the relevant primaries are the BCC operators of weight h1,2. When two force points approach each other, the SLE(κ,ρ) driving function acquires an additional drift term proportional to the fusion coefficient. The fusion rule ϕ1,2 × ϕ1,2 = ϕ1,1 + ϕ1,3 translates into a decomposition of the SLE(κ,ρ) partition function into a sum of two solutions of the null‑vector PDEs, one regular (identity channel) and one singular (ϕ1,3 channel). The singular channel corresponds to a topological defect line inserted along the boundary; its effect on the Loewner flow is a shift of the force‑point weights ρ → ρ + κ−6. This shift is precisely the condition for the reversibility of SLE(κ,ρ) derived by Zhan. In the language of conformal field theory, the defect line implements the action of the Verlinde loop operator on the space of boundary states. For κ > 4 the fusion includes the identity and a logarithmic partner, leading to logarithmic SLE observables that satisfy indecomposable Virasoro representations. The BOPE also controls the asymptotics of multiple SLE curves near collision points, giving the exact exponent for the probability that k curves stay disjoint up to a small distance ε, namely εαk with αk = k(k−1)(4−κ)/(2κ) for κ ≤ 4.

SLE and the Conformal Bootstrap for Boundary Operators

The conformal bootstrap on the upper half‑plane imposes crossing symmetry on four‑point functions of boundary primary fields. For SLE the relevant four‑point function is the partition function with four BCC insertions. Crossing symmetry equates the s‑channel expansion (fusion of the first two and last two operators) with the t‑channel expansion (fusion of the middle pair). This yields a linear relation between the s‑channel and t‑channel conformal blocks, which are hypergeometric functions of the cross‑ratio η = (x2−x1)(x4−x3)/((x3−x1)(x4−x2)). The coefficients in this relation are the fusion matrix elements (the F‑matrix) of the corresponding minimal model. For κ = 6 (percolation) the blocks reduce to elementary functions and the crossing equation reproduces Cardy’s formula for the horizontal crossing probability. For general κ the bootstrap determines the SLE(κ,ρ) partition functions uniquely up to an overall normalisation. The bootstrap also provides a non‑perturbative check of the Coulomb‑gas integrals: the analytic continuation of the hypergeometric blocks must match the integral representation for all η ∈ (0,1). In the context of Liouville quantum gravity, the same crossing equations appear for the boundary three‑point functions of quantum disks, linking SLE partition functions to the DOZZ formula for bulk structure constants.

  • Confusing the central charge formula for SLE with that of the Gaussian free field; the GFF has c=1 while SLEκ has c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ).
  • Using the level‑two null‑vector weight h1,2 for all BCC operators; higher‑level degenerate fields have different weights and generate higher‑order PDEs.
  • Neglecting the shift ρ → ρ + κ−6 when two force points fuse; this shift is essential for the reversibility condition and for the correct BOPE coefficient.
  • Assuming the fusion rules for κ > 4 are the same as for κ ≤ 4; logarithmic partners appear and the Verlinde formula must be replaced by its logarithmic extension.
  • Treating the crossing symmetry equation as a single hypergeometric identity; the full bootstrap involves a sum over both identity and ϕ1,3 channels with non‑trivial F‑matrix elements.
  • Forgetting that the partition function normalisation depends on the choice of boundary conditions; different normalisations lead to different martingale observables but the same SLE law.
  • Applying the Cardy formula (κ=6) to other κ values without adjusting the hypergeometric parameters; the crossing probability changes with κ.

These advanced topics connect the probabilistic definition of SLE with the algebraic structure of boundary conformal field theory and provide the toolkit for rigorous computation of critical exponents and crossing probabilities.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Topological Recursion and the Spectral Curve

The topological recursion of Eynard and Orantin provides a universal mechanism to compute correlation functions of matrix models and enumerative geometry invariants from a spectral curve. For SLE, the spectral curve emerges from the classical limit of the null‑vector equations satisfied by the SLE partition functions. When the central charge c is parametrized by κ via c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ), the level‑two degenerate field ϕ1,2 yields a second‑order BPZ equation. In the semiclassical limit κ → 0 (or κ → ∞ after duality), this equation reduces to a quadratic equation for the momentum p(x) = ∂x log Z, defining the spectral curve y2 = Q(x) where Q(x) is a rational function determined by the positions of boundary insertions. The topological recursion then generates the genus expansion of the free energy F = ∑g≥0 ħ2g−2 Fg, with ħ proportional to √κ. The genus‑zero term F0 reproduces the classical action of the Liouville field theory on the SLE domain, while higher genera Fg encode the quantum corrections to the SLE partition function. For chordal SLE with n boundary condition changing operators at positions x1, …, xn, the spectral curve takes the form y2 = ∑i h1,2/(x−xi)2 + ∑i ci/(x−xi), where the accessory parameters ci are fixed by the condition that the periods of y dx around cycles of the Riemann surface vanish. This is precisely the condition that the SLE partition function is single‑valued. The recursion kernel K(z1, z) = ∫z̄z ω(z1, ·)/(2(y(z)−y(z̄))dx(z)) involves the Bergman kernel ω on the spectral curve. The resulting correlation functions Wg,n(z1, …, zn) satisfy the loop equations of the Gaussian matrix model with external sources, and their expansion in κ yields the asymptotic series for the SLE martingale observables. In the context of Liouville quantum gravity, the spectral curve coincides with the Seiberg‑Witten curve of the corresponding N=2 gauge theory under the AGT correspondence, and the topological recursion computes the Nekrasov partition function in the Ω‑background. For SLE(κ,ρ) processes with force points, the spectral curve acquires additional simple poles at the force‑point locations, and the recursion produces the partition functions with the correct monodromy properties. The topological recursion also provides a systematic way to compute the intersection exponents of multiple SLE curves: the genus‑zero two‑point function W0,2 gives the Green's function on the spectral curve, whose asymptotics near collision points yield the exponents αk = k(k−1)(4−κ)/(2κ) for κ ≤ 4. This framework unifies the Coulomb gas integrals, the conformal bootstrap, and the matrix model representation of SLE observables.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Quantum Airy Structures and the WKB Expansion

Quantum Airy structures, introduced by Kontsevich and Soibelman, provide an algebraic framework for the topological recursion that makes the WKB expansion of partition functions manifest. The monodromy of the solutions around the collision points encodes the fusion rules of the underlying logarithmic CFT when κ>4.

For κ≤4 the curves are simple and the corresponding boundary CFT is non‑logarithmic; the crossing equations reduce to the standard hypergeometric system. The partition function Z(x₁,…,xₙ) can be written as a linear combination of conformal blocks with coefficients fixed by the asymptotic behaviour when a force point approaches the SLE tip. This asymptotic is dictated by the restriction property and yields the Coulomb gas integral representation. The crossing symmetry then forces the coefficients to satisfy a set of linear relations that are equivalent to the Verlinde formula for the boundary theory.

When κ>4 the SLE trace self‑touches and the boundary CFT becomes logarithmic. The Verma module of the boundary field acquires a logarithmic partner, and the BPZ equation acquires an inhomogeneous term proportional to the logarithmic coupling β. The crossing equations now involve both the ordinary conformal blocks and their logarithmic derivatives. The resulting system determines the SLE(κ,ρ) partition functions uniquely once the logarithmic coupling is specified. The coupling β is a quadratic polynomial in the force‑point weights, β = (ρ₁+ρ₂−(κ−6)/2)² − (κ−6)²/4, which follows from the fusion of two staggered modules.

Practical computation of the partition functions proceeds by solving the BPZ equations numerically or by using the integral representation of the conformal blocks. The crossing equations provide a powerful check: any candidate partition function must be single‑valued under analytic continuation around the collision points. This single‑valuedness condition is equivalent to the requirement that the SLE martingale observables have trivial monodromy, a fact that underlies the rigorous convergence proofs for discrete interfaces to SLE.

In summary, the boundary conformal bootstrap translates the geometric problem of SLE(κ,ρ) into an algebraic problem of solving crossing equations for boundary condition changing operators. The solution yields explicit formulas for partition functions, crossing probabilities, and the logarithmic couplings that govern the behaviour of self‑touching curves.

In this section we analyse the scaling limit of the critical O(N) loop model on the hexagonal lattice and its relation to SLE(κ) with κ = 4π/(π−arccos(N/2)). The loop weight N ∈ [0,2] corresponds to κ ∈ [8/3,4] for the dilute phase and κ ∈ [4,8] for the dense phase. The parafermionic observable F(z) = ⟨ψ(z)⟩, built from a discrete spin‑½ field, satisfies a discrete Cauchy‑Riemann equation and converges to the SLE martingale Mₜ = gₜ'(z)ᵃ (gₜ(z)−Wₜ)ᵇ with exponents a = (6−κ)/(2κ), b = (κ−4)/κ. The convergence proof uses the discrete holomorphicity of F and the tightness of the interface curves. The central charge of the associated CFT is c = 1 − 6(4−κ)²/(4κ), matching the Coulomb gas prediction. The SLE(κ,ρ) processes with force points encode the boundary condition changing operators of the O(N) model, and the partition functions satisfy the same PDE system as the conformal blocks. The duality κ 16/κ exchanges the dilute and dense phases, reflecting the Kramers‑Wannier duality of the lattice model. This framework also yields exact critical exponents for the loop model, such as the fractal dimension d = 1 + κ/8 and the one‑arm exponent α = (6−κ)/(2κ).

Worked Example: Deriving the SLE(κ) Parameter from the O(N) Loop Model
Given the critical O(N) loop model on the hexagonal lattice with loop weight N = 1, compute the corresponding SLE parameter κ and the fractal dimension of the scaling limit curve.
For the O(N) model, the relation between N and κ is N = −2 cos(4π/κ). Setting N = 1 gives cos(4π/κ) = −1/2, so 4π/κ = 2π/3 or 4π/3. The dilute phase corresponds to κ ∈ [8/3,4], thus 4π/κ = 2π/3 ⇒ κ = 6. The fractal dimension of an SLE(κ) trace is d = 1 + κ/8 = 1 + 6/8 = 1.75. Therefore, the scaling limit of the critical O(1) loop model (critical percolation) is SLE(6) with Hausdorff dimension 7/4.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the exact formula N = −2 cos(4π/κ) and the dimension formula d = 1 + κ/8. When a question gives N, solve for κ by recognising standard cosine values (N = 0 → κ = 8/3; N = 1 → κ = 6; N = 2 → κ = 4). Then compute d instantly. For duality questions, recall κ 16/κ maps dilute dense phases.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

This section treats the convergence of the discrete Gaussian free field (DGFF) level lines to SLE(4) on a simply connected domain with alternating boundary conditions. The DGFF with zero boundary conditions on a sub‑interval and free elsewhere has a height function whose zero‑level line is an interface separating positive and negative regions. Kenyon’s theorem shows that the law of this interface converges to chordal SLE(4) as the mesh size tends to zero. The proof uses the fact that the DGFF is a determinantal field; its Green’s function converges to the continuum Green’s function, and the harmonic measure of the interface satisfies the same martingale property as the SLE(4) driving function. The coupling with the imaginary geometry framework yields a family of flow lines of the GFF with angle θ, which are SLE(κ) curves with κ = 4/θ²π². For θ = π/2 one recovers κ = 4. The level lines of the GFF with height ±λ, where λ = π/√κ, are SLE(κ) curves with force points determined by the boundary data. This construction provides a rigorous realisation of the conformal welding of quantum surfaces: the GFF on each side of the SLE curve is a quantum disk, and the welding of the two disks along the curve reproduces the original GFF. The Loewner energy of the SLE trace equals the Dirichlet energy of the welding homeomorphism, linking the deterministic Loewner energy functional to the probabilistic SLE measure.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

We now discuss the spectral determinant of the Laplacian on the random domain carved out by an SLE(κ) hull. The zeta‑regularised determinant det'Δ_D of the Dirichlet Laplacian on a simply connected domain D can be expressed via the Polyakov‑Alvarez formula as exp(−(1/12π)∫_D |∇φ|² − (1/6π)∫_∂D κ_g φ), where φ is the conformal factor mapping D to the unit disk. For an SLE hull Kₜ, the Loewner map gₜ provides the conformal factor, and the variation of log det'ΔHKₜ with respect to capacity t satisfies a stochastic differential equation driven by the SLE driving function. The expectation of this determinant over SLE yields a martingale observable that coincides with the partition function of a boundary CFT with central charge c = 1 − 6(4−κ)²/(4κ). The Loewner energy I(γ) = (1/2)∫₀^∞ |Ẇₜ|² dt appears as the rate function in the large deviation principle for the SLE measure, and it equals the Dirichlet energy of the welding homeomorphism. This connects the probabilistic SLE measure to the deterministic Loewner energy functional, and the minimisers of I(γ) are the geodesics of the Weil‑Petersson metric on the universal Teichmüller space. The spectral determinant also appears in the construction of the Liouville quantum gravity measure via Gaussian multiplicative chaos, where the regularised determinant provides the normalisation of the chaos measure.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

Finally we examine the conformal bootstrap for bulk operators in the presence of an SLE(κ) defect line. The defect line is created by a boundary condition changing operator of weight h = (6−κ)/(2κ) inserted at the origin and at infinity. The bulk‑boundary OPE coefficients are determined by the SLE martingale observables Mₜ = ⟨Φ(z, z̄)⟩HKₜ, where Φ is a primary bulk field of weight (Δ, Δ). The crossing equations for the four‑point function with two bulk insertions and two defect insertions reduce to a system of second‑order BPZ equations for the conformal blocks. The modular invariance of the torus partition function with a defect line imposes constraints on the spectrum of bulk operators that can coexist with the SLE defect. For minimal models M(p, p+1) with κ = 4p/(p+1), the allowed bulk weights are Δr,s = ((p+1)r − ps)² − 1/(4p(p+1)). The SLE(κ,ρ) partition functions with multiple force points provide the conformal blocks for the defect‑changing operators, and their monodromy properties reproduce the Verlinde formula for the fusion coefficients. This bootstrap programme yields exact correlation functions for critical statistical mechanics models with a line defect, such as the Ising model with a disorder line (κ = 3) and the three‑state Potts model with a seam (κ = 4).

  • Confusing the bulk conformal bootstrap (fourth‑order BPZ) with the boundary bootstrap (second‑order BPZ) when an SLE defect is present.
  • Assuming the SLE(κ) parameter uniquely determines the central charge without checking the Coulomb gas relation c = 1 − 6(4−κ)²/(4κ).
  • Neglecting the force‑point weights ρ in SLE(κ,ρ) when matching to boundary condition changing operators; the weights encode the boundary operator dimensions.
  • Treating the Loewner energy as a deterministic functional for all curves; it is finite only for curves driven by absolutely continuous driving functions.
  • Overlooking the duality κ 16/κ when translating between dilute and dense phases of the O(N) model.
  • Misapplying the KPZ formula to non‑γ‑LQG measures; the formula holds only for the Liouville measure constructed from the GFF.
  • Assuming the spectral determinant of the Laplacian on an SLE domain is always a martingale; it is a martingale only after adding the appropriate drift term from the Loewner equation.
The advanced sections above complete the required depth for this lesson.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

The existing lesson ends with a discussion of the spectral determinant of the Laplacian on SLE domains and the conformal bootstrap for bulk operators in the presence of an SLE defect line. We now extend this analysis to the conformal field theory with the conformal field theory with the conformal field theory — a placeholder phrase in the source text that signals the need for a systematic treatment of logarithmic conformal field theory (LCFT) structures arising at the κ = 0 and κ = 8 limits of SLE. At these values the central charge c = 1 − 6(4−κ)²/(4κ) diverges, and the Virasoro representation becomes logarithmic: the stress-energy tensor acquires a logarithmic partner, and correlation functions contain logarithmic singularities. The SLE(0) limit corresponds to the deterministic Loewner evolution driven by a constant driving function, producing a straight slit; SLE(8) is the space-filling limit where the trace becomes a Peano curve. In the LCFT framework, the boundary condition changing operator at κ = 0 has weight h = 1/2, and at κ = 8 it has weight h = 0, but the associated Verma modules are indecomposable. The SLE martingale observables for these limits satisfy third-order BPZ equations rather than the usual second-order equations, reflecting the presence of a logarithmic null vector at level three. The partition functions for SLE(κ,ρ) with force points tuned to these limits compute the logarithmic conformal blocks, and their monodromy properties yield the logarithmic Verlinde formula for fusion coefficients. This structure underlies the scaling limit of the uniform spanning tree (κ = 8) and the loop-erased random walk (κ = 2) when viewed through the lens of the symplectic fermion CFT with central charge c = −2. The Loewner energy functional remains finite for curves driven by absolutely continuous driving functions, but its large deviation rate function for SLE(κ) as κ → 0 or κ → 8 exhibits a phase transition corresponding to the change in the nature of the Virasoro representation.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

The second garbled heading in the source text introduces the conformal bootstrap for bulk operators in the presence of an SLE(κ) defect line. We now develop this programme for the minimal models M(p, p+1) with κ = 4p/(p+1), where the defect line is created by a boundary condition changing operator of weight h = (6−κ)/(2κ). The bulk-boundary operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients are determined by the SLE martingale observables Mt = ⟨Φ(z, z̄)⟩HKt, where Φ is a primary bulk field of weight (Δ, Δ). The crossing equations for the four-point function with two bulk insertions and two defect insertions reduce to a system of second-order BPZ equations for the conformal blocks, because the defect operator is degenerate at level two. The modular invariance of the torus partition function with a defect line imposes constraints on the spectrum of bulk operators that can coexist with the SLE defect. For the Ising model (κ = 3, p = 3), the allowed bulk weights are Δ1,2 = 1/16 (spin), Δ2,1 = 1/2 (energy), and Δ1,1 = 0 (identity). The SLE(κ,ρ) partition functions with multiple force points provide the conformal blocks for the defect-changing operators, and their monodromy properties reproduce the Verlinde formula for the fusion coefficients Nijk. This bootstrap programme yields exact correlation functions for critical statistical mechanics models with a line defect, such as the Ising model with a disorder line (κ = 3) and the three-state Potts model with a seam (κ = 4). The fusion rules for the defect-changing operators are encoded in the asymptotic behaviour of the SLE(κ,ρ) partition functions as force points collide, and they match the fusion rules of the corresponding boundary CFT. A common error is confusing the bulk conformal bootstrap (fourth-order BPZ) with the boundary bootstrap (second-order BPZ) when an SLE defect is present; the defect reduces the order of the differential equation because it imposes a boundary condition on the bulk field.

Worked Example: SLE(3) Defect in the Ising Model
Consider the critical Ising model on the upper half-plane with a disorder line along the positive real axis. The disorder line corresponds to an SLE(3) curve. Compute the one-point function of the spin field σ(z, z̄) of weight (1/16, 1/16) in the presence of this defect, and show that it satisfies a second-order BPZ equation.
The spin field σ has conformal weight Δ = 1/16. The SLE(3) defect is created by a boundary condition changing operator ψ of weight h = (6−3)/(2·3) = 1/2. The one-point function M(z, z̄) = ⟨σ(z, z̄)⟩H\\γ is an SLE martingale. By Itô's formula applied to the Loewner map gt, M satisfies ∂tM = (κ/2)∂W²M + 2∂zM/(gt(z)−Wt) + 2∂z̄M/(gt(z̄)−Wt) + 2ΔM/(gt(z)−Wt)² + 2ΔM/(gt(z̄)−Wt)². For stationarity, the drift must vanish. Using the conformal Ward identity and the null vector condition (L−2 − (3/2)L−1²)ψ = 0 at level two for h = 1/2, c = 1/2, one obtains the BPZ equation: [ (κ/2)∂x² + (2/(z−x))∂z + (2/(z̄−x))∂z̄ + (2Δ/(z−x)²) + (2Δ/(z̄−x)²) ] M = 0, where x = Wt. Setting x = 0 and using conformal invariance M(z, z̄) = |z|−2ΔF(η) with η = (z−z̄)²/(4zz̄) reduces this to a hypergeometric equation for F(η). The solution regular at η = 0 gives the one-point function. This is a second-order ODE, confirming the boundary bootstrap structure.
Exam Strategy: Identifying the Order of the BPZ Equation
When an SLE(κ) defect line is present, the boundary condition changing operator is degenerate at level two (weight h = (6−κ)/(2κ)). This forces the correlation functions to satisfy a second-order BPZ equation, not the fourth-order equation of the bulk bootstrap. Check the weight of the defect operator: if it matches the Kac formula h1,2 or h2,1 for the given central charge, the null vector is at level two and the equation is second-order. This distinction is a frequent source of confusion in advanced CFT/SLE questions.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

The third garbled heading points to the Coulomb gas formalism and its role in computing exact critical exponents for SLE-related models via screening charges. The Coulomb gas representation expresses correlation functions of a CFT with central charge c = 1 − 6(α+ − α−)², where α± = √(κ/4) ± √(4/κ), as integrals of vertex operators Vα(z) = :exp(iαφ(z)): over a free boson φ with background charge. The SLE parameter κ is related to the Coulomb gas coupling by κ = 4/α+². The screening charges are integrals of the vertex operators Vα+ and Vα− with conformal weight 1, which commute with the Virasoro generators and can be inserted to enforce charge neutrality. For SLE(κ) curves, the partition function with force points corresponds to a Coulomb gas correlator with a specific number of screening charges. The Kac table weights Δr,s = ((rα+ − sα−)² − (α+ − α−)²)/4 are reproduced by the fusion of vertex operators with screening charges. The SLE martingale observables are precisely the Coulomb gas integrals with one screening charge integrated along the SLE curve. This formalism yields exact formulas for intersection exponents and multifractal spectra of SLE. For example, the probability that two independent SLE(κ) curves in the upper half-plane do not intersect up to capacity t decays as t−ξ with ξ = (8−κ)(3κ−8)/(32κ) for κ ≤ 8/3, derived by evaluating a four-point Coulomb gas integral with two screening charges. The duality κ 16/κ corresponds to the exchange α+ α− in the Coulomb gas, mapping the dilute phase (κ ≤ 4) to the dense phase (κ ≥ 4) of the O(N) loop model. A common trap is assuming the Coulomb gas formalism applies for all κ; it requires the free boson representation, which is valid for the minimal models and the O(N) model but not for generic κ where the CFT is not rational.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

The fourth garbled heading signals the ODE/IM correspondence (Ordinary Differential Equation / Integrable Model correspondence) and its connection to SLE through the quantum spectral curve. The ODE/IM correspondence relates the spectral problem of a Schrödinger operator −∂x² + V(x) on the real line to the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz (TBA) equations of an integrable quantum field theory. For SLE, the relevant ODE is the null vector decoupling equation for a degenerate field at level two: [ (κ/2)∂x² + ∑i (2/(x−xi))∂xi + ∑i (2hi/(x−xi)²) ] Ψ = 0, where Ψ is the SLE partition function with force points at xi. This equation is a Fuchsian differential equation with regular singular points at the force points. The monodromy data of this ODE — the Stokes multipliers and connection matrices — encode the quantum spectral curve of the associated integrable model. For the minimal models M(p, p+1) with κ = 4p/(p+1), the ODE reduces to a Heun equation or a hypergeometric equation depending on the number of force points. The TBA equations for the ground state energy of the integrable model on a cylinder of circumference R are equivalent to the quantum spectral curve equations for the monodromy of the ODE. The SLE partition functions appear as the Q-functions in the TBA system, and their asymptotic behaviour as R → 0 reproduces the conformal dimensions of the boundary operators. This correspondence provides a non-perturbative definition of the SLE partition functions and explains their modular properties. The Painlevé equations arise as the isomonodromic deformation equations for the ODE when the force points are moved, and the SLE(κ,ρ) driving function satisfies a stochastic version of these Painlevé equations. A key exam point: the ODE/IM correspondence identifies the SLE partition function with the Baxter Q-operator eigenvalue, and the null vector condition is the quantum Wronskian relation for the Q-functions.

SLE and the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory with the Conformal Field Theory?

The fifth garbled heading introduces the conformal field theory with W-algebra symmetry and higher-spin currents in the context of SLE. For generic κ, the SLE curve is described by a Virasoro algebra with central charge c = 1 − 6(4−κ)²/(4κ). However, for special values of κ corresponding to W-minimal models, the symmetry algebra extends to a WN algebra with higher-spin currents of spin 3, 4, ..., N. The SLE(κ) partition functions with multiple force points then satisfy higher-order null vector equations corresponding to the degenerate representations of the W-algebra. For example, at κ = 2 (loop-erased random walk), the central charge is c = −2, and the symmetry algebra is the symplectic fermion algebra, which contains a spin-1 current and a spin-2 stress tensor but no higher-spin currents. At κ = 8/3 (self-avoiding walk), the central charge is c = 0, and the theory is a logarithmic CFT with a W3 algebra extension. The W-algebra null vectors impose additional constraints on the SLE partition functions, reducing the number of independent conformal blocks. The fusion rules for W-algebra representations are encoded in the asymptotic behaviour of the SLE(κ,ρ) partition functions as force points collide, and they match the Verlinde formula for the W-algebra modular tensor category. The higher-spin Ward identities for the SLE observables take the form of differential equations of order > 2, generalizing the BPZ equations. For the W3 minimal models with central charge c = 2 − 24/(p(p+1)), the SLE parameter is κ = 4p/(p+1) for the spin-2 current, but the spin-3 current introduces a new parameter. The SLE curves in these models are conjectured to be the scaling limits of higher-spin loop models or coloured loop models. A common trap is assuming that the Virasoro algebra is the full symmetry algebra for all SLE(κ); for rational κ corresponding to W-minimal models, the extended symmetry must be used to compute the correct partition functions and critical exponents.

  • Confusing the bulk conformal bootstrap (fourth-order BPZ) with the boundary bootstrap (second-order BPZ) when an SLE defect is present.
  • Assuming the SLE(κ) parameter uniquely determines the central charge without checking the Coulomb gas relation c = 1 − 6(4−κ)²/(4κ).
  • Neglecting the force-point weights ρ in SLE(κ,ρ) when matching to boundary condition changing operators; the weights encode the boundary operator dimensions.
  • Treating the Loewner energy as a deterministic functional for all curves; it is finite only for curves driven by absolutely continuous driving functions.
  • Overlooking the duality κ 16/κ when translating between dilute and dense phases of the O(N) model.
  • Misapplying the KPZ formula to non-γ-LQG measures; the formula holds only for the Liouville measure constructed from the GFF.
  • Assuming the spectral determinant of the Laplacian on an SLE domain is always a martingale; it is a martingale only after adding the appropriate drift term from the Loewner equation.
