The pullback f*Lψ is the Artin–Schreier sheaf Lψ∘f. Its Fourier transform is, by definition, F(f*Lψ) = p2,!(p1*Lψ∘f ⊗ m*Lψ)[1]. The trace of Frobenius at y equals Σx∈k ψ(f(x) + xy). This is exactly the exponential sum S(y) = Σx∈k ψ(xp - x + xy). Because the map x ↦ xp - x is an 𝔽p-linear endomorphism of the additive group of k, its kernel has size p. The sum S(y) is a Gauss sum over the kernel; it equals p if y lies in the image of the dual map (which is the same map), and 0 otherwise. Hence the trace is p when y ∈ Im(f) and 0 otherwise. This matches the fact that the number of solutions of f(x) = y is p for y in the image and 0 otherwise, confirming the trace formula interpretation of the Fourier transform.
Exam‑day strategy
Remember that the ℓ‑adic Fourier transform shifts the perverse t‑structure by +1, so a perverse sheaf becomes a perverse sheaf placed in degree -1. This shift is often compensated by a Tate twist (-1) in normalisations; check the convention used in the problem. When computing exponential sums via the trace formula, always verify that the sheaf is constructible and that the projections in the correspondence are finite, otherwise the local terms are not defined.

Étale Cohomology and the Tame Fundamental Group in Anabelian Geometry

The tame fundamental group π1t(X) of a smooth variety X over a field k classifies finite étale covers of X that are tamely ramified along a given normal crossings divisor at infinity. When X is a hyperbolic curve (genus g ≥ 2, or genus 1 with at least one puncture, or genus 0 with at least three punctures), Grothendieck’s anabelian conjectures assert that the isomorphism class of X over a finitely generated field can be recovered from its tame fundamental group equipped with the natural outer Galois action. Mochizuki proved the full anabelian reconstruction for hyperbolic curves over p-adic fields, using the theory of the tame fundamental group and the associated weight filtration coming from the lower central series. The tame fundamental group fits into an exact sequence 1 → π1t(X¯k) → π1t(X) → Gal(ksep/k) → 1, and the outer action of the absolute Galois group on the geometric tame fundamental group encodes the arithmetic of X. The weight filtration on π1t(X¯k) is defined by the lower central series of the pro‑ℓ completion; its graded pieces are isomorphic to the ℓ‑adic realisations of the motivic Lie algebra of X. Nakamura and Tamagawa extended the anabelian results to higher-dimensional varieties with ample canonical bundle, showing that the tame fundamental group determines the variety up to isomorphism under certain conditions. The tame fundamental group also appears in the study of the étale homotopy type of X: the pro‑ℓ completion of the tame fundamental group is the fundamental group of the tame étale homotopy type, which is a pro‑ℓ homotopy type that captures the tame covers. In the context of the weight spectral sequence, the monodromy action on the nearby cycles of a semistable degeneration induces an action on the tame fundamental group of the generic fibre, and the weight filtration on the tame fundamental group is compatible with the monodromy weight filtration on cohomology. This compatibility is a key ingredient in the proof of the weight monodromy conjecture for curves and in the construction of the pro‑ℓ abelianised tame fundamental group as a Galois module. The theory of the tame fundamental group is also essential for the definition of the ℓ‑adic local systems with tame ramification, which form the coefficients for the geometric Langlands correspondence on curves with punctures.

Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Principal Bundles on Curves for Non‑Reductive Group Schemes

The moduli stack BunG of principal G-bundles on a smooth projective curve C over a finite field has been extensively studied when G is a reductive group. For non‑reductive group schemes — such as unipotent groups, Borel subgroups, or more general solvable groups — the geometry of BunG is considerably more subtle. The stack is no longer of finite type, and its cohomology does not satisfy the same finiteness properties. Heinloth and Yun have analysed the case where G is a Borel subgroup B of a reductive group Gred; they show that BunB stratifies by the Harder–Narasimhan type of the associated Gred-bundle, and the ℓ‑adic cohomology of each stratum can be expressed in terms of the cohomology of BunGred and the cohomology of the flag variety. For a unipotent group U, the stack BunU is an infinite‑dimensional ind‑scheme, but its ℓ‑adic cohomology can be computed using the theory of factorisation algebras and the geometric Satake equivalence for the dual group, which in this case is a pro‑unipotent group. The work of Drinfeld and Gaitsgory on the geometric Langlands correspondence for GLn uses the Whittaker sheaf on BunN, where N is the maximal unipotent subgroup; the cohomology of this sheaf is related to the space of automorphic forms. In positive characteristic, the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence of Lan–Sheng–Zuo relates the étale cohomology of BunG for a non‑reductive G to the cohomology of the moduli stack of Higgs bundles with structure group the Langlands dual of G. For a parabolic subgroup P, the stack BunP maps to BunL where L is the Levi quotient; the fibres are affine spaces, so the cohomology of BunP is a direct sum of shifted copies of the cohomology of BunL. This inductive structure allows one to compute the ℓ‑adic cohomology of BunP in terms of the cohomology of BunGred. The trace of Frobenius on these cohomology groups gives rise to automorphic forms for the non‑reductive group, which appear in the spectral decomposition of the space of functions on the adelic quotient G(k)\G(𝔸k). The main open problem is to extend the geometric Langlands correspondence to arbitrary non‑reductive groups, where the dual group is not a reductive algebraic group but a pro‑algebraic group; recent work of Gaitsgory and Raskin on the spectral action for non‑reductive groups provides a framework using the theory of D‑modules on the Ran space, but the ℓ‑adic analogue remains largely unexplored.

Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Stable Maps to Algebraic Stacks and Stacky Gromov–Witten Theory

The extension of Gromov–Witten theory to target algebraic stacks was pioneered by Abramovich, Graber, and Vistoli. Let X be a smooth proper Deligne–Mumford stack over a finite field k. The moduli stack Mg,n(X, β) of stable maps from n-pointed genus g curves to X with curve class β is a proper Deligne–Mumford stack equipped with a perfect obstruction theory in the sense of Behrend–Fantechi. The virtual fundamental class [Mg,n(X, β)]vir lives in the étale Chow group A•(Mg,n(X, β)) ⊗ ℚℓ, and its ℓ‑adic cycle class defines a class in the compactly supported étale cohomology H•c(Mg,n(X, β), ℚℓ). The stacky Gromov–Witten invariants are defined by integrating tautological classes against this virtual class; they take values in the étale cohomology of the inertia stack IX, which encodes the orbifold structure. The inertia stack decomposes as a disjoint union of components indexed by the conjugacy classes of stabiliser groups, and the cohomology of each component carries a natural grading by the age (or degree shifting number). The crepant resolution conjecture, proved in many cases by Coates, Iritani, Jiang, and others, relates the stacky Gromov–Witten invariants of X to the ordinary Gromov–Witten invariants of a crepant resolution Y → X via a symplectic transformation on the Givental space. In the ℓ‑adic setting, the comparison is mediated by the étale realisation of the motivic Donaldson–Thomas invariants of the derived category of coherent sheaves on X. The moduli stack of stable maps to a stack also appears in the geometric Langlands program for non‑simply connected groups: the Hecke correspondence for G-bundles on a curve can be interpreted as a correspondence of moduli stacks of stable maps to the classifying stack BG. The étale cohomology of these moduli stacks carries an action of the spherical Hecke algebra, and the trace of Frobenius computes the orbital integrals that appear in the Arthur–Selberg trace formula. Recent work of Ciocan‑Fontanine, Kim, and Maulik has developed a virtual fundamental class for stable maps to Artin stacks with finite inertia, using the theory of derived algebraic geometry; the ℓ‑adic realisation of this virtual class is expected to satisfy the same functorial properties as in the Deligne–Mumford case, opening the way to a stacky Gromov–Witten theory for general algebraic stacks.

  • Confusing the weight spectral sequence with the Leray spectral sequence; the former computes the cohomology of the generic fibre from the special fibre strata, the latter computes the cohomology of the total space from the fibres.
  • Assuming the ℓ‑adic Fourier transform preserves the perverse t‑structure without the shift [1]; the correct statement is that it exchanges the perverse t‑structure with its shift by one.
  • Neglecting that the tame fundamental group classifies only tamely ramified covers; wild ramification is captured by the full étale fundamental group and requires the theory of higher ramification groups.
  • Thinking the moduli stack BunG for a non‑reductive G is of finite type; it is typically an ind‑stack of infinite type, and its cohomology must be defined via a limit process.
  • Equating the virtual fundamental class in stacky Gromov–Witten theory with the ordinary fundamental class of the coarse moduli space; the virtual class lives in the Chow group of the stack and incorporates the obstruction theory.
  • Overlooking that the inertia stack components are indexed by conjugacy classes of stabilisers, not by the stabilisers themselves; the age grading depends on the choice of a representative in each conjugacy class.
  • Believing the crepant resolution conjecture holds for all Deligne–Mumford stacks without the condition that the resolution is crepant and that the stack has projective coarse moduli space.

Étale Cohomology and Anabelian Geometry: The Section Conjecture and Grothendieck's Program

Anabelian geometry, initiated by Grothendieck in his 1983 letter to Faltings and developed in Esquisse d'un Programme, posits that the étale fundamental group of a hyperbolic curve over a number field encodes the curve itself up to isomorphism. The central conjecture, the section conjecture, asserts that for a smooth projective curve X of genus g ≥ 2 over a number field K, the set of rational points X(K) is in bijection with the set of conjugacy classes of sections of the exact sequence 1 → π₁(XK̄) → π₁(X) → Gal(K̄/K) → 1, where π₁ denotes the étale fundamental group. This sequence arises from the functoriality of the étale fundamental group for the structure morphism X → Spec K. A section corresponds to a Galois-equivariant map Spec K → X, i.e., a K-rational point. The conjecture implies that the birational anabelian property holds: the isomorphism class of X over K is determined by the outer Galois representation Gal(K̄/K) → Out(π₁(XK̄)). Mochizuki proved the birational anabelian conjecture for hyperbolic curves over p-adic fields using his theory of p-adic Teichmüller theory and the theory of Frobenioids. For number fields, the section conjecture remains open; it is known for K = ℚ and certain modular curves by work of Stix and Harari–Stix, using the non-abelian Chabauty method of Kim. The étale cohomology of the moduli stack of curves enters via the action of the mapping class group on the pro-ℓ completion of π₁, and the Galois representation on the étale cohomology of the moduli stack Mg,n provides a linearised shadow of the anabelian picture. The Grothendieck–Teichmüller group GT, defined as the automorphism group of the tower of profinite completions of mapping class groups, acts on the étale fundamental group of Mg,n and is conjecturally isomorphic to the absolute Galois group Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ). The section conjecture for Mg,n itself would imply the injectivity of the map Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) → GT, a central problem in anabelian geometry.

Étale Cohomology and the Motivic t-Structure: The Category of Mixed Motives and the Standard Conjectures

The search for a universal cohomology theory led to the conjectural abelian category of mixed motives MM(k) over a field k, equipped with a motivic t-structure on Voevodsky's triangulated category of motives DM(k). The heart of this t-structure should be MM(k), and the ℓ-adic realisation functor Rℓ : DM(k) → Db(Repℓ(Gal(k̄/k))) is expected to be t-exact, inducing a fibre functor on MM(k) with values in ℓ-adic Galois representations. The standard conjectures of Grothendieck — Lefschetz type, Hodge type, Künneth type, and numerical equivalence equals homological equivalence — are sufficient to construct MM(k) as a Tannakian category with the Betti realisation as fibre functor. Over finite fields, the Tate conjecture implies the standard conjectures for abelian varieties (Milne), and the Weil conjectures provide the weight filtration. The motivic Galois group Gmot is the automorphism group of the fibre functor; its representations correspond to motives. The ℓ-adic realisation gives a homomorphism Gal(k̄/k) → Gmot(ℚℓ), which is expected to be faithfully flat. The Bloch–Kato conjecture (now a theorem of Voevodsky–Rost–Weibel) identifies motivic cohomology with étale cohomology: Himot(X, ℤ/ℓn(j)) ≅ Hiét(X, μℓn⊗j). The motivic t-structure would yield a weight filtration on mixed motives whose graded pieces are pure motives, compatible with the weight filtration on ℓ-adic cohomology via the realisation functor. The conservativity conjecture asserts that a morphism in DM(k) is an isomorphism if and only if its ℓ-adic realisation is an isomorphism for all ℓ ≠ char k; this is known for k finite or algebraically closed by work of Cisinski–Déglise. The Tate motive ℚ(1) corresponds to H2ét(ℙ1, ℚℓ(1)), and the motivic cohomology of a point is the Milnor K-theory of k by the norm residue isomorphism.

Worked Example: Section Conjecture for ℙ¹ {0,1,∞}
Let X = ℙ¹ℚ {0,1,∞}. Describe the exact sequence of étale fundamental groups and explain why the section conjecture predicts that the set of ℚ-rational points of X corresponds to conjugacy classes of sections.
The geometric fundamental group π₁(Xℚ̄) is the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group of ℙ¹(ℂ) {0,1,∞}, which is the free profinite group on two generators x, y corresponding to loops around 0 and 1 (the loop around ∞ is xy). The exact sequence is 1 → π₁(Xℚ̄) → π₁(X) → Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) → 1. A section s : Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) → π₁(X) is a continuous homomorphism splitting the projection. By functoriality of π₁, a ℚ-rational point P ∈ X(ℚ) gives a morphism Spec ℚ → X, inducing a section of fundamental groups. Conversely, a section gives a Galois-equivariant map from the geometric point to X, which by the anabelian property of X (a hyperbolic curve) corresponds to a rational point. The conjugacy class of the section corresponds to the choice of basepoint in the geometric fibre. For X = ℙ¹ {0,1,∞}, the rational points are ℚ {0,1}, and the section conjecture (proved for this case by Ihara and others using the theory of Galois representations on the pro-ℓ completion of the free group on two generators) asserts the bijection between ℚ {0,1} and conjugacy classes of sections.
Exam Strategy: Anabelian Geometry Keywords
When a question mentions "section conjecture", "Grothendieck's anabelian program", or "hyperbolic curve over a number field", immediately recall the exact sequence 1 → π₁(XK̄) → π₁(X) → Gal(K̄/K) → 1. The bijection is between X(K) and conjugacy classes of sections. For ℙ¹ {0,1,∞}, the geometric π₁ is the free profinite group on two generators. Mochizuki's work is for p-adic fields; over number fields the conjecture is open in general. Do not confuse the section conjecture with the birational anabelian conjecture (isomorphism of curves from outer Galois representation).

Étale Cohomology and Derived Algebraic Geometry: The Cotangent Complex and the Derived Étale Site

Derived algebraic geometry, developed by Toën–Vezzosi and Lurie, replaces schemes by derived schemes or spectral schemes, where the structure sheaf takes values in connective E∞-ring spectra (or simplicial commutative rings). The cotangent complex LX/S of a morphism f : X → S of derived schemes is a connective quasi-coherent complex on X that controls deformation theory: for a square-zero extension X′ → X with ideal I, the obstruction to lifting a map Y → X lies in Ext1(f*LX/S, I). In the étale setting, a morphism f is étale if and only if LX/S ≃ 0. The derived étale site of a derived scheme X has as objects derived schemes U equipped with an étale morphism U → X; the topology is generated by covers that are surjective on π₀. The ∞-topos of étale sheaves of spaces on this site is equivalent to the ∞-topos of étale sheaves on the underlying classical scheme π₀X (Lurie, Spectral Algebraic Geometry). This implies that the étale cohomology of a derived scheme with coefficients in a discrete sheaf depends only on its truncation. However, for coefficients in derived ℓ-adic sheaves (objects of the stable ∞-category Dlis(X, ℤℓ) of Lurie), the derived structure matters: the cotangent complex appears in the derived de Rham complex and in the Hodge–Tate comparison for p-adic derived schemes. The derived loop space LX = X ×X×X X has tangent complex LX[1], and its étale cohomology computes the Hochschild homology of X. The derived moduli stack of local systems LocSysG(X) parametrises G-local systems on a derived scheme X; its cotangent complex at a point ρ is the shifted cohomology complex RΓ(X, ad ρ)[1], where ad ρ is the adjoint local system. This derived enhancement is essential for the geometric Langlands correspondence in the sense of Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum, where the category of D-modules on BunG is replaced by the category of ind-coherent sheaves on the derived stack LocSysG(X). The ℓ-adic analogue uses the derived category of ℓ-adic sheaves on the derived moduli stack.

Étale Cohomology and (φ, Γ)-Modules: The p-adic Local Langlands Correspondence via (φ, Γ)-Modules

The p-adic local Langlands correspondence for GL₂(ℚp) establishes a bijection between irreducible admissible Banach space representations of GL₂(ℚp) over a p-adic field E and 2-dimensional continuous representations of Gal(ℚ̄p/ℚp) on E-vector spaces. Fontaine's theory of (φ, Γ)-modules provides an equivalence between the category of p-adic Galois representations of Gal(ℚ̄p/ℚp) and the category of étale (φ, Γ)-modules over the Robba ring ℛE. A (φ, Γ)-module is a finite free ℛE-module D equipped with a semilinear Frobenius φ and a continuous semilinear action of Γ = Gal(ℚp(μp∞)/ℚp) ≅ ℤp×, commuting with φ, such that the linearised Frobenius φ*D → D is an isomorphism. The étale condition is precisely that the map φ*D → D is an isomorphism. The functor V ↦ D(V) = (ℬrig† ⊗ℚp V)Gal(ℚ̄p/ℚp(μp∞)) realises this equivalence, where ℬrig† is the ring of p-adic periods of bounded Robba type. The p-adic Langlands correspondence of Colmez associates to a (φ, Γ)-module D a locally analytic representation Π(D) of GL₂(ℚp) via the Colmez functor using the p-adic local Langlands correspondence for (φ, Γ)-modules. The étale cohomology of the modular curve enters via the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for p-adic coefficients: the completed cohomology H1(X(p∞), ℤp) carries an action of GL₂(ℚp) × Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ), and its (φ, Γ)-module structure over the Robba ring interpolates the Galois representations attached to p-adic modular forms. The Breuil–Mézard conjecture (proved by Emerton–Gee–Savitt) relates the Hilbert–Samuel multiplicities of potentially crystalline deformation rings to the reduction mod p of the corresponding (φ, Γ)-modules. For GLn, the theory of (φ, Γ)-modules over the Robba ring in several variables (Kedlaya–Liu) classifies p-adic Galois representations of Gal(ℚ̄p/ℚp) of dimension n, but the local Langlands correspondence for GLn(ℚp) in the p-adic setting remains conjectural beyond n = 2.

Étale Cohomology and the Bloch–Beilinson Filtration: The Conjecture of Bloch and Beilinson on Algebraic Cycles

The Bloch–Beilinson filtration is a conjectural decreasing filtration Fν on the Chow group CHi(X)ℚ of codimension i cycles on a smooth projective variety X over a field k, such that F0 = CHi(X)ℚ, F1 = CHi(X)hom (cycles homologically equivalent to zero), and the graded pieces GrFν CHi(X)ℚ are related to the motivic cohomology H2i-νmot(X, ℚ(i)). The Bloch–Beilinson conjectures predict that this filtration is induced by the weight filtration on the mixed motive h2i-1(X)(i) and that the cycle class map CHi(X)ℚ → H2iét(X, ℚℓ(i))Gal has kernel exactly F1. The generalised Hodge conjecture (Grothendieck) and the Tate conjecture imply the existence of such a filtration. For k a number field, the étale Abel–Jacobi map AJét : CHi(X)hom → H1(Gal(k̄/k), H2i-1ét(Xk̄, ℚℓ/ℤℓ(i))) factors through the conjectural GrF1. The Bloch–Kato exponential map relates the p-adic étale cohomology to the de Rham cohomology via the period ring ℬdR, and the Tamagawa number conjecture of Bloch–Kato predicts the leading term of the L-function L(h2i-1(X)(i), s) at s = 0 in terms of the regulator on the motivic cohomology. The étale realisation of the motivic complex ℤ(i)mot gives a map H2i-1mot(X, ℤ(i)) → H2i-1ét(X, ℤℓ(i)), whose image is expected to be the Selmer group of the Galois representation H2i-1ét(Xk̄, ℤℓ(i)). The conjecture of Beilinson on special values of L-functions asserts that the regulator map from motivic cohomology to Deligne cohomology (or étale cohomology via the comparison isomorphism) computes the leading coefficient. The weight filtration on the mixed motive h2i-1(X)(i) has graded pieces that are pure motives of weight ≤ -1, and the Bloch–Beilinson filtration is the filtration induced by the weight filtration on the Ext-groups in the category of mixed motives.

  • Confusing the section conjecture (bijection between rational points and conjugacy classes of sections of the fundamental group exact sequence) with the birational anabelian conjecture (isomorphism of curves from the outer Galois representation); the former implies the latter but is strictly stronger.
  • Assuming the motivic t-structure exists unconditionally on DM(k); its existence is equivalent to the standard conjectures, and only the weight filtration is known unconditionally via the ℓ-adic realisation.
  • Thinking the derived étale site of a derived scheme has more cohomology than the classical étale site of its truncation; for discrete coefficients they are equivalent, but for derived ℓ-adic sheaves the cotangent complex enters.
  • Equating (φ, Γ)-modules over the Robba ring with all p-adic Galois representations without the étale condition (φ*D → D isomorphism); the étale condition is essential for the equivalence.
  • Believing the Bloch–Beilinson filtration is known to exist for all smooth projective varieties; it is conditional on the standard conjectures and the Tate conjecture, and only the first step F1 = CHihom is unconditional.
  • Overlooking that the étale Abel–Jacobi map takes values in continuous Galois cohomology H1(Gal(k̄/k), H2i-1ét(Xk̄, ℚℓ/ℤℓ(i))), not in the étale cohomology of X itself.
  • Confusing the Colmez functor (from (φ, Γ)-modules to locally analytic representations of GL₂(ℚp)) with the global Langlands correspondence; the former is purely local and does not involve automorphic forms on adele groups.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Higgs Bundles on Higher Dimensional Varieties

The extension of the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence from curves to higher dimensional bases replaces the moduli stack of Higgs bundles on a smooth projective curve by the moduli stack HiggsX(G) of semistable G‑Higgs bundles on a smooth projective variety X of dimension d ≥ 2. The étale cohomology of this stack carries a natural perverse Leray filtration induced by the Hitchin fibration h : HiggsX(G) → A, where A is an affine space of Hitchin base parameters. The decomposition theorem for the proper map h (proved by Ngô for curves and extended by Maulik–Shen for higher dimensions under semistability hypotheses) yields a direct sum decomposition of the derived pushforward Rh*ℚℓ into shifted perverse sheaves on A. The associated graded pieces of the perverse filtration on H*ét(HiggsX(G), ℚℓ) are identified with the cohomology of the global nilpotent cone and with the cohomology of the moduli stack of G‑local systems on X via the non‑abelian Hodge isomorphism. In particular, the weight filtration on the mixed ℓ‑adic sheaves matches the perverse filtration, giving a geometric realization of the P = W conjecture for higher dimensional X. The presence of strictly semistable Higgs bundles forces one to work with the good moduli space in the sense of Alper, and the étale cohomology of the stack differs from that of the good moduli space by contributions from the stabilizer groups, which are recorded by the inertia stack. These contributions are controlled by the theory of twisted sectors and the orbifold cohomology of the stack, a feature absent in the curve case.

Key technical points for examiners: (1) the Hitchin map is only proper after restricting to the semistable locus; (2) the decomposition theorem requires the base field to be algebraically closed of characteristic zero or ℓ ≠ p in positive characteristic; (3) the perverse filtration is defined via the perverse t‑structure on the derived category of constructible ℓ‑adic sheaves on A; (4) the identification of the associated graded with the cohomology of the character stack uses the Simpson correspondence, which in higher dimensions is known only for GLn and under restrictive stability conditions. A typical exam question asks to explain why the weight filtration on H*ét(HiggsX(G)) coincides with the perverse filtration, and to indicate where the proof uses the purity of the Hitchin fibres.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of G‑Bundles on Curves with Parabolic Structure and the Geometric Langlands Correspondence with Parabolic Level

Let C be a smooth projective curve over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic not dividing the order of a reductive group G. Fix a finite set of marked points D ⊂ C and parabolic weights λ at each point. The moduli stack BunG,par(C,D,λ) of G‑bundles with parabolic structure at D is a smooth Artin stack of finite type. Its étale cohomology with ℓ‑adic coefficients carries an action of the spherical Hecke algebra at the unramified places and of the ramified Hecke algebra at the marked points, where the ramified Hecke operators are defined by modifications of the parabolic structure. The geometric Langlands correspondence with parabolic level predicts an equivalence between the derived category of D‑modules on BunG,par and the derived category of coherent sheaves on the stack LocSysǦ,par(C,D,λ∨) of Ǧ‑local systems with compatible parabolic data. On the level of étale cohomology this translates into a compatibility between the Hecke eigensheaf property and the spectral decomposition of the cohomology of LocSysǦ,par. The trace formula for the stack BunG,par (proved by Yun and extended by Chen–Zhu) expresses the trace of Hecke operators on H*ét(BunG,par, ℚℓ) as a sum over automorphic representations with prescribed ramification at D. The parabolic weights enter the formula through the central character of the local Langlands parameters at the marked points. A crucial technical ingredient is the factorisation property of the Hecke stack with parabolic level, which allows one to reduce the computation to local contributions at each marked point. The local contribution is the cohomology of the affine Grassmannian with parabolic Iwahori level structure, computed by the geometric Satake equivalence for the parahoric group scheme. The resulting cohomology groups are graded by the dominant coweights satisfying the parabolic weight inequalities, and the Hecke eigenvalues are given by the Satake parameters of the corresponding Ǧ‑local system.

Examiner's trap: Parabolic Hecke eigenvalues vs. Satake parameters
A question states: "Let G = GL2 and let D = {x} be a single marked point with parabolic weight λ = (1,0). Compute the eigenvalue of the Hecke operator Tx acting on the étale cohomology H1ét(BunGL2,par, ℚℓ) corresponding to a Ǧ‑local system with Satake parameter diag(α, β) at x."
The parabolic Hecke operator at x with weight λ acts via the modification of the parabolic structure of type λ. Under the geometric Satake equivalence for the parahoric subgroup Iwλ ⊂ GL2(𝒪x), the Hecke eigenvalue is the trace of the Satake parameter on the representation of Ǧ = GL2 with highest weight λ. The representation with highest weight (1,0) is the standard representation V of dimension 2. Its character evaluated on diag(α, β) is α + β. Therefore the eigenvalue of Tx on the Hecke eigensheaf attached to the given local system is α + β. The trap is to answer αβ (the determinant) or α² + β²; the correct answer uses the weight λ to pick the appropriate representation.
Exam‑day strategy
When a problem asks for a Hecke eigenvalue on a parabolic moduli stack, first identify the dominant coweight λ defining the parabolic level. Then recall the geometric Satake equivalence for the corresponding parahoric group: the eigenvalue is the character of the irreducible representation of the Langlands dual group with highest weight λ evaluated on the Satake parameter. Write down the representation explicitly (standard, symmetric power, etc.) before computing the trace.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Local Systems on Varieties with Boundary

Let X be a smooth variety over an algebraically closed field k, and let D ⊂ X be a simple normal crossing divisor. The moduli stack LocSysG(X D) of G‑local systems on the open complement U = X D with prescribed monodromy around the components of D is an Artin stack locally of finite type. Its étale cohomology H*ét(LocSysG(U), ℚℓ) carries a mixed Hodge structure (in characteristic zero) and a weight filtration in positive characteristic via the theory of weights for ℓ‑adic sheaves on stacks. The presence of the boundary divisor introduces a monodromy weight filtration on the nearby cycles complex ΨDℚℓ on the compactification of LocSysG(U) inside the stack of meromorphic connections. The graded pieces of this filtration are identified with the cohomology of the moduli stack of local systems on the strata of D with induced monodromy data, a result of Sabbah and Mochizuki in the complex analytic setting and of D. A. Kedlaya in the ℓ‑adic setting. The weight spectral sequence degenerates at E2 under the assumption that the monodromy is quasi‑unipotent, yielding a pure weight decomposition on the cohomology of the open moduli stack. This degeneration is the geometric counterpart of the Clemens–Schmid exact sequence for degenerating families of varieties. In the Langlands program, the boundary strata correspond to Levi subgroups of G, and the spectral decomposition of H*ét(LocSysG(U)) reflects the endoscopic classification of automorphic forms with prescribed ramification at D. The trace formula for the stack with boundary (proved by Ngô–Yun for curves and conjectural in higher dimensions) expresses the trace of Hecke operators away from D as a sum over automorphic representations whose local components at D match the prescribed monodromy. The ℓ‑adic cohomology of the compactified stack thus provides a geometric realisation of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula with ramification.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Coherent Sheaves on Fano Varieties and the Categorical Enumerative Geometry

Let Y be a smooth Fano variety of dimension n over an algebraically closed field k. The moduli stack CohY(v) of coherent sheaves on Y with fixed Chern character v is an Artin stack of finite type. Its étale cohomology with ℓ‑adic coefficients is the target of the categorical enumerative invariants defined by Joyce and by Kontsevich–Soibelman via the motivic Hall algebra. The Hall algebra product on H*ét(CohY, ℚℓ) is induced by the correspondence of short exact sequences of sheaves, and the integration map to the motivic quantum torus sends the fundamental class of the stack to the generating series of Donaldson–Thomas invariants. For Fano varieties, the stability condition is given by the slope with respect to the anticanonical polarization, and the Harder–Narasimhan filtration yields a stratification of CohY by semistable loci. The étale cohomology of each semistable stratum carries a pure weight (by the Weil conjectures for the corresponding moduli spaces of stable sheaves), and the wall‑crossing formula for the Hall algebra product translates into the Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing identity for the DT invariants. The categorification of the DT invariants is achieved by constructing a perverse sheaf of vanishing cycles on the critical locus of the Chern–Simons functional on the derived moduli stack; its hypercohomology recovers H*ét(CohY) and the weight filtration matches the perverse filtration. In the case of a Fano threefold, the virtual fundamental class of the moduli space of stable sheaves is identified with the fundamental class of the critical locus, and the étale cohomology of the stack computes the categorified DT invariants. The main technical input is the existence of a symmetric perfect obstruction theory on the moduli stack, which in the ℓ‑adic setting is provided by the derived deformation theory of coherent sheaves and the comparison theorem between the étale and the analytic cotangent complexes.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Stable Maps to Varieties with Target a Stack

Let 𝒳 be a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack of finite type over an algebraically closed field k, and let β be a curve class in the Chow group of 𝒳. The moduli stack 𝔐g,n(𝒳, β) of stable maps from n‑pointed genus g curves to 𝒳 representing β is a proper Deligne–Mumford stack with a perfect obstruction theory. Its étale cohomology H*ét(𝔐g,n(𝒳, β), ℚℓ) carries a virtual fundamental class [𝔐]vir in the Chow group of the stack, constructed by Behrend–Fantechi using the intrinsic normal cone. The Gromov–Witten invariants of 𝒳 are defined by integrating tautological classes against this virtual class. The comparison theorem of Abramovich–Graber–Vistoli shows that the étale virtual fundamental class coincides with the analytic virtual class after base change to ℂ, so the ℓ‑adic Gromov–Witten invariants satisfy the same axioms (splitting, divisor, topological recursion) as their complex counterparts. The orbifold cohomology of 𝒳 enters through the evaluation maps evi : 𝔐g,n(𝒳, β) → I𝒳 to the inertia stack; the pullback of the orbifold Poincaré pairing on H*ét(I𝒳) yields the genus zero three‑point correlators. The quantum product on the orbifold cohomology is defined by the genus zero potential, and the associativity (WDVV equations) follows from the gluing axiom for the virtual class on the boundary strata of 𝔐0,4(𝒳, β). In positive characteristic, the ℓ‑adic theory provides a Weil cohomology for the stack 𝔐, and the Frobenius action on H*ét(𝔐) yields a p‑adic analytic continuation of the quantum product via the Dwork–Monsky trace formula. The main open problem is the construction of a categorical lift of the virtual class to a perverse sheaf of vanishing cycles on the derived moduli stack, which would categorify the Gromov–Witten invariants in the sense of the cohomological Hall algebra.

  • Confusing the perverse filtration on the Hitchin fibration for higher dimensional Higgs bundles with the weight filtration on the curve case; the former requires the decomposition theorem for a non‑proper map after semistable restriction.
  • Assuming the geometric Satake equivalence for parahoric groups gives the same eigenvalues as for the Iwahori level; the representation attached to a parabolic weight λ is the irreducible representation of the dual group with highest weight λ, not the regular representation.
  • Neglecting the monodromy weight filtration on the nearby cycles complex when computing the étale cohomology of local systems on varieties with boundary; the Clemens–Schmid sequence is essential for the weight spectral sequence.
  • Treating the Hall algebra product on the moduli stack of coherent sheaves on a Fano variety as commutative; it is associative but graded‑commutative only after passing to the motivic quantum torus via the integration map.
  • Equating the virtual fundamental class of the moduli stack of stable maps to a stack with the fundamental class of the underlying coarse moduli space; the stacky structure contributes orbifold cohomology classes from the inertia stack.
  • Overlooking that the trace formula for BunG,par involves the central character of the local Langlands parameter at the marked points, which is determined by the parabolic weight λ, not merely by the unramified Satake parameter.
  • Assuming the weight filtration on H*ét(LocSysG(U)) is pure without checking quasi‑unipotence of the monodromy; wild ramification breaks purity and introduces non‑trivial weight monodromy.

These advanced topics illustrate how étale cohomology interacts with modern geometric representation theory, enumerative geometry, and the Langlands program, and they are precisely the areas where examiners test depth of understanding beyond textbook statements.

Étale Cohomology and the Motivic t‑Structure on Derived Categories

The motivic t‑structure, conjectured by Beilinson and constructed in various settings by Bondarko, Hébert, and others, provides a filtration on the triangulated category of mixed motives that mirrors the weight filtration on ℓ‑adic cohomology. When one passes to the ℓ‑adic realization functor, the heart of the motivic t‑structure maps to the category of mixed ℓ‑adic sheaves equipped with the weight filtration of Deligne. The key mechanism is the compatibility of the six operations (f∗, f!, f∗, f!, ⊗, Hom) with the t‑structures: the realization functor is t‑exact for the perverse t‑structure on constructible sheaves and for the motivic t‑structure on motives. This exactness yields a comparison isomorphism between the motivic weight spectral sequence and the ℓ‑adic weight spectral sequence, allowing one to read off the graded pieces of the weight filtration on Hⁱₑₜ(X, ℚℓ) from the motivic cohomology groups Hp,q_M(X, ℚ). In practice, the motivic t‑structure gives a conceptual explanation for the purity of smooth projective varieties: the motive of such a variety lies in the heart, so its realization is pure of weight i in degree i.

For non‑complete varieties the motivic t‑structure predicts a non‑trivial weight filtration that matches the one constructed by Deligne using compactifications and the nearby cycles functor. The recent work of Ayoub and Cisinski‑Déglise shows that the motivic t‑structure exists on the stable homotopy category of motives over a perfect field, and that the ℓ‑adic realization is a morphism of t‑structures. This result is essential for the proof of the weight‑monodromy conjecture in many cases, because the monodromy operator on nearby cycles corresponds under realization to the nilpotent operator on the graded pieces of the motivic weight filtration. Examiners often test the distinction between the motivic t‑structure (which is defined on the level of motives) and the perverse t‑structure (which lives on constructible sheaves), and they expect candidates to explain why the realization functor is t‑exact for the perverse t‑structure but only right t‑exact for the motivic t‑structure in general.

An important subtlety is that the motivic t‑structure is not known to exist over arbitrary bases; its construction uses resolution of singularities and the existence of a suitable category of motives. Over fields of characteristic zero the work of Voevodsky and Morel provides the necessary framework, while in positive characteristic one relies on alterations and the theory of motives with rational coefficients. The failure of the motivic t‑structure in certain positive‑characteristic situations is a common trap: students may assume that the weight filtration on ℓ‑adic cohomology always comes from a motivic t‑structure, which is false without the appropriate hypotheses.

Étale Cohomology and the Derived Satake Equivalence for Reductive Groups

The derived Satake equivalence, formulated by Bezrukavnikov‑Finkelberg and proved in the ℓ‑adic setting by Zhu, identifies the derived category of constructible ℓ‑adic sheaves on the affine Grassmannian Gr_G with the derived category of coherent sheaves on the Langlands dual group ^L G‑equivariant derived category of the Steinberg variety. This equivalence is a categorification of the classical Satake isomorphism, which matches the spherical Hecke algebra of G(ℚₚ) with the representation ring of ^L G. In the ℓ‑adic world the convolution product on D^b_c(Gr_G, ℚℓ) corresponds under the equivalence to the derived tensor product on Coh^L G(St), and the perverse t‑structure on the left matches the coherent t‑structure on the right. The geometric Satake correspondence thus becomes an equivalence of monoidal triangulated categories, preserving the six operations and the weight structures.

The mechanism relies on the nearby cycles functor for the loop group LG → Gr_G and the fact that the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the fibers of the affine Grassmannian carries a natural action of the dual group. The weight filtration on the ℓ‑adic side corresponds to the filtration by support on the coherent side, and the purity of the intersection cohomology complexes of Schubert varieties translates into the fact that the structure sheaves of the corresponding subvarieties in the Steinberg variety are pure. This compatibility is crucial for the proof of the local Langlands correspondence for GL_n via the Harris‑Taylor method, because the ℓ‑adic sheaves on the Lubin‑Tate tower are matched with coherent sheaves on the deformation space of p‑divisible groups through the derived Satake equivalence.

A frequent examination trap is to confuse the derived Satake equivalence with the classical (abelian) Satake isomorphism. The classical statement only concerns the spherical Hecke algebra and the representation ring, whereas the derived version works at the level of derived categories and respects the full monoidal structure. Another trap is to assume that the equivalence holds for all reductive groups without qualification; it requires the group to be split and the coefficient field to be of characteristic zero (or ℓ invertible in the residue field). In the non‑split case one must replace the affine Grassmannian by the affine flag variety and work with the Iwahori‑Hecke algebra, leading to the derived affine Hecke category.

Worked Example: Compatibility of t‑Structures
Let G be a split reductive group over ℚₚ and let IC_λ denote the intersection cohomology complex on the Schubert variety Gr_λ ⊂ Gr_G. Show that under the derived Satake equivalence the perverse sheaf IC_λ corresponds to a coherent sheaf placed in cohomological degree zero, and explain why this implies purity of the ℓ‑adic cohomology of Gr_λ.
The derived Satake equivalence Φ: D^b_c(Gr_G, ℚℓ) → D^b Coh^L G(St) is t‑exact for the perverse t‑structure on the left and the standard coherent t‑structure on the right. The intersection cohomology complex IC_λ is perverse, hence lies in the heart of the perverse t‑structure. By t‑exactness, Φ(IC_λ) lies in the heart of the coherent t‑structure, i.e. it is a coherent sheaf (concentrated in degree zero). The weight filtration on IC_λ is trivial because IC_λ is pure of weight zero (Deligne’s purity theorem for intersection cohomology of projective varieties, applied to the projective Schubert variety Gr_λ). Under Φ, the weight filtration corresponds to the filtration by support on the coherent side; a pure object of weight zero maps to a coherent sheaf with no non‑trivial sub‑quotients of different weights, which forces the sheaf to be a vector bundle on its support. Consequently the ℓ‑adic cohomology groups H^i(Gr_λ, IC_λ) are pure of weight i, matching the expected purity of intersection cohomology.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the relationship between a perverse sheaf on the affine Grassmannian and a coherent sheaf on the Steinberg variety, first state the derived Satake equivalence and its t‑exactness. Then identify the relevant Schubert variety and its IC complex. Use the fact that purity of IC_λ forces the image to be a coherent sheaf in degree zero. Mention the weight‑support correspondence to earn full marks.

Étale Cohomology and the p‑adic Period Map for Shimura Varieties

The p‑adic period map, constructed by Scholze and Caraiani‑Scholze, provides a morphism from the étale cohomology of a Shimura variety to the p‑adic Hodge theory of its associated p‑divisible groups. Concretely, for a Shimura variety Sh_K(G, X) with good reduction at p, the period map π_HT: Sh_K → Flag sends a point to the Hodge‑Tate filtration on the Tate module of the universal abelian variety. On ℓ‑adic cohomology (ℓ ≠ p) this map induces a Galois‑equivariant isomorphism between the étale cohomology of the Shimura variety and the cohomology of the flag variety with coefficients in certain automorphic vector bundles. The mechanism uses the pro‑étale site and the theory of diamonds to compare the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the infinite‑level Shimura variety with the p‑adic cohomology of the period domain.

The key input is the primitive comparison theorem of Scholze, which identifies the ℓ‑adic cohomology of a perfectoid space with its p‑adic étale cohomology after tensoring with ℂₚ. Applying this to the perfectoid Shimura variety at infinite level yields a Hodge‑Tate decomposition of the ℓ‑adic cohomology groups: H^i_et(ShK^pK_p, ℚℓ) ⊗ ℂₚ ≅ ⊕a+b=i H^a(Flag, Ω^b) ⊗ ℂₚ(−b). This decomposition is compatible with the action of the Hecke operators and the Galois group, and it realizes the local Langlands correspondence in the cohomology of Shimura varieties. The period map also controls the weight filtration: the graded pieces of the weight filtration on H^i_et correspond to the Hodge‑Tate weights appearing in the decomposition.

A common pitfall is to confuse the Hodge‑Tate period map (which lands in the flag variety) with the de Rham period map (which lands in the de Rham period domain). The Hodge‑Tate map is defined over ℂₚ and is Galois‑equivariant, while the de Rham map is defined over the reflex field and is not directly Galois‑equivariant. Examiners often ask to state the precise target of the period map and to explain why the Hodge‑Tate map is the correct one for ℓ‑adic cohomology comparisons. Another trap is to assume the period map exists for all Shimura varieties; it requires the Shimura variety to be of Hodge type or at least to admit a good integral model with a universal p‑divisible group.

Étale Cohomology and the Cohomological Dimension of Algebraic Groups over Global Fields

The cohomological dimension of an algebraic group G over a global field K governs the vanishing range of the étale cohomology groups H^i_et(G, ℚℓ) for torsion sheaves. For a connected reductive group G, the cohomological dimension equals the rank of G plus the number of real places of K where G is anisotropic, a result due to Borel‑Serre and refined by Harder. The mechanism uses the Bruhat‑Tits building of G over each completion K_v: the building is a contractible simplicial complex on which G(K_v) acts with compact stabilizers, and its dimension equals the rank of G over K_v. The global cohomological dimension is then the supremum of the local dimensions plus the contribution from the archimedean places.

In the ℓ‑adic setting, the cohomological dimension controls the finiteness properties of the ℓ‑adic cohomology of arithmetic quotients ΓG(K)/K_∞. For example, if cd_ℓ(G) = d, then H^i_et(ΓG, ℚℓ) = 0 for i > d, and the groups are finite‑dimensional ℚℓ‑vector spaces for i ≤ d. This vanishing is crucial for the proof of the Matsushima formula, which expresses the L²‑cohomology of the locally symmetric space in terms of automorphic representations. The weight filtration on these cohomology groups is trivial (pure of weight i) because the locally symmetric space is a rational homology manifold and the ℓ‑adic cohomology satisfies Poincaré duality with a pure weight.

Examiners frequently test the distinction between the ℓ‑adic cohomological dimension (which depends on ℓ) and the virtual cohomological dimension (which is independent of ℓ). For arithmetic groups the virtual cohomological dimension equals the dimension of the associated symmetric space minus the rank of the maximal ℚ‑split torus. A typical trap is to state that cd_ℓ(G) = dim(G) for all ℓ, which is false; the correct formula involves the rank and the anisotropic kernel. Another trap is to ignore the contribution of the archimedean places when computing the global cohomological dimension, leading to an underestimate by the number of real places where G is compact.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Fundamental Group of Higher Stacks

The étale fundamental group π₁^et(𝒳, x̄) of a higher Artin stack 𝒳 classifies finite étale covers of 𝒳 in the ∞‑categorical sense. For a Deligne‑Mumford stack the definition coincides with the classical one, but for general Artin stacks one must work with the pro‑étale site or the ∞‑topos of étale sheaves of spaces. The fundamental group fits into an exact sequence 1 → π₁^et(𝒳k) → π₁^et(𝒳) → Gal(k) → 1 when 𝒳 is defined over a field k, and the outer action of Gal(k) on the geometric fundamental group encodes the Galois representation on the étale homotopy type. The mechanism uses the shape functor from the ∞‑topos of étale sheaves to the ∞‑category of pro‑spaces, and the fundamental group is the first homotopy group of the shape.

In the ℓ‑adic setting, the profinite completion of π₁^et(𝒳) controls the category of ℓ‑adic local systems on 𝒳 via the equivalence LocSys_ℓ(𝒳) ≅ Rep_ℓ(π₁^et(𝒳)^∧_ℓ). For higher stacks such as the moduli stack of G‑bundles Bun_G on a curve, the fundamental group is closely related to the geometric Langlands correspondence: the ℓ‑adic local systems on Bun_G correspond to D‑modules on the de Rham stack, and the fundamental group of Bun_G maps to the Langlands dual group. The weight filtration on the cohomology of ℓ‑adic local systems is governed by the monodromy action of the fundamental group, and the decomposition theorem for the Hitchin fibration yields a description of the graded pieces in terms of perverse sheaves on the Hitchin base.

A frequent examination error is to treat the étale fundamental group of a stack as the same as that of its coarse moduli space. The stacky structure contributes inertia groups at points with non‑trivial stabilizers, and these appear as additional finite quotients in π₁^et. For instance, the fundamental group of the classifying stack BG_m is the profinite completion of ℤ, whereas the coarse space is a point with trivial fundamental group. Another trap is to assume that the étale fundamental group of a higher stack is always profinite; in the ∞‑categorical setting it is a pro‑group object in spaces, and its profinite completion is needed to match ℓ‑adic local systems. Candidates should be prepared to explain the exact sequence for a gerbe banded by a finite group and how the band contributes a central extension of the fundamental group.

  • Confusing the motivic t‑structure with the perverse t‑structure; they live on different categories and the realization functor is only right t‑exact for the motivic one.
  • Assuming the derived Satake equivalence holds for non‑split groups without passing to the affine flag variety and the Iwahori‑Hecke category.
  • Mixing up the Hodge‑Tate period map with the de Rham period map; the former is Galois‑equivariant and lands in the flag variety, the latter does not.
  • Stating that the ℓ‑adic cohomological dimension of a reductive group equals its dimension; the correct formula involves rank and anisotropic kernel.
  • Identifying the étale fundamental group of a stack with that of its coarse moduli space, ignoring inertia contributions from stabilizers.
  • Neglecting the need for profinite completion when relating the étale fundamental group of a higher stack to ℓ‑adic local systems.
  • All of the above traps illustrate the precision required when moving between geometric, categorical, and Galois‑theoretic incarnations of étale cohomology.

Étale Cohomology and the Artin Comparison Theorem for Complex Varieties

The Artin comparison theorem asserts that for a smooth proper variety X over the complex numbers the ℓ‑adic étale cohomology groups H^i_et(XC̄, Q_ℓ) are canonically isomorphic to the singular cohomology groups H^i(X(C), Q) ⊗ Q_ℓ. The isomorphism respects cup products, cycle class maps, and the action of the absolute Galois group of C (which is trivial). The proof proceeds by reducing to the case of projective space via the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem for étale cohomology and then using the proper base change theorem together with the comparison for projective space, where the étale site is equivalent to the analytic site. A key point is that the theorem fails for non‑proper varieties; for example the affine line has trivial étale cohomology in positive degrees while its singular cohomology is non‑zero. The theorem also extends to smooth proper Deligne‑Mumford stacks, where the inertia groups contribute finite group cohomology that matches the orbifold singular cohomology. In examinations the distinction between proper and non‑proper cases is a frequent source of error, as is the mistaken belief that the comparison holds integrally; torsion phenomena such as the Brauer group require the use of the Kummer sequence and the identification H2_et(X, Z_ℓ(1)) ≅ H2(X(C), Z_ℓ(1)).

When X is defined over a subfield k ⊂ C, the comparison isomorphism is Gal(k)-equivariant after choosing an embedding k → C. This compatibility underlies the construction of the ℓ‑adic Galois representation on the cohomology of varieties over number fields. The weight filtration on H^i_et(Xk̄, Q_ℓ) corresponds under the comparison to the Hodge filtration on H^i(X(C), Q) via the Hodge‑Tate decomposition in p‑adic Hodge theory. Candidates should be able to state the precise hypotheses: X smooth, proper, geometrically connected over C, and ℓ a prime different from the characteristic (which is zero). The theorem does not require ℓ to be invertible on X because char(C)=0, but the same statement in positive characteristic requires ℓ ≠ p and the use of the proper smooth base change theorem.

Étale Cohomology and the Cohomological Dimension of Arithmetic Groups

Let G be a linear algebraic group defined over Q and Γ ⊂ G(Q) an arithmetic subgroup. The ℓ‑adic cohomological dimension cd_ℓ(Γ) is the supremum of integers i such that H^i(Γ, M) ≠ 0 for some ℓ‑adic Γ‑module M. The virtual cohomological dimension vcd(Γ) is the cohomological dimension of a torsion‑free subgroup of finite index; it is independent of ℓ. Borel and Serre proved that vcd(Γ) equals the dimension of the associated symmetric space X = G(R)/K minus the Q‑rank of G. For G = SL_n the symmetric space has dimension n(n−1)/2 and Q‑rank n−1, giving vcd(SL_n(Z)) = n(n−1)/2 − (n−1) = (n−1)(n−2)/2. The ℓ‑adic cohomological dimension can be larger because of ℓ‑torsion in the finite subgroups of Γ; for example cd_ℓ(SL2(Z)) = 1 for ℓ ≠ 2,3 but cd2(SL2(Z)) = 2 due to the presence of a 2‑Sylow subgroup. The Borel‑Serre compactification provides a manifold with corners whose cohomology computes the group cohomology of Γ and exhibits the weight filtration predicted by the theory of mixed sheaves. In the context of the Arthur‑Selberg trace formula, the cohomology of locally symmetric spaces ΓX appears as the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the associated Shimura variety, and the weight filtration is pure of weight i because the Shimura variety is a rational homology manifold.

A common examination task is to compute vcd for a given arithmetic group. The steps are: (1) identify the real Lie group G(R) and a maximal compact subgroup K; (2) compute dim X = dim G(R) − dim K; (3) determine the Q‑rank of G; (4) subtract the Q‑rank from dim X. For G = Sp2g the symmetric space has dimension g(g+1)/2 and Q‑rank g, yielding vcd = g(g−1)/2. Another trap is to confuse the ℓ‑adic cohomological dimension of the group with that of the associated locally symmetric space; the latter satisfies Poincaré duality and has dimension equal to dim X, while the former may be smaller because of the presence of cuspidal cohomology. The distinction between cd_ℓ and vcd is essential when applying the Grothendieck trace formula to the cohomology of Shimura varieties.

Computing virtual cohomological dimension
Compute the virtual cohomological dimension of the arithmetic group Γ = SL3(Z).
The group G = SL3 has real Lie group G(R) = SL3(R) of dimension 8. A maximal compact subgroup is K = SO(3) of dimension 3, so the symmetric space X = SL3(R)/SO(3) has dimension 5. The Q‑rank of SL3 is 2 (the maximal split torus over Q has dimension 2). Therefore vcd(Γ) = dim X − Q‑rank = 5 − 2 = 3. This matches the known result that the cohomology of SL3(Z) vanishes above degree 3 for torsion‑free subgroups of finite index.
Exam‑day strategy
When asked for vcd, first write down the formula vcd = dim(G(R)/K) − rank_Q(G). Memorise the dimensions of the classical symmetric spaces: SL_n gives n(n−1)/2, Sp2g gives g(g+1)/2, SO(p,q) gives pq. Then recall the Q‑rank: for split groups it equals the absolute rank. Subtract and state the result. If the question asks for cd_ℓ, check whether ℓ divides the order of any finite subgroup of Γ; if so, cd_ℓ may exceed vcd.

Étale Cohomology and the p-adic Langlands Correspondence for GL_n

The p‑adic Langlands correspondence for GL_n(Q_p) relates continuous representations of GL_n(Q_p) on p‑adic Banach spaces to n‑dimensional continuous representations of the absolute Galois group Gal(Q̄_p/Q_p) on Q_p‑vector spaces. For n = 2 the correspondence was established by Colmez using the theory of (φ,Γ)‑modules and the étale cohomology of modular curves. For general n the correspondence is conjectural, but significant progress has been made by Emerton, Breuil, Schneider, and others using the étale cohomology of Shimura varieties for GL_n and the theory of completed cohomology. The key geometric input is the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the tower of modular curves (or higher‑dimensional Shimura varieties) with level structure at p, which carries an action of GL_n(Q_p) × Gal(Q̄_p/Q_p). By passing to the limit over level subgroups one obtains the completed cohomology groups H^î, which are admissible Banach representations of GL_n(Q_p). The p‑adic local Langlands correspondence is then expected to be realized inside the derived category of these completed cohomology groups. The weight filtration on the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the Shimura variety translates into a filtration on the Banach representations, and the graded pieces are conjecturally described by the p‑adic Hodge theory of the associated Galois representations. In examinations the distinction between the ℓ‑adic (ℓ ≠ p) and p‑adic settings is crucial: the ℓ‑adic correspondence is a theorem (via the work of Harris‑Taylor, Henniart, Scholze) while the p‑adic correspondence remains largely conjectural for n > 2.

A typical question asks to explain how the étale cohomology of the Lubin‑Tate tower or the Drinfeld upper half‑space provides a geometric realization of the local Langlands correspondence for GL_n. The answer should mention that the Lubin‑Tate tower is a formal scheme whose generic fibre is a rigid analytic space whose ℓ‑adic cohomology carries an action of GL_n(Q_p) × WQ_p × D^× (where D is the division algebra of invariant 1/n). The cohomology realizes the local Langlands correspondence for GL_n and the Jacquet‑Langlands correspondence for D^×. For the p‑adic correspondence one replaces ℓ‑adic coefficients by p‑adic coefficients and uses the theory of (φ,Γ)‑modules to relate the Galois side to the Banach representations of GL_n(Q_p). The role of the weight monodromy conjecture in predicting the structure of the graded pieces of the weight filtration should also be mentioned.

Étale Cohomology and the Motivic t-Structure on the Derived Category of Étale Sheaves

Voevodsky's triangulated category of motives DM(k) admits a motivic t‑structure whose heart is conjecturally the abelian category of mixed motives MM(k). The ℓ‑adic realization functor R_ℓ: DM(k) → D^b_c(k, Q_ℓ) is a triangulated functor compatible with the six operations. A fundamental theorem of Ayoub and Cisinski‑Déglise shows that R_ℓ is right t‑exact for the motivic t‑structure and the perverse t‑structure on the étale derived category. This means that for a motivic complex M in the heart MM(k), the étale cohomology sheaves H^i_et(R_ℓ(M)) vanish for i > 0. The weight filtration on the étale realization corresponds to the motivic weight filtration, and the graded pieces are pure motives of the expected weight. The motivic t‑structure is characterized by the property that its heart consists of those complexes whose ℓ‑adic realizations have cohomology sheaves concentrated in non‑positive degrees for all ℓ. In practice, verifying that a given complex lies in the heart often reduces to checking the weight bounds on its ℓ‑adic realizations, which is a concrete computational task using the Weil conjectures.

An important application is the construction of the motivic cohomology groups Hi,j_M(X, Q) as HomDM(k)(Q(i)[j], M(X)). The ℓ‑adic realization identifies these groups with the étale cohomology groups Hi_et(X, Q_ℓ(j)) after tensoring with Q_ℓ, and the Bloch‑Kato conjecture (now a theorem of Voevodsky‑Rost) identifies the latter with Milnor K‑theory modulo ℓ. The motivic t‑structure also controls the behavior of the cycle class map: a cycle class in CH^j(X) maps to a class in H2j_et(X, Q_ℓ(j)) which lies in the weight zero part of the motivic filtration. Examiners often test the distinction between the motivic t‑structure and the perverse t‑structure: the former lives on DM(k), the latter on D^b_c(k, Q_ℓ), and the realization functor is only right t‑exact for the motivic one, not left t‑exact. Confusing the two leads to incorrect statements about the vanishing of negative motivic cohomology.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Higgs Bundles on Higher Dimensional Varieties

The moduli stack Higgs_G(X) of G‑Higgs bundles on a smooth projective variety X of dimension d > 1 carries a natural Hitchin fibration h: Higgs_G(X) → A, where A is an affine space of invariant polynomials. The non‑abelian Hodge correspondence identifies the ℓ‑adic cohomology of Higgs_G(X) with the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the character stack LocSys_G(X) of G‑local systems on X. For curves the decomposition theorem for h yields a direct sum decomposition of the pushforward h_* Q_ℓ into shifted perverse sheaves on A, and the support of these perverse sheaves is described by the nilpotent cone. In higher dimensions the Hitchin map is no longer proper, and the decomposition theorem must be replaced by the theory of perverse sheaves on Artin stacks and the weight filtration on the cohomology of the fibers. The work of Hausel‑Thaddeus, Maulik‑Okounkov, and others shows that the ℓ‑adic cohomology of Higgs_G(X) carries a natural action of the Weyl group and a mixed Hodge structure (in the complex case) which is reflected in the weight filtration on the ℓ‑adic side. The P = W conjecture, proved for curves by de Cataldo‑Hausel‑Migliorini, predicts that the perverse filtration on the cohomology of the character variety coincides with the weight filtration coming from the mixed Hodge structure. For higher dimensional X the conjecture is open, but recent work using the six operations formalism on stacks has established a version of the decomposition theorem for the Hitchin fibration on the moduli stack of Higgs bundles on surfaces, yielding a description of the graded pieces in terms of perverse sheaves on the Hitchin base.

A typical examination question asks to explain how the weight filtration on the ℓ‑adic cohomology of Higgs_G(X) is related to the perverse filtration via the Hitchin fibration. The answer should outline the following steps: (1) the Hitchin map h is a projective morphism of Artin stacks after suitable compactification; (2) the decomposition theorem for h (or its stacky analogue) gives a direct sum decomposition of Rh_* Q_ℓ into intersection cohomology complexes of the supports; (3) the perverse filtration on H^*(Higgs_G(X)) is induced by the truncation functors on the perverse t‑structure; (4) the weight filtration comes from the mixed sheaf structure on Q_ℓ; (5) the P = W conjecture asserts the equality of these two filtrations after passing to the associated graded. Candidates should also mention that for X a surface the Hitchin base is no longer an affine space but a more complicated stack, and the supports of the perverse sheaves are related to the nilpotent cone in the cotangent bundle of the moduli stack of bundles.

  • Assuming the Artin comparison theorem holds for non‑proper varieties; it requires properness and smoothness over C.
  • Confusing the ℓ‑adic cohomological dimension cd_ℓ(Γ) with the virtual cohomological dimension vcd(Γ); cd_ℓ can be larger due to ℓ‑torsion in finite subgroups.
  • Stating that the p‑adic Langlands correspondence for GL_n is a theorem for all n; it is only proved for n = 2.
  • Treating the motivic t‑structure and the perverse t‑structure as identical; they live on different categories and the realization functor is only right t‑exact for the motivic one.
  • Believing the Hitchin fibration is proper for higher dimensional base varieties; it is proper only for curves, and the decomposition theorem must be adapted using stacky perverse sheaves.
  • Neglecting the weight monodromy conjecture when describing the graded pieces of the weight filtration on the cohomology of Higgs bundles; the conjecture predicts the precise structure of these pieces.
  • Identifying the étale cohomology of the moduli stack of Higgs bundles on a surface with that of the coarse moduli space; the stacky inertia contributes additional finite group cohomology that must be accounted for.

Anabelian Geometry and Grothendieck's Section Conjecture

Anabelian geometry, initiated by Grothendieck in his 1983 letter to Faltings and developed in Esquisse d'un Programme, studies the extent to which the étale fundamental group π₁^ét(X) of a hyperbolic curve X over a number field k determines the isomorphism class of X. The central conjecture, the section conjecture, asserts that for a smooth projective curve X of genus g ≥ 2 over a number field k, the set of rational points X(k) is in bijection with the set of conjugacy classes of sections of the exact sequence 1 → π₁^ét(Xk) → π₁^ét(X) → Gal(k/k) → 1. Here π₁^ét(Xk) is the geometric fundamental group, a profinite group isomorphic to the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group of a genus g surface. A section s: Gal(k/k) → π₁^ét(X) corresponds to a rational point x ∈ X(k) via the functoriality of the fundamental group: x induces a map Spec(k) → X, hence a homomorphism Gal(k/k) ≅ π₁^ét(Spec(k)) → π₁^ét(X). The conjecture predicts that every section arises this way, and that two points give conjugate sections iff they are equal.

The section conjecture is known in very few cases. Stix (2002) proved it for curves over p-adic fields under certain conditions on the reduction type. Harari and Szamuely (2012) established a version for curves over finite fields. The birational anabelian geometry program, advanced by Mochizuki, extends these ideas to higher-dimensional varieties: the Grothendieck conjecture for hyperbolic curves over finitely generated fields asserts that the isomorphism class of the curve is determined by its étale fundamental group as a profinite group equipped with the outer action of the absolute Galois group of the base field. Mochizuki's inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUTT) claims a proof of the abc conjecture via anabelian methods, but its acceptance remains contested. For examiners, the key distinction is between the section conjecture (rational points sections) and the birational anabelian conjecture (isomorphism class of variety fundamental group). The étale fundamental group of a hyperbolic curve over a number field is a profinite group of rank 2g + r - 1 (where r is the number of punctures), and its outer Galois representation encodes the arithmetic of the curve. The Neukirch–Uchida theorem for number fields is the archetypal anabelian result: a number field is determined by its absolute Galois group as a topological group.

In the étale cohomological context, the section conjecture relates to the non-abelian cohomology set H¹(Gal(k/k), π₁^ét(Xk)). The set of sections modulo conjugation injects into this pointed set. The obstruction to a section coming from a rational point lies in the kernel of the map X(k) → H¹(Gal(k/k), π₁^ét(Xk)). The Chabauty–Kim method uses the non-abelian fundamental group and its ℓ-adic pro-unipotent completion to bound rational points, providing a higher non-abelian analogue of Chabauty's method. The ℓ-adic pro-unipotent completion of π₁^ét(Xk) carries a mixed Hodge structure (in the complex case) and a weight filtration, and the Selmer variety parametrizes certain torsors under this group. The non-abelian cohomology H¹(Gal(k/k), π₁^ét(Xk)un,ℓ) is a pro-algebraic variety whose k-points correspond to Galois-equivariant torsors. The section conjecture predicts that the image of X(k) in this Selmer variety is precisely the set of sections. This connects anabelian geometry to the theory of mixed motives and the motivic fundamental group.

The Fundamental Lemma and Ngô's Proof via the Hitchin Fibration

The fundamental lemma, conjectured by Langlands and Shelstad in the 1980s, is a combinatorial identity between orbital integrals on a reductive group G over a local field F and stable orbital integrals on its endoscopic groups H. It is the keystone of the stabilization of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula, which expresses the trace of Hecke operators on the space of automorphic forms in terms of geometric data. The lemma asserts that for a regular semisimple element γ ∈ G(F) and its transfer δ ∈ H(F), the orbital integral O_γ(1K) equals the stable orbital integral SO_δ(1K_H) up to a transfer factor Δ(γ, δ), where K ⊂ G(F) and K_H ⊂ H(F) are hyperspecial maximal compact subgroups. The proof by Ngô Bào Châu (2008, Fields Medal 2010) uses the geometry of the Hitchin fibration on the moduli stack of G-Higgs bundles on a smooth projective curve X over a finite field 𝔽_q.

Let M_G be the moduli stack of G-Higgs bundles (E, φ) where E is a G-bundle on X and φ ∈ H⁰(X, ad(E) ⊗ K_X). The Hitchin map h: M_G → A = ⊕i=1^r H⁰(X, K_Xd_i) sends (E, φ) to the characteristic polynomial of φ, where d_i are the degrees of the basic invariants of G. The fibers of h are (possibly singular) Lagrangian subvarieties. Ngô's insight was to consider the perverse sheaf R h_* ℚ_ℓ on A and its decomposition theorem. The support of the perverse cohomology sheaves ^p H^i(R h_* ℚ_ℓ) is a union of irreducible components of the nilpotent cone N = h-1(0). The fundamental lemma is equivalent to an identity between the weighted orbital integrals on G and stable orbital integrals on H, which Ngô interprets as the equality of the Frobenius traces on the stalks of certain perverse sheaves on the Hitchin base A. Specifically, the orbital integral O_γ(1_K) equals the trace of Frobenius on the stalk of the intersection cohomology complex IC(A^γ) at a point a ∈ A(𝔽_q), where A^γ is the open subset of A where the fiber is a torsor under the centralizer of γ. The endoscopic transfer corresponds to the decomposition of the perverse sheaf R h_* ℚ_ℓ into a direct sum of intersection cohomology complexes of the supports, indexed by endoscopic data. The transfer factor Δ(γ, δ) arises from the comparison of the Weil group actions on the cohomology of the fibers.

The proof proceeds by constructing a global argument over the curve X, using the fact that the Hitchin fibration is proper and the decomposition theorem holds. The key geometric input is the support theorem: the supports of the perverse cohomology sheaves ^p H^i(R h_* ℚ_ℓ) are precisely the closures of the images of the Hitchin bases of the endoscopic groups H under the natural maps A_H → A. This is proved using the affine Springer fibers and the geometric Satake equivalence. The fundamental lemma for the unit element of the Hecke algebra follows from the equality of the Frobenius traces on the stalks of the perverse sheaves, which in turn follows from the fact that the perverse sheaves on A_G and A_H are related by a Fourier transform (the Ngô support theorem). The general fundamental lemma (for arbitrary test functions) is reduced to the unit case by the transfer of orbital integrals and the stabilization of the trace formula. Examiners often test the distinction between the local fundamental lemma (orbital integrals on G(F) vs H(F)) and the global geometric proof (Hitchin fibration over a curve). The local statement is a combinatorial identity; the proof is global and geometric, using the cohomology of the Hitchin fibration over a finite field. The weighted fundamental lemma (for the derivative of orbital integrals) is proved by Chaudouard and Laumon using similar methods but with the perverse sheaf of vanishing cycles on the Hitchin base.

Worked Example: Section Conjecture for a Hyperbolic Curve
Let X be a smooth projective curve of genus 2 over ℚ. Describe the exact sequence relating π₁^ét(X), π₁^ét(Xℚ), and Gal(ℚ/ℚ). Explain how a rational point x ∈ X(ℚ) gives a section of this sequence, and state the section conjecture for X.
The étale fundamental group fits into the exact sequence 1 → π₁^ét(Xℚ) → π₁^ét(X) → Gal(ℚ/ℚ) → 1, where π₁^ét(Xℚ) is the geometric fundamental group, isomorphic to the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group of a genus 2 surface (a profinite group on 4 generators with one relation). A rational point x: Spec(ℚ) → X induces a map on fundamental groups π₁^ét(Spec(ℚ)) → π₁^ét(X). Since π₁^ét(Spec(ℚ)) ≅ Gal(ℚ/ℚ), this gives a homomorphism s_x: Gal(ℚ/ℚ) → π₁^ét(X) which splits the projection π₁^ét(X) → Gal(ℚ/ℚ), i.e., a section. Two points x, y give conjugate sections iff x = y. The section conjecture asserts that the map X(ℚ) → {sections modulo conjugation} is a bijection. In particular, every section arises from a unique rational point. This is an open problem for genus 2 curves over ℚ; it is known only in special cases (e.g., certain curves over p-adic fields by Stix).
Exam Strategy: Anabelian Geometry vs. Classical Galois Theory
Distinguish clearly: classical Galois theory studies Gal(L/K) for field extensions; anabelian geometry studies π₁^ét(X) for varieties. The section conjecture is about sections of 1 → π₁^ét(Xk) → π₁^ét(X) → Gal(k/k) → 1, not about field extensions. For the fundamental lemma, remember: the statement is local (orbital integrals on G(F)), but Ngô's proof is global (Hitchin fibration over a curve X/𝔽_q). The decomposition theorem for h: M_G → A and the support theorem are the geometric engines. Do not confuse the Hitchin base A (an affine space) with the nilpotent cone N = h-1(0). The perverse sheaf R h_* ℚ_ℓ decomposes into IC complexes of the supports, which are the images of endoscopic Hitchin bases.

Motivic Homotopy Theory and the A¹-Homotopy Category

Motivic homotopy theory, developed by Morel and Voevodsky in the 1990s, constructs the A¹-homotopy category H(k) = Ho(Spc_•(Sm_k)A¹) as the homotopy category of simplicial sheaves on the site of smooth schemes over a field k, localized with respect to the A¹-homotopy equivalence X × A¹ ≃ X. This provides a framework where algebraic varieties behave like topological spaces, and cohomology theories (étale, de Rham, Betti) become representable by motivic spectra. The motivic sphere spectrum 𝟙 represents motivic cohomology, and its stable homotopy groups πp,q(𝟙) are the motivic stable homotopy groups of the base field. The motivic cohomology Hp,q(X, ℤ) = HomDM(k)(M(X), ℤ(q)[p]) is represented by the motivic Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum Hℤ. The Suslin–Voevodsky theorem (proved by Voevodsky, 2003) identifies motivic cohomology with higher Chow groups: Hp,q(X, ℤ) ≅ CH^q(X, 2q-p). The Bloch–Kato conjecture (norm residue isomorphism theorem, proved by Voevodsky, Rost, Weibel et al.) states that the Galois symbol K^M_n(k)/ℓ → H^n_et(k, μ_ℓ⊗n) is an isomorphism; this is equivalent to the vanishing of certain motivic cohomology groups and the computation of πn,n(𝟙) ⊗ ℤ/ℓ.

The étale realization functor Re_et: SH(k) → SH_et(k) from the motivic stable homotopy category to the étale stable homotopy category sends the motivic sphere spectrum to the étale sphere spectrum and induces a map on homotopy groups πp,q(𝟙) → πp,q^et(𝟙). For a smooth variety X over a field k of characteristic not ℓ, the étale cohomology H^i_et(X, ℤ/ℓ^r(j)) is computed as HomSH_et(k)(Σ^∞_T X_+, Σi,j Hℤ/ℓ^r). The motivic Steenrod algebra acts on motivic cohomology, and its étale realization recovers the classical Steenrod algebra on étale cohomology. The Morel's connectivity theorem states that the motivic sphere spectrum is (0,0)-connective, and π0,0(𝟙) ≅ GW(k), the Grothendieck–Witt group of quadratic forms over k. The Milnor conjecture (proved by Voevodsky) identifies K^M_*(k)/2 with H^*_et(k, μ2⊗*), which is equivalent to π*,*(𝟙) ⊗ ℤ/2 being generated by the motivic Hopf map η ∈ π1,1(𝟙). The A¹-homotopy invariance of étale cohomology with finite coefficients (for ℓ invertible in k) is a theorem of Gabber: H^i_et(X × A¹, ℤ/ℓ^r) ≅ H^i_et(X, ℤ/ℓ^r). This is the cohomological shadow of the A¹-localization.

The motivic t-structure on the category of motives DM(k) (constructed by Bondarko, Hébert, and others) has heart the category of effective motives, and its realization to D^b_c(k, ℚ_ℓ) is only right t-exact. The perverse t-structure on D^b_c(k, ℚ_ℓ) is different; the realization functor does not preserve perversity. The weight structure on DM(k) (Bondarko) and the weight filtration on mixed motives are related to the weight filtration on ℓ-adic sheaves via the realization functor. The motivic Galois group G_mot(k) is the Tannakian fundamental group of the category of mixed motives (conjecturally), and its action on motivic cohomology recovers the Galois action on étale cohomology. The period isomorphism between Betti and de Rham cohomology lifts to a map of motivic spectra, and the motivic fundamental group π₁^mot(X, x) is a pro-algebraic group whose ℓ-adic realization is the pro-ℓ completion of π₁^ét(X, x). The Kim–Hain theory of the non-abelian fundamental group in motivic homotopy provides the geometric Selmer varieties used in the Chabauty–Kim method. Examiners test the distinction between the unstable A¹-homotopy category H(k) (where the motivic sphere is not invertible) and the stable motivic homotopy category SH(k) (where the Tate sphere 𝔾_m becomes invertible). The Tate sphere S1,1 = 𝔾_m is the motivic analogue of the circle; its suspension gives the Tate twist. The motivic Hopf map η: S2,1 → S1,0 is the first non-trivial stable motivic homotopy group, and its étale realization is the Kummer map.

The Theory of Diamonds and v-Stacks: Scholze's New Foundations
