This estimate follows from the Hadamard variation formula for eigenvalues combined with the evolution of the first eigenfunction u₁ under the flow. The key computation uses the identity ∂ₜu₁ = −H ∂ₙu₁ on Mₜ, where H is the mean curvature and ∂ₙ the outward normal derivative. Integrating by parts and applying the Reilly formula yields a bound on the time derivative of the Rayleigh quotient. A landmark result of Haslhofer (2019) shows that if the initial domain is mean convex and the flow exists smoothly until extinction at time T, then the quantity λ₁(t) (T−t) is non-decreasing. This monotonicity implies a sharp Faber–Krahn inequality for the extinction profile: the limit of λ₁(t) (T−t) as t→T is minimized by the round sphere. The proof uses the Łojasiewicz–Simon gradient inequality for the Dirichlet energy functional along the rescaled flow. For higher eigenvalues, the evolution is more subtle due to possible eigenvalue crossings; however, the sum of the first k eigenvalues satisfies a similar differential inequality. These spectral estimates have been used to prove uniqueness of tangent flows at singularities for mean convex MCF and to derive quantitative stability for the isoperimetric inequality under the flow. The techniques extend to Neumann and Robin boundary conditions, where the boundary term in the Hadamard formula involves the second fundamental form of Mₜ.

The Mean Curvature Flow of Hypersurfaces with Free Boundary on a Manifold with Corners: The Work of Hershkovits and the Regularity Theory

Free-boundary MCF asks for a family of hypersurfaces Mₜ ⊂ N meeting a fixed supporting hypersurface ∂N orthogonally along their common boundary. When ∂N has corners — i.e., it is a piecewise smooth hypersurface with edges and vertices — the regularity theory requires new barrier arguments and a refined blow-up analysis. Hershkovits (2019) established short-time existence and uniqueness for smooth initial hypersurfaces meeting ∂N at a prescribed contact angle, even when ∂N has edges of dihedral angle less than π. The key innovation is a family of barrier hypersurfaces constructed via the method of reflections, adapted to the corner geometry. For a dihedral angle α ∈ (0, π), the barrier is built from a rotationally symmetric self-shrinker in a wedge of angle α, whose existence follows from a shooting argument for the profile ODE. The regularity theory up to the corner uses a boundary monotonicity formula of Grüter–Jost type, modified by a cut-off function that respects the corner geometry. At a corner point, the Gaussian density of the flow is bounded below by the density of the static union of two half-planes meeting at angle α. If the density equals this lower bound, the blow-up limit is exactly that static union, and Allard-type regularity implies the flow is smooth near the corner. For higher codimension corners (vertices where three or more faces meet), the classification of tangent flows is open; however, the work of Edelen (2020) shows that any tangent flow at a vertex is a union of half-hyperplanes meeting at the vertex with angles determined by the geometry of ∂N. The free-boundary condition also interacts with the Huisken–Sinestrari convexity estimates: if the initial hypersurface is mean convex and ∂N is convex, the flow preserves mean convexity up to the corners, and the cylindrical neck detection algorithm extends to necks that intersect the boundary. This has applications to the construction of MCF with surgery for domains with corners, where the surgery parameters must be chosen uniformly away from the corners to avoid degeneracy.

Worked Example: First Eigenvalue Monotonicity under MCF
Let Ω(t) ⊂ ℝ³ be a family of smooth domains evolving by MCF with boundary Mₜ = ∂Ω(t), extinct at time T. Let λ₁(t) be the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of −Δ on Ω(t) with eigenfunction u₁ > 0 normalized by ∫Ω(t) u₁² = 1. Show that d/dt [λ₁(t) (T−t)] ≥ 0.
The Hadamard formula gives dλ₁/dt = −∫Mₜ H (∂ₙu₁)² dμ. The eigenfunction satisfies ∂ₜu₁ = −H ∂ₙu₁ on Mₜ. Differentiate the normalization: 0 = d/dt ∫ u₁² = 2∫ u₁ ∂ₜu₁ + ∫Mₜ H u₁². Using the Reilly identity ∫Ω (Δu₁)² = ∫Ω |∇²u₁|² + ∫Mₜ H (∂ₙu₁)² + II(∇u₁, ∇u₁) and Δu₁ = −λ₁u₁, we get λ₁² = ∫ |∇²u₁|² + ∫Mₜ H (∂ₙu₁)² + II(∇u₁, ∇u₁). By Cauchy–Schwarz, ∫ |∇²u₁|² ≥ (1/3)λ₁². For mean convex flow, H ≥ 0 and II ≥ 0 on Mₜ, so ∫Mₜ H (∂ₙu₁)² ≤ (2/3)λ₁². Thus dλ₁/dt ≥ −(2/3)λ₁². Now compute d/dt [λ₁(T−t)] = (T−t) dλ₁/dt − λ₁ ≥ −(2/3)λ₁²(T−t) − λ₁. Using the a priori bound λ₁(t) ≤ C/(T−t) (from the extinction profile), the right-hand side is non-negative for t close to T. A maximum principle argument extends this to all t.
Exam Strategy: Spectral Monotonicity
When asked to prove monotonicity of a spectral quantity under MCF, always start with the Hadamard variation formula. Identify the boundary term involving H and the normal derivative of the eigenfunction. Use the eigenfunction evolution equation ∂ₜu = −H ∂ₙu to convert time derivatives into boundary integrals. The Reilly formula (or Bochner identity) is the standard tool to relate ∫ H (∂ₙu)² to the eigenvalue. Remember the dimensional constant in the Cauchy–Schwarz estimate for ∫ |∇²u|² depends on the dimension of the domain (n+1), not the hypersurface (n). For free-boundary problems, the boundary term in Hadamard's formula includes the second fundamental form of the supporting hypersurface — do not omit it.

The Mean Curvature Flow and the Theory of Viscosity Solutions for Fully Nonlinear Geometric Equations: The Level Set Method and Its Extensions

The level set method of Chen–Giga–Goto (1991) and Evans–Spruck (1991) represents the evolving hypersurface Mₜ as the zero level set of a function u(x,t) solving the degenerate parabolic equation uₜ = |Du| div(Du/|Du|). This equation is the viscosity solution formulation of MCF, which allows for fattening (non-uniqueness of the level set flow) and handles topological changes without surgery. The theory of viscosity solutions for fully nonlinear equations of the form uₜ = F(D²u, Du) with F geometric (i.e., F(OᵀMO, Oᵀp) = F(M,p) for O ∈ O(n)) was developed by Ishii and Souganidis. For MCF, F(M,p) = tr(M) − ⟨M p/|p|, p/|p|⟩. The comparison principle holds for bounded uniformly continuous initial data, yielding a unique viscosity solution. The geometric property that the zero level set evolves by MCF in the classical sense wherever it is smooth is proved using the strict maximum principle for semicontinuous functions. Extensions to anisotropic MCF replace F by F_γ(M,p) = tr(A_γ(p) M) where A_γ is the Cahn–Hoffman ξ-vector of the surface energy γ. For crystalline energies, γ is not C¹, and the level set equation becomes a system of variational inequalities; the theory of Giga–Gurtin–Matias handles this via the subdifferential of γ. The level set method also applies to MCF with forcing terms uₜ = |Du| (div(Du/|Du|) + f(x,t)) and to the Allen–Cahn approximation uₜ^ε = Δu^ε − (1/ε²)W'(u^ε), where the zero level set of u^ε converges to the viscosity solution as ε→0 (Ilmanen, 1993). A key open problem is the uniqueness of the level set flow for non-convex initial data in dimensions n ≥ 3; the work of White (2000) shows that fattening occurs if and only if the initial hypersurface has a point of positive mean curvature where the inward and outward parallel flows meet. The viscosity framework is essential for numerical schemes: the monotone finite difference scheme of Oberbeck–Rumpf converges to the viscosity solution by the Barles–Souganidis theorem.

The Mean Curvature Flow in the Context of the Ricci Flow: Perelman's W-Entropy and the Hamilton-Huisken Monotonicity Formula

The coupling of MCF with Ricci flow arises naturally in the study of singularities of the Ricci flow via the Hamilton–Huisken monotonicity formula. Perelman's W-entropy for Ricci flow, W(g,f,τ) = ∫_M [τ(|∇f|² + R) + f − n] (4πτ)⁻ⁿ/² e⁻ᶠ dV, has a direct analogue for MCF discovered by Colding–Minicozzi (2012). For a hypersurface Mₜ evolving by MCF in ℝⁿ⁺¹, define the entropy functional E(M) = supx₀,t₀ ∫_M (4π(t₀−t))⁻ⁿ/² exp(−|x−x₀|²/4(t₀−t)) dμₜ. This is precisely the Gaussian density of the flow. The Hamilton–Huisken monotonicity formula states that for any fixed (x₀,t₀), the quantity Θ(x₀,t₀,t) = ∫_M (4π(t₀−t))⁻ⁿ/² exp(−|x−x₀|²/4(t₀−t)) dμₜ is non-increasing in t < t₀. Perelman's insight was to interpret this as the derivative of a functional along a gradient flow in a suitable metric space. For MCF, the gradient flow structure is in the space of immersions with the L² metric, and the entropy is the logarithm of the Gaussian density. The W-entropy for MCF is W(M,f,τ) = ∫_M [τ|H + ∇f|² + f − n] (4πτ)⁻ⁿ/² e⁻ᶠ dμ, where f is a weight function. Its monotonicity under the coupled flow (∂ₜM = H, ∂ₜf = −Δf + |∇f|² − n/2τ, ∂ₜτ = −1) was proved by Haslhofer–Kleiner (2017) and is the key to their proof of the mean convex neighborhood conjecture. The connection to Ricci flow is via the fact that a translating soliton of MCF corresponds to a steady Ricci soliton on the product manifold M × ℝ. The entropy stability of self-shrinkers (Colding–Minicozzi) is equivalent to the non-negativity of the second variation of Perelman's W-entropy at the corresponding Gaussian soliton. This dictionary has been used to transfer results: the classification of low-entropy self-shrinkers by Bernstein–Wang (2017) uses the entropy stability of the cylinder, which corresponds to the stability of the Bryant soliton in Ricci flow. The Hamilton–Huisken formula also implies the pseudo-locality theorem for MCF: if the initial hypersurface is close to a plane in a ball, the flow remains graphical for a short time with curvature bounds.

The Mean Curvature Flow and the Classification of Ancient Solutions in ℝ⁴: The Work of Brendle, Choi, Daskalopoulos, and Sesum

The classification of ancient solutions to MCF in ℝ⁴ represents a major breakthrough in the understanding of Type II singularities. An ancient solution is a smooth MCF Mₜ defined for all t ∈ (−∞, T) for some T ≤ ∞. In ℝ³, the only compact ancient solutions are the shrinking sphere and the Angenent oval (Daskalopoulos–Hamilton–Sesum, 2010). In ℝ⁴, the topology of the hypersurface can be more complicated: the Clifford torus S¹(√2) × S¹(√2) is a self-shrinker, and there exist ancient solutions asymptotic to it. Brendle (2016) proved that any compact ancient solution in ℝ⁴ with entropy ≤ λ(S¹×S¹) + ε is either a shrinking sphere, a shrinking cylinder S²×ℝ, or the Angenent oval. The proof uses the Hamilton–Huisken monotonicity formula and a refined analysis of the asymptotic behavior as t→−∞. The key step is to show that the rescaled flow Mₜ/√(−t) converges to a self-shrinker as t→−∞, and then to classify the possible limits. For non-compact ancient solutions, Choi–Daskalopoulos–Sesum (2018) classified all ancient solutions in ℝ⁴ that are graphical over a plane and have polynomial volume growth: they are either the translating bowl soliton, the grim reaper cylinder, or a family of ancient solutions asymptotic to the grim reaper cylinder constructed via a gluing method. The classification of ancient solutions with low entropy in ℝ⁴ is complete up to entropy λ(S¹×S¹) ≈ 1.85; above this threshold, the desingularized Clifford tori of Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller (2018) provide examples of embedded self-shrinkers with genus ≥ 2, and it is unknown whether ancient solutions asymptotic to them exist. The techniques involve the Łojasiewicz–Simon inequality for the F-functional, the spectral analysis of the linearized operator L = Δ − ½⟨x,∇⟩ + 1 + |A|² on the self-shrinker, and a delicate neck analysis using the Huisken–Sinestrari convexity estimates adapted to the ancient setting. The result has implications for the mean convex neighborhood conjecture in ℝ⁴: any Type II singularity of a mean convex flow in ℝ⁴ is modeled on one of the classified ancient solutions.

  • Confusing the entropy of the Clifford torus in ℝ⁴ with that of the cylinder in ℝ³; the Clifford torus has entropy strictly between the sphere and the cylinder in ℝ⁴, but its entropy in ℝ⁴ is not the same as the cylinder's entropy in ℝ³.
  • Assuming the Angenent oval exists in all dimensions; it exists only in ℝ³ (and as a product with ℝᵏ in ℝ³⁺ᵏ), but there is no rotationally symmetric ancient oval in ℝ⁴ with S²×S¹ symmetry.
  • Applying the Hamilton–Huisken monotonicity formula without checking the polynomial volume growth hypothesis; the formula holds for all smooth flows, but the convergence of the rescaled flow as t→−∞ requires polynomial volume growth to apply the compactness theorem.
  • Overlooking the role of the Łojasiewicz–Simon exponent in the convergence rate of ancient solutions to self-shrinkers; the exponent depends on the spectrum of the linearized operator and can be strictly less than ½ for degenerate shrinkers.
  • Confusing the grim reaper cylinder (translating soliton) with an ancient solution; the grim reaper cylinder is eternal (defined for all t ∈ ℝ), not just ancient, and its entropy equals that of the cylinder.
  • Assuming the desingularized Clifford tori are ancient solutions; they are self-shrinkers (defined only for t ∈ (−∞,0)), not ancient solutions extending to −∞.
  • Neglecting the difference between Type I and Type II ancient solutions in the classification; Type I ancient solutions have bounded curvature on parabolic balls, while Type II solutions require a separate blow-up analysis at infinity.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Classification of Ancient Solutions in ℝⁿ for n≥5

The study of ancient solutions — smooth flows defined for all t∈(−∞,T) — is central to understanding Type II singularities. In dimensions n=2,3 the classification is essentially complete: the only compact ancient solutions are the shrinking sphere and, in ℝ³, the Angenent oval (Daskalopoulos–Hamilton–Sesum, 2010). For n=4, Brendle (2016) and Choi–Daskalopoulos–Sesum (2018) extended the picture, showing that any compact ancient solution with entropy below λ(S¹×S¹)+ε is a sphere, a cylinder S²×ℝ, or the Angenent oval, while non‑compact graphical ancient solutions are the translating bowl, the grim reaper cylinder, or a glued family asymptotic to the grim reaper.

When n≥5 the landscape becomes dramatically richer. The entropy of the Clifford torus Sᵏ(√(2k))×Sⁿ⁻ᵏ⁻¹(√(2(n−k−1))) lies strictly between the sphere and the cylinder, and Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller (2018) constructed desingularized Clifford tori — embedded self‑shrinkers of arbitrarily high genus — whose entropy can be made arbitrarily close to that of the cylinder. It is unknown whether ancient solutions asymptotic to these high‑genus shrinkers exist. Moreover, the Hamilton–Huisken monotonicity formula still holds, but the compactness theorem for rescaled flows as t→−∞ requires a polynomial volume growth hypothesis; without it, subsequential limits may fail to be self‑shrinkers. Recent work of Hershkovits–White (2020) on the mean convex neighborhood conjecture in ℝⁿ shows that any Type II singularity of a mean convex flow is modeled on an ancient solution, but the full classification of low‑entropy ancient solutions in ℝⁿ for n≥5 remains open.

A key technical tool is the Łojasiewicz–Simon inequality for the F‑functional F(M)=∫_M e−|x|²/4 dμ. On a non‑degenerate self‑shrinker the inequality gives a convergence rate of the rescaled flow to the shrinker with exponent ½; for degenerate shrinkers (e.g. the cylinder) the exponent can be strictly smaller, which complicates the neck analysis. The Huisken–Sinestrari convexity estimates, adapted to the ancient setting, provide cylindrical neck detection, but their constants depend on dimension and deteriorate as n grows. Consequently, the classification program in high dimensions proceeds by a combination of entropy bounds, spectral analysis of the linearized operator L=Δ−½⟨x,∇⟩+1+|A|², and delicate gluing constructions.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Construction of Ancient Solutions via the Gluing Method of Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller

The gluing method produces new ancient solutions by perturbing a known singular configuration — typically a union of intersecting cylinders or grim reaper cylinders — into a smooth embedded flow. Kapouleas, Kleene and Møller (2018) desingularized the intersection of two orthogonal cylinders Sᵏ(√(2k))×ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ and Sⁿ⁻ᵏ⁻¹(√(2(n−k−1)))×ℝᵏ⁺¹ in ℝⁿ⁺¹, obtaining a family of embedded self‑shrinkers with genus growing with the gluing parameter. The construction proceeds in three stages: (1) an approximate solution built from the exact shrinkers cut off at a small radius and interpolated by a neck region modeled on a catenoid; (2) a Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction that solves the projected nonlinear equation on the orthogonal complement of the kernel of the linearized operator L; (3) a finite‑dimensional balancing condition that matches the asymptotic expansions of the neck and the cylindrical ends, yielding a genuine self‑shrinker.

The same philosophy extends to ancient solutions. By gluing a grim reaper cylinder to a translating bowl soliton along a common asymptotic cylinder, one obtains an ancient solution defined for all t<0 that is asymptotic to the grim reaper as t→−∞ and to the bowl as t→0⁻. The linearized operator around the grim reaper cylinder has a one‑dimensional kernel generated by the translation mode; the balancing condition fixes the relative shift of the two ends. The resulting ancient flow has entropy equal to that of the cylinder, and its existence demonstrates that the entropy threshold λ(cylinder) is not a barrier for ancient solutions in dimensions n≥4. The method also produces ancient solutions with higher entropy by gluing multiple grim reaper cylinders in a chain, each additional link increasing the genus and the entropy by a quantized amount.

Analytically, the gluing construction relies on precise weighted Schauder estimates for L on the neck region, where the weight captures the exponential decay of the cylindrical ends. The kernel of L on the cylinder consists of the translational modes and the dilation mode; the dilation mode is excluded by the self‑shrinker equation, leaving only translations. The balancing equations are then a finite‑dimensional nonlinear system whose solvability is guaranteed by the implicit function theorem once the gluing parameter is sufficiently small. This technique has become a standard tool for producing exotic ancient solutions and for testing the sharpness of entropy‑based classification conjectures.
