Write down the ordering sphere < cylinder < Clifford torus for ℝ⁴; this single fact resolves many multiple‑choice traps.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Theory of Viscosity Solutions for the Level Set Equation with Obstacle Constraints

The level set method represents an evolving hypersurface as the zero level set of a function u:ℝⁿ⁺¹×[0,T)→ℝ satisfying the degenerate parabolic equation ∂ₜu = |∇u| div(∇u/|∇u|). Evans and Spruck (1991) and Chen–Giga–Goto (1991) independently developed the viscosity solution framework for this equation, proving existence, uniqueness and a comparison principle for continuous initial data. The definition of viscosity sub‑ and super‑solutions uses test functions φ touching u from above or below; the geometric nature of the equation allows the comparison principle to hold despite the lack of uniform ellipticity.

When an obstacle constraint is imposed — for instance, the flow must stay outside a fixed closed set K — the level set function must satisfy u≥0 on K and the complementary slackness condition (∂ₜu − |∇u| div(∇u/|∇u|))·u = 0. This leads to a variational inequality of obstacle type. Barles and Souganidis (1991) extended the viscosity theory to such problems by introducing the notion of constrained viscosity solutions: a sub‑solution must satisfy the usual inequality on the open set {u>0} and a boundary condition on the free boundary ∂{u>0}. The comparison principle still holds provided the obstacle set K has a uniform exterior sphere condition, which guarantees that the distance function to K is a suitable barrier.

Regularity of the free boundary is a deep issue. For the classical obstacle problem for the heat equation, Caffarelli (1998) proved that the free boundary is C¹,α in space‑time. For the geometric obstacle problem, the work of Dirr, Dragoni and von Renesse (2010) shows that, under a convexity assumption on K, the free boundary is a C¹ hypersurface away from a singular set of parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n−1. The proof adapts the monotonicity formula of Almgren to the level set setting and uses a blow‑up analysis at free boundary points. These results are essential for numerical schemes that approximate the constrained flow by penalization, because they guarantee convergence of the discrete free boundary to the true one.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Evolution of the Gauss Map and its Role in Convexity Preservation

The Gauss map ν:Mₜ→Sⁿ assigns to each point its outward unit normal. Under MCF the normal evolves by ∂ₜν = ∇H, where H is the mean curvature. Differentiating the Weingarten relation ∇ᵢν = hᵢⱼ gʲᵏ ∂ₖ gives the evolution of the second fundamental form hᵢⱼ: ∂ₜhᵢⱼ = Δhᵢⱼ + |A|² hᵢⱼ. The maximum principle applied to the scalar quantity |ν−ν₀|² for a fixed direction ν₀ yields Huisken’s celebrated convexity preservation theorem: if the initial hypersurface is convex (all principal curvatures positive), then it remains convex until extinction. The proof uses the fact that the smallest principal curvature λ₁ satisfies ∂ₜλ₁ ≥ Δλ₁ + |A|² λ₁, so the minimum of λ₁ cannot become negative if it is initially positive.

The Gauss map also controls the avoidance principle. If two disjoint hypersurfaces evolve by MCF, the distance between their images under the Gauss map is non‑increasing; this prevents them from intersecting. More quantitatively, Andrews (1994) introduced the pinching quantity Q = (λₙ−λ₁)/H and proved that Q satisfies a differential inequality that forces it to decay, implying that the flow becomes asymptotically round near a Type I singularity. The evolution of the Gauss map is the geometric counterpart of the heat flow on the sphere, and its spectral gap provides the rate of convergence to a sphere for convex flows.

In higher codimension the Gauss map takes values in the Grassmannian of normal planes. The evolution equation acquires an extra term involving the normal connection, and convexity is replaced by the notion of mean convexity (H·ν ≥ 0 for all normal directions). The preservation of mean convexity under MCF was proved by Huisken and Sinestrari (1999) using a maximum principle for the smallest eigenvalue of the second fundamental form in the direction of the mean curvature vector. This result underpins the surgery program for mean convex flows in all dimensions.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Classification of Self‑Similar Solutions in Higher Codimensions

Self‑similar solutions — shrinkers, translators, expanders — are the building blocks of singularity models. In codimension one, Huisken (1990) classified all compact self‑shrinkers with polynomial volume growth as generalized cylinders Sᵏ×ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ, and Colding–Minicozzi (2012) proved uniqueness of the tangent flow for generic initial data using the entropy functional. In higher codimension the picture is far less complete. Smoczyk (1996) showed that any compact Lagrangian self‑shrinker in ℂⁿ must be a product of circles (the Clifford torus) up to unitary transformation. Wang (2001) constructed non‑Lagrangian self‑shrinkers in ℝⁿ⁺² by rotating a curve in a plane, yielding a family of embedded shrinkers with topology S¹×Sⁿ⁻¹.

Self‑translating solitons in higher codimension have been studied by Martín, Savas‑Halilaj and Smoczyk (2015), who proved that any complete translating soliton in ℝⁿ⁺² with bounded second fundamental form and polynomial volume growth is a product of a curve translator in ℝ² with a minimal submanifold. The grim reaper cylinder generalizes to a product of the grim reaper curve with ℝⁿ⁻¹. Self‑expanders are even more mysterious; the only known compact examples are the spheres and the Clifford tori, but non‑compact expanders with asymptotic cones exist and are related to the inverse mean curvature flow.

The entropy functional λ(Σ)=supx₀,t₀ ∫_Σ (4π(t₀−t))−n/2 e−|x−x₀|²/4(t₀−t) dμₜ remains the primary invariant for classifying self‑similar solutions. In codimension one, the entropy of the Clifford torus Sᵏ(√(2k))×Sⁿ⁻ᵏ⁻¹(√(2(n−k−1))) is strictly increasing in k and lies between the sphere and the cylinder. In higher codimension, the entropy of a product of two shrinkers is the product of their entropies, which can produce values not attainable in codimension one. This richness suggests that a full classification of self‑similar solutions in higher codimension will require new invariants beyond entropy, possibly involving the topology of the normal bundle.

  • Confusing the entropy ordering in ℝ⁴: the sphere has entropy 1, the cylinder S²×ℝ has entropy ≈1.52, and the Clifford torus S¹×S¹ has entropy ≈1.85; the Clifford torus is the largest, not the smallest.
  • Assuming the gluing construction of Kapouleas–Kleene–Møller produces ancient solutions for all dimensions; the method requires the linearized operator to have a one‑dimensional kernel, which fails for certain high‑genus desingularizations.
  • Applying the viscosity comparison principle for the level set equation without checking the exterior sphere condition on the obstacle set; the principle fails if the obstacle has inward cusps.
  • Using the Gauss map evolution ∂ₜν = ∇H in higher codimension without the normal connection term; the correct formula is ∂ₜν = ∇H + A(ν,·) where A is the second fundamental form of the normal bundle.
  • Believing that all self‑shrinkers in higher codimension are products of lower‑dimensional shrinkers; Smoczyk’s Lagrangian classification is a special case, and many non‑product examples exist.
  • Neglecting the polynomial volume growth hypothesis when invoking the Hamilton–Huisken monotonicity formula to extract a tangent flow at −∞; without it the rescaled flow may not converge.
  • Overlooking that the Łojasiewicz–Simon exponent for degenerate shrinkers can be strictly less than ½, which changes the convergence rate of ancient solutions to their asymptotic shrinkers.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Evolution of the Spectral Gap of the Laplacian on Evolving Hypersurfaces

The first non‑zero eigenvalue λ₁(t) of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on a closed hypersurface Mₜ moving by mean curvature flow satisfies a differential inequality discovered by Huisken (1990) and later refined by Cao (2007). If the flow exists on a maximal time interval [0,T) and the hypersurfaces remain uniformly convex, then λ₁(t) is non‑decreasing and blows up at the rate (T−t)⁻¹ as t→T. The proof uses the evolution equation for the metric gᵢⱼ and the Rayleigh quotient, together with the maximum principle applied to the quantity λ₁(t)−c/(T−t) for a suitable constant c depending only on the initial hypersurface. For non‑convex flows the spectral gap can drop, but Colding–Minicozzi (2012) showed that the entropy functional controls the λ₁‑behaviour near singularities: any tangent flow with entropy below the cylinder entropy has λ₁ bounded away from zero. In the setting of mean convex flows with surgery, the spectral gap provides a quantitative measure of the neck‑pinch region; the work of Brendle–Huisken (2017) proves that λ₁ on the rescaled neck converges to the first eigenvalue of the cylinder Sⁿ⁻¹×ℝ, which equals 1. This convergence is exponential in the rescaled time and its rate is dictated by the spectral gap of the linearised operator L = Δ + |A|² on the cylinder. The spectral gap also appears in the Łojasiewicz–Simon inequality for the area functional: the exponent θ = 1/2 is valid precisely when λ₁ of the linearised operator on the limit self‑shrinker is positive. For the sphere the gap is 2, for the cylinder it is 1, and for the Clifford torus it is 2/3. These numbers determine the convergence speed of ancient solutions to their asymptotic shrinkers.

Mean Curvature Flow with Nonlinear Mobility: The Porous Medium Type Flow

Replacing the linear mobility in the normal velocity V = H by a power law V = Hᵐ with m>1 yields the porous medium mean curvature flow, first studied by Ecker and Huisken (1991) for entire graphs and later by Kim and Lee (2005) for closed hypersurfaces. The equation becomes degenerate parabolic where H=0, so the flow instantaneously develops a free boundary separating the region of positive curvature from the flat region. Short‑time existence for smooth, strictly mean convex initial data follows from a De Giorgi–Nash–Moser iteration adapted to the geometric setting; the key estimate is a Harnack inequality for the pressure function p = Hᵐ⁻¹/(m−1). Long‑time behaviour differs sharply from the linear case: the extinction time is finite and the rescaled flow converges to a self‑similar Barenblatt profile rather than a sphere. For m>1 the extinction profile is a compactly supported solution of the stationary equation Δp + (1/(m−1))|∇p|²/p = 0, which in the radial case reduces to an explicit algebraic profile. The waiting‑time phenomenon — the interface does not move until the curvature exceeds a threshold depending on m — was proved by DiBenedetto and Friedman (1986) in the Euclidean setting and carries over to the geometric flow via the comparison principle with suitable barrier functions. In the anisotropic case where the mobility depends on the normal direction, the Wulff shape replaces the sphere as the asymptotic profile; the convergence rate is governed by the spectral gap of the linearised operator on the Wulff shape, which can be computed from the second variation of the anisotropic surface energy.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap Monotonicity
Let Mₜ be a smooth family of closed, uniformly convex hypersurfaces in ℝⁿ⁺¹ evolving by mean curvature flow on [0,T). Show that the quantity Q(t) = λ₁(t)(T−t) is non‑decreasing.
The evolution of the metric is ∂ₜgᵢⱼ = −2Hhᵢⱼ. For the first eigenfunction φ>0 with ∫φ²=1 we have λ₁ = ∫|∇φ|². Differentiating and using the Rayleigh quotient yields ∂ₜλ₁ = 2∫Hhᵢⱼ∇ⁱφ∇ʲφ + 2∫φΔφ ∂ₜφ. Integration by parts and the eigenfunction equation Δφ = −λ₁φ give ∂ₜλ₁ = 2∫Hhᵢⱼ∇ⁱφ∇ʲφ + 2λ₁∫Hφ². By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the convexity assumption hᵢⱼ ≥ (H/n)gᵢⱼ, the first term is at least (2/n)∫H|∇φ|². Since H>0, we obtain ∂ₜλ₁ ≥ (2/n)λ₁ min H. Huisken's estimate min H ≥ 1/(n(T−t)) then gives ∂ₜλ₁ ≥ (2/n²)λ₁/(T−t). Multiplying by (T−t) and adding λ₁ shows ∂ₜ[λ₁(T−t)] ≥ 0. Hence Q(t) is non‑decreasing.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for monotonicity of a geometric quantity under MCF, first write the evolution equations for the metric and the relevant operator. Identify the sign of the curvature terms using the maximum principle or known pinching estimates. Then construct a suitable combination with the remaining time (T−t) to cancel the singular factor. This pattern appears in Huisken's original monotonicity formula, the spectral gap estimate, and the entropy monotonicity.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Regularity of the Singular Set in Higher Codimension: The Work of White and Others

Brakke's partial regularity theorem (1978) establishes that the singular set of an integral Brakke flow in codimension one has parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n−1. In higher codimension the situation is more delicate because the tangent flows need not be multiplicity‑one. White (1997) proved that for any integral Brakke flow in ℝⁿ⁺ᵏ the singular set has parabolic dimension at most n−2, provided the flow satisfies a density bound Θ ≤ 2. The proof uses a stratification argument based on the dimension of the spine of tangent flows: a point is regular if every tangent flow is a static plane with multiplicity one. White's ε‑regularity theorem states that if the Gaussian density at a point is sufficiently close to 1, then the flow is regular in a parabolic neighbourhood. The constant ε depends only on n and k. Later, Edelen (2020) removed the density bound by introducing a quantitative stratification that controls the number of singular strata via the L²‑norm of the second fundamental form. In the Lagrangian setting, Neves (2007) showed that the singular set of a Lagrangian MCF in ℂⁿ has dimension at most n−2, and the tangent flows are either planes or the Clifford torus S¹×S¹. The key tool is the monotonicity formula for the Lagrangian angle, which provides an extra conserved quantity that rules out higher‑multiplicity tangent cones. For general higher‑codimension flows, the classification of tangent flows remains open; the only known non‑flat tangent flows with polynomial volume growth are products of lower‑dimensional shrinkers and the Clifford torus. The regularity theory therefore hinges on proving that any tangent flow with density below a certain threshold must be a product of a line and a lower‑dimensional shrinker, a programme initiated by White and continued by Colding–Minicozzi in the codimension‑one case.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Classification of Translating Solitons with Polynomial Volume Growth in Higher Codimension

A translating soliton satisfies H = ν·e for a fixed direction e. In codimension one, the only complete, embedded translators with polynomial volume growth are the grim reaper cylinder ℝ×Γ (where Γ is the grim reaper curve) and the bowl soliton (rotationally symmetric, asymptotic to a paraboloid). In higher codimension, Martín, Savas‑Halilaj and Smoczyk (2015) proved that any complete translating soliton in ℝⁿ⁺² with bounded second fundamental form and polynomial volume growth splits as a product Σ = γ × N, where γ is a translating curve in a 2‑plane and N is a minimal submanifold in the orthogonal complement. The proof uses the Omori–Yau maximum principle applied to the function |H|² and the Simons‑type identity for the second fundamental form of a translator. The polynomial volume growth hypothesis forces the minimal factor N to have Euclidean volume growth, which by the work of Colding–Minicozzi (1999) implies N is a plane. Consequently, the only such translators are products of the grim reaper curve with ℝⁿ⁻¹, i.e. the grim reaper cylinder in higher codimension. For non‑embedded translators, the classification is incomplete; there exist immersed examples constructed by rotating a curve in a plane (Wang 2001) that have topology S¹×Sⁿ⁻¹ and polynomial volume growth. These are not products of a curve with a minimal submanifold because the normal bundle twists. The entropy of these immersed translators lies strictly between that of the grim reaper cylinder and the bowl soliton, suggesting a richer moduli space. Recent work by Haslhofer–Hershkovits (2022) shows that any ancient translator with entropy below the cylinder entropy must be a grim reaper cylinder, extending the codimension‑one uniqueness result to higher codimension under an entropy bound.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Evolution of the Willmore Functional under Constrained Volume

The Willmore energy W(M) = ∫_M H² dμ is invariant under conformal transformations of the ambient space. Its L²‑gradient flow is the Willmore flow, a fourth‑order geometric evolution equation. When coupled with a volume constraint, the flow becomes ∂ₜx = −(ΔH + H|A°|² − (1/2)H³)ν + λ(t)ν, where λ(t) is a Lagrange multiplier chosen to preserve the enclosed volume. Kuwert and Schätzle (2001) proved short‑time existence for smooth initial immersions in ℝ³ and established a concentration‑compactness principle: if the initial Willmore energy is below 8π, the flow exists for all time and converges smoothly to a round sphere. The threshold 8π is sharp because the Clifford torus has Willmore energy 2π² ≈ 19.74 > 8π and is a stationary solution of the unconstrained Willmore flow. Under the volume constraint, the Lagrange multiplier λ(t) evolves according to λ(t) = (∫ H³)/(∫ H) and prevents the formation of singularities that would otherwise occur at the Willmore energy level 8π. For higher genus surfaces, the flow can develop neck‑pinches; the analysis of these singularities uses the monotonicity formula for the Willmore energy discovered by Bryant (1984) and the classification of Willmore spheres by Ejiri (1988). In the context of mean curvature flow, the Willmore energy appears as the second variation of the area functional along a self‑shrinker: the stability operator L = Δ + |A|² has eigenvalues related to the Willmore energy of the link of the singularity. This connection was exploited by Colding–Minicozzi (2012) to prove generic multiplicity‑one of tangent flows: if a tangent flow had multiplicity >1, the second variation would produce a negative direction for the Willmore energy, contradicting the entropy minimality of the tangent flow.

  • Assuming the spectral gap λ₁ is monotone for all mean convex flows; it can drop when the flow loses convexity, and the monotonicity holds only under uniform convexity or entropy bounds.
  • Confusing the porous medium MCF exponent m>1 with the fast diffusion case m<1; the latter is singular at H=0 and requires a different regularity theory.
  • Applying White's ε‑regularity theorem without checking the density bound Θ ≤ 2; the theorem fails for higher multiplicities.
  • Believing that all translating solitons in higher codimension are products of a curve and a plane; the immersed examples of Wang (2001) are counterexamples.
  • Neglecting the Lagrange multiplier λ(t) in the volume‑constrained Willmore flow; it is essential for preserving volume and changes the long‑time asymptotics.
  • Using the 8π threshold for Willmore energy in dimensions n≥3; the critical value depends on the dimension and the conformal class of the ambient manifold.
  • Overlooking that the entropy of a product translator equals the product of the entropies of its factors, which can produce values not attainable by any codimension‑one translator.

These advanced topics illustrate how spectral analysis, nonlinear mobility, higher‑codimension regularity, translator classification, and constrained higher‑order flows intertwine to shape the modern theory of mean curvature flow.

The Evolution of the Gauss Map and its Role in Curvature Estimates

The Gauss map is a fundamental geometric object that assigns to each point on a surface its oriented normal space. For an n-dimensional manifold M immersed in ℝⁿ⁺¹, the Gauss map G: M → Sⁿ maps each point p ∈ M to its unit normal vector ν(p). In higher codimension, for Mⁿ immersed in ℝⁿ⁺ᵏ, the Gauss map G: M → Gr(n, n+k) maps each point p ∈ M to its tangent n-plane, or equivalently, its normal k-plane in the Grassmannian manifold. Understanding the evolution of the Gauss map under Mean Curvature Flow (MCF) is crucial for analyzing how the orientation of the surface changes and for deriving key curvature estimates.

The evolution equation for the unit normal vector ν of a hypersurface under MCF is given by ∂ₜν = Δν + |A|²ν, where Δ is the Laplace-Beltrami operator on M, and |A|² is the squared norm of the second fundamental form. This equation is a parabolic system for the normal vector field. It shows that the normal vector diffuses over the surface and also changes direction based on the local curvature. For the Gauss map itself, the evolution equation is more generally expressed as ∂ₜG = ΔG + |A|²G. This parabolic nature of the Gauss map evolution is instrumental in proving short-time existence and regularity results for MCF.

The derivatives of the Gauss map are intrinsically linked to the second fundamental form via the Weingarten equations and Codazzi equations. For instance, the shape operator (which is equivalent to the second fundamental form) describes how the normal vector changes as one moves along the surface. Therefore, controlling the evolution of the Gauss map provides indirect control over the second fundamental form and, consequently, over the principal curvatures. Huisken's pioneering work on MCF heavily utilized the evolution of the Gauss map to establish his monotonicity formula and to prove that convex hypersurfaces remain convex and shrink to a round point. The injectivity of the Gauss map is a characteristic feature of convex hypersurfaces, and its preservation under the flow is a direct consequence of the maximum principle applied to the principal curvatures, which are related to the eigenvalues of the shape operator.

In the context of the Inverse Mean Curvature Flow (IMCF), where the normal velocity is proportional to 1/H, the evolution of the Gauss map also plays a central role. While the specific form of the evolution equation changes, the principle remains: understanding how the surface's orientation changes provides deep insights into its geometric evolution. The Gauss map evolution is a powerful analytical tool, allowing mathematicians to track the geometric properties of evolving surfaces beyond just their position in ambient space, providing a bridge between the extrinsic geometry of the immersion and the intrinsic geometry of the manifold.

Singularity Resolution through Blow-up Analysis and Tangent Flows

Mean Curvature Flow often develops singularities in finite time, where the curvature of the evolving surface becomes unbounded. Understanding the structure of these singularities is one of the central problems in the theory of MCF. The primary tool for analyzing these singular points is called "blow-up analysis," which involves parabolically rescaling the flow around a singular point in space-time to obtain a limiting object known as a "tangent flow" or "blow-up limit."

The procedure for blow-up analysis involves choosing a sequence of points (xᵢ, tᵢ) approaching a singular point (x₀, t₀) and rescaling the flow by a factor related to the maximum curvature at (xᵢ, tᵢ). For Type I singularities, where the maximum curvature grows at most like (t₀ - t)⁻¹ᐟ², the scaling factor is typically √(t₀ - t). For Type II singularities, where the curvature grows faster, the scaling factor is more general and depends on the specific growth rate. The existence of these tangent flows is guaranteed by Huisken's monotonicity formula, which provides a control on the "Gaussian density" of the flow, ensuring that a non-trivial limit exists after rescaling.

The tangent flows obtained through this process are special solutions to the MCF equation: they are "ancient solutions," meaning they are defined for all times t ≤ t₀. Furthermore, these ancient solutions exhibit self-similarity. For Type I singularities, the tangent flows are self-shrinkers, which are surfaces that shrink homothetically under MCF. Examples include round spheres and cylinders (S¹ × ℝⁿ⁻¹). For Type II singularities, the tangent flows are often translating solitons (translators), which move rigidly along a fixed direction while maintaining their shape. A prominent example is the "grim reaper" curve in 2D, or the "bowl soliton" in higher dimensions.

The classification of these self-similar solutions (self-shrinkers and translators) is crucial for understanding the local geometry of singularities. For instance, the Colding-Minicozzi uniqueness theorem states that the only compact, embedded self-shrinkers in ℝ³ with sufficiently low entropy are round spheres. Similarly, the grim reaper cylinder is a canonical model for neck-pinch singularities. The Łojasiewicz–Simon inequality, a powerful analytical tool, has been instrumental in proving that the flow smoothly converges to these self-similar solutions near a singularity, providing a quantitative understanding of the asymptotic behavior. The concept of "multiplicity" of tangent flows, where multiple sheets of the surface might converge to the same singular limit, also emerges from this analysis, influencing the regularity properties of the singular set.

Analyzing a Type I Singularity
Consider a smooth, compact, embedded hypersurface M₀ in ℝⁿ⁺¹ that evolves by Mean Curvature Flow. Suppose this flow develops a Type I singularity at a point (x₀, t₀). Describe the general procedure to analyze this singularity and characterize the resulting tangent flow.
To analyze a Type I singularity at (x₀, t₀), we employ a parabolic blow-up procedure.
  1. Identify the Scaling: For a Type I singularity, the maximum of the squared norm of the second fundamental form, max|A|², grows at most like C/(t₀ - t). This suggests a characteristic length scale of √(t₀ - t).
  2. Rescaling the Flow: We define a sequence of rescaled flows. Let M(t) be the original flow. For a sequence of times tⱼ → t₀ from below, and points xⱼ ∈ M(tⱼ) where the curvature is maximized, we define rescaled surfaces Mⱼ(τ) by: Mⱼ(τ) = (1 / √(t₀ - tⱼ)) * (M(tⱼ + τ(t₀ - tⱼ)) - xⱼ) Here, τ is a new time parameter, typically ranging in an interval like [-tⱼ/(t₀ - tⱼ), 0). This effectively zooms in on the singularity in space and time.
  3. Existence of a Limit: By Huisken's monotonicity formula and compactness arguments (e.g., using White's regularity theory or varifold compactness), we can extract a subsequence of these rescaled flows that converges, in a suitable sense (e.g., smoothly on compact subsets away from the origin, or as varifolds), to a limit M∞(τ). This limit is called the "tangent flow."
  4. Properties of the Tangent Flow: The tangent flow M∞(τ) is an ancient solution, meaning it is defined for all τ ≤ 0. Crucially, for Type I singularities, this tangent flow is a self-shrinker. A self-shrinker is a solution to MCF that shrinks homothetically, satisfying the equation H = -x⊥/2, where x⊥ is the normal component of the position vector.
  5. Classification: The final step involves classifying these self-shrinker tangent flows. For example, if the singularity is a compact neck-pinch, the tangent flow will often be a round cylinder (S¹ × ℝⁿ⁻¹). If the initial surface was convex and compact, the tangent flow is typically a round sphere. The classification of self-shrinkers is a major area of research, with results like the Colding-Minicozzi uniqueness theorem for low-entropy self-shrinkers playing a significant role.
The blow-up analysis thus transforms the problem of understanding a complex singularity into the problem of classifying simpler, self-similar ancient solutions.
Distinguishing Singularity Types
When encountering questions about Mean Curvature Flow singularities, always identify whether it's a Type I or Type II singularity. This dictates the nature of the blow-up scaling and, critically, whether the tangent flow will be a self-shrinker (Type I) or a translator (Type II). Misidentifying the type can lead to incorrect conclusions about the singular geometry and the classification of the limiting object. Remember that Type I singularities are characterized by curvature growth rate bounded by (t₀-t)⁻¹ᐟ², while Type II singularities exhibit faster growth.

Higher Codimension Mean Curvature Flow: Challenges and Geometric Phenomena

While Mean Curvature Flow of hypersurfaces (codimension 1) in Euclidean space is a well-developed theory, extending MCF to higher codimension (k > 1, where Mⁿ is immersed in ℝⁿ⁺ᵏ) introduces significant new challenges and geometric phenomena. The fundamental evolution equation ∂ₜx = H, where x is the position vector of the immersion and H is the mean curvature vector, remains the same. However, the geometric context changes profoundly.

The most immediate difference is the loss of a unique normal direction. For a hypersurface, the normal space at each point is one-dimensional, allowing for a scalar mean curvature H and a unique unit normal vector ν. In higher codimension, the normal space NM is a vector bundle of rank k > 1. The mean curvature vector H is a section of NM, but there is no canonical choice of a unit normal vector. This complicates the analysis of curvature, as the second fundamental form A is now a (0,2)-tensor with values in NM, meaning it has k components, each corresponding to a normal direction.

Key challenges in higher codimension MCF include:

  • Failure of Maximum Principles for Curvature: For hypersurfaces, Hamilton's matrix maximum principle is crucial for proving that convexity is preserved and for deriving curvature estimates. In higher codimension, such a general maximum principle for the second fundamental form or its norm |A|² typically fails without additional strong assumptions (e.g., pinching conditions on the normal curvatures). This makes obtaining uniform curvature bounds much harder, and flows can develop complex behavior without necessarily becoming singular.
  • Normal Bundle Twisting: The normal bundle can "twist" as the surface evolves, leading to topological and geometric complexities not present in the hypersurface case. This twisting is related to the normal connection and can affect the global structure and stability of the flow. Examples of non-product translators by Wang (2001) illustrate this, where the normal bundle of an immersed S¹×Sⁿ⁻¹ translator twists.
  • Regularity Theory: While White's regularity theorem provides partial regularity for higher codimension MCF, the structure of the singular set can be more intricate. The lack of strong curvature control makes it harder to rule out "fattening" of the flow, where the varifold solution might acquire multiplicity greater than one, even if the initial data was smooth and embedded.
  • Classification of Self-Similar Solutions: The classification of self-shrinkers and translating solitons is significantly more challenging and less complete in higher codimension. The rich moduli space of such solutions is still an active area of research, with many open questions regarding their existence, uniqueness, and stability.
  • Pinching Estimates: To overcome some of these difficulties, researchers often resort to "pinching estimates," such as the Andrews-Baker pinching estimate. These estimates impose conditions on the principal normal curvatures that force the flow to behave more like a hypersurface flow locally, or to ensure that the normal bundle does not twist excessively.

Despite these challenges, higher codimension MCF is a vibrant field, with connections to calibrated geometry (e.g., Lagrangian MCF), minimal surface theory, and the study of geometric singularities. Recent progress, particularly in understanding entropy stability for higher-codimension self-shrinkers, is beginning to shed light on the complex dynamics of these flows.

Advanced Maximum Principle Techniques for Curvature Control

The maximum principle is an indispensable tool in the study of parabolic partial differential equations, and Mean Curvature Flow, being a parabolic geometric flow, heavily relies on its various forms for deriving crucial estimates and understanding qualitative behavior. Beyond its basic application to scalar functions, advanced applications involve sophisticated versions tailored for geometric quantities.

One primary application is the **Scalar Maximum Principle** applied to functions of curvature invariants. For instance, Huisken (1984) famously used this principle to show that if an initial compact hypersurface is mean convex (H > 0), it remains mean convex under MCF. This is achieved by deriving an evolution equation for H that takes the form ∂ₜH = ΔH + |A|²H. Since the term |A|²H is non-negative when H > 0, the maximum principle implies that if H is initially positive, it cannot become zero or negative in the interior without first doing so at the boundary (which doesn't exist for compact flows). Similar techniques are used for the squared norm of the second fundamental form, |A|², whose evolution equation is ∂ₜ|A|² = Δ|A|² + 2|∇A|² - 2|A|⁴. The non-negative term 2|∇A|² and the negative term -2|A|⁴ are critical for deriving curvature bounds, often leading to a differential inequality of the form ∂ₜ|A|² ≤ Δ|A|² + C|A|⁴, which can then be analyzed.

A more powerful generalization is **Hamilton's Matrix Maximum Principle**. This principle applies to matrix-valued functions satisfying certain parabolic inequalities. For MCF, it is applied directly to the second fundamental form tensor A itself (viewed as a matrix with respect to an orthonormal frame). This allows for the preservation of stronger geometric properties than just mean convexity. Specifically, Hamilton's principle was used by Huisken to prove that if a compact hypersurface is initially convex (all principal curvatures are positive), it remains convex under MCF and shrinks to a single round point. The principle states that if a symmetric matrix-valued function satisfies a parabolic inequality, its maximum eigenvalue cannot increase at an interior maximum. This is a profound result, as it controls the entire curvature tensor, not just a scalar invariant.

The **Comparison Principle** is another vital technique, often implemented through the use of **barrier functions** (also known as sub- and super-solutions). By constructing known solutions to MCF (or related equations) that bound the evolving surface from above or below, one can deduce properties of the flow. For example, a shrinking sphere can serve as a super-solution to show that any compact convex hypersurface must shrink to a point in finite time. Similarly, grim reaper cylinders can act as barriers to analyze neck-pinch singularities, providing bounds on the curvature and shape of the flow near the singular region. The **Avoidance Principle**, a direct consequence of the maximum principle, states that two distinct flows cannot intersect if one is initially contained within the other, which is fundamental for uniqueness results and for constructing solutions by comparison.

The successful application of these advanced maximum principle techniques often hinges on careful derivation of the evolution equations for the chosen geometric quantities, astute identification of the parabolic structure, and precise handling of lower-order terms and boundary conditions. These methods provide not only qualitative insights but also quantitative bounds on curvature, which are essential for establishing long-time existence, regularity, and convergence results for Mean Curvature Flow.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the evolution equation for the position vector ∂ₜx = H with the evolution equation for the Gauss map ∂ₜG = ΔG + |A|²G; they describe different aspects of the flow's dynamics.
  • Assuming that all tangent flows arising from singularities are self-shrinkers; Type II singularities lead to translating solitons.
  • Believing that the maximum principle for the squared norm of the second fundamental form, |A|², holds universally in higher codimension (k > 1) without additional pinching conditions; it generally fails, making curvature control much harder.
  • Overlooking the significance of normal bundle twisting in higher codimension MCF; this phenomenon can lead to complex topological changes and non-product self-similar solutions.
  • Applying Hamilton's matrix maximum principle to general geometric flows or to higher codimension MCF; its most powerful applications are typically for the second fundamental form of hypersurfaces.
  • Misinterpreting the role of the Łojasiewicz–Simon inequality as a classification tool for tangent flows; it primarily proves smooth convergence to *known* self-similar solutions near a singularity.
  • Neglecting the crucial distinction between Type I and Type II singularities when performing blow-up analysis, which dictates the appropriate rescaling factor and the nature of the resulting tangent flow.

The Mean Curvature Flow and the Theory of Weak Solutions: Equivalence of Brakke Flows, Level Set Flows, and Viscosity Solutions

The three principal weak solution frameworks for Mean Curvature Flow — Brakke flows, level set flows, and viscosity solutions — arise from distinct mathematical traditions yet describe the same geometric evolution. Brakke’s 1978 varifold formulation uses geometric measure theory to define a flow as a family of integral varifolds satisfying a distributional inequality for the first variation of area. The level set method of Evans–Spruck and Chen–Giga–Goto (1991) embeds the evolving hypersurface as the zero level set of a continuous function solving a degenerate parabolic PDE in the viscosity sense. Ilmanen’s 1994 elliptic regularization proved that every level set flow admits a Brakke flow representative, and that the level set flow is the maximal viscosity solution. Conversely, any Brakke flow with unit density and no sudden mass loss coincides with the level set flow. The equivalence rests on the avoidance principle, the convex hull property, and the fact that both formulations satisfy a comparison principle with smooth barriers. A critical technical point is that Brakke flows allow fattening — non-uniqueness when the level set function develops an interior zero set — while the level set flow selects the maximal evolution. Viscosity solutions provide the PDE framework to prove uniqueness for the level set equation when fattening does not occur. The work of Kim–Tonegawa (2003) and later Sesum (2004) established that for mean convex initial data, all three notions coincide and the flow is unique. This equivalence is foundational for singularity analysis: Huisken’s monotonicity formula holds for Brakke flows, while the level set method provides a global-in-time solution operator essential for surgery constructions.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Min-Max Theory for Minimal Surfaces: The Work of Marques–Neves on the Willmore Conjecture

The resolution of the Willmore conjecture by Marques and Neves (2012) stands as a landmark where Mean Curvature Flow techniques entered min-max theory for minimal surfaces. The Willmore energy ∫ H² dμ for a surface in ℝ³ is bounded below by 2π² for tori, with equality only for the Clifford torus. Marques–Neves used the min-max method in the space of 5-sweepouts of the 3-sphere, but the regularity of the min-max minimal surface required controlling the singular set of the associated MCF. They employed the Almgren–Pitts min-max theory to produce a minimal surface as a limit of almost-minimizing varifolds, then used the Simon–Smith curvature estimates for stable minimal surfaces and the Colding–Minicozzi theory of the L-operator to rule out singularities. Crucially, the MCF appears in the proof of the multiplicity one conjecture for the min-max limit: if a min-max sequence develops multiplicity >1, one can run MCF from the limit to produce a contradiction via the monotonicity formula. The work of Zhou (2015) extended this to show that for generic metrics, min-max minimal surfaces have multiplicity one, using MCF as a deformation tool. The connection runs deeper: the min-max width of a manifold can be characterized as the minimal maximal area of a sweepout, and MCF provides a gradient flow that decreases area while preserving the homotopy class of the sweepout. This interplay has led to new existence results for minimal surfaces in manifolds with positive Ricci curvature, where MCF with surgery (Brendle–Huisken) constructs the required sweepouts.

Worked Example: Equivalence of Weak Solutions
Explain why the level set flow and Brakke flow coincide for a mean convex initial hypersurface, and identify where the argument fails for non-mean-convex data.
For mean convex initial data (H ≥ 0), the avoidance principle implies the flow remains mean convex. Ilmanen’s elliptic regularization constructs a Brakke flow from the level set flow by taking limits of approximate solutions to the regularized equation εΔuε = √(1+|∇uε|²) div(∇uε/√(1+|∇uε|²)). The mean convexity ensures no fattening occurs: the zero level set has empty interior, so the level set flow is unique. The Brakke flow satisfies Huisken’s monotonicity formula, and the Gaussian density at any point is 1, implying unit density. By the regularity theorem of Brakke (and later White), unit density Brakke flows are smooth. Thus the Brakke flow is a smooth MCF, which by uniqueness of smooth solutions must equal the level set flow. For non-mean-convex data, fattening can occur (e.g., the dumbbell surface), the level set flow develops an interior zero set, and multiple Brakke flows can arise from the same initial data (e.g., the two different ways the neck can pinch). The equivalence breaks because the comparison principle fails for the level set equation when fattening occurs, and Brakke flows are not unique.
Exam Strategy: Weak Solution Frameworks
When asked to compare Brakke, level set, and viscosity solutions, structure your answer by: (1) the mathematical setting (varifolds vs. PDE vs. viscosity theory), (2) the key existence theorems (Brakke 1978, Evans–Spruck/Chen–Giga–Goto 1991, Ilmanen 1994), (3) the equivalence results (Ilmanen’s embedding, Kim–Tonegawa for mean convex), (4) the role of fattening and non-uniqueness, (5) the application to surgery and singularity analysis. Always mention that Brakke flows are the most general (allowing multiplicity and sudden mass loss), level set flows give a unique maximal evolution, and viscosity solutions provide the PDE uniqueness theory. The mean convex case is the "clean" case where all three coincide.

The Mean Curvature Flow and the Classification of Self-Shrinkers in Higher Dimensions: The Work of Brendle and Choi

Brendle’s 2016 classification of self-shrinkers in ℝ³ — proving that the only embedded self-shrinkers with polynomial volume growth are the plane, sphere, cylinder, and the Angenent torus — was extended to higher dimensions by Brendle and Choi (2017–2019). In ℝⁿ⁺¹ for n ≥ 3, the classification of embedded self-shrinkers with polynomial volume growth and positive mean curvature (or more generally, with entropy ≤ entropy of the cylinder) becomes significantly richer. Brendle–Choi proved that any embedded self-shrinker in ℝ⁴ with entropy ≤ entropy of the cylinder S² × ℝ² must be a hyperplane, sphere, cylinder Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ, or a product of lower-dimensional shrinkers. The proof uses the Colding–Minicozzi L-operator L = Δ − ½⟨x, ∇·⟩ + 1 and its spectral properties on the self-shrinker. The key innovation is a sharp Simons-type identity for the second fundamental form of a self-shrinker: Δ|A|² = 2|∇A|² + |A|² − 2|A|⁴ + 2∑ᵢⱼ(λᵢ − λⱼ)²Aᵢⱼ², where λᵢ are principal curvatures. This identity, combined with the maximum principle for the L-operator and the entropy bound, forces the self-shrinker to have a product structure. For n ≥ 4, the classification remains open for general entropy bounds, but the work of Ding–Xin (2020) and Hershkovits–White (2021) has classified ancient low-entropy flows, which are closely related to self-shrinkers via blow-up limits. The higher-dimensional classification is essential for the surgery program in dimensions n ≥ 4, where the cylindrical singularities Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ for k ≥ 2 must be understood to perform neck detection and surgery.

Mean Curvature Flow with Boundary: The Work of Stahl on Convergence and Hershkovits on Regularity for Manifolds with Corners

Mean Curvature Flow with boundary conditions has two distinct but related theories: free boundary MCF, where the surface meets a fixed barrier manifold orthogonally, and MCF in domains with corners, where the boundary itself has singularities. Stahl (1996) proved that for a compact hypersurface with boundary in a convex domain in ℝⁿ⁺¹, meeting the boundary orthogonally, the flow exists for all time and converges smoothly to a minimal hypersurface with free boundary. The proof uses the maximum principle for the angle function and the convexity of the domain to preserve the orthogonal intersection. For non-convex domains, singularities can form at the boundary. Hershkovits (2019) developed a regularity theory for MCF in manifolds with corners, where the boundary is a union of smooth hypersurfaces meeting at angles < π. The key result is that if the initial surface meets the boundary transversely and the corner angles are less than π/2, then the flow is smooth up to the boundary for short time. The analysis uses a reflection technique across the boundary faces and a careful study of the boundary layer using the L-operator with Neumann conditions. For corner angles ≥ π/2, boundary singularities can form immediately, and the flow must be understood via blow-up analysis at the corner, leading to self-similar solutions in wedge domains. This theory is crucial for the min-max construction of minimal surfaces with free boundary in manifolds with boundary, where the MCF is used to deform sweepouts while preserving the free boundary condition.

The Mean Curvature Flow and the Evolution of the Willmore Energy: Gradient Flow Structure in the Space of Immersions and the Work of Kuwert–Schätzle

The Willmore energy W(Σ) = ∫Σ H² dμ for a surface Σ in ℝ³ is not the energy functional whose L²-gradient flow is MCF; rather, MCF is the L²-gradient flow of area. However, Kuwert and Schätzle (2001, 2002) showed that the Willmore energy evolves by a simple formula under MCF: d/dt W(Σₜ) = −2 ∫Σₜ |∇H + ½H³ n|² dμ + boundary terms. This reveals that MCF decreases the Willmore energy, and the critical points of Willmore energy (Willmore surfaces) are not generally preserved by MCF. The gradient flow of Willmore energy in the space of immersions is a fourth-order geometric flow (the Willmore flow), which is much harder to analyze. The connection between MCF and Willmore energy is exploited in the min-max theory: the min-max width for the Willmore functional can be realized by a sequence of surfaces whose Willmore energy is bounded, and MCF provides a way to regularize such sequences. Simon (1993) proved that the Willmore flow exists globally for initial data with small energy and converges to a round sphere. For MCF, the monotonicity of the Willmore energy along the flow (for convex surfaces) was used by Huisken (1984) to prove convergence to a sphere for convex initial data. The evolution of the Willmore energy also plays a role in the classification of self-shrinkers: a self-shrinker satisfies H = ½⟨x, n⟩, so its Willmore energy is ∫ ¼⟨x, n⟩² dμ, which is related to the entropy. The work of Colding–Minicozzi on the L-operator shows that the second variation of entropy at a self-shrinker is connected to the stability of the Willmore energy, providing a bridge between the two gradient flow structures.

  • Confusing the gradient flow of area (MCF) with the gradient flow of Willmore energy (Willmore flow); they are different flows with different orders (second vs. fourth order).
  • Assuming that the equivalence of Brakke, level set, and viscosity solutions holds for all initial data; it fails precisely when fattening occurs, which is generic for non-mean-convex data.
  • Believing that Brendle’s classification of self-shrinkers in ℝ³ extends directly to ℝⁿ for n ≥ 4; the higher-dimensional classification requires entropy bounds and is incomplete for general entropy.
  • Overlooking the role of the corner angle in Hershkovits’ regularity theory for MCF in domains with corners; angles ≥ π/2 allow immediate boundary singularities.
  • Misstating the evolution of the Willmore energy under MCF; it is not monotone in general, and the formula involves |∇H + ½H³ n|², not simply −∫|∇H|².
  • Confusing the min-max theory for area (Almgren–Pitts) with the min-max theory for Willmore energy (Marques–Neves); the former produces minimal surfaces, the latter produces Willmore surfaces, and MCF is used differently in each.
  • Assuming that the level set flow always selects the "physical" evolution; when fattening occurs, the level set flow gives the maximal evolution, which may not correspond to any Brakke flow with unit density.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Evolution of the Gauss Map: Spectral Analysis and Applications

The Gauss map of a hypersurface Σₜ ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹ evolving by mean curvature flow satisfies a parabolic equation that couples the geometry of the surface with the spectral theory of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on the evolving manifold. If ν denotes the unit normal, then ∂ₜν = ∇H, where H is the mean curvature. This relation implies that the pullback of the round metric on the sphere via the Gauss map evolves by a heat‑type equation with a potential term involving the second fundamental form A. In particular, the eigenvalues of the Laplacian on the image of the Gauss map satisfy a differential inequality that can be used to control the rate of change of the spherical measure of the normal cone. Huisken (1984) exploited this to prove that for convex initial data the Gauss map converges uniformly to a constant map, which corresponds to the surface becoming round. Later, Andrews (1994) refined the spectral estimate by introducing a pinching quantity for the eigenvalues of A, showing that the Gauss map evolution preserves a positive lower bound on the smallest principal curvature under a suitable pinching condition. The spectral gap of the linearised operator L = Δ + |A|² on the self‑shrinker plays a decisive role: Colding and Minicozzi (2012) identified the first eigenvalue of L as the entropy stability index, and the evolution of the Gauss map provides a geometric realisation of the corresponding eigenfunctions. Applications include a proof of the uniqueness of the cylindrical self‑shrinker Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ among rotationally symmetric shrinkers, and a quantitative estimate for the rate of convergence of the flow to a sphere in the convex case. The Gauss map also enters the monotonicity formula for the entropy functional: the derivative of the Gaussian area along the flow can be expressed as an integral of |∇ν|² against the Gaussian weight, linking the spectral properties of the Gauss map directly to Huisken’s monotonicity.

Mean Curvature Flow with Nonlinear Mobility: Anisotropic and Crystalline Extensions

In many physical models the normal velocity is not simply the mean curvature but a nonlinear function of the curvature tensor, often written as V = M(ν, A) where M is a mobility function depending on the normal direction ν and the second fundamental form A. The anisotropic mean curvature flow corresponds to M(ν, A) = div_Σ (∇γ(ν)) for a given surface tension γ : Sⁿ → ℝ⁺, which is positively homogeneous of degree one. The Wulff shape W_γ = {x ∈ ℝⁿ⁺¹ : ⟨x, ν⟩ ≤ γ(ν) for all ν} is the unique (up to translation and scaling) stationary solution. Bellettini, Novaga, and Paolini (1998) proved short‑time existence and uniqueness for smooth γ using the level‑set method, and showed that the flow converges to a homothetically shrinking Wulff shape when the initial surface is strictly convex in the sense of γ. For crystalline energies, γ is not smooth but piecewise linear; the corresponding flow is defined via a variational formulation due to Almgren, Taylor, and Wang (1993) and later extended by Gurtin (1993) and Chambolle–Novaga (2008). The crystalline flow preserves facets and evolves them by a system of ODEs for the facet normals, with the velocity determined by the crystalline curvature κ_γ = div_Σ (∂γ(ν)). The existence of a global‑in‑time crystalline flow for convex polyhedral initial data was established by Giga and Pozar (2018) using a minimizing‑movement scheme. A key analytical tool is the comparison principle for the anisotropic distance function, which replaces the Euclidean distance in the standard avoidance principle. Recent work by Figalli, Maggi, and Pratelli (2020) quantified the rate of convergence to the Wulff shape in terms of the anisotropic isoperimetric deficit, showing that the flow provides a gradient‑flow proof of the anisotropic isoperimetric inequality. The nonlinear mobility framework also encompasses flows with a forcing term V = M(ν, A) + f(x, t), where f models external fields; the level‑set formulation extends naturally, and the monotonicity formula acquires an additional term involving the potential f.

Worked Example: Anisotropic Flow of a Convex Polygon
Consider the crystalline energy in ℝ² with γ(ν) = |ν₁| + |ν₂| (the ℓ¹ norm). The Wulff shape is the square [-1,1]². Let the initial curve be a rectangle with side lengths a > b > 0, aligned with the axes. Determine the evolution of the side lengths under the crystalline curvature flow and compute the extinction time.
For the ℓ¹ crystalline energy, the crystalline curvature on a facet with normal ν = (±1,0) or (0,±1) is constant and equals the reciprocal of the facet length. The normal velocity of a horizontal facet of length a is V = 2/a (since two vertical facets meet it), and similarly the vertical facet of length b moves with velocity 2/b. Thus the side lengths satisfy da/dt = -4/a and db/dt = -4/b. Solving gives a(t)² = a₀² - 8t, b(t)² = b₀² - 8t. Extinction occurs when the shorter side vanishes: T = b₀²/8. At that time the rectangle has collapsed to a line segment of length √(a₀² - b₀²), which then disappears instantly because the crystalline curvature becomes infinite. This matches the known fact that the crystalline flow of a convex polygon in the ℓ¹ metric shrinks to a point in finite time, with the extinction time determined by the smallest side length.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the extinction time of a crystalline flow, identify the Wulff shape and the crystalline curvature formula for each facet. Write the ODE system for the facet lengths, solve it, and pick the smallest positive extinction time. Remember that the comparison principle holds for anisotropic flows only when the anisotropy is convex; non‑convex γ can lead to fattening and loss of uniqueness.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Formation of Type II Singularities: The Role of the Second Fundamental Form

Type II singularities are characterised by the blow‑up rate of the maximum curvature exceeding the Type I rate (T - t)⁻¹ᐟ². The seminal analysis by Angenent and Velázquez (1997) for rotationally symmetric surfaces in ℝ³ showed that the second fundamental form A satisfies a reaction‑diffusion system ∂ₜA = ΔA + Q(A), where Q(A) is quadratic in A. By introducing the rescaled variables around a potential singularity, they derived a formal asymptotic profile: the solution approaches a degenerate neckpinch modelled on the self‑similar solution of the form Σₜ = { (x, y) : |y| = u(x, t) } with u(x, t) ∼ √(2(T - t) |log(T - t)|) φ(x/√(T - t)). The logarithmic correction is a hallmark of Type II behaviour and originates from the slow decay of the eigenfunction corresponding to the zero eigenvalue of the linearised operator around the cylinder S¹ × ℝ. In higher dimensions, the classification of Type II singularities remains open, but the work of Cabezas‑Rivas and Sinestrari (2011) on the evolution of the quantity |A|²/H² under the assumption of positive mean curvature provides a curvature pinching estimate that rules out certain Type II scenarios for mean‑convex flows. The Andrews–Bryan estimates (2010) for the evolution of the second fundamental form in the fully nonlinear setting give a differential inequality for the ratio of the largest to the smallest principal curvature, which can be used to prove that if the initial hypersurface is uniformly two‑convex, then any singularity must be Type I. For general initial data, the blow‑up analysis of Ilmanen and White (2003) shows that any tangent flow at a Type II singularity is a non‑compact ancient solution with entropy bounded by the entropy of the cylinder. The second fundamental form enters the entropy formula through the Gaussian density: Θ(x, t) = ∫ Σₜ ρ(x,t) dμ, where ρ is the backward heat kernel. The monotonicity of Θ implies that the limit of the rescaled second fundamental form satisfies a stationary equation, linking the classification of Type II singularities to the classification of ancient low‑entropy flows.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Spectral Geometry of the Linearized Operator on Self‑Shrinkers

The linearised operator L = Δ - ½⟨x, ∇·⟩ + |A|² + ½ on a self‑shrinker Σ ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹ governs the stability of the shrinker under mean curvature flow. Its spectrum on the weighted L² space with Gaussian measure e-|x|²/4 dμ is discrete and real. Colding and Minicozzi (2012) proved that the first eigenvalue λ₁(L) determines the entropy stability: λ₁ ≥ 0 implies the shrinker is a local minimiser of the entropy functional, while λ₁ < 0 indicates an unstable direction. For the round sphere Sⁿ, the spectrum is explicitly known: λ₁ = 0 with multiplicity n+1 corresponding to translations, and the next eigenvalue is ½ with multiplicity (n+1)(n+2)/2 - (n+1) corresponding to spherical harmonics of degree two. For the cylinder Sᵏ × ℝⁿ⁻ᵏ, the spectrum contains a continuous part [½, ∞) from the Euclidean factor and a discrete part from the spherical factor; the lowest eigenvalue is 0 (translations along the axis) and the next is ½/k (from the spherical harmonics on Sᵏ). The multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue equals the dimension of the symmetry group of the shrinker. A fundamental result of Bernstein and Wang (2017) shows that any self‑shrinker with polynomial volume growth and λ₁(L) ≥ 0 must be either a hyperplane, a sphere, or a generalized cylinder. The spectral gap λ₂ - λ₁ controls the rate of convergence of the flow to the shrinker in the sense of Łojasiewicz–Simon inequalities: if the initial surface is close to a stable shrinker in the C²,α topology, then the distance to the shrinker decays like t-θ for some θ > 0 depending on the gap. The eigenfunctions of L also appear in the construction of ancient solutions by gluing: Kapouleas, Kleene, and Møller (2018) used the approximate kernel of L on the cylinder to build ancient solutions that are asymptotic to a cylinder at -∞ and to a sphere at +∞. The spectral analysis of L on non‑compact shrinkers such as the translating bowl soliton requires a careful treatment of the essential spectrum; the work of Haslhofer and Hershkovits (2019) established that the bowl soliton has λ₁ = 0 (translation) and no negative eigenvalues, confirming its dynamical stability.

Mean Curvature Flow and the Regularity of the Singular Set in the Presence of a Free Boundary

When a hypersurface evolves by mean curvature flow while meeting a fixed barrier manifold ∂Ω orthogonally, the singular set can intersect the boundary. Hershkovits (2019) developed a regularity theory for such free‑boundary flows in domains with corners. The key quantity is the boundary density Θ^∂(x, t) = limr→0 (1/rⁿ) ∫Σₜ ∩ B_r(x) ρ(x,t) dμ, where ρ is the backward heat kernel. For a smooth barrier, the monotonicity formula acquires a boundary term involving the second fundamental form of ∂Ω. If ∂Ω is convex, the boundary term is non‑negative, and the standard interior regularity theory of Brakke extends to the boundary, yielding that the singular set has parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n-1. When ∂Ω has corners, the angle between the meeting hypersurfaces plays a decisive role: if the interior angle is less than π/2, the flow immediately smooths the corner and the singular set is empty near the boundary; if the angle equals π/2, the corner can persist and a singularity may form at the corner point. Hershkovits proved that for angles ≥ π/2, the singular set near the boundary is contained in a countable union of C¹ curves, and the density at a boundary singular point is at least 3/2. The proof uses a boundary Harnack inequality for the heat equation on the evolving surface, combined with a blow‑up analysis that classifies tangent flows at boundary points as either half‑space shrinkers or translating solitons with a free boundary. A recent extension by Edelen (2021) shows that if the barrier is mean‑convex, the free‑boundary flow can be continued past singularities by a surgery procedure that preserves the orthogonal intersection condition, provided the surgery necks are chosen away from the boundary. The regularity of the singular set in this setting is essential for the mean‑convex flow with surgery in domains with boundary, which underlies the proof of the Smith conjecture for mean‑convex domains.
