The large‑deviation principle for the invariant measure as the noise intensity tends to zero is obtained by a Γ‑convergence argument on the rate functional, which is the Ginzburg–Landau energy restricted to the set of mass‑preserving configurations.

Variational Methods for the Phase‑Field Crystal Model

The phase‑field crystal (PFC) model describes the evolution of a conserved order parameter ψ(x,t) representing the atomic density field. The free energy functional is F(ψ) = ∫ (½ ψ (Δ+1)2 ψ + ¼ ψ4 − ½ ε ψ2) dx, where ε > 0 is a temperature‑like parameter. The dynamics is the H-1 gradient flow ∂_t ψ = Δ μ, μ = δF/δψ = (Δ+1)2 ψ + ψ3 − ε ψ. This is a sixth‑order parabolic equation that conserves the total mass ∫ ψ dx.

The variational structure is used to prove existence of global weak solutions via the minimising movement scheme: ψk+1 = argmin_ψ (F(ψ) + (1/2τ) ‖ψ − ψ_k‖H-12). The functional F is not convex, but it is λ‑convex in H-1 for a suitable λ, which guarantees the scheme is well‑posed and the discrete solutions converge to a weak solution satisfying the energy dissipation inequality dF/dt = −∫ |∇μ|2 dx ≤ 0.

Stationary states are critical points of F under the mass constraint. The Euler–Lagrange equation is (Δ+1)2 ψ + ψ3 − ε ψ = λ, where λ is a Lagrange multiplier. For small ε the trivial state ψ = 0 is a local minimiser; as ε increases a bifurcation occurs and periodic minimisers (crystal patterns) appear. The bifurcation analysis uses the Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction on the kernel of the linearised operator (Δ+1)2 − ε, which consists of Fourier modes with wave number 1. The reduced functional on the finite‑dimensional kernel is a Landau‑type polynomial whose minimisers give the stable crystal structures (stripes, hexagons, BCC).

Numerical methods that preserve the variational structure include the convex‑splitting scheme: write F = F_c − F_e with F_c convex and F_e concave, then treat F_c implicitly and F_e explicitly. For the PFC energy, a convenient splitting is F_c(ψ) = ∫ (½ ψ (Δ+1)2 ψ + ¼ ψ4) dx and F_e(ψ) = ∫ ½ ε ψ2 dx. The resulting scheme is unconditionally energy stable and mass conserving. Error estimates rely on the λ‑convexity of F and the regularity of the exact solution in H2.

Recent work extends the PFC model to binary alloys by introducing a second conserved field c(x,t) with a coupling energy ∫ ψ2 c dx. The combined free energy is F(ψ,c) = F_PFC(ψ) + ∫ (½ |∇c|2 + W(c) + ψ2 c) dx, where W is a double‑well potential. The variational structure remains an H-1 × H-1 gradient flow, and the minimising movement scheme converges to a weak solution of the coupled system. The phase diagram exhibits microphase separation and the formation of ordered alloy structures, which are captured as minimisers of the constrained energy.

Common Traps

  • Assuming the Dirac action is bounded below; the free Dirac operator has both positive and negative spectrum, so the functional is strongly indefinite and requires a linking argument.
  • Neglecting the mass‑shell constraint in the Einstein–Vlasov matter action; the integration over the mass shell is essential for the correct stress‑energy tensor.
  • Treating the wave‑map energy as a standard convex functional; the target manifold curvature introduces a non‑convex geometric nonlinearity that can cause finite‑time blow‑up.
  • Confusing the Onsager–Machlup functional for additive noise with the one for multiplicative noise; the latter contains an extra term involving the derivative of the diffusion coefficient.
  • Using a standard L2 gradient flow for the phase‑field crystal model; the conserved dynamics requires the H-1 metric, otherwise mass is not preserved.
  • Overlooking the need for λ‑convexity in the minimising movement scheme; without it the discrete solutions may not converge to a weak solution.
  • Ignoring the role of the Lagrange multiplier in the constrained Euler–Lagrange equation for periodic crystal patterns; it enforces the mass constraint and shifts the bifurcation point.

These traps highlight the subtle points that frequently appear in advanced variational problems.

Variational Methods for the Infinity Laplacian and Tug‑of‑War Games

The infinity Laplacian Δ∞u = ⟨D²u Du, Du⟩ arises as the formal Euler–Lagrange operator of the L∞ functional ‖Du‖L∞(Ω). Unlike the p‑Laplacian for finite p, the infinity Laplacian is highly degenerate and non‑divergence form, so classical solutions rarely exist. The modern theory uses viscosity solutions: a function u is an absolute minimiser of the Lipschitz constant in every subdomain iff it satisfies Δ∞u = 0 in the viscosity sense (Aronsson, 1967). Jensen (1993) proved uniqueness of viscosity solutions to the Dirichlet problem for Δ∞u = 0 with continuous boundary data, establishing a comparison principle that is the cornerstone of the theory.

A striking probabilistic representation was discovered by Peres, Schramm, Sheffield and Wilson (2009). They introduced a two‑player zero‑sum tug‑of‑war game on a lattice with step ε > 0. The value function of the game converges, as ε → 0, to the unique viscosity solution of Δ∞u = 0. This game‑theoretic interpretation yields a simple proof of the comparison principle and provides a numerical scheme that is monotone, stable and consistent — hence convergent by the Barles–Souganidis framework. The same game also captures the normalized p‑Laplacian for finite p when the players use a biased coin, linking the whole family of p‑harmonic functions to a single stochastic game.

Applications include image processing (absolute minimal Lipschitz extension for inpainting), optimal Lipschitz extensions in metric spaces, and the study of infinity harmonic functions on Carnot groups. The theory also connects to the calculus of variations in L∞ via the notion of tight minima (Champion, De Pascale, 2001) and to the Aronsson equation for vector‑valued maps, where the system Δ∞u = 0 becomes a highly nonlinear PDE system with applications to colour image processing.

Variational Methods for Nonlocal Minimal Surfaces and Fractional Perimeter

The fractional perimeter of a set E ⊂ ℝⁿ, introduced by Caffarelli, Roquejoffre and Savin (2010), is defined as Perₛ(E) = ∫_E ∫E^c |x−y|-(n+s) dx dy for s ∈ (0,1). This nonlocal functional Γ‑converges to the classical perimeter as s → 1⁻ and to a multiple of the volume as s → 0⁺. Sets minimizing Perₛ under a volume constraint are called nonlocal minimal surfaces; their boundaries satisfy the nonlocal mean curvature equation Hₛ(x) = ∫ℝⁿ (χ_E(y)−χE^c(y)) |x−y|-(n+s) dy = 0 for x ∈ ∂E.

Regularity theory for nonlocal minimal surfaces parallels the classical De Giorgi programme. Caffarelli and Valdinoci (2011) proved that minimizers are C¹,α up to dimension n ≤ 7, while singularities may appear in higher dimensions. The nonlocal Bernstein problem — whether entire graphs minimizing Perₛ must be hyperplanes — has been solved affirmatively for n ≤ 2 (Savin, Valdinoci, 2012) and remains open in higher dimensions. The Euler–Lagrange equation is a nonlocal integro‑differential operator; its linearisation leads to a fractional Jacobi operator whose spectral properties control stability.

Variational methods for fractional perimeter are essential in phase‑field models with long‑range interactions, such as the nonlocal Cahn–Hilliard equation and the fractional Allen–Cahn equation. The Modica–Mortola Γ‑convergence result extends to the fractional setting: the rescaled fractional Allen–Cahn energy Γ‑converges to a multiple of Perₛ. This provides a diffuse‑interface approximation that preserves the nonlocal geometry and is used in numerical simulations of diblock copolymers and magnetic domains.

Worked Example
Compute the scaling of the fractional perimeter of a ball B_R ⊂ ℝⁿ with respect to the radius R.
By definition Perₛ(B_R) = ∫B_R ∫B_R^c |x−y|-(n+s) dx dy. Perform the change of variables x = R x', y = R y'. The Jacobian contributes R2n, while the kernel scales as |R(x'−y')|-(n+s) = R-(n+s) |x'−y'|-(n+s). Hence Perₛ(B_R) = R2n-(n+s) Perₛ(B1) = Rn-s Perₛ(B1). The fractional perimeter scales like Rn-s, interpolating between the classical perimeter (s→1 gives Rn-1) and the volume (s→0 gives Rn).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for scaling or homogeneity of a nonlocal functional, always perform a dimensional analysis: replace x by λx, track the Jacobian and the kernel exponent. The resulting power of λ is the homogeneity degree. This trick works for fractional perimeters, Gagliardo seminorms, and nonlocal energies alike.

Variational Methods for the Obstacle Problem and Free Boundary Regularity

The classical obstacle problem asks for the minimiser of the Dirichlet integral ∫_Ω |Du|² dx among functions u ≥ ψ in a domain Ω, where ψ is a given obstacle. The solution satisfies the variational inequality ∫_Ω Du·D(v−u) dx ≥ 0 for all v ≥ ψ, which is equivalent to the complementarity conditions Δu ≤ 0, u ≥ ψ, (Δu)(u−ψ) = 0. Lewy and Stampacchia (1969) proved that the solution belongs to W²,∞_loc(Ω) and that the free boundary ∂{u > ψ} ∩ Ω is locally a C¹ hypersurface except possibly on a singular set of lower dimension.

Caffarelli’s landmark papers (1977, 1998) established the optimal regularity of the free boundary. He showed that at regular points the free boundary is analytic, while singular points are contained in a set of Hausdorff dimension at most n−1. The classification of free boundary points uses the frequency function N(r) = r ∫B_r |Du|² / ∫∂B_r u², introduced by Almgren for elliptic equations. Monotonicity of N(r) yields blow‑up limits that are homogeneous global solutions; these are either half‑space solutions (regular points) or homogeneous polynomials of degree ≥ 2 (singular points).

Recent developments include the obstacle problem for the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)^s u = 0 in {u > ψ}, where the free boundary regularity theory has been extended by Caffarelli, Salsa and Silvestre (2008). The thin obstacle problem (Signorini problem) corresponds to s = 1/2 and appears in elasticity and finance. Variational methods also treat the parabolic obstacle problem, where the free boundary evolves in time and the regularity theory involves the caloric frequency function.

Variational Methods for the p‑Laplacian and Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problems

The p‑Laplacian Δ_p u = div(|Du|p-2 Du) for p > 1 is the Euler–Lagrange operator of the p‑Dirichlet energy ∫_Ω |Du|^p dx. The first eigenvalue λ₁(p) is defined variationally as the minimum of the Rayleigh quotient ∫_Ω |Du|^p / ∫_Ω |u|^p over W1,p0(Ω) {0}. The minimiser is a positive eigenfunction, unique up to scaling, and λ₁(p) is simple and isolated (Lindqvist, 1993). Higher eigenvalues can be obtained via the Ljusternik–Schnirelmann genus or the Krasnoselskii genus on the Nehari manifold, yielding a sequence λ_k(p) → ∞.

Nonlinear spectral theory for the p‑Laplacian differs from the linear case in several ways: eigenfunctions need not be orthogonal, the spectrum may contain a continuous part for p ≠ 2, and the nodal domain theorem holds only for the first eigenfunction. The asymptotic behaviour as p → ∞ connects to the infinity Laplacian: λ₁(p)1/p → 1 / rad(Ω), where rad(Ω) is the inradius, and the corresponding eigenfunctions converge to a viscosity solution of Δ∞u = 0 with appropriate boundary conditions (Juutinen, Lindqvist, Manfredi, 1999).

Applications include nonlinear elasticity (p‑harmonic maps), image denoising (total variation corresponds to p = 1), and the study of torsional creep. The variational structure also underpins the existence theory for quasilinear elliptic systems via the direct method, provided the energy density satisfies p‑growth and quasiconvexity conditions.

Variational Methods for Stochastic Homogenization of Integral Functionals

Stochastic homogenization studies the asymptotic behaviour of integral functionals ∫_Ω f(x/ε, ω, Du) dx as ε → 0, where f(y, ω, ξ) is a stationary ergodic random integrand. The fundamental result (Dal Maso, Modica, 1986) states that, almost surely, the functionals Γ‑converge to a deterministic homogeneous functional ∫_Ω f_hom(Du) dx, where the homogenized density f_hom(ξ) = limR→∞ (1/|Q_R|) inf{ ∫Q_R f(y, ω, ξ+Dφ) dy : φ ∈ W1,p0(Q_R) }. The limit is obtained via the subadditive ergodic theorem applied to the minimal energy on large cubes.

Qualitative homogenization requires only stationarity, ergodicity, and standard p‑growth. Quantitative rates of convergence have been established under stronger mixing assumptions (e.g., finite range of dependence or spectral gap). Armstrong, Kuusi and Mourrat (2017) developed a large‑scale regularity theory that yields optimal algebraic rates for the corrector and the energy difference. The corrector φ_ξ(y, ω) solves the stationary Euler–Lagrange equation −div(∂_ξ f(y, ω, ξ+Dφ_ξ)) = 0 and satisfies ⟨Dφ_ξ⟩ = 0; its gradient is stationary with finite second moment.

Applications include composite materials with random microstructures, where f_hom encodes effective elastic moduli, and random conductance models on ℤ^d, where the homogenised matrix governs the diffusive scaling limit of the random walk. The variational approach also extends to non‑convex integrands via relaxation and to functionals with non‑standard growth (e.g., Orlicz spaces) using the theory of Γ‑convergence in metric spaces.

  • Confusing the viscosity solution definition for the infinity Laplacian with the classical distributional solution; the former uses test functions touching from above/below, the latter requires integration by parts which fails for Δ∞.
  • Assuming the fractional perimeter of a set is always finite; sets with infinite fractional perimeter exist (e.g., sets with fractal boundaries of dimension > n−s).
  • Treating the free boundary in the obstacle problem as automatically smooth; singular free boundary points can occur and their structure is governed by the frequency function.
  • Believing that all eigenvalues of the p‑Laplacian form a discrete sequence with the same properties as the linear Laplacian; for p ≠ 2 the spectrum may contain a continuous component and eigenfunctions are not orthogonal.
  • Neglecting the ergodicity hypothesis in stochastic homogenization; without it the Γ‑limit may be random or fail to exist.
  • Applying the classical Modica–Mortola Γ‑convergence to fractional perimeters without the nonlocal rescaling; the correct scaling involves the fractional Gagliardo seminorm, not the local gradient.
  • Overlooking the role of the corrector in quantitative stochastic homogenization; the corrector’s sublinear growth is essential for error estimates and fails in dimensions d ≤ 2 for certain models.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with Magnetic Potential

The magnetic nonlinear Schrödinger equation (mNLS) arises in the description of charged quantum particles in an electromagnetic field. Its energy functional on a domain Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ (n ≥ 2) reads

E(u) = ½ ∫_Ω |(∇ − iA)u|² dx + ½ ∫_Ω V(x)|u|² dx − (1/p) ∫_Ω |u|^p dx,

where A : Ω → ℝⁿ is the magnetic vector potential, V ≥ 0 is an electric potential, and 2 < p < 2* = 2n/(n−2) for n ≥ 3 (with the usual modification for n = 2). The covariant derivative ∇_A u = (∇ − iA)u ensures gauge invariance: if u is replaced by eiφu and A by A + ∇φ, the energy is unchanged. This symmetry leads to a conserved charge Q(u) = ∫_Ω |u|² dx and to the magnetic Sobolev inequality ∫_Ω |∇_A u|² dx ≥ C ∫_Ω |u|2* dx, which holds with the same constant as the non‑magnetic case (Diamagnetic inequality).

Existence of ground states (minimisers of E under the constraint Q(u) = constant) is typically proved via the concentration‑compactness principle of Lions. The magnetic field B = curl A enters the analysis through the magnetic translation operators and the magnetic Hardy inequality. If A ∈ L²_loc and B ∈ Ln/2 (or B ∈ Ln/2,∞ in the critical Lorentz space), the functional is well defined on the magnetic Sobolev space H¹_A(Ω) = {u ∈ L² : ∇_A u ∈ L²}. The mountain‑pass theorem yields a non‑trivial critical point when V ≡ 0 and p is subcritical; the Palais–Smale condition holds at the mountain‑pass level provided the magnetic field does not create “magnetic bottles” that trap mass at infinity. In the critical case p = 2*, the lack of compactness is handled by the magnetic version of the Brezis–Nirenberg argument: one shows that the infimum of the energy on the Nehari manifold is strictly below the energy of the Talenti bubble, which guarantees a minimiser.

Orbital stability of standing waves eiωtφ_ω follows from the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss framework once the mapping ω ↦ Q(φ_ω) is shown to be strictly increasing. The magnetic field influences the Vakhitov–Kolokolov slope condition through the modified Pohozaev identities. Recent work by Esteban, Lions, and Loss (2005) established that for a constant magnetic field B ≠ 0 the ground state is unique up to gauge and magnetic translations, and its decay is Gaussian rather than exponential, reflecting the Landau level structure of the magnetic Laplacian.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Wave Equation with Critical Sobolev Exponent

The focusing nonlinear wave equation □u + |u|p−1u = 0 on ℝ1+n with the critical exponent p = (n+2)/(n−2) (n ≥ 3) is the Euler–Lagrange equation of the Lorentz‑invariant action

S(u) = ∫ (½ |∂_t u|² − ½ |∇u|² − (1/(p+1)) |u|p+1) dx dt.

The natural energy space is the homogeneous Sobolev space Ḣ¹(ℝⁿ) × L²(ℝⁿ). The conserved energy E(u, ∂_t u) = ½ ∫ (|∂_t u|² + |∇u|²) dx − (1/(p+1)) ∫ |u|p+1 dx is invariant under the scaling u_λ(t,x) = λ(n−2)/2 u(λt, λx). This scaling symmetry is the source of the criticality: the energy is scale‑invariant, and the Strichartz estimates for the linear wave equation are exactly at the endpoint of the admissible range.

Kenig and Merle (2008) developed the concentration‑compactness/rigidity method to prove global existence and scattering for radial data with energy below the ground state threshold. The ground state W is the unique positive radial solution of −ΔW = W^p, which minimises the Sobolev quotient ∫ |∇u|² / (∫ |u|p+1)2/(p+1). The variational characterisation of W yields the sharp Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality ∫ |u|p+1 ≤ Copt (∫ |∇u|²)(p+1)/2 with equality exactly for the family of rescaled ground states. If the initial energy E(u₀,u₁) < E(W,0) and the Ḣ¹ norm of u₀ is less than that of W, then the solution exists globally and scatters to a linear solution as t → ±∞.

For non‑radial data, the profile decomposition of Bahouri and Gérard (1999) replaces the radial compactness. One extracts a sequence of profiles that are either dispersive (scattering) or concentrate along a scaling parameter. The “critical element” — a minimal‑energy non‑scattering solution — is shown to be almost periodic modulo symmetries. A virial/Morawetz argument then forces this element to be zero, completing the proof. The variational structure is essential: the energy functional provides the coercivity needed for the profile decomposition, and the ground state W serves as the threshold between blow‑up and scattering.

Mountain Pass Theorem Application
Consider the magnetic NLS energy E(u) on H¹_A(ℝ³) with A ∈ L⁴(ℝ³) and V ≡ 0. Show that E satisfies the Palais–Smale condition at the mountain‑pass level c = infγ∈Γ maxt∈[0,1] E(γ(t)), where Γ = {γ ∈ C([0,1], H¹_A) : γ(0)=0, E(γ(1))<0}.
1. The diamagnetic inequality |∇|u|| ≤ |∇_A u| implies the embedding H¹_A L^p is compact for 2 < p < 6. 2. Any Palais–Smale sequence (u_k) at level c is bounded in H¹_A by the geometry of the mountain pass and the subcritical growth. 3. By Rellich–Kondrachov, up to a subsequence u_k ⇀ u weakly in H¹_A and strongly in L^p_loc. 4. The magnetic potential A ∈ L⁴ ensures the nonlinear term ∫ A·Im(ū_k∇u_k) is continuous under weak convergence (Hölder with exponents 4, 4, 2). 5. The Brezis–Lieb lemma splits the energy: E(u_k) = E(u) + E(u_k−u) + o(1). 6. If u ≠ 0, then u is a critical point and c = E(u) + lim E(u_k−u) ≥ c + 0, forcing u_k → u strongly. 7. If u = 0, then c = lim E(u_k) ≥ 0, contradicting c < 0 from the mountain‑pass geometry. Hence strong convergence holds and the Palais–Smale condition is satisfied.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a variational problem involves a magnetic field, first write the covariant derivative and verify gauge invariance. Then check the diamagnetic inequality to transfer standard Sobolev embeddings. For critical exponent wave equations, remember the Kenig–Merle roadmap: (i) identify the ground state via the sharp Sobolev inequality, (ii) set up the concentration‑compactness profile decomposition, (iii) construct the critical element, (iv) apply a virial/Morawetz estimate to rule it out. Cite the key papers (Kenig–Merle 2008, Bahouri–Gérard 1999) to show awareness of the modern rigidity method.

Variational Methods for the Nonlocal Cahn–Hilliard Equation and Phase Separation

The nonlocal Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂_t u = Δ( (−Δ)^s u + f(u) ) with s ∈ (0,1) models phase separation with long‑range interactions. Its energy functional on the torus 𝕋ⁿ is

E_s(u) = ½ ∫ |(−Δ)s/2 u|² dx + ∫ F(u) dx,

where F' = f and F is a double‑well potential (e.g., F(u) = (1−u²)²/4). The fractional Laplacian (−Δ)^s is defined via Fourier multiplier |ξ|2s or the singular integral (−Δ)^s u(x) = Cn,s P.V. ∫ (u(x)−u(y))/|x−y|n+2s dy. The variational structure yields the gradient flow in the H−s metric: ∂_t u = −∇H−s E_s(u).

Existence of global weak solutions follows from the minimizing movement scheme (De Giorgi’s minimizing movements) applied to the functional E_s on the convex set of functions with prescribed mass. The scheme produces a discrete sequence u_k^τ solving u_k^τ = argmin_v { E_s(v) + (1/(2τ)) ‖v − uk−1^τ‖H−s² }. Compactness in L²(0,T; H^s) and the energy dissipation inequality E_s(u(t)) + ∫0^t ‖∂_t u‖H−s² ≤ E_s(u₀) pass to the limit τ → 0.

The sharp‑interface limit s → 1⁻ (or the simultaneous limit ε → 0 with ε2s scaling) has been analysed by Savin and Valdinoci (2012) using Γ‑convergence. They prove that the rescaled energies ε2s−1 E_s Γ‑converge to the classical perimeter functional ∫_∂*Ω dℋn−1 for sets of finite perimeter, where the fractional perimeter P_s(Ω) = ∫_Ω ∫Ω^c |x−y|−n−2s dx dy appears as the nonlocal analogue. The Γ‑limit identifies the motion by mean curvature as the limit of the nonlocal Cahn–Hilliard dynamics, with a mobility factor depending on the double‑well potential.

Recent work by Figalli and Ros‑Oton (2020) established regularity of minimisers of the fractional perimeter: if s > 1/2, the reduced boundary is C1,α except for a singular set of dimension at most n−2. For s ≤ 1/2, stickiness phenomena occur and the boundary may develop cusps. The variational approach also yields the existence of non‑trivial periodic patterns (lamellar, hexagonal) as minimisers under a volume constraint, with the optimal period scaling like ε−1/(2s+1).

Variational Methods for the Fractional p‑Laplacian and Nonlocal Eigenvalue Problems

The fractional p‑Laplacian (−Δ)_p^s for s ∈ (0,1), p > 1 is the Euler–Lagrange operator of the Gagliardo seminorm

[u]s,p^p = ∫ℝⁿ ∫ℝⁿ |u(x)−u(y)|^p / |x−y|n+sp dx dy.

The associated eigenvalue problem (−Δ)_p^s u = λ |u|p−2 u in Ω, u = 0 in Ω^c, admits a variational characterisation of the first eigenvalue

λ₁(s,p) = inf { [u]s,p^p / ∫_Ω |u|^p dx : u ∈ Ws,p0(Ω), u ≠ 0 }.

The infimum is attained by a positive eigenfunction φ₁ ∈ Ws,p0(Ω) which is unique up to scaling (Lindgren–Lindqvist 2018). The simplicity of λ₁ follows from the strict convexity of the functional u ↦ [u]s,p^p on the Nehari manifold. Higher eigenvalues are obtained via the Krasnoselskii genus on the symmetric Nehari manifold, yielding a sequence λ_k(s,p) → ∞.

As s → 1⁻, the fractional p‑Laplacian converges to the local p‑Laplacian in the sense of Mosco convergence of the corresponding energies. The eigenvalues satisfy λ_k(s,p) → λ_k(p) (the eigenvalues of the local p‑Laplacian) and the eigenfunctions converge strongly in W1,p0(Ω). Conversely, as p → ∞ with s fixed, one recovers the fractional infinity Laplacian (−Δ)_∞^s, whose viscosity solutions are characterised by the asymptotic mean value property u(x) = (1/2)(supB_r(x) u + infB_r(x) u) + o(r2s).

Regularity of eigenfunctions: for p ≥ 2, φ₁ ∈ Cα_loc(Ω) with α = min(s, 1−sp/n) (Brasco–Lindgren 2020). For 1 < p < 2, the eigenfunction is locally bounded and Hölder continuous up to the boundary if Ω satisfies the exterior ball condition. The fractional Hardy inequality ∫ |u|^p / dist(x,∂Ω)sp dx ≤ C [u]s,p^p holds for all u ∈ Ws,p0(Ω) and is sharp; it plays a crucial role in the analysis of the eigenvalue problem near the boundary.

Variational Methods for the Euler Equations of Incompressible Fluids and the Arnold Stability Criterion

The incompressible Euler equations ∂_t v + (v·∇)v = −∇p, ∇·v = 0 on a domain Ω ⊂ ℝ³ describe the motion of an ideal fluid. Arnold (1966) recognised that the Euler flow is a geodesic flow on the infinite‑dimensional manifold SDiff(Ω) of volume‑preserving diffeomorphisms, equipped with the right‑invariant L² metric. The kinetic energy E(v) = ½ ∫_Ω |v|² dx serves as the Hamiltonian, and the vorticity ω = curl v is transported by the flow: ∂_t ω + (v·∇)ω = (ω·∇)v.

The variational principle states that a steady solution v_s is a critical point of the energy restricted to the coadjoint orbit of the vorticity, i.e., among all divergence‑free fields with the same vorticity distribution. The second variation of the energy at v_s, restricted to perturbations preserving the vorticity invariants (Casimirs), yields the Arnold stability criterion: if the second variation δ²E(v_s) is positive definite on the subspace of divergence‑free fields tangent to the coadjoint orbit, then v_s is nonlinearly stable in the L² norm.

Concretely, for a two‑dimensional flow on a simply connected domain with stream function ψ_s (v_s = ∇^⊥ψ_s), the condition reduces to the existence of a constant c > 0 such that f'(ψ_s) ≤ −c, where f = −Δψ_s is the vorticity as a function of the stream function. This is the celebrated Arnold’s first stability theorem. The second theorem replaces the pointwise condition by an integral inequality involving the Hessian of the energy‑Casimir functional.

The energy‑Casimir method extends to three dimensions: one constructs a Lyapunov functional H_C(v) = E(v) + C(ω) where C is a Casimir functional (any functional of the vorticity that is conserved by the Euler flow, e.g., ∫ Φ(ω) dx). If v_s is a critical point of H_C and the second variation δ²H_C(v_s) is positive definite on the whole space of divergence‑free fields, then v_s is formally stable. The choice of C is guided by the specific steady state; for columnar vortices, C(ω) = ∫ F(ω) dx with F'' > 0 yields stability criteria that match the Rayleigh criterion for inviscid shear flows.

Recent developments by Brenier (1999) and Shnirelman (1994) use the convex integration technique to construct wild solutions that violate the energy conservation, showing that the variational structure on SDiff(Ω) is subtle: the geodesic equation is well‑posed only for short time in the smooth category, and the L² metric completion leads to measure‑valued solutions. Nevertheless, the Arnold criterion remains the cornerstone of nonlinear hydrodynamic stability for ideal fluids.

  • Confusing the magnetic Sobolev space H¹_A with the standard H¹; the covariant derivative must be used in all embeddings and compactness arguments.
  • Assuming the critical wave equation scattering threshold is the same for radial and non‑radial data; the non‑radial case requires the profile decomposition and a rigidity argument.
  • Treating the fractional Cahn–Hilliard energy as a local functional; the nonlocal term (−Δ)^s requires the Gagliardo seminorm and the correct scaling for Γ‑convergence.
  • Neglecting the exterior ball condition when citing boundary regularity for fractional p‑Laplacian eigenfunctions; the condition is essential for Hölder continuity up to the boundary.
  • Applying Arnold’s stability criterion without verifying that the perturbation preserves the Casimir invariants; the second variation must be restricted to the coadjoint orbit.
  • Overlooking the role of the diamagnetic inequality in transferring compactness from H¹ to H¹_A; it is the key estimate that allows standard variational methods to work with magnetic potentials.
  • Believing that the fractional perimeter Γ‑limit holds for any scaling; the correct scaling is ε2s−1 for the Modica–Mortola type approximation, otherwise the limit is trivial or infinite.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Choquard Equation and Nonlocal Nonlinearities

The Choquard equation, also known as the nonlinear Schrödinger–Newton or Hartree equation, takes the form i∂tu + Δu = (|x|−α * |u|p)|u|p−2u with 0 < α < n and p ≥ 2. Its stationary counterpart −Δu + u = (|x|−α * |u|p)|u|p−2u arises in quantum mechanics (mean‑field limit of many‑body systems) and in the description of self‑gravitating matter. The variational functional is E(u) = ½∫|∇u|2 + ½∫u2 − (1/2p)∫∫|u(x)|p|u(y)|p/|x−y|α dx dy. Lieb (1977) proved existence of ground states for the critical exponent p = (2n−α)/(n−2) using the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality and a concentration‑compactness argument. Lions (1984) extended the method to subcritical exponents and established orbital stability of standing waves via the Cazenave–Lions framework. Later, Moroz and Van Schaftingen (2013) developed a unified variational approach for a wide class of nonlocal nonlinearities, introducing the notion of nonlocal Nehari manifold and proving multiplicity results through the symmetric mountain‑pass theorem. The main analytical difficulty is the lack of compactness due to the convolution term; the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality provides the necessary control, while the Rellich–Kondrachov theorem fails at the critical exponent. Recent work by D'Avenia, Pomponio, and others (2020) treats the Choquard equation with magnetic potentials, showing that the diamagnetic inequality still holds for the nonlocal term, allowing the transfer of compactness from the magnetic Sobolev space H1A to the standard H1. These results are essential for the analysis of Bose–Einstein condensates with long‑range interactions and for the justification of the mean‑field limit in the Hartree dynamics.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with Magnetic Fields and the Diamagnetic Inequality

The magnetic nonlinear Schrödinger equation i∂tu + (∇ − iA)2u + V(x)u = |u|p−2u couples the gauge potential A with the wave function. The associated energy functional on the magnetic Sobolev space H1A(ℝn) is EA(u) = ½∫|(∇ − iA)u|2 + ½∫V|u|2 − (1/p)∫|u|p. The diamagnetic inequality |∇|u|| ≤ |(∇ − iA)u| a.e., proved by Avron, Herbst, and Simon (1978), is the cornerstone that allows one to compare the magnetic functional with the non‑magnetic one. Esteban and Lions (1990) used this inequality to show that the infimum of EA on the Nehari manifold is attained for subcritical p provided the magnetic field satisfies suitable decay conditions. For critical exponent p = 2n/(n−2), the lack of compactness is handled by the concentration‑compactness principle adapted to the magnetic setting by Cingolani (1997). The presence of a non‑trivial magnetic field can create multiple solutions via the topological structure of the gauge group; for instance, when A corresponds to an Aharonov–Bohm solenoid, the functional exhibits a ℤk symmetry leading to at least k distinct solutions by the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category theory. Recent advances by Bonheure, Nys, and Van Schaftingen (2021) treat the case of a critical magnetic nonlinearity combined with a Hardy potential, proving existence of ground states under a magnetic Hardy inequality. The variational framework also extends to the time‑dependent problem: the Strichartz estimates for the magnetic Schrödinger group, established by Erdogan, Goldberg, and Schlag (2009), yield local well‑posedness in H1A and allow the construction of global solutions for energy‑subcritical powers. These results are directly relevant to the modeling of superconductivity (Ginzburg–Landau theory) and to the study of quantum particles in electromagnetic fields.

Worked Example: Diamagnetic Inequality and Ground State Existence
Let A ∈ L2loc(ℝ3; ℝ3) and consider the functional EA(u) = ½∫|(∇ − iA)u|2 + ½∫|u|2 − (1/4)∫|u|4 on H1A(ℝ3). Show that any minimizing sequence for the constrained problem inf{EA(u) : ∫|u|4 = 1} is bounded in H1A and, up to a subsequence, converges strongly in L4 to a minimizer.
1. By the diamagnetic inequality, ∫|∇|u||2 ≤ ∫|(∇ − iA)u|2. Hence EA(u) ≥ E0(|u|) where E0 is the non‑magnetic functional. 2. The Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality gives ∫|u|4 ≤ C‖∇|u|‖23‖u‖2. With the constraint ∫|u|4 = 1, this yields a uniform bound on ‖∇|u|‖2 and thus on ‖(∇ − iA)u‖2. 3. Therefore the minimizing sequence is bounded in H1A. By the Rellich–Kondrachov theorem applied to |u|, we obtain strong convergence in L4 after passing to a subsequence. 4. Weak lower semicontinuity of the magnetic kinetic term and strong convergence of the nonlinear term imply the limit attains the infimum. Hence a ground state exists.
Exam Strategy
When a problem involves a magnetic potential, always check whether the diamagnetic inequality can reduce the estimate to the non‑magnetic case. Write the inequality explicitly and cite Avron–Herbst–Simon (1978). For compactness, remember that the magnetic Sobolev space embeds compactly into Lp only after taking absolute values; the gauge invariance of the norm ‖(∇ − iA)u‖2 is the key to applying standard concentration‑compactness.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Wave Equation with Critical Sobolev Exponent and Concentration Compactness

The energy‑critical nonlinear wave equation □u = |u|4/(n−2)u on ℝ1+n (n ≥ 3) possesses the scaling symmetry uλ(t,x) = λ(n−2)/2u(λt,λx) which leaves the conserved energy E(u) = ½∫(|∂tu|2 + |∇u|2) − (n−2)/2n ∫|u|2n/(n−2) invariant. The variational structure is encoded in the action functional S(u) = ∫0TE(u(t)) dt. The breakthrough by Struwe (1988) and Grillakis (1990) used the concentration‑compactness principle of Lions (1984) to prove global existence and scattering for radial data below the ground state energy. The profile decomposition of Bahouri and Gérard (1999) extended the result to non‑radial data by showing that any bounded sequence in the energy space Ḣ1 × L2 can be written as a sum of rescaled profiles plus a remainder that vanishes in the Strichartz norm. The critical element method of Kenig and Merle (2006) then identified the minimal‑energy blow‑up solution, which must be almost periodic modulo symmetries. A rigidity argument based on the virial identity and the Morawetz estimate rules out such a solution, establishing scattering for all data with energy below the ground state. For the focusing equation, the ground state W solves −ΔW = W(n+2)/(n−2) and its energy E(W,0) is the threshold. Duyckaerts, Kenig, and Merle (2011) classified all solutions at the threshold energy, showing they are either the stationary solution W or a soliton‑like solution converging to W in the energy space. These variational and concentration‑compactness techniques have been adapted to the wave maps equation, the Yang–Mills equation, and the Einstein vacuum equations, demonstrating the universality of the critical element approach.

Variational Methods for Nonlinear Elliptic Systems via the Nehari Manifold and the Fountain Theorem

Systems of elliptic equations such as −Δu = λ|u|p−2u + α|u|α−2u|v|β, −Δv = μ|v|q−2v + β|u|α|v|β−2v with α,β > 1, α+β = 2* (critical Sobolev exponent) arise in nonlinear optics and Bose–Einstein condensates. The associated energy functional E(u,v) = ½∫(|∇u|2 + |∇v|2) − (λ/p)∫|u|p − (μ/q)∫|v|q − ∫|u|α|v|β is defined on H1 × H1. The Nehari manifold 𝒩 = {(u,v) ≠ (0,0) : ⟨E'(u,v),(u,v)⟩ = 0} is a natural constraint; it is a C1 manifold of codimension one when the coupling term satisfies the condition α,β ≥ 2. Szulkin and Weth (2010) proved that the ground state energy c = inf𝒩 E is attained for subcritical couplings by showing that the Nehari manifold is homeomorphic to the unit sphere in H1 × H1 via the fibering map t ↦ E(tu,tv). For the critical case, the lack of compactness is overcome by the concentration‑compactness principle for systems developed by Alves, do Ó, and Souto (2011). The Fountain Theorem of Bartsch (1993) provides infinitely many solutions when the functional is even and satisfies the Palais–Smale condition on symmetric subsets. By constructing a sequence of finite‑dimensional subspaces Xk and radii ρk > rk > 0 such that supXk∩Sρk E ≤ 0 and infYk∩Srk E → ∞, one obtains a sequence of critical points with energies tending to infinity. Recent work by Chen and Zou (2018) extends the Fountain Theorem to systems with indefinite linear parts, using the spectral decomposition of the linear operator and a generalized Nehari–Pankov manifold. These variational tools are essential for proving multiplicity of bound states in coupled nonlinear Schrödinger systems and for the analysis of phase separation in binary mixtures.

Variational Methods for Nonlinear Parabolic Equations and the Gradient Flow Structure in Metric Spaces

Many nonlinear parabolic equations can be written as gradient flows of a convex functional in a suitable metric space. The prototype is the heat equation ∂tu = Δu, which is the gradient flow of the Dirichlet energy E(u) = ½∫|∇u|2 in the Hilbert space L2. For the porous medium equation ∂tu = Δ(um) (m > 1), Otto (2001) identified the Wasserstein distance W2 as the underlying metric and the internal energy E(u) = ∫um/(m−1) as the driving functional. The minimizing movement scheme (De Giorgi, 1993) constructs discrete solutions by solving uk ∈ argminv { E(v) + (1/2τ)W22(v,uk−1) } and passing to the limit τ → 0. Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré (2005) developed the abstract theory of gradient flows in metric spaces, introducing the notions of metric derivative, slope, and the energy dissipation inequality E(u(t)) + ½∫0t|u'|2 + ½∫0t|∂E|2(u) ≤ E(u(0)). This framework applies to the Fokker–Planck equation, the Cahn–Hilliard equation (with the H−1 Wasserstein metric), and the fourth‑order thin‑film equation. For the Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂tu = Δ(−ε2Δu + F'(u)), the energy is the Ginzburg–Landau functional E(u) = ∫(ε2/2|∇u|2 + F(u)) and the metric is the H−1 norm. The minimizing movement scheme yields existence of weak solutions and provides a natural discretization for numerical approximation. Recent extensions by Lisini, Matthes, and Savaré (2016) treat gradient flows of non‑convex functionals using the De Giorgi variational interpolation, allowing the analysis of the Allen–Cahn equation with a double‑well potential. The metric‑space gradient flow perspective unifies the variational structure of a wide class of dissipative PDEs and provides powerful tools for proving convergence to equilibrium, quantitative rates, and stability under perturbations.

  • Assuming the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality holds with the same constant for all α; the sharp constant depends on α and n and must be used in critical exponent calculations.
  • Neglecting the gauge invariance of the magnetic kinetic term when applying the diamagnetic inequality; the inequality applies to |u|, not to u itself, and the magnetic field must be real‑valued.
  • Applying the concentration‑compactness principle to the wave equation without verifying the Strichartz estimates for the linear propagator; the profile decomposition relies on the linear estimate.
  • Treating the Nehari manifold for systems as a product of scalar Nehari manifolds; the coupling term creates a non‑separable constraint that requires a joint fibering map.
  • Using the Wasserstein distance W2 for the Cahn–Hilliard equation; the correct metric is the H−1 Wasserstein distance, which accounts for mass conservation.
  • Overlooking the need for the energy functional to be lower semicontinuous with respect to the metric convergence in the minimizing movement scheme; without it the limit may not satisfy the energy dissipation inequality.
  • Confusing the Fountain Theorem with the Symmetric Mountain Pass Theorem; the Fountain Theorem requires a sequence of finite‑dimensional subspaces and yields infinitely many critical points with unbounded energy.

Variational Methods for the Fractional Laplacian and Nonlocal Operators

The fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s with 0 < s < 1 arises as the infinitesimal generator of a symmetric Lévy process and appears in models of anomalous diffusion, finance, and nonlocal elasticity. Its variational structure is built on the Gagliardo seminorm

[u]Hs2 = ∫∫ℝn×ℝn |u(x) − u(y)|2 / |x − y|n+2s dx dy

which defines the homogeneous fractional Sobolev space Ḣs(ℝn). The associated energy functional for a semilinear problem (−Δ)s u = f(u) is E(u) = ½[u]Hs2 − ∫ F(u) dx, where F′ = f. Critical points of E correspond to weak solutions. The Caffarelli–Silvestre extension (2007) realizes (−Δ)s as a Dirichlet‑to‑Neumann map for a degenerate elliptic problem in ℝn+1+ with weight y1−2s, turning the nonlocal variational problem into a local one on a half‑space. This extension preserves the variational structure and enables the use of classical regularity theory. Compactness issues are handled via the fractional Sobolev embedding Ḣs(ℝn) L2*s(ℝn) with 2*s = 2n/(n−2s). For subcritical nonlinearities the direct method yields minimizers on the Nehari manifold; for the critical exponent the concentration‑compactness principle of Lions (1984) adapted by Palatucci–Pisante (2014) provides existence of ground states. The fractional Brezis–Nirenberg problem, studied by Servadei–Valdinoci (2012), shows that the lack of compactness can be overcome by a careful analysis of the best constant in the Sobolev inequality. Recent work on nonlocal minimal surfaces (Caffarelli–Roquejoffre–Savin, 2010) uses the same energy with a characteristic function, leading to a variational formulation of the fractional perimeter.

Variational Methods for the Mean Curvature Flow and Level Set Formulations

Mean curvature flow (MCF) evolves a hypersurface Σt by normal velocity equal to its mean curvature H. Brakke (1978) introduced a variational formulation using integral varifolds: a family of rectifiable varifolds Vt satisfies the inequality d/dt μVt(φ) ≤ −∫ φ |H|2 dμVt + ∫ ∇φ·H dμVt for all test functions φ ≥ 0. This yields a weak solution that can pass through singularities. Ilmanen (1994) constructed MCF via elliptic regularization, minimizing the functional ∫ (ε|∇u|2 + (1/ε)W(u)) dx with a double‑well potential W, and proved convergence to Brakke’s flow as ε → 0. The level set method of Osher–Sethian (1988) represents the evolving interface as the zero level set of a function u solving the degenerate parabolic PDE ut = |∇u| div(∇u/|∇u|). Evans–Spruck (1991) and Chen–Giga–Goto (1991) independently established a viscosity solution theory for this PDE, providing a unique weak solution for any compact initial set. The variational structure appears in the minimizing movement scheme of Almgren–Taylor–Wang (1993): given a set Ek−1, define Ek as a minimizer of Per(E) + (1/τ)∫E Δ Ek−1 d(x,∂Ek−1) dx, where Per is the perimeter. As τ → 0 the discrete solutions converge to the viscosity solution of MCF. This scheme is the foundation of the threshold dynamics algorithm (Merriman–Bence–Osher, 1992) used in image processing. Recent advances by Kim–Tonegawa (2019) extend the varifold approach to anisotropic surface energies, while Laux–Otto (2021) developed a gradient flow structure in the space of varifolds with the Wasserstein metric.

Technique: Constructing a Minimizing Movement for Mean Curvature Flow
Given a smooth bounded domain Ω ⊂ ℝ2 and an initial set E0 ⊂ Ω with finite perimeter, describe the discrete minimizing movement scheme with time step τ > 0 and explain why the limit as τ → 0 yields a weak solution of mean curvature flow.
For each k ≥ 1, define Ek as a minimizer of the functional Fτ(E) = Per(E;Ω) + (1/τ)∫E Δ Ek−1 d(x,∂Ek−1) dx among all sets E ⊂ Ω of finite perimeter. The first term is the perimeter (total variation of the characteristic function), the second penalizes the symmetric difference weighted by the distance to the previous interface. Existence follows from the direct method in BV(Ω): the functional is lower semicontinuous with respect to L1 convergence and coercive. The piecewise constant interpolation Eτ(t) = Ek for t ∈ ((k−1)τ, kτ] satisfies the energy dissipation inequality Per(Eτ(t)) + (1/2)∫0t (1/τ)∫ d(x,∂Eτ(s−τ))2 dx ds ≤ Per(E0). Compactness in BV and the De Giorgi interpolation yield a limit set E(t) as τ → 0. By the work of Almgren–Taylor–Wang and later Luckhaus–Sturzenhecker, the limit satisfies the viscosity formulation of mean curvature flow, hence is a weak solution in the sense of Brakke.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a variational formulation of a geometric evolution, first identify the energy (perimeter, Dirichlet energy, etc.) and the metric (L2, Wasserstein, flat norm). Write the minimizing movement functional explicitly, state the lower semicontinuity and compactness arguments, and cite the key convergence theorem (Almgren–Taylor–Wang for MCF, De Giorgi for gradient flows). This template works for MCF, Allen–Cahn, and many other gradient flows.

Variational Methods for the Euler–Arnold Equations on Diffeomorphism Groups

Arnold (1966) showed that the Euler equations for an ideal incompressible fluid describe geodesics on the group of volume‑preserving diffeomorphisms SDiff(M) equipped with the right‑invariant L2 metric. The kinetic energy E(u) = ½∫M |u|2 dμ defines a Lagrangian on the Lie algebra of divergence‑free vector fields. The Euler–Poincaré reduction yields the Euler–Arnold equation ∂t u + ∇u u = −∇p, div u = 0. Ebin–Marsden (1970) proved local well‑posedness by viewing SDiff(M) as a smooth Hilbert manifold modeled on Hs vector fields (s > n/2 + 1) and applying the abstract Picard theorem on the geodesic spray. The variational principle is the least action principle δ∫ E(u(t)) dt = 0 among curves in SDiff(M) with fixed endpoints. For the Camassa–Holm equation, the metric is the H1 norm E(u) = ½∫ (u2 + ux2) dx on the diffeomorphism group of the circle; the corresponding geodesic equation exhibits peakon solutions. Misiołek (1998) established a conjugate point criterion for stability of fluid flows using the second variation of the energy. The Euler–Arnold framework extends to the Korteweg–de Vries equation (Ovsienko–Khesin, 1987) and to the incompressible magnetohydrodynamics equations (Holm–Marsden–Ratiu, 1998) where the configuration space is a semidirect product of diffeomorphisms and vector fields. Recent work by Bauer–Bruveris–Michor (2014) develops a Riemannian geometry on the full diffeomorphism group Diff(M) with Sobolev metrics of order k ≥ 1, providing a unified variational setting for many integrable PDEs.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Schrödinger–Poisson System

The Schrödinger–Poisson (or Schrödinger–Newton) system couples a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a Poisson equation for the self‑consistent potential: i∂t ψ = −Δψ + (V * |ψ|2)ψ + f(|ψ|2)ψ, where V(x) = |x|2−n (n ≥ 3) is the Coulomb kernel. Standing waves ψ(t,x) = eiωt u(x) lead to the elliptic system −Δu + ωu + (V * u2)u = f(u2)u. The associated energy functional on H1(ℝn) is E(u) = ½∫ |∇u|2 + ½ω∫ u2 + ¼∫ (V * u2)u2 − ∫ F(u2) dx, where F′ = f. The nonlocal term is well defined by the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality: ∫ (V * u2)u2 ≤ CHLS ‖u‖L12/54 for n = 3. Lions (1980) proved existence of ground states for subcritical power nonlinearities f(s) = sp with 1 < p < 2 using the concentration‑compactness principle. The critical exponent p = 2 (L2‑critical) was treated by Cazenave–Lions (1982) via the sharp Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality. For the repulsive case (negative sign in front of the nonlocal term) the functional is not bounded below; however, a constrained minimization on the Nehari manifold yields mountain‑pass solutions (Ambrosetti–Rabinowitz, 1973). The orbital stability of standing waves follows from the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss (1987) framework once the Vakhitov–Kolokolov slope condition d/dω ‖uω‖L22 > 0 is verified. Recent results by Bellazzini–Jeanjean–Luo (2020) address the case of combined local and nonlocal nonlinearities, showing the existence of normalized solutions with prescribed L2 mass using a variational approach on the Pohozaev manifold.

Variational Methods for the Relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell System

The Vlasov–Maxwell system describes a collisionless plasma: ∂t f + v·∇x f + (E + v × B)·∇v f = 0, coupled with Maxwell’s equations for the electromagnetic fields E, B. Low (1958) and later Ye–Morrison (1992) formulated a Lagrangian action principle on the space of particle trajectories and field potentials. The action is S = ∫ (½|E|2 − ½|B|2 − ∫ f (√(1+|v|2) − 1) dv) dx dt + ∫ (A·J − φρ) dx dt, where f is the distribution function, ρ = ∫ f dv, J = ∫ v f dv, and the fields derive from potentials φ, A. Critical points of S with respect to variations of f, φ, A yield the Vlasov–Maxwell equations. The Hamiltonian structure was clarified by Marsden–Weinstein (1982) using the Poisson bracket on the cotangent bundle of the field configuration space. Glassey–Strauss (1986) proved global existence of classical solutions for small initial data by exploiting the conservation of the total energy H = ∫ (½|E|2 + ½|B|2 + ∫ f √(1+|v|2) dv) dx. The variational formulation is essential for the construction of weak solutions via the DiPerna–Lions (1989) renormalization theory and for the recent work of Luk–Strain (2014) on the Cauchy problem with large data in 3D. In the nonrelativistic limit c → ∞ the action reduces to the Vlasov–Poisson action, and the variational structure underlies the derivation of the quasineutral limit (Golse–Saint‑Raymond, 2004). The existence of time‑periodic solutions via a variational mountain‑pass argument was established by Guo–Strauss (1995) for the Vlasov–Poisson system; the relativistic analogue remains an open problem.

  • Confusing the fractional Sobolev embedding exponent 2*s = 2n/(n−2s) with the classical 2* = 2n/(n−2); the former depends on s and is critical for compactness.
  • Assuming the minimizing movement scheme for mean curvature flow converges in the classical sense without invoking the viscosity solution framework; the limit is only a weak (Brakke) solution.
  • Neglecting the right‑invariant nature of the metric on the diffeomorphism group when deriving the Euler–Arnold equation; the geodesic equation involves the adjoint of the inertia operator.
  • Applying the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality with the wrong exponent for the Coulomb kernel in the Schrödinger–Poisson system; the sharp constant is essential for the critical case.
  • Treating the Vlasov–Maxwell action as a standard Lagrangian on a fixed manifold; the configuration space is an infinite‑dimensional Lie group and the action includes both particle and field variables.
  • Overlooking the need for the energy functional to be lower semicontinuous with respect to the weak topology in the direct method for nonlocal problems; the nonlocal term may fail weak continuity.
  • Confusing the Nehari manifold for the Schrödinger–Poisson system with the scalar case; the nonlocal term couples the L2 norm and the H1 norm in a non‑separable way.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Klein–Gordon Equation

The nonlinear Klein–Gordon equation in ℝn reads

∂ttu − Δu + m2u + f(u) = 0, m > 0,

where the nonlinearity f is typically a power f(u)=|u|p−1u with 1 < p < 1+4/(n−2) for n ≥ 3 (subcritical) or the critical exponent p = 1+4/(n−2). The equation is the Euler–Lagrange equation of the action functional

S(u) = ∫ℝ∫ℝn [½(∂tu)2 − ½|∇u|2 − ½m2u2 − F(u)] dx dt, F′ = f.

Standing waves u(t,x)=eiωtφ(x) with |ω| < m reduce the problem to the elliptic equation

−Δφ + (m2−ω2)φ = f(φ) in ℝn.

The associated energy on H1(ℝn) is

Eω(φ) = ½∫|∇φ|2 + ½(m2−ω2)∫φ2 − ∫F(φ).

Berestycki and Lions (1983) proved existence of a positive radial ground state for subcritical f by minimizing Eω on the Nehari manifold {φ≠0 : ⟨Eω′(φ),φ⟩=0}. The mountain‑pass geometry yields a second solution when f is odd. For the critical exponent the lack of compactness is overcome by the concentration‑compactness principle of Lions (1984); the sharp Sobolev constant determines the threshold for existence.

Orbital stability of the standing wave follows from the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss (1987) framework once the Vakhitov–Kolokolov slope condition d/dω ‖φω‖L22 > 0 is verified. In the repulsive case (negative sign before F) the functional is unbounded below, but constrained minimization on the Nehari manifold still produces mountain‑pass solutions (Ambrosetti–Rabinowitz, 1973). Recent work by Bellazzini–Jeanjean–Luo (2020) treats combined local and nonlocal nonlinearities using a Pohozaev manifold to prescribe the L2 mass.

Variational Methods for the Camassa–Holm Equation and Peakons

The Camassa–Holm (CH) equation

ut − uxxt + 3uux = 2uxuxx + uuxxx

models shallow water waves and is completely integrable. It arises as the Euler–Poincaré equation on the diffeomorphism group of the circle equipped with the H1 right‑invariant metric. The Lagrangian action is

ℒ(u) = ∫0T [½∫S1 (u2 + ux2) dx − ⅙∫S1 u3 dx] dt.

Introducing the momentum m = u − uxx, the CH equation takes the transport form mt + umx + 2uxm = 0. This structure reveals a bi‑Hamiltonian formulation with the Poisson operators J1 = −∂x + ∂x3 and J2 = −m∂x − ∂xm.

Peakons are weak solutions of the form u(x,t) = c e−|x−ct| (periodic version uses cosh). They correspond to momentum m = 2c δx=ct and solve the CH equation in the sense of distributions. Constantin and Strauss (2000) proved orbital stability of peakons by showing they are constrained minimizers of the Hamiltonian H(u)=½∫(u2+ux2) under fixed momentum I(u)=½∫(u3+uux2). The variational characterization uses the fact that the CH flow preserves both H and I, and the peakon profile minimizes H on the level set of I.

Multi‑peakon solutions u(x,t)=∑i=1N pi(t) e−|x−qi(t)| reduce the PDE to a finite‑dimensional Hamiltonian system for (qi,pi) with Hamiltonian H = ½∑i,j pipj e−|qi−qj|. This system is integrable and its solutions can be obtained by the inverse scattering transform. The variational approach also yields global existence of weak conservative solutions for initial data in H1 (Bressan–Constantin, 2007) by interpreting the CH equation as a geodesic flow on the diffeomorphism group with the H1 metric.

Technique: Variational Characterization of Peakons
Show that the single peakon u(x)=c e−|x| is a critical point of the Hamiltonian H(u)=½∫(u2+ux2) subject to the constraint I(u)=½∫(u3+uux2) = constant.
Compute the first variations. For H, δH = ∫(u−uxx)δu dx = ∫m δu dx. For I, δI = ½∫(3u2δu + ux2δu + 2uuxδux) dx = ∫(3/2 u2 + 1/2 ux2 − (uux)x)δu dx. Using u = c e−|x|, one finds m = 2c δ0 and ux = −c sign(x) e−|x|. Substituting shows the Euler–Lagrange equation δH = λ δI holds with λ = c, confirming the peakon is a constrained critical point. The second variation is positive on the tangent space of the constraint, giving orbital stability.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a variational derivation of a known PDE, write the action functional first, then compute the first variation carefully. For peakon‑type problems, remember that the momentum m = u − uxx is a measure; treat distributional derivatives explicitly. The constrained minimization argument (H under fixed I) is a standard template — memorize the steps: (1) define functionals, (2) compute variations, (3) identify Lagrange multiplier, (4) verify second variation positivity.

Variational Methods for the Fractional p‑Laplacian and Nonlocal Eigenvalue Problems

The fractional p‑Laplacian (−Δ)ps for s∈(0,1), p>1 is defined via the Gagliardo seminorm

[u]s,pp = ∫ℝn∫ℝn |u(x)−u(y)|p / |x−y|n+sp dx dy.

The eigenvalue problem (−Δ)ps u = λ |u|p−2u in Ω, u=0 in ℝn∖Ω, has a variational formulation: the first eigenvalue λ1 is the minimum of the Rayleigh quotient

λ1 = infu∈W0s,p(Ω), u≠0 [u]s,pp / ‖u‖Lp(Ω)p.

The space W0s,p(Ω) is the closure of Cc∞(Ω) under the norm (‖u‖Lpp+[u]s,pp)1/p. The direct method applies because the embedding W0s,p(Ω) Lp(Ω) is compact for bounded Ω (Rellich‑Kondrachov for fractional spaces). A minimizer exists and satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation in the weak sense.

Higher eigenvalues are obtained by the Ljusternik–Schnirelmann genus or the Krasnoselskii genus on the Nehari manifold. The fractional p‑Laplacian is homogeneous of degree p−1, so the spectrum is a sequence 0 < λ1 < λ2 ≤ λ3 ≤ … → ∞. For p=2 the operator is linear and the eigenvalues coincide with those of the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s.

Nonlocal eigenvalue problems appear in models of anomalous diffusion, finance (Lévy processes), and image processing (nonlocal total variation). The asymptotic behavior as s→1− recovers the classical p‑Laplacian eigenvalues (Bourgain–Brezis–Mironescu, 2001). As p→∞ one obtains the fractional infinity Laplacian and the associated eigenvalue problem for the nonlocal Lipschitz constant.

Variational Methods for Mean Field Games with Common Noise

Mean field games (MFG) describe the limit of N‑player stochastic differential games as N→∞. When a common noise W0 drives all players, the system becomes a pair of stochastic PDEs: a backward Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation for the value function u(t,x,ω) and a forward Fokker–Planck (FP) equation for the conditional law m(t,·,ω) of a representative player given the common noise path ω.

Carmona and Delarue (2018) formulated a variational principle on the space of flows of probability measures 𝒫(C([0,T];ℝd)). The MFG equilibrium corresponds to a minimizer of the functional

J(μ) = 𝔼[ ∫0T L(t, Xt, αt, μt) dt + G(XT, μT) ]

over all admissible controls α, where μt = Law(Xt | W0) and the dynamics are dXt = b(t,Xt,αt,μt) dt + σ dWt + σ0 dW0t. The expectation is taken over both the idiosyncratic noise W and the common noise W0.

The direct method works because the cost functional is convex in the control and lower semicontinuous with respect to the weak convergence of measures in the Wasserstein space 𝒫2(ℝd). The common noise breaks the symmetry of the problem and often restores uniqueness of the MFG equilibrium, which may fail in the deterministic case. The master equation, an infinite‑dimensional PDE on the space of measures, can be derived as the dynamic programming equation for this stochastic control problem.

Applications include systemic risk in finance (Carmona–Lacker, 2015), crowd motion with environmental uncertainty, and optimal execution with market impact. The variational approach also enables numerical approximation via the stochastic gradient descent on the space of measure flows (the “fictitious play” algorithm).

Variational Methods for Wasserstein Gradient Flows and the JKO Scheme

Many evolution PDEs can be interpreted as gradient flows of a functional ℱ in the Wasserstein space (𝒫2(ℝd), W2). The Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (JKO) scheme (1998) constructs the flow by implicit time discretization: given τ>0 and μ0∈𝒫2, define recursively

μk+1 ∈ argminμ∈𝒫2 [ ℱ(μ) + (1/(2τ)) W22(μ, μk) ].

The minimizer exists if ℱ is lower semicontinuous and has compact sublevels. As τ→0, the piecewise constant interpolation converges to a curve μ(t) satisfying the Evolution Variational Inequality (EVI)

½ d/dt W22(μ(t), ν) + ℱ(μ(t)) ≤ ℱ(ν) for all ν∈𝒫2.

Classical examples: the heat equation is the gradient flow of the Boltzmann entropy ℱ(μ)=∫ ρ log ρ dx (μ=ρ dx); the porous medium equation ∂tρ = Δρm is the gradient flow of the internal energy ℱ(μ)=1/(m−1)∫ ρm dx; the Fokker–Planck equation ∂tρ = div(ρ∇V) + Δρ is the gradient flow of the free energy ℱ(μ)=∫ ρV dx + ∫ ρ log ρ dx.

The Benamou–Brenier formula gives a dynamical representation of W22 as an action minimization over curves of measures and velocity fields, linking the JKO scheme to the theory of optimal transport. The scheme is also the basis for numerical algorithms (e.g., entropic regularization à la Cuturi, 2013) and for proving convergence of particle methods.

Recent extensions treat gradient flows in metric measure spaces (Ambrosio–Gigli–Savaré, 2005), non‑convex energies (e.g., the Keller–Segel model), and flows with constraints (e.g., incompressible Euler as a gradient flow in the space of volume‑preserving diffeomorphisms). The variational structure provides a unified framework for existence, uniqueness, and long‑time behavior of a vast class of PDEs.

  • Confusing the fractional Sobolev embedding exponent 2*s = 2n/(n−2s) with the classical 2* = 2n/(n−2); the former depends on s and is critical for compactness.
  • Assuming the minimizing movement scheme for mean curvature flow converges in the classical sense without invoking the viscosity solution framework; the limit is only a weak (Brakke) solution.
  • Neglecting the right‑invariant nature of the metric on the diffeomorphism group when deriving the Euler–Arnold equation; the geodesic equation involves the adjoint of the inertia operator.
  • Applying the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality with the wrong exponent for the Coulomb kernel in the Schrödinger–Poisson system; the sharp constant is essential for the critical case.
  • Treating the Vlasov–Maxwell action as a standard Lagrangian on a fixed manifold; the configuration space is an infinite‑dimensional Lie group and the action includes both particle and field variables.
  • Overlooking the need for the energy functional to be lower semicontinuous with respect to the weak topology in the direct method for nonlocal problems; the nonlocal term may fail weak continuity.
  • Confusing the Nehari manifold for the Schrödinger–Poisson system with the scalar case; the nonlocal term couples the L2 norm and the H1 norm in a non‑separable way.

Variational Methods for the Choquard Equation and Nonlocal Nonlinearities

The Choquard equation, also known as the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a nonlocal Hartree‑type nonlinearity, arises in quantum mechanics (polaron models) and in the description of self‑gravitating matter. Its energy functional on ℝⁿ (n ≥ 3) reads

E(u) = ½ ∫ |∇u|² dx − ¼ ∫∫ |u(x)|² |x−y|-(n−2) |u(y)|² dx dy,

where the double integral is the Coulomb interaction. The Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality guarantees that the nonlocal term is well defined on H¹(ℝⁿ) and scales like the kinetic term, making the problem critical in the sense of scaling. Lieb (1977) proved existence of a minimizer for the constrained minimization problem inf{E(u) : ‖u‖₂² = λ} by a concentration‑compactness argument that predates Lions’ general theory. The minimizer is radially symmetric, positive, and solves the Euler–Lagrange equation −Δu + u = (|x|-(n−2) * |u|²) u. Uniqueness of the positive radial solution for n = 3 was established by Lieb and Yau (1988) using an ODE shooting method combined with a nonlocal Pohozaev identity. For n ≥ 4 the uniqueness remains open, and the variational structure is used to derive Morse index estimates for excited states. The functional is not convex, but it satisfies the Palais–Smale condition at energy levels below the threshold given by the best constant in the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality. This threshold is exactly the energy of the ground state of the limiting problem on ℝⁿ, and it governs the dichotomy between compactness and loss of mass at infinity. In applications to optical media with long‑range interactions, the same variational framework yields existence of standing waves for the nonlocal nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a Riesz potential of order α ∈ (0,n). The critical exponent α = n−2 corresponds to the Choquard case; for α < n−2 the problem is subcritical and standard mountain‑pass arguments apply, while for α > n−2 the functional is unbounded below and no ground state exists.

Variational Methods for the Fractional p‑Laplacian and Nonlocal Eigenvalue Problems

The fractional p‑Laplacian (−Δ)ₚˢ, with s ∈ (0,1) and p > 1, is defined via the Gagliardo seminorm

[u]s,pᵖ = ∫∫ |u(x)−u(y)|ᵖ / |x−y|n+sp dx dy.

The associated energy functional on the fractional Sobolev space Ws,p(ℝⁿ) is Φ(u) = (1/p)[u]s,pᵖ. The first eigenvalue λ₁ of the Dirichlet problem on a bounded domain Ω is variationally characterized by the Rayleigh quotient

λ₁ = inf { [u]s,pᵖ / ∫_Ω |u|ᵖ dx : u ∈ W₀s,p(Ω), u ≠ 0 }.

Existence of a minimizer follows from the compact embedding W₀s,p(Ω) Lᵖ(Ω) for sp < n, and from the direct method using the lower semicontinuity of the Gagliardo seminorm with respect to weak convergence. The eigenfunction is positive, unique up to scaling, and satisfies a Harnack inequality (Kassmann, 2007). For sp ≥ n the embedding is not compact, but the eigenvalue problem can still be treated via the Caffarelli–Silvestre extension, which realizes the fractional operator as a Dirichlet‑to‑Neumann map for a degenerate elliptic equation in one higher dimension. This extension transforms the nonlocal variational problem into a local one with a weight y1−sp, allowing the use of standard elliptic regularity theory. The asymptotic behavior of λ₁ as s → 1⁻ recovers the classical p‑Laplacian eigenvalue, while as s → 0⁺ the eigenvalue scales like s(1−s) and converges to a nonlocal limit related to the logarithmic Laplacian. In the non‑variational setting, the fractional p‑Laplacian appears in the Euler–Lagrange equation of the nonlocal p‑energy, and the same Rayleigh quotient provides a min‑max characterization of higher eigenvalues via the Krasnoselskii genus. Recent work (Brasco–Lindgren, 2018) shows that the second eigenvalue can be obtained by minimizing the Rayleigh quotient on the Nehari manifold associated with the odd symmetry constraint. These variational techniques are essential for proving existence of nontrivial solutions to fractional p‑Laplacian equations with critical growth, where the Sobolev exponent is p*ₛ = np/(n−sp).

Worked Example: First Eigenvalue of the Fractional Laplacian on an Interval
Let Ω = (0,1) and consider the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)ˢ with s ∈ (0,1) and Dirichlet exterior condition. Show that the first eigenvalue λ₁(s) satisfies λ₁(s) ≥ Cₛ, where Cₛ is the best constant in the fractional Poincaré inequality on (0,1).
The Rayleigh quotient for the fractional Laplacian on (0,1) is R(u) = [u]s,2² / ∫₀¹ u² dx, where [u]s,2² = ∫∫ℝ² |u(x)−u(y)|² / |x−y|1+2s dx dy and u ≡ 0 outside (0,1). By definition, λ₁(s) = infu≠0 R(u). The fractional Poincaré inequality states that there exists a constant Cₛ > 0 such that ∫₀¹ u² dx ≤ Cₛ [u]s,2² for all u ∈ H₀ˢ(0,1). Rearranging gives [u]s,2² / ∫₀¹ u² dx ≥ 1/Cₛ. Taking the infimum over all admissible u yields λ₁(s) ≥ 1/Cₛ. The constant Cₛ is known explicitly: Cₛ = (π2s Γ(1−s)) / (22s Γ(1+s)) for the interval, so λ₁(s) ≥ 22s Γ(1+s) / (π2s Γ(1−s)). This lower bound is sharp as s → 1⁻, where λ₁(s) → π², the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the classical Laplacian on (0,1).
Exam Strategy
When a problem asks for a variational characterization of a nonlocal eigenvalue, write the Rayleigh quotient explicitly, identify the correct function space (usually W₀s,p), and cite the compact embedding condition (sp < n). If the embedding fails, mention the Caffarelli–Silvestre extension as the standard tool to recover a local variational formulation. Always check whether the nonlinearity is subcritical, critical, or supercritical with respect to the fractional Sobolev exponent p*ₛ = np/(n−sp); this determines which compactness argument (Palais–Smale, concentration‑compactness, or none) applies.

Variational Methods for Nonlinear Elasticity with Quasiconvexity and Relaxation

In finite‑strain elasticity the stored‑energy function W(F) depends on the deformation gradient F ∈ ℝn×n. The total energy of a deformation u : Ω → ℝⁿ is I(u) = ∫_Ω W(∇u) dx. Classical existence theory requires W to be quasiconvex in the sense of Morrey: for every F and every φ ∈ W₀1,∞(Q;ℝⁿ) (Q the unit cube),

W(F) ≤ ⨏_Q W(F + ∇φ) dx.

Quasiconvexity is necessary and sufficient for sequential weak lower semicontinuity of I on W1,p (p > 1). However, many physically relevant energy densities (e.g., those modeling martensitic phase transitions) are not quasiconvex. The relaxation theorem (Dacorogna, 1982) states that the lower semicontinuous envelope of I is given by the integral of the quasiconvex envelope QW, defined as the greatest quasiconvex function not exceeding W. Computing QW explicitly is possible only in special cases, such as for two‑well energies where the wells are rank‑one connected; then QW coincides with the convex hull on the lamination convex hull of the wells. Ball and James (1987) showed that microstructures (fine‑scale oscillations) correspond to minimizing sequences that generate Young measures supported on the wells. The variational problem is then reformulated in the space of gradient Young measures, and existence of a relaxed minimizer follows from the fundamental theorem of Young measures combined with the lower semicontinuity of the relaxed functional. In the context of shape memory alloys, the relaxed energy predicts the formation of austenite‑martensite interfaces and the hysteresis loop observed experimentally. Numerical approximation of relaxed problems uses finite‑element discretizations of the quasiconvex envelope via lamination convexification algorithms (Kohn–Strang, 1986). The lack of quasiconvexity also leads to the Lavrentiev phenomenon, where the infimum over smooth maps is strictly larger than the infimum over Sobolev maps; this is a genuine variational obstruction that must be addressed in any rigorous treatment.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Wave Equation with Critical Sobolev Exponent

The focusing nonlinear wave equation □u = |u|p−1u on ℝ1+n with the critical Sobolev exponent p = (n+2)/(n−2) (n ≥ 3) is the Euler–Lagrange equation of the action functional

S(u) = ½ ∫ (|∂ₜu|² − |∇u|²) dx dt − 1/(p+1) ∫ |u|p+1 dx dt.

The functional is indefinite due to the Lorentzian signature, so standard minimization fails. Instead, one seeks critical points via the mountain‑pass theorem on the energy space Ḣ¹ × L². The ground state solution W(x) = (1 + |x|²/(n(n−2)))-(n−2)/2 solves the elliptic equation −ΔW = W^p and provides the threshold for scattering versus blow‑up. Kenig and Merle (2008) introduced the concentration‑compactness/rigidity method: they proved that any solution with energy below E(W,0) and ‖∇u₀‖₂ < ‖∇W‖₂ exists globally and scatters, while solutions with energy equal to E(W,0) and ‖∇u₀‖₂ = ‖∇W‖₂ are exactly the solitary waves up to symmetries. The variational structure enters through the profile decomposition of bounded sequences in Ḣ¹, which is a consequence of the Bahouri–Gérard lemma adapted to the wave equation. The linear profile decomposition yields a sum of rescaled linear waves plus a remainder that goes to zero in the Strichartz norm. The nonlinear profiles are then constructed via perturbation theory, and the Pythagorean expansion of the energy allows one to isolate a minimal‑energy blow‑up solution. The rigidity step uses a localized virial identity (Morawetz estimate) to rule out the existence of such a minimal blow‑up solution unless it is the stationary ground state. This variational‑dynamical approach has been extended to the energy‑critical wave maps equation, the Yang–Mills equation, and the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with critical nonlinearity. In all cases the key variational ingredient is the characterization of the ground state as the optimizer of the Sobolev inequality, which provides the sharp constant for the Gagliardo–Nirenberg estimate used in the virial argument.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation on Compact Riemannian Manifolds

On a compact Riemannian manifold (M,g) without boundary, the nonlinear Schrödinger equation i∂ₜu + Δ_g u = |u|p−1u conserves the mass ‖u‖L²² and the energy E(u) = ½ ∫_M |∇_g u|² dV_g − 1/(p+1) ∫_M |u|p+1 dV_g. The variational problem for standing waves u(t,x) = eiωt φ(x) reduces to finding critical points of the action functional S_ω(φ) = E(φ) + ½ ω ‖φ‖L²² on H¹(M). When M = 𝕊ⁿ or a Zoll manifold, the spectrum of −Δ_g has high multiplicities, and the lack of dispersion leads to a different variational landscape than on ℝⁿ. For subcritical exponents p < 1 + 4/(n−2) (n ≥ 3), the embedding H¹(M) Lp+1(M) is compact, so the direct method yields a minimizer of S_ω on the Nehari manifold {φ ≠ 0 : ⟨S_ω'(φ), φ⟩ = 0}. The minimizer is a ground state, and its Morse index is one. For the critical exponent p = 1 + 4/(n−2), the embedding is not compact, and the Palais–Smale condition fails at energy levels equal to the best Sobolev constant on ℝⁿ. However, the concentration‑compactness principle on manifolds (Hebey–Vaugon, 1995) shows that loss of compactness can only occur by bubbling at a point, and the bubble profile is the Euclidean ground state. If the Yamabe invariant of (M,g) is positive and the manifold is not conformally equivalent to the sphere, one can prove existence of a ground state by a min‑max argument on the Nehari manifold combined with a careful analysis of the interaction between bubbles and the geometry (the so‑called “bubble‑tree” decomposition). For the sphere 𝕊ⁿ, the problem is completely symmetric and the ground states are exactly the conformal images of the Euclidean optimizer; the variational problem reduces to a finite‑dimensional minimization over the conformal group. In the focusing case, the variational structure also yields orbital stability of standing waves via the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss framework, provided the mapping ω ↦ ‖φ_ω‖L²² is strictly increasing. On compact manifolds this derivative can be computed using the spectral flow of the linearized operator, linking stability to the sign of the first eigenvalue of the linearized operator on the orthogonal complement of the gauge direction.

  • Confusing the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev critical exponent for the Choquard equation with the Sobolev critical exponent; they coincide only for the Coulomb potential (α = n−2).
  • Assuming the fractional p‑Laplacian eigenvalue problem is compact for all s,p; compactness requires sp < n, otherwise the Caffarelli–Silvestre extension must be used.
  • Treating quasiconvexity as equivalent to convexity in nonlinear elasticity; rank‑one convexity is necessary but not sufficient, and explicit counterexamples exist (Šverák, 1992).
  • Applying the mountain‑pass theorem directly to the wave action functional without first restricting to the Nehari manifold or using the concentration‑compactness/rigidity scheme; the indefinite metric prevents a straightforward minimax.
  • Overlooking the role of the Yamabe invariant in the critical NLS on manifolds; a negative Yamabe invariant can prevent existence of ground states even when the subcritical problem has solutions.
  • Neglecting the gauge invariance when computing the Morse index of a standing wave on a manifold; the kernel of the linearized operator always contains the derivative with respect to the phase, which must be factored out.
  • Using the Euclidean Sobolev constant as the threshold for blow‑up in the critical wave equation on a curved background; the threshold is the energy of the ground state of the associated elliptic problem on the manifold, which may differ from the Euclidean optimizer.

These advanced variational topics illustrate how geometric, analytic, and algebraic structures intertwine to determine existence, uniqueness, and stability of critical points in nonlinear field theories.

Variational Methods for the Choquard Equation — Nonlocal Nonlinearity

The Choquard equation, also called the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with Hartree‑type nonlocal nonlinearity, reads i∂ₜu + Δu = (|x|⁻ᵅ * |u|²) u on ℝⁿ, where 0 < α < n and * denotes convolution. Its stationary states u(t,x)=eiωtφ(x) satisfy −Δφ + ωφ = (|x|⁻ᵅ * |φ|²) φ, which is the Euler–Lagrange equation of the action functional S_ω(φ)=½∫(|∇φ|²+ω|φ|²)dx − ¼∫∫|φ(x)|²|x−y|⁻ᵅ|φ(y)|²dxdy. The double integral is well defined on H¹(ℝⁿ) by the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality, which requires α < n and gives the critical exponent p_c = (2n−α)/(n−2) for the associated power‑type nonlinearity. When α = n−2 the Choquard equation coincides with the classical Schrödinger–Newton system and the critical exponent matches the Sobolev critical exponent 2* = 2n/(n−2). Existence of ground states for ω>0 follows from the concentration‑compactness principle applied to the minimisation of S_ω on the Nehari manifold N_ω={φ≠0: ⟨S_ω'(φ),φ⟩=0}. Lions (1984) proved that a minimiser exists for all subcritical α and that the minimiser is radially symmetric, positive, and exponentially decaying. For the critical case α = n−2, the lack of compactness is exactly the same as for the Sobolev critical NLS; the threshold energy is the Euclidean optimiser of the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality, explicitly known from Lieb’s sharp constant. Orbital stability of the standing waves is obtained via the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss framework once one verifies the Vakhitov–Kolokolov slope condition d/dω ‖φ_ω‖₂² > 0, which holds for the whole subcritical range. In the critical case the slope condition fails at the threshold, leading to a sharp dichotomy between global existence and blow‑up analogous to the Kenig–Merle result for the local NLS.

Variational Methods for the Gross–Pitaevskii Equation with Harmonic Trapping

The Gross–Pitaevskii (GP) equation i∂ₜψ = (−½Δ + V(x) + g|ψ|²)ψ models a Bose–Einstein condensate at zero temperature. The external trap V(x)=½|x|² is harmonic, and the coupling constant g>0 corresponds to repulsive interactions. Stationary states ψ(t,x)=e-iμtφ(x) satisfy the elliptic problem −½Δφ + ½|x|²φ + g|φ|²φ = μφ, which is the Euler–Lagrange equation of the energy functional E(φ)=∫(½|∇φ|² + ½|x|²|φ|² + ½g|φ|⁴)dx under the mass constraint ‖φ‖₂² = N (particle number). The direct method on the constrained manifold {φ∈H¹(ℝⁿ): ‖φ‖₂²=N} yields a unique (up to phase) minimiser because the harmonic potential provides compact embedding of the weighted Sobolev space H¹_V into L⁴. The minimiser φ₀ is positive, radially symmetric, and satisfies the Thomas–Fermi approximation φ_TF(x) = √((μ−½|x|²)/g)_+ for large gN, where the kinetic term becomes negligible. The chemical potential μ scales like (gN)2/3 in three dimensions. Excited states correspond to higher critical points of E on the Nehari manifold; their Morse index equals the number of nodal domains. The Bogoliubov–de Gennes linearisation around φ₀ gives the excitation spectrum; the lowest eigenvalue is zero (phase mode) and the next eigenvalue is positive, confirming dynamical stability. For rotating condensates one adds the term −ΩL_z to the Hamiltonian; the variational problem then includes the angular momentum constraint and leads to vortex lattice solutions whose existence is proved by Γ‑convergence of the rescaled energy to a Ginzburg–Landau type functional as Ω approaches the trap frequency.

Worked Example: Ground State of the Choquard Equation
Show that the functional S_ω(φ)=½∫(|∇φ|²+ω|φ|²)dx − ¼∫∫|φ(x)|²|x−y|⁻ᵅ|φ(y)|²dxdy is well defined and C¹ on H¹(ℝ³) for 0<α<3, and compute its Fréchet derivative.
By the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequality, for φ∈H¹(ℝ³) we have ‖|x|⁻ᵅ * |φ|²‖6/(3−α) ≤ C‖φ‖12/(3+α)². Sobolev embedding gives H¹L12/(3+α) for α<3, so the double integral is finite. The map φ↦|x|⁻ᵅ * |φ|² is C¹ from H¹ to L6/(3−α); differentiating under the integral sign yields ⟨S_ω'(φ),η⟩ = ∫(∇φ·∇η + ωφ η)dx − ∫(|x|⁻ᵅ * |φ|²) φ η dx. Hence S_ω'(φ) = −Δφ + ωφ − (|x|⁻ᵅ * |φ|²) φ, which is exactly the stationary Choquard equation.
