Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for the Euler–Lagrange equation of a nonlocal functional, first verify the functional is well defined using the appropriate Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev or Sobolev embedding. Then differentiate the nonlocal term by treating the convolution as a bilinear form; the derivative is twice the convolution of the kernel with the product of the function and the test function. Remember the factor ½ from the double integral.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with Magnetic Potential

The magnetic NLS i∂ₜu = (−i∇−A(x))²u + V(x)u − |u|p−1u arises in superconductivity and quantum mechanics with a magnetic field B = curl A. The stationary equation (−i∇−A)²φ + Vφ = |φ|p−1φ is the Euler–Lagrange equation of the magnetic energy functional E_A(φ)=½∫|(−i∇−A)φ|²dx + ½∫V|φ|²dx − 1/(p+1)∫|φ|p+1dx on the magnetic Sobolev space H¹_A = {φ∈L²: (−i∇−A)φ∈L²}. Diamagnetic inequality |∇|φ|| ≤ |(−i∇−A)φ| guarantees that the embedding H¹_A Lp+1 holds under the same conditions as the standard Sobolev embedding, provided A∈L²_loc and V≥0. Existence of ground states for subcritical p follows from minimisation on the magnetic Nehari manifold N_A = {φ≠0: ⟨E_A'(φ),φ⟩=0}. The presence of a magnetic field breaks translation invariance, so concentration‑compactness must be applied to the magnetic gradient; the lack of compactness is still governed by the usual Sobolev critical exponent. For critical exponent p = 2*−1 = (n+2)/(n−2) the best constant in the magnetic Sobolev inequality equals the Euclidean one, and the minimisers are the standard Aubin–Talenti bubbles multiplied by a magnetic phase factor eiχ where χ is a line integral of A. Orbital stability of magnetic standing waves is again governed by the Vakhitov–Kolokolov condition d/dω ‖φ_ω‖₂² > 0; the magnetic field does not alter the slope because the mass is gauge invariant. In the case of a constant magnetic field B = (0,0,b) in ℝ³, the Landau levels give an explicit spectral decomposition of (−i∇−A)², and the ground state can be constructed by a Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction near the lowest Landau level.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation on Metric Graphs

A metric graph Γ consists of a finite set of edges identified with intervals [0,ℓ_e] (ℓ_e may be infinite) and vertices where Kirchhoff (continuity and sum of derivatives zero) or δ‑type conditions are imposed. The NLS on Γ reads i∂ₜu = −∂ₓₓu − |u|p−1u on each edge, with the chosen vertex conditions. The energy functional is E(u)=½∑_e∫0ℓ_e|u'_e|²dx − 1/(p+1)∑_e∫0ℓ_e|u_e|p+1dx, defined on the Sobolev space H¹(Γ) = {u∈⊕_e H¹(0,ℓ_e): u continuous at vertices}. The mass ‖u‖₂² is conserved. Ground states for a prescribed mass μ>0 are minimisers of E on the mass‑constraint manifold M_μ = {u∈H¹(Γ): ‖u‖₂²=μ}. For subcritical p<5 (the L²‑critical exponent on a line) the embedding H¹(Γ)Lp+1(Γ) is compact on compact graphs, so the direct method yields a minimiser. On non‑compact graphs (e.g. a half‑line or a star graph with infinite edges) compactness fails; one uses concentration‑compactness adapted to graphs, where loss of mass can only occur by translation to infinity along an infinite edge. The ground state on a star graph with N half‑lines and Kirchhoff conditions is symmetric (equal on each edge) for p<5 and becomes asymmetric for p>5, a bifurcation phenomenon proved by Adami–Cacciapuoti–Finco–Noja (2015). The critical exponent p=5 is the threshold where the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality on Γ has the same best constant as on ℝ; the minimiser is the soliton restricted to a single edge and vanishing on the others. Orbital stability of the symmetric ground state for p<5 follows from the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss theory once the slope condition d/dω ‖φ_ω‖₂² > 0 is verified; the derivative can be computed explicitly using the scaling relation φ_ω(x)=ω1/(p−1)φ1(√ω x). For δ‑type conditions with strength α at the vertex, the ground state exists for all α∈ℝ when p<5, and the energy level is strictly decreasing in α.

Variational Methods for the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation with Critical Exponential Growth (Trudinger–Moser)

In two dimensions the Sobolev embedding H¹(ℝ²)L^p fails at p=∞, but the Trudinger–Moser inequality gives ∫(e4π|u|²/‖∇u‖₂²−1)dx ≤ C for ‖∇u‖₂≤1. The NLS with exponential nonlinearity i∂ₜu + Δu = u(e|u|²−1) has the energy functional E(u)=½∫|∇u|²dx − ½∫(e|u|²−1−|u|²)dx. The natural space is the Orlicz space associated with the Young function Φ(t)=et²−1−t². Existence of ground states for a prescribed mass is delicate because the functional is not bounded below on the whole H¹; one restricts to the Nehari manifold N={u≠0: ⟨E'(u),u⟩=0} where the kinetic and potential parts balance. Adachi–Tanaka (2000) proved that a minimiser exists for any mass μ>0 by a concentration‑compactness argument in the Orlicz setting; the lack of compactness is again due to translations, and the threshold is given by the best constant in the Trudinger–Moser inequality. The ground state is radially symmetric, positive, and solves −Δφ + λφ = φ(eφ²−1) with a Lagrange multiplier λ>0. Orbital stability follows from the convexity of the mapping ω↦‖φ_ω‖₂², which can be shown using the Pohozaev identity and the strict monotonicity of the mass with respect to λ. For the critical exponential growth on a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝ² with Dirichlet boundary condition, the same variational structure yields existence of a positive solution for any λ<λ₁ (first Dirichlet eigenvalue), while for λ≥λ₁ the problem has no nontrivial solution. The borderline case λ=λ₁ is related to the Moser–Onofri inequality on the sphere via stereographic projection.

  • Confusing the Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev critical exponent for the Choquard equation with the Sobolev critical exponent; they coincide only for the Coulomb potential (α = n−2).
  • Assuming the magnetic Sobolev embedding is compact for all magnetic potentials; compactness requires the magnetic field to vanish at infinity or the domain to be bounded.
  • Treating the mass constraint on a metric graph as a simple Lagrange multiplier problem without checking the Kirchhoff vertex conditions are preserved by the minimiser.
  • Overlooking the role of the Trudinger–Moser constant 4π as the sharp threshold for the exponential NLS; using any larger constant leads to non‑existence of minimisers.
  • Applying the standard Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss stability criterion without factoring out the gauge symmetry in the magnetic case; the kernel of the linearised operator always contains the phase derivative.
  • Neglecting the possibility of asymmetric ground states on star graphs for p>5; the symmetric state becomes a saddle point and the true minimiser breaks symmetry.
  • Using the Euclidean Aubin–Talenti bubble as a trial function for the magnetic critical NLS without adding the magnetic phase factor; the magnetic gradient of the bare bubble is larger, so the energy is not optimal.

These advanced variational topics illustrate how nonlocal interactions, external fields, discrete geometries, and critical exponential growth each require tailored functional‑analytic tools while preserving the core principle that critical points of an action functional govern the dynamics of nonlinear dispersive equations.

Variational Methods for the Fractional p‑Laplacian and Nonlocal Eigenvalue Problems

The fractional p‑Laplacian (−Δ)ps for s∈(0,1) and p>1 is defined via the singular integral (−Δ)psu(x)=2limε→0∫|x−y|>ε|u(x)−u(y)|p−2(u(x)−u(y))|x−y|−n−spdy. Its variational structure lives in the fractional Sobolev–Slobodeckij space Ws,p(ℝn) with the Gagliardo seminorm [u]s,pp=∬ℝ2n|u(x)−u(y)|p|x−y|−n−spdxdy. The Dirichlet eigenvalue problem (−Δ)psu=λ|u|p−2u in Ω, u=0 in ℝn∖Ω, admits a variational formulation: the first eigenvalue λ1(Ω)=inf{[u]s,pp/‖u‖Lpp : u∈W0s,p(Ω), u≠0} where W0s,p(Ω) is the closure of Cc∞(Ω) in Ws,p(ℝn). The infimum is attained by a positive eigenfunction φ1∈W0s,p(Ω)∩L∞(ℝn) which satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation in the weak sense. Higher eigenvalues are obtained via the Ljusternik–Schnirelmann genus or the Krasnoselskii genus on the Nehari manifold N={u∈W0s,p(Ω)∖{0} : [u]s,pp=λ‖u‖Lpp}. A key difference from the local case p=2 is the lack of a Hilbert space structure; the energy functional J(u)=1/p[u]s,pp−λ/p‖u‖Lpp is C1 but not C2 when p≠2, so the Palais–Smale condition must be verified directly using the compact embedding W0s,p(Ω)Lp(Ω) for bounded Lipschitz domains. The fractional Faber–Krahn inequality states that among all domains of fixed volume, the ball minimizes λ1; the proof uses the fractional Polya–Szegő inequality [u*]s,p≤[u]s,p for the symmetric decreasing rearrangement u*. For the critical exponent ps*=np/(n−sp), the embedding W0s,p(Ω)Lps*(Ω) is continuous but not compact, leading to the Brezis–Nirenberg type problem (−Δ)psu=λ|u|p−2u+|u|ps*−2u. The existence threshold depends on the best constant Ss,p in the fractional Sobolev inequality and the geometry of Ω; for star‑shaped domains the Pohozaev identity rules out nontrivial solutions when λ≤0. Nonlocal eigenvalue problems also arise in the spectral theory of the regional fractional Laplacian (−ΔΩ)ps where integration is restricted to Ω×Ω; its first eigenvalue converges to the local p‑Laplacian eigenvalue as s→1− with rate O(1−s).

Variational Methods for Double Phase Functionals and Variable Exponent Spaces

Double phase functionals J(u)=∫Ω(|∇u|p+a(x)|∇u|q)dx with 1

Φ(Ω) with Φ(x,t)=tp+a(x)tq, or equivalently the sum space W1,p(Ω)∩W1,qa(Ω) where W1,qa(Ω)={u∈Lq(Ω) : a1/q∇u∈Lq(Ω)}. The modular ρΦ(u)=∫Φ(x,|u|)dx replaces the norm in the lack of uniform convexity when a(x) vanishes on a set of positive measure. The Euler–Lagrange equation −div(|∇u|p−2∇u+a(x)|∇u|q−2∇u)=f is degenerate where a(x)=0 and singular where a(x)→∞. Regularity theory developed by Colombo–Mingione (2015) shows that local minimizers are C1,α provided q

0,α; the proof uses a fractional Caccioppoli inequality and a non‑uniform version of the Gehring lemma. For variable exponent problems J(u)=∫|∇u|p(x)dx with p∈C0,γ(Ω̄), 1

−≤p(x)≤p+<n, the space W<sup>1,p(·)(Ω) is reflexive and separable but not uniformly convex when p(x) is not constant. The log‑Hölder continuity condition |p(x)−p(y)|≤C/−log|x−y| for |x−y|<1/2 guarantees the density of smooth functions and the validity of the Poincaré inequality. The eigenvalue problem −Δp(x)u=λ|u|p(x)−2u has a sequence of variational eigenvalues obtained by the genus on the Nehari manifold N={u≠0 : ∫|∇u|p(x)dx=λ∫|u|p(x)dx}. The first eigenvalue λ1 is simple, isolated, and its eigenfunction does not change sign. The (p,q)‑Laplacian −Δpu−Δqu=λ|u|r−2u with p<r<q exhibits a bifurcation from infinity at λ=λ<sub>1(−Δp) and from zero at λ=λ1(−Δq); the variational structure is captured by the functional J(u)=1/p∫|∇u|p+1/q∫|∇u|q−λ/r∫|u|r. In the double phase case with a(x)=|x|α, the Hardy inequality ∫|u|p/|x|pdx≤C∫(|∇u|p+|x|α|∇u|q)dx holds for α<q−p, and the best constant is attained only when α=0. These problems require a careful blend of modular convergence, the De Giorgi–Nash–Moser iteration adapted to non‑standard growth, and the concentration‑compactness principle in Musielak–Orlicz spaces.</p>

Worked Problem: First Eigenvalue of the Fractional p‑Laplacian on a Ball
Let Ω=B1(0)⊂ℝn, s∈(0,1), p>1 with sp<n. Show that the first eigenvalue λ<sub>1 of (−Δ)ps with Dirichlet exterior condition is simple and its eigenfunction can be chosen positive and radially symmetric decreasing.
Step 1: Variational characterization. λ1=inf{[u]s,pp/‖u‖Lpp : u∈W0s,p(B1), u≠0}. The embedding W0s,p(B1)Lp(B1) is compact (Rellich–Kondrachov for fractional spaces), so a minimizer φ1 exists by the direct method. Normalize ‖φ1‖Lp=1. Step 2: Positivity. The functional [u]s,p is convex and satisfies [|u|]s,p≤[u]s,p (by the triangle inequality for |·|p−2·). Hence |φ1| is also a minimizer. The strong maximum principle for the fractional p‑Laplacian (Iannizzotto–Mosconi–Squassina, 2016) implies |φ1|>0 in B1. Step 3: Radial symmetry. Let φ1* be the symmetric decreasing rearrangement. The fractional Polya–Szegő inequality [φ1*]s,p≤[φ1]s,p holds with equality iff φ1 is already radially symmetric decreasing up to translation. Since φ1 vanishes outside B1, its rearrangement is supported in B1 and ‖φ1*‖Lp=‖φ1‖Lp=1. Thus φ1* is also a minimizer, so equality holds in Polya–Szegő, forcing φ1 to be radially symmetric decreasing. Step 4: Simplicity. Suppose ψ is another eigenfunction for λ1 with ‖ψ‖Lp=1. By the Picone identity for the fractional p‑Laplacian (Alberico–Cianchi–Pick, 2020), ∫(|∇φ1|p−|∇ψ|p)≥0 with equality iff ψ=cφ1. Since both have the same Rayleigh quotient, equality holds, so ψ=±φ1. Hence the eigenspace is one‑dimensional.
Exam Strategy: Nonlocal vs Local Eigenvalue Problems
When comparing fractional and local p‑Laplacian eigenvalues, remember three key differences: (1) the fractional Rayleigh quotient uses the Gagliardo seminorm, not ∫|∇u|p; (2) the exterior condition u=0 in ℝn∖Ω is nonlocal and stronger than the local Dirichlet condition; (3) as s→1−, (1−s)[u]s,pp→Cn,p∫|∇u|p (Bourgain–Brezis–Mironescu), so λ1(s)∼λ1(1)/(1−s). In multiple‑choice questions, check whether the limit s→1 is taken with or without the (1−s) factor — this is a common trap.

Variational Methods for the Concentration‑Compactness Principle and Profile Decomposition

The concentration‑compactness principle (Lions, 1984) addresses the failure of compactness in critical Sobolev embeddings W1,p(ℝn)Lp*(ℝn) where p*=np/(n−p). A bounded sequence (uk) in W1,p may lose mass by three mechanisms: (i) vanishing: supy∈ℝn∫BR(y)|uk|p*→0 for all R>0; (ii) dichotomy: the sequence splits into two asymptotically disjoint parts with nontrivial energy; (iii) compactness: up to translation, a subsequence converges strongly in Lp*. The principle states that for any bounded sequence, one of these three occurs after passing to a subsequence. The profile decomposition (Bahouri–Gérard, 1999; Gérard, 1998) refines this for the critical wave and Schrödinger equations: any bounded sequence (uk) in Ḣ1(ℝn) can be written as uk=∑j=1Jφjk+wkJ where φjk(x)=λj,k(n−2)/2φj(λj,kx−xj,k) are rescaled and translated profiles with orthogonal parameters (λj,k/λi,k+λi,k/λj,k+|xj,k−xi,k|/λj,k→∞ for i≠j), and the remainder satisfies limJ→∞limsupk→∞‖wkJ‖L2n/(n−2)=0. The Pythagorean expansion ‖∇uk‖22=∑j=1J‖∇φj‖22+‖∇wkJ‖22+o(1) holds. This decomposition is the backbone of the Kenig–Merle roadmap for critical dispersive equations: one assumes a minimal‑mass blowup solution, extracts its profile decomposition, and shows that the nonlinear profile must be a soliton, leading to rigidity theorems. In the variational context, the concentration‑compactness principle is used to prove existence of minimizers for the Sobolev quotient Q(u)=‖∇u‖22/‖u‖2*2 on ℝn; the Aubin–Talenti bubbles Uλ,x0(x)=cn(λ/(λ2+|x−x0|2))(n−2)/2 are the only minimizers. For the Brezis–Nirenberg problem −Δu=λu+u2*−1 on a bounded domain, the threshold λ* depends on whether the domain is star‑shaped (Pohozaev obstruction) or has nontrivial topology (Bahri–Coron). The profile decomposition also yields the sharp Strichartz estimates and the soliton resolution conjecture for energy‑critical NLS: any global solution decomposes into a sum of solitary waves plus a radiation term that scatters to zero.

Variational Methods for the Min‑Max Theory and the Almgren–Pitts Construction

While the mountain pass theorem and linking arguments produce critical points of C1 functionals on Banach spaces, the Almgren–Pitts min‑max theory constructs minimal hypersurfaces in a Riemannian manifold (Mn+1,g) by minimizing the area functional over sweepouts. A sweepout is a continuous map Φ: [0,1]→Zn(M) into the space of integral n‑currents with Φ(0)=Φ(1)=0. The width is L(Φ)=supt∈[0,1]M(Φ(t)) where M is the mass (area). The min‑max value is W=infΦL(Φ) over all sweepouts in a given homotopy class. Almgren (1965) proved that for 2≤n≤6, there exists an integral current T with ∂T=0, M(T)=W, which is a stationary varifold and regular except for a singular set of dimension ≤n−7. Pitts (1981) extended this to n≥7 using the regularity theory of Schoen–Simon. The key technical tool is the pull‑tight procedure: given a minimizing sequence of sweepouts, one deforms each slice by the mean curvature flow for a short time to reduce area while preserving the homotopy class, then takes a limit. The resulting min‑max minimal hypersurface has Morse index bounded by the number of parameters in the sweepout (Marques–Neves, 2016). For the Weyl law for the volume spectrum ωp(M)=infΦ∈Πpsupx∈XM(Φ(x)) where Πp are p‑sweepouts, Liokumovich–Marques–Neves (2018) proved ωp(M)∼a(n)vol(M)n/(n+1)p1/(n+1). In the variational setting for the Allen–Cahn equation −εΔu+ε−1W'(u)=0 with W(u)=(1−u2)2/4, the Modica–Mortola Γ‑convergence shows that the energy Eε(u)=∫(ε|∇u|2/2+W(u)/ε)dx Γ‑converges to c0Per(E) where c0=∫−11√(2W(s))ds. The min‑max critical points of Eε converge as ε→0 to minimal hypersurfaces, providing a PDE‑based proof of the Almgren–Pitts theorem (Guaraco, 2018; Gaspar–Guaraco, 2019). The Morse index of the Allen–Cahn min‑max solution converges to the Morse index of the limiting minimal hypersurface, establishing a precise correspondence between the variational structures.

Variational Methods for Evolutionary Γ‑Convergence and Gradient Flow Convergence

The Sandier–Serfaty theory (2004) of evolutionary Γ‑convergence provides a framework to pass to the limit in gradient flows when the energy functionals Eε Γ‑converge to E0. Let (X,d) be a metric space, Eε: X→[0,∞] a family of functionals Γ‑converging to E0. A curve uε: [0,T]→X is an ε‑gradient flow if it satisfies the energy‑dissipation inequality Eε(uε(t))+1/2∫0t|u̇ε|2ds+1/2∫0t|∂Eε|2(uε(s))ds≤Eε(uε(0)) where |u̇| is the metric derivative and |∂E| is the strong slope. If Eε Γ‑converges to E0 and the slopes satisfy a lower semicontinuity condition liminfε→0|∂Eε|(uε)≥|∂E0|(u) whenever uε→u and sup Eε(uε)<∞, then any limit of ε‑gradient flows is a 0‑gradient flow. This abstract result applies to the Allen–Cahn to mean curvature flow convergence: Eε(u)=∫(ε|∇u|2/2+W(u)/ε)dx Γ‑converges to c0Per(E) in L1, and the L2‑gradient flow ∂tu=Δu−ε−2W'(u) converges to the mean curvature flow of the interface ∂{u≈1}. The key is the Modica–Mortola trick: the energy‑dissipation identity for Allen–Cahn reads Eε(u(t))+∫0t∫(∂tu)2dxds=Eε(u(0)). Passing to the limit requires the equipartition of energy limε→0∫(ε|∇u|2/2−W(u)/ε)dx=0, which holds for well‑prepared initial data. For the Ginzburg–Landau vortices, Eε(u)=1/2∫|∇u|2+(1−|u|2)2/(2ε2)dx Γ‑converges to π∑di2δai in the sense of Jacobians, and the heat flow ∂tu=Δu+ε−2u(1−|u|2) converges to the vortex motion law diȧi=−∇aiW where W is the renormalized energy. The evolutionary Γ‑convergence framework also covers the convergence of the Cahn–Hilliard equation to the Hele–Shaw flow, the phase‑field crystal model to the sharp interface limit, and the Landau–de Gennes Q‑tensor model to the Oseen–Frank line defects. The main technical condition is the existence of a recovery sequence for the slope: for every u with |∂E0|(u)<∞, there exists uε→u such that limsup|∂Eε|(uε)≤|∂E0|(u). This is often the hardest part to verify and requires constructing explicit interpolations between the discrete and continuous energies.

  • Confusing the fractional p‑Laplacian eigenvalue scaling: forgetting the factor (1−s) in the limit s→1−; λ1(s)∼λ1(1)/(1−s), not λ1(1).
  • Misapplying the Polya–Szegő inequality: it holds for the Gagliardo seminorm [u*]s,p≤[u]s,p but the equality case requires u to be a translate of a radially symmetric decreasing function; on a bounded domain, the rearrangement may not preserve the exterior condition.
  • Overlooking the modular vs norm distinction in double phase spaces: the Luxemburg norm ‖u‖Φ=inf{λ>0 : ρΦ(u/λ)≤1} is not equivalent to the modular ρΦ(u) when a(x) vanishes; boundedness in norm does not imply boundedness in modular and vice versa.
  • Assuming the concentration‑compactness principle gives strong convergence in W1,p: it only gives strong convergence in Lp*; the gradient may still concentrate (e.g., Aubin–Talenti bubbles have ‖∇Uλ‖2→Sn/2 but do not converge strongly in Ḣ1).
  • Neglecting the orthogonality condition in profile decomposition: the parameters (λj,k,xj,k) must satisfy λj,k/λi,k+λi,k/λj,k+|xj,k−xi,k|/λj,k→∞ for i≠j; without this, the Pythagorean expansion of the energy fails.
  • Treating the Almgren–Pitts width as a standard min‑max value: the width is defined over sweepouts of currents, not maps into a manifold; the pull‑tight procedure is essential to ensure the limit is stationary, not just a critical point of the discretized problem.
  • Forgetting the slope lower semicontinuity in evolutionary Γ‑convergence: Γ‑convergence of energies alone does not guarantee convergence of gradient flows; the Mosco convergence of the subdifferentials (or the slope condition) must be checked separately.

Variational Methods for the Nonlocal Porous Medium Equation

The nonlocal porous medium equation ∂ₜu + (−Δ)ˢ(uᵐ) = 0 with m > 1 and s ∈ (0,1) arises as the gradient flow of the nonlocal interaction energy E(u) = 1/(m−1) ∫ uᵐ dx + 1/2 ∬ (u(x)−u(y))²/|x−y|ⁿ⁺²ˢ dx dy in the Wasserstein space of probability measures. The fractional Laplacian (−Δ)ˢ is defined via the principal value integral (−Δ)ˢφ(x) = Cₙ,ₛ PV ∫ (φ(x)−φ(y))/|x−y|ⁿ⁺²ˢ dy. Existence of weak solutions follows from the minimizing movement scheme (JKO scheme) where one constructs a discrete sequence uᵏ by minimizing E(u) + (1/2τ) W₂²(u, uᵏ⁻¹) with W₂ the quadratic Wasserstein distance. The Γ‑convergence of the discrete energies to the continuous energy and the lower semicontinuity of the slope yield a curve of maximal slope satisfying the energy‑dissipation inequality E(u(t)) + ½∫₀ᵗ |u̇|² ds + ½∫₀ᵗ |∂E|²(u(s)) ds ≤ E(u(0)). Regularity theory developed by Caffarelli, Soria, and Vázquez shows that solutions become instantly Hölder continuous and satisfy a Harnack inequality with constants independent of the initial datum. The asymptotic behaviour is governed by the Barenblatt profile B(x,t) = t⁻ᵅ (C − k |x|² t⁻²ᵝ/ⁿ)₊¹/(ᵐ⁻¹) where α = n/(n(m−1)+2s) and β = α/n. Convergence to the Barenblatt solution in relative entropy is proved using the Csiszár–Kullback inequality and the functional inequality ∫ uᵐ log(u/B) dx ≤ C (E(u)−E(B)).

Key references include the work of Vázquez (2012) on the fractional porous medium equation, the JKO framework by Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré (2005), and the regularity results of Caffarelli and Vasseur (2010). The variational structure also allows the derivation of a nonlocal version of the Otto calculus, where the formal Riemannian metric on the space of densities is given by the inverse of the fractional Laplacian. This metric structure is essential for proving displacement convexity of the energy along generalized geodesics, which in turn yields contraction estimates in Wasserstein distance.

Variational Methods for the Fractional Obstacle Problem

The fractional obstacle problem seeks a function u minimizing the Gagliardo seminorm [u]²Hˢ = ∬ (u(x)−u(y))²/|x−y|ⁿ⁺²ˢ dx dy among all functions u ≥ ψ a.e. with prescribed exterior data. The obstacle ψ is typically smooth and compactly supported. The minimizer satisfies the complementarity conditions u ≥ ψ, (−Δ)ˢu ≥ 0, and (u−ψ)(−Δ)ˢu = 0 in the distributional sense. Caffarelli, Salsa, and Silvestre (2008) proved optimal regularity: u ∈ C¹,ˢ⁻¹/² locally and the free boundary ∂{u > ψ} is C¹,ᵅ outside a lower‑dimensional singular set. The proof uses the extension technique of Caffarelli and Silvestre, which realizes the fractional Laplacian as the Dirichlet‑to‑Neumann map for a degenerate elliptic equation in one higher dimension: div(y¹⁻²ˢ ∇U) = 0 in ℝⁿ⁺¹₊ with U(x,0)=u(x). The obstacle problem then becomes a thin obstacle problem for U, allowing the use of monotonicity formulas of Almgren type. The variational formulation also yields a nonlocal version of the Signorini problem, relevant in fracture mechanics and contact problems with long‑range interactions.

Recent developments include the analysis of the parabolic fractional obstacle problem ∂ₜu + (−Δ)ˢu ∈ ∂I[ψ,∞)(u) where I is the indicator functional. The existence of a unique strong solution follows from the theory of maximal monotone operators in Hilbert spaces. The regularity of the free boundary in the parabolic setting has been studied by Petrosyan and Shahgholian, who established a nonlocal version of the Caffarelli‑Friedman monotonicity formula. Numerical approximation via the finite element method on the extended problem uses graded meshes in the extended variable y to capture the degeneracy of the weight y¹⁻²ˢ. The discrete variational inequality inherits the Γ‑convergence properties of the continuous energy, guaranteeing convergence of discrete free boundaries to the continuous one.

Worked Example: Energy Minimization for the Fractional Obstacle
Let Ω = (−1,1), s = 1/2, ψ(x) = 1−x². Consider the minimization of [u]²H¹/²(ℝ) among u ∈ H¹/²(ℝ) with u ≥ ψ in Ω and u = 0 outside Ω. Show that the minimizer satisfies (−Δ)¹/²u = λ in {u > ψ} for some nonnegative measure λ supported on the contact set {u = ψ}.
The admissible set K = {u ∈ H¹/²(ℝ) : u ≥ ψ a.e. in Ω, u = 0 in ℝ\Ω} is convex and closed. The functional J(u) = ½[u]²H¹/² is strictly convex, coercive, and lower semicontinuous, hence admits a unique minimizer u* ∈ K. For any v ∈ K, the directional derivative gives [u*, v−u*]H¹/² ≥ 0. By the definition of the fractional Laplacian, this is equivalent to ∫ (−Δ)¹/²u* (v−u*) dx ≥ 0. Since v−u* can be chosen arbitrarily nonnegative in Ω and zero outside, we deduce (−Δ)¹/²u* ≥ 0 in Ω in the sense of distributions. Moreover, taking v = ψ on the contact set and v = u* elsewhere yields ∫u*=ψ (−Δ)¹/²u* (ψ−u*) dx = 0, so (−Δ)¹/²u* = 0 a.e. on {u* > ψ}. Defining λ = (−Δ)¹/²u* restricted to {u* = ψ} gives a nonnegative measure supported on the contact set, and (−Δ)¹/²u* = λ in Ω. This is the desired complementarity formulation.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the variational formulation of a fractional obstacle problem, write the energy functional explicitly, state the admissible convex set, and invoke the direct method. Then derive the Euler‑Lagrange inequality and identify the Lagrange multiplier as a measure on the contact set. Remember to mention the Caffarelli‑Silvestre extension if regularity of the free boundary is required.

Variational Methods for Nonconvex Elasticity and the Formation of Microstructures

In nonlinear elasticity the stored energy density W(F) depends on the deformation gradient F ∈ ℝⁿˣⁿ and is typically nonconvex due to frame indifference and material symmetry. The total energy E(u) = ∫_Ω W(∇u) dx is minimized subject to boundary conditions. Because W is not quasiconvex, minimizers may not exist; instead minimizing sequences develop fine‑scale oscillations called microstructures. Ball (1977) introduced the notion of quasiconvexification QW(F) = inf { ⨏_D W(F+∇φ) dx : φ ∈ W₀¹,∞(D;ℝⁿ) } and proved that the relaxed functional Ē(u) = ∫_Ω QW(∇u) dx is the lower semicontinuous envelope of E with respect to weak convergence in W¹,ᵖ. The lack of quasiconvexity leads to the formation of laminates: rank‑one connections between energy wells produce simple laminates, while higher‑order laminates arise from iterative rank‑one convexification. The microstructure is described by a gradient Young measure νₓ generated by the minimizing sequence; the relaxed energy equals ∫_Ω ⟨νₓ, W⟩ dx. Kinderlehrer and Pedregal (1991) characterized gradient Young measures by the Jensen inequality ⟨νₓ, f⟩ ≥ f(⟨νₓ, id⟩) for all quasiconvex f. This variational framework explains the experimentally observed martensitic twins in shape‑memory alloys.

Numerical approximation of nonconvex problems requires relaxation or the use of finite element spaces that can capture oscillations. The relaxation approach replaces W by its quasiconvex envelope QW, which can be computed for two‑well problems via the lamination convex hull. Alternatively, the finite element method with mesh refinement aligned to the expected laminate direction yields convergence of the discrete energies to the relaxed energy (Müller, 1999). The variational theory also extends to multiwell energies with more than two wells, where the quasiconvex envelope may involve complex branching microstructures. Recent work by Conti and Theil (2005) on the single‑slip model in crystal plasticity shows that the relaxed energy can be expressed in terms of a single scalar slip variable, leading to a tractable variational problem.

Variational Methods for Mean Field Games with Common Noise

Mean field games (MFG) describe the limit of N‑player stochastic differential games as N → ∞. When a common noise W⁰ drives all players, the state dynamics are dXᵗ = αᵗ dt + σ dWᵗ + σ⁰ dW⁰ᵗ. The variational formulation due to Carmona and Delarue (2018) expresses the MFG equilibrium as a saddle point of the Lagrangian L(μ, α) = 𝔼[ ∫₀ᵀ (½|αᵗ|² + F(Xᵗ, μᵗ)) dt + G(Xᵀ, μᵀ) ] where μᵗ = Law(Xᵗ | W⁰) is the conditional law. The master equation is a PDE on the space of probability measures: ∂ₜU + H(x, ∂ₓU) + ∫ ∂_μU(x, μ, y) · H_p(y, ∂ᵧU(y, μ)) μ(dy) + ½σ⁰² Tr(∂ₓₓU) = 0. The variational structure yields a convex‑concave optimization problem: the value function U(t, μ) = inf_α sup_ν L(μ, α, ν) where ν is a measure‑valued control representing the common noise. The existence of a classical solution to the master equation requires the monotonicity condition (Lasry‑Lions) ∫ (F(x, μ)−F(x, ν)) (μ−ν)(dx) ≥ 0. Under this condition, the MFG system admits a unique solution, and the value function is the unique viscosity solution of the master equation.

The probabilistic approach uses the stochastic maximum principle: the optimal control α* = −∂ₓU(t, Xᵗ, μᵗ) and the adjoint process satisfies a backward SDE driven by both idiosyncratic and common noises. The variational formulation also leads to a numerical scheme based on the fictitious play algorithm, where players iteratively best‑respond to the empirical distribution of the population. Convergence of the algorithm is proved using the contraction property of the best‑response map in the Wasserstein space. Recent extensions to major‑minor player games and to MFG with absorption at the boundary preserve the variational structure by adding appropriate boundary terms to the Lagrangian.

Variational Methods for Stochastic Variational Inequalities and the Skorokhod Problem

Stochastic variational inequalities (SVI) arise in models with constraints, such as reflected diffusions and optimal stopping. The Skorokhod problem in a convex domain D ⊂ ℝⁿ asks for a pair (X, K) such that Xᵗ = x + ∫₀ᵗ b(Xˢ) ds + ∫₀ᵗ σ(Xˢ) dWˢ + Kᵗ, with Xᵗ ∈ D, K of bounded variation, and ∫₀ᵀ 1∂D(Xˢ) d|K|ˢ = ∫₀ᵀ n(Xˢ) dKˢ where n is the inward normal. This is equivalent to the variational inequality: for all φ ∈ C¹([0,T]; D), 𝔼[ ∫₀ᵀ (Xᵗ−φᵗ)·(dXᵗ−b(Xᵗ)dt) ] ≥ 0. Lions and Stampacchia (1967) proved existence and uniqueness for deterministic variational inequalities; the stochastic extension by Bensoussan and Lions (1982) uses the theory of maximal monotone operators in L²(Ω×[0,T]). The solution map is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the driving noise in the Wasserstein metric, which is crucial for the stability of numerical schemes.

The variational formulation also covers optimal stopping problems: the value function V(t,x) = sup_τ 𝔼[ g(X_τ) 1τ≤T + h(X_T) 1τ>T ] satisfies the obstacle problem ∂ₜV + ℒV ≤ 0, V ≥ g, (∂ₜV + ℒV)(V−g) = 0, where ℒ is the infinitesimal generator of the diffusion. The connection with the Skorokhod problem is made via the Snell envelope: the optimal stopping time is the first hitting time of the set {V = g}. Numerical approximation uses the penalization method: replace the constraint by a penalty term (1/ε) (Xᵗ−Π_D(Xᵗ)) in the drift, where Π_D is the projection onto D. As ε → 0, the penalized solutions converge to the solution of the Skorokhod problem. The rate of convergence in L² is O(√ε) under uniform ellipticity of σσᵀ.

  • Confusing the fractional porous medium exponent: the Barenblatt scaling exponent α = n/(n(m−1)+2s) not n/(n(m−1)+2).
  • Assuming the fractional obstacle problem has the same regularity as the classical obstacle: optimal regularity is C¹,ˢ⁻¹/², not C¹,¹.
  • Treating quasiconvexification as convexification: QW is generally larger than the convex envelope and requires rank‑one convexity tests.
  • Neglecting the common noise term in the master equation: the σ⁰² Tr(∂ₓₓU) term is essential for well‑posedness.
  • Applying the deterministic Skorokhod reflection map pathwise to stochastic integrals: the stochastic Skorokhod problem requires the normal reflection condition in the sense of stochastic differentials.
  • Overlooking the monotonicity condition in mean field games: without Lasry‑Lions monotonicity the master equation may have multiple solutions.
  • Using the wrong scaling for the penalization parameter in reflected diffusions: the convergence rate is O(√ε), not O(ε).

These advanced variational topics illustrate how modern analysis combines geometric measure theory, stochastic calculus, and convex optimization to solve problems that are inaccessible to classical methods.

Variational Structure of the Porous Medium Equation as a Wasserstein Gradient Flow

The porous medium equation ∂ₜρ = Δ(ρᵐ) for m > 1 admits a variational formulation as the gradient flow of the internal energy functional ℰ(ρ) = ∫ ρᵐ/(m−1) dx in the Wasserstein space 𝒫₂(ℝⁿ) equipped with the 2-Wasserstein distance W₂. This interpretation, due to Otto (2001), identifies the tangent space at ρ with the space of velocity fields v such that ∂ₜρ + ∇·(ρv) = 0, and the metric tensor is given by the Benamou–Brenier formula W₂²(ρ₀, ρ₁) = inf ∫₀¹ ∫ |vₜ|² ρₜ dx dt. The first variation of ℰ yields δℰ/δρ = mρᵐ⁻¹/(m−1), and the Wasserstein gradient is ∇_W ℰ = −∇·(ρ∇(δℰ/δρ)) = −∇·(ρ∇(mρᵐ⁻¹/(m−1))) = Δ(ρᵐ), recovering the porous medium equation. The JKO minimizing movement scheme constructs discrete-time approximations ρᵏ⁽ᵗ⁾ = argmin_ρ [ W₂²(ρ, ρᵏ⁻¹)/(2τ) + ℰ(ρ) ], and as τ → 0 the piecewise constant interpolation converges to the unique weak solution. The displacement convexity of ℰ along geodesics in 𝒫₂ (McCann, 1997) guarantees contractivity of the flow: W₂(ρₜ, σₜ) ≤ W₂(ρ₀, σ₀). For the fast diffusion equation m ∈ (1−2/n, 1), the energy ℰ is still displacement convex but the flow exhibits finite-time extinction when m < 1. The Barenblatt profile B(x,t) = t⁻ᵅ (C − k|x|²t⁻²ᵝ/ᵅ)₊¹/(ᵐ⁻¹) with α = n/(n(m−1)+2), β = 1/(n(m−1)+2) is a self-similar solution that arises as the minimizer of ℰ under mass constraint, and its linearization governs the asymptotic convergence rate in relative entropy. The entropy–entropy dissipation inequality d/dt Ent(ρ|B) ≤ −C Ent(ρ|B) yields exponential convergence to the Barenblatt profile in rescaled variables. This variational framework extends to the fractional porous medium equation ∂ₜρ + (−Δ)ˢ(ρᵐ) = 0, where the dissipation is the fractional Fisher information, and to the porous medium equation on Riemannian manifolds where the Wasserstein geometry incorporates the Ricci curvature lower bound via the Lott–Sturm–Villani theory.

Variational Methods for the Thin Film Equation and Higher-Order Degenerate Parabolic Equations

The thin film equation ∂ₜh + ∇·(hⁿ∇Δh) = 0 for n > 0 models the evolution of a viscous fluid film on a solid substrate under surface tension and lubrication approximation. It is the gradient flow of the surface energy ℰ(h) = ½∫ |∇h|² dx in the Wasserstein-type metric induced by the mobility m(h) = hⁿ, where the distance between two film profiles h₀, h₁ is defined via the Benamou–Brenier action inf ∫₀¹ ∫ hₜ|vₜ|² dx dt subject to ∂ₜh + ∇·(hv) = 0. The first variation δℰ/δh = −Δh yields the chemical potential, and the flux is hⁿ∇(δℰ/δh) = −hⁿ∇Δh. For n ≥ 2, the mobility degenerates sufficiently at the contact line h = 0 to allow finite speed of propagation and waiting-time phenomena, while for n < 2 the solutions become instantaneously positive. The JKO scheme ρᵏ = argmin_h [ dₙ²(h, hᵏ⁻¹)/(2τ) + ℰ(h) ] with the distance dₙ induced by mobility hⁿ constructs weak solutions, and the convergence proof relies on the displacement convexity of ℰ along generalized geodesics. The energy dissipation identity d/dt ℰ(hₜ) = −∫ hⁿ|∇Δh|² dx provides a priori estimates in the weighted Sobolev space L²(0,T; H²(hⁿ/² dx)). For the critical exponent n = 3, the equation arises from the Navier–Stokes equations with no-slip boundary condition, and the variational structure is linked to the gradient flow of the Dirichlet energy in the H⁻¹ metric with weight h³. The fourth-order degenerate parabolic equation ∂ₜu = −∇·(uⁿ∇Δu) also appears in the context of quantum drift-diffusion models (n = 1) and the Derrida–Lebowitz–Speer–Spohn equation (n = 1) for interface fluctuations. The variational formulation enables the construction of entropy solutions via the minimizing movement scheme even when classical solutions cease to exist due to singularity formation at the contact line. The long-time behavior is governed by the self-similar source-type solution h(x,t) = t⁻ᵅ f(|x|t⁻ᵝ) with α = 1/(n+4), β = 1/(n+4) in one dimension, which minimizes the energy under mass constraint. The linearization around this profile yields a spectral gap in the weighted space L²(fⁿ⁻² dx) that determines the convergence rate. For the thin film equation with slip (mobility hⁿ + νhᵐ, ν > 0), the variational structure is preserved and the waiting-time phenomenon disappears, illustrating how the degeneracy of the mobility controls the geometric properties of the flow.

Worked Example: Displacement Convexity of the Porous Medium Energy
Show that the internal energy ℰ(ρ) = ∫ ρᵐ/(m−1) dx is displacement convex in 𝒫₂(ℝⁿ) for m ≥ 1 − 1/n, and compute the second variation along a geodesic ρₜ = (Tₜ)#ρ₀ where Tₜ(x) = (1−t)x + t∇φ(x) for a convex function φ.
A functional ℰ is displacement convex if t ↦ ℰ(ρₜ) is convex for every geodesic ρₜ in 𝒫₂. For ρₜ = (Tₜ)#ρ₀ with Tₜ = (1−t)Id + t∇φ, the density satisfies ρₜ(Tₜ(x)) det DTₜ(x) = ρ₀(x). The energy is ℰ(ρₜ) = ∫ ρₜᵐ/(m−1) dx = ∫ [ρ₀(x)/det DTₜ(x)]ᵐ/(m−1) det DTₜ(x) dx = ∫ ρ₀(x)ᵐ/(m−1) [det DTₜ(x)]¹⁻ᵐ dx. Since DTₜ(x) = (1−t)I + tD²φ(x) and D²φ ≥ 0, the map t ↦ det DTₜ(x) is log-concave (Minkowski's inequality for mixed volumes). Thus t ↦ [det DTₜ(x)]¹⁻ᵐ is convex if 1−m ≤ 0 (i.e., m ≥ 1) or if 1−m > 0 but the log-concavity is strong enough. McCann's condition: the function ψ(s) = s⁻ⁿ⁽ᵐ⁻¹⁾ is convex on (0,∞) iff m ≥ 1 − 1/n. For m ≥ 1 − 1/n, ψ(det DTₜ) is convex in t because det DTₜ is log-concave and ψ is convex and decreasing. Hence ℰ(ρₜ) = ∫ ρ₀ᵐ/(m−1) ψ(det DTₜ) dx is convex in t. The second variation is d²/dt² ℰ(ρₜ)|ₜ₌₀ = ∫ ρ₀ᵐ [ (m−1)|∇·v|² + (1−1/n)(Δv)² ] dx where v = ∇φ − x, confirming non-negativity for m ≥ 1 − 1/n.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Gradient Flow Structures
When a PDE has the form ∂ₜu = ∇·(M(u)∇(δℰ/δu)) with a symmetric positive mobility M(u) ≥ 0, it is a gradient flow of ℰ in a metric induced by M. Identify the energy ℰ and the mobility M. The JKO scheme minimizes ℰ + (1/2τ)distance². Displacement convexity of ℰ along geodesics of the metric implies uniqueness and contractivity. For porous medium, M(ρ) = ρ, ℰ(ρ) = ∫ ρᵐ/(m−1). For thin film, M(h) = hⁿ, ℰ(h) = ½∫ |∇h|². The critical exponent for displacement convexity often involves the dimension n (e.g., m ≥ 1 − 1/n for porous medium). Memorize the McCann condition and the Barenblatt scaling exponents α = n/(n(m−1)+2), β = 1/(n(m−1)+2).

Variational Methods for the Harmonic Map Heat Flow and Geometric Evolution Equations

The harmonic map heat flow ∂ₜu = τ(u) = Δu + A(u)(∇u, ∇u) for maps u: M → N between Riemannian manifolds is the gradient flow of the Dirichlet energy ℰ(u) = ½∫_M |du|² dvol_M in the L² metric on the mapping space. The tension field τ(u) = trace ∇du is the negative L²-gradient of ℰ. For N isometrically embedded in ℝᴷ, the flow becomes ∂ₜu = Δu + A(u)(∇u, ∇u) where A is the second fundamental form of N ⊂ ℝᴷ. The variational structure yields the energy dissipation identity d/dt ℰ(uₜ) = −∫_M |∂ₜu|² dvol_M. Short-time existence and uniqueness hold for smooth initial data; singularities may form in finite time when dim M ≥ 3 (Struwe, 1985). The blow-up analysis uses the monotonicity formula for the rescaled energy Θ(x₀,t₀,r) = r²⁻ᵐ ∫Bᵣ(x₀) |∇u|² dx, which is non-decreasing in r for stationary harmonic maps. At a singularity, a non-trivial harmonic sphere S² → N bubbles off, and the energy identity ℰ(u₀) = ℰ(u_∞) + Σ ℰ(ωᵢ) holds where ωᵢ are the bubbles. The variational formulation extends to the p-harmonic map heat flow ∂ₜu = div(|du|ᵖ⁻² du) + A(u)(∇u, ∇u) for p > 2, which is the gradient flow of the p-energy ℰₚ(u) = 1/p ∫ |du|ᵖ. For the Landau–Lifshitz equation ∂ₜm = m × Δm (m: M → S²), the variational structure is symplectic rather than gradient: it is the Hamiltonian flow of the Dirichlet energy with respect to the symplectic form ω(ξ, η) = ∫ m·(ξ × η) on the tangent bundle of the mapping space. The Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation ∂ₜm = m × Δm + α m × (m × Δm) combines the Hamiltonian and gradient parts, with the Gilbert damping α > 0 providing energy dissipation d/dt ℰ = −α ∫ |m × Δm|². The variational approach to geometric flows also covers the mean curvature flow as the gradient flow of the area functional in the L² metric on hypersurfaces, and the Willmore flow as the gradient flow of the Willmore energy ∫ H². The De Giorgi minimizing movement scheme constructs weak solutions for these flows even past singularities, using the metric space structure of varifolds or integral currents.

Variational Methods for the von Kármán Plate Equations and Nonlinear Elasticity

The von Kármán equations model the large deflections of a thin elastic plate: Δ²w = [w, χ] + f, Δ²χ = −½[w, w], where w is the vertical displacement, χ is the Airy stress function, [u, v] = uₓₓvᵧᵧ + uᵧᵧvₓₓ − 2uₓᵧvₓᵧ is the Monge–Ampère bracket, and f is the transverse load. This system is the Euler–Lagrange equation of the von Kármán energy functional ℰ(w, χ) = ½∫_Ω (|Δw|² − 2(1−ν)(wₓₓwᵧᵧ − wₓᵧ²)) dx + ½∫_Ω (|Δχ|² − 2(1+ν)(χₓₓχᵧᵧ − χₓᵧ²)) dx − ∫_Ω [w, χ] dx − ∫_Ω fw dx, where ν ∈ (−1, ½) is the Poisson ratio. The first term is the bending energy, the second is the stretching energy, and the coupling term ∫ [w, χ] = ∫ (wₓₓχᵧᵧ + wᵧᵧχₓₓ − 2wₓᵧχₓᵧ) encodes the geometric nonlinearity. The functional is not convex due to the indefinite coupling term, but it is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous in H²(Ω) × H²(Ω) for ν ∈ (−1, ½). The direct method yields existence of minimizers for clamped boundary conditions w = ∂ₙw = χ = ∂ₙχ = 0 on ∂Ω. The linearized operator at a solution (w, χ) is the Hessian of ℰ, and its Morse index determines stability. The buckling load corresponds to the first eigenvalue of the linearized problem Δ²w = λ[w, χ₀] where χ₀ solves Δ²χ₀ = −½[w₀, w₀] for a pre-buckling state. For the full nonlinear elasticity model in 3D, the stored energy function W(F) = μ|F|² + (λ/2)(det F − 1)² − μ log det F (neo-Hookean) or W(F) = μ/2(|F|² − 3) − μ log det F + λ/2(log det F)² (Ogden) is polyconvex (Ball, 1977), meaning W(F) = g(F, cof F, det F) with g convex. Polyconvexity implies weak lower semicontinuity of the total energy ∫ W(∇u) dx in W¹ᵖ(Ω; ℝ³) for p > 3, enabling the direct method for existence of minimizers under Dirichlet boundary conditions. The variational structure also underlies the derivation of plate theories from 3D elasticity via Γ-convergence: as the thickness h → 0, the rescaled 3D energy (1/h)∫ W(∇ₕu) dx Γ-converges to the von Kármán functional for scalings where the displacement is of order h². The limiting theory captures the interplay between bending and stretching, and the Γ-limit identifies the correct effective energy for the plate. The variational approach extends to the Föppl–von Kármán equations for inextensible plates (isometric immersions) where the stretching energy is replaced by a constraint det ∇²w = 0, leading to the Monge–Ampère equation as a constraint in the minimization problem.

Variational Methods for the Stefan Problem and Free Boundary Phase Transitions

The Stefan problem describes the evolution of a phase boundary between ice and water: ∂ₜu = Δu in {u > 0}, u = 0 on the free boundary ∂{u > 0}, and the normal velocity V = −∂ₙu on the free boundary (Stefan condition). This is the gradient flow of the enthalpy functional ℰ(u) = ∫ (½|∇u|² + χu>0) dx in the H⁻¹ metric, where the indicator function χu>0 represents the latent heat. The variational formulation uses the enthalpy variable h = u + χu>0, which satisfies the degenerate parabolic equation ∂ₜh = Δu with u = max(h−1, 0). The energy dissipation identity d/dt ℰ(uₜ) = −∫ |∇u|² dx holds for weak solutions. The minimizing movement scheme constructs solutions via hᵏ = argmin_h [ ∫ (½|∇max(h−1,0)|² + χh>1) dx + (1/2τ)‖h − hᵏ⁻¹‖²H⁻¹ ]. The Γ-convergence of the discrete energies to the continuous energy as τ → 0 yields existence of weak solutions. The regularity of the free boundary is a central topic: Caffarelli (1977) proved that the free boundary is C¹,α except for a singular set of parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n−1. The variational approach also covers the two-phase Stefan problem with different conductivities in each phase, where the energy is ℰ(u) = ∫ (½a(u)|∇u|² + χu>0) dx with a(u) = a₊ for u > 0 and a₋ for u < 0. The quasi-stationary approximation (Hele-Shaw flow) corresponds to the limit where the time derivative is neglected, leading to the variational inequality ∫ ∇u·∇(v−u) dx ≥ 0 for all v ≥ 0 with v = u on ∂Ω, which is the obstacle problem for the Laplacian. The connection with optimal transport appears in the work of Otto (1998) who showed that the Hele-Shaw flow is the gradient flow of the perimeter functional in the Wasserstein metric. The Stefan problem with surface tension adds a curvature term to the Stefan condition: V = −∂ₙu + κ, where κ is the mean curvature of the free boundary. This is the gradient flow of the energy ℰ(u) = ∫ (½|∇u|² + χu>0) dx + σ Per({u > 0}) in a suitable metric. The variational formulation enables the use of geometric measure theory tools (varifolds, Caccioppoli sets) to construct weak solutions past topological changes of the free boundary. The large-time behavior is governed by the self-similar solutions, and the stability of the planar front is analyzed via the linearized operator around the traveling wave, which has a spectral gap in weighted spaces.

  • Confusing the displacement convexity condition for porous medium energy: it is m ≥ 1 − 1/n, not m ≥ 1.
  • Misidentifying the mobility in the thin film equation: the metric is induced by mobility hⁿ, not hⁿ⁻¹ or hⁿ⁺¹.
  • Overlooking the role of the Monge–Ampère bracket [w, χ] in the von Kármán energy: it is the coupling term, not a separate bending or stretching term.
  • Assuming the harmonic map heat flow is the gradient flow of the Dirichlet energy in the H¹ metric: it is the L² gradient flow.
  • Neglecting the enthalpy variable h = u + χu>0 in the Stefan problem: the equation ∂ₜh = Δu is the correct variational form, not ∂ₜu = Δu everywhere.
  • Treating the Landau–Lifshitz equation as a gradient flow: it is a Hamiltonian flow with symplectic structure, not a gradient flow.
  • Using the wrong scaling exponent for the Barenblatt profile: α = n/(n(m−1)+2), not n/(n(m−1)+2s) which is for the fractional porous medium equation.

Variational Methods for the Fractional Laplacian and Nonlocal Operators

The fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s for s ∈ (0,1) is defined via the singular integral

(−Δ)s u(x) = Cn,s P.V. ∫ℝn (u(x) − u(y)) / |x − y|n+2s dy,

where Cn,s is a normalization constant. Its natural variational structure lives in the Gagliardo seminorm

[u]Hs2 = ∫ℝn∫ℝn (u(x) − u(y))2 / |x − y|n+2s dx dy.

The Dirichlet energy functional ℰ(u) = ½ [u]Hs2 − ∫ f u dx is strictly convex on the fractional Sobolev space Hs0(Ω), so the direct method yields a unique minimizer solving (−Δ)s u = f in Ω with u = 0 in ℝn\\Ω. The Euler–Lagrange equation is exactly the fractional Poisson problem.

A landmark breakthrough is the Caffarelli–Silvestre extension (2007): the nonlocal problem in ℝn is realized as a local degenerate elliptic equation in ℝn+1+. For U(x,y) solving div(y1−2s ∇U) = 0 with U(x,0)=u(x), one has (−Δ)s u = −ks limy→0 y1−2s ∂yU. This local formulation enables the use of standard elliptic regularity, barrier arguments, and monotonicity formulas.

Nonlocal minimal surfaces arise as critical points of the fractional perimeter functional Pers(E) = ∫E∫ℝnE dx dy / |x−y|n+2s. The first variation yields the nonlocal mean curvature Hs(x) = ∫ℝn (χE(y)−χE(x)) / |x−y|n+2s dy. Regularity theory (Caffarelli, Roquejoffre, Savin, Valdinoci) shows that s-minimal surfaces are C1,α outside a singular set of dimension at most n−2.

Applications span finance (fractional diffusion models for option pricing), image processing (nonlocal total variation denoising), and ecology (long-range dispersal). The variational framework also underpins the spectral fractional Laplacian on bounded domains, where the energy is ∑ λks uk2 for eigenpairs (λk, φk) of −Δ with Dirichlet conditions.

Variational Methods for the Ricci Flow and Perelman's Entropy

The Ricci flow ∂tg = −2 Ric(g) introduced by Hamilton (1982) deforms a Riemannian metric in the direction of its Ricci curvature. Perelman (2002–2003) discovered two monotone quantities that give the flow a variational interpretation. The F-functional

F(g,f) = ∫M (R + |∇f|2) e−f dV,

where f is a scalar function with ∫ e−f dV = 1, satisfies d/dt F ≥ 2 ∫ |Ric + Hess f|2 e−f dV along the coupled system ∂tg = −2 Ric, ∂tf = −Δf − R + |∇f|2. The infimum over f yields Perelman's λ-functional λ(g) = inff F(g,f), which is non-decreasing along the flow and constant only on gradient Ricci solitons.

The W-entropy W(g,f,τ) = ∫M [τ(R + |∇f|2) + f − n] (4πτ)−n/2 e−f dV, with τ > 0, satisfies d/dt W ≥ 2τ ∫ |Ric + Hess f − (1/2τ)g|2 (4πτ)−n/2 e−f dV. Its monotonicity implies the no local collapsing theorem: if |Rm| ≤ r−2 on a parabolic ball, then the volume of the time slice is bounded below by κ rn for a universal κ > 0.

Perelman's reduced length ℓ(q,τ) and reduced volume Ṽ(τ) = ∫ (4πτ)−n/2 e−ℓ dV provide a distance-like functional whose monotonicity yields the κ-noncollapsing estimate essential for surgery. The variational structure also underlies the classification of ancient κ-solutions, which are limits of blow-ups at singularities and are gradient shrinking solitons.

These entropy functionals can be viewed as the Boltzmann entropy of a diffusion process on the space of metrics, and the Ricci flow as the gradient flow of the entropy with respect to the Wasserstein metric on the space of probability measures (Otto, 2001). This connection links geometric analysis to optimal transport and has inspired variational approaches to the Ricci flow on metric measure spaces (Lott–Villani, Sturm).

Variational Derivation of the Fractional Laplacian
Show that the first variation of the Gagliardo seminorm [u]Hs2 = ∫∫ (u(x)−u(y))2/|x−y|n+2s dx dy yields the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s u up to a constant factor.
Consider a perturbation u + εη with η ∈ Cc∞(Ω). The derivative at ε=0 is d/dε|0 ½[u+εη]Hs2 = ∫∫ (u(x)−u(y))(η(x)−η(y))/|x−y|n+2s dx dy. Split the integral: ∫ η(x) [∫ (u(x)−u(y))/|x−y|n+2s dy] dx − ∫ η(y) [∫ (u(x)−u(y))/|x−y|n+2s dx] dy. By symmetry of the kernel, the two terms are equal, giving 2 ∫ η(x) [∫ (u(x)−u(y))/|x−y|n+2s dy] dx. The inner integral is, up to the constant Cn,s, the fractional Laplacian (−Δ)s u(x). Hence the Euler–Lagrange equation for the minimizer of ℰ(u) = ½[u]Hs2 − ∫ f u is (−Δ)s u = f in Ω.
Exam Strategy: Recognize Variational Structures in Nonlocal Problems
When a problem involves a singular integral kernel homogeneous of degree −n−2s, immediately write the associated Gagliardo seminorm. The Euler–Lagrange equation will be the corresponding fractional operator. Remember the Caffarelli–Silvestre extension: a nonlocal problem in ℝn becomes a local degenerate elliptic problem in ℝn+1+ with weight y1−2s. This trick converts nonlocal regularity questions into local ones and is a frequent source of exam questions on monotonicity formulas and boundary Harnack principles.

Variational Methods for the Euler–Arnold Equations on Diffeomorphism Groups

Arnold (1966) showed that the Euler equations for an ideal incompressible fluid describe geodesics on the infinite‑dimensional Lie group SDiff(M) of volume‑preserving diffeomorphisms of a compact manifold M, equipped with the right‑invariant L2 metric ⟨u,v⟩ = ∫M u·v dμ. The kinetic energy functional

E(φ) = ½ ∫01 ∫M |∂tφ(t,x)|2 dμ(x) dt

is minimized over curves φ(t) in SDiff(M) with fixed endpoints. The Euler–Poincaré reduction yields the Euler equation ∂tu + ∇uu = −∇p, div u = 0, where u = ∂tφ ∘ φ−1 is the Eulerian velocity.

Changing the metric leads to other celebrated equations. The H1 metric ⟨u,v⟩H1 = ∫ (u·v + α2 ∇u:∇v) dμ gives the Camassa–Holm equation ut − uxxt + 3uux = 2uxuxx + uuxxx on the circle, which models shallow water waves and possesses peaked solitons (peakons). The Korteweg–de Vries equation arises from a right‑invariant metric on the Virasoro–Bott group, and the Burgers equation from the L2 metric on the full diffeomorphism group without the volume constraint.

Well‑posedness in the geometric setting was established by Ebin and Marsden (1970) using the Nash–Moser implicit function theorem on Sobolev completions of SDiff(M). The geodesic spray is smooth on Hs for s > n/2 + 1, giving local existence and uniqueness. Global existence for 2D Euler follows from vorticity conservation; in 3D the Beale–Kato–Majda criterion ∫0T ‖ω‖L∞ dt < ∞ is the sharp blow‑up condition.

The variational principle also underlies the Arnold stability criterion: a steady flow u0 is nonlinearly stable if the second variation of the energy restricted to coadjoint orbits is definite. This connects to the energy–Casimir method and the convexity of the Hamiltonian on symplectic leaves of the Lie–Poisson structure on the dual of the Lie algebra of divergence‑free vector fields.

Variational Methods for the Mumford–Shah Functional and Image Segmentation

The Mumford–Shah functional (1989) for image segmentation is

MS(u,K) = ∫ΩK |∇u|2 dx + α ∫ΩK (u − g)2 dx + β Hn−1(K),

where g ∈ L∞(Ω) is the observed image, K ⊂ Ω is a rectifiable set of discontinuities (edges), u ∈ SBV(Ω) is the piecewise smooth approximation, and Hn−1 is the (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure. The first term penalizes oscillations inside regions, the second enforces fidelity to data, and the third penalizes total edge length.

Ambrosio (1989) proved existence of minimizers in the space SBV(Ω) of special functions of bounded variation, where the distributional derivative Du splits into an absolutely continuous part ∇u dx and a jump part (u+−u−) νu dHn−1 on the jump set Ju. The functional is lower semicontinuous with respect to the weak* topology of SBV, and the direct method applies.

The Ambrosio–Tortorelli approximation (1990) replaces the sharp edge set K by a phase field v ∈ H1(Ω) with v ≈ 0 near edges and v ≈ 1 away from them:

ATε(u,v) = ∫Ω v2|∇u|2 dx + α ∫Ω (u−g)2 dx + β ∫Ω (ε|∇v|2 + (1−v)2/(4ε)) dx.

As ε → 0, ATε Γ‑converges to MS, providing a practical numerical scheme. The Blake–Zisserman weak membrane model discretizes the problem on a graph, leading to the famous graph‑cut algorithms (Boykov–Jolly, 2001) that compute global minima for binary labeling via max‑flow/min‑cut.

Regularity of minimizers: the edge set K is C1,α except for a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most n−2 (De Giorgi–Carriero–Leaci). In 2D, the singular set is finite. The Mumford–Shah functional also appears in fracture mechanics (Francfort–Marigo, 1998) where u is the displacement and K the crack set, and the energy release rate drives crack propagation.

Variational Methods for the Wasserstein Gradient Flows and the JKO Scheme

Otto (2001) endowed the space P2(ℝn) of probability measures with finite second moment with a formal Riemannian structure: the tangent space at ρ is {∇φ : φ ∈ Cc∞}, with metric ⟨∇φ, ∇ψ⟩ρ = ∫ ∇φ·∇ψ dρ. The induced distance is the quadratic Wasserstein distance W2(μ,ν) = (infπ∈Π(μ,ν) ∫ |x−y|2 dπ)1/2.

The Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto (JKO) scheme (1998) constructs the gradient flow of a functional ℰ(ρ) by the minimizing movement

ρk+1 = argminρ∈P2 [ ℰ(ρ) + (1/2τ) W22(ρ, ρk) ],

with time step τ > 0. As τ → 0, the piecewise constant interpolation converges to the Wasserstein gradient flow ∂tρ = div(ρ ∇(δℰ/δρ)).

Key examples: ℰ(ρ) = ∫ ρ log ρ dx (Boltzmann entropy) gives the heat equation ∂tρ = Δρ. ℰ(ρ) = 1/(m−1) ∫ ρm dx (m > 1) yields the porous medium equation ∂tρ = Δρm. ℰ(ρ) = ∫ V ρ dx + ½ ∫ W*ρ ρ dx (interaction energy) gives the aggregation equation ∂tρ = div(ρ ∇(V + W*ρ)).

McCann's displacement convexity (1997) provides the geometric condition for contractivity of the flow: if ℰ is λ‑convex along Wasserstein geodesics, then W2(ρt, σt) ≤ e−λt W2(ρ0, σ0). The Boltzmann entropy is 0‑convex, the power‑law entropy is λ‑convex for m ≥ 1 − 1/n, and the interaction energy is λ‑convex if W is λ‑convex.

Ambrosio, Gigli, and Savaré (2005) developed a rigorous theory of gradient flows in metric spaces, establishing existence, uniqueness, and stability of curves of maximal slope. The JKO scheme is the cornerstone of numerical methods for Wasserstein gradient flows, including the proximal point algorithm for optimal transport and the Sinkhorn algorithm for entropic regularization.

  • Confusing the Gagliardo seminorm with the spectral fractional Laplacian energy: the former uses the full ℝn kernel, the latter uses eigenfunction expansion on a bounded domain.
  • Assuming the Ricci flow is the gradient flow of the Einstein–Hilbert action in the L2 metric on metrics: it is the gradient flow of Perelman's F-functional in the DeTurck‑modified metric, not the standard L2 metric.
  • Treating the Euler–Arnold framework as only formal: the Ebin–Marsden theorem gives rigorous local well‑posedness on Sobolev completions, and the geodesic spray is smooth for s > n/2 + 1.
  • Neglecting the jump set Ju in SBV when writing the Mumford–Shah functional: the perimeter term is exactly Hn−1(Ju), not an arbitrary set K.
  • Misidentifying the displacement convexity threshold for the porous medium equation: it is m ≥ 1 − 1/n, not m ≥ 1.
  • Overlooking the role of the Caffarelli–Silvestre extension in regularity proofs for the fractional Laplacian: the local degenerate problem in one higher dimension is the standard tool for boundary Harnack and monotonicity formulas.
  • Assuming the JKO scheme converges for any functional ℰ: λ‑convexity along Wasserstein geodesics (or at least lower semicontinuity and coercivity) is required for the minimizing movement to be well defined and converge.

hand/perverse-sheaves.html:
Weight Filtration and the Mixed Hodge Module Formalism

Morihiko Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge modules (1990) provides a Hodge‑theoretic lift of the category of perverse sheaves. For a complex algebraic variety X, the abelian category MHM(X) of mixed Hodge modules is equipped with a weight filtration W• such that the associated graded pieces Gr^W_k are pure Hodge modules of weight k. The forgetful functor rat: MHM(X) → Perv(X, ℚ) sending a mixed Hodge module to its underlying perverse sheaf is exact and faithful. The weight filtration on a mixed Hodge module M induces a filtration on the perverse sheaf rat(M) which coincides with the perverse Leray filtration for a proper morphism. In particular, for a proper map f: X → Y, the decomposition theorem Rf_* IC_X ≅ ⊕ ICZ_k(L_k)[d_k] lifts to an isomorphism in the derived category of mixed Hodge modules, and the summands inherit pure Hodge structures of weight dim Z_k. This Hodge‑theoretic refinement explains why the intersection cohomology groups IH^i(X) carry pure Hodge structures of weight i, a fact that cannot be seen at the level of perverse sheaves alone. The construction uses the nearby and vanishing cycle functors ψ_f, φ_f on mixed Hodge modules, which are compatible with the corresponding functors on perverse sheaves and preserve the weight filtration. Saito’s proof relies on the strictness of the Hodge filtration for the de Rham complex of a regular holonomic D‑module, a deep analytic result due to Kashiwara and Kawai. The mixed Hodge module formalism also yields a canonical extension of the weight filtration to the derived category D^b MHM(X), making it a filtered triangulated category. This framework is essential for modern applications such as the proof of the Kähler package for intersection cohomology and the study of motivic weights in the geometric Langlands program.

The Decomposition Theorem in Families and the Relative Hard Lefschetz

The Beilinson–Bernstein–Deligne–Gabber decomposition theorem extends from a single proper morphism to a family of proper morphisms. Let f: X → S be a proper morphism of complex algebraic varieties with S smooth and connected. For each s ∈ S, the fiber f_s: X_s → Y_s satisfies Rfs* ICX_s ≅ ⊕_k ICZk,s(Lk,s)[d_k]. The theorem asserts that the formation of this decomposition commutes with base change: the direct sum decomposition of Rf_* IC_X in D^b_c(Y) is locally constant in the analytic topology on S. This local constancy is a consequence of the relative hard Lefschetz theorem. For a relatively ample line bundle L on X/S, the cup product L^k: R-kf_* IC_X → Rkf_* IC_X is an isomorphism of perverse sheaves on Y for all k. The proof uses the theory of polarizable Hodge modules: the relative hard Lefschetz isomorphism is induced by a morphism of mixed Hodge modules which is strict with respect to the Hodge and weight filtrations. As a corollary, the perverse cohomology sheaves ^pH^i(Rf_* IC_X) are semisimple local systems on a dense open subset of Y, and their monodromy representations are completely reducible. This semisimplicity is the geometric incarnation of the fact that the monodromy of the Gauss–Manin connection on the intersection cohomology of the fibers is semisimple. The relative hard Lefschetz also implies the relative Hodge–Riemann bilinear relations, which give a positive definite pairing on the primitive parts of the perverse cohomology. These results have been used by de Cataldo and Migliorini to prove the topological invariance of intersection cohomology Betti numbers for projective morphisms and to establish the hard Lefschetz theorem for the intersection cohomology of singular projective varieties.

Worked Example: Relative Hard Lefschetz for a Family of Nodal Curves
Let π: C → Δ be a proper flat family of curves over the unit disc Δ such that the generic fiber C_t (t ≠ 0) is smooth of genus g and the central fiber C0 is a nodal curve with a single node. Let L be a relatively ample line bundle on C. Show that the cup product L: R-1π_* IC_C → R1π_* IC_C is an isomorphism of perverse sheaves on Δ.
The intersection complex IC_C on the total space C is the shifted constant sheaf ℚ_C[2] because C is a surface with at worst a nodal singularity in the central fiber; the node is a rational double point, so IC_C = ℚ_C[2]. The higher direct images R^iπ_* ℚ_C[2] are perverse sheaves on Δ. For i = -1, R-1π_* ℚ_C[2] = R1π_* ℚ_C[1] is the local system on Δ* given by H1(C_t, ℚ) extended across 0 as the nearby cycles ψ_π ℚ_C[2]. For i = 1, R1π_* ℚ_C[2] = R3π_* ℚ_C[1] is the dual local system by Verdier duality. The relatively ample line bundle L restricts to an ample line bundle on each fiber, giving a Lefschetz operator L: H1(C_t) → H3(C_t) ≅ H1(C_t)^∨. By the classical hard Lefschetz theorem on the smooth fibers, this is an isomorphism for t ≠ 0. The relative hard Lefschetz theorem (Saito, 1990) asserts that this isomorphism extends across the singular fiber because the morphism of mixed Hodge modules induced by L is strict. Hence the map of perverse sheaves L: R-1π_* IC_C → R1π_* IC_C is an isomorphism on Δ.
Exam Strategy: Recognising Relative Hard Lefschetz in Disguise
Questions often ask for the isomorphism type of Rf_* IC_X for a projective morphism f. If the morphism is a family over a curve, the relative hard Lefschetz forces the perverse cohomology sheaves to be semisimple local systems. Look for keywords such as “relatively ample”, “proper flat family”, or “semisimple monodromy”. The answer is usually a direct sum of intersection complexes of subvarieties of the base twisted by semisimple local systems. Do not confuse this with the ordinary hard Lefschetz on a single variety, which concerns the cohomology of the variety itself.

Perverse Sheaves on Stratified Spaces and Verdier Duality

Verdier duality D_X: D^b_c(X) → D^b_c(X) is an anti‑equivalence of triangulated categories sending a constructible complex ℱ to Rℋom(ℱ, ω_X), where ω_X is the dualizing complex. On a smooth variety of dimension n, ω_X ≅ ℚ_X[2n]; on a singular variety, ω_X is the intersection cohomology complex IC_X shifted by the dimension. The perverse t‑structure is self‑dual: D_X(Perv(X)) = Perv(X). This means that for any perverse sheaf P, its Verdier dual D_X(P) is again a perverse sheaf. The self‑duality is a key ingredient in the proof of the decomposition theorem because it forces the direct summands of Rf_* IC_X to be self‑dual up to shift, which characterises intersection complexes of subvarieties with semisimple local systems. On a stratified space X = ∪_α X_α, a perverse sheaf can be described by gluing data: for each stratum inclusion i_α: X_α → X, the costalk and stalk cohomology groups H^*(i_α^! P) and H^*(i_α^* P) satisfy support and cosupport conditions. The gluing formalism of MacPherson and Vilonen (1986) expresses the category of perverse sheaves on X as the category of diagrams of vector spaces attached to the strata, with linear maps given by the nearby and vanishing cycles along the inclusions of closures. This combinatorial description makes it possible to compute perverse sheaves on toric varieties, Schubert varieties, and nilpotent cones by reducing to quiver representations. Verdier duality acts on the diagram by reversing arrows and dualising vector spaces. The self‑duality of the perverse t‑structure implies that the category of perverse sheaves is a Frobenius category, and its stable category is equivalent to the derived category of constructible sheaves modulo the subcategory of complexes with zero perverse cohomology. This perspective underlies the geometric Satake correspondence, where the category of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian Gr_G is identified with the category of representations of the Langlands dual group ^L G.

Geometric Langlands and the Role of Perverse Sheaves

The geometric Langlands program seeks a categorical equivalence between D‑modules on the moduli stack Bun_G of G‑bundles on a smooth projective curve X and coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSys^L G of local systems for the Langlands dual group ^L G. Perverse sheaves enter through the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence: regular holonomic D‑modules on Bun_G correspond to perverse sheaves on the associated analytic stack. The Hecke operators act on D‑modules on Bun_G by convolution with perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian Gr_G. The geometric Satake equivalence (Mirković–Vilonen, 2007) identifies the category PervG(O)(Gr_G) of G(O)‑equivariant perverse sheaves on Gr_G with the category Rep(^L G) of finite‑dimensional representations of ^L G. Under this equivalence, the convolution product corresponds to the tensor product of representations. A Hecke eigensheaf is a perverse sheaf (or D‑module) on Bun_G which is an eigenobject for all Hecke operators; its eigenvalues are given by a local system on X, i.e., a point of LocSys^L G. The work of Lafforgue (2002) for GL_n over function fields and of Gaitsgory, Lurie, and others for the categorical version over ℂ uses the theory of perverse sheaves on the moduli stack of shtukas and on the affine Grassmannian. The decomposition theorem guarantees that the pushforward of the constant sheaf along the Hitchin fibration h: M_H → A decomposes into a sum of intersection complexes of the fibers, which are Lagrangian subvarieties. This decomposition is the geometric counterpart of the spectral decomposition of the space of automorphic forms. The perverse Leray filtration on the cohomology of the Hitchin moduli space coincides with the weight filtration on the corresponding mixed Hodge modules, providing a bridge between the topological and Hodge‑theoretic aspects of the correspondence. Recent advances by Arinkin–Gaitsgory (2015) on the categorical geometric Langlands for GL_n use the theory of ind‑perverse sheaves on the Ran space to construct the required equivalence. The perverse t‑structure remains the central organising principle throughout these developments.

Computational Aspects: Algorithms for Intersection Cohomology and Perverse Sheaves

Effective computation of intersection cohomology groups and perverse sheaf cohomology has become feasible through algorithms implemented in computer algebra systems. The de Cataldo–Migliorini algorithm (2009) computes the decomposition of Rf_* IC_X for a projective morphism f: X → Y by reducing to the computation of the perverse Leray filtration on the cohomology of the fibers. For a toric variety X_Σ defined by a fan Σ, the intersection cohomology Betti numbers are given by the h‑vector of the associated polytope, which can be computed via the Stanley–Reisner ring of Σ. The software package “Perverse” for Macaulay2 (developed by M. Saito and collaborators) constructs the perverse sheaf associated to a given stratification by building the gluing diagram of vector spaces and linear maps. For Schubert varieties in the flag variety G/B, the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials Pw,v(q) can be computed recursively using the Hecke algebra multiplication rules; the coefficients give the stalk dimensions of the intersection cohomology complexes ICX_w. The algorithm of Braden–MacPherson (1999) computes the intersection cohomology of a stratified space by a sequence of pushforwards and nearby cycles along a filtration by closed subvarieties; this algorithm has been implemented in the “IntersectionCohomology” package for SageMath. In practice, one often works with the Verdier dual of a perverse sheaf to obtain the costalk data, which is easier to compute because it involves only local cohomology with support. The complexity of these algorithms is polynomial in the number of strata and the Betti numbers of the links, but exponential in the dimension of the variety in the worst case. For exam purposes, it is sufficient to know that intersection cohomology of toric varieties is combinatorial, that Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials are computable via the Hecke algebra, and that the decomposition theorem can be checked on a case‑by‑case basis using the perverse Leray spectral sequence.

  • Confusing the weight filtration on mixed Hodge modules with the perverse Leray filtration; they coincide only after applying the forgetful functor to perverse sheaves.
  • Assuming the decomposition theorem holds for non‑proper morphisms; properness is essential for semisimplicity of the pushforward.
  • Neglecting the shift by dimension in the definition of IC_X = j!* ℚ_U[dim X]; forgetting the shift leads to incorrect Poincaré duality statements.
  • Treating Verdier duality as an equivalence of abelian categories on Perv(X) without the shift; D_X is an anti‑equivalence of the derived category but restricts to an equivalence Perv(X) ≅ Perv(X)^op only after accounting for the perverse t‑structure.
  • Misidentifying the geometric Satake category as all perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian; it is the subcategory of G(O)‑equivariant perverse sheaves.
  • Believing that the relative hard Lefschetz isomorphism holds for any ample line bundle on the total space; it requires relative ampleness over the base.
  • Overlooking the necessity of regular holonomicity in the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence; irregular D‑modules correspond to enhanced perverse sheaves, not ordinary constructible sheaves.
