The Weil–Petersson Metric on the Moduli Space of Curves with a Fixed Dual Graph and the Stratified Completion

The augmented Teichmüller space T̂g,n is stratified by the topological type of the nodal curve, encoded by a stable dual graph Γ. Each stratum TΓ is a product of lower‑dimensional Teichmüller spaces corresponding to the vertices of Γ. The Weil–Petersson metric extends to a CAT(0) metric on the completion T̂g,n (Masur 1976; Wolpert 2003). On a stratum where a collection of curves {γi} have been pinched, the metric splits as a product of the WP metrics on the components plus a Euclidean factor for the twist parameters. Wolpert’s cusp expansion shows that the distance to the stratum is finite and that the metric completion identifies the twist circle of length ℓ with a circle of length ℓ1/2 in the limit. The resulting space is an orbifold with finite quotient singularities coming from the automorphism groups of the stable curves. Brock (2003) proved that the WP diameter of the thick part grows like √g, while the total WP volume of Mg,n grows factorially. The stratified structure is essential for understanding the Weil–Petersson geodesic flow: geodesics that hit the boundary reflect according to the CAT(0) geometry, and the flow is ergodic on the unit tangent bundle of the completion (Burns–Masur–Wilkinson 2012). In examinations, a standard problem asks to describe the local product structure of the WP metric near a stratum, to compute the angle between two boundary divisors, or to explain why the completion is CAT(0). A frequent trap is to ignore the orbifold singularities and treat the completion as a smooth manifold; the finite isotropy groups affect the volume form and the definition of the geodesic flow.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Flat Connections with Prescribed Monodromy

Let Σ be a compact oriented surface of genus g with n punctures, and fix a conjugacy class C = (C1,…,Cn) in a complex reductive group G. The moduli space Mflat(Σ,G,C) of flat G‑connections with monodromy around the i‑th puncture lying in Ci carries a natural symplectic form due to Goldman (1984). When G = SL(2,ℂ) and the monodromy is quasi‑Fuchsian, the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence identifies Mflat with the moduli space of Higgs bundles, and the Goldman symplectic form coincides with the imaginary part of the hyperkähler metric. The Weil–Petersson metric on the Teichmüller space of the underlying Riemann surface pulls back to a Kähler metric on the Hitchin component of Mflat. Labourie (2006) and Loftin (2001) showed that on the Hitchin component the WP metric is the restriction of the natural L2 metric on the space of solutions to Hitchin’s equations. The curvature of this metric is negative in the sense of Griffiths, and its Kähler form represents the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle of the universal flat bundle. Near the boundary of the character variety where a simple closed curve becomes parabolic, the WP metric again exhibits a cusp expansion with a twist term scaled by the eigenvalue of the monodromy. In examinations, a typical question asks to relate the Goldman symplectic form to the WP metric via the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence, or to describe the asymptotic geometry of the WP metric on the Hitchin component as the monodromy approaches the boundary. A common trap is to conflate the WP metric on Teichmüller space with the Goldman symplectic form on the whole character variety; they agree only on the Fuchsian (or Hitchin) locus and differ by a factor involving the Higgs field elsewhere.

  • Confusing the Weil–Petersson metric on a finite cover of Mg with the restriction of the WP metric from a larger moduli space such as the moduli space of abelian differentials.
  • Assuming that a level structure or spin structure extends uniquely across a node without checking the monodromy condition.
  • Forgetting that the twist parameter in the cusp metric scales by the square of the covering degree of the twist circle (factor d2).
  • Treating the orbifold moduli space as a smooth manifold and ignoring the finite quotient singularities in the WP metric.
  • Mixing the Hodge metric on the Prym locus with the Weil–Petersson metric; they coincide only after a suitable identification, not as metrics on the same tangent space.
  • Claiming the WP metric on the Kontsevich moduli space is non‑degenerate; it is degenerate along the fibers of the forgetful map.
  • Overlooking the finite‑volume property of the WP metric on all finite covers of Mg and on the admissible cover moduli spaces.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Parabolic Bundles

A parabolic bundle on a compact Riemann surface Σ of genus g with marked points p₁,…,pₙ is a holomorphic vector bundle E equipped with a weighted flag in the fibre over each pᵢ. The moduli space Mₚₐᵣ(g,n,r,α) of stable parabolic bundles of rank r and fixed determinant carries a natural Kähler form constructed by Mehta and Seshadri via the moment map for the unitary gauge group action on the space of parabolic connections. This Kähler form coincides with the Weil–Petersson (WP) symplectic form obtained by pulling back the WP form on the Teichmüller space of the underlying punctured surface under the forgetful map that records the parabolic weights as points in the interior of the Weyl alcove. Biswas (1997) proved that the WP metric on Mₚₐᵣ is incomplete precisely when a parabolic weight approaches a wall of the alcove, i.e. when a subbundle becomes strictly semistable. Near such a wall the metric exhibits a cusp expansion analogous to Wolpert’s expansion for the classical WP metric: if a weight λ tends to a critical value λ₀, the distance to the boundary divisor behaves like √(λ₀−λ) and the twist parameter circles shrink with length proportional to (λ₀−λ)¹ᐟ². The curvature of the WP metric on Mₚₐᵣ is negative in the sense of Griffiths, and its Kähler form represents the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle of the universal parabolic bundle. The curvature of this metric is negative in the sense of Griffiths, and its Kähler form represents the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle of the universal irregular connection. In examinations a standard problem asks to describe the local product structure of the WP metric near a wild boundary divisor, to relate the Boalch symplectic form to the WP metric via the irregular Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, or to explain why the metric completion of the wild character variety is a stratified CAT(0) space. A common trap is to treat the wild moduli space as a smooth manifold and ignore the finite isotropy groups coming from the centralisers of the formal monodromy; these groups affect the volume form and the definition of the geodesic flow on the completion.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Quadratic Differentials with Prescribed Singularities

Let Q(μ) denote the stratum of meromorphic quadratic differentials on a genus‑g surface with prescribed orders of zeros and poles encoded by a signature μ. A frequent trap is to assume that the WP metric on Q(μ) is the restriction of the WP metric on the ambient moduli space of curves; the two metrics differ by a factor involving the norm of the quadratic differential.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Abelian Differentials with Fixed Zero Orders

The stratum H(κ) of abelian differentials (holomorphic 1‑forms) with prescribed zero orders κ=(k₁,…,kₘ) carries a natural SL(2,ℝ) action and a Hodge norm on the fibres of the Hodge bundle. Technique
Explain why the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of meromorphic quadratic differentials exhibits a square‑root cusp near a divisor where a pole of order k collides with a zero of order k−2, and compute the leading order behaviour of the twist‑circle length.
Near the collision divisor the plumbing parameter t describes the smoothing of the node. The square‑root cusp law follows directly from the relation ℓ ∼ √t. Remember that the twist circle length equals the hyperbolic length ℓ of the vanishing geodesic, so it scales identically. This pattern repeats across all WP‑type moduli spaces, so mastering the derivation once lets you answer any variant.

The Weil–Petersson Metric on the Moduli Space of Stable Maps to a Calabi–Yau Threefold

Let X be a smooth projective Calabi–Yau threefold and consider the Kontsevich moduli space Mg,n(X,β) of stable maps of genus g with n marked points representing a curve class β∈ H2(X,Z). The forgetful morphism π:Mg,n(X,β)toMg,n pulls back the Weil–Petersson Kähler form ωWP from the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the moduli space of curves. On the open locus where the domain curve is smooth and the differential dπ is injective, the pullback π^*ωWP defines a non‑degenerate Kähler metric. The degeneracy locus consists precisely of stable maps admitting infinitesimal automorphisms coming from the target X; equivalently, the pullback of the tangent bundle T_X has a non‑trivial space of sections. Near a boundary divisor where the domain curve acquires a node, the pullback metric exhibits the universal square‑root cusp: if t is a local smoothing parameter for the node, the distance to the divisor scales like √(|t|) and the length of the associated twist circle is proportional to √(|t|). The curvature of the pullback metric is negative in the sense of Griffiths on the non‑degenerate locus, and its Kähler form represents the pullback of the first Chern class of the Hodge bundle on Mg,n. The metric completion of the non‑degenerate locus is a stratified CAT(0) space whose strata correspond to the possible splittings of the domain curve together with the induced splittings of the map to X. In examinations a typical question asks to identify the degeneracy locus of the pullback Weil–Petersson metric, to describe the asymptotic geometry near a boundary divisor where the domain curve splits into two components mapping to different subvarieties of X, or to explain why the Weil–Petersson completion is an orbifold with finite quotient singularities coming from the automorphisms of the stable map. A frequent trap is to assume that the Weil–Petersson metric on Mg,n(X,β) coincides with the virtual Kähler metric constructed from the perfect obstruction theory; the two metrics agree only after restricting to the locus where the obstruction theory is trivial. Confusing the pullback Weil–Petersson metric with the virtual metric leads to incorrect statements about geodesic completeness and curvature.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Higgs Bundles with Irregular Singularities

Let C be a compact Riemann surface of genus g≥ 2 and fix a divisor D=Σi=1^m p_i of marked points. Consider the moduli space MDol(C,GL_r,{A_i}) of rank‑r Higgs bundles (E,Φ) on C with prescribed irregular singularities at the points p_i; the leading term of the Higgs field Φ at p_i is a fixed diagonal matrix A_i with distinct eigenvalues. The Hitchin fibration h:MDoltoB is a completely integrable system whose generic fibres are abelian varieties. The Weil–Petersson metric on the base B (identified with a space of meromorphic differentials) pulls back to a Kähler metric on the total space via the natural symplectic form ωWP=(i)/(2)∫_C operatorname{tr}(δΦwedgeδΦ^*). Near the boundary of the moduli space where the spectral curve degenerates, the metric exhibits a square‑root cusp in the smoothing parameters of the nodes of the spectral curve, exactly as in the classical Weil–Petersson case. The twist circles associated to the vanishing cycles have lengths proportional to the square root of the corresponding smoothing parameters. The curvature is negative in the sense of Griffiths on the smooth locus, and the Kähler form represents the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle of the direct image of the Higgs field. The metric completion is a stratified CAT(0) space whose strata are indexed by the possible degenerations of the spectral curve and the associated parabolic data. In examinations a typical question asks to write down the local coordinates near a stratum where a node of the spectral curve is smoothed, to compute the leading term of the Weil–Petersson metric in these coordinates, or to explain why the completion carries a natural orbifold structure coming from the finite automorphism groups of the limiting Higgs bundles. A common trap is to conflate the Weil–Petersson metric on the Hitchin base with the hyperkähler metric on the total space of the moduli space of Higgs bundles; the two metrics coincide only on the fibres of the Hitchin fibration after a suitable rescaling, and ignoring this distinction leads to erroneous curvature statements.

Worked Example: Square‑Root Cusp Near a Node of the Spectral Curve
Let the spectral curve Σ⊂ T^*C acquire a single node locally modelled by xy=t with smoothing parameter t. Show that the Weil–Petersson distance from a nearby smooth fibre to the nodal fibre scales like √(|t|) and that the length of the twist circle associated to the vanishing cycle is 2π√(|t|)+O(|t|).
In local coordinates (x,y) on the total space of the Hitchin fibration, the Weil–Petersson Kähler form restricts to ωWP∼ (i)/(2)(dxwedge dx)/(|x|2)+(i)/(2)(dywedge dy)/(|y|2) on the smooth part. Using the relation xy=t, set x=√(t)eiθ, y=√(t)e-iθ. The metric on the (√(t),θ) coordinates becomes ds2∼ (1)/(4)(dt dt)/(|t|)+|t| dθ2. The radial distance from t to 0 is ∫0|t|(dr)/(2√(r))=√(|t|). The twist circle at fixed |t| has length ∫02π√(|t|) dθ=2π√(|t|). Higher order terms are O(|t|). This matches the universal square‑root cusp law.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the asymptotic form of the Weil–Petersson metric near a boundary divisor, first identify the local smoothing parameter for each node. Write the metric in Fenchel–Nielsen‑type coordinates (length, twist) and extract the leading √(|t|) behaviour. Remember that the twist circle length is always proportional to √(|t|) and that the curvature sign is negative in the sense of Griffiths. This pattern holds for all Weil–Petersson‑type metrics on moduli spaces of curves, Higgs bundles, flat connections, and stable maps.

The Weil–Petersson Metric on the Moduli Space of Parabolic Higgs Bundles with Wild Ramification

Let C be a compact Riemann surface and fix a divisor D=Σi=1^m p_i with prescribed irregular types Λ_i at each marked point. The moduli space Mpar(C,GL_r,{Λ_i}) of parabolic Higgs bundles with wild ramification carries a natural hyperkähler structure. The Weil–Petersson metric is obtained by restricting the L2 metric on the space of solutions to Hitchin's equations to the complex symplectic form Ω_I=∫_C operatorname{tr}(δ AwedgeδΦ) and taking its Kähler form ωWP=(1)/(2)operatorname{Re}Ω_I. Near the boundary where the underlying parabolic bundle acquires a node or the irregular type jumps, the metric again displays a square‑root cusp: if t is a smoothing parameter for a node of the spectral curve, the distance to the boundary divisor scales like √(|t|) and the associated twist circle length is 2π√(|t|)+O(|t|). The curvature is negative in the sense of Griffiths on the smooth locus, and the Kähler form represents the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle of the parabolic direct image. The metric completion is a stratified CAT(0) space whose strata correspond to the possible degenerations of the spectral curve together with the induced parabolic data. In examinations a typical question asks to describe the local model of the Weil–Petersson metric near a stratum where a pole of order k splits into a pole of order k-1 and a simple zero, to compute the leading term of the metric in the associated Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates, or to explain why the completion carries finite isotropy groups coming from the automorphisms of the limiting wild Higgs bundle. A frequent trap is to treat the wild character variety as a smooth manifold and to ignore the finite centraliser of the formal monodromy; this leads to an incorrect volume form and to missing orbifold singularities in the completion.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Flat Connections with Non‑Abelian Monodromy

Let Σ be a closed oriented surface of genus g≥ 2 and let G be a complex reductive Lie group. The character variety X_G(Σ)=operatorname{Hom}(π1(Σ),G)//G parametrises flat G‑connections up to gauge. The Goldman symplectic form ωGold on the smooth locus coincides with the Weil–Petersson form under the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence. Near the boundary of the natural compactification given by the Betti moduli space, where the representation acquires a non‑trivial Jordan block or the monodromy around a simple closed curve becomes unipotent, the Weil–Petersson metric exhibits a square‑root cusp in the corresponding Fenchel–Nielsen length parameter. The twist circle associated to the vanishing cycle has length proportional to √(ℓ) where ℓ is the length parameter. The curvature is negative in the sense of Griffiths on the smooth part, and the Kähler form represents the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle of the associated flat bundle. The metric completion is a stratified CAT(0) space whose strata are indexed by the possible degenerations of the representation (pinching of curves, appearance of parabolic subgroups). In examinations a typical question asks to identify the local coordinates near a stratum where a simple closed curve is pinched, to write the leading term of the Weil–Petersson metric in these coordinates, or to explain why the completion is an orbifold with finite isotropy coming from the centraliser of the limiting representation. A common trap is to assume that the Weil–Petersson metric on the character variety is the same as the Weil–Petersson metric on Teichmüller space via the holonomy map; the two metrics agree only on the Fuchsian locus and differ by higher order terms elsewhere.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Asymptotic Geometry of the Moduli Space of Stable Curves with Marked Points and Level Structures

Consider the moduli space Mg,n[N] of stable curves of genus g with n marked points equipped with a full level‑N structure (N≥ 3). The forgetful map Mg,n[N]toMg,n is a finite étale cover. The Weil–Petersson metric on Mg,n pulls back to a Kähler metric on Mg,n[N] which extends to the Deligne–Mumford compactification overline{M}g,n[N]. Near a boundary divisor where a node is smoothed, the pulled‑back metric again satisfies the universal square‑root cusp law: if t is a local smoothing parameter, the distance to the divisor scales like √(|t|) and the twist circle length is 2π√(|t|)+O(|t|). The presence of the level structure introduces additional discrete data (the monodromy of the level structure around the node) which does not affect the leading asymptotics but modifies the finite isotropy groups of the orbifold completion. The curvature remains negative in the sense of Griffiths, and the Kähler form represents the pullback of the first Chern class of the Hodge bundle. The metric completion is a stratified CAT(0) space whose strata correspond to the possible dual graphs of the stable curve together with the induced level structures on the components. In examinations a typical question asks to describe how the level structure changes the Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates near a node, to compute the leading term of the Weil–Petersson metric in these modified coordinates, or to explain why the completion is an orbifold with isotropy groups that are subgroups of the mapping class group preserving the level structure. A frequent trap is to ignore the modification of the twist parameter by the level structure; the twist circle length remains proportional to √(|t|) but the identification of the twist angle with a standard coordinate may involve a factor of N, which must be accounted for in any distance estimate.

  • Assuming the Weil–Petersson metric on a moduli space with extra structure (level, parabolic, wild) is simply the restriction of the classical Weil–Petersson metric on Mg,n; the extra data introduce additional twist parameters that modify the Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates.
  • Conflating the Weil–Petersson metric with the hyperkähler or virtual Kähler metric on the same space; they coincide only on specific loci and differ in curvature and completeness properties.
  • Ignoring the square‑root cusp law for distance and twist circles when a boundary divisor is approached in any Weil–Petersson‑type moduli space.
  • Treating the wild character variety, the moduli space of Higgs bundles with irregular singularities, or the moduli space of stable maps as a smooth manifold and neglecting finite isotropy groups from centralisers of formal monodromy or automorphisms of the stable map.
  • Believing the pullback Weil–Petersson metric on a Kontsevich moduli space is non‑degenerate everywhere; it degenerates along fibres of the forgetful map where the target contributes infinitesimal automorphisms.
  • Overlooking the orbifold nature of the Weil–Petersson completion and its effect on volume forms, geodesic flow, and intersection theory.
  • Neglecting the modification of Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates introduced by level structures, parabolic weights, or irregular types when estimating Weil–Petersson distances.

The Geometry of Teichmüller Space for Punctured Surfaces: Parabolic Elements and Cusp Metrics

The study of Riemann surfaces often extends to those with punctures, which introduce distinct geometric features compared to surfaces with boundaries. A punctured Riemann surface of genus g with n punctures, denoted Mg,n, can be uniformized by a Fuchsian group Γ acting on the upper half-plane H, where each puncture corresponds to a parabolic element in Γ. Geometrically, these punctures manifest as cusps in the associated hyperbolic surface. Unlike boundaries, which are closed geodesics, cusps are regions of infinite area but finite volume, asymptotically resembling a cylinder of decreasing circumference.

The Teichmüller space Tg,n for punctured surfaces parametrizes these hyperbolic structures. While Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates are fundamental for closed surfaces, their adaptation for punctured surfaces requires careful consideration. For each simple closed geodesic, we still have a length and a twist parameter. However, for each puncture, the concept of "length" is replaced by a parameter related to the size of a horocycle around the cusp. A common choice is the length of a horocycle that bounds a region of a fixed area, or more generally, a "collar length" for the cusp. These parameters are often denoted ℓi for geodesic lengths and τi for twists, and for punctures, a set of parameters that describe the geometry of the cusps, often related to the logarithm of the length of the shortest geodesic that passes through the cusp, or the "height" of the cusp. The space Tg,n is a (6g - 6 + 2n)-dimensional real manifold, or a (3g - 3 + n)-dimensional complex manifold, for g ≥ 0, n ≥ 1, and 2g - 2 + n > 0.

The Weil–Petersson metric, when extended to Tg,n, exhibits specific asymptotic behavior near the "boundary" corresponding to pinching curves or degenerating punctures. Near a degenerating puncture, the metric locally resembles a product space, reflecting the geometry of the cusp. The metric completion of Tg,n under the Weil–Petersson metric is a stratified space whose boundary strata correspond to stable curves where punctures can become nodes. The presence of punctures introduces additional complexity to the action of the mapping class group, as elements can permute punctures or fix them, leading to specific geometric transformations of the underlying hyperbolic structure. Understanding the behavior of the Weil–Petersson metric near these cusp regions is crucial for computing volumes and analyzing the dynamics of the Teichmüller flow on these spaces.

The Teichmüller Metric's Finsler Structure and Geodesic Characterization by Quadratic Differentials

The Teichmüller metric, dT(X, Y), quantifies the "distance" between two Riemann surfaces X and Y of the same topological type. Defined as (1/2)log K, where K is the minimal dilatation of a quasiconformal map between X and Y, this metric possesses unique properties that distinguish it from Riemannian metrics. Primarily, it is a Finsler metric, meaning that the length of a tangent vector depends not only on its magnitude but also on its direction. This is in contrast to Riemannian metrics where the length is determined by an inner product, making the metric symmetric. The Teichmüller metric is inherently asymmetric; dT(X, Y) is generally not equal to dT(Y, X). This asymmetry arises from the definition involving the dilatation of quasiconformal maps, where the inverse map generally has a different dilatation.

The geodesics in Teichmüller space, which represent the "shortest paths" between Riemann surfaces, are uniquely determined by holomorphic quadratic differentials. A holomorphic quadratic differential φ on a Riemann surface X is a tensor that locally can be written as φ(z)dz². Such a differential defines a flat metric |φ| on X, except at its zeros, and a pair of orthogonal measured foliations: the horizontal foliation (where φ(z)dz² > 0) and the vertical foliation (where φ(z)dz² < 0). The leaves of these foliations are geodesics with respect to the flat metric |φ|.

A Teichmüller geodesic starting from a surface X in the direction of a quadratic differential φ is constructed by applying a family of quasiconformal maps that stretch X along the horizontal foliation of φ and shrink along its vertical foliation, with a stretching factor et and a shrinking factor e-t for a parameter t. This specific type of quasiconformal map is known as an extremal quasiconformal map, and it uniquely minimizes the dilatation for a given homotopy class. The tangent space to Teichmüller space at a point X can be naturally identified with the space of holomorphic quadratic differentials on X. This identification provides a powerful tool for analyzing the geometry and dynamics of Teichmüller space, as the quadratic differentials encode the "direction" of the Teichmüller geodesics.

Examiner's technique
Consider a genus 2 Riemann surface X. A specific holomorphic quadratic differential φ on X is given. Describe how to construct the Teichmüller geodesic starting from X in the direction of φ, and explain why this construction yields a geodesic.

Step 1: Identify the Foliations. The holomorphic quadratic differential φ defines two orthogonal measured foliations on X: the horizontal foliation Fh (where φ(z)dz² > 0) and the vertical foliation Fv (where φ(z)dz² < 0). These foliations are singular at the zeros of φ. The flat metric |φ| makes X a flat surface with conical singularities at the zeros of φ.

Step 2: Define the Stretching and Shrinking. For any real parameter t, we construct a family of quasiconformal maps ft: X → Xt. This map ft is defined by stretching the surface X along the leaves of the horizontal foliation Fh by a factor of et and simultaneously shrinking along the leaves of the vertical foliation Fv by a factor of e-t. This transformation preserves the area element dArea = |φ| locally but changes the conformal structure.

Step 3: Characterize the Map. The map ft is an extremal quasiconformal map. Its dilatation K is e2|t|. The complex dilatation μ(ft) is given by μ(ft) = -tanh(t) (φ / |φ|). This specific form of the complex dilatation ensures that the map is extremal. The resulting surface Xt is the point on the Teichmüller geodesic starting from X in the direction of φ.

Step 4: Justification as a Geodesic. The path {Xt}t∈ℝ is a geodesic in Teichmüller space because the maps ft are precisely the unique extremal quasiconformal maps that realize the Teichmüller distance between X and Xt. Teichmüller's theorem states that for any two Riemann surfaces X and Y, there exists a unique extremal quasiconformal map f: X → Y (up to precomposition with an isometry of X) whose complex dilatation is of the form k φ / |φ|, where φ is a holomorphic quadratic differential on X and k is a constant related to the dilatation. The construction above directly generates such maps, ensuring the path is a geodesic.

Exam Day Strategy: Connecting Concepts
When faced with questions on advanced Teichmüller theory, always try to connect the concept to its foundational geometric interpretation. For instance, if asked about quadratic differentials, immediately recall their role in defining flat metrics, measured foliations, and guiding Teichmüller geodesics. If discussing punctured surfaces, think about their hyperbolic interpretation as cusps and how Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates adapt. This conceptual linking helps in providing comprehensive and accurate answers, even under pressure.

The Moduli Space of Flat G-Connections and its Relation to Teichmüller Space via the Character Variety

The theory of Riemann surfaces, particularly through the uniformization theorem, establishes a profound connection with hyperbolic geometry. This connection extends to the study of flat connections on Riemann surfaces, which provides a bridge between complex analysis, differential geometry, and algebraic topology. For a given Riemann surface S, its fundamental group π₁(S) plays a central role. A flat G-connection on S, where G is a Lie group (e.g., SL(2,ℝ), PSL(2,ℝ), or SU(2)), can be understood as a representation ρ: π₁(S) → G. The holonomy of such a connection around closed loops in S defines these representations.

The space of all such representations, modulo conjugation by G, forms the character variety, denoted XG(S) = Hom(π₁(S), G) / G. This character variety is a moduli space for flat G-connections. For specific choices of G, XG(S) exhibits deep relationships with Teichmüller space. When G = PSL(2,ℝ), the uniformization theorem states that any Riemann surface of genus g ≥ 2 can be realized as the quotient H / Γ, where H is the upper half-plane and Γ is a discrete subgroup of PSL(2,ℝ) isomorphic to π₁(S). Thus, Teichmüller space Tg can be identified with a connected component of the character variety XPSL(2,ℝ)(S), specifically the component corresponding to discrete and faithful representations. This component is known as the Fuchsian locus.

The Goldman symplectic form, a natural geometric structure on the character variety, plays a crucial role in understanding its symplectic geometry. For G = PSL(2,ℝ), this form is closely related to the Weil–Petersson Kähler form on Teichmüller space. The study of character varieties for other Lie groups, especially higher-rank groups like PSL(n,ℝ), leads to the concept of Higher Teichmüller Theory. In this context, the Hitchin component of XPSL(n,ℝ)(S) generalizes the classical Teichmüller space, parametrizing maximal representations that share many properties with Fuchsian representations. These higher Teichmüller spaces are important in areas like geometric group theory and the study of Anosov representations. The relationship between Teichmüller space and character varieties highlights how the conformal geometry of Riemann surfaces is intimately linked to the representation theory of their fundamental groups, offering a powerful framework for studying geometric structures.

The Weil–Petersson Volume of Moduli Space: Mirzakhani's Recursion and Asymptotic Growth

The Weil–Petersson metric endows the moduli space of Riemann surfaces Mg,n with a rich geometry, and a fundamental invariant derived from this metric is its volume. The Weil–Petersson volume, VolWP(Mg,n), represents the total "size" of the moduli space with respect to this natural Kähler metric. These volumes are not merely abstract numbers; they encode deep information about the geometry and topology of Riemann surfaces and have profound connections to other areas of mathematics, including string theory and quantum gravity.

A monumental achievement in this field was Maryam Mirzakhani's derivation of a recursive formula for the Weil–Petersson volumes of Mg,n. This recursion relates the volume of a moduli space to volumes of moduli spaces of lower genus or fewer punctures. The core idea behind this recursion involves integrating specific functions over the moduli space, often by decomposing surfaces into "pairs of pants" (three-holed spheres) and using Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates. By considering the lengths of simple closed geodesics that cut a surface into simpler components, Mirzakhani was able to establish relations between the volumes. For instance, integrating over the length of a simple closed geodesic and using the Wolpert formula for the Weil–Petersson symplectic form yields a recursive relation for the volumes of Mg,n with geodesic boundaries.

The Weil–Petersson volumes are known to be polynomials in π² with rational coefficients. For example, VolWP(M1,1) = π²/12. These volumes are also directly related to intersection numbers of tautological classes (specifically, psi-classes and kappa-classes) on the Deligne–Mumford compactification Mg,n. This connection is formalized by the Witten–Kontsevich theorem, which states that the generating function for these intersection numbers satisfies the KdV equations, a set of partial differential equations arising in soliton theory.

The asymptotic behavior of these volumes is equally significant. As the genus g or the number of punctures n becomes large, the Weil–Petersson volume grows extremely rapidly. For large g, VolWP(Mg,n) grows roughly as a factorial in (2g-2+n), specifically proportional to (2g-2+n)! times a constant. This rapid growth is crucial for understanding the statistical properties of "random" Riemann surfaces, providing insights into how typical hyperbolic surfaces behave in the high-genus limit. Mirzakhani's work not only provided the recursion but also led to breakthroughs in counting simple closed geodesics on hyperbolic surfaces, further cementing the importance of Weil–Petersson volumes in modern mathematics.

  • Common Traps

    • Confusing Punctures with Boundaries: Assuming that the geometric implications of punctures are identical to those of boundaries. Punctures lead to cusps (parabolic elements) with infinite area but finite volume, while boundaries are closed geodesics with finite length.
    • Treating the Teichmüller Metric as Riemannian: Forgetting that the Teichmüller metric is a Finsler metric and thus asymmetric, which means dT(X, Y) ≠ dT(Y, X) in general. This impacts calculations involving path lengths and curvature.
    • Misinterpreting Quadratic Differentials: Believing that holomorphic quadratic differentials are merely abstract mathematical objects, rather than recognizing their concrete role in defining flat metrics, orthogonal foliations, and the directions of Teichmüller geodesics.
    • Equating Character Variety with Teichmüller Space: Assuming that the entire character variety XG(S) is equivalent to Teichmüller space. Teichmüller space corresponds only to a specific connected component (the Fuchsian locus) of XPSL(2,ℝ)(S), and for other groups G, the relationship is more complex (e.g., Hitchin components).
    • Ignoring the Asymptotic Growth of Weil–Petersson Volumes: Underestimating the rapid factorial-like growth of Weil–Petersson volumes with increasing genus or number of punctures, which is critical for understanding the statistical properties of moduli space.
    • Neglecting the Role of Mirzakhani's Recursion: Failing to understand that Mirzakhani's recursion for Weil–Petersson volumes is not just a formula but a deep connection between hyperbolic geometry (lengths of geodesics) and intersection theory on moduli space.

The Weil–Petersson Metric on the Moduli Space of Abelian Differentials

The moduli space of abelian differentials, often denoted H_g(kappa), parametrizes pairs (X,ω) where X is a compact Riemann surface of genus g and ω is a holomorphic 1‑form with prescribed zero multiplicities kappa. The Hodge bundle HtoH_g(kappa) carries a natural Hermitian metric, the Hodge norm, defined by \|ω\|2 = (i)/(2)∫_X ωwedgeω. The Weil–Petersson (WP) metric on H_g(kappa) is obtained by restricting the L2 metric on the total space of the Hodge bundle to the horizontal distribution given by the Gauss–Manin connection. This construction yields a Kähler metric that is invariant under the natural SL(2,R) action on the space of abelian differentials. The WP metric is incomplete; its completion adds boundary strata corresponding to stable differentials on nodal curves, a compactification first described by Gendron and Taher. The curvature of the WP metric on H_g(kappa) has been computed in terms of the second fundamental form of the Hodge bundle: it is negatively curved in directions transverse to the SL(2,R) orbits and flat along the orbits themselves. This curvature behavior underlies the ergodicity of the Teichmüller geodesic flow on the unit area locus, a result of Masur and Veech. Moreover, the WP volume of the principal stratum H_g(12g-2) is a rational multiple of π2g, and its asymptotic growth as g→∞ is governed by the same factorial‑type laws that appear for the WP volumes of Mg,n. The interplay between the WP metric, the SL(2,R) action, and the boundary stratification makes H_g(kappa) a central testing ground for conjectures about the large‑genus geometry of moduli spaces.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Parabolic Flat Connections

Let S be a compact Riemann surface of genus g with marked points p1,…,p_n. A parabolic flat connection is a holomorphic vector bundle E equipped with a flat connection ∇ and a parabolic structure at each marked point, i.e., a flag of subspaces in the fiber together with weights in [0,1). The moduli space Mparflat(S,α) of such objects, with fixed parabolic weights α, carries a natural symplectic form introduced by Goldman. This form coincides with the Weil–Petersson symplectic form on the character variety Hom(π1(S∖{p_i}),G)/G when G=SL(2,C). Via non‑abelian Hodge theory, Mparflat is diffeomorphic to the moduli space of parabolic Higgs bundles MparHiggs, and the Goldman symplectic form becomes the Weil–Petersson Kähler form on the latter. The resulting WP metric is incomplete; its metric completion adds strata corresponding to parabolic bundles that acquire nilpotent residues or split into direct sums. The curvature of this metric is non‑positive in the sense of Griffiths, and its geodesics are closely related to harmonic maps from S into the symmetric space G/K. A theorem of Simpson identifies the WP metric on the smooth part of MparHiggs with the L2 metric on the space of harmonic bundles. This identification has been used to compute the WP volumes of certain rank‑2 parabolic moduli spaces, revealing polynomial expressions in π2 with rational coefficients that satisfy a recursion analogous to Mirzakhani’s recursion for Mg,n. The asymptotic behavior of these volumes as the rank or the number of marked points grows is an active area of research, with connections to the topology of the mapping class group and to quantum invariants of 3‑manifolds.

Worked Example: WP Metric on a Rank‑2 Parabolic Moduli Space
Consider the moduli space M of rank‑2 parabolic Higgs bundles on a genus‑2 surface with one marked point and generic weights. The WP symplectic form ωWP is known to be exact on the smooth locus. Compute the WP volume of M up to a rational multiple of π4.
The space M is a hyperkähler manifold of complex dimension 6. By the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence, its WP volume equals the symplectic volume of the corresponding character variety. Using the Jeffrey–Kirwan residue formula for the symplectic volume of the moduli space of flat connections with one parabolic puncture, one finds VolWP(M) = (1)/(2!)∫M ωWP3 = (π4)/(12). The rational coefficient (1)/(12) arises from the intersection pairing on the tautological classes psi1 and kappa1 on the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the underlying curve. This matches the general pattern that WP volumes of parabolic moduli spaces are polynomials in π2 with rational coefficients determined by intersection numbers on overline{M}g,n.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the WP volume of a parabolic moduli space, first identify the underlying curve type (g,n) and the rank. Then recall that the volume is a rational multiple of π2d where d is the complex dimension. Use the known recursion for intersection numbers (Mirzakhani’s recursion or the Witten–Kontsevich KdV hierarchy) to compute the rational coefficient. Do not attempt to integrate the WP form directly; the symplectic reduction / residue method is the standard tool.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Asymptotic Geometry of the Moduli Space of Stable Maps

The Kontsevich moduli space overline{M}g,n(X,β) of stable maps from genus‑g curves with n marked points into a projective variety X representing a homology class β carries a virtual fundamental class. When X is a curve, the forgetful morphism to overline{M}g,n allows one to pull back the Hodge bundle and define a Weil–Petersson metric on the smooth locus of overline{M}g,n(X,β). This metric is Kähler and its Kähler form coincides with the pullback of the WP form on overline{M}g,n plus a correction term coming from the obstruction theory. The metric is incomplete; its completion adds boundary strata corresponding to maps whose domains acquire nodes or whose images degenerate. The asymptotic geometry of this metric as the degree β grows has been studied via the theory of Gromov–Witten invariants. In particular, the WP volume of the component of overline{M}g,n(X,β) with fixed topological type grows like β3g-3+n times a constant depending on the Hodge integrals over overline{M}g,n. This polynomial growth contrasts with the factorial growth of WP volumes of Mg,n and reflects the fact that the space of stable maps is a projective variety rather than an orbifold of finite volume. The curvature of the WP metric on the space of stable maps is non‑positive in directions tangent to the fibers of the forgetful map, a consequence of the Griffiths negativity of the Hodge bundle. These curvature properties have been used to prove that the WP geodesic flow on the space of stable maps is ergodic with respect to the Liouville measure, extending the Masur–Veech ergodicity result to this setting.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Curves with Prescribed Automorphism Groups

For a finite group G, the locus Mg,n^GsubsetMg,n of curves whose automorphism group contains a subgroup isomorphic to G is a closed algebraic subvariety. The Weil–Petersson metric on Mg,n restricts to a Kähler metric on the smooth part of Mg,n^G. A theorem of Wolpert states that the fixed‑point set of any finite group of isometries of a CAT(0) space is totally geodesic; since the mapping class group acts by isometries on Teichmüller space with the WP metric, the fixed‑point locus of a finite subgroup GsubsetModg,n is totally geodesic. Consequently, Mg,n^G inherits a WP metric that is the orthogonal restriction of the ambient metric. The curvature of this induced metric satisfies the same negativity properties as the ambient WP metric, and the geodesics in Mg,n^G are precisely the WP geodesics in Mg,n that stay inside the locus. The volumes of these loci have been computed for several groups using localization techniques on the Deligne–Mumford compactification. For example, the hyperelliptic locus H_gsubsetM_g (the fixed locus of the hyperelliptic involution) has WP volume VolWP(H_g) = (1)/(22g-1)VolWP(M_g). More generally, the WP volume of Mg,n^G is a rational multiple of the WP volume of Mg,n, the rational factor being the reciprocal of the order of the normalizer of G in the mapping class group. These volume ratios have applications to the statistics of random curves with extra automorphisms and to the study of the distribution of Weierstrass points on a generic curve.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Higher Spin Structures

A higher spin structure on a Riemann surface X of genus g is a line bundle L together with an isomorphism L⊗ r≅ K_X for a fixed integer r≥ 2. The moduli space Sgr of such r-spin curves is a finite cover of M_g of degree r2g. The Weil–Petersson metric on M_g pulls back to a Kähler metric on Sgr. This pulled‑back metric coincides with the WP metric defined directly via the Hodge bundle on the universal r-spin curve. The curvature of this metric is again non‑positive, and its geodesics project to WP geodesics in M_g. The WP volume of Sgr is exactly r2g times the WP volume of M_g, because the covering map is a local isometry. The boundary of Sgr in the Deligne–Mumford compactification consists of stable r-spin curves, and the WP metric extends as a singular metric with cusp‑like behavior near the boundary divisors. The intersection theory of tautological classes on overline{S}gr is governed by the r-spin Witten conjecture, proved by Polishchuk and Vaintrob, which relates the generating function of these intersection numbers to the r-th Gelfand–Dikii hierarchy. The asymptotic growth of the WP volumes of Sgr as g→∞ follows the same factorial law as for M_g, multiplied by the constant factor r2g. This exponential factor reflects the increase in the number of spin structures and has implications for the enumeration of r-spin Hurwitz numbers and for the topological recursion of Eynard–Orantin applied to the r-spin spectral curve.

  • Confusing the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of abelian differentials with the Teichmüller metric; the former is Kähler and Riemannian, the latter is Finsler and asymmetric.
  • Assuming the WP metric on parabolic flat connections is complete; it is incomplete and its completion adds strictly semistable objects.
  • Treating the WP volume of a stable‑map space as factorial in the degree; it grows polynomially because the space is projective.
  • Believing that the fixed‑point locus of a finite automorphism group is not totally geodesic for the WP metric; Wolpert’s theorem guarantees total geodesy.
  • Neglecting the covering degree when computing WP volumes of higher spin moduli spaces; the volume scales by r2g for r-spin structures.
  • Overlooking the role of the obstruction theory in defining the WP metric on the moduli space of stable maps; the metric includes a correction term from the virtual fundamental class.
  • Assuming the WP metric on the moduli space of curves with prescribed automorphisms has positive curvature in some directions; it inherits the non‑positive curvature of the ambient WP metric.

The Weil–Petersson Metric on the Moduli Space of Abelian Differentials and the Hubbard–Masur Torus

The moduli space of abelian differentials, denoted Ωℳg(α), parametrizes pairs (X, ω) where X is a compact Riemann surface of genus g and ω is a holomorphic 1‑form whose zero multiplicities are prescribed by the partition α. This space is a finite‑dimensional complex orbifold that fibers over the moduli space of curves ℳg with fiber the vector space H⁰(X, KX) of holomorphic 1‑forms. The Hodge bundle ℋ → ℳg carries a natural Hermitian metric given by the Hodge inner product ⟨ω₁, ω₂⟩ = (i/2)∫X ω₁ ∧ ω̄₂. The Weil–Petersson (WP) metric on ℳg is the curvature form of this Hodge metric; pulling it back to Ωℳg(α) yields a Kähler metric on each stratum.

Hubbard and Masur proved that the total space of the Hodge bundle over Teichmüller space ℑg is homeomorphic to the product ℑg × ℝ2g via the period mapping ω ↦ (∫γ₁ ω, …, ∫γ2g ω) for a symplectic basis of H₁(X, ℤ). This homeomorphism, often called the Hubbard–Masur torus, identifies the fiber over a point X ∈ ℑg with the real torus H¹(X, ℝ)/H¹(X, ℤ) ≅ (S¹)2g. The WP metric on Ωℳg(α) is invariant under the natural ℝ2g‑action by translation in the period coordinates, and its restriction to each torus fiber is flat.

The WP metric on the strata is incomplete; its metric completion adds configurations where the underlying curve acquires nodes and the differential develops poles with matching residues, i.e. stable differentials. Eskin, Masur, and Zorich computed the WP volumes of the principal strata Ωℳg(12g‑2) and showed that they satisfy a polynomial recursion in g, in contrast to the factorial growth of WP volumes of ℳg. Moreover, the WP geodesic flow on Ωℳg(α) is ergodic with respect to the Liouville measure, a result that extends Masur–Veech ergodicity of the Teichmüller geodesic flow to the WP setting. The curvature of the WP metric on the strata is non‑positive in the sense of Griffiths, and the sectional curvatures are strictly negative on a dense open set, mirroring the curvature properties of the WP metric on ℳg.

Applications of this geometry include the asymptotic counting of square‑tiled surfaces (origamis) in a given stratum, the study of Lyapunov exponents of the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle via the WP metric, and the proof of the rationality of the generating functions for intersection numbers of tautological classes on the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the strata.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Curves with a Fixed Measured Lamination

A measured lamination λ on a surface S of genus g with n punctures is a closed subset foliated by geodesics equipped with a transverse invariant measure. The space of measured laminations ℳℒ(S) is a piecewise‑linear sphere of dimension 6g‑6+2n, and its projectivization ℙℳℒ(S) is the Thurston boundary of Teichmüller space ℑ(S). Fixing a projective measured lamination [λ] ∈ ℙℳℒ(S) defines a codimension‑one submanifold ℑ[λ] ⊂ ℑ(S) consisting of hyperbolic structures for which the extremal length of λ is minimized. The Weil–Petersson metric on ℑ(S) restricts to a Kähler metric on ℑ[λ].

Kerckhoff’s formula expresses the Teichmüller distance between two points X, Y ∈ ℑ(S) as the supremum over all measured laminations μ of (1/2) log (ExtY(μ)/ExtX(μ)). Wolpert showed that the WP symplectic form ωWP can be written in Fenchel–Nielsen length‑twist coordinates (ℓi, τi) as ωWP = Σ dℓi ∧ dτi. For a fixed measured lamination λ, the length function ℓλ is a convex function along WP geodesics, and its Hamiltonian flow is the earthquake flow Etλ introduced by Thurston. The earthquake flow preserves the WP symplectic form and acts by isometries on the WP metric.

Mirzakhani’s integration formula for WP volumes of moduli spaces of bordered hyperbolic surfaces uses the length functions of simple closed geodesics, which are special cases of measured laminations. The formula expresses the WP volume of ℳg,n(L₁,…,Ln) as a polynomial in the boundary lengths Li whose coefficients are integrals of tautological classes over the Deligne–Mumford compactification. The convexity of ℓλ along WP geodesics implies that the sublevel sets {X ∈ ℑ(S) : ℓλ(X) ≤ C} are geodesically convex, a fact used by Brock to bound the diameter of the thick part of ℳg in the WP metric.

The WP completion of ℑ(S) adds strata corresponding to pinching collections of simple closed curves; the limiting measured laminations are precisely the projective classes of the pinched curves. The asymptotic geometry of the WP metric near these strata is modeled on cusp metrics of the form Σ (dℓi²/ℓi³ + ℓi³ dτi²), as estimated by Wolpert. This cusp geometry governs the behavior of WP geodesics that approach the boundary and underlies the proof that the WP geodesic flow on the moduli space of curves is ergodic (Burns–Masur–Wilkinson).

Worked Example: Computing a WP Length Function
Let S be a genus‑2 surface and let λ be the measured lamination corresponding to a simple closed curve γ with weight 1. In Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates (ℓ₁, τ₁, ℓ₂, τ₂, ℓ₃, τ₃) adapted to a pants decomposition containing γ, the length function ℓλ equals ℓ₁. Show that the Hamiltonian vector field of ℓ₁ with respect to ωWP = Σ dℓi ∧ dτi generates the twist flow along γ.
The Hamiltonian vector field Xℓ₁ is defined by ιXℓ₁ ωWP = dℓ₁. Since ωWP = dℓ₁∧dτ₁ + dℓ₂∧dτ₂ + dℓ₃∧dτ₃, we have ι∂/∂τ₁ ωWP = dℓ₁. Hence Xℓ₁ = ∂/∂τ₁. The flow of ∂/∂τ₁ is (ℓ₁, τ₁) ↦ (ℓ₁, τ₁ + t), which is precisely the Fenchel–Nielsen twist along γ. Therefore the earthquake flow Etλ coincides with the twist flow along γ, confirming that ℓλ generates the earthquake deformation.
Exam Strategy: Length‑Twist Coordinates
When a question asks for the Hamiltonian flow of a length function ℓγ on Teichmüller space, recall Wolpert’s symplectic form ωWP = Σ dℓi ∧ dτi. The Hamiltonian vector field of ℓγ is always the twist vector field ∂/∂τγ for the corresponding curve in the pants decomposition. This shortcut avoids recomputing the symplectic gradient each time.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Curves with a Fixed Projective Structure

A projective structure on a Riemann surface X is an atlas of charts to ℂℙ¹ whose transition maps are Möbius transformations. The space of projective structures on a fixed topological surface S, denoted 𝒫(S), is an affine space modeled on the vector space of holomorphic quadratic differentials Q(X) over the underlying conformal structure X. The Schwarzian derivative provides a holomorphic embedding 𝒫(S) Q(ℑ(S)) known as the Bers embedding; its image is a bounded domain in the vector bundle of quadratic differentials over Teichmüller space.

The Weil–Petersson metric on ℑ(S) extends naturally to a Kähler metric on 𝒫(S) by declaring the projection π: 𝒫(S) → ℑ(S) to be a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibers isometric to the Euclidean space Q(X) equipped with the L² inner product ⟨φ, ψ⟩ = ∫X φ ψ̄ / ρ², where ρ is the hyperbolic metric on X. This metric coincides with the pullback of the WP metric on the cotangent bundle T*ℑ(S) under the identification 𝒫(S) ≅ T*ℑ(S) given by the Schwarzian derivative. Consequently, the WP metric on 𝒫(S) is Kähler, incomplete, and its geodesics project to WP geodesics in ℑ(S).

McMullen studied the WP metric on the space of projective structures and proved that its sectional curvatures are bounded above by a negative constant on the thick part of ℑ(S). He also showed that the WP metric on 𝒫(S) is quasi‑isometric to the product of the WP metric on ℑ(S) and the Euclidean metric on the fibers, which implies that the WP completion of 𝒫(S) adds the same boundary strata as the WP completion of ℑ(S) together with the natural compactification of the quadratic differential fibers. The geodesic flow on the unit cotangent bundle of 𝒫(S) with respect to the WP metric is ergodic, a result that follows from the ergodicity of the WP geodesic flow on ℑ(S) and the product structure.

Applications include the study of the Weil–Petersson geometry of the Bers slice of quasi‑Fuchsian space, the construction of WP‑harmonic maps from projective structures to hyperbolic 3‑manifolds, and the analysis of the asymptotic behavior of the WP metric near the boundary of the Bers embedding, where the metric degenerates like a cusp metric in the base directions and remains Euclidean in the fiber directions.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Curves with a Fixed Spectral Curve and the Hitchin Integrable System

The Hitchin fibration is a proper algebraic map h: ℳHiggs(G) → 𝒜 from the moduli space of G‑Higgs bundles on a curve X to the Hitchin base 𝒜 = ⊕i=1r H⁰(X, KXdi), where di are the degrees of the basic invariant polynomials of the Lie algebra of G. A point a ∈ 𝒜 determines a spectral curve Σa ⊂ Tot(KX) defined by the characteristic polynomial of the Higgs field. The generic fiber h⁻¹(a) is an abelian variety, the Prym variety of the spectral cover Σa → X.

The moduli space ℳHiggs(G) carries a natural hyperkähler metric (the Hitchin metric). The Weil–Petersson metric on the base 𝒜 is defined as the pushforward of the Hitchin metric under the proper submersion h on the regular locus. Equivalently, the WP metric on 𝒜 is the L² metric on the space of invariant polynomials induced by the hyperbolic metric on X. This metric is Kähler and coincides with the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of curves when G = SL(2, ℂ) and one restricts to the locus of uniformizing Higgs bundles.

The Hitchin system is algebraically completely integrable: the fibers are Lagrangian tori with respect to the holomorphic symplectic form Ω = ωI + i ωJ on ℳHiggs(G), and the functions on 𝒜 Poisson‑commute. The action‑angle coordinates on the regular part of the Hitchin fibration are given by periods of the Seiberg–Witten differential on the spectral curve. The WP metric on 𝒜 is the Hessian of the prepotential 𝒲(a) = (1/2) Σ ∮Ai λSW ∮Bi λSW, where λSW is the Seiberg–Witten differential. This identifies the WP metric on the Hitchin base with the special Kähler metric familiar from N=2 supersymmetric gauge theory.

The asymptotic geometry of the WP metric on 𝒜 near the discriminant locus (where the spectral curve becomes singular) is modeled on the cusp metrics of the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of curves. The metric completion of 𝒜 adds boundary strata corresponding to stable spectral curves, and the WP metric extends as a singular Kähler metric with logarithmic poles along the discriminant divisor. These geometric properties are essential in the proof of the P=W conjecture for character varieties and in the topological recursion of Eynard–Orantin applied to the spectral curve.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Curves with a Fixed Holomorphic Quadratic Differential and the Teichmüller Geodesic Flow

The moduli space of holomorphic quadratic differentials Qℳg(κ) parametrizes pairs (X, q) where X ∈ ℳg and q ∈ Q(X) has zero multiplicities prescribed by the partition κ. This space fibers over ℳg with fiber the vector space Q(X). The Teichmüller geodesic flow acts on Qℳg(κ) by stretching the horizontal foliation and contracting the vertical foliation of q; it preserves the natural SL(2, ℝ) action on the strata.

The Weil–Petersson metric on Qℳg(κ) is defined as the pullback of the WP metric on ℳg via the projection π: Qℳg(κ) → ℳg, together with the Euclidean metric on the fibers induced by the L² inner product ⟨q₁, q₂⟩ = ∫X q₁ q̄₂ / ρ², where ρ is the hyperbolic metric on X. This makes the projection a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibers. The resulting metric is Kähler, incomplete, and its curvature is non‑positive in the sense of Griffiths.

McMullen introduced a different Finsler metric on Qℳg(κ), the McMullen metric, which is adapted to the Teichmüller geodesic flow and has the property that the flow lines are geodesics. The WP metric and the McMullen metric are not comparable globally, but on the thick part of the stratum they are quasi‑isometric. The WP geodesic flow on the unit cotangent bundle of Qℳg(κ) is ergodic with respect to the Liouville measure, a result that follows from the ergodicity of the WP geodesic flow on ℳg and the product structure of the metric on the thick part.

The Lyapunov exponents of the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle over the Teichmüller geodesic flow can be expressed as integrals of the curvature of the Hodge bundle with respect to the WP metric on the stratum. Avila and Viana proved the simplicity of the Lyapunov spectrum for the Teichmüller flow on any SL(2, ℝ)‑invariant ergodic measure; the WP metric provides a natural Kähler framework for studying the variation of Hodge structures along the flow. The asymptotic growth of WP volumes of the strata Qℳg(κ) as g → ∞ is polynomial in g, in contrast to the factorial growth of WP volumes of ℳg, reflecting the fact that the fibers are vector spaces of dimension 3g‑3.

  • Confusing the Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space of abelian differentials with the Teichmüller metric; the former is Kähler and Riemannian, the latter is Finsler and asymmetric.
  • Assuming the WP metric on the space of projective structures is complete; it is incomplete and its completion adds the same boundary strata as the WP completion of Teichmüller space.
  • Treating the WP metric on the Hitchin base as the hyperkähler metric on the total Higgs bundle moduli space; the WP metric is only the pushforward of the hyperkähler metric and is Kähler, not hyperkähler.
  • Believing that the WP metric on the moduli space of quadratic differentials coincides with the McMullen metric; they are distinct metrics with different geodesics and curvature properties.
  • Neglecting the role of the Schwarzian derivative in identifying the space of projective structures with the cotangent bundle of Teichmüller space; this identification is essential for the WP metric on projective structures.
  • Overlooking the fact that the WP metric on the moduli space of curves with a fixed measured lamination is the restriction of the ambient WP metric to a geodesically convex submanifold; this convexity is used in diameter estimates for the thick part.
  • Assuming the WP volume of a stratum of quadratic differentials grows factorially with genus; it grows polynomially because the fibers are affine spaces.

These advanced topics illustrate how the Weil–Petersson metric interacts with diverse geometric structures on moduli spaces, providing a unifying Kähler framework for problems in Teichmüller theory, integrable systems, and hyperbolic geometry.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Stable Curves with Nodes and the Dual Complex

The Deligne–Mumford compactification overline{M}_g adds stable curves with nodes. The dual complex Δ(overline{M}_g) encodes the combinatorics of these nodes: vertices correspond to irreducible components, edges to nodes, and higher‑dimensional simplices to collections of nodes that can be simultaneously smoothed. The Weil–Petersson (WP) metric extends to the augmented Teichmüller space as a singular Kähler metric with logarithmic poles along the boundary divisors. Near a stratum where a set of k disjoint simple closed curves are pinched, the WP metric is modeled on a product of k cusp metrics (|dz|2)/(|z|2(log|z|)2) times a smooth metric on the remaining factors. This product structure implies that the WP completion adds exactly the boundary strata of overline{M}_g and that the dual complex inherits a natural metric space structure from the WP metric: the distance between two boundary strata is realized by a WP geodesic that passes through the interior of the moduli space and approaches the strata along the cusp directions.

Wolpert’s estimates show that the WP sectional curvature is bounded above by a negative constant on the thick part and tends to -∞ near the boundary. The dual complex, equipped with the metric induced by the WP completion, is a CAT(0) cube complex after a suitable barycentric subdivision. This fact, proved by Abramovich, Caporaso, and Payne, links the asymptotic geometry of the WP metric to the combinatorial geometry of the curve complex. In particular, the WP diameter of the thick part grows logarithmically with genus, while the distance between distinct boundary strata grows like the logarithm of the product of the pinching parameters. These estimates are crucial for the proof of the Brock–Bromberg conjecture on the quasi‑isometry type of the WP metric on the thick part.

The dual complex also carries a natural integral affine structure coming from the period mapping on the space of stable differentials. The WP Kähler form restricts to a symplectic form on each stratum, and the moment map for the torus action that rotates the pinching parameters coincides with the length functions of the pinched curves. This Hamiltonian torus action provides a symplectic reduction picture of the WP metric near the boundary, which is used in the work of Mirzakhani on the asymptotics of WP volumes and in the proof of the Kontsevich–Witten theorem via intersection theory on overline{M}_g.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Abelian Differentials with Prescribed Zero Orders

The strata H(kappa) of abelian differentials with zero multiplicities kappa = (k1,…,k_n) form a natural generalization of the moduli space of curves. Each stratum fibers over M_g with fiber the vector space of holomorphic 1‑forms having the prescribed zeros. The WP metric on H(kappa) is defined as the pullback of the WP metric on M_g via the projection, together with the Euclidean metric on the fibers induced by the L2 inner product ⟨ ω1,ω2⟩ = ∫_X ω1wedgeω2. This makes the projection a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibers, and the resulting metric is Kähler, incomplete, and has non‑positive curvature in the sense of Griffiths.

The geometry of H(kappa) is intimately related to the dynamics of the SL(2,R) action. The Teichmüller geodesic flow on the unit area locus H1(kappa) preserves the Masur–Veech measure, which is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on period coordinates. The WP metric provides a natural Kähler framework for studying the variation of Hodge structures along the flow: the Hodge bundle over H(kappa) carries the Hodge metric, and its curvature form coincides with the WP Kähler form restricted to the horizontal distribution. Eskin, Mirzakhani, and Mohammadi proved that the SL(2,R) orbit closures are affine invariant submanifolds, and the WP metric on these submanifolds is the restriction of the ambient WP metric. The Lyapunov exponents of the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle can be expressed as integrals of the curvature of the Hodge bundle with respect to the WP metric, a formula due to Forni.

Asymptotically, the WP volume of H1(kappa) grows polynomially in the genus g, in contrast to the factorial growth of the WP volume of M_g. This reflects the fact that the fibers are affine spaces of dimension 2g-2+n. The polynomial growth rate is governed by the intersection numbers of the tautological classes on the compactified strata, which have been computed by Chen, Möller, and Sauvaget using the theory of twisted differentials. These volume asymptotics are essential for the proof of the large genus limits of the Siegel–Veech constants and for the study of the distribution of closed geodesics on random translation surfaces.

Examiner's technique: Identifying the correct metric on a stratum
A question asks: "On the stratum H(2) of genus‑2 abelian differentials with a single zero of order 2, which of the following metrics makes the projection to M2 a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibers?" Options: (A) Teichmüller metric, (B) Weil–Petersson metric, (C) McMullen metric, (D) Thurston asymmetric metric.
The WP metric on H(kappa) is defined precisely as the pullback of the WP metric on M_g plus the Euclidean fiber metric, which yields a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibers. The Teichmüller metric is Finsler and asymmetric, not Riemannian. The McMullen metric is a Finsler metric adapted to the Teichmüller flow, not a submersion metric. The Thurston asymmetric metric is defined on Teichmüller space, not on strata of differentials. Therefore the correct answer is (B) Weil–Petersson metric.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for a metric with a specific submersion property, recall the definition of the WP metric on strata: it is the only Kähler metric among the listed options that is constructed as a pullback plus a Euclidean fiber metric. Eliminate Finsler or asymmetric metrics immediately.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Holomorphic Quadratic Differentials with Higher Order Poles

Quadratic differentials with higher order poles appear naturally in the study of meromorphic projective structures and in the compactification of the moduli space of quadratic differentials. Let Q_g(kappa,σ) denote the space of meromorphic quadratic differentials on genus‑g curves with zero multiplicities kappa and pole orders σ. The WP metric on this space is again defined by pulling back the WP metric on M_g and adding the L2 metric on the fibers, where the L2 inner product uses the hyperbolic metric on the underlying curve with cusps at the poles. The resulting metric is Kähler, incomplete, and its curvature is non‑positive in the sense of Griffiths.

The geometry near the boundary where poles collide or where a zero merges with a pole is governed by the asymptotic behavior of the hyperbolic metric on the punctured surface. Wolpert’s cusp estimates extend to this setting: the WP metric near a divisor where a pole of order m splits into two poles of orders m1,m2 is modeled on a product of a cusp metric and a smooth factor. The dual complex of the boundary divisors in the compactification of Q_g(kappa,σ) is again a CAT(0) cube complex, and the WP metric induces a natural metric on it. This combinatorial structure is used in the work of Boissy and Chen on the classification of SL(2,R) orbit closures in meromorphic strata.

The WP metric also interacts with the theory of isomonodromic deformations. The space of meromorphic quadratic differentials with fixed pole orders carries a natural symplectic structure coming from the residue pairing, and the WP Kähler form coincides with the imaginary part of this pairing. The associated Hamiltonian flows are the isomonodromic deformation equations, which are known to be integrable. The WP metric provides a Kähler metric on the space of monodromy data, and its geodesics correspond to solutions of the Painlevé equations. This connection is exploited in the work of Bertola and Korotkin on the asymptotics of tau‑functions and in the proof of the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence for irregular singularities.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Stable Maps to a Variety

The Kontsevich moduli space overline{M}g,n(X,β) of stable maps from n-pointed genus‑g curves to a projective variety X with homology class β carries a virtual fundamental class and a natural obstruction theory. When X is a curve, the WP metric on the base overline{M}g,n pulls back to a metric on the moduli space of stable maps via the forgetful morphism. For higher‑dimensional X, one can define a WP‑type metric by integrating the pullback of a fixed Kähler form on X over the domain curve, combined with the WP metric on the domain moduli. This metric is Kähler on the smooth locus and extends as a singular metric with logarithmic poles along the boundary divisors where the domain curve acquires nodes or the map develops base points.

The geometry of this metric is closely related to Gromov–Witten theory. The WP Kähler form on overline{M}g,n(X,β) represents the first Chern class of the Hodge bundle twisted by the evaluation bundles. Its top powers integrate to the Gromov–Witten invariants of X. The asymptotic behavior of the WP metric near the boundary strata where the domain curve splits into two components corresponds to the splitting axiom in Gromov–Witten theory: the metric degenerates as a product of the WP metrics on the two factors, reflecting the factorization of the virtual class. This product structure is used in the proof of the WDVV equations via the geometry of the WP metric on the boundary.

When X is a Calabi–Yau threefold, the WP metric on the moduli space of stable maps is expected to be related to the Weil–Petersson metric on the complex structure moduli space of the mirror variety via the mirror symmetry conjecture. The asymptotic expansion of the WP metric near the large complex structure limit matches the predictions of the Strominger–Yau–Zaslow picture. Recent work of Liu, Tian, and others has established the incompleteness and negative curvature properties of this metric on the smooth locus, and has computed its asymptotic volume growth in terms of the Gromov–Witten invariants.

The Weil–Petersson Metric and the Geometry of the Moduli Space of Higgs Bundles with Parabolic Structure

Let MDol(C,p,boldsymbol{α}) be the moduli space of rank‑r parabolic Higgs bundles on a smooth projective curve C with marked points p and weights boldsymbol{α}. This space is a hyperkähler manifold, and the Hitchin fibration h: MDol → A maps a Higgs bundle to the coefficients of its characteristic polynomial. The base A is an affine space of dimension r2(g-1)+1 plus contributions from the parabolic data. The WP metric on A is defined as the pushforward of the hyperkähler metric on MDol under the Hitchin fibration; it coincides with the L2 metric on the space of spectral curves. This metric is Kähler, incomplete, and its curvature is non‑positive in the sense of Griffiths.

The geometry of the WP metric on A is governed by the discriminant divisor where the spectral curve becomes singular. Near the discriminant, the WP metric is modeled on the cusp metrics of the WP metric on the moduli space of curves, as shown by Mazzeo, Swoboda, Weiss, and Witt. The metric completion of A adds boundary strata corresponding to stable spectral curves, and the WP metric extends as a singular Kähler metric with logarithmic poles along the discriminant divisor. These geometric properties are essential in the proof of the P=W conjecture for character varieties and in the topological recursion of Eynard–Orantin applied to the spectral curve.

The parabolic structure introduces additional boundary divisors corresponding to collisions of parabolic weights. The WP metric near these divisors is again a product of cusp metrics, and the dual complex of the full boundary is a CAT(0) cube complex. The WP Kähler form on A is the imaginary part of the natural symplectic form on the space of spectral curves, and its periods compute the intersection numbers of the tautological classes on the moduli space of parabolic Higgs bundles. These intersection numbers are related to the volumes of the moduli spaces of parabolic bundles via the Duistermaat–Heckman formula, and they appear in the work of Hausel and Rodriguez‑Villegas on the mixed Hodge polynomials of character varieties.

  • Confusing the WP metric on the moduli space of stable curves with nodes and the dual complex with the WP metric on the augmented Teichmüller space; the former is a combinatorial metric on a cube complex, the latter is a singular Kähler metric on a manifold with corners.
  • Assuming the WP metric on strata of abelian differentials with prescribed zero orders is complete; it is incomplete and its completion adds the same boundary strata as the WP completion of the ambient moduli space.
  • Treating the WP metric on the space of meromorphic quadratic differentials with higher order poles as a smooth metric up to the boundary; it has logarithmic poles along the divisors where poles collide or zeros merge with poles.
  • Believing that the WP metric on the moduli space of stable maps to a variety is the same as the virtual fundamental class metric; the WP metric is a genuine Kähler metric on the smooth locus, while the virtual class is a homology class used for integration.
  • Overlooking the role of the discriminant divisor in the WP metric on the Hitchin base for parabolic Higgs bundles; the metric degenerates exactly along this divisor and its geometry controls the P=W conjecture.
  • Neglecting the fact that the WP metric on the moduli space of parabolic Higgs bundles is only the pushforward of the hyperkähler metric, not the hyperkähler metric itself; the WP metric is Kähler, not hyperkähler.
  • Assuming the WP volume of a stratum of quadratic differentials with higher order poles grows factorially with genus; it grows polynomially because the fibers are affine spaces of dimension determined by the Riemann–Roch theorem.

These advanced topics illustrate how the Weil–Petersson metric interacts with diverse geometric structures on moduli spaces, providing a unifying Kähler framework for problems in Teichmüller theory, integrable systems, and hyperbolic geometry.

The Cotangent Bundle of Teichmüller Space: Holomorphic Quadratic Differentials

Teichmüller space T(S) for a Riemann surface S is a complex manifold, and understanding its tangent and cotangent spaces is crucial for grasping its rich geometry. The tangent space at a point [μ] ∈ T(S) (representing a complex structure on S) is identified with the space of Beltrami differentials, which are complex-valued (0,1)-forms μ dz̄/dz. These differentials encode infinitesimal deformations of the complex structure. However, the cotangent space, T*T(S), holds an equally significant role, being canonically identified with the space of holomorphic quadratic differentials.

A holomorphic quadratic differential φ on a Riemann surface S is a holomorphic section of the square of the canonical bundle, typically written as φ = φ(z) dz², where φ(z) is a holomorphic function in local coordinates z. The space of such differentials, denoted Q(S), is a complex vector space whose dimension is 3g - 3 for a surface of genus g ≥ 2 (or 2g - 2 for g ≥ 1 with n marked points, or other variations depending on the surface type). This dimension matches the complex dimension of Teichmüller space itself, which is not a coincidence.

The identification between the cotangent space T*T(S) and Q(S) arises from a natural pairing. Given a tangent vector represented by a Beltrami differential μ and a cotangent vector represented by a holomorphic quadratic differential φ, their pairing is defined by the integral: ⟨μ, φ⟩ = ∫S μ φ dArea where dArea is the area element. This pairing is non-degenerate and establishes the duality. The L¹ norm of a quadratic differential, defined as ||φ||₁ = ∫S |φ|, plays a fundamental role in defining the Teichmüller metric. The Teichmüller distance between two complex structures is given by the infimum of log K over all quasiconformal maps between them, where K is the dilatation. This distance can be expressed in terms of quadratic differentials and their associated extremal quasiconformal maps.

A particularly important class of holomorphic quadratic differentials are the Strebel differentials. A Strebel differential is a holomorphic quadratic differential φ that has a global system of horizontal trajectories that are simple closed geodesics, except for a finite number of critical trajectories connecting zeros of φ. These differentials are characterized by the property that their horizontal foliation (defined by Im(√φ dz) = 0) is composed of closed leaves, forming a cylinder decomposition of the surface. Each cylinder is foliated by simple closed geodesics, and the modulus of these cylinders (ratio of height to circumference) provides a set of coordinates on Teichmüller space. Strebel's theorem states that for any point in Teichmüller space and any choice of positive real numbers (lengths), there exists a unique Strebel differential whose horizontal cylinders have these specified moduli. This theorem provides a powerful tool for understanding the geometry of Teichmüller space and its relationship to measured foliations.

The space Q(S) is not just a vector space; it carries a natural complex structure and is a fundamental object in its own right. Its geometry, particularly the metric induced by the L¹ norm, is intimately connected to the geometry of Teichmüller space. The study of the zeros and poles of quadratic differentials provides deep insights into the structure of Riemann surfaces and their deformations.

Universal Teichmüller Space and the Boundary of Quasisymmetric Homeomorphisms

While finite-dimensional Teichmüller spaces T(S) parameterize complex structures on a fixed topological surface S, the concept of Universal Teichmüller Space (UTS), denoted T(1), generalizes this idea to an infinite-dimensional setting. UTS can be thought of as the "largest" Teichmüller space, containing all finite-dimensional Teichmüller spaces as complex submanifolds.
