Logarithmic Picard Varieties and Logarithmic Albanese Varieties

The logarithmic Picard functor assigns to a fine saturated log scheme X a group scheme Piclog(X) representing line bundles equipped with a log structure compatible with the given one. Kato proved that when X is proper and log smooth over a field, Piclog(X) is represented by a separated group scheme of finite type whose identity component is a semi‑abelian variety. The log structure contributes a toric part coming from the divisor at infinity; the character group of this torus is canonically identified with the group of log line bundles trivial on the interior. The logarithmic Albanese variety Alblog(X) is defined dually as the universal recipient of a log morphism from X to a semi‑abelian log variety. Kato and Nakayama showed that the natural map X → Alblog(X) induces an isomorphism on log H1 and that the log Albanese fits into an exact sequence 0 → T → Alblog(X) → Alb(X∘) → 0, where T is the torus associated to the log structure and X∘ is the interior. The duality between Piclog and Alblog extends the classical Poincaré duality: there is a perfect pairing Piclog(X) × Alblog(X) → Gm,log compatible with the log Kummer sequence. In the case of a log curve (C,D) with D a reduced divisor, the log Picard variety is an extension of the usual Jacobian by a torus of rank |D|−1, and the log Albanese coincides with the generalized Jacobian of the curve with modulus D. These constructions are functorial for log morphisms and play a central role in the logarithmic version of the Mordell–Weil theorem for semi‑abelian log varieties over number fields.

Logarithmic Chow Motives and Logarithmic Correspondences

The category of logarithmic Chow motives Chowlog(k) over a perfect field k was introduced by Kahn, Saito and Yamazaki to provide a universal cohomology theory for log smooth varieties. Objects are triples (X, p, n) where X is a smooth projective log scheme, p is an idempotent logarithmic correspondence of degree 0, and n ∈ ℤ denotes the Tate twist. A logarithmic correspondence from (X, MX) to (Y, MY) of degree r is a cycle class on the log product X ×log Y supported on a closed subscheme whose log structure is the pullback of the product log structure; equivalently it is a morphism in the log Chow group CHrlog(X × Y). Composition uses the log Fulton–MacPherson intersection product, which respects the log structure because the excess intersection formula holds in the log setting (Kato–Saito). The resulting category is rigid symmetric monoidal with the log Tate motive 𝟙(1) = (Spec k, id, −1) as the tensor unit. The realization functors to log étale, log de Rham, log crystalline and log Hodge cohomology are compatible with the six operations on log motives constructed by Ayoub and extended by Déglise–Jin. A key theorem (Kahn–Saito) states that the log motive of a log smooth compactification of a smooth variety U depends only on the log structure, giving a well‑defined motive Mlog(U) for any smooth U with a chosen modulus. This allows one to formulate a logarithmic version of the standard conjectures: the log Künneth projectors are algebraic, and the log Lefschetz operator is induced by a log ample line bundle. The category Chowlog(k) is expected to be the heart of a log motivic t‑structure on the log stable homotopy category SHlog(k).

Worked Example: Computing a Logarithmic Correspondence
Let (X, D) be a smooth projective curve with a reduced divisor D = {P1, P2}. Consider the log structure MX associated to D. Compute the group of logarithmic correspondences of degree 0 from (X, D) to itself, i.e. CH0log(X × X).
The log product X ×log X carries the log structure pulled back from the two factors; its divisor is (D × X) ∪ (X × D). A degree‑0 logarithmic correspondence is a 0‑cycle on this log scheme, i.e. a finite formal sum of closed points with multiplicities, modulo rational equivalence respecting the log structure. Because the log structure is vertical over the diagonal, the log Chow group CH0log(X × X) fits into an exact sequence 0 → CH0(X × X) → CH0log(X × X) → ⊕i,j ℤ → 0, where the last term records the multiplicities along the log strata Di × Dj. For a curve, CH0(X × X) ≅ ℤ generated by the class of a point. The log strata are the four points (Pi, Pj). Hence CH0log(X × X) ≅ ℤ ⊕ ℤ4. The identity correspondence corresponds to (1, 0,0,0,0). The additional ℤ4 summands correspond to the log modifications supported on the boundary strata.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the group of log correspondences, first identify the log strata of the product. Write the exact sequence relating ordinary Chow groups to log Chow groups; the cokernel is a free abelian group on the log strata. Remember that the log structure is vertical for the projection maps, so the excess intersection formula simplifies to a direct sum decomposition.

Logarithmic p-adic Hodge Theory for Logarithmic Varieties over Imperfect Fields

Classical p‑adic Hodge theory compares étale cohomology of a smooth proper variety over a perfectoid field with its de Rham cohomology via the period rings BdR, Bcris, Bst. For log smooth varieties over an imperfect field k of characteristic p, the log structure on the base introduces a non‑trivial log monodromy operator Nlog on the log crystalline cohomology H•cris,log(X/W(k)). Nizioł and later Bhatt–Lurie–Morrow constructed a logarithmic version of the Fontaine functors DlogdR, Dlogcris, Dlogst taking values in the category of filtered (φ, Nlog)‑modules over the log Robba ring. The key input is the log prismatic cohomology Δlog(X) which carries a Frobenius φlog and a log Nygaard filtration. The logarithmic Hyodo–Kato isomorphism identifies H•cris,log(X/W(k)) ⊗ K0 with H•dR,log(X/K) compatibly with φlog and the log monodromy Nlog. When the base log structure is non‑trivial (e.g. k = Fp(t) with the log structure given by the valuation), the operator Nlog does not vanish even for semistable reduction; it encodes the variation of the log structure along the special fibre. The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism extends to this setting: for a log smooth proper X over OK with K a finite extension of Qp and a log structure on OK given by a valuation, there is a functorial isomorphism Hiét(XK̄, Zp) ⊗ Blog,cris ≅ Hicris,log(X/OK) ⊗ Blog,cris compatible with Galois action, φlog and Nlog. This theory underpins the logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture for varieties over imperfect fields, where the weight filtration on log étale cohomology is expected to be the monodromy filtration of Nlog.

Logarithmic Motivic Homotopy Theory with Modulus and the Logarithmic Suslin Complex

Voevodsky’s motivic homotopy theory has a logarithmic analogue developed by Binda, Park and Østvær. The log motivic homotopy category SHlog(k) is obtained by localizing the category of log smooth schemes with respect to the log Nisnevich topology and the log A1-homotopy invariance. A crucial new feature is the modulus condition: a log scheme (X, M) is said to have modulus D if the log structure is generated by a divisor D. The logarithmic Suslin complex Clog•(X) is defined as the simplicial abelian group whose n‑simplices are finite correspondences from the log standard simplex Δnlog to X satisfying the modulus condition. The log motivic cohomology groups Hp,qlog(X) are the cohomology of the complex Clog•(X)(q). The main theorem (Binda–Park–Østvær) states that for a log smooth pair (X, D) over a perfect field, the log motivic cohomology with modulus coincides with the higher Chow groups with modulus defined by Kahn–Saito–Yamazaki. Moreover, the log motivic cohomology satisfies a logarithmic version of the Beilinson–Lichtenbaum conjecture: the natural map Hp,qlog(X, Z/ℓ) → Hpét,log(X, μℓ⊗q) is an isomorphism for p ≤ q and injective for p = q+1. The log motivic Steenrod algebra acts on these groups, and the log motivic spectral sequence converges to the log algebraic K‑theory of X. The logarithmic six functors formalism (Ayoub, Déglise–Jin) lifts to SHlog(k), giving a log motivic version of the Grothendieck–Verdier duality. This framework is essential for formulating the logarithmic Bloch–Kato conjecture and for constructing the logarithmic regulator map from log K‑theory to log motivic cohomology.

Logarithmic Hodge Theory for Logarithmic Varieties with Non-Log Smooth Morphisms

When a morphism f : (X, MX) → (Y, MY) of fine saturated log schemes is not log smooth, the logarithmic de Rham complex Ω•X/Y,log fails to be locally free and the naive Hodge filtration does not satisfy Griffiths transversality. Ogus and later Kato–Nakayama introduced the logarithmic Hodge filtration using the log cotangent complex LX/Y,log. The log cotangent complex fits into a distinguished triangle f*LY,log → LX,log → LX/Y,log →, and its cohomology sheaves control the obstruction to log smoothness. The logarithmic Hodge filtration Fplog on the log de Rham complex is defined by the image of the wedge powers of the log relative differentials ΩpX/Y,log in the derived category. For a log smooth morphism this recovers the usual filtration; for a general morphism the associated graded pieces are expressed in terms of the log cotangent complex via the log HKR isomorphism: grpF,log Ω•X/Y,log ≅ ∧p LX/Y,log[−p]. The logarithmic Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence E1p,q = Hq(X, grpF,log) ⇒ Hp+qdR,log(X/Y) degenerates at E1 when f is log smooth and proper, but in the non‑log‑smooth case the differentials are governed by the log Kodaira–Spencer class in Ext1(Ω1X/Y,log, OX). This theory provides the correct framework for the logarithmic variation of Hodge structure on the base of a degenerating family with non‑normal crossing singularities, and it underlies the logarithmic version of the Clemens–Schmid exact sequence for semi‑stable reduction with non‑log‑smooth total space.

  • Confusing the logarithmic Picard variety with the ordinary Picard variety of the interior; the log Picard contains a toric part coming from the boundary divisor.
  • Assuming logarithmic correspondences are ordinary correspondences on the product; they must respect the log structure on the product, which adds boundary strata contributions.
  • Neglecting the log monodromy operator Nlog in p‑adic Hodge theory over imperfect fields; it is non‑zero even for semistable reduction when the base log structure is non‑trivial.
  • Treating the logarithmic Suslin complex as the ordinary Suslin complex; the modulus condition forces correspondences to have prescribed behaviour along the log divisor.
  • Applying the classical Hodge filtration to a non‑log‑smooth morphism; one must use the log cotangent complex to define the correct filtration.
  • Overlooking that the logarithmic Albanese variety is a semi‑abelian log variety, not an abelian variety, and its toric part is dual to the toric part of the log Picard.
  • Believing the logarithmic weight monodromy conjecture follows directly from the classical case; the log monodromy on the base introduces extra weight filtration steps.

The Logarithmic Étale Site: Construction and Properties for Degenerations

The ordinary étale site, while powerful for smooth schemes, proves insufficient for studying schemes with degenerations or boundaries. Logarithmic geometry addresses this by introducing the logarithmic étale site, which is specifically designed to capture the additional structure provided by a log scheme. This site is built upon the Kummer flat topology, a refinement of the flat topology that incorporates the log structure. A morphism f : (X, MX) → (Y, MY) of log schemes is defined as log étale if it is étale in the usual sense on the underlying schemes X → Y, and additionally, the induced map of log structures f-1MY → MX is a Kummer flat morphism of sheaves of monoids. This dual condition ensures that the morphism respects both the geometric and the logarithmic structure.

The objects of the log étale site are log schemes (U, MU) over a base log scheme (S, MS), and the morphisms are log étale morphisms. The crucial difference from the standard étale site lies in the definition of covering families. A family of log étale morphisms {(Ui, MUi) → (U, MU)} is a log étale covering if the underlying morphisms Ui → U form an étale covering, and for each i, the induced map of log structures is Kummer flat. This allows for a richer class of coverings that "see" the boundary components and their interactions. For instance, if X is a scheme with a normal crossing divisor D, and (X, MD) is the associated log scheme, then a log étale cover of (X, MD) can resolve singularities or degenerations that an ordinary étale cover of X might not. The log étale site provides the correct framework for defining log étale cohomology, which is a cohomology theory that is sensitive to the log structure and behaves well with respect to degenerations.

The relationship between log étale cohomology and ordinary étale cohomology is intricate. For a log scheme (X, MX), one can consider the generic fiber Xo (where the log structure is trivial) and the boundary components. Log étale cohomology groups Hqét,log(X, F) for a log étale sheaf F often relate to the ordinary étale cohomology of Xo and the cohomology of the boundary. For example, if (X, M) is a log smooth scheme over a field, the log étale cohomology of X with coefficients in Z/nZ can be understood as the ordinary étale cohomology of the generic part Xo, but with additional information encoded by the boundary. This is particularly evident in the construction of the Kato–Nakayama space, which provides a topological space whose ordinary cohomology is isomorphic to the log étale cohomology of the log scheme. This construction topologically "unfolds" the singularities encoded by the log structure, making them amenable to standard topological methods.

The log étale site is fundamental for defining the logarithmic fundamental group π1,log(X, MX), which is a generalization of the classical fundamental group. This group classifies log étale covers of (X, MX) and captures the monodromy around the boundary components in a precise algebraic manner. Its construction involves considering log étale pointed covers, and it plays a crucial role in the logarithmic version of the Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem and the arithmetic Langlands program, where it provides the appropriate Galois group for arithmetic schemes with boundaries. Understanding the Kummer flat topology and the precise definition of log étale morphisms is key to navigating the subtleties of this advanced cohomology theory.

Logarithmic Moduli Spaces: Universal Properties and Boundary Behavior

The construction of moduli spaces for geometric objects, such as curves or abelian varieties, often leads to non-compact spaces. Compactifying these spaces is crucial for many applications, including intersection theory and the study of degenerations. However, naive compactifications often result in highly singular spaces, making them difficult to work with. Logarithmic moduli spaces provide a canonical and well-behaved framework for compactifying moduli spaces by explicitly incorporating the degeneration data into the structure of the compactified space.

The core idea is that a family of geometric objects degenerating over a base space S can be viewed as a family of log objects over a log scheme (S, MS), where MS encodes the boundary behavior. For instance, a family of smooth curves degenerating to a stable nodal curve over the origin of the disk can be reinterpreted as a family of log smooth curves over the log point (Spec k[[t]], N → k[[t]] via t ↦ t). The log structure on the base "remembers" the fact that the family degenerates, and the log structure on the total space of the family precisely describes the stable degeneration.

A key feature of logarithmic moduli spaces is their universal property. For example, the moduli space of stable log curves Mg,n,log classifies families of n-pointed log smooth curves of genus g over log schemes. This means that any family of stable log curves over a log scheme (S, MS) corresponds to a unique log morphism from (S, MS) to Mg,n,log. This universal property ensures that the compactification is canonical and behaves functorially with respect to base changes. The points on the boundary of Mg,n,log correspond to stable curves with nodes, and the log structure at these points encodes the combinatorial data of the dual graph of the nodal curve, including the number of irreducible components and their intersection patterns.

For abelian varieties, the compactification typically involves toroidal compactifications. The logarithmic moduli space of abelian varieties provides a framework where the boundary components correspond to degenerate abelian varieties (semi-abelian varieties) which have a toric part. The log structure at the boundary points precisely records the data of the toric degeneration, such as the fan associated with the toroidal compactification. This allows for a smooth compactification in the log sense, even if the underlying scheme is singular. The theory of log structures ensures that the families of degenerating objects extend uniquely over the compactified base, preserving the desired properties like log smoothness.

The construction of these spaces often involves techniques from toric geometry and the theory of stacks. The log structure on the moduli space itself is often a fine saturated (fs) log structure, which means it is locally isomorphic to the log structure associated with a cone in a lattice. This combinatorial data is essential for understanding the local structure of the boundary and for performing calculations, such as intersection theory, on these compactified spaces. The log structure provides the necessary "bookkeeping" to handle the complexities of degenerations in a coherent and geometrically meaningful way, making logarithmic moduli spaces indispensable tools in modern algebraic geometry.

Examiner's Twist on Log Étale Cohomology
Consider a scheme X = Spec k[x,y]/(xy) over an algebraically closed field k, equipped with the log structure MD associated with the normal crossing divisor D = {xy=0}. Let Xo = Spec k[x,y]/(xy) - {0} be the generic part. Which of the following statements about the relationship between H1ét,log(X, MD; G) and H1ét(Xo; G) for a finite abelian group G is generally true, and why?
  1. They are always isomorphic.
  2. H1ét,log(X, MD; G) contains H1ét(Xo; G) as a direct summand.
  3. H1ét,log(X, MD; G) is related to H1ét(Xo; G) by an exact sequence involving boundary terms.
  4. There is no general relationship between them.
The correct statement is 3.

Explanation:

The log étale cohomology of a log scheme (X, MD) for a normal crossing divisor D is not simply the ordinary étale cohomology of its generic part Xo. The log structure MD encodes information about the boundary D, which consists of the two lines x=0 and y=0 intersecting at the origin. The log étale site is designed to capture this boundary behavior.

For a log scheme (X, MD) where D is a normal crossing divisor, there is a fundamental exact sequence relating log étale cohomology to ordinary étale cohomology of the generic fiber Xo and the boundary components. This sequence arises from the localization sequence in log étale cohomology and captures the contribution of the boundary. Specifically, for a suitable sheaf G, one often finds exact sequences of the form:

... → Hqét,log(X, MD; G) → Hqét(Xo; G) → Hq-1ét(Dred; G(-log D)) → ...

or more generally, sequences involving the cohomology of the components of D and their intersections. The term G(-log D) or similar constructions account for the "logarithmic" twist induced by the boundary. This means that the log étale cohomology groups are generally richer than the ordinary étale cohomology of the generic part, incorporating information from the boundary components and their intersections. Therefore, statement 3, which posits a relationship via an exact sequence involving boundary terms, is the most accurate description of the general connection.

Statements 1 and 2 are too simplistic. The log structure provides additional data that cannot simply be ignored or treated as a direct summand without accounting for the boundary's contribution to the cohomology.

Mastering Logarithmic Geometry for Exams
Logarithmic geometry is a highly abstract and technical field. For competitive exams, focus on understanding the *purpose* and *consequences* of log structures rather than memorizing every definition. Key areas to prioritize include:
  1. Why log structures are needed: To handle degenerations, compactify moduli spaces, and provide well-behaved cohomology theories for singular schemes.
  2. Core concepts: Log scheme, log smooth morphism, log étale site (Kummer flat topology), semistable reduction. Understand how these differ from their non-log counterparts.
  3. Comparison theorems: Know the significance of isomorphisms like Kato–Nakayama (log étale log Betti) and Hyodo–Kato (log de Rham log crystalline). These show how different cohomology theories are fundamentally related through log structures.
  4. Applications: Recognize the role of log structures in moduli space compactifications, p-adic Hodge theory, and arithmetic geometry.
When encountering a problem, identify if it involves a singular scheme or a family degenerating. If so, consider how log structures might provide a more refined or "correct" framework for analysis.

The Logarithmic Riemann-Hilbert Correspondence: From Connections to Monodromy

The classical Riemann-Hilbert correspondence establishes an equivalence between the category of flat connections on a complex manifold and the category of local systems of vector spaces. This correspondence is fundamental in connecting differential equations with topology. When dealing with schemes that have singularities or degenerations, particularly those arising from arithmetic contexts, the classical theory needs refinement. The Logarithmic Riemann-Hilbert Correspondence extends this profound connection to the setting of log schemes, providing a bridge between logarithmic differential equations and logarithmic local systems.

On the algebraic side, the objects are logarithmic connections. For a log smooth scheme (X, MX) over C, a logarithmic connection on a vector bundle E is a connection ∇: E → E ⊗ Ω1X/C,log that has regular singularities along the boundary divisor D = X Xo. The sheaf of logarithmic differentials Ω1X/C,log is a key ingredient; it is the sheaf of relative differentials of the log scheme (X, MX) over (Spec C, MC), where MC is the trivial log structure. These logarithmic differentials are locally free and incorporate poles of at most order one along the boundary, reflecting the regular singularity condition. The category of logarithmic connections is closely related to the category of logarithmic D-modules, which are modules over the sheaf of logarithmic differential operators DX,log.

On the topological side, the objects are logarithmic local systems. These are not just ordinary local systems, but rather local systems on the generic fiber Xo equipped with additional data that describes the monodromy around the boundary components. Specifically, for each irreducible component Di of the boundary divisor D, the local system is equipped with a unipotent monodromy operator around Di. This monodromy data precisely captures the behavior of solutions to differential equations with regular singularities. The Kato–Nakayama space Xanlog, which is a topological space associated with the log scheme (X, MX), provides the appropriate topological setting for these logarithmic local systems; they are local systems on Xanlog.

The correspondence states that there is an equivalence of categories between the category of logarithmic connections (or logarithmic D-modules) on (X, MX) and the category of logarithmic local systems on Xanlog. This equivalence is functorial and respects tensor products and duality. It is a powerful tool because it allows one to translate problems from the world of differential equations (which are often hard to solve explicitly) to the world of topology (where techniques from algebraic topology can be applied), and vice-versa. For example, the existence of a logarithmic connection with certain properties can imply the existence of a corresponding logarithmic local system with specific monodromy properties.

The logarithmic Riemann-Hilbert correspondence is particularly important in the study of variations of mixed Hodge structure, where the periods of algebraic varieties with degenerations are encoded by logarithmic connections. It provides a concrete realization of the abstract connections between algebraic geometry, differential geometry, and topology in the presence of singularities, making it a cornerstone of modern research in arithmetic geometry and complex analysis.

Logarithmic Intersection Theory: Virtual Cycles and Enumerative Geometry

Classical intersection theory on smooth projective varieties provides powerful tools for enumerating geometric objects, such as counting curves of a certain genus passing through given points. However, when working with singular spaces or with moduli spaces whose compactifications are singular, the standard intersection theory often breaks down. The notion of a virtual fundamental class, developed in the context of Gromov-Witten theory and related enumerative theories, addresses this by providing a way to define an intersection product even on spaces that are not smooth, but are equipped with a "virtual" tangent bundle. Logarithmic intersection theory extends these ideas to log schemes, offering a robust framework for enumerative geometry in the presence of degenerations.

A central application is in Logarithmic Gromov-Witten (GW) theory, which studies stable maps from curves to target varieties. In the classical setting, stable maps are maps from nodal curves to a target variety. In the logarithmic setting, we consider log stable maps from log curves to a log target variety (X, MX). A log curve is a curve equipped with a log structure that encodes information about its nodes and marked points. A log stable map is a stable map that respects the log structures, meaning it maps the boundary of the log curve to the boundary of the log target, and the map on the monoids satisfies certain properties. This allows for a more refined study of curves that degenerate onto the boundary of the target space.

The moduli space of log stable maps, denoted Mg,n(X, MX, β)log, is generally a singular space. To define intersection numbers on this space, one constructs a log virtual fundamental class. This class is an element in the Chow group or homology group of the moduli space, even if the space itself is singular. The construction of the log virtual cycle involves a careful analysis of the deformation theory of log stable maps. The log cotangent complex plays a crucial role here, as its cohomology groups control the obstructions to deforming a log stable map. The log virtual fundamental class is then defined using techniques from derived algebraic geometry, effectively "desingularizing" the moduli space in a virtual sense.

The log virtual fundamental class allows for the definition of logarithmic Gromov-Witten invariants, which are intersection numbers computed on the moduli space of log stable maps. These invariants count log stable maps with specified properties, such as passing through certain cycles on the target space. They are particularly powerful for studying enumerative problems on varieties with boundaries or in degenerating families. For example, in mirror symmetry, logarithmic GW invariants on a Calabi-Yau variety with a boundary are conjectured to correspond to certain invariants on its mirror partner.

Logarithmic intersection theory provides a precise way to account for the contributions of curves that "touch" or "cross" the boundary of a log scheme. The log structure ensures that these boundary interactions are handled combinatorially and algebraically, leading to well-defined and geometrically meaningful enumerative invariants. Without the log structure, the deformation theory would be ill-behaved, and the virtual fundamental class would not be well-defined, highlighting the essential role of logarithmic geometry in modern enumerative geometry.

Logarithmic Prismatic Cohomology: A Unifying Framework for p-adic Cohomologies

The landscape of p-adic cohomology theories is vast and complex, encompassing crystalline, de Rham, syntomic, and étale cohomologies, each with its own strengths and applications. A major challenge has been to find a unified framework that can relate these theories and simplify their comparison isomorphisms. Logarithmic prismatic cohomology, introduced by Bhatt and Scholze, provides such a powerful and unifying perspective, especially for schemes with degenerations over p-adic fields.

The foundation of prismatic cohomology lies in the construction of the prismatic site. For a scheme X over a p-adic base S, the prismatic site Pris(X/S) consists of pairs (A, I), where A is a p-adic ring and I is a prism ideal in A, satisfying certain properties. A prism is a pair (A, I) where A is a p-adic complete P-ring (a ring complete with respect to a regular sequence (p, d)) and I is an ideal such that A/I is p-torsion free. This abstract construction provides a flexible environment for defining cohomology theories. Logarithmic prismatic cohomology extends this to log schemes (X, MX), where the prisms are equipped with additional log structure data, allowing them to capture the boundary behavior of the log scheme.

The logarithmic prismatic cohomology groups HqPris,log(X, MX) are defined as the cohomology of certain complexes of sheaves on the logarithmic prismatic site. A key feature is that these groups naturally carry a Frobenius action and a filtration, making them suitable for p-adic Hodge theory. What makes logarithmic prismatic cohomology particularly powerful is its ability to recover other p-adic cohomology theories as special cases or via natural comparison isomorphisms. For instance:

  • Log Crystalline Cohomology: Logarithmic prismatic cohomology specializes to logarithmic crystalline cohomology when considering prisms of the form (W(OK), (p)), where W(OK) is the ring of Witt vectors of the ring of integers OK of a p-adic field K. The log Hyodo-Kato isomorphism, which relates log de Rham and log crystalline cohomology, can be seen as a consequence of the prismatic framework.
  • Log de Rham Cohomology: By inverting p and taking the derived de Rham complex of the prismatic cohomology, one recovers logarithmic de Rham cohomology. This provides a direct link between the p-adic world and the world of differential forms.
  • Log Syntomic Cohomology: Logarithmic syntomic cohomology, which combines features of crystalline and étale cohomology, also arises naturally from logarithmic prismatic cohomology by taking certain fixed points under the Frobenius action and considering specific filtrations. The logarithmic Fontaine–Messing isomorphism, relating log syntomic to log crystalline cohomology, is thus unified.

This unifying power simplifies many arguments in p-adic Hodge theory. Instead of constructing separate comparison isomorphisms between each pair of theories, one can often establish a single comparison from prismatic cohomology to each of them. This makes logarithmic prismatic cohomology an indispensable tool for researchers working on the arithmetic of schemes with degenerations, providing a coherent and comprehensive framework for understanding their p-adic invariants. It is particularly relevant for the study of logarithmic Shimura varieties and other objects in arithmetic geometry.

Common Traps in Advanced Logarithmic Geometry

  • Confusing Log Étale and Ordinary Étale Sites: Assuming that log étale covers are simply ordinary étale covers. The Kummer flat topology is a finer topology, and log étale morphisms require conditions on both the underlying scheme and the log structure, leading to a different category of sheaves and cohomology.
  • Ignoring Boundary Contributions in Logarithmic Cohomology: Treating log étale or log crystalline cohomology as merely the cohomology of the generic fiber. Log structures explicitly encode boundary data, and this data contributes non-trivially to the cohomology groups, often via exact sequences involving boundary components.
  • Applying Classical Riemann-Hilbert to Singularities: Attempting to use the classical Riemann-Hilbert correspondence for connections with non-regular singularities or on schemes with non-trivial log structures. The logarithmic version is necessary to correctly handle regular singularities and the associated monodromy.
  • Misinterpreting Virtual Fundamental Classes: Believing that a virtual fundamental class implies the underlying moduli space is smooth or has a classical fundamental class. The virtual class exists even for highly singular spaces and is a construct in derived categories, not a direct geometric cycle in the classical sense.
  • Overlooking the Prismatic Site's Structure: Assuming prismatic cohomology is just another p-adic cohomology without understanding its foundational role. The prismatic site and the concept of prisms are crucial for its unifying power, and it's not simply a variant of crystalline cohomology.
  • Neglecting the Log Structure on the Base: When dealing with families of log schemes, forgetting that the base itself must often be a log scheme, and the log structure on the base encodes the degeneration of the family. This is critical for universal properties of log moduli spaces.
  • Simplifying Monodromy in Logarithmic Contexts: Assuming that monodromy in logarithmic local systems is always trivial or simple. The unipotent monodromy operators around boundary components are specific and essential data that distinguish logarithmic local systems from ordinary ones.

Logarithmic Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves and the Logarithmic Bondal–Orlov Reconstruction

The derived category of coherent sheaves on a log scheme (X, MX) is defined as the derived category of the abelian category of coherent OX-modules equipped with a compatible log structure. When f : (X, MX) → (Y, MY) is a proper log smooth morphism, the pushforward Rf* preserves coherence and admits a right adjoint f! given by the log twisted inverse image. The log canonical bundle ωX/Y = det(LX/Y), where LX/Y is the log cotangent complex, plays the role of the relative dualizing sheaf. A log version of the Bondal–Orlov reconstruction theorem states that if (X, MX) and (Y, MY) are smooth proper log Calabi–Yau varieties (i.e. ωX ≃ OX and ωY ≃ OY in the log sense) and there exists an exact equivalence of triangulated categories Dbcoh(X, MX) ≃ Dbcoh(Y, MY) commuting with the log Serre functors, then the log schemes are isomorphic. The proof adapts the classical argument by using the log Hochschild cohomology HH*(X, MX) and the log Mukai pairing. In particular, the log Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg isomorphism identifies HH*(X, MX) with the log polyvector fields ⊕p Hp(X, ∧p TX(-log D)), where D is the boundary divisor. This identification is functorial for log étale morphisms and underlies the log Fourier–Mukai transform: any kernel K ∈ Dbcoh(X × Y, MX×Y) defines an exact functor ΦK which preserves the log structure if K is log perfect. The reconstruction theorem has been used to classify log derived equivalences for log K3 surfaces and log abelian varieties, showing that the log Picard group and the log Néron–Severi lattice are derived invariants.

Logarithmic Categorical Enumerative Geometry and Logarithmic Gopakumar–Vafa Invariants

Logarithmic Gromov–Witten theory counts log stable maps f : (C, MC) → (X, MX) from log curves to a log smooth target. The moduli stack Mg,n((X, MX), β) of such maps carries a virtual fundamental class [M]vir constructed via the log perfect obstruction theory of Abramovich–Chen–Gross–Siebert. The log Gromov–Witten invariants Ng,β are defined by integrating tautological classes against this virtual class. The logarithmic Gopakumar–Vafa invariants ng,β are extracted from the generating series of log GW invariants by the same multiple cover formula as in the classical case, but the log structure ensures that the contributions from boundary strata are correctly accounted for. In the Gross–Siebert program, the log GW invariants of a log Calabi–Yau variety are computed by tropicalizing the moduli space: each log stable map corresponds to a tropical curve in the intersection complex B of the log structure, and the log GW invariant equals a weighted count of tropical curves with multiplicities given by the log structure. This tropical correspondence theorem has been proved for toric degenerations and for log Calabi–Yau surfaces by Gross–Siebert and by Ruddat–Siebert. The log GV invariants are conjecturally integers and satisfy the log version of the integrality conjecture. They have been computed explicitly for the log quintic threefold and for log K3 surfaces, matching the predictions from mirror symmetry. The log DT/PT correspondence, relating log Donaldson–Thomas invariants of the log Calabi–Yau to log Pandharipande–Thomas invariants, provides an alternative definition of log GV invariants via the log DT vertex.

Logarithmic Curve Counting via Tropicalization
Let (X, MX) be the log Calabi–Yau surface obtained from ℙ² by taking the toric boundary divisor D = {xyz = 0} as the log structure. Compute the genus‑0 log Gromov–Witten invariant N0,β for the curve class β = [line] using the tropical correspondence.
The intersection complex B is ℝ² with the standard fan of ℙ². A tropical line in B is a trivalent graph with three unbounded edges in directions (−1,0), (0,−1), (1,1) meeting at a vertex. The log structure assigns multiplicity 1 to each vertex because the lattice length of each edge is 1. There is exactly one such tropical line up to translation, so the weighted count is 1. By the tropical correspondence theorem, N0,β = 1. This matches the classical count of lines through two points in ℙ², and the log structure ensures that no extra contributions arise from maps meeting the boundary D.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorize the definition of a log stable map (stability of the underlying curve plus minimality of the log structure) and the statement of the tropical correspondence theorem. Examiners often ask to identify the tropical curve corresponding to a given log map or to explain why the log structure removes boundary contributions. Practice drawing the fan of a toric log Calabi–Yau and listing the possible tropical curves of low degree.

Logarithmic Arithmetic Intersection Theory and the Logarithmic Arithmetic Riemann–Roch Theorem

Arithmetic intersection theory on log regular schemes extends the Gillet–Soulé framework by incorporating log structures on the boundary. Let (X, MX) be an arithmetic log variety over Spec ℤ with a fine saturated log structure. The log arithmetic Chow groups CĤp(X, MX) are generated by pairs (Z, g) where Z is a codimension‑p cycle on X meeting the boundary properly and g is a log Green current for Z, i.e. a current on X(ℂ) with logarithmic singularities along the boundary divisor D satisfying ddc g + δZ = [ω] for a smooth log form ω. The log arithmetic intersection product is defined by the *-product of log Green currents, which is associative and commutative up to homotopy. The log arithmetic Riemann–Roch theorem, proved by Burgos Gil–Kramer–Kühn, states that for a log hermitian vector bundle (E, h) on (X, MX), the log arithmetic Chern character cĥ(E, h) satisfies cĥ(Rf*(E, h)) = f*(cĥ(E, h) · Td̂(Tf)) in CĤ*(Y, MY) ⊗ ℚ, where f : (X, MX) → (Y, MY) is a proper log smooth morphism, Tf is the log relative tangent bundle, and Td̂ is the log arithmetic Todd class. The proof uses the log version of the Bismut–Köhler analytic torsion form and the log anomaly formula for the Quillen metric. Applications include the computation of log Faltings heights of log abelian varieties and the log arithmetic Hilbert–Samuel formula for log ample line bundles. The log arithmetic intersection theory also provides a natural setting for the log version of the Bogomolov conjecture, where the log essential minimum of a subvariety is related to its log arithmetic self‑intersection.

Logarithmic Topological Cyclic Homology and the Logarithmic Trace Map

Topological cyclic homology TC for log schemes is constructed by equipping the cyclotomic spectra THH(X, MX) with a log structure compatible with the circle action. For a log smooth ℤ-algebra (A, M), the log THH is the geometric realization of the cyclic bar construction in the category of log animated rings. The log cyclotomic trace K(X, MX) → TC(X, MX) is a map of log ring spectra induced by the log Dennis trace. The logarithmic Dundas–Goodwillie–McCarthy theorem asserts that for a nilpotent extension of log rings (A, M) → (B, N), the relative log K‑theory and relative log TC are equivalent. This reduces the computation of log K‑theory of log schemes to log TC, which is more accessible via the log Bökstedt periodicity theorem: THH(A, M) ≃ (A, M) ⊗ 𝕊1 as log cyclotomic spectra. The log TC groups carry a natural filtration, the log Nygaard filtration, whose associated graded pieces are identified with log prismatic cohomology via the log prismatic–TC comparison of Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze. In particular, for a log smooth proper scheme over a perfectoid field, the log TC groups recover the log p‑adic étale cohomology after p‑completion. The log trace map has been used to compute the log K‑theory of log toric varieties and to prove the log version of the Bloch–Kato conjecture for log motives over finite fields.

Logarithmic Motivic Homotopy Theory and the Logarithmic Slice Filtration

The log motivic homotopy category SHlog(S) over a log base scheme (S, MS) is obtained by inverting the log affine line 𝔸1log = (𝔸1, ℕ → 𝔸1) in the category of log motivic spaces. The log sphere spectrum 𝕊log represents log stable motivic homotopy groups. The log slice filtration, constructed by adapting Voevodsky's slice tower to the log setting, yields a tower of localizing subcategories ⋯ ⊂ slogq+1 ⊂ slogq ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ SHlog(S) where slogq consists of objects whose log motivic cohomology vanishes below weight q. The log slice associated graded pieces slogq/slogq+1 are equivalent to shifts of the log motivic Eilenberg–MacLane spectra Hℤlog(q). Morel's connectivity theorem extends: the log motivic Hopf map ηlog is non‑zero in π1,1log(𝕊log) and the log motivic Steenrod algebra acts on log motivic cohomology. The log slice spectral sequence converges to the log motivic stable homotopy groups and degenerates at the E2-page for log cellular schemes. This machinery computes the log algebraic K‑theory of log regular schemes via the log motivic spectral sequence E2p,q = Hp-q,-qlog(X, ℤ) ⇒ K-p-qlog(X). The log slice filtration also controls the log motivic Tate conjecture: a log motive is log Tate if and only if its slice tower splits.

  • Assuming log Gopakumar–Vafa invariants are always integers without checking the log integrality conjecture; counterexamples exist for non‑saturated log structures.
  • Neglecting the log Green current condition in arithmetic intersection theory; ordinary Green currents do not satisfy the required logarithmic singularity along the boundary.
  • Treating log TC as ordinary TC of the underlying scheme; the log cyclotomic structure and the log Nygaard filtration are essential for the comparison with log prismatic cohomology.

Logarithmic Fukaya Categories and Logarithmic Symplectic Geometry

The logarithmic Fukaya category Fuk(X, D) of a log Calabi–Yau pair (X, D) with D a normal crossing divisor is constructed by equipping the Fukaya category of the complement X D with a wrapping structure controlled by the log structure. Objects are exact Lagrangian branes L ⊂ X D with boundary on the divisor at infinity, graded by the log canonical bundle KX + D. The log wrapping Hamiltonian is chosen to be compatible with the log symplectic form ωlog = ω + d log |sD|2, where sD is a defining section of D. Morphism spaces are generated by intersection points weighted by counts of log holomorphic disks with boundary on the Lagrangians and interior punctures mapping to the divisor strata. The log A∞ structure satisfies the log Maurer–Cartan equation, where the curvature term records the log disk potential. For a log toric variety (X, D) with moment polytope Δ, the log Fukaya category is quasi-equivalent to the category of matrix factorizations of the log Landau–Ginzburg potential Wlog = Σi zvi on the log mirror (X∨, D∨), where vi are the primitive normal vectors to the facets of Δ. The log closed-open string map factors through the log quantum cohomology QHlog•(X, D), which carries a log quantum product deformed by log Gromov–Witten invariants with tangency conditions along D. The log Seidel representation π1(Hamlog(X, ω)) → Aut(Fuklog(X, D)) is constructed using log Hamiltonian isotopies preserving the log structure. In the case of a log K3 surface (X, D) with D an anti-canonical cycle of rational curves, the log Fukaya category is expected to be equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the mirror log K3 surface, realizing log homological mirror symmetry. The log wrapped Fukaya category admits a log cyclic symmetry, and its log Hochschild homology is isomorphic to the log quantum cohomology via the log closed-open map. Applications include the computation of log Gromov–Witten invariants of log Fano varieties via log mirror symmetry and the construction of log categorical enumerative invariants for log Calabi–Yau 3-folds.

Logarithmic Categorical Enumerative Geometry and the Logarithmic DT/PT Correspondence

Logarithmic Donaldson–Thomas theory assigns invariants to a log Calabi–Yau 3-fold (X, D) by counting stable log maps from log curves to (X, D) with prescribed contact orders along D. The log DT invariants DTlog(β, k) are defined as the weighted Euler characteristic of the moduli stack Mlog(X, D; β, k) of log stable maps of class β with contact order vector k along the divisor components. The log PT invariants PTlog(β, k) count stable pairs (F, s) where F is a pure 1-dimensional sheaf on X with log structure along D and s: OX(−D) → F is a section with 0-dimensional cokernel. The log DT/PT correspondence asserts that the generating series of log DT and log PT invariants are related by a universal log wall-crossing formula: Σ DTlog(β, k) qβ yk = M(q, y) ⋅ Σ PTlog(β, k) qβ yk, where M(q, y) is the log MacMahon function encoding contributions from log ideal sheaves supported on the divisor strata. The proof uses the log Joyce–Song wall-crossing formula in the log Hall algebra of the log category of coherent sheaves on (X, D). The log Hall algebra Hlog(X, D) is the algebra of constructible functions on the moduli stack of log coherent sheaves, with product given by log extensions. The log integration map Ilog: Hlog(X, D) → Q[[q, y]] sends a log sheaf to its log DT invariant. The log DT/PT correspondence follows from the identity Ilog([MlogDT]) = Ilog([MlogPT] ⋆ [Mlogideal]) in the log quantum torus, where ⋆ is the log Hall product. For a log toric Calabi–Yau 3-fold (X, D) with toric diagram Δ, the log DT invariants are computed by the log topological vertex, a combinatorial formula summing over 3D partitions with asymptotic boundary conditions determined by the log structure. The log PT invariants are computed by the log Pandharipande–Thomas vertex, which counts log stable pairs on the toric log Calabi–Yau. The log DT/PT correspondence for log toric Calabi–Yau 3-folds reduces to an identity of symmetric functions involving log skew Schur functions. The log categorical DT invariants are defined as the cohomology of the log DT moduli stack with coefficients in the log vanishing cycle complex φlog(W), where W is the log Chern–Simons functional on the log derived moduli stack. The log categorical DT/PT correspondence is an equivalence of log dg-categories between the log DT category and the log PT category, induced by a log spherical twist functor associated to the log structure sheaf OD.

Worked Computation: Log DT Invariants of the Log Resolved Conifold
Let (X, D) be the log resolved conifold: X = Tot(Oℙ1(−1) ⊕ Oℙ1(−1)) with D the union of the zero section ℙ1 and the divisor at infinity. Compute the log DT invariant DTlog(d[ℙ1], k) for degree d = 1 and contact order k = (1, 1) along the two divisor components.
The moduli space Mlog(X, D; [ℙ1], (1,1)) parametrizes log stable maps f: (C, p1, p2) → (X, D) where C ≅ ℙ1, f∗[C] = [ℙ1], and f has contact order 1 at p1 with the zero section and contact order 1 at p2 with the divisor at infinity. Such a map is uniquely determined by the image of C, which must be a fiber of the projection X → ℙ1 intersecting both divisor components transversely. The space of such fibers is ℙ1 itself. The log virtual dimension is vdim = ∫[ℙ1] c1(TX(−log D)) + (1+1) − 3 = 0 + 2 − 3 = −1. However, the log obstruction theory has a 1-dimensional obstruction space coming from the log structure, so the log virtual class is a 0-cycle. The log DT invariant is the weighted Euler characteristic of this 0-cycle with Behrend function weights. The log Behrend function νlog is constant −1 on the moduli space because the log obstruction theory is symmetric. The moduli space is isomorphic to ℙ1 with its log structure, which has log Euler characteristic χlog(ℙ1) = 2. Therefore DTlog([ℙ1], (1,1)) = −χlog(ℙ1) = −2. This matches the log topological vertex computation: the log vertex for the resolved conifold with boundary conditions (1,1) gives −2.
Exam Strategy: Log DT/PT Correspondence
When a question asks for the log DT/PT correspondence, write the generating series identity with the log MacMahon function. Remember that the log MacMahon function M(q, y) = ∏n≥1 (1 − qn y)−n ∏m≥1 (1 − qm y−1)−m encodes log ideal sheaves on the divisor. For log toric Calabi–Yau 3-folds, cite the log topological vertex and log PT vertex as computational tools. The key mechanism is the log Hall algebra and log Joyce–Song wall-crossing; mention the log integration map Ilog and the log quantum torus. Do not confuse the log DT/PT correspondence with the ordinary DT/PT correspondence — the log version has contact order vectors k and the log MacMahon function depends on both q and y.

Logarithmic Factorization Homology and Logarithmic Topological Field Theories

Logarithmic factorization homology ∫M A of a log En-algebra A over a log n-manifold M is the colimit of the log factorization diagram indexed by the log Ran space Ranlog(M). The log Ran space parametrizes finite non-empty subsets of M with a log structure recording collisions along the boundary strata. For a log En-algebra A in a symmetric monoidal ∞-category C, the log factorization homology satisfies log excision: if M = M1 ∪N M2 is a log decomposition along a log (n−1)-manifold N, then ∫M A ≃ ∫M1 A ⊗∫N A ∫M2 A. The log En-algebra structure on the log Hochschild cochains HHlog•(X, D) of a log Calabi–Yau pair (X, D) is constructed using the log Fukaya category: the log E2-structure comes from the log pair-of-pants product on log wrapped Floer cohomology. The log factorization homology of HHlog•(X, D) over a log surface Σ computes the log Fukaya category of the log symplectic manifold (X, D) × Σ with appropriate boundary conditions. A log topological field theory Zlog: Bordnlog → C is a symmetric monoidal functor from the log bordism ∞-category to C. The log bordism category has objects closed log (n−1)-manifolds and morphisms log n-manifolds with corners. The log cobordism hypothesis classifies log TFTs by fully dualizable objects in C equipped with a log SO(n)-action. For a log Calabi–Yau n-fold (X, D), the log Fukaya category Fuklog(X, D) is a fully dualizable object in the ∞-category of log A∞-categories, and the associated log TFT ZFuk assigns to a log n-manifold M the log factorization homology ∫M Fuklog(X, D). The log TFT partition function on a closed log n-manifold M is the log Hochschild homology HHlog•(∫M Fuklog(X, D)). In dimension 2, the log TFT associated to a log Calabi–Yau surface (X, D) computes the log Gromov–Witten invariants of (X, D) via the log closed-open map. The log factorization homology of the log E2-algebra of log coherent sheaves Cohlog(X, D) over a log curve C computes the log derived category of the log mapping stack Maplog(C, (X, D)). This provides a categorical framework for the log geometric Langlands correspondence: the log Hecke eigensheaves are constructed as log factorization homology of the log spherical Hecke category over the log curve.

Logarithmic Microlocal Sheaf Theory and Logarithmic Singular Support

The logarithmic microlocal sheaf theory on a log manifold (X, MX) studies sheaves on the log cotangent bundle T∗logX with singular support contained in the log conormal variety. The log cotangent bundle is the vector bundle associated to the log cotangent sheaf Ω1X/log = Ω1X(log D), where D is the divisor defined by the log structure. The log singular support SSlog(F) of a constructible sheaf F on X is a closed conical log Lagrangian subset of T∗logX, defined as the complement of the set of log covectors (x, ξ) where F is locally constant in the log microlocal sense. The log microlocalization functor μlog: Shc(X) → Shc(T∗logX) sends F to its log microlocal stalk along the log conormal directions. The log microsupport satisfies the log Kashiwara–Schapira estimate: SSlog(F ⊗L G) ⊂ SSlog(F) + SSlog(G) and SSlog(Rf!F) ⊂ fπ(fd−1SSlog(F)) for a log morphism f: X → Y. The log Nadler–Zaslow correspondence establishes an equivalence between the derived category of constructible sheaves on a log Weinstein manifold (X, D) with log singular support in the log Lagrangian skeleton Λlog and the wrapped log Fukaya category Fuklog(X, D). The log skeleton Λlog is the union of the log core and the log conormal bundles to the divisor strata. The log microlocal monodromy along the divisor D is encoded in the log Stokes data of the sheaf, which matches the log wrapping in the Fukaya category. For a log holonomic Dlog-module M on (X, D), the log characteristic variety Chlog(M) is a log Lagrangian subvariety of T∗logX, and the log Riemann–Hilbert correspondence identifies M with a constructible sheaf whose log singular support is Chlog(M). The log microlocal Euler characteristic χlog(F) = Σ (−1)i dim Hilog(X, F) is computed by the log microlocal index formula: χlog(F) = ∫T∗logX CClog(F) ⋅ Tdlog(TlogX), where CClog(F) is the log characteristic cycle and Tdlog is the log Todd class. The log characteristic cycle is a log Lagrangian cycle on T∗logX representing the log singular support with multiplicities given by the log microlocal multiplicities. The log microlocal sheaf theory provides the categorical foundation for the log geometric Langlands program: log Hecke eigensheaves are log microlocal sheaves on the log moduli stack of G-bundles with log singular support on the log spectral variety.

Logarithmic Categorical Mirror Symmetry for Logarithmic Landau–Ginzburg Models

Logarithmic categorical mirror symmetry relates the log Fukaya–Seidel category FSlog(X, D, W) of a log Landau–Ginzburg model (X, D, W) to the log matrix factorization category MFlog(X∨, D∨, W∨) of the mirror log Landau–Ginzburg model. Here (X, D) is a log Calabi–Yau pair, W: X → 𝔸1 is a log regular function with log critical locus Critlog(W) proper over 𝔸1, and the log Fukaya–Seidel category has objects graded log Lagrangian branes with boundary on the log fiber W−1(t) for t ≫ 0. The log wrapping is controlled by the log Liouville form λlog = λ + d log |W|2. The log matrix factorization category MFlog(X∨, D∨, W∨) consists of log coherent sheaves E on X∨ with a log endomorphism dE: E → E ⊗ OX∨(D∨) satisfying dE2 = W∨ ⋅ idE. The log mirror functor Φlog: FSlog(X, D, W) → MFlog(X∨, D∨, W∨) is constructed by associating to a log Lagrangian brane L its log Floer cohomology with the log thimble, which carries a log matrix factorization structure via the log open-closed map. The log closed-open map COlog: QHlog•(X, D) → HHlog•(FSlog(X, D, W)) is a map of log BV-algebras, where the log quantum cohomology QHlog•(X, D) carries the log quantum product and the log BV operator Δlog counts log holomorphic disks with one interior marked point. The log open-closed map OClog: HHlog•(FSlog(X, D, W)) → QHlog•(X, D) is the log trace map. The log categorical mirror symmetry conjecture asserts that Φlog is an equivalence of log A∞-categories. For a log toric Landau–Ginzburg model (X, D, W) with moment polytope Δ and log superpotential W = Σ zvi, the mirror is the log Landau–Ginzburg model on the log toric variety X∨ with log superpotential W∨ = Σ yi zvi. The log mirror functor is computed by the log tropical vertex: the log thimble associated to a tropical disk in Δ corresponds to a log matrix factorization given by a log Koszul complex. The log Hochschild homology of FSlog(X, D, W) is isomorphic to the log Jacobian ring Jaclog(W) = OX(log D) / (∂logW), where ∂logW are the log partial derivatives. The log categorical mirror symmetry implies the log Hori–Vafa mirror symmetry for log Gromov–Witten invariants: the log I-function of (X, D, W) matches the log period integral of the mirror log Landau–Ginzburg model. The log categorical mirror symmetry for log Landau–Ginzburg models with non-isolated log critical loci is formulated using the log singularity category Dsg,log(X, W) = Dblog(X) / Perflog(X), which is equivalent to the log matrix factorization category MFlog(X, W) by the log Orlov equivalence.
