Derived Autoequivalences and Their Action on the Stability Manifold

One of the most powerful tools for probing the geometry of the space of stability conditions Stab(D) is the group of exact autoequivalences Aut(D) of the underlying triangulated category D. For a Calabi‑Yau category of dimension d, each autoequivalence Φ induces a biholomorphic map

Φ∗: Stab(D) → Stab(D), Φ∗(Z, 𝒫) = (Z ∘ Φ⁻¹, Φ(𝒫)).

The image of the central charge under Φ is obtained by pre‑composing with the induced map on the numerical Grothendieck group Knum(D). When D is the derived category of coherent sheaves on a smooth projective variety X, the standard generators of Aut(D) are:

  1. Shifts: [1] acts trivially on the central charge but rotates the slicing 𝒫 by one unit.
  2. Tensor by line bundles: ⊗ L for L∈Pic(X) changes the central charge by Z(E)↦Z(E⊗L). On a K3 surface, the Mukai vector v(E) transforms by v(E)↦v(E)·exp(c₁(L)).
  3. Spherical twists: For a spherical object S (i.e. Hom⁎(S,S)=ℂ⊕ℂ[−d]), the twist TS is defined by the exact triangle Hom⁎(S,E)⊗S → E → TS(E) → . The induced action on Knum is the reflection v↦v−⟨v,v(S)⟩v(S), where ⟨·,·⟩ is the Euler pairing. This mirrors the Weyl group action on the root lattice of the associated ADE quiver.
  4. Fourier–Mukai transforms: Any equivalence Φ: D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh X) → D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh Y) is given by a kernel 𝒦∈D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh X×Y). The induced map on K‑theory is v↦πY∗(πX⁎v·ch(𝒦)·td(TX)). For abelian varieties, the standard Poincaré line bundle yields the classical Fourier–Mukai involution, which exchanges the complex and Kähler parameters in the central charge.

These actions generate a discrete subgroup Γ⊂Aut(D) that often acts properly discontinuously on a connected component of Stab(D). The quotient ΓStab(D) can be identified with a moduli space of “geometric” stability conditions. For example, on a generic K3 surface, Bridgeland proved that the distinguished component Stab⁰(D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh X)) is a covering of the period domain ℙ⁺(H̃⁎(X,ℂ)) \ ⋃δ⊥, where δ runs over (−2)‑classes. The deck transformation group is precisely the subgroup generated by spherical twists in the (−2)‑classes, i.e. the Weyl group of the Mukai lattice.

In practice, exam‑level problems ask candidates to compute the effect of a given autoequivalence on a known stability condition. A typical scenario: start with the “large volume limit” central charge ZLV(E)=−∫Xe−iω}ch(E)√tdX, apply a spherical twist TS and determine the new heart. The answer hinges on recognizing that TS sends the standard heart Coh(X) to the tilt heart generated by Coh(X) and S[1]. The resulting slicing often lies on a wall where objects of class v(S) become semistable, illustrating the intimate link between autoequivalences and wall‑crossing.

Stability Conditions for Quivers with Superpotentials and the Role of Non‑Commutative Donaldson‑Thomas Theory

Quivers equipped with a potential W (a cyclic linear combination of oriented cycles) give rise to 3‑Calabi‑Yau (3‑CY) categories via the Ginzburg differential graded algebra Γ(Q,W). The derived category D(Γ) carries a natural t‑structure whose heart is the category of finite‑dimensional modules over the Jacobian algebra J(Q,W)=H⁰(Γ). Bridgeland stability on D(Γ) can be described explicitly in terms of King’s θ‑stability for representations of (Q,W). The central charge is a group homomorphism

Z: K₀(J(Q,W)) → ℂ, Z(α)=∑i ziαi,

where the complex numbers zi lie in the upper half‑plane and encode a choice of stability parameters (θ, φ). An object M is Z‑stable iff for every proper submodule N⊂M one has arg Z(N) < arg Z(M). This recovers the usual notion of θ‑stability when all zi have the same modulus.

The non‑commutative Donaldson‑Thomas (ncDT) invariants of (Q,W) are defined by counting Z‑semistable objects in D(Γ) with fixed class γ∈K₀(J(Q,W)). Kontsevich–Soibelman showed that the generating series

A(γ)=∑n≥0Ω(γ,n) qⁿ

obeys the quantum dilogarithm identity

∏γ∈Δ⁺𝔈(−q½xγ)Ω(γ) = 1,

where Δ⁺ is the set of positive roots of the associated Kac–Moody algebra and 𝔈 denotes the quantum dilogarithm. The wall‑crossing formula for ncDT invariants is precisely the Kontsevich–Soibelman factorization, and the “BPS invariants” Ω(γ) are integers counting stable representations.

Several concrete examples appear in exam questions:

  • For the A₂ quiver with potential W=0, the Jacobian algebra is just the path algebra kQ. The stability space is two‑dimensional; walls are given by lines arg z₁=arg z₂. The ncDT invariant Ω(α₁+α₂)=1, reflecting the unique indecomposable representation of dimension (1,1).
  • For the conifold quiver (two vertices, four arrows, superpotential W=ab‑cd), the Jacobian algebra is the non‑commutative crepant resolution of the conifold singularity. The central charge can be chosen so that the wall‑crossing reproduces the Pandharipande‑Thomas invariants of the resolved conifold. The BPS spectrum consists of an infinite tower Ω(k·δ)=1 for the primitive class δ, encoding the D0‑D2 bound states.

In a competitive exam, a typical problem asks to compute the change in Ω(γ) when the stability parameters cross a wall defined by a short exact sequence 0→M₁→M→M₂→0. The answer follows from the “wall‑crossing product”:

𝔈(−xγ₁)Ω(γ₁) · 𝔈(−xγ₂)Ω(γ₂) = 𝔈(−xγ₂)Ω'(γ₂) · 𝔈(−xγ₁)Ω'(γ₁) · 𝔈(−xγ₁+γ₂)Ω'(γ₁+γ₂).

Understanding this identity and being able to read off the new invariants Ω' from a given quiver diagram is a decisive skill for high‑level problem solving.

Technique: Translating a wall in the stability space to a short exact sequence
Consider the A₃ quiver 1→2→3 with zero potential. Let the stability parameters be (z₁,z₂,z₃) with arg z₁

At the wall arg z₂=arg z₃ the objects of class (0,1,1) become semistable. The indecomposable representation of dimension (1,1,1) fits into the exact sequence

0 → S₁ → M → S₂⊕S₃ → 0,

where Sᵢ denotes the simple at vertex i. Since S₂ and S₃ have the same phase, they can combine to form a strictly semistable object S₂⊕S₃. The wall‑crossing formula yields

Ω'(1,1,1)=Ω(1,1,1)+Ω(1,0,0)·Ω(0,1,1)=1+1·1=2.

Thus after crossing the wall there are two stable objects: the original indecomposable and the extension of S₁ by S₂⊕S₃.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question involves a quiver with potential, first write down the Jacobian algebra and identify the simples. Then list the possible dimension vectors up to the total class asked. Sketch the stability half‑plane: order the arguments of the central charges. Any time two arguments coincide, a wall appears; use the short exact sequence picture to compute the change in BPS invariants via the Kontsevich–Soibelman product. Keeping a small table of Ω values for simple roots saves time.

Bridgeland Stability on Non‑Compact Calabi‑Yau Threefolds via Tilting and Perverse Sheaves

For a non‑compact Calabi‑Yau threefold Y, such as the total space of the canonical bundle KS over a smooth projective surface S, the derived category D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh Y) does not admit a bounded t‑structure coming from Coh(Y) alone, because Coh(Y) is not Noetherian. The standard remedy is to use a tilting construction that produces a heart 𝒜t consisting of perverse coherent sheaves relative to the projection π:Y→S. Concretely, define

𝒜t = {E∈D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh Y) | H⁰(π_*E)∈Coh(S), H⁻¹(π_*E)∈Coh(S), Hⁱ(π_*E)=0 for i≠0,−1}.

This heart fits into a torsion pair (𝒯,𝔽) on Coh(Y) with 𝒯={sheaves supported in dimension ≤1} and 𝔽={torsion‑free sheaves of dimension 2 or 3}. The tilt 𝒜t

The central charge is taken to be

Zω,B(E)=−∫_Y e−(B+iω)·ch(E)·√td_Y,

where ω is a Kähler form pulled back from S and B∈H²(Y,ℝ) is a B‑field. Because Y is non‑compact, the integral is interpreted via compactly supported cohomology; the contribution from the fiber direction reduces to a factor of the volume of the line ℂ. The support property holds with respect to the lattice Knum(Y)≅Knum(S)⊕ℤ·[𝒪_Y], and the quadratic form Q(α)=|Z(α)|²−C·‖α‖² can be chosen using the Bogomolov–Gieseker inequality on S.

One of the most celebrated applications is the computation of Donaldson‑Thomas invariants for the resolved conifold X=Tot(𝒪ℙ¹(−1)⊕𝒪ℙ¹(−1)). The tilting heart 𝒜t coincides with the category of “perverse coherent sheaves” introduced by Bridgeland. The wall‑crossing from the large volume limit to the “orbifold point” reproduces the generating function

∑n,d DTn,d qⁿ tᵈ = M(−q)χ(ℙ¹) · ∏k≥1(1−(−q)kt)k,

where M(q) is the MacMahon function. The factorization reflects the infinite series of spherical twists around the exceptional ℙ¹, each twist corresponding to a wall where a D2‑brane wrapping the ℙ¹ becomes marginally stable.

Exam‑level questions often ask candidates to justify why the perverse heart satisfies the Harder–Narasimhan property for the chosen central charge. The key steps are:

  1. Show that any object E∈𝒜t admits a finite filtration whose successive quotients are either torsion sheaves supported on curves (phase determined by ω·[C]) or torsion‑free sheaves of rank ≥1 (phase determined by the slope μω,B).
  2. Use the Bogomolov–Gieseker inequality on S to bound the discriminant Δ(E) and thereby control the imaginary part of Z.
  3. Verify the support property by constructing a quadratic form Q that dominates |Z|² on the image of Knum(Y).

These arguments illustrate how non‑compact geometry forces a blend of algebraic and analytic techniques, a theme that frequently appears in advanced problem sets.

Stability Conditions in the Context of the Gross–Siebert Program and Mirror Symmetry for Log Calabi‑Yau Pairs

The Gross–Siebert program aims to construct mirrors of log Calabi‑Yau (log CY) pairs (X,D) by means of tropical and toric degenerations. A crucial intermediate object is the “scattering diagram” Σ in the real vector space Nℝ, whose walls encode counts of rational curves meeting the boundary divisor D. Kontsevich–Soibelman showed that a consistent scattering diagram gives rise to a formal deformation of the algebra of functions on the mirror torus, and the wall‑crossing automorphisms are precisely the quantum dilogarithms attached to BPS invariants.

Bridgeland stability enters the picture through the derived category D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh X) equipped with a “log” central charge

Zlog(E)=−∫_X e−(B+iω)·ch(E)·√td_X · ∏i=1r(1−e−D_i),

where D=∑D_i is the normal crossings boundary. The factor ∏(1−e−D_i) forces objects supported on the boundary to have smaller phase, mirroring the tropical picture where broken lines stop upon hitting a wall.

In the simplest case of (ℙ², line L), the scattering diagram consists of three rays emanating from the origin, each labeled by the count of lines meeting L. The associated stability condition has a heart generated by the line bundle 𝒪ℙ² and the skyscraper sheaf 𝒪_L[1]. The central charge values are

Z(𝒪ℙ²)=−(B+iω)³/6, Z(𝒪_L[1])=−(B+iω)·[L].

Crossing a wall where arg Z(𝒪_L[1])=arg Z(𝒪ℙ²) corresponds to a mutation in the scattering diagram: the ray associated to L is replaced by a new ray reflecting the count of rational curves of degree 2 meeting L twice. The resulting wall‑crossing automorphism matches the cluster transformation of the mirror Landau‑Ginzburg potential.

For higher‑dimensional log CY pairs, the same mechanism produces a family of stability conditions parametrised by the Kähler cone of X together with “log” parameters controlling the contribution of each component of D. The support property is verified using the log version of the Bogomolov–Gieseker inequality proved by Bayer–Macrí for pairs (X,D). Moreover, the space Stablog(X) often fibres over the secondary fan of the toric degeneration, and the monodromy of this fibration recovers the integral affine structure on the base of the SYZ fibration.

In exams, a common task is to identify the wall in Stablog(X) that corresponds to a given tropical mutation. The answer requires matching the change in the central charge of a boundary sheaf with the slope of the corresponding ray in the scattering diagram. Mastery of this correspondence demonstrates a deep integration of stability theory, enumerative geometry, and mirror symmetry.

Bridgeland Stability for Derived Categories of Stacks and the Role of Inertia

When the underlying space is a Deligne–Mumford stack 𝔛, the derived category D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh 𝔛) carries extra information coming from the inertia stack I𝔛, which records automorphism groups of points. The numerical Grothendieck group Knum(𝔛) splits as a direct sum

Knum(𝔛) ≅ Knum(X) ⊕ ⊕g≠1 Knum(𝔛_g),

where X is the coarse moduli space and 𝔛_g denotes the component of the inertia fixed by an element g of the generic stabiliser. Consequently, a central charge Z must assign complex numbers to each twisted sector.

For a global quotient stack [Y/G] with Y smooth projective and G finite, the central charge can be written as

Z(E)=−∑[g] ∫Yg e−(B+iω)·ch_g(E)·√tdYg·(1)/(|C(g)|),

where the sum runs over conjugacy classes [g]⊂G, Yg is the fixed locus, ch_g is the equivariant Chern character, and C(g) is the centraliser. The factor 1/|C(g)| reflects the contribution of the inertia.

Stability conditions on D⁽ᵇ⁾(Coh [ℙ¹/μ_r]) provide a concrete illustration. The stack has r twisted sectors corresponding to the μ_r‑gerbe at the two orbifold points. The heart 𝒜 can be taken as the extension‑closure of the line bundles 𝒪(k) together with the skyscraper sheaves supported at the orbifold points, shifted by one. The central charge assigns

Z(𝒪(k))=−(B+iω)·(k+½), Z(𝒪p_i[1])=−(B+iω)·θ_i,

where θ_i∈(0,1) encodes the age grading of the i‑th twisted sector. Walls occur when a linear combination a·Z(𝒪(k))+b·Z(𝒪p_i[1]) has zero imaginary part, leading to explicit rational slopes a/b that can be tabulated.

From the perspective of Donaldson‑Thomas theory, the motivic Hall algebra of 𝔛 incorporates the inertia by adjoining variables x[g],α for each class α in Knum(𝔛_g). The integration map to the quantum torus then involves the orbifold Euler characteristic χorb(𝔛), which equals the usual Euler characteristic of the coarse space divided by |G| plus contributions from the twisted sectors. The resulting orbifold DT invariants satisfy a modified wall‑crossing formula where the quantum dilogarithm is replaced by its “orbifold” version 𝔈orb(x)=∏m≥1(1−xm)−1/m raised to the age grading.

Exam questions may ask to compute the central charge for a given stacky line bundle or to describe the wall structure for a simple global quotient. The decisive step is to keep track of the age shifts and the normalisation by the order of the stabiliser; overlooking these leads to incorrect phase calculations and loss of marks.

  • Confusing the numerical Grothendieck group of a stack with that of its coarse space; the inertia contribution is essential.
  • Omitting the age grading when writing the central charge for twisted sectors, which changes the argument of Z.
  • Assuming the support property automatically holds for non‑compact Calabi‑Yau threefolds without checking the Bogomolov–Gieseker inequality on the base surface.
  • Treating spherical twists as commuting operations; in general they satisfy braid relations that affect wall‑crossing.
  • Applying the standard Kontsevich–Soibelman factorization to quivers with potential without first verifying the 3‑CY condition of the Ginzburg algebra.
  • Neglecting the monodromy of the Dubrovin connection when relating quantum DT invariants to mirror symmetry, leading to wrong transformation rules.
  • Using the ordinary MacMahon function for orbifold DT invariants; the correct generating series involves the orbifold quantum dilogarithm.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi‑Yau Threefolds with Non‑Trivial B‑Field and the Twisted DT/PT Correspondence

A B‑field is a closed two‑form B ∈ H²(X, ℝ/ℤ) on a Calabi‑Yau threefold X. It twists the derived category Dᵇ(Coh X) by modifying the Chern character to chᴮ(E) = eᴮ · ch(E) and the Mukai pairing accordingly. The twisted central charge becomes Zᴮ(E) = −∫ₓ e⁻⁽ᴮ⁺ⁱᵠ⁾ · ch(E) · √td(X), where ω is the Kähler form. Bridgeland stability conditions on the twisted category depend on the pair (B, ω) modulo the action of the integral cohomology H²(X, ℤ) shifting B by integral classes. The space Stabᴮ(X) fibres over the complexified Kähler cone with fibre the set of stability conditions for a fixed B‑field. Wall‑crossing in Stabᴮ(X) is governed by the same Kontsevich‑Soibelman factorization, but the BPS invariants Ωᴮ(γ) now count twisted semistable objects. The twisted DT/PT correspondence relates the generating series of twisted DT invariants DTᴮ(β, n) to twisted Pandharipande‑Thomas invariants PTᴮ(β, n) via the same rational function identity DTᴮ = PTᴮ · M(−q)ᵡ⁽ˣ⁾, where M(q) is the MacMahon function and χ(X) the topological Euler characteristic. The proof uses the twisted motivic Hall algebra of Joyce‑Song, where the integration map lands in a quantum torus with commutation relations xᵅ xᵝ = (−q)ᵡ⁽ᵅ,ᵝ⁾ xᵝ xᵅ and the pairing χᴮ(α, β) = χ(α, β) + ∫ₓ B · (ch₁(α) ch₂(β) − ch₂(α) ch₁(β)). For local Calabi‑Yau threefolds such as the resolved conifold, the B‑field can be absorbed into a shift of the Kähler parameter, but for compact X with non‑trivial H²(X, ℤ) the twisted theory is genuinely new. Exam questions often ask to compute the twisted central charge for a given B‑field and to identify the wall where a twisted stable pair becomes unstable. The key step is to expand chᴮ(E) = ch(E) + B · ch₁(E) + ½ B² · ch₀(E) + … and track the imaginary part of Zᴮ(E). Overlooking the B² term for sheaves with non‑zero rank leads to incorrect phase calculations.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps to Varieties with Non‑Trivial Fundamental Group and the DT Invariants for Local Systems

When the target variety X has non‑trivial fundamental group π₁(X), the moduli space of stable maps M̄g,₀(X, β) carries a natural local system ℒ_ρ associated to a representation ρ: π₁(X) → GL(r, ℂ). The DT invariants for local systems are defined by integrating the Behrend function weighted by the trace of the monodromy of ℒ_ρ over the virtual fundamental class. In the categorical framework, one considers the derived category Dᵇ(Coh(M̄g,₀(X, β), ℒ_ρ)) of coherent sheaves twisted by the local system. A stability condition on this category requires a central charge Z: K₀(M̄g,₀(X, β), ℒ_ρ) → ℂ that factors through the twisted Chern character ch^ρ. The heart of the t‑structure is the extension‑closure of twisted stable maps with fixed monodromy data. Wall‑crossing for these invariants is controlled by a generalized Kontsevich‑Soibelman formula where the quantum dilogarithm is replaced by its “monodromy‑twisted” version 𝔈_ρ(x) = ∏k≥1 (1 − ρ(γ) xᵏ)⁻¹ for each class γ ∈ π₁(X). The DT/GW correspondence for local systems states that the generating series of twisted DT invariants equals the twisted Gromov‑Witten potential after the change of variables q = eⁱᵘ. For X a K3 surface with a non‑trivial π₁ (e.g., an Enriques surface), the twisted DT invariants recover the Donaldson invariants of the universal cover via the orbifold correspondence. A concrete computational example: let X be a quintic threefold with a free ℤ/5 action, so π₁(X) = ℤ/5. The local system ℒ_ρ for a non‑trivial character ρ: ℤ/5 → ℂ× gives twisted DT invariants DT^ρ(β, n) that satisfy a wall‑crossing formula with quantum dilogarithms 𝔈(x) replaced by 𝔈_ρ(x) = ∏m≥1 (1 − ρ(1) xᵐ)⁻¹. The support property is verified using the twisted Bogomolov‑Gieseker inequality proved by Toda for local systems on projective varieties. In exams, a typical task is to write the twisted central charge for a given local system on a curve and to determine the walls where the phase of a twisted stable map crosses that of a twisted line bundle. The critical point is to remember that the twisted Chern character ch^ρ(E) = ch(E) ⊗ ρ lives in H*(X, ℒ_ρ ⊗ ℒ_ρ∨) and that the pairing involves the trace of the monodromy.

Worked Example: Twisted Central Charge on an Enriques Surface
Let X be an Enriques surface with π₁(X) = ℤ/2, and let ρ be the non‑trivial character. Consider the twisted sheaf E = 𝒪_X ⊕ 𝒪_X(−K_X) with the ℤ/2‑action swapping the summands. Compute the twisted central charge Z^ρ(E) for B = 0, ω = H an ample divisor, and explain why the phase of E differs from the untwisted case.
The twisted Chern character is ch^ρ(E) = ch(𝒪_X) ⊗ 1 + ch(𝒪_X(−K_X)) ⊗ ρ(1). Since ρ(1) = −1, we have ch^ρ(E) = (1, 0, 1) + (1, −K_X, ½ K_X²) ⊗ (−1) = (0, K_X, 1 − ½ K_X²). On an Enriques surface K_X is 2‑torsion with K_X² = 0, so ch^ρ(E) = (0, K_X, 1). The central charge is Z^ρ(E) = −∫ₓ e⁻ⁱᴴ · ch^ρ(E) = −∫ₓ (1 − iH − ½ H²) · (0, K_X, 1) = −(∫ₓ K_X · H − i ∫ₓ H²). Since K_X is numerically trivial, ∫ₓ K_X · H = 0, so Z^ρ(E) = i ∫ₓ H². The phase is φ(E) = ½. In the untwisted case ch(E) = (2, −K_X, 1 + ½ K_X²) = (2, 0, 1), giving Z(E) = −∫ₓ (1 − iH − ½ H²) · (2, 0, 1) = −(2 − ½ ∫ₓ H²) + i ∫ₓ H², whose phase is arctan(∫ₓ H² / (½ ∫ₓ H² − 2)) ≠ ½. The twist by ρ changes the rank from 2 to 0, shifting the phase to the maximal value. This illustrates how local systems can create new stable objects that are unstable in the untwisted theory.
Exam Strategy: Twisted DT Invariants
When a question mentions a non‑trivial fundamental group or a local system, immediately write down the twisted Chern character ch^ρ = ch ⊗ ρ and the twisted pairing χ^ρ(α, β) = χ(α, β) with monodromy trace. The wall‑crossing formula uses the twisted quantum dilogarithm 𝔈_ρ(x) = ∏ (1 − tr(ρ(γ)) xᵏ)⁻¹. For a free quotient X = Y/G, the twisted DT invariants on X equal the G‑invariant part of the DT invariants on Y. Always check whether the support property is cited (Toda’s twisted BG inequality) — this is a frequent mark‑earning point.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi‑Yau Threefolds with Boundary Conditions Given by Coisotropic Branes and the Open‑Closed DT Correspondence

Coisotropic branes are D‑branes wrapping a coisotropic submanifold C ⊂ X with a Chan‑Paton bundle V and a non‑degenerate two‑form F on C such that ω|_C + F has constant rank. In the derived category, they correspond to objects in the Fukaya category Fuk(X) that are not Lagrangian. The open‑closed DT correspondence relates the generating series of open DT invariants counting stable pairs with boundary on C to the closed DT invariants of X via a wall‑crossing formula in the extended stability manifold Stab^ext(X) that includes both closed and open sectors. The central charge for an open‑closed object (E, ∂E) is Z(E, ∂E) = Z_closed(E) + Z_open(∂E), where Z_open(∂E) = −∫_C e⁻⁽ᴮ⁺ⁱᵠ⁾ · ch(∂E) · √td(C) and the boundary condition ∂E is a coherent sheaf on C twisted by the restriction of the B‑field. The heart of the t‑structure is the extension‑closure of closed stable pairs and open stable pairs with fixed boundary conditions. Walls occur when the phase of a closed object aligns with that of an open object, leading to a decay of the closed object into an open‑closed bound state. The wall‑crossing formula is a factorization in the extended quantum torus with generators x_γ for closed classes and y_δ for open classes, satisfying x_γ y_δ = (−q)⟨γ, δ⟩ y_δ x_γ where ⟨γ, δ⟩ is the open‑closed pairing. For the resolved conifold X = Tot(𝒪(−1)⊕𝒪(−1) → ℙ¹) with a coisotropic brane on the zero section ℙ¹, the open DT invariants count stable pairs on ℙ¹ with a framing given by the normal bundle. The generating series is the open topological string partition function Z_open = ∑d≥0 N_d q^d, where N_d are the open Gopakumar‑Vafa invariants. The open‑closed correspondence states Z_open = Z_closed1/2 · Z_brane, where Z_brane is the contribution of the coisotropic brane. In exams, a common question is to write the extended central charge for a given coisotropic brane and to identify the wall where a closed stable pair decays into an open‑closed bound state. The key is to compute the open‑closed pairing ⟨γ, δ⟩ = ∫_C ch₁(γ) · ch₀(δ) and to track the phase of Z_open relative to Z_closed.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps to Varieties with Non‑Trivial Hodge Structure and the Hodge‑Theoretic DT Invariants

For a projective variety X with non‑trivial Hodge structure, the DT invariants can be refined to Hodge‑theoretic DT invariants taking values in the Grothendieck ring of mixed Hodge structures K₀(MHS). The motivic Hall algebra of Joyce is replaced by the Hodge‑theoretic Hall algebra of Davison‑Meinhardt, where the integration map lands in a quantum torus over K₀(MHS). A stability condition in this setting is a pair (Z, 𝒫) where Z: K₀(Dᵇ(Coh X)) → ℂ is a central charge and 𝒫(φ) are subcategories of semistable objects of phase φ, but now the DT invariant DT(γ) is an element of K₀(MHS) rather than an integer. The wall‑crossing formula becomes an identity in the completed quantum torus over K₀(MHS) with the quantum dilogarithm replaced by its Hodge‑theoretic version 𝔈^H(x) = ∏k≥1 (1 − ℒk/2 x^k)⁻¹, where ℒ = [𝔸¹] is the Lefschetz motive. For a K3 surface X, the Hodge‑theoretic DT invariants of the Hilbert scheme of points X[n] are given by the Hodge numbers of the Hilbert scheme, which are known via Göttsche’s formula. The generating series ∑n≥0 DT^H(X[n]) q^n = ∏m≥1 (1 − ℒm/2 q^m)−χ(X). For a Calabi‑Yau threefold X, the Hodge‑theoretic DT invariants of the moduli space of stable sheaves M_σ(v) are conjecturally given by the cohomology of the perverse sheaf of vanishing cycles on the critical locus of the Chern‑Simons functional. The support property is verified using the Hodge‑theoretic Bogomolov‑Gieseker inequality proved by Bayer‑Macrì for varieties with a Hodge structure. In exams, a typical task is to compute the Hodge‑theoretic DT invariant for a simple sheaf on a K3 surface and to write the wall‑crossing formula in K₀(MHS). The critical step is to replace the integer Euler characteristic χ(M) with the Hodge‑Deligne polynomial E(M; u, v) and to remember that the quantum parameter q is replaced by ℒ1/2.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi‑Yau Threefolds with Non‑Trivial Algebraic Cycles and the DT Invariants for Algebraic Cycles

Algebraic cycles on a Calabi‑Yau threefold X give rise to a filtration on the numerical Grothendieck group K_num(X) by coniveau. The DT invariants for algebraic cycles are defined by restricting the integration map in the motivic Hall algebra to the subalgebra generated by classes supported on cycles of a given codimension. A stability condition for algebraic cycles is a central charge Z: K_num(X) → ℂ that factors through the cycle class map cl: K_num(X) → H2*(X, ℤ) and satisfies the support property with respect to the coniveau filtration. The heart of the t‑structure is the extension‑closure of sheaves whose support has a fixed coniveau. Wall‑crossing for these invariants is governed by a truncated Kontsevich‑Soibelman formula where the product runs only over classes γ with coniveau ≥ c. For X a quintic threefold, the coniveau 1 classes are those supported on curves, and the DT invariants for curves are the usual DT invariants of one‑dimensional sheaves. The coniveau 2 classes are supported on divisors, and their DT invariants are related to the DT invariants of surfaces via the DT/PT correspondence for divisors. The generating series of DT invariants for algebraic cycles of coniveau c is conjecturally a rational function in q with denominator ∏m≥1 (1 − q^m)χ_c(X), where χ_c(X) is the Euler characteristic of the c‑th coniveau piece. In exams, a common question is to describe the coniveau filtration on K_num(X) for a given threefold and to write the central charge for a sheaf supported on a divisor. The key is to use the cycle class map cl(E) = (ch₀(E), ch₁(E), ch₂(E), ch₃(E)) and to note that ch_i(E) = 0 for i < c if E has coniveau ≥ c. The support property then follows from the Hodge index theorem on the support of E.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi-Yau Threefolds with Non-Trivial Brauer Groups and the Twisted DT/PT Correspondence

A Brauer class α ∈ Br(X) on a Calabi-Yau threefold X twists the derived category Dᵇ(Coh(X, α)) of α-twisted coherent sheaves. The numerical Grothendieck group K_num(X, α) carries a twisted Mukai pairing ⟨γ, δ⟩_α = −∫_X ch(γ)ᵀ ch(δ) td(X) where the twisted Chern character ch^α = e^B ch for a B-field lift of α. The wall-crossing formula for twisted stability conditions involves the twisted Kontsevich-Soibelman product ∏φ 𝔈_α(x_γ)Ω_α(γ) where Ω_α(γ) are the twisted BPS invariants. In exams, a typical problem asks to write the twisted central charge Z_α(E) = −∫_X e−(B+iω) ch(E) √td(X) for an α-twisted sheaf E and to verify the support property using the twisted Bogomolov-Gieseker inequality Δ_α(E) = (ch₁^α(E))² − 2 ch₀^α(E) ch₂^α(E) ≥ 0.

Exam Strategy: Twisted vs Untwisted Computations
When a problem involves a B-field or Brauer class, always write ch^B = e^B ch explicitly before computing the central charge. The B² term contributes to ch₂^B and ch₃^B for rank ≥ 2 sheaves. Derived DT invariants incorporate the full derived structure of the moduli stack M_σ(v) rather than its truncation to a classical scheme. For a Calabi-Yau threefold X, the derived DT invariants of the Hilbert scheme of points X[n] are related to the cohomology of the derived Hilbert scheme: DT^der(n) = [X[n],der] ∈ K₀(dSt/ℂ). The derived DT/PT correspondence states that the derived generating series are related by the derived MacMahon function M^der(q) = ∏m≥1 (1 − ℒm/2 q^m)−m χ(X). For X = ℂ³, the derived DT invariants are computed via the derived vertex formalism: DT^der(n) = [Hilb^n(ℂ³)der] = coefficient of q^n in ∏m≥1 (1 − ℒm/2 q^m)−m. Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi-Yau Threefolds with Non-Trivial Categorical Symmetries and the Categorical DT/PT Correspondence

The categorical PT invariants PT^cat(β, n) are defined for the category of stable pairs in 𝒞. For the cluster category 𝒞_Q of a quiver Q with potential W, the categorical DT invariants are the cluster characters X_γ = ∑M χ(Gr(M)) xdim M where Gr(M) is the quiver Grassmannian. The categorical BPS invariants Ω^cat(γ) are the indecomposable objects in the heart of the categorical t-structure. In exams, a typical problem is to compute the categorical DT invariant for the Kronecker quiver with two arrows: the category of representations is equivalent to Coh(ℙ¹), and the categorical DT generating series is Z^cat_DT = ∏n≥1 (1 − x_n)−1 where x_n corresponds to the simple representation of dimension n. The categorical DT/PT correspondence for the conifold quiver relates the categorical DT series for the resolved conifold to the categorical PT series for the deformed conifold via the categorical mutation functor. The key insight is that categorical DT invariants are independent of the choice of stability condition up to the categorical wall-crossing equivalence, making them intrinsic invariants of the 2-Calabi-Yau category.

The Gopakumar-Vafa (GV) invariants n^g_β ∈ ℤ are integer invariants of a Calabi-Yau threefold X that count BPS states of M-theory on X. Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi-Yau Threefolds with Surface Defects and the 2d-4d Wall-Crossing

Surface defects in Donaldson-Thomas theory are codimension-two operators supported on a divisor D ⊂ X. They are engineered by coupling the 4d topological string on X to a 2d supersymmetric gauge theory on D. The moduli space of stable pairs with a surface defect is the moduli space of pairs (F, s) where F is a pure dimension-one sheaf on X and s is a section of F|D satisfying a stability condition relative to the defect. The central charge for the defect theory is Z_defect(E) = ∫_D ch(E) · eB+iJ · √td(D) where the integral is over the divisor D. The space of stability conditions Stab_defect(D^b(Coh(X))) fibers over the space of stability conditions on D^b(Coh(D)) via the restriction functor. Wall-crossing in the defect theory is governed by the 2d-4d wall-crossing formula of Gaiotto-Moore-Neitzke: the BPS spectrum of the 4d theory jumps across walls of marginal stability in the 2d parameter space, and the jump is computed by the Kontsevich-Soibelman product of quantum dilogarithms associated to the 2d BPS states. For X = O(-1) ⊕ O(-1) → ℙ¹ (the resolved conifold) and D = ℙ¹ the zero section, the defect partition function is the open topological string amplitude on the conifold with a D-brane on the zero section. The 2d-4d wall-crossing reproduces the open-closed duality of the conifold: the open string amplitude on the resolved conifold equals the closed string amplitude on the deformed conifold. The categorical formulation uses the category of matrix factorizations of the superpotential W = xy - uv on the conifold, with the defect corresponding to a boundary condition preserving B-type supersymmetry. The stability condition on the category of matrix factorizations is constructed by Orlov's equivalence with the derived category of the singularity. The wall-crossing formula for the defect DT invariants takes the form Z_defect(ζ_+) = 𝕊_defect(ζ) ⋆ Z_defect(ζ_-) where 𝕊_defect is the 2d-4d wall-crossing operator, a product of quantum dilogarithms indexed by the 2d BPS states. The 2d BPS states are counted by the Euler characteristic of the moduli space of vortices on D, which for D = ℙ¹ is the moduli space of stable maps to ℙ¹. The generating series of 2d BPS states is the J-function of ℙ¹, and the wall-crossing operator is the quantum differential equation of ℙ¹. This identifies the 2d-4d wall-crossing with the Givental quantization of the mirror map. In exams, a standard problem is to compute the defect DT invariant for the conifold with a single D2-brane on the zero section: the answer is the open Gromov-Witten invariant of the conifold, which equals the closed Gromov-Witten invariant of the deformed conifold via the open-closed duality. The key computational tool is the topological vertex with a boundary leg, which computes the open string amplitude as a sum over plane partitions with a fixed boundary condition.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps to Varieties with Non-Trivial Fundamental Group and the Monodromy Data

When the target variety X has non-trivial fundamental group π₁(X), the moduli space of stable maps M_g(X, β) carries a local system ℒ_ρ associated to a representation ρ: π₁(X) → GL(r, ℂ). The heart of the t-structure is the category of ρ-equivariant coherent sheaves on the universal cover X̃, which is equivalent to the category of coherent sheaves on X with a flat connection with monodromy ρ. The wall-crossing formula for twisted DT invariants involves the quantum dilogarithm with matrix coefficients: 𝔈_ρ(x) = ∏k≥0 (1 - ρ(γ) q^k x)-1 where ρ(γ) is the monodromy matrix of the local system along the class γ. The Kontsevich-Soibelman factorization holds in the group of matrix-valued formal power series. For X an abelian variety, π₁(X) = H₁(X, ℤ) and the twisted DT invariants are the Fourier-Mukai transforms of the ordinary DT invariants with respect to the Poincaré bundle twisted by ρ. The generating series Z_DT^ρ = ∑ DT_ρ(β, n) q^n y^β satisfies the twisted wall-crossing formula Z_DT^ρ(ζ_+) = 𝕊_ρ(ζ) ⋆ Z_DT^ρ(ζ_-) where 𝕊_ρ is the twisted KS operator. For X a K3 surface with a non-symplectic automorphism of finite order, the twisted DT invariants compute the orbifold DT invariants of the quotient X/G. The categorical formulation uses the category of G-equivariant coherent sheaves on X, and the stability condition is the G-equivariant Bridgeland stability condition. The wall-crossing formula for equivariant DT invariants is the G-equivariant KS formula, where the quantum dilogarithm is replaced by the G-equivariant quantum dilogarithm 𝔈_G(x) = ∏k≥0 (1 - g q^k x)-1 for g ∈ G. In exams, a typical computation is the twisted DT invariant for X = T² × ℙ¹ with ρ a non-trivial character of π₁(T²) = ℤ²: the moduli space of stable maps is a product of the moduli space of maps to ℙ¹ and the Jacobian of T², and the twisted invariant factors as the product of the ordinary DT invariant of ℙ¹ and the Fourier coefficient of the theta function of the Jacobian twisted by ρ.

Worked Problem: Twisted DT Invariant for T² × ℙ¹
Let X = T² × ℙ¹ where T² = ℂ/(ℤ + τℤ) is an elliptic curve. Let ρ: π₁(T²) → ℂ* be a non-trivial character ρ(m, n) = e2πi(mα + nβ) with (α, β) ∉ ℤ². Compute the twisted DT invariant DT_ρ(β, n) for β = d[ℙ¹] ∈ H₂(X) and n ∈ ℤ.
The moduli space of stable maps M_g(X, d[ℙ¹]) is isomorphic to M_g(ℙ¹, d) × T² because any map f: C → T² × ℙ¹ factors as f = (f_T, f_ℙ) where f_T: C → T² is constant (since C is a curve of genus g and T² has no non-constant maps from C unless g=1, but for stable maps we consider the moduli space of maps with fixed homology class, so f_T is constant). The universal curve π: C → M_g(ℙ¹, d) × T² has evaluation map ev: C → T² × ℙ¹. The pullback local system ev*ℒ_ρ is the pullback of ℒ_ρ from the T² factor. The monodromy trace is Tr(ρ_*([f])) = ρ([f_T]) where [f_T] ∈ H₁(T², ℤ) is the homology class of the constant map, which is zero. Wait: for a constant map, the induced map on π₁ is trivial, so the monodromy is ρ(0) = 1. But the twisted DT invariant uses the monodromy of the local system on the moduli space itself. The correct interpretation: the local system ℒ_ρ on X pulls back to a local system on the moduli space via the evaluation map at a marked point. For M_g(X, β) with one marked point, ev: M_g(X, β) → X. The twisted invariant is ∫M_g(X,β) ν · ev*Tr(ℒ_ρ) dχ. Since ev = (ev_T, ev_ℙ) and ev_T: M_g(X, β) → T² is the projection onto the T² factor (because f_T is constant), ev*ℒ_ρ = pr_T*ℒ_ρ where pr_T: M_g(ℙ¹, d) × T² → T². The Behrend function ν on the product is the product of the Behrend functions. The integral factors: DT_ρ(d, n) = DT_ℙ¹(d, n) · ∫T² Tr(ℒ_ρ) dχ. The integral of the trace of a non-trivial local system over T² is zero because the character is non-trivial. Therefore DT_ρ(d, n) = 0 for all d, n when ρ is non-trivial. If ρ is trivial, we recover the ordinary DT invariant. This matches the Fourier-Mukai prediction: the twisted DT generating series is the Fourier transform of the ordinary DT series with respect to the Poincaré bundle twisted by ρ, and the Fourier coefficient of a non-trivial character vanishes.
Exam Strategy: Twisted Invariants and Vanishing Theorems
When a problem asks for twisted DT invariants with a non-trivial local system on a variety with non-trivial π₁, first check if the moduli space fibers over the variety with the local system pulled back from the base. If the fiber integral of the Behrend function is the ordinary DT invariant and the base integral is the trace of the local system over the base, the answer is often zero for non-trivial characters due to orthogonality of characters. Always verify whether the evaluation map pulls back the local system from a factor where the map is constant — this is the most common source of vanishing results in exam problems.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi-Yau Threefolds with Non-Geometric Phases and the Landau-Ginzburg/Calabi-Yau Correspondence

Non-geometric phases in the space of stability conditions Stab(D^b(Coh(X))) are connected components that do not contain any geometric stability condition (i.e., no heart equivalent to Coh(X) for any variety X). For a Calabi-Yau threefold X that is a hypersurface in a toric variety, the Landau-Ginzburg/Calabi-Yau correspondence relates the derived category of X to the category of matrix factorizations of the Landau-Ginzburg superpotential W on the mirror toric variety. The stability conditions on the LG side are constructed by Takahashi using the category of graded matrix factorizations MF^gr(W). The central charge is Z(E) = ∫_γ e-W/ℏ ch(E) where γ is a Lefschetz thimble. The space of stability conditions on MF^gr(W) is isomorphic to the space of stability conditions on D^b(Coh(X)) via the Orlov equivalence. Wall-crossing between geometric and non-geometric phases corresponds to the monodromy of the Picard-Fuchs equation around the large volume limit and the LG point. The DT invariants in the non-geometric phase are the BPS invariants of the LG model, which are the open string invariants of the mirror symmetry. For X the quintic threefold, the LG model is the Fermat quintic W = x₁⁵ + x₂⁵ + x₃⁵ + x₄⁵ + x₅⁵ - 5ψ x₁x₂x₃x₄x₅ in ℙ⁴ with a ℤ₅ action. The category of matrix factorizations MF^gr(W) has a stability condition whose heart is the category of graded matrix factorizations of the Fermat quintic. The DT invariants in this phase are the FJRW invariants of the LG model, which are the genus-zero Gromov-Witten invariants of the quintic via the LG/CY correspondence. The wall-crossing formula for the DT generating series across the LG/CY wall is the quantum differential equation of the quintic: the generating series Z_DT(ζ) satisfies the Picard-Fuchs equation, and the monodromy around the LG point is the KS transformation associated to the vanishing cycles. The categorical wall-crossing functor is the spherical twist associated to the spherical object in MF^gr(W) corresponding to the vanishing cycle. For a general toric Calabi-Yau threefold X, the non-geometric phases correspond to the different chambers in the secondary fan of the toric variety. The stability conditions in each chamber are constructed by the method of iterated tilts of the heart of the standard t-structure on the category of matrix factorizations. The DT invariants in each chamber are the generalized DT invariants of Joyce-Song for the quiver with potential associated to the toric diagram. The wall-crossing between chambers is the mutation of the quiver with potential, which corresponds to the Seiberg duality in the gauge theory. In exams, a standard problem is to identify the non-geometric phase for the resolved conifold: the LG model is the A₁ singularity W = x² + y² + z² + w², and the category of matrix factorizations is equivalent to the derived category of the resolved conifold. The non-geometric stability condition is the one whose heart is the category of matrix factorizations of the A₁ singularity, and the DT invariants are the open string invariants of the conifold with a D-brane on the exceptional ℙ¹.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps to Varieties with Non-Trivial Torsion in Cohomology and the Discrete Torsion

Discrete torsion in string theory is a choice of a class in H²(X, U(1)) that modifies the orbifold partition function by a phase factor. In Donaldson-Thomas theory, discrete torsion appears when the target variety X has torsion in its cohomology groups, specifically when H³(X, ℤ) has torsion. The moduli space of stable maps M_g(X, β) then carries a gerbe banded by the torsion subgroup Tor H³(X, ℤ). The DT invariants with discrete torsion are defined by integrating the Behrend function twisted by the gerbe: DT_τ(β, n) = ∫M_g(X,β) ν · τ dχ where τ ∈ H²(M_g(X,β), U(1)) is the pullback of the discrete torsion class. The stability condition on the derived category of coherent sheaves on the gerbe is a twisted stability condition in the sense of Huybrechts-Stellari, where the central charge takes values in the twisted K-theory K^τ(X) = K0(X, τ). The heart of the t-structure is the category of τ-twisted coherent sheaves on X, which are sheaves of modules over the Azumaya algebra associated to τ. The wall-crossing formula for twisted DT invariants involves the quantum dilogarithm with coefficients in the twisted K-theory: the KS operator is an element of the completed twisted Hall algebra H_τ = ⊕γ K^τ(M_γ) where M_γ is the moduli stack of τ-twisted sheaves of class γ. The Kontsevich-Soibelman factorization holds in the group of automorphisms of the twisted quantum torus. For X a Calabi-Yau threefold with H³(X, ℤ) = ℤ^b₃ ⊕ Tor, the discrete torsion classes are elements of Tor H³(X, ℤ) ≅ Tor H²(X, U(1)). The twisted DT invariants DT_τ(β, n) are the Fourier coefficients of the twisted topological string partition function Z_top^τ = ∑ DT_τ(β, n) q^n y^β. The twisted partition function satisfies the holomorphic anomaly equation with a twisted boundary condition at the conifold point. The categorical formulation uses the derived category of τ-twisted coherent sheaves D^b(Coh(X, τ)), which is equivalent to the derived category of modules over the Azumaya algebra A_τ. The stability condition on D^b(Coh(X, τ)) is constructed by lifting a geometric stability condition on X to the Azumaya algebra via the Morita equivalence. The wall-crossing functor is the spherical twist associated to the spherical object in D^b(Coh(X, τ)) corresponding to the torsion class. For X a rigid Calabi-Yau threefold with H³(X, ℤ) = ℤ/2ℤ, there is a unique non-trivial discrete torsion class τ. The twisted DT invariants DT_τ(β, n) differ from the ordinary DT invariants by a sign factor (-1)∫_β w₂ where w₂ is the second Stiefel-Whitney class of the normal bundle. In exams, a typical computation is the twisted DT invariant for X = (T⁶/ℤ₂) with discrete torsion: the moduli space of stable pairs is a product of the moduli space on T⁶ and the fixed locus of the ℤ₂ action, and the twisted invariant is the ordinary invariant multiplied by the sign of the ℤ₂ action on the obstruction theory.

Stability Conditions on Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves on Moduli Spaces of Stable Pairs on Calabi-Yau Threefolds with Non-Compact Divisors and the Relative Donaldson-Thomas Theory

Relative Donaldson-Thomas theory studies stable pairs on a Calabi-Yau threefold X relative to a non-compact divisor D ⊂ X. The moduli space of relative stable pairs P_n(X/D, β) parametrizes pairs (F, s) where F is a sheaf on X with support proper over XD, and s is a section of F with zero-dimensional cokernel, together with a framing at D given by a trivialization of F|D ≅ O_D^r. The stability condition for relative pairs is a stability condition on the derived category of coherent sheaves on the expanded degeneration X_D = X ∪_D (D × ℙ¹) ∪_D ... where the central charge is Z(E) = ∫_X ch(E) · eB+iJ · √td(X) + ∫_D ch(E|D) · eB_D+iJ_D · √td(D). The space of relative stability conditions Stab_rel(D^b(Coh(X/D))) fibers over the space of stability conditions on D^b(Coh(D)) via the restriction to the divisor. The relative DT invariants DT_rel(β, n) are defined by integrating the relative Behrend function on P_n(X/D, β). The wall-crossing formula for relative DT invariants is the relative KS formula: Z_rel(ζ_+) = 𝕊_rel(ζ) ⋆ Z_rel(ζ_-) where 𝕊_rel is the relative wall-crossing operator, a product of quantum dilogarithms indexed by the relative BPS states. The relative BPS states are the BPS states of the 4d theory on X with a surface defect on D, which are counted by the relative DT invariants of the local Calabi-Yau D × ℂ. For X a toric Calabi-Yau threefold and D a toric divisor, the relative DT invariants are computed by the topological vertex with a preferred direction, which gives the open string amplitude on X with a D-brane on D. The relative DT/PT correspondence relates the relative DT invariants to the relative PT invariants of stable pairs with a relative condition. The categorical formulation uses the category of relative matrix factorizations of the superpotential W on X with boundary condition on D. The stability condition on the relative category is constructed by the method of gluing stability conditions on XD and D × ℂ. The wall-crossing between relative and absolute DT invariants is the degeneration formula: the absolute DT invariant of X is the sum over splittings β = β₁ + β₂ of the product of relative DT invariants of X/D and the local DT invariants of D × ℂ, glued by the relative insertion. For X = O(-1) ⊕ O(-1) → ℙ¹ and D = ℙ¹ the zero section, the relative DT invariants are the open DT invariants of the conifold, and the degeneration formula reproduces the open-closed duality. In exams, a standard problem is to compute the relative DT invariant for X = ℂ³ and D = ℂ² (the xy-plane): the moduli space of relative stable pairs is the Hilbert scheme of points on ℂ³ relative to ℂ², which is isomorphic to the Hilbert scheme of points on ℂ² × ℂ, and the relative DT generating series is the MacMahon function M(q) = ∏n≥1 (1 - q^n)-n with a framing factor qλ²/2 for the partition λ labeling the framing at D.

  • Confusing the 2d-4d wall-crossing operator with the ordinary 4d KS operator; the 2d-4d operator acts on the defect partition function and involves the 2d BPS spectrum, not the 4d BPS spectrum.
  • Forgetting that the twisted central charge for discrete torsion takes values in twisted K-theory, not ordinary K-theory; the Chern character must be replaced by the twisted Chern character ch_τ = ch · eB_τ where B_τ is the B-field representing the torsion class.
  • Treating the non-geometric phase stability condition as a geometric stability condition on some variety; the heart is not equivalent to Coh(Y) for any variety Y, but to a category of matrix factorizations.
  • Neglecting the framing factor in relative DT invariants; the relative partition function depends on the choice of framing at the divisor, and the wall-crossing formula includes a framing-dependent phase.
  • Assuming the monodromy trace in twisted DT invariants is always the character of the representation; for non-abelian representations, the trace is the trace of the monodromy matrix, which depends on the conjugacy class.
  • Overlooking that the support property for relative stability conditions requires the relative Bogomolov-Gieseker inequality, which has an extra boundary term involving the restriction to the divisor.
  • Confusing the LG/CY wall-crossing with the large volume wall-crossing; the LG/CY wall is a wall in the space of stability conditions where the central charge of the spherical object vanishes, not a wall of marginal stability between two geometric phases.

hand/infinite-lie-algebras.html:
Generalized Kac‑Moody Algebras and Borcherds’ Denominator Identity

Generalized Kac‑Moody algebras, introduced by Borcherds, relax the requirement that the Cartan matrix be symmetrizable and allow simple roots of non‑positive norm. A generalized Cartan matrix A = (aij) still satisfies aii=2, aij≤0 for i≠j, and aij=0 ⇔ aji=0, but the associated bilinear form on the root lattice need not be positive definite. Imaginary simple roots (those with (α|α)≤0) appear, and the Weyl group is generated only by reflections in real simple roots. The denominator identity for a generalized Kac‑Moody algebra 𝔤 takes the form

eρ ∏α>0 (1−e−α)mult(α) = ∑w∈W ε(w) w( eρ ∑α∈Q c(α) eα ),

where ρ is the Weyl vector, W the Weyl group, mult(α) the root multiplicity, and the coefficients c(α) are determined by the simple root multiplicities. For the Monster Lie algebra 𝔪, the simple roots are the vectors (1,n) in the Lorentzian lattice II1,1 with multiplicity given by the coefficients of the j‑function: j(τ)=q−1+744+196884q+…. Borcherds showed that the denominator identity of 𝔪 is exactly the product expansion

j(σ)−j(τ) = p−1 ∏m>0, n∈ℤ (1−pm qn)c(mn),

where p=e2πiσ, q=e2πiτ, and c(n) are the Fourier coefficients of j. This identity implies that the graded traces of Monster elements on the Moonshine module V♮ are Hauptmoduls, proving the Conway‑Norton conjecture. The construction also yields a family of automorphic products on orthogonal groups of signature (2,n), linking generalized Kac‑Moody algebras to Siegel modular forms.

Quantum Affine Algebras and the Yang‑Baxter Equation

Quantum affine algebras U_q(ĝ) are Hopf algebra deformations of the universal enveloping algebras of affine Lie algebras. For a simple Lie algebra 𝔤 with Cartan matrix (aij), the Drinfeld‑Jimbo presentation gives generators e_i, f_i, k_i±1 (i=0,…,r) with relations

k_i k_j = k_j k_i, k_i e_j k_i−1 = qaij e_j, k_i f_j k_i−1 = q−aij f_j,

[e_i, f_j] = δij (k_i−k_i−1)/(q−q−1),

together with the quantum Serre relations. The parameter q is generic (not a root of unity) for the standard representation theory. The universal R‑matrix ℛ ∈ U_q(ĝ)⊗U_q(ĝ) satisfies the quantum Yang‑Baxter equation

ℛ12 ℛ13 ℛ23 = ℛ23 ℛ13 ℛ12

and intertwines the coproduct: ℛ Δ(x) = Δop(x) ℛ for all x∈U_q(ĝ). Finite‑dimensional irreducible representations are classified by Drinfeld polynomials; for U_q(ŝl2) they are the evaluation modules V_z(ℓ) of highest weight ℓ with spectral parameter z. The R‑matrix on V_z(ℓ)⊗V_w(m) yields the Boltzmann weights of the XXZ spin chain, and the Yang‑Baxter equation guarantees integrability. At roots of unity q^N=1 the representation theory truncates, leading to modular tensor categories that underlie topological quantum field theories and the Verlinde formula for fusion rules.

Identifying the quantum parameter from the level
In the quantum affine algebra U_q(ŝl2) at positive integer level k, the central element c acts as k. The deformation parameter q is related to the level by q = exp(π i / (k+2)). Derive this relation from the requirement that the quantum Casimir eigenvalue matches the affine Sugawara construction.
The affine Sugawara construction gives the Virasoro central charge c = 3k/(k+2). In the quantum group, the ribbon element v = u-1 Σ S(b_i) a_i (with ℛ = Σ a_i⊗b_i) acts on the highest weight module of spin ℓ/2 as qℓ(ℓ+2)/2. Matching the conformal weight h_ℓ = ℓ(ℓ+2)/4(k+2) from the Sugawara formula with the eigenvalue of the Virasoro generator L0 = (1/2π i) log v yields qℓ(ℓ+2)/2 = exp(2π i h_ℓ) = exp(π i ℓ(ℓ+2)/(2(k+2))). Hence q = exp(π i/(k+2)).
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the level‑parameter relation q = exp(π i/(k+2)) for U_q(ŝl2); it appears in Bethe ansatz equations, fusion category classifications, and the identification of minimal model central charges. Write it on a flash card with the corresponding central charge c = 3k/(k+2).

Minimal Models, Null Vectors, and the BPZ Differential Equations

The unitary Virasoro minimal models M(p,p') are labelled by coprime integers p,p'≥2 with central charge

c = 1 − 6(p−p')2/(pp').

Highest weights are parametrised by Kac indices 1≤r

:

hr,s = ((rp'−sp)2 − (p−p')2)/(4pp').

At level rs the Verma module M(hr,s,c) contains a singular vector (null vector) |χr,s⟩ which generates a proper submodule. The decoupling of this null vector from correlation functions yields the Belavin‑Polyakov‑Zamolodchikov (BPZ) differential equations. For a four‑point function ⟨φr1,s1(z1) φr2,s2(z2) φr3,s3(z3) φr4,s4(z4)⟩ with a degenerate field φ2,1 or φ1,2, the null vector condition translates into a second‑order Fuchsian differential equation for the conformal blocks. The solutions are hypergeometric functions; their monodromy gives the fusion matrices (braiding) and the Verlinde formula for fusion coefficients

Nij^k = ∑_m (Sim Sjm Skm^*)/S0m,

where S is the modular S‑matrix of characters. The Coulomb gas (free field) representation realises minimal model correlators as integrals of screening charges, providing explicit integral formulas for conformal blocks and proving the AGT correspondence for N=2 gauge theories.

Vertex Operator Algebras: Axioms, Zhu’s Algebra, and Classification

A vertex operator algebra (VOA) (V,Y,1,ω) consists of a ℤ‑graded vector space V = ⊕n∈ℤ V_n, a linear map Y: V → (End V)[[z,z−1]] (Y(v,z)=∑n∈ℤ v_n z−n−1), a vacuum vector 1∈V0, and a conformal vector ω∈V2 such that the modes L_n = ωn+1 satisfy the Virasoro algebra with central charge c. The axioms are:

  • Vacuum: Y(1,z)=Id, Y(v,z)1∈V[[z]] and limz→0 Y(v,z)1 = v.
  • Translation: [L−1, Y(v,z)] = ∂_z Y(v,z).
  • Locality: for any u,v∈V there exists N≥0 with (z−w)^N [Y(u,z), Y(v,w)] = 0.

Zhu’s algebra A(V) is the associative algebra V/O(V) where O(V) is spanned by residues Res_z Y(u,z) v (z+1)wt u / z. Its irreducible modules correspond bijectively to irreducible V‑modules. Classification results: for c<1 the only simple VOAs are the minimal models M(p,p'); for c=1 they are lattice VOAs V_L with L an even positive‑definite lattice of rank one; for c=24 the unique holomorphic VOA with V1=0 is the Moonshine module V♮. The C2‑cofiniteness condition (finite‑dimensionality of V/C2(V)) guarantees rationality and modular invariance of characters, and is satisfied by all known unitary VOAs.

  • Confusing the generalized Cartan matrix of a Borcherds algebra with an ordinary symmetrizable Cartan matrix; the former allows non‑positive diagonal entries for imaginary simple roots.
  • Assuming the quantum parameter q is always a root of unity; generic q gives infinite‑dimensional representation categories, while roots of unity give modular tensor categories.
  • Misidentifying the level‑parameter relation for U_q(ŝl2) as q = exp(2π i/(k+2)) instead of q = exp(π i/(k+2)).
  • Overlooking that null vectors exist only at specific levels rs in minimal models; using the wrong level leads to incorrect BPZ equations.
  • Treating Zhu’s algebra as commutative; it is generally non‑commutative and its representation theory classifies VOA modules.
  • Believing all VOAs of central charge 24 are isomorphic to V♮; there are 71 known holomorphic VOAs of c=24, distinguished by their weight‑one Lie algebra.
  • Neglecting the C2‑cofiniteness hypothesis when invoking modular invariance of characters; without it the Verlinde formula need not hold.

These advanced topics complete the structural picture of infinite‑dimensional Lie algebras and their quantum, conformal, and moonshine extensions.

english/comprehension.html:
Passage Architecture: Identifying Macro‑Structure and Micro‑Cohesion

Every well‑crafted passage follows a discernible macro‑structure: an opening that frames the issue, a development section that presents evidence, counter‑arguments, or elaboration, and a closing that synthesises or proposes a direction. Recognising this skeleton allows a reader to locate the main idea without reading every sentence in detail. At the micro level, cohesion devices — pronouns, lexical chains, conjunctions, and thematic progression — bind sentences into a logical flow. When a test‑taker maps these devices, the location of answer‑bearing sentences becomes predictable: factual details cluster in the development, evaluative language appears in the closing, and definitional vocabulary often surfaces early.

Paragraph‑level signals such as topic sentences, transitional adverbs (however, consequently, moreover), and enumerative markers (first, second, finally) reveal the author’s organisational pattern — cause‑effect, problem‑solution, compare‑contrast, or chronological. A quick scan of the first and last sentence of each paragraph, combined with a note of recurring key terms, yields a skeletal outline that can be consulted while answering. This outline also guards against the common error of importing outside knowledge; the passage’s internal logic alone determines the correct response.

Practice with diverse genres — scientific abstracts, policy briefs, literary essays — sharpens the ability to spot structural variants. For instance, a scientific abstract compresses the macro‑structure into a single paragraph, while a policy brief may use explicit headings. Adapting the same mapping technique across formats builds flexibility, a crucial asset when the exam presents an unfamiliar passage type.

Inference Hierarchies: From Textual Entailment to Authorial Implication

Inference questions operate on a hierarchy. The lowest tier, textual entailment, asks what follows directly from a stated proposition — essentially a restatement with a logical connector. The middle tier, implicature, requires the reader to recognise what the author suggests without stating, often signalled by hedging (suggests, indicates, points to) or by juxtaposition of contrasting data. The highest tier, authorial implication, probes the writer’s underlying stance, purpose, or unstated assumption; answering these demands synthesis of tone, structure, and lexical choice.

Distinguishing the tier is essential because answer options are calibrated: entailment options are usually close paraphrases, implicature options introduce a plausible but unexpressed consequence, and implication options capture a broader thematic judgment. A systematic approach — first locate the exact sentence(s) referenced, then classify the logical relation (deductive, inductive, abductive) — prevents the trap of over‑inferring. For example, a passage noting “revenue fell while expenses rose” entails a deficit; it implicates pressure on budgets; it may imply the need for restructuring, but only if the author’s tone signals advocacy.

Training with annotated passages that label each inference tier accelerates mastery. Over time, the reader internalises a mental checklist: (1) Is the answer directly supported? (2) Does it require a reasonable bridge? (3) Does it demand a judgment about the author’s purpose? This checklist mirrors the examiner’s design and reduces guesswork.

Inference Tier Identification
Passage: “The new regulation requires all manufacturers to disclose carbon emissions. Industry groups have warned that compliance costs will erode profit margins, yet consumer surveys show a growing preference for transparent brands.” Question: What can be inferred at the implicature level? a) Manufacturers will immediately reduce emissions. b) Compliance costs may be offset by increased consumer loyalty. c) The regulation will be repealed within a year. d) Consumer surveys are unreliable.
The passage states a regulation and two opposing facts: industry warns of cost, consumers prefer transparency. At the entailment level we only know the regulation exists. At the implicature level we can reasonably bridge that the cost pressure might be mitigated by consumer preference, making option b the best implicature. Option a over‑states immediate action; option c predicts a future political move not supported; option d attacks the survey without basis. Therefore b is correct.
Exam‑Day Inference Shortcut
When facing an inference question, underline the exact clause the question references. Then ask: “Does the answer restate, extend, or judge?” Choose the option that matches the required tier. This three‑second classification eliminates two distractors instantly.

Contextual Vocabulary Decoding: Morphology, Collocation, and Register

Vocabulary‑in‑context questions test the ability to infer meaning from surrounding linguistic cues rather than from dictionary definitions. Three reliable cues are morphology (prefixes, roots, suffixes), collocation (habitual word partners), and register (formal, technical, colloquial). A word like “unprecedented” yields “un‑” (not) + “precedent” (prior example) + “‑ed” (adjective), signalling “without prior example”. Even if the root is unfamiliar, the negative prefix narrows the field to options conveying novelty or rarity.

Collocational patterns are equally powerful. In a passage on economics, “fiscal” almost always partners with “policy”, “deficit”, or “stimulus”. If the target word appears in “fiscal ______”, the missing noun is likely one of those partners. Register clues further discriminate: a scientific passage will favour “hypothesis” over “guess”, “empirical” over “observed”. Recognising the register prevents selecting a synonym that fits the definition but clashes with the passage’s tone.

Practice drills that isolate a target word, list its morphological breakdown, note the immediate left/right collocates, and label the register, then ask the learner to choose among four options, build automaticity. Over time, the process becomes sub‑second, turning vocabulary questions from a time sink into a scoring opportunity.

Tone Detection: Categorising Authorial Stance Across Genres

Tone questions ask for the author’s attitude toward the subject. A reliable taxonomy distinguishes five primary tones: objective/neutral, analytical, appreciative, critical, and skeptical. Objective tone presents facts without evaluative adjectives; analytical tone adds logical connectors (therefore, consequently) and weighs evidence; appreciative tone uses positive affect words (remarkable, pioneering); critical tone employs negative affect (flawed, inadequate) and often juxtaposes shortcomings; skeptical tone hedges (claims, purported) and highlights gaps.

Genre influences baseline expectations. A scientific abstract defaults to objective/analytical; an editorial leans critical or appreciative; a historical narrative may be neutral but can embed subtle skepticism. The test‑taker should first note the genre, then scan for affect‑laden lexical items, modal verbs (must, should, might), and the balance of positive versus negative descriptors. A quick tally — more negative than positive → critical; balanced with hedging → skeptical; predominantly positive → appreciative; neutral language with logical structuring → analytical.

Edge cases arise when a passage mixes tones — e.g., an analytical overview that ends with a critical recommendation. In such cases the question usually targets the dominant tone or the tone of a specific segment. Marking the segment referenced by the question (often indicated by line numbers) isolates the relevant tone and avoids the “whole‑passage” trap.

Cross‑Passage Synthesis: Comparative Reading for Paired‑Passage Sets

Some examinations present two passages on a related theme and ask comparative questions — agreement, contradiction, complementary evidence, or differing perspectives. Effective synthesis begins with a parallel outline: for each passage note the thesis, key evidence, and concluding stance. Align the outlines side by side; overlapping points indicate agreement, divergent evidence signals contradiction, and distinct angles reveal complementarity.

Comparative questions often use phrasing such as “Both authors would agree that…” or “Passage 1 supports the claim in Passage 2 by…”. The answer must be derivable from both texts simultaneously. A common error is to select a statement true in only one passage. To avoid this, verify each candidate against both outlines before committing. When the question asks for a difference, look for a point where one passage explicitly states X while the other states not‑X or remains silent.

Time management for paired sets: allocate an initial 90‑second skim of both passages to build the parallel outline, then answer the comparative items before tackling passage‑specific questions. This order exploits the fresh comparative map and prevents re‑reading. Regular practice with paired passages from varied domains — science vs. policy, history vs. memoir — builds the mental agility required for rapid synthesis.

  • Assuming the main idea resides in the first paragraph only.
  • Treating every hedging word as a sign of authorial doubt rather than rhetorical caution.
  • Choosing a vocabulary option that matches a dictionary definition but violates the passage’s register.
  • Assigning a single tone label to a passage that shifts tone across sections.
  • Answering a comparative question using evidence from only one passage.
  • Over‑inferring by importing real‑world knowledge that the passage does not contain.
  • Neglecting to verify that an inference option is logically entailed rather than merely plausible.
