Once an embedding is found, many NP‑hard problems become polynomial on graphs of bounded genus via dynamic programming on branch decompositions of width O(√{g·n}). For example, graph coloring, Hamiltonian cycle, and maximum independent set can be solved in time 2^{O(√{g·n})}·nO(1). The theorem also implies that the class of graphs of genus at most g has bounded local treewidth, which yields PTASes for many optimization problems via Baker’s layering technique.

It is important to distinguish genus from crossing number. A graph may have crossing number 1 but arbitrarily large genus (e.g., a large planar graph plus one crossing edge). Conversely, bounded genus implies bounded crossing number, but the converse fails. The excluded‑minor sets for bounded crossing number are not known to be finite for crossing number ≥ 2; this is a major open problem.

Typical exam tasks: (i) list the forbidden minors for the projective plane, (ii) explain why the existence of a finite forbidden‑minor set for each surface follows from the Robertson–Seymour theorem, (iii) describe how an embedding on a fixed surface can be used to obtain a branch decomposition of width O(√{g·n}). A frequent trap is to claim that the set of forbidden minors for the torus is known to be exactly the 16 000+ graphs found by computer; the proof of completeness relies on the graph minor theorem, not on exhaustive enumeration alone.

The Graph Minor Theorem for Graphs of Bounded Pathwidth

Pathwidth is a graph parameter defined via path decompositions: a sequence of bags (vertex subsets) such that each vertex appears in a contiguous subsequence, each edge has both ends in some bag, and the width is the maximum bag size minus one. Pathwidth is minor‑monotone (taking a minor never increases pathwidth) and satisfies pw(G) ≤ tw(G) ≤ pw(G)·log₂|V(G)| for general graphs, while for trees pw = tw. The class of graphs with pathwidth at most k is minor‑closed, so by the Robertson–Seymour theorem it is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors Forb(k). For k = 1 the forbidden minors are exactly the cycles (graphs of pathwidth 1 are forests). For k = 2 the set Forb(2) is known and contains 110 graphs (Kinnersley 1992). For k ≥ 3 the exact forbidden sets are unknown, but finiteness is guaranteed.

Algorithmic applications of bounded pathwidth are often sharper than those for treewidth. Many dynamic‑programming algorithms on path decompositions run in time 2O(pw)·n, whereas the treewidth analogue may have a factor nO(tw). For instance, Hamiltonian path can be solved in 2pw·nO(1) time, and the graph searching number (node search) equals pw + 1. The vertex separation number, which is the minimum over all linear layouts of the maximum number of vertices to the left of a cut that have neighbours to the right, equals pathwidth. This equivalence yields a simple linear‑time algorithm to compute pathwidth on interval graphs.

The excluded‑minor characterization for bounded pathwidth also implies that the class of graphs with pathwidth ≤ k is well‑quasi‑ordered by the minor relation, and that any property expressible in monadic second‑order logic (MSO₂) can be decided in linear time on this class (by Courcelle’s theorem, since bounded pathwidth implies bounded treewidth). However, the dependence on k in the MSO₂ algorithm is non‑elementary because the forbidden‑minor set is not explicitly known.

Exam questions may ask to (i) construct a path decomposition of width 2 for a given graph, (ii) prove that pathwidth is minor‑monotone, (iii) explain why the node search number equals pw + 1, or (iv) contrast the known forbidden minors for pathwidth 1 and 2 with the unknown situation for higher k. A common error is to state that pathwidth ≤ treewidth; the correct inequality is treewidth ≤ pathwidth. Another trap is to assume that the forbidden‑minor set for pathwidth k is the same as for treewidth k; they are different because the classes are not identical.

  • Confusing clique‑width with treewidth; remember that cliques have clique‑width 2 but unbounded treewidth.
  • Assuming bounded expansion implies bounded treewidth; planar graphs have bounded expansion but unbounded treewidth.
  • Applying the undirected grid theorem to directed graphs without respecting edge directions.
  • Mixing up genus and crossing number; a graph of crossing number 1 can have arbitrarily large genus.
  • Stating that pathwidth ≤ treewidth; the correct relation is treewidth ≤ pathwidth.
  • Believing the forbidden‑minor set for bounded pathwidth is known for all k; it is known only for k = 1,2.
  • Thinking that the directed grid theorem gives a polynomial bound N(k); the bound is non‑elementary.

Pathwidth, Vertex Separation, and Linear Layouts

Pathwidth is a graph parameter defined via a path decomposition: a sequence of bags (vertex subsets) such that each vertex appears in a contiguous subsequence, each edge has both ends in some bag, and the width is the maximum bag size minus one. The vertex separation number of a linear layout (an ordering of the vertices) is the maximum, over all cuts between a prefix and its suffix, of the number of vertices in the prefix that have neighbours in the suffix. A fundamental theorem states that the pathwidth of a graph equals its vertex separation number. Consequently, computing pathwidth is equivalent to finding an optimal linear layout.

Pathwidth is minor‑monotone: taking a minor never increases pathwidth. By the Robertson–Seymour theorem, for every fixed k the class of graphs with pathwidth at most k is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. For k = 1 the forbidden minors are exactly the cycles (graphs of pathwidth 1 are forests). For k = 2 the forbidden set is known and contains 110 graphs (Kinnersley 1992). For k ≥ 3 the exact forbidden sets are unknown, but finiteness is guaranteed.

Relation to treewidth: for any graph G, tw(G) ≤ pw(G) ≤ tw(G)·log₂|V(G)|. For trees the two parameters coincide. Many dynamic‑programming algorithms on path decompositions run in time 2O(pw)·n, which is often sharper than the nO(tw) dependence for treewidth. For example, Hamiltonian path can be solved in 2pw·nO(1) time, and the node‑search number (graph searching with node searchers) equals pw + 1.

Algorithmic applications: bounded pathwidth yields fixed‑parameter tractable algorithms for a host of NP‑hard problems (Independent Set, Dominating Set, Chromatic Number, etc.) with running time 2O(pw)·nO(1). Courcelle’s theorem also applies because bounded pathwidth implies bounded treewidth, but the dependence on k is non‑elementary when the forbidden‑minor set is not explicitly known.

Common exam tasks: (i) construct a path decomposition of width 2 for a given graph, (ii) prove that pathwidth is minor‑monotone, (iii) explain why the node‑search number equals pw + 1, (iv) contrast the known forbidden minors for pathwidth 1 and 2 with the unknown situation for higher k.

Boolean‑Width: Definition, Properties, and Algorithmic Uses

Boolean‑width is a graph parameter defined via branch decompositions. For a partition (A, B) of the vertex set, consider the bipartite graph between A and B. Over the field GF(2), each vertex a ∈ A defines a characteristic vector of its neighbours in B. The boolean dimension of the cut is the dimension of the subspace spanned by these vectors. The boolean‑width of a branch decomposition is the maximum boolean dimension over all its cuts; the boolean‑width of the graph is the minimum over all branch decompositions.

Key inequalities: for every graph G, mim‑width(G) ≤ boolw(G) ≤ rw(G) ≤ cw(G), where mim‑width is maximum induced matching width, rw is rank‑width, and cw is clique‑width. Boolean‑width is not minor‑monotone, but it is monotone under taking induced subgraphs. Graph classes of bounded boolean‑width include interval graphs, permutation graphs, trapezoid graphs, and more generally all graphs of bounded rank‑width.

Algorithmic meta‑theorem: any problem expressible in monadic second‑order logic with quantification over vertex sets only (MSO₁) can be solved in time nO(boolw) on graphs of boolean‑width at most boolw. This yields polynomial‑time algorithms for Independent Set, Dominating Set, and many other problems on graph classes where boolean‑width is bounded by a constant. Computing the exact boolean‑width is NP‑hard, but there exist approximation algorithms that produce a branch decomposition of width at most 2boolw in polynomial time.

Typical exam questions: (i) define boolean‑width formally, (ii) prove boolw(G) ≤ rw(G), (iii) explain why MSO₁ model‑checking is fixed‑parameter tractable parameterized by boolean‑width, (iv) give an example of a graph class with bounded boolean‑width but unbounded treewidth.

Worked Example
Let G be a graph with boolean‑width 2. Show that the Independent Set problem can be solved in polynomial time on G.
Since boolw(G) = 2, there exists a branch decomposition of G where every cut has boolean dimension at most 2. Independent Set is expressible in MSO₁ (∃S ⊆ V: ∀u,v ∈ S, ¬E(u,v)). By the algorithmic meta‑theorem for boolean‑width, MSO₁ model‑checking runs in time nO(boolw) = nO(1). Therefore Independent Set is solvable in polynomial time on G.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a width parameter that guarantees polynomial‑time MSO₁ model‑checking, recall the hierarchy mim‑width ≤ boolw ≤ rw ≤ cw. Boolean‑width is the weakest parameter among them that still yields an nO(k) algorithm for MSO₁. If the problem is MSO₂ (edge‑set quantification), you need treewidth or rank‑width, not boolean‑width.

Mim‑Width: A Unified Width Parameter for Graph Classes

Maximum induced matching width (mim‑width) is defined via branch decompositions. For a cut (A, B) of a branch decomposition, consider the bipartite graph H with parts A and B and edges those of G crossing the cut. The mim‑width of the cut is the size of a maximum induced matching in H. The mim‑width of the decomposition is the maximum over its cuts; the mim‑width of G is the minimum over all branch decompositions.

Mim‑width generalizes several classical parameters: interval graphs and permutation graphs have mim‑width 1; more generally, any graph class with a linear ordering where the neighbourhoods of vertices in one part form a chain has mim‑width 1. Bounded mim‑width also holds for H‑graphs, circular‑arc graphs, and many others. Importantly, mim‑width is not minor‑monotone and not closed under taking minors.

Algorithmic consequences: a large family of problems (Independent Set, Dominating Set, r‑Dominating Set, Induced Matching, etc.) can be solved in time nO(mimw) on graphs of mim‑width at most mimw. This is achieved by dynamic programming on a branch decomposition, where the state space at each cut is bounded by the number of induced matchings. Computing mim‑width exactly is NP‑hard, but for many graph classes a decomposition of constant mim‑width can be found in polynomial time.

Relation to other widths: mim‑width ≤ boolw ≤ rw ≤ cw. There are graph classes with bounded mim‑width but unbounded treewidth (e.g., interval graphs have treewidth equal to the size of the maximum clique minus one, which can be arbitrarily large while mim‑width stays 1). Conversely, bounded treewidth does not imply bounded mim‑width.

Exam focus: (i) define mim‑width and give an example of a graph with mim‑width 1, (ii) explain why mim‑width is not minor‑monotone, (iii) describe the dynamic‑programming paradigm that yields nO(mimw) algorithms, (iv) contrast mim‑width with pathwidth and treewidth.

Excluded Minor Characterizations for Graphs of Bounded Boolean‑Width

Unlike treewidth, pathwidth, or rank‑width, boolean‑width is not minor‑monotone. Therefore the Robertson–Seymour theorem does not apply, and the class of graphs with boolean‑width at most k is not characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. In fact, for any fixed k ≥ 1 there exist graphs of boolean‑width greater than k that contain arbitrarily large minors of boolean‑width at most k, showing that the class is not minor‑closed.

However, boolean‑width is monotone under taking induced subgraphs, and it is characterized by a finite set of forbidden vertex‑minors for each fixed k? This is an open problem. For rank‑width, Oum (2005) proved that graphs of rank‑width at most k are characterized by a finite set of forbidden vertex‑minors. For boolean‑width, no such characterization is known, and it is conjectured that the class of graphs of bounded boolean‑width may not admit a finite forbidden vertex‑minor characterization.

What is known: if a graph class has bounded boolean‑width, then it also has bounded rank‑width, and therefore it is characterized by forbidden vertex‑minors for rank‑width. But the converse fails: there are graph classes of bounded rank‑width (hence characterized by forbidden vertex‑minors) that have unbounded boolean‑width. This separation shows that boolean‑width captures a strictly smaller family of graph classes than rank‑width.

Typical exam traps: assuming that bounded boolean‑width implies a finite forbidden‑minor set (it does not), confusing vertex‑minor and minor characterizations, and believing that the algorithmic meta‑theorem for boolean‑width extends to MSO₂ (it does not; MSO₂ requires treewidth or rank‑width).

The Directed Grid Theorem and Parameterized Algorithms on Directed Graphs

The directed grid theorem (Kawarabayashi & Kreutzer 2015) states that for every integer k there exists a number N(k) such that every directed graph with directed treewidth at least N(k) contains a directed grid of order k as a butterfly minor. The directed grid of order k is a directed graph on a k × k grid where each horizontal edge points right and each vertical edge points down, together with all edges of the form (i, j) → (i+1, j+1). The function N(k) is known to be non‑elementary (a tower of exponentials of height proportional to k).

Directed treewidth is a parameter for directed graphs that generalizes undirected treewidth. Many problems that are fixed‑parameter tractable parameterized by undirected treewidth become W[1]‑hard when parameterized by directed treewidth (e.g., Directed Hamiltonian Cycle). However, on classes of directed graphs that exclude a fixed directed grid as a butterfly minor, several problems admit subexponential or even polynomial‑time parameterized algorithms. This mirrors the bidimensionality theory for undirected graphs.

Algorithmic applications: the directed grid theorem is used to prove that problems such as Directed Disjoint Paths, Directed Feedback Vertex Set, and Directed Cycle Packing are fixed‑parameter tractable on directed graphs of bounded directed treewidth, but the dependence on the parameter is typically non‑elementary due to the bound N(k). Recent work has developed approximation algorithms for directed treewidth and fixed‑parameter algorithms for specific problems on graphs excluding a directed grid.

Exam focus: (i) state the directed grid theorem precisely, (ii) explain why the bound N(k) is non‑elementary, (iii) contrast directed treewidth with undirected treewidth, (iv) give an example of a problem that is FPT on undirected graphs of bounded treewidth but W[1]‑hard on directed graphs of bounded directed treewidth.

  • Confusing pathwidth ≤ treewidth; the correct inequality is treewidth ≤ pathwidth.
  • Assuming the forbidden‑minor set for bounded pathwidth is known for all k; it is known only for k = 1,2.
  • Treating boolean‑width as minor‑monotone; it is not, so Robertson–Seymour does not give a finite forbidden‑minor characterization.
  • Believing that bounded boolean‑width implies bounded treewidth; interval graphs have boolean‑width 1 but unbounded treewidth.
  • Thinking mim‑width is minor‑monotone; it is not, and bounded mim‑width does not imply bounded treewidth.
  • Assuming the directed grid theorem gives a polynomial bound N(k); the bound is non‑elementary.
  • Applying the undirected grid theorem to directed graphs without respecting edge directions.

Graph Minor Theory: Excluding a Fixed Topological Minor

The Robertson–Seymour Graph Minor Theorem establishes that the class of all finite graphs is well‑quasi‑ordered by the minor relation. A parallel line of work, completed in the 1990s, shows that the same well‑quasi‑ordering holds for the topological‑minor relation when a fixed graph H is forbidden as a topological minor. In other words, for every graph H there are only finitely many minimal graphs that contain H as a topological minor, and any infinite sequence of H‑topological‑minor‑free graphs contains a pair where one is a topological minor of the other. This result is often called the Topological Minor Theorem and its proof uses the same structural decomposition ideas — tree‑decompositions, vortices, and apex vertices — that appear in the full minor theorem, but the analysis of how edges can be subdivided adds a layer of technical complexity.

A concrete consequence is that many algorithmic problems that are fixed‑parameter tractable parameterized by treewidth remain FPT on H‑topological‑minor‑free graphs. For example, the Disjoint Paths problem, which is NP‑complete in general, can be solved in time f(k)·n³ on graphs excluding a fixed topological minor, where k is the number of terminal pairs. The function f depends on H but not on n. This mirrors the bidimensionality framework for ordinary minors, yet the constants hidden in f are typically larger because the structural theorem for topological minors yields a larger “grid‑like” obstruction.

Examiners frequently test the distinction between minor‑closed and topological‑minor‑closed classes. A classic trap is to assume that every minor‑closed class is also topological‑minor‑closed; the converse fails because a graph may contain H as a minor without containing it as a topological minor (e.g., a large clique contains a small clique as a minor but not as a topological minor unless the host graph has sufficiently high degree). Remember that the set of forbidden topological minors for a given property can be infinite even when the forbidden minor set is finite, so the Robertson–Seymour finiteness theorem does not automatically transfer.

Graph Minor Theory: Excluding a Fixed Immersion

An immersion of a graph H in a graph G is a mapping that sends vertices of H to distinct vertices of G and edges of H to edge‑disjoint paths in G whose internal vertices are distinct from the images of vertices. Robertson and Seymour proved in 2010 that the class of all finite graphs is well‑quasi‑ordered by the immersion relation. Consequently, for any fixed graph H the class of H‑immersion‑free graphs admits a finite set of minimal immersion obstructions. This Immersion Theorem is strictly weaker than the minor theorem: every minor is an immersion, but not every immersion is a minor (consider a subdivision of a vertex of degree three). The proof introduces the notion of “edge‑cut” decompositions and a new type of “wall” structure that respects edge‑disjoint routing.

Algorithmic applications are striking. The Edge‑Disjoint Paths problem, which asks for k pairwise edge‑disjoint paths connecting prescribed terminal pairs, becomes fixed‑parameter tractable on graphs excluding a fixed immersion. The parameter is k, and the running time is f(k)·n² where f depends on the excluded immersion H. This is a rare example where a problem that is W[1]‑hard on general graphs becomes FPT on a structurally restricted class without bounding treewidth. The key insight is that bounded immersion‑width (the analogue of treewidth for immersions) yields a tree‑like decomposition where each bag has a bounded number of “edge‑boundary” vertices, enabling dynamic programming.

A common exam mistake is to conflate immersion‑width with treewidth. While treewidth ≤ immersion‑width always holds, the converse is false: a large complete bipartite graph Kₙ,ₙ has treewidth n but immersion‑width 2. Therefore, algorithms that rely on bounded treewidth cannot be directly transferred to bounded immersion‑width settings, and vice‑versa. The exam may ask you to identify which width parameter is appropriate for a given problem — edge‑disjoint routing favours immersion‑width, vertex‑disjoint routing favours treewidth.

Worked Example: Deciding Immersion‑Free Membership
Given a graph G with 12 vertices and 18 edges, determine whether G contains K₄ as an immersion. Outline the steps of an FPT algorithm parameterized by the size of the excluded immersion.
1. Compute the immersion‑width of G using the known O(n³) approximation algorithm for immersion‑width (since K₄ has immersion‑width 3, any graph with immersion‑width ≤ 2 is K₄‑immersion‑free). 2. If the computed width ≤ 2, answer NO. 3. Otherwise, construct the immersion‑decomposition tree of width w. 4. Run dynamic programming on the decomposition: each bag stores a partition of its boundary vertices into at most 3 groups representing the images of the three vertices of K₄, together with a record of which edge‑disjoint paths have been used. 5. Because the boundary size is bounded by a function of w, the DP table size is f(w)·n. 6. If the DP finds a consistent assignment for all four vertices of K₄, output YES; otherwise NO. The overall running time is f(3)·n², which is polynomial for this fixed H.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions “edge‑disjoint paths” or “immersion”, immediately think of immersion‑width and the Robertson–Seymour Immersion Theorem. Write down the inequality treewidth ≤ immersion‑width and note that complete bipartite graphs separate the two parameters. This single observation often earns the majority of marks for a comparison‑type question.

Graph Minor Theory: Boolean‑Width and Its Algorithmic Meta‑Theorem

Boolean‑width was introduced by Bui‑Xuan, Telle, and Vatshelle in 2013 as a width measure that captures the complexity of a graph’s vertex partition via the Boolean algebra generated by neighbourhoods across a cut. Formally, for a branch decomposition (T,δ) of a graph G, the boolean‑width of a cut (A,Ā) is log₂ of the number of distinct neighbourhoods of vertices in A into Ā, viewed as subsets of Ā. The boolean‑width of the decomposition is the maximum over all cuts, and the boolean‑width of G is the minimum over all branch decompositions. Unlike treewidth or rank‑width, boolean‑width is not minor‑monotone; contracting an edge can increase the number of distinct neighbourhoods. However, it is monotone under taking induced subgraphs, which makes it suitable for dense graph classes such as interval graphs, permutation graphs, and more generally graphs of bounded clique‑width.

The central algorithmic result is a meta‑theorem: every graph problem expressible in Monadic Second‑Order logic with quantification over vertex sets only (MSO₁) can be solved in time O*(2O(bw)) on graphs given with a branch decomposition of boolean‑width bw. This matches the classic Courcelle theorem for treewidth but applies to many dense graphs where treewidth is unbounded. For instance, Maximum Independent Set, Dominating Set, and q‑Coloring are all MSO₁‑expressible, so they become polynomial‑time solvable on any class of bounded boolean‑width provided a suitable decomposition is supplied. Finding an optimal decomposition is NP‑hard, but a 2‑approximation can be computed in polynomial time using the rank‑width approximation algorithm of Oum and Seymour, because boolean‑width ≤ rank‑width + 1.

Exam traps often involve the mistaken belief that bounded boolean‑width implies bounded treewidth or that the MSO₂ version of Courcelle’s theorem (which quantifies over edge sets) holds for boolean‑width. Neither is true: interval graphs have boolean‑width 1 but arbitrarily large treewidth, and MSO₂ problems such as Hamiltonian Cycle remain NP‑hard on graphs of boolean‑width 2. Remember also that the class of graphs with boolean‑width ≤ k is not characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors; the Robertson–Seymour theorem does not apply because boolean‑width is not minor‑closed.

Graph Minor Theory: Mim‑Width and Its Applications to Dense Graph Classes

Maximum induced matching width (mim‑width) was introduced by Vatshelle in 2012 to capture the difficulty of finding large induced matchings across a cut of a branch decomposition. For a cut (A,Ā), the mim‑value is the size of a maximum induced matching in the bipartite graph between A and Ā. The mim‑width of a decomposition is the maximum mim‑value over all cuts, and the mim‑width of G is the minimum over all branch decompositions. Mim‑width is bounded for many dense graph classes that have unbounded treewidth and unbounded clique‑width, including interval graphs, permutation graphs, circular‑arc graphs, and more generally graphs of bounded interval‑width. Crucially, mim‑width is not minor‑monotone and not even monotone under induced subgraphs, but it is monotone under taking induced subgraphs of the *complement* graph.

The algorithmic payoff is a meta‑theorem for problems expressible in a fragment of MSO₁ called “MSO₁ with cardinality constraints” or, equivalently, problems that can be solved by dynamic programming where the state at a cut depends only on the partition of the boundary vertices into equivalence classes of having identical neighbourhoods into the opposite side. Many classic problems — Independent Set, Dominating Set, q‑Coloring, and even Weighted versions — fall into this fragment and can be solved in time nO(w) where w is the mim‑width, provided a decomposition of width w is given. For interval graphs, a decomposition of mim‑width 1 can be constructed in linear time from the interval representation, yielding linear‑time algorithms for all these problems.

A frequent exam confusion is to treat mim‑width as a minor‑monotone parameter and to invoke the Graph Minor Theorem for it. Because mim‑width can increase under edge contraction, the class of graphs with mim‑width ≤ k is not minor‑closed and has no finite forbidden‑minor characterization. Another trap is to assume that bounded mim‑width implies bounded boolean‑width; the two parameters are incomparable. There exist graph families (e.g., certain bipartite chain graphs) with boolean‑width 1 but arbitrarily large mim‑width, and conversely interval graphs have mim‑width 1 but unbounded boolean‑width. Knowing these separations is essential for selecting the right width parameter in a parameterized‑complexity question.

Graph Minor Theory: The Graph Minor Theorem for Graphs of Bounded Genus and Surface Embeddings

Robertson and Seymour extended their well‑quasi‑ordering result to graphs embeddable on a fixed surface Σ. The Surface Minor Theorem states that for any compact surface Σ (orientable or non‑orientable) the class of graphs that embed in Σ is well‑quasi‑ordered by the minor relation. The proof builds on the Graph Minor Structure Theorem: any H‑minor‑free graph can be decomposed into pieces that are “almost embeddable” on a surface of bounded genus, glued together along vortices and apex vertices. When the host surface Σ is fixed, the genus of the almost‑embeddable pieces is bounded by the genus of Σ, which yields a finite set of minimal obstructions for embeddability on Σ. This finite obstruction set is precisely the set of forbidden minors for the surface Σ.

Algorithmic consequences are profound. Many NP‑hard problems become polynomial‑time solvable on graphs of bounded genus because the surface embedding provides a branch decomposition of width O(√g·n) where g is the genus, and dynamic programming on this decomposition runs in time 2O(√g)·n. For example, the Independent Set problem on graphs embeddable on a surface of genus g can be solved in time 2O(√g)·n, which is subexponential for fixed g. Moreover, the Excluded Grid Theorem for surfaces guarantees that any graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains a large grid minor that respects the surface embedding, enabling bidimensionality‑style subexponential algorithms for a wide range of problems.

Exam questions often ask you to distinguish between the genus of a graph (the minimum genus of a surface into which it embeds) and the Euler genus (twice the orientable genus for non‑orientable surfaces). A typical trap is to claim that the forbidden‑minor set for the torus is known and small; in fact, the complete list of forbidden minors for the torus contains thousands of graphs and is not fully enumerated in any textbook. What is known is that the set is finite (by the Surface Minor Theorem) and that the projective plane has exactly 35 forbidden minors. When a problem asks for the number of forbidden minors for a given surface, the correct answer is “finite but not explicitly known in general; only for the sphere (planar graphs, two minors) and the projective plane (35 minors) are the complete lists known.”

  • Assuming that bounded boolean‑width implies bounded treewidth; interval graphs disprove this.
  • Believing that the MSO₂ version of Courcelle’s theorem holds for boolean‑width; it does not.
  • Treating mim‑width as minor‑monotone and invoking Robertson–Seymour for it.
  • Confusing immersion‑width with treewidth; Kₙ,ₙ separates them.
  • Thinking the forbidden‑minor set for the torus is small or fully known; it is finite but huge.
  • Assuming that a graph class closed under topological minors is automatically closed under minors; the converse fails.
  • Using the directed grid theorem bound N(k) as if it were polynomial; it is non‑elementary.

These advanced topics illustrate how structural graph theory provides a hierarchy of width parameters, each with its own algorithmic meta‑theorems and well‑quasi‑ordering results, and how examiners test the precise boundaries between them.

Boolean‑Width and Its Algorithmic Applications

Boolean‑width is a graph parameter introduced by Bui‑Xuan, Telle and Vatshelle to capture the complexity of a graph with respect to a branch decomposition where each cut is measured by the number of distinct neighbourhoods that can appear across the cut. Formally, for a partition (A, B) of the vertex set, the Boolean dimension is the logarithm (base 2) of the number of distinct subsets of B that can be realised as neighbourhoods of vertices in A. The boolean‑width of a graph is the minimum, over all branch decompositions, of the maximum Boolean dimension of its cuts. This parameter is incomparable with treewidth, rank‑width and clique‑width: there are graph families of bounded boolean‑width and unbounded treewidth (e.g. certain bipartite chain graphs) and families of bounded treewidth but unbounded boolean‑width (e.g. interval graphs).

The algorithmic significance of boolean‑width lies in its connection to monadic second‑order logic (MSO₁). For any fixed MSO₁ formula φ, the model‑checking problem on graphs of boolean‑width at most w can be solved in time f(|φ|, w)·n, where f is a computable function. This yields fixed‑parameter tractable algorithms for a wide range of problems — Independent Set, Dominating Set, q‑Coloring, Hamiltonian Cycle — provided a decomposition of bounded boolean‑width is given. Computing an optimal boolean‑width decomposition is NP‑hard, but for many graph classes (distance‑hereditary graphs, graphs of bounded clique‑width, certain permutation graphs) a decomposition of width O(1) can be constructed in polynomial time.

Boolean‑width also interacts with the theory of graph limits. For a sequence of dense graphs, the cut‑norm distance used in graphon theory can be approximated by the Boolean dimension of cuts, giving a bridge between structural sparsity parameters and analytic limit objects. In practice, examiners often test the distinction between MSO₁ and MSO₂ expressibility: boolean‑width captures MSO₁ but not MSO₂ (which quantifies over edge sets). Consequently, problems like Edge‑Dominating Set or Hamiltonicity (which require edge‑set quantification) are not known to be FPT parameterised by boolean‑width alone.

Key Properties

  • Boolean‑width ≤ rank‑width + 1 and ≤ clique‑width.
  • Graphs of boolean‑width 1 are exactly the graphs that admit a branch decomposition where every cut has at most two distinct neighbourhood types; these are precisely the graphs of linear rank‑width 1.
  • The class of graphs with boolean‑width ≤ k is not closed under edge contraction, so it is not minor‑closed and has no finite forbidden‑minor characterisation.

Mim‑Width: Maximum Induced Matching Width and Parameterized Algorithms

Mim‑width (maximum induced matching width) was introduced by Vatshelle as a refinement of boolean‑width tailored for problems that are naturally expressed by induced matchings across a cut. For a partition (A, B), the mim‑value is the size of a maximum induced matching in the bipartite graph formed by the edges between A and B. The mim‑width of a graph is the minimum, over all branch decompositions, of the maximum mim‑value of its cuts. Unlike boolean‑width, mim‑width is monotone under taking induced subgraphs but can increase under edge contraction, so it is not minor‑monotone either.

The algorithmic power of mim‑width stems from the fact that many classic NP‑hard problems — Independent Set, Dominating Set, q‑Coloring, and their weighted variants — can be solved in time nO(w) on graphs given with a decomposition of mim‑width w. For interval graphs, a decomposition of mim‑width 1 can be built in linear time from the interval representation, yielding linear‑time algorithms for all these problems. For permutation graphs and convex graphs the same holds. This makes mim‑width a practical parameter for algorithm design on dense graph classes where treewidth is large.

A frequent exam confusion is to treat mim‑width as a minor‑monotone parameter and to invoke the Graph Minor Theorem for it. Because mim‑width can increase under edge contraction, the class of graphs with mim‑width ≤ k is not minor‑closed and has no finite forbidden‑minor characterisation. Another trap is to assume that bounded mim‑width implies bounded boolean‑width; the two parameters are incomparable. There exist graph families (e.g. certain bipartite chain graphs) with boolean‑width 1 but arbitrarily large mim‑width, and conversely interval graphs have mim‑width 1 but unbounded boolean‑width. Knowing these separations is essential for selecting the right width parameter in a parameterized‑complexity question.

Distinguishing Width Parameters
Consider the following statements about a graph class 𝒞: 1. 𝒞 has bounded boolean‑width but unbounded mim‑width. 2. 𝒞 has bounded mim‑width but unbounded boolean‑width. 3. 𝒞 is minor‑closed. Which of the statements can simultaneously hold for a non‑trivial graph class? Choose the correct combination.
Statement 1 holds for bipartite chain graphs: they have boolean‑width 1 (the neighbourhoods across any cut are linearly ordered) but mim‑width can be arbitrarily large because large induced matchings can be forced across a cut. Statement 2 holds for interval graphs: they have mim‑width 1 (an interval representation yields a branch decomposition where each cut induces at most one edge in any induced matching) but boolean‑width is unbounded (the number of distinct neighbourhood types grows with the number of intervals). Statement 3 cannot hold together with either 1 or 2 because both boolean‑width and mim‑width are not minor‑monotone; a minor‑closed class with bounded width would have a finite forbidden‑minor set, which is known not to exist for these parameters. Hence the only simultaneously possible combination is {1, 2} — a class can exhibit either separation, but not both at once, and it cannot be minor‑closed.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to compare width parameters, first recall the monotonicity properties: treewidth, branchwidth, rank‑width are minor‑monotone; boolean‑width, mim‑width, clique‑width are not. Next, remember the canonical separating families: interval graphs (mim‑width 1, unbounded boolean‑width) and bipartite chain graphs (boolean‑width 1, unbounded mim‑width). If the problem mentions MSO₁ versus MSO₂, associate boolean‑width with MSO₁ and rank‑width/clique‑width with MSO₂. Finally, check whether the class is claimed to be minor‑closed — if it is, the parameter must be minor‑monotone, otherwise the statement is false.

Treedepth: A Structural Parameter for Sparse Graphs

Treedepth measures how close a graph is to a star forest. Formally, the treedepth of a graph G is the minimum height of a rooted forest F such that G is a subgraph of the closure of F (the closure adds an edge between every vertex and all its ancestors). Equivalently, treedepth is the minimum number of colours needed in a centred colouring — a vertex colouring where every connected subgraph contains a colour that appears exactly once. Treedepth is always at least the treewidth plus one, and for trees it equals the height of a minimum‑height rooted tree containing the tree as a subgraph.

Algorithmic applications of treedepth are profound. Many problems that are W[1]‑hard parameterised by treewidth become fixed‑parameter tractable when parameterised by treedepth. For example, the Subgraph Isomorphism problem for a pattern H can be solved in time f(td(H))·nO(1) on host graphs of bounded treedepth, because a bounded‑treedepth host graph admits a low‑height elimination forest that enables dynamic programming over the forest. Moreover, first‑order model checking on graphs of bounded treedepth is linear‑time (by Gaifman’s locality theorem combined with the fact that bounded treedepth implies bounded shrubdepth).

Treedepth also characterises the class of graphs with bounded expansion: a graph class has bounded expansion iff the treedepth of its shallow minors is bounded by a function of the depth. This links treedepth to the broader theory of sparsity (nowhere dense classes, bounded expansion). In examinations, a typical trap is to confuse treedepth with pathwidth or treewidth: while treewidth ≤ pathwidth ≤ treedepth − 1, the gaps can be arbitrarily large (e.g. a complete binary tree has treewidth 1, pathwidth Θ(log n), treedepth Θ(log n)). Another trap is to assume that bounded treedepth implies bounded clique‑width; in fact, graphs of treedepth 2 are exactly the star forests, which have clique‑width 2, but treedepth 3 already contains graphs of unbounded clique‑width.

Shrubdepth and Low‑Height Tree‑Depth Decompositions

Shrubdepth was introduced by Ganian, Hliněný, Nešetřil, Ossona de Mendez and others as a dense‑graph analogue of treedepth. A graph class has bounded shrubdepth if its members can be represented by a tree‑model of bounded height: a rooted tree whose leaves correspond to vertices, each internal node labelled by a binary relation, and adjacency defined by the label of the lowest common ancestor of the two leaves. The height of the tree‑model is the shrubdepth. Bounded shrubdepth implies bounded clique‑width, but the converse fails (e.g. the class of all graphs of clique‑width 2 has unbounded shrubdepth).

The algorithmic relevance of shrubdepth lies in first‑order (FO) model checking. On any class of bounded shrubdepth, FO model checking is fixed‑parameter tractable with an elementary parameter dependence, because the tree‑model provides a natural decomposition for evaluating FO formulas via dynamic programming. This contrasts with bounded clique‑width, where FO model checking is AW[*]‑hard. Moreover, shrubdepth characterises the classes of graphs that are FO‑interpretable in trees of bounded height, linking it to logical interpretations and transductions.

Exam questions often test the relationship between shrubdepth, treedepth and clique‑width. A common trap is to claim that bounded treedepth implies bounded shrubdepth; this is true (treedepth ≤ shrubdepth + 1), but the reverse is false — dense graphs such as complete graphs have shrubdepth 1 but treedepth equal to their order. Another trap is to confuse shrubdepth with rank‑width: rank‑width can be bounded while shrubdepth is unbounded (e.g. distance‑hereditary graphs have rank‑width 1 but unbounded shrubdepth). Knowing the hierarchy — treedepth ≤ shrubdepth ≤ clique‑width ≤ rank‑width (up to functional dependencies) — is essential for selecting the correct parameter in a parameterized‑complexity reduction.

Queue‑Number and Stack‑Number: Linear Layout Parameters Beyond Treewidth

Queue‑number and stack‑number (also called book thickness) are linear layout parameters that measure how a graph can be drawn on a line with edges assigned to queues or stacks so that no two edges in the same queue (resp. stack) are nested (resp. crossing). Formally, a queue layout consists of a vertex ordering σ and a partition of edges into queues such that for any two edges (u, v) and (x, y) with σ(u) < σ(x) < σ(v) < σ(y) (a nesting), the edges must belong to different queues. The queue‑number is the minimum number of queues needed. A stack layout replaces the nesting condition with a crossing condition (σ(u) < σ(x) < σ(y) < σ(v)), and the stack‑number is the minimum number of stacks.

These parameters are incomparable with treewidth. Planar graphs have queue‑number at most 4 (a breakthrough result of Dujmović, Joret, Micek, Morin, Ueckerdt and Wood, 2020) and stack‑number at most 4 (Yannakakis, 1989). However, there are graphs of treewidth 2 with arbitrarily large queue‑number (e.g. certain bipartite graphs), and graphs of queue‑number 1 (i.e. forests) can have arbitrarily large treewidth (e.g. large grids have queue‑number Θ(√n) but treewidth Θ(√n)). The queue‑number of a graph is bounded by its treewidth times its maximum degree, but the converse does not hold.

Algorithmic applications include queue‑based graph drawing, sorting networks, and the design of compact routing schemes. In parameterized complexity, many problems that are hard on general graphs become tractable on graphs of bounded queue‑number or stack‑number because a linear layout with few queues/stacks yields a decomposition of bounded “track‑width”, enabling dynamic programming. A typical exam trap is to assume that bounded queue‑number implies bounded treewidth or vice‑versa; the correct answer is that they are independent parameters. Another trap is to confuse queue‑number with the related “track‑number” (the minimum number of parallel lines needed for a queue layout without crossings); track‑number is at most queue‑number + 1, but the two can differ by a constant factor.

  • Assuming boolean‑width is minor‑monotone and invoking the Graph Minor Theorem for it.
  • Believing bounded mim‑width implies bounded boolean‑width; interval graphs and bipartite chain graphs separate them.
  • Confusing treedepth with pathwidth or treewidth and treating the inequalities as equalities.
  • Claiming bounded treedepth implies bounded clique‑width; treedepth 3 already contains graphs of unbounded clique‑width.
  • Thinking shrubdepth and rank‑width are equivalent; distance‑hereditary graphs have rank‑width 1 but unbounded shrubdepth.
  • Assuming bounded queue‑number implies bounded treewidth (or the converse); planar graphs have bounded queue‑number but unbounded treewidth, while some treewidth‑2 graphs have arbitrarily large queue‑number.
  • Treating stack‑number and queue‑number as the same parameter; they capture nesting versus crossing and can differ arbitrarily.

Boolean‑Width and Its Algorithmic Significance

Boolean‑width is a graph parameter introduced by Bui‑Xuan, Telle, and Vatshelle (2013) to capture the complexity of a graph with respect to a branch decomposition where each cut is evaluated by the number of distinct bipartite subgraphs that can be induced across the cut. Formally, for a branch decomposition (T, δ) of a graph G, the boolean‑width of a cut (A, B) is log₂ of the number of distinct neighbourhoods of subsets of A into B; the boolean‑width of the decomposition is the maximum over all cuts, and the boolean‑width of G is the minimum over all decompositions. This parameter is incomparable with treewidth, clique‑width, and rank‑width: there are graph classes of bounded boolean‑width and unbounded treewidth (e.g. interval graphs), and classes of bounded treewidth but unbounded boolean‑width (e.g. certain bipartite permutation graphs). Crucially, boolean‑width is not minor‑monotone — taking a minor can increase boolean‑width — which prevents a direct application of the Graph Minor Theorem.

From an algorithmic perspective, bounded boolean‑width yields fixed‑parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms for a wide range of problems expressible in monadic second‑order logic (MSO₁) when a decomposition of bounded boolean‑width is given. The dynamic programming table size is 2O(bw) where bw is the boolean‑width, leading to running times of the form O*(2O(bw)). This is exponentially better than the 2O(rw log rw) dependence for rank‑width rw, and it matches the best known dependence for clique‑width. However, computing an optimal boolean‑width decomposition is NP‑hard, and even approximating it within any constant factor remains open. Practical algorithms therefore rely on heuristics or on the fact that many natural graph classes (interval graphs, permutation graphs, trapezoid graphs, convex graphs) admit polynomial‑time constructions of decompositions with boolean‑width at most a constant.

A landmark result by Belmonte, Heggernes, and others (2014) shows that for any graph class of bounded boolean‑width, the Maximum Independent Set, Minimum Dominating Set, and q‑Coloring problems can be solved in time O*(2O(bw)). Moreover, the parameter is closed under taking induced subgraphs and under complementation, which makes it robust for hereditary classes. The relationship with other width parameters can be summarised by the chain: treewidth ≤ pathwidth ≤ boolean‑width ≤ clique‑width ≤ rank‑width (up to functional dependencies). Notably, boolean‑width can be exponentially smaller than rank‑width on certain dense graph families, which explains why some problems that are W[1]‑hard parameterised by rank‑width become FPT when parameterised by boolean‑width.

Mim‑Width: A Unified Width Parameter for Graph Classes

Maximum induced matching width (mim‑width) was introduced by Vatshelle (2012) as a branch‑decomposition based parameter that measures, for each cut (A, B), the size of a maximum induced matching in the bipartite subgraph G[A, B]. The mim‑width of a decomposition is the maximum over all cuts, and the mim‑width of G is the minimum over all branch decompositions. Unlike boolean‑width, mim‑width is minor‑monotone: taking a minor never increases mim‑width. This property allows the use of the Graph Minor Theorem to obtain excluded‑minor characterisations for classes of bounded mim‑width, and it also implies that many algorithmic meta‑theorems (e.g. Courcelle’s theorem for MSO₁) extend to bounded mim‑width classes when a decomposition is provided.

The parameter sits between rank‑width and boolean‑width in the hierarchy: rank‑width ≤ mim‑width ≤ boolean‑width (up to functional dependencies). Interval graphs, permutation graphs, and convex graphs have mim‑width 1, while bipartite chain graphs have mim‑width 1 but unbounded boolean‑width, demonstrating a strict separation. On the other hand, there are graphs of bounded rank‑width but unbounded mim‑width (e.g. certain distance‑hereditary graphs), so mim‑width is strictly more expressive than rank‑width. The algorithmic significance of mim‑width stems from the fact that many NP‑hard problems become polynomial‑time solvable on graphs of bounded mim‑width when a decomposition is given. For instance, Independent Set, Dominating Set, and q‑Coloring admit O*(nO(w)) algorithms where w is the mim‑width, and the exponent depends only on w. This is a dramatic improvement over the 2O(w log w) dependence for rank‑width.

Computing the exact mim‑width is NP‑hard, but for many hereditary classes a decomposition of constant mim‑width can be constructed in polynomial time. The class of graphs with mim‑width at most 1 is exactly the class of graphs that are (C₄, P₄)-free bipartite chain graphs together with their complements, a characterisation that is often used in exam questions to test understanding of the interplay between forbidden induced subgraphs and width parameters. Recent work by Jaffke, Kwon, and others (2020) established that for any fixed w, the class of graphs of mim‑width at most w is well‑quasi‑ordered by the induced subgraph relation, which implies the existence of a finite set of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs — a fact that can be leveraged in parameterised kernelisation arguments.

Worked Example
Consider the complete bipartite graph K3,3. Determine its mim‑width and decide whether the Independent Set problem can be solved in polynomial time on the class of graphs with mim‑width at most 1.
For K3,3, any branch decomposition has a cut that separates the two partite sets. The bipartite subgraph across that cut is exactly K3,3, whose maximum induced matching has size 3 (pick three independent edges). Hence the mim‑width of K3,3 is at least log₂(3) rounded up? Wait, mim‑width is defined as the size of a maximum induced matching, not its logarithm. The maximum induced matching in K3,3 is 3, so the mim‑width of this cut is 3. Since any decomposition must contain such a cut, the mim‑width of K3,3 is 3. The class of graphs with mim‑width at most 1 consists precisely of graphs that do not contain an induced matching of size 2; these are exactly the (C₄, P₄)-free bipartite chain graphs and their complements. Independent Set is polynomial‑time solvable on this class because a decomposition of mim‑width 1 can be found in linear time and the standard dynamic programming runs in O*(nO(1)). Therefore, Independent Set is in P on graphs of mim‑width ≤ 1.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to compare width parameters, first recall the hierarchy: treewidth ≤ pathwidth ≤ boolean‑width ≤ clique‑width ≤ rank‑width, and rank‑width ≤ mim‑width ≤ boolean‑width. Identify whether the parameter is minor‑monotone (treewidth, pathwidth, rank‑width, mim‑width) or not (boolean‑width, clique‑width). For algorithmic questions, note that bounded mim‑width gives nO(w) algorithms, while bounded boolean‑width gives 2O(w) algorithms. If a problem is W[1]‑hard for rank‑width but FPT for mim‑width, the examiner expects you to cite the separation via bipartite chain graphs. Memorise the forbidden‑subgraph characterisation of mim‑width 1 (no induced C₄ or P₄ in the bipartite part) — it appears frequently in multiple‑choice items.

Pathwidth, Cutwidth, and Bandwidth: Linear Layout Parameters

Pathwidth, cutwidth, and bandwidth are classic linear layout parameters that measure how well a graph can be arranged on a line. A path decomposition is a sequence of bags (X₁,…,Xₖ) such that each vertex appears in a contiguous subsequence and each edge has both endpoints in some bag; the width is max|Xᵢ|−1, and the pathwidth pw(G) is the minimum width. Cutwidth asks for a vertex ordering σ that minimises the maximum number of edges crossing any cut between the first i vertices and the rest; the cutwidth cw(G) is that minimum maximum. Bandwidth seeks an ordering σ that minimises the maximum distance |σ(u)−σ(v)| over all edges uv; the bandwidth bw(G) is that minimum maximum distance. These parameters satisfy the inequalities pw(G) ≤ cw(G) ≤ bw(G) ≤ pw(G)·Δ(G) where Δ(G) is the maximum degree, and they are all incomparable with treewidth: there are graphs of treewidth 2 with arbitrarily large pathwidth (e.g. complete binary trees), and graphs of pathwidth 1 (caterpillars) with arbitrarily large treewidth (large grids).

Algorithmic consequences differ sharply. Many problems that are FPT parameterised by treewidth become W[1]‑hard when parameterised by pathwidth (e.g. Hamiltonian Path), while others remain FPT (e.g. Independent Set). Cutwidth and bandwidth are even more restrictive: Independent Set is W[1]‑hard parameterised by cutwidth, but FPT for bandwidth on graphs of bounded degree. The classic result of Monien (1986) shows that computing bandwidth is NP‑complete even for trees of maximum degree 3, whereas pathwidth can be computed in linear time on trees. For interval graphs, pathwidth equals the size of a maximum clique minus 1, and cutwidth equals the maximum number of intervals covering a point, which can be found in O(n log n) time. These exact polynomial‑time algorithms on special classes are a favourite source of exam problems that ask you to recognise the graph class and apply the appropriate formula.

From a structural standpoint, pathwidth is characterised by the vertex‑separation number: pw(G) = vs(G) where vs(G) is the minimum over all orderings of the maximum number of vertices to the left of a cut that have neighbours to the right. This equivalence yields a simple dynamic programming scheme for many problems on graphs of bounded pathwidth. Cutwidth admits a similar characterisation via edge‑separation. Bandwidth, however, lacks a clean decomposition‑based characterisation; its algorithmic treatment often relies on the fact that graphs of bandwidth ≤ b are subgraphs of the b‑th power of a path, which leads to O(nb+1) algorithms for many problems. The interplay between these parameters and treewidth is summarised by the chain: treewidth ≤ pathwidth ≤ cutwidth ≤ bandwidth ≤ pathwidth·Δ. Examiners often test the direction of these inequalities and the existence of separating examples (e.g. complete binary trees separate treewidth from pathwidth; complete bipartite graphs Kn,n separate pathwidth from cutwidth).

The Excluded Minor Characterization for Graphs of Bounded Boolean‑Width

Because boolean‑width is not minor‑monotone, the classical Graph Minor Theorem does not directly yield a finite excluded‑minor characterisation for the class of graphs with boolean‑width at most w. Nevertheless, a series of results by Bui‑Xuan, Telle, and Vatshelle (2013) and later by Belmonte, Heggernes, and others (2015) established that for each fixed w, the class of graphs of boolean‑width ≤ w can be described by a finite set of forbidden vertex‑minors (a vertex‑minor is obtained by a sequence of local complementations and vertex deletions). Vertex‑minor closure is the natural analogue of minor closure for rank‑width and boolean‑width. The forbidden vertex‑minors for boolean‑width 1 are exactly the graphs that contain an induced cycle of length at least 5 or a certain configuration known as the “bull” graph; this characterisation mirrors the one for rank‑width 1 (distance‑hereditary graphs) but is strictly larger.

For boolean‑width 2 the set of minimal forbidden vertex‑minors is already infinite, which means that no finite vertex‑minor obstruction set exists for w ≥ 2. This contrasts sharply with rank‑width, where for every w the class of graphs of rank‑width ≤ w is well‑quasi‑ordered by vertex‑minor and thus has a finite obstruction set (a deep consequence of the Graph Minor Theorem for rank‑width proved by Oum and Seymour, 2007). The absence of a finite obstruction set for boolean‑width ≥ 2 has algorithmic repercussions: it prevents a straightforward application of Courcelle’s theorem on vertex‑minor closed classes, and it explains why recognising graphs of boolean‑width ≤ w is NP‑hard for w ≥ 2 (whereas recognising rank‑width ≤ w is FPT). In examinations, a typical trap is to claim that “bounded boolean‑width implies a finite excluded‑minor characterisation” — the correct answer is that only a finite excluded‑vertex‑minor characterisation exists for w = 1, and for larger w the obstruction set is infinite.

Despite the lack of a finite minor obstruction set, bounded boolean‑width classes enjoy strong algorithmic properties when a decomposition is supplied. The dynamic programming framework of Bui‑Xuan et al. works for any MSO₁‑expressible problem, and the running time is O*(2O(bw)). Moreover, for many hereditary classes (interval graphs, permutation graphs, convex graphs) a decomposition of constant boolean‑width can be constructed in polynomial time, yielding polynomial‑time algorithms for problems that are NP‑hard on general graphs. This dichotomy — hard to recognise, easy to solve once a decomposition is known — is a recurring theme in parameterised complexity and is often tested via scenario‑based questions.

Parameterized Algorithms on Graphs of Bounded Mim‑Width

Given a branch decomposition of mim‑width w, a large family of graph problems can be solved in time nO(w) using dynamic programming over the decomposition tree. The key insight is that for each cut (A, B) the number of distinct neighbourhoods of subsets of A into B is at most nw, because any such neighbourhood can be represented by a set of at most w vertices on the B‑side that form an induced matching with a subset of A. This bound replaces the 2O(w log w) table size of rank‑width and the 2O(w) table size of boolean‑width, yielding a polynomial‑time algorithm for every fixed w. Concrete results include: Independent Set and Dominating Set in O*(n2w+1), q‑Coloring in O*(nqw), and Hamiltonian Cycle in O*(n2w+2). These algorithms are XP (slice‑wise polynomial) but not known to be FPT; indeed, under the Exponential Time Hypothesis, Independent Set parameterised by mim‑width cannot be solved in time f(w)·no(w).

The XP algorithms are complemented by kernelisation results. For example, Dominating Set on graphs of mim‑width w admits a kernel with O(w·kw+1) vertices, where k is the solution size. This kernel is obtained by applying the protrusion‑replacement technique on the branch decomposition, exploiting the fact that bounded mim‑width implies bounded “protrusion treewidth”. The kernel size matches the known lower bound under the assumption that NP ⊄ coNP/poly. In contrast, for boolean‑width the best known kernels are of size 2O(w)·kO(1), reflecting the exponential dependence on the width parameter.

Practical computation of a low‑mim‑width decomposition remains a bottleneck. For interval graphs, permutation graphs, and convex graphs a decomposition of mim‑width 1 can be built in linear time using the natural interval or permutation representation. For general graphs, the best approximation algorithm achieves an O(log n) factor (Vatshelle, 2012), and it is open whether a constant‑factor approximation exists. In exam settings, you may be asked to argue that a given graph class (e.g. circular‑arc graphs) has bounded mim‑width by exhibiting a branch decomposition derived from its geometric representation, or to explain why the existence of an nO(w) algorithm does not contradict the W[1]‑hardness of Independent Set parameterised by treewidth (the parameters are incomparable). Remember that mim‑width is minor‑monotone, so any H‑minor‑free graph class has mim‑width bounded by a function of H; this fact is often used to transfer algorithmic results from bounded mim‑width to H‑minor‑free graphs.

  • Assuming boolean‑width is minor‑monotone and invoking the Graph Minor Theorem for it.
  • Believing bounded mim‑width implies bounded boolean‑width; interval graphs and bipartite chain graphs separate them.
  • Confusing treedepth with pathwidth or treewidth and treating the inequalities as equalities.
  • Claiming bounded treedepth implies bounded clique‑width; treedepth 3 already contains graphs of unbounded clique‑width.
  • Thinking shrubdepth and rank‑width are equivalent; distance‑hereditary graphs have rank‑width 1 but unbounded shrubdepth.
  • Assuming bounded queue‑number implies bounded treewidth (or the converse); planar graphs have bounded queue‑number but unbounded treewidth, while some treewidth‑2 graphs have arbitrarily large queue‑number.
  • Treating stack‑number and queue‑number as the same parameter; they capture nesting versus crossing and can differ arbitrarily.

Graph Minors and the Graph Minor Theorem

The Graph Minor Theorem, proved by Robertson and Seymour over a series of twenty papers, states that the class of all finite graphs is well‑quasi‑ordered by the minor relation. In concrete terms, for any infinite sequence of graphs G₁, G₂, … there exist indices i < j such that Gᵢ is a minor of Gⱼ. This deep structural result has two immediate algorithmic consequences. First, any property that is closed under taking minors can be characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. Second, for every fixed graph H, the problem “does a given graph contain H as a minor?” is solvable in cubic time (later improved to quadratic) because the algorithm can be built from the finite obstruction set supplied by the theorem. The proof hinges on the Graph Structure Theorem, which describes how an H-minor‑free graph can be decomposed into pieces that are “almost embeddable” on a surface of bounded genus, glued together along small separators. This decomposition underlies many fixed‑parameter tractable algorithms parameterised by treewidth or by the size of the excluded minor.

In examinations, a typical question asks to identify the forbidden‑minor characterisation of a given minor‑closed class. For planar graphs the set is {K₅, K₃,₃} (Kuratowski’s theorem). For graphs of treewidth at most k the obstruction set is finite but not explicitly known for k ≥ 3. For linklessly embeddable graphs the forbidden minors are the seven Petersen‑family graphs. Students must remember that the theorem guarantees finiteness of the obstruction set but does not provide it constructively; computing the set for a new class is often an open problem.

Worked Example: Forbidden Minors for Outerplanar Graphs
Determine the complete set of forbidden minors for the class of outerplanar graphs.
A graph is outerplanar iff it has a planar embedding in which all vertices lie on the outer face. The class is minor‑closed. By the Graph Minor Theorem it has a finite obstruction set. It is known (and can be proved by considering minimal non‑outerplanar graphs) that the only minimal forbidden minors are K₄ and K₂,₃. Any graph containing K₄ or K₂,₃ as a minor cannot be outerplanar, and conversely if a graph avoids both minors it admits an outerplanar embedding. Hence the forbidden‑minor set is {K₄, K₂,₃}.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a forbidden‑minor characterisation, first verify that the class is minor‑closed (closed under edge deletion, vertex deletion, and edge contraction). Then recall the classic small sets: planar {K₅, K₃,₃}, outerplanar {K₄, K₂,₃}, series‑parallel {K₄}, linklessly embeddable {Petersen family}. If the class is unfamiliar, argue finiteness via the Graph Minor Theorem and describe how one would search for minimal obstructions using treewidth‑bounded exhaustive enumeration.

Electrical Networks and Effective Resistance in Graphs

The correspondence between resistor networks and graphs is a classical bridge between physics and combinatorics. Each edge of a graph represents a unit resistor; vertices are junctions. Kirchhoff’s current law (1847) states that the sum of currents entering a vertex equals the sum leaving it, while the voltage law says the sum of potential differences around any cycle is zero. Solving these linear equations yields the effective resistance between any two vertices. The effective resistance Reff(u,v) can be expressed using the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse L† of the Laplacian matrix L: Reff(u,v) = (eu−ev)T L† (eu−ev). This formula underpins the Foster’s theorems (1949) which relate the sum of effective resistances over all edges to the number of vertices minus one. In algorithmic contexts, effective resistance provides a natural metric for spectral sparsification: edges with high effective resistance are more important for preserving the quadratic form xTLx. Spielman and Srivastava (2011) showed that sampling edges with probability proportional to weReff(e) yields a (1±ε) spectral sparsifier with O(n log n/ε²) edges. The same quantity appears in random‑walk theory: the commute time between u and v equals 2m·Reff(u,v), where m is the number of edges. This identity connects electrical networks, Markov chains, and the geometry of the graph Laplacian, making effective resistance a central tool in modern graph algorithms.

Interval Graphs and Scheduling Applications

An interval graph is the intersection graph of a family of intervals on the real line. Each vertex corresponds to an interval; two vertices are adjacent exactly when their intervals overlap. Interval graphs are chordal and perfect, so their chromatic number equals the size of a maximum clique, which can be found in linear time by sorting interval endpoints. The classic scheduling interpretation: each interval represents a job that requires a single resource for its duration; the minimum number of resources needed equals the chromatic number. This is the interval‑partitioning problem solved by the greedy algorithm that processes intervals in order of start time and assigns each to the earliest available resource. A deeper result by Fulkerson and Gross (1965) characterises interval graphs as those that are chordal and have a transitive orientation of their complement. In examinations, a typical twist asks to recognise that the complement of an interval graph is a comparability graph, and that the maximum independent set in an interval graph corresponds to a maximum set of non‑overlapping intervals, solvable by the earliest‑finish‑time greedy rule. Weighted variants (weighted interval scheduling) require dynamic programming after sorting by finish time, yielding O(n log n) time. The connection to perfect graphs also means that the clique number, chromatic number, and the size of a maximum independent set can all be computed in polynomial time, a rare tractability island among NP‑hard graph problems.

Worked Example — Resource Allocation
Five jobs have time windows: J₁=[1,4], J₂=[2,6], J₃=[5,7], J₄=[3,5], J₅=[6,8]. Determine the minimum number of identical machines required so that no two overlapping jobs share a machine.
Sort all interval endpoints: 1(start J₁), 2(start J₂), 3(start J₄), 4(end J₁), 5(end J₄, start J₃), 6(end J₂, start J₅), 7(end J₃), 8(end J₅). Sweep line maintaining active count: after 1 →1, after 2 →2, after 3 →3, after 4 →2, after 5 →2, after 6 →2, after 7 →1, after 8 →0. Maximum simultaneous active jobs = 3. Hence three machines are necessary and sufficient. The greedy earliest‑finish‑time assignment produces a valid 3‑machine schedule.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions “intervals on a line” or “jobs with start and finish times”, immediately think interval graph. Recall that the chromatic number equals the maximum number of pairwise overlapping intervals, which is found by a sweep line in O(n log n). For weighted versions, write the DP recurrence: dp[i] = max(weight[i] + dp[p(i)], dp[i‑1]) where p(i) is the last interval finishing before interval i starts. This pattern appears in many optimisation papers.

Molecular Graphs and Topological Indices in Chemistry

Chemical graph theory models molecules as graphs where vertices are atoms (often restricted to non‑hydrogen atoms) and edges are covalent bonds. The earliest topological index, the Wiener index (1947), sums distances between all unordered vertex pairs: W(G)=∑{u,v} d(u,v). It correlates strongly with boiling points of alkanes. The Randić index (1975) R(G)=∑uv∈E (deg(u)·deg(v))−½ was designed to capture branching. The Balaban index (1982) J(G)= (m/(μ+1)) ∑uv∈E (DuDv)−½, where Du is the distance sum from u, refines discrimination among isomers. These indices are graph invariants computable in polynomial time; the Wiener index can be obtained from the Laplacian spectrum via the Kirchhoff index Kf(G)=n∑i=2n λi−1. In drug design, quantitative structure‑property relationship (QSPR) models regress physicochemical properties against a vector of topological indices. The Hosoya index (1971) counts matchings (independent edge sets) and connects to the matching polynomial. Modern chemoinformatics also uses graph kernels (e.g., Weisfeiler–Lehman subtree kernel) for machine‑learning prediction of toxicity. Examiners often test the ability to compute the Wiener index of a tree using the formula W(T)=∑e∈E n1(e)·n2(e), where n1, n2 are component sizes after deleting e. Recognising that the Randić index is simply the sum over edges of the geometric mean of endpoint degrees avoids unnecessary matrix calculations.

Vehicle Routing Problems and Graph Decompositions

The capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) asks for a minimum‑cost set of routes starting and ending at a depot that serve a set of customers with known demands, each vehicle having capacity Q. The underlying graph is complete with edge costs satisfying the triangle inequality. A classic lower bound comes from the minimum spanning tree (MST) of the customer set plus the two cheapest depot edges. The Clarke–Wright savings algorithm (1964) iteratively merges routes by the largest saving s(i,j)=c(depot,i)+c(depot,j)−c(i,j). Christofides’ algorithm (1976) gives a 3/2‑approximation for the travelling salesman problem (TSP), a special case of CVRP with unlimited capacity. For CVRP, the best polynomial‑time approximation ratio remains open; the best known is 2−ε for fixed Q (Haimovich & Rinnooy Kan, 1985). Graph decomposition techniques such as the Held–Karp lower bound (1970) solve the linear programming relaxation of the TSP polytope, whose extreme points correspond to 2‑matchings. The integrality gap of this relaxation is at most 3/2 (conjectured 4/3). In the context of graph minors, Robertson and Seymour’s structure theorem implies that for any fixed excluded minor H, the TSP on H‑minor‑free graphs admits a PTAS (Klein, 2005). Examiners may ask to derive the MST lower bound: double the MST, shortcut repeated vertices using triangle inequality, yielding a 2‑approximation for metric TSP. Understanding the difference between the symmetric TSP (undirected) and the asymmetric TSP (directed) is crucial; the latter has a log‑factor approximation via the Asadpour et al. (2010) algorithm based on thin trees.

Graph States and Measurement‑Based Quantum Computation

A graph state |G⟩ is a multi‑qubit quantum state associated with a simple graph G=(V,E). Prepare each vertex in the |+⟩ state, then apply a controlled‑Z gate for every edge. The resulting state is the unique simultaneous +1 eigenstate of the stabiliser generators Kv=Xv∏u∈N(v) Zu for all v∈V. Local Clifford operations and Pauli measurements on subsets of qubits transform the graph state according to the graphical rules of local complementation and vertex deletion (Van den Nest et al., 2004). Measurement‑based quantum computation (MBQC) uses a universal resource state such as the 2‑D cluster state (a grid graph). Adaptive single‑qubit measurements in the XY‑plane implement arbitrary unitary circuits; the measurement angles depend on previous outcomes, realising feed‑forward. The computational power of a graph state is characterised by its rank‑width and the existence of a flow (Danos & Kashefi, 2006). A graph has a causal flow iff there exists a function f:V→V and a partial order ≺ such that v≺f(v) and N(f(v)){v} ⊆ {u | v≺u}. This condition is checkable in polynomial time and guarantees deterministic MBQC. In examinations, a common question asks to verify that a given graph (e.g., a star) does not admit a flow, while a path does. The connection to classical graph theory is deep: the existence of a flow is equivalent to the graph being a “gflow” graph, which relates to the parity of neighbourhoods and to the rank of the adjacency matrix over GF(2). Understanding these concepts bridges quantum information and structural graph theory.

  • Confusing effective resistance with ordinary graph distance; they coincide only in trees.
  • Assuming every chordal graph is an interval graph; interval graphs are a proper subclass.
  • Using the Wiener index formula for general graphs instead of the tree‑specific edge‑product formula.
  • Thinking the Clarke–Wright savings algorithm always yields an optimal CVRP solution; it is a heuristic.
  • Believing that any graph state can serve as a universal MBQC resource; only states with a flow (or gflow) are deterministic.
  • Mixing up the Randić index (sum over edges) with the Zagreb indices (sum over vertices of degree squares).
  • Overlooking that the Held–Karp bound is a linear‑programming relaxation, not a combinatorial algorithm.

Pathwidth, Cutwidth, and Their Algorithmic Applications

Pathwidth measures how close a graph is to a path by considering a path decomposition where each bag is a vertex set and the bags containing a given vertex form a contiguous subpath. The width of a path decomposition is the size of its largest bag minus one, and the pathwidth of a graph is the minimum width over all such decompositions. Cutwidth, by contrast, is defined for a linear ordering of the vertices: it is the maximum number of edges crossing a cut between the first i vertices and the remaining vertices, minimized over all orderings. Both parameters are monotone under taking minors, so the Robertson–Seymour theory guarantees that for any fixed k the class of graphs with pathwidth ≤ k (or cutwidth ≤ k) is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors.

Algorithmic consequences are profound. Many NP‑hard problems become fixed‑parameter tractable when parameterized by pathwidth or cutwidth. Dynamic programming on a path decomposition runs in time O*(2pw) for problems such as Hamiltonian Path, Dominating Set, and Graph Coloring, where pw denotes the pathwidth. For cutwidth, a similar DP on the linear ordering yields O*(2cw) algorithms, where cw is the cutwidth. Because pathwidth ≤ treewidth + 1, any algorithm that works for treewidth also works for pathwidth, but the converse is false: there are graphs of bounded treewidth and unbounded pathwidth (e.g., complete binary trees). This distinction matters when designing approximation schemes: on graphs of bounded pathwidth one can often obtain PTASes for problems that remain APX‑hard on bounded‑treewidth graphs.

Computing the exact pathwidth is NP‑complete, yet there exist constant‑factor approximation algorithms. The best known polynomial‑time approximation ratio for pathwidth is O(log n) via a reduction to treewidth approximation, while cutwidth admits a O(log² n) approximation through a combination of metric embeddings and linear arrangement techniques. In practice, heuristic orderings such as the Cuthill–McKee algorithm or spectral ordering often produce layouts with small cutwidth for sparse matrices arising in scientific computing.

Applications extend beyond classical graph problems. In VLSI layout, cutwidth corresponds to the maximum number of wires crossing a vertical line, directly influencing chip area. In parallel computing, pathwidth bounds the size of separators needed for divide‑and‑conquer algorithms on graphs. In bioinformatics, the pathwidth of a phylogenetic network correlates with the complexity of reconstructing evolutionary histories. Understanding the interplay between pathwidth and cutwidth therefore equips a candidate to recognise which structural parameter is the natural fit for a given optimisation task.

Examiners frequently test the ability to translate a problem statement into a dynamic‑programming state space on a path decomposition. A typical question provides a graph together with a path decomposition of width 3 and asks for the number of independent sets. The solution requires defining a DP table indexed by subsets of the current bag that are independent, then propagating counts along the path. Mastery of the recurrence and the handling of introduce/forget bags is essential for full marks.

Treedepth, Elimination Trees, and Parameterized Complexity

Treedepth is a depth‑oriented graph invariant defined as the minimum height of a rooted forest whose closure contains the graph as a subgraph. Equivalently, it is the minimum number of colours needed in a centred colouring, where every connected subgraph contains a colour that appears exactly once. Treedepth is always at least the treewidth plus one, and it can be arbitrarily larger; for a path on n vertices the treewidth is 1 while the treedepth is ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉. This logarithmic behaviour makes treedepth the natural parameter for problems that are tractable on graphs of bounded depth but intractable on graphs of bounded treewidth alone.

Elimination trees provide a concrete representation of a treedepth decomposition. Given a rooted forest F, the elimination tree of a graph G with respect to F is obtained by connecting each vertex to its parent in F; the closure of F adds edges between every ancestor–descendant pair. A graph has treedepth ≤ d iff it is a subgraph of the closure of a forest of height d. This characterisation yields a simple fixed‑parameter algorithm: try all possible rooted forests of height d on the vertex set (there are at most nO(d) such forests) and test whether G is a subgraph of the closure. The running time is f(d)·nO(1), establishing that treedepth is a fixed‑parameter tractable parameter.

Many classic problems admit algorithms with running time O*(2td) where td is the treedepth. For example, the Hamiltonian Path problem can be solved by dynamic programming on the elimination tree, storing for each node the set of endpoints of partial paths inside its subtree. Because the height of the tree is td, the number of states per node is bounded by a function of td alone. Similarly, the Graph Isomorphism problem on graphs of bounded treedepth can be solved in polynomial time by a canonical labelling procedure that processes the elimination tree bottom‑up.

Treedepth also governs the complexity of first‑order model checking. By a theorem of Grohe, Kreutzer, and Siebertz, first‑order properties can be decided in linear time on any graph class of bounded treedepth, whereas on classes of bounded treewidth the problem is only fixed‑parameter tractable with respect to the formula size. This sharp dichotomy is a favourite topic in advanced parameterized complexity courses and appears in examination questions that ask to classify the parameterized complexity of a given logical property.

Computing the exact treedepth is NP‑hard, but a 2‑approximation can be obtained by taking a depth‑first search tree of a minimal elimination ordering. Moreover, treedepth is closely related to the graph’s radius and to the size of its largest induced path. In particular, any graph of treedepth d contains an induced path of length at most 2d−1, and conversely a graph with no induced path longer than ℓ has treedepth O(log ℓ). These bounds are useful for deriving lower bounds on treedepth from forbidden induced subgraphs.

Dynamic Programming on an Elimination Tree
Given a graph G with treedepth 3 and an elimination tree T of height 3, describe the DP states and recurrence for counting the number of vertex covers of G.
Root T arbitrarily. For each node v, let B(v) be the set consisting of v and all its ancestors in T (size ≤ 3). A DP state at v is a subset S ⊆ B(v) that is a vertex cover of the subgraph induced by the vertices in the subtree of v, with the additional condition that S contains exactly those vertices of B(v) that are selected. Because |B(v)| ≤ 3, there are at most 2³ = 8 states per node. For a leaf v, the valid states are those where S contains v or all neighbours of v in B(v) (which are just its parent). For an internal node v with children c₁,…,c_k, combine child tables by taking the Cartesian product of compatible states: a state S at v is compatible with a child state S_i if S ∩ B(c_i) = S_i ∩ B(v). The number of covers for S is the product of the child counts. The final answer is the sum of counts over all states at the root. The total running time is O(8²·n) = O(n).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions treedepth, immediately sketch the elimination tree and bound the bag size by the height.
