For the interaction energy F(μ) = ½ ∫∫ W(x-y) dμ(x)dμ(y), it yields the aggregation equation ∂_t ρ = ∇·(ρ ∇W*ρ). For the porous medium energy F(μ) = (1/(m-1))∫ ρᵐ dx, it yields ∂_t ρ = Δρᵐ. The JKO scheme provides existence, uniqueness, and stability of solutions without requiring smoothness, and it underpins the Otto calculus which formally identifies the tangent space of P₂ at μ = ρ dx with the weighted Sobolev space H¹(ρ) with metric ⟨v,w⟩_ρ = ∫ v·w ρ dx. The scheme extends to metric measure spaces satisfying CD(K,∞) (Ambrosio-Gigli-Savaré, 2005), to the Schrödinger problem (Léonard, 2012), and to unbalanced optimal transport (Liero-Mielke-Savaré, 2016). Numerical implementations use entropic regularisation (Cuturi, 2013) and the Sinkhorn algorithm.

Stein's Method and Malliavin-Stein Bounds for Normal Approximation

Stein's method (1972) characterises the standard normal distribution N(0,1) by the equation 𝔼[f'(Z) - Zf(Z)] = 0 for all absolutely continuous f with 𝔼|f'(Z)| < ∞. For a random variable W, the distance to N(0,1) is bounded by solving the Stein equation f'(w) - wf(w) = h(w) - 𝔼[h(Z)] for a test function h. The Malliavin-Stein method combines this with Malliavin calculus on Wiener space. Let F be a centred random variable in the Wiener chaos of order q ≥ 2, with Malliavin derivative DF and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck generator L. The Nourdin-Peccati criterion (2009) states that dTV(F, N(0,σ²)) ≤ (2/σ²)√Var(⟨DF, -DL⁻¹F⟩L²) where dTV is total variation distance. For the Wasserstein distance, d_W(F, N(0,σ²)) ≤ (1/σ²)𝔼|σ² - ⟨DF, -DL⁻¹F⟩L²|. The fourth moment theorem (Nualart-Peccati, 2005) is a special case: a sequence F_n in a fixed Wiener chaos converges in law to N(0,σ²) iff 𝔼[F_n⁴] → 3σ⁴. This is equivalent to ⟨DF_n, -DL⁻¹F_n⟩L² → σ² in L². The method extends to multivariate normal approximation (Nourdin-Peccati-Reinert, 2010) using the Malliavin matrix Γij = ⟨DF_i, DF_j⟩L², to Poisson chaos (Peccati-Zheng, 2010), to free probability (Nourdin-Peccati-Speicher, 2011), and to quantitative invariance principles (Mossel-O'Donnell-Oleszkiewicz, 2010). The bounds are computable for concrete statistics: for the number of triangles in an Erdős-Rényi graph G(n,p), the Malliavin-Stein bound gives a rate of convergence O(n-1/2) in Kolmogorov distance, improving on classical CLT rates. The method also yields Berry-Esseen bounds for dependent sequences via the exchangeable pair approach (Stein, 1986; Chatterjee, 2008).

  • Confusing the Calderón-Zygmund decomposition with the Whitney decomposition: the former splits a function at a height λ using dyadic cubes, the latter covers an open set by dyadic cubes with controlled overlap.
  • Assuming the T(1) theorem applies to all singular integrals: it requires the kernel to satisfy the standard estimates and the weak boundedness property; counterexamples exist without it.
  • Treating H¹ atoms as having vanishing moments of all orders: a (1,∞)-atom only has zeroth moment zero; higher-order atoms are needed for Hardy spaces Hᵖ with p < 1.
  • Neglecting the λ-convexity requirement in the JKO scheme: without it, the minimising movement may not converge to a gradient flow, and the EVI formulation fails.
  • Applying the fourth moment theorem outside a fixed Wiener chaos: the theorem characterises convergence to normality only for sequences living in a single chaos of order q ≥ 2.
  • Confusing the Bakry-Émery CD(ρ,n) condition with the Lott-Villani-Sturm CD(K,N) condition: the former is defined via Γ-calculus on a Markov semigroup, the latter via displacement convexity on the Wasserstein space; they coincide for Riemannian manifolds but differ in generality.
  • Using the Malliavin-Stein bound without verifying the Malliavin differentiability of the random variable: the bounds require F ∈ D1,2 and -DL⁻¹F ∈ D1,2, which fail for some discrete chaos.
The advanced topics above complete the measure-theoretic toolkit needed for research-level problems in harmonic analysis, optimal transport, and stochastic analysis.

Calderón–Zygmund Singular Integrals and the T(1) Theorem

The Calderón–Zygmund theory provides the modern framework for singular integral operators (SIOs) of convolution type Tf = K * f where the kernel K satisfies the size estimate |K(x)| ≤ C|x|−n and the Hölder-type smoothness condition |K(x−y)−K(x)| ≤ C|y|δ|x|−n−δ for |x| > 2|y|. The classical Calderón–Zygmund decomposition splits a function f ∈ L1(ℝn) at height λ into a “good” part g bounded by Cλ and a “bad” part b = Σ bj supported on disjoint dyadic cubes Qj with ∫ bj = 0 and ‖bj‖L1 ≤ Cλ|Qj|. This yields the weak-type (1,1) bound and, by Marcinkiewicz interpolation, strong Lp boundedness for 1 < p < ∞. The T(1) theorem of David and Journé (1984) characterises L2 boundedness for non-convolution SIOs with standard kernels: a linear operator T initially defined on Cc∞ extends boundedly to L2 iff T(1) ∈ BMO, T*(1) ∈ BMO, and T satisfies the weak boundedness property |⟨TφQ, ψQ⟩| ≤ C|Q| for all test functions φQ, ψQ adapted to a cube Q with ‖φQ‖∞, ‖ψQ‖∞ ≤ 1 and support in Q. The proof uses a dyadic decomposition of the kernel and a paraproduct expansion T = Πb + Πb* + Td where b = T(1), b* = T*(1), and Td is a diagonal operator. The T(1) theorem fails without the weak boundedness property; counterexamples by Hofmann (1986) show that T(1), T*(1) ∈ BMO alone are insufficient. The theorem extends to T(b) theorems for accretive systems bQ (Nazarov–Treil–Volberg, 1998), enabling L2 theory on spaces of homogeneous type and for non-doubling measures (Tolsa, 2001).

Hardy Spaces Hp for p ≤ 1 and Atomic Decomposition

The real Hardy space Hp(ℝn) for 0 < p ≤ 1 replaces the Lp norm by the maximal function norm ‖f‖Hp = ‖supt>0 |φt * f|‖Lp where φ ∈ S is a fixed Schwartz function with ∫ φ ≠ 0. For p = 1, Fefferman and Stein (1972) proved the duality (H1)* = BMO, where BMO is the space of functions with bounded mean oscillation ‖b‖BMO = supQ ⨍Q |b−⨍Q b|. The atomic decomposition theorem states that every f ∈ Hp (0 < p ≤ 1) can be written as f = Σ λj aj where aj are (p, q, s)-atoms: supp aj ⊂ Qj, ‖aj‖Lq ≤ |Qj|1/q−1/p, and ∫ xα aj(x) dx = 0 for |α| ≤ s with s ≥ ⌊n(1/p−1)⌋. The sum converges in Hp and Σ |λj|p ≈ ‖f‖Hpp. For p = 1, (1,∞)-atoms have only zeroth moment zero; higher-order atoms are needed for p < 1. Calderón–Zygmund operators extend boundedly from H1 to L1 and from L∞ to BMO, but not on L1 or L∞ themselves. The H1–BMO duality underpins the compensated compactness theory of Coifman–Lions–Meyer–Semmes (1993): if div u = 0 and curl v = 0 then u·v ∈ H1 with ‖u·v‖H1 ≤ C‖u‖L2‖v‖L2. The space VMO (vanishing mean oscillation) is the closure of Cc∞ in BMO and equals the predual of H1. The Fefferman–Stein sharp maximal function f#(x) = supQ∋x ⨍Q |f−⨍Q f| characterises BMO: ‖f‖BMO ≈ ‖f#‖∞.

Worked Example: Atomic Decomposition of an H1 Function
Let f(x) = χ[0,1](x) − χ[1,2](x) on ℝ. Show that f ∈ H1(ℝ) and construct its atomic decomposition.
Step 1: Verify f ∈ H1. The function has integral zero and is supported on [0,2]. Its maximal function is bounded by C/|x|2 for large |x|, hence in L1. Alternatively, f = a1 + a2 where a1 = χ[0,1] − 1/2, a2 = 1/2 − χ[1,2] are not atoms (support not a single cube).
Step 2: Construct atoms. Take Q1 = [0,1], Q2 = [1,2]. Define a1 = χ[0,1] − χ[1,2] on Q1∪Q2? No — atoms must be supported on a single cube. Instead, use the dyadic grid: let Q = [0,2]. Define a = (1/2)f. Then supp a ⊂ Q, ‖a‖∞ = 1/2 ≤ |Q|−1 = 1/2, and ∫ a = 0. So f = 2a with |λ| = 2. Hence ‖f‖H1 ≈ 2.
Step 3: Check duality. For any b ∈ BMO, |∫ f b| = |∫01 b − ∫12 b| ≤ 2‖b‖BMO, confirming ‖f‖H1 ≤ 2.
Exam Strategy: Recognising H1 vs L1
In multiple-choice questions, a function with ∫ f = 0 and compact support is often in H1 but not necessarily in L1 with additional regularity. The key test: if a Calderón–Zygmund operator T maps f to an L1 function, then f ∈ H1. Conversely, if Tf ∉ L1 for some SIO T, then f ∉ H1. Remember that H1 ⊂ L1 strictly; the inclusion fails for p < 1.

Carleson Measures and the Fefferman–Stein Duality of BMO

A positive Borel measure μ on the upper half-space ℝn+1+ = {(x, t) : x ∈ ℝn, t > 0} is a Carleson measure if supQ⊂ℝn μ(T(Q))/|Q| < ∞, where T(Q) = Q × (0, ℓ(Q)) is the Carleson box over the cube Q. The Carleson embedding theorem (1962) states that for f ∈ L2(ℝn), the measure dμ(x, t) = |t∇x,t u(x, t)|2 dx dt/t is Carleson iff u is the Poisson extension of some b ∈ BMO(ℝn), with ‖b‖BMO ≈ supQ (μ(T(Q))/|Q|)1/2. Fefferman and Stein (1972) used this to prove (H1)* = BMO: every continuous linear functional on H1 is represented by a BMO function via ⟨f, b⟩ = ∫ f b, and the pairing extends to f ∈ H1, b ∈ BMO by duality. The proof constructs a Carleson measure from the tent space T2 of functions F(x, t) with ‖F‖T2 = ‖(∫Γ(x) |F(y, t)|2 dy dt/tn+1)1/2‖L2, where Γ(x) is the cone {(y, t) : |x−y| < t}. The dual of T2 is the tent space T2,∞ of Carleson measures. The atomic decomposition of H1 corresponds to the fact that H1 embeds into T1 via the Lusin area integral. Carleson measures also characterise the boundedness of the Littlewood–Paley g-function: ‖g(f)‖Lp ≈ ‖f‖Lp for 1 < p < ∞, and the failure at p = 1 is measured by the Carleson norm of |t∇u|2 dx dt/t. The T(b) theorem of Nazarov–Treil–Volberg (1998) generalises the T(1) theorem by testing on accretive functions bQ adapted to a dyadic grid; the testing conditions involve Carleson measures |⟨T(bQφQ), ψQ⟩|2 dx dt/t. This framework underpins the solution of the L2 boundedness problem for the Cauchy integral on Lipschitz curves (Coifman–McIntosh–Meyer, 1982) and the L2 theory of singular integrals on non-doubling measure spaces (Tolsa, 2001).

Lévy Processes, the Lévy–Itô Decomposition, and Stochastic Integration

A Lévy process (Xt)t≥0 on ℝd is a càdlàg stochastic process with independent and stationary increments, X0 = 0 a.s., and continuous in probability. The Lévy–Khintchine formula gives the characteristic exponent: 𝔼[ei⟨ξ,Xt⟩] = e−tΨ(ξ) with Ψ(ξ) = −i⟨γ, ξ⟩ + ½⟨ξ, Aξ⟩ + ∫ℝd∖{0} (1 − ei⟨ξ,x⟩ + i⟨ξ, x⟩1{|x|<1}) ν(dx), where γ ∈ ℝd, A is a positive semidefinite matrix, and ν is a Lévy measure satisfying ∫ min(1, |x|2) ν(dx) < ∞. The Lévy–Itô decomposition (1940s) splits Xt into three independent components: Xt = γt + Bt + ∫0t∫|x|<1 x (N−ν)(ds dx) + ∫0t∫|x|≥1 x N(ds dx), where B is a Brownian motion with covariance A, and N is a Poisson random measure on ℝ+ × (ℝd∖{0}) with intensity ds ν(dx). The compensated small jumps form a square-integrable martingale; the large jumps form a compound Poisson process. Stochastic integration with respect to X is defined for predictable processes H satisfying ∫0T (|Hs|2‖A‖ + ∫ |Hsx|2 ∧ |Hsx| ν(dx)) ds < ∞. The integral ∫0t Hs dXs decomposes into a continuous martingale part ∫ Hs dBs, a compensated small-jump martingale ∫∫|x|<1 Hsx (N−ν)(ds dx), and a large-jump integral ∫∫|x|≥1 Hsx N(ds dx). The Itô formula for C2 functions f reads f(Xt) = f(0) + ∫0t ∇f(Xs−)·dXsc + ½∫0t Tr(∇2f(Xs−)A) ds + Σs≤t [f(Xs) − f(Xs−) − ∇f(Xs−)·ΔXs], where Xc is the continuous martingale part. The semimartingale characteristics (B, C, ν) of X are Bt = γt, Ct = At, and ν(dt dx) = dt ν(dx). Infinitely divisible distributions correspond bijectively to Lévy triplets (γ, A, ν). Stable processes have ν(dx) = |x|−d−α dx for α ∈ (0,2); the fractional Laplacian −(−Δ)α/2 is their infinitesimal generator. Subordinators are increasing Lévy processes with ν supported on (0,∞) and zero Gaussian part; they provide time changes for Brownian motion yielding variance-gamma and normal inverse Gaussian processes used in finance.

Dirichlet Forms, Fukushima's Decomposition, and Quasi-Regularity

A Dirichlet form on L2(E, m) is a closed, symmetric, Markovian bilinear form (ℰ, ℱ) with ℱ ⊂ L2 dense, satisfying the Beurling–Deny criteria: ℰ(u+ ∧ 1, u+ ∧ 1) ≤ ℰ(u, u) for all u ∈ ℱ. The associated generator L is a negative self-adjoint operator with domain 𝒟(L) ⊂ ℱ. The Beurling–Deny decomposition (1958) splits ℰ into a strongly local part ℰc (diffusion), a jump part ℰj = ∫E×E∖diag (u(x)−u(y))2 J(dx dy), and a killing part ℰk(u) = ∫ u2 k(dx). A Dirichlet form is quasi-regular (Ma–Röckner, 1992) if there exists an ℰ-nest of compact sets, a dense subset of ℱ ∩ Cc(E) in the ℰ1-norm, and an ℰ-quasi-continuous m-version for each u ∈ ℱ. Quasi-regularity is equivalent to the existence of an associated Hunt process (a strong Markov process with càdlàg paths and quasi-left-continuity). Fukushima's decomposition (1980) states that for any u ∈ ℱloc (local Dirichlet space), the additive functional u(Xt) − u(X0) decomposes uniquely as M[u]t + N[u]t, where M[u] is a martingale additive functional (MAF) of finite energy and N[u] is a continuous additive functional (CAF) of zero energy. The MAF further splits into a continuous part M[u]c and a purely discontinuous part M[u]d. The energy measure μu of u satisfies ℰ(u, v) = ½∫ dμu,v for u, v ∈ ℱloc ∩ L∞. For the classical Dirichlet form ℰ(u, v) = ∫ ∇u·∇v dx on ℝd, μu = |∇u|2 dx, M[u]c is the stochastic integral ∫ ∇u(Xs)·dBs, and N[u] = 0. For jump-type forms, M[u]d is the compensated sum of jumps. The Revuz correspondence gives a bijection between positive smooth measures μ and positive continuous additive functionals A via limt↓0 (1/t) 𝔼m[∫0t f(Xs) dAs] = ∫ f dμ. This identifies the killing measure k with the CAF of zero energy that terminates the process. The theory extends to non-symmetric forms (Stroock–Varadhan, Ouhabaz) and to metric measure spaces via the Cheeger energy Ch(u) = ½∫ |∇u|2 dm, whose relaxation yields a Dirichlet form on RCD(K, N) spaces (Ambrosio–Gigli–Savaré, 2014).

  • Confusing the Calderón–Zygmund decomposition with the Whitney decomposition: the former splits a function at height λ using dyadic cubes with mean-zero bad parts; the latter covers an open set by dyadic cubes with controlled overlap and no cancellation.
  • Assuming the T(1) theorem applies to all singular integrals: it requires the kernel to satisfy standard estimates and the weak boundedness property; counterexamples exist without it.
  • Treating H1 atoms as having vanishing moments of all orders: a (1,∞)-atom only has zeroth moment zero; higher-order atoms are needed for Hardy spaces Hp with p < 1.
  • Neglecting the accretivity condition in the T(b) theorem: the testing functions bQ must satisfy Re bQ ≥ δ > 0; without it, the paraproduct expansion fails.
  • Confusing the Lévy measure ν with the jump measure of the process: ν is the intensity of the Poisson random measure N; the actual jumps are the atoms of N, and ∫|x|≥1 ν(dx) < ∞ ensures finitely many large jumps per unit time.
  • Applying the Itô formula for continuous semimartingales to Lévy processes without the jump correction: the term Σ [f(Xs) − f(Xs−) − ∇f(Xs−)·ΔXs] is essential and cannot be omitted.
  • Assuming every Dirichlet form is quasi-regular: quasi-regularity is a non-trivial condition equivalent to the existence of an associated Hunt process; general Dirichlet forms on non-locally-compact spaces may fail it.

Hausdorff Measures and Fractal Dimension

The Hausdorff measure generalises length, area, and volume to non‑integer dimensions. For a metric space X and s ≥ 0, the s‑dimensional Hausdorff measure ℋs is defined by the Carathéodory construction: for each δ > 0 let ℋsδ(E) = inf{ Σi (diam Ui)s : E ⊂ ⋃ Ui, diam Ui ≤ δ }; then ℋs(E) = limδ→0 ℋsδ(E). Felix Hausdorff introduced this in 1918; Carathéodory’s 1914 outer measure framework makes it a metric outer measure. The Hausdorff dimension dimH(E) = inf{ s : ℋs(E) = 0 } = sup{ s : ℋs(E) = ∞ }.

Key tools include Frostman’s lemma (1935): a Borel set E ⊂ ℝd has dimH(E) ≥ s iff there exists a non‑zero Borel measure μ supported on E with μ(B(x,r)) ≤ C rs for all balls. This links capacity and dimension. The Marstrand projection theorem (1954) states that for a Borel set E ⊂ ℝ2 with dimH(E) = s ≤ 1, almost every orthogonal projection onto a line has Hausdorff dimension s; if s > 1, almost every projection has positive length. The Besicovitch covering theorem (1945) guarantees a bounded overlap covering by balls, essential for differentiation of measures.

Classic examples: the middle‑third Cantor set has dimH = log 2 / log 3 and 0 < ℋlog 2/log 3(C) < ∞. The von Koch curve has dimension log 4 / log 3. For Brownian motion paths in ℝd (d ≥ 2), S. J. Taylor (1953) proved dimH = 2 almost surely; Kaufman (1969) showed that for any analytic map f, dimH(f(B[0,1])) ≤ 2 dimH(B[0,1]). These results underpin modern fractal geometry and the analysis of stochastic processes.

Carleson Measures and the Corona Theorem

A positive Borel measure μ on the unit disc 𝔻 is a Carleson measure if there exists C > 0 such that for every arc I ⊂ ∂𝔻, μ(S(I)) ≤ C |I|, where S(I) = { reiθ : eiθ ∈ I, 1−|I|/(2π) ≤ r < 1 } is the Carleson square. The Carleson embedding theorem (1962) asserts that the identity map H1(𝔻) → L1(μ) is bounded iff μ is a Carleson measure. This characterises the boundedness of the Hilbert transform on weighted spaces and underlies the duality (H1)* = BMO proved by Fefferman (1971).

The Corona theorem (Carleson 1962) solved a long‑standing problem: given f1,…,fn ∈ H∞(𝔻) with Σ |fk(z)| ≥ δ > 0 for all z ∈ 𝔻, there exist g1,…,gn ∈ H∞(𝔻) such that Σ fk gk = 1. Carleson’s proof introduced the Carleson measure condition on the measure |∂f|2 (1−|z|) dA(z) and a sophisticated stopping‑time argument. Later, Wolff (1980) gave a simpler proof using BMO and the John–Nirenberg inequality. The theorem has deep consequences for control theory (the matrix corona problem) and for the structure of maximal ideal spaces of H∞.

Applications extend to the T(1) theorem of David and Journé (1984), where Carleson measures control the boundedness of singular integral operators on non‑homogeneous spaces. In several complex variables, the Carleson measure for the Bergman space Ap(𝔻) is defined by μ(S(I)) ≤ C |I|p+1; the embedding Ap Lp(μ) is bounded exactly for such measures (Luecking 1985).

Technique: Verifying the Carleson Measure Condition
Show that the discrete measure μ = Σn=1∞ 2−n δzn with zn = 1 − 2−n is a Carleson measure on 𝔻.

For an arc I ⊂ ∂𝔻 of length |I|, the Carleson square S(I) contains those zn with 1−|zn| ≤ |I|/(2π). Since 1−|zn| = 2−n, the condition is 2−n ≤ |I|/(2π), i.e. n ≥ log2(2π/|I|). The sum of masses in S(I) is Σn ≥ N 2−n = 2−N+1 ≤ 4π |I|. Hence μ(S(I)) ≤ C |I| with C = 4π, so μ is a Carleson measure.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When asked to test whether a discrete measure is Carleson, first express the distance of each atom to the boundary in terms of its index. Then estimate the tail sum of masses for atoms whose distance is smaller than the arc length. A geometric series bound almost always yields the required constant.

SRB Measures and Statistical Properties of Chaotic Systems

For a C2 diffeomorphism f on a compact manifold M preserving a hyperbolic attractor, a Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen (SRB) measure μ is an f‑invariant probability measure whose conditional measures on unstable manifolds are absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Ya. Sinai (1972) constructed SRB measures for Anosov diffeomorphisms; Ruelle (1976) and Bowen (1975) extended the theory to Axiom A attractors. The physical measure property means that for Lebesgue‑almost every initial point x in the basin, time averages converge to space averages: limn→∞ (1/n) Σk=0n−1 φ(fk(x)) = ∫ φ dμ for all continuous φ.

Key results: Existence and uniqueness of SRB measures for transitive Axiom A attractors (Bowen–Ruelle). Exponential decay of correlations for Hölder observables (Dolgopyat 1998 for certain non‑uniformly hyperbolic systems). The Pesin entropy formula hμ(f) = ∫ Σ λi+ dμ relates metric entropy to positive Lyapunov exponents. The Ledrappier–Young formula (1985) gives the Hausdorff dimension of μ in terms of Lyapunov exponents and entropy. For the Hénon map (Benedicks–Carleson 1991) and the Lorenz attractor (Tucker 1999, computer‑assisted), SRB measures have been rigorously established, confirming that these systems exhibit genuine chaotic statistics.

Applications: In smooth ergodic theory, SRB measures provide the rigorous foundation for the fluctuation–dissipation theorem and linear response (Ruelle 1997). In numerical analysis, they justify the use of time averages to approximate space averages in molecular dynamics and climate models.

Patterson–Sullivan Measures on Hyperbolic Groups

Let Γ be a non‑elementary Kleinian group acting on hyperbolic space ℍn+1. The critical exponent δ(Γ) = inf{ s > 0 : Σγ∈Γ e−s d(o,γo) < ∞ } equals the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set Λ(Γ) ⊂ ∂ℍn+1. S. J. Patterson (1976) constructed a family of conformal densities {μx}x∈ℍ of dimension δ(Γ) on Λ(Γ) satisfying μγx = γ*μx and dμy/dμx(ξ) = e−δ βξ(y,x), where β is the Busemann function. D. Sullivan (1979) used these measures to prove that δ(Γ) = dimH(Λ(Γ)) and to establish the Sullivan rigidity theorem: if two geometrically finite Kleinian groups are topologically conjugate on their limit sets, the conjugacy is the restriction of a Möbius transformation.

The Bowen–Margulis measure on the unit tangent bundle T1(ℍ/Γ) is the product of Patterson–Sullivan measures on stable and unstable foliations; it is the unique measure of maximal entropy for the geodesic flow. This yields precise asymptotics for closed geodesics: the number of closed geodesics of length ≤ T grows like eδT/(δT) (Margulis 1969). For convex‑cocompact groups, the Patterson–Sullivan measure coincides with the harmonic measure of the Brownian motion on ℍ/Γ (Sullivan 1983). The construction extends to word‑hyperbolic groups (Coornaert 1993), where the visual metric on the Gromov boundary makes the Patterson–Sullivan measure a δ‑conformal density.

Information Geometry: Fisher–Rao Metric and Exponential Families

Information geometry studies statistical models as differentiable manifolds endowed with the Fisher–Rao metric gij(θ) = 𝔼θ[ ∂i log p(x;θ) ∂j log p(x;θ) ]. N. N. Chentsov (1972) proved that this metric is the unique (up to scale) Riemannian metric on the simplex of probability distributions invariant under sufficient statistics. For an exponential family p(x;θ) = exp( θ·T(x) − ψ(θ) ) h(x), the Fisher metric is the Hessian of the log‑partition function: gij = ∂i∂j ψ(θ). The manifold is dually flat with respect to the α‑connections ∇(α) introduced by Amari (1982); the mixture connection (α = −1) and the exponential connection (α = +1) are dual with respect to g.

The Kullback–Leibler divergence DKL(p‖q) = ∫ p log(p/q) acts as a Bregman divergence generated by ψ. The Cramér–Rao bound states that for any unbiased estimator θ̂, Cov(θ̂) ≥ g(θ)−1. In machine learning, the natural gradient ∇̃L = g(θ)−1∇L follows the steepest descent direction under the Fisher metric, leading to faster convergence in policy‑gradient reinforcement learning (Kakade 2001). The Amari–Chentsov tensor Tijk = 𝔼[ ∂i∂j log p ∂k log p ] measures the skewness of the statistical manifold; it vanishes exactly for exponential families, characterising their dually flat structure.

  • Confusing Hausdorff dimension with box‑counting dimension: the latter may be strictly larger (e.g. for certain Moran sets).
  • Assuming every Carleson measure is a discrete sum of point masses; continuous Carleson measures (e.g. |f′|2(1−|z|) dA) are equally important.
  • Treating SRB measures as invariant under all diffeomorphisms; they exist only for systems with some hyperbolicity (Axiom A or non‑uniform hyperbolicity).
  • Neglecting the conformal factor in Patterson–Sullivan measures: the density transformation involves the Busemann function, not just the Jacobian of the boundary map.
  • Believing the Fisher–Rao metric is flat for all statistical models; flatness holds only for exponential families (α = ±1 connections).
  • Applying the Cramér–Rao bound without checking regularity conditions (differentiability under the integral, support independence of θ).
  • Overlooking that the Corona theorem fails for H∞ of the polydisc (n ≥ 2); the multivariable case requires the Briançon–Skoda type conditions.

Non‑Atomic Measures and the Construction of Lebesgue‑Stieltjes Measures on ℝ

While the Lebesgue measure on ℝ is the prototypical non‑atomic (or continuous) measure, many problems in analysis and probability require a more flexible family of non‑atomic measures that arise from monotone functions. Given a right‑continuous, non‑decreasing function F : ℝ → ℝ, the Lebesgue‑Stieltjes measure μ_F is defined by

μ_F((a,b]) = F(b) – F(a) for all a < b.

Key properties of μ_F follow directly from the structure of F:

  • Non‑atomicity. μ_F({x}) = F(x) – limy↑xF(y). If F is continuous at x, the atom at x vanishes. Thus any continuous F yields a purely non‑atomic measure.
  • σ‑finiteness. Since ℝ can be written as a countable union of bounded intervals, each of finite μ_F‑measure, μ_F is σ‑finite whenever F is of bounded variation on every compact set.
  • Absolute continuity. μ_F is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure λ iff F is absolutely continuous in the classical sense; then the Radon‑Nikodym derivative dμ_F/dλ exists a.e. and equals F′.

Two classical examples illustrate the breadth of this construction:

  1. Uniform distribution on an interval. Take F(x)=0 for x≤a, F(x)=(x−a)/(b−a) for a<x<b, and F(x)=1 for x≥b. Then μ_F coincides with λ restricted to (a,b) and scaled by 1/(b−a). This is the standard continuous uniform probability law.</li>
  2. Cantor‑Lebesgue measure. Let C be the middle‑third Cantor set and define F as the Cantor function (also called the Devil’s staircase). F is continuous, non‑decreasing, and constant on each removed interval, yet increases from 0 to 1 on C. The resulting μ_F is a singular continuous probability measure: it assigns zero mass to every interval (hence non‑atomic) but is supported entirely on a set of Lebesgue measure zero.

In probability theory, the correspondence “distribution function probability measure” is precisely the Lebesgue‑Stieltjes construction. The Kolmogorov extension theorem (see later sections) uses this to define stochastic processes from consistent finite‑dimensional distributions, each of which is a product of Lebesgue‑Stieltjes measures.

When solving exam problems, it is crucial to recognise whether a given distribution function is continuous, has jump discontinuities, or possesses a singular component. The decomposition theorem for measures states that any finite Borel measure μ on ℝ can be uniquely written as

μ = μ_ac + μ_sc + μ_pp,

where μ_ac is absolutely continuous w.r.t. λ, μ_sc is singular continuous (as in the Cantor case), and μ_pp is purely atomic (a sum of point masses). This trichotomy often appears in questions that ask for the Lebesgue decomposition of a given probability law.

Outer Regularity, Inner Regularity, and the Role of Regular Measures in Locally Compact Spaces

In many applications—particularly in harmonic analysis and potential theory—one needs measures that interact well with the topology of the underlying space. A Borel measure μ on a metric space (X,d) is called regular if it satisfies two complementary approximation properties:

  • Outer regularity. For every Borel set A,

    • μ(A) = inf{ μ(U) : A ⊂ U, U open }.

  • Inner regularity. For every open set U,

    • μ(U) = sup{ μ(K) : K ⊂ U, K compact }.

When X is locally compact and Hausdorff, every finite Borel measure admits a unique regular extension from the algebra of compact sets. This is the content of the Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem, which identifies the dual of C_c(X) (continuous functions with compact support) with the space of regular Borel measures.

Key consequences for exam‑level problems include:

  1. Approximation of integrals. If μ is regular and f∈L¹(μ) is non‑negative, then for any ε>0 there exists a compact K⊂X such that ∫XK f dμ < ε. This allows one to replace integrals over the whole space by integrals over compact subsets, a technique frequently used in proofs of the dominated convergence theorem on non‑σ‑compact spaces.
  2. Portmanteau theorem for weak convergence. In the setting of probability measures on a Polish space, weak convergence μ_n ⇒ μ is equivalent to convergence of μ_n(F) to μ(F) for all closed sets F, provided the limit measure μ is regular. This regularity hypothesis is often implicit in exam statements that invoke “convergence in distribution”.
  3. Product regularity. If μ and ν are regular Borel measures on locally compact spaces X and Y, then the product measure μ×ν on X×Y is regular. This fact underlies the validity of Fubini’s theorem for a broad class of measures beyond Lebesgue, such as Haar measure on locally compact groups.

Typical pitfalls arise when students assume regularity for arbitrary Borel measures on non‑locally‑compact spaces (e.g., infinite‑dimensional Banach spaces). In such settings, inner regularity may fail, and one must work with the weaker notion of Radon measures (inner regular on all Borel sets, not just open ones). Recognising the ambient topology is therefore essential.

Martingale Problems, Uniqueness of Solutions, and the Stroock‑Varadhan Framework

The martingale problem, introduced by Stroock and Varadhan in the 1970s, provides a measure‑theoretic formulation of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) that bypasses explicit construction of stochastic integrals. Given a linear operator A defined on a core 𝔇⊂C_b(ℝ^d), the (A,𝔇)-martingale problem asks for a probability measure P on the canonical path space C([0,∞),ℝ^d) such that for every f∈𝔇, the process

M_f(t) = f(X_t) – f(X0) – ∫0^t A f(X_s) ds

is a P‑martingale with respect to the natural filtration.

When A is the generator of a diffusion, i.e.

A f(x) = ∑i=1^d b_i(x) ∂x_i f(x) + ½ ∑i,j=1^d aij(x) ∂x_i∂x_j f(x),

with drift b and diffusion matrix a = σσ^T, the martingale problem is equivalent to the SDE

dX_t = b(X_t) dt + σ(X_t) dW_t.

Two fundamental results shape the exam syllabus:

  1. Existence under bounded measurable coefficients. If b and σ are bounded and σ is uniformly non‑degenerate (i.e., there exists λ>0 such that ξ^T a(x) ξ ≥ λ|ξ|² for all ξ and x), then the (A,𝔇)-martingale problem admits a solution. The proof uses the Krylov–Safonov estimate and tightness of approximating measures.
  2. Uniqueness via the Stroock‑Varadhan support theorem. If the coefficients are Lipschitz continuous, the martingale problem has a unique solution, which coincides with the strong solution of the SDE. Moreover, the support of the law of X under P is the closure of the set of solutions to the associated deterministic control system ẋ = b(x) + σ(x)u, u∈L².

Exam questions often ask to verify whether a given operator defines a well‑posed martingale problem. A common strategy is to check the following checklist:

  • Domain 𝔇 contains C_c^∞(ℝ^d) (smooth compactly supported functions).
  • Coefficients satisfy linear growth: |b(x)| + |σ(x)| ≤ C(1+|x|).
  • Uniform ellipticity or non‑degeneracy condition for a(x).

If any of these fail, one must either construct a counterexample (e.g., a diffusion with degenerate σ leading to non‑uniqueness) or invoke a more refined theorem such as Engelbert–Schmidt’s criteria for one‑dimensional SDEs.

Entropy Methods in Measure‑Theoretic Probability: Log‑Sobolev Inequalities and Hypercontractivity

Entropy techniques connect functional inequalities with the speed of convergence of Markov semigroups to equilibrium. Let (P_t)t≥0 be a symmetric Markov semigroup on L²(μ), where μ is a probability measure invariant under P_t. The relative entropy of a density f ≥ 0 with ∫ f dμ =1 is

Ent_μ(f) = ∫ f log f dμ.

A measure μ satisfies a log‑Sobolev inequality (LSI) with constant C>0 if

Ent_μ(f) ≤ 2C ∫ |∇√f|² dμ for all smooth f≥0.

Key implications for exam problems:

  1. Hypercontractivity. Gross’s theorem states that LSI with constant C is equivalent to the semigroup being hypercontractive: for t≥C log(p−1), the operator P_t maps L²(μ) into L^p(μ) with norm ≤1. This provides a quantitative bound on how quickly moments improve under the flow.
  2. Exponential convergence in entropy. If μ satisfies LSI(C), then for any initial density f₀, the entropy decays exponentially:

    3. Ent_μ(P_t f₀) ≤ e-2t/C Ent_μ(f₀).

  3. Tensorisation. If μ₁ and μ₂ each satisfy LSI with constants C₁ and C₂, then the product measure μ₁⊗μ₂ satisfies LSI with constant max(C₁,C₂). This property is frequently used to handle high‑dimensional product spaces, such as the Gaussian measure on ℝⁿ.

Classical examples:

  • Standard Gaussian measure γ_n on ℝⁿ. LSI holds with constant C=1. The associated Ornstein‑Uhlenbeck semigroup is hypercontractive, a fact that underlies many concentration‑of‑measure results.
  • Uniform measure on the sphere Sn‑1. By the Bakry‑Émery curvature‑dimension condition, the spherical measure satisfies LSI with constant C = 1/(n‑2) for n≥3, leading to sharp concentration inequalities for Lipschitz functions on the sphere.

In competitive examinations, a typical question may present a Markov chain with transition matrix P and ask whether the stationary distribution π satisfies an LSI. The correct approach is to compute the spectral gap λ₁ of the generator (I‑P) and use the inequality C ≤ 1/λ₁ when the chain is reversible. Misidentifying the constant or overlooking reversibility is a frequent source of error.

Technique: Using the Portmanteau Theorem with Regular Measures
Let μ_n be a sequence of probability measures on ℝ defined by μ_n(A) = ∫_A (1+sin(nx))⁺ / (2π) dx, where (·)⁺ denotes the positive part. Show that μ_n converges weakly to the Lebesgue measure λ restricted to [0,2π] and compute the limit of μ_n([0,π]).

Step 1 – Identify the limit candidate. The function f_n(x)= (1+sin(nx))⁺ / (2π) oscillates rapidly between 0 and 1/π. By the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma, the average of sin(nx) over any interval tends to zero, so the weak limit of μ_n should be the measure with density 1/(2π) on [0,2π], i.e. λ[0,2π]/(2π).

Step 2 – Verify tightness. Since each μ_n is supported on [0,2π] and total mass equals 1, the family is tight.

Step 3 – Apply the Portmanteau theorem. For any closed set F⊂[0,2π],

limsupn→∞ μ_n(F) ≤ λ(F)/(2π).

For any open set G⊂[0,2π],

liminfn→∞ μ_n(G) ≥ λ(G)/(2π).

Because λ is regular, these inequalities together imply μ_n ⇒ λ/(2π) on [0,2π].

Step 4 – Compute the limit of μ_n([0,π]). The limit measure assigns mass λ([0,π])/(2π)=π/(2π)=½. Hence

limn→∞ μ_n([0,π]) = ½.

Thus the sequence converges weakly to the uniform probability measure on [0,2π], and the required limit is ½.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question involves weak convergence or limit theorems for measures, first check whether the underlying measures are regular (or Radon). Regularity guarantees that you can replace arbitrary Borel sets by open or compact approximations, which is exactly what the Portmanteau theorem requires. Write down the open/closed set inequalities explicitly; this often earns partial credit even if you do not finish the full proof.

Disintegration of Measures and Regular Conditional Probabilities in Product Spaces

Disintegration formalises the intuitive idea of “splitting” a measure on a product space into a family of conditional measures on one factor, parametrised by points of the other factor. Let (X,𝔅_X,μ) and (Y,𝔅_Y,ν) be σ‑finite measure spaces and consider the product measure μ⊗ν on X×Y. A regular conditional probability (RCP) of μ⊗ν given the σ‑algebra 𝔅_X is a measurable map

y ↦ μ_y with μ_y ∈ 𝔐⁺(Y), such that for every measurable A⊂Y, the function x↦μ_x(A) is 𝔅_X‑measurable and

(μ⊗ν)(B×A) = ∫_B μ_x(A) dμ(x) for all B∈𝔅_X, A∈𝔅_Y.

The existence of such a family relies on two structural facts:

  1. Standard Borel spaces. If X and Y are Polish (complete separable metric) spaces equipped with their Borel σ‑algebras, then every probability measure on X×Y admits a disintegration relative to the projection onto X. This is a consequence of the existence of regular conditional probabilities on standard Borel spaces.
  2. Uniqueness up to μ‑null sets. If {μ_x} and {μ'_x} are two disintegrations, then μ_x = μ'_x for μ‑almost every x. Hence the conditional law is well defined μ‑a.e.

Applications in exam settings:

  • Conditional expectation as an integral of conditional measures. For an integrable random variable Z on X×Y, the conditional expectation E[Z|𝔅_X] can be written as x ↦ ∫_Y Z(x,y) dμ_x(y). This representation is often used to prove the tower property or to compute explicit conditional expectations in problems involving mixtures of distributions.
  • Bayes’ formula in abstract form. If μ is a joint distribution of (Θ,X) and ν is the marginal of Θ, the disintegration yields the posterior distribution μ_θ(dx) = P(X∈dx | Θ=θ). The Bayes update becomes a concrete integral against μ_θ, which is useful when the prior or likelihood is given in measure‑theoretic language.
  • Fubini’s theorem for non‑σ‑finite measures. When ν is not σ‑finite, the usual Fubini theorem may fail, but a disintegration still provides a way to integrate first with respect to the conditional measures μ_x, provided the family satisfies appropriate integrability conditions.

Typical exam traps involve neglecting the measurability requirement of the map x↦μ_x(A). One must verify that for each fixed A, the function is indeed 𝔅_X‑measurable; otherwise the integral ∫ μ_x(A) dμ(x) is not defined. In practice, when X and Y are Euclidean spaces with the Borel σ‑algebra, this measurability follows from the standard construction using regular versions of conditional probabilities.

  • Confusing the Lebesgue‑Stieltjes measure of a discontinuous distribution function with its atomic part; always separate jump contributions from the continuous component.
  • Assuming every Borel measure on a metric space is regular; inner regularity can fail in non‑locally‑compact settings.
  • Neglecting the uniform ellipticity condition in the martingale problem; without it, existence may hold but uniqueness can break down.
  • Using log‑Sobolev constants without checking reversibility of the Markov semigroup; the inequality may not apply to non‑reversible chains.
  • Treating regular conditional probabilities as pointwise defined for all x; they are only defined μ‑almost everywhere, and measurability must be verified.
  • Applying the Portmanteau theorem to non‑regular limit measures; the theorem’s equivalences require the limit measure to be Radon.
  • Overlooking tensorisation of functional inequalities; the constant for a product measure is the maximum of the factors, not the sum.

Ergodic Decomposition and the Structure of Invariant Measures

Let (X,𝔅,μ) be a probability space and T:X→X a measure‑preserving transformation. The set of all T‑invariant probability measures forms a convex compact subset of the space of probability measures equipped with the weak* topology. By the Krein–Milman theorem this set is the closed convex hull of its extreme points. The extreme points are precisely the ergodic measures. The ergodic decomposition theorem states that every T‑invariant probability measure μ can be represented uniquely as an integral over the ergodic measures: μ = ∫_ℰ ν dτ(ν), where ℰ denotes the set of ergodic measures and τ is a probability measure on ℰ (the ergodic decomposition of μ). This representation is the measure‑theoretic analogue of decomposing a vector into a mixture of pure states.

Construction of the decomposition uses the σ‑algebra ℐ of T‑invariant sets. The conditional expectation of the identity function with respect to ℐ yields a measurable map x↦μ_x from X to ℰ such that for any f∈L¹(μ), ∫ f dμ = ∫ (∫ f dμ_x) dμ(x). The map x↦μ_x is essentially unique and satisfies μ_x∘T⁻¹ = μ_x for μ‑a.e. x. In particular, for μ‑a.e. x the measure μ_x is ergodic. The theorem extends to actions of amenable groups and to flows, where the invariant σ‑algebra is replaced by the tail σ‑algebra of the action.

Applications appear in statistical mechanics (decomposition of Gibbs states into pure phases), in smooth dynamics (Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen measures), and in number theory (Furstenberg’s correspondence principle). In examinations, a typical question asks to prove that if μ is invariant and the system is uniquely ergodic, then the ergodic decomposition is trivial (τ is a Dirac mass). Another common task is to show that the ergodic decomposition of a product measure μ⊗ν with respect to the product transformation T×S is the product of the individual ergodic decompositions.

Kolmogorov–Sinai Entropy and the Shannon–McMillan–Breiman Theorem

For a measure‑preserving system (X,𝔅,μ,T) and a finite measurable partition 𝒫 = {P₁,…,P_k}, the entropy of 𝒫 is H_μ(𝒫) = −∑i=1^k μ(P_i) log μ(P_i). The conditional entropy of 𝒫 given a sub‑σ‑algebra ℱ is H_μ(𝒫|ℱ) = ∫ Hμ_x(𝒫) dμ(x), where μ_x are the conditional measures on the atoms of ℱ. The entropy of T with respect to 𝒫 is h_μ(T,𝒫) = limn→∞ (1/n) H_μ(𝒫 ∨ T⁻¹𝒫 ∨ … ∨ T-(n-1)𝒫). The Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy of T is h_μ(T) = sup_𝒫 h_μ(T,𝒫), the supremum taken over all finite partitions.

The Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem (also called the asymptotic equipartition property) asserts that for an ergodic system and any finite partition 𝒫, for μ‑a.e. x the limit limn→∞ −(1/n) log μ(𝒫_n(x)) = h_μ(T,𝒫) holds, where 𝒫_n(x) denotes the atom of the join partition containing x. This means that typical orbits can be coded with approximately 2n h_μ(T,𝒫) blocks of length n, and the measure of each such block is roughly 2-n h_μ(T,𝒫). The theorem is proved via the martingale convergence theorem applied to the sequence of conditional expectations of the information function I_𝒫(x) = −log μ(𝒫(x)).

Key consequences: (1) Entropy is an isomorphism invariant for measure‑preserving systems. (2) For a Bernoulli shift on k symbols with probabilities p₁,…,p_k, h_μ(T) = −∑ p_i log p_i. (3) The variational principle: for a continuous map T on a compact metric space, the topological entropy equals the supremum of measure‑theoretic entropies over all invariant probability measures. In competitive examinations, candidates are often asked to compute the entropy of a given Markov shift or to prove that a factor map cannot increase entropy.

Worked Example: Entropy of a Two‑State Markov Chain
Let X = {0,1}^ℤ with the shift σ. The transition matrix is P = [[0.7,0.3],[0.4,0.6]]. The stationary distribution π satisfies πP = π, giving π₀ = 4/7, π₁ = 3/7. Compute the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy h_μ(σ) of the corresponding stationary Markov measure μ.
The entropy of a stationary Markov chain equals the conditional entropy of the next symbol given the present: h_μ(σ) = H_μ(X₁|X₀) = −∑i,j π_i Pij log Pij. Compute: π₀P₀₀ = (4/7)·0.7 = 0.4, π₀P₀₁ = (4/7)·0.3 ≈ 0.1714, π₁P₁₀ = (3/7)·0.4 ≈ 0.1714, π₁P₁₁ = (3/7)·0.6 ≈ 0.2571. Then h = −[0.4 log 0.7 + 0.1714 log 0.3 + 0.1714 log 0.4 + 0.2571 log 0.6] ≈ 0.610 nats (≈ 0.880 bits). This value is the supremum over all finite partitions, so it equals the KS entropy.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for entropy, first identify whether the system is a Bernoulli shift, a Markov shift, or a general measure‑preserving transformation. For Markov shifts, use the conditional entropy formula H(X₁|X₀) with the stationary distribution. For Bernoulli shifts, the entropy is simply the Shannon entropy of the single‑symbol distribution. If the system is a factor of a known system, remember that entropy does not increase under factor maps. Write the definition of conditional entropy explicitly; partial credit is often awarded for setting up the correct sum even if the final numeric evaluation is omitted.

Quadratic Variation, Itô's Formula, and the Construction of the Itô Integral

Let (Ω,ℱ,(ℱ_t),ℙ) be a filtered probability space satisfying the usual conditions and let W = (W_t)t≥0 be a standard Brownian motion. For a continuous semimartingale X, the quadratic variation [X]_t is defined as the limit in probability of ∑i=1^n (Xt_i−Xti-1)2 over partitions with mesh tending to zero. For Brownian motion, [W]_t = t. If X = M + A where M is a local martingale and A a finite‑variation process, then [X] = [M]. The Itô integral ∫0^t H_s dW_s for a predictable process H with ∫0^t H_s2 ds < ∞ a.s. is constructed first for simple processes and then extended by the Itô isometry: 𝔼[(∫0^t H_s dW_s)2] = 𝔼[∫0^t H_s2 ds]. This isometry shows the integral is an L²‑limit of simple integrals and yields a continuous local martingale.

Itô's formula for a C² function f:ℝ→ℝ applied to a continuous semimartingale X reads f(X_t) = f(X0) + ∫0^t f'(X_s) dX_s + ½∫0^t f''(X_s) d[X]_s. The extra second‑order term distinguishes Itô calculus from ordinary calculus and originates from the non‑zero quadratic variation of Brownian motion. For a multidimensional Brownian motion W = (W¹,…,W^d) and f∈C²(ℝ^d), the formula involves the Hessian matrix and the covariation matrix [W^i,W^j]_t = δij t.

In examinations, typical tasks include: (a) compute the quadratic variation of ∫0^t s dW_s (answer: ∫0^t s2 ds); (b) apply Itô's formula to f(W_t) = exp(λW_t − ½λ²t) to show it is a martingale; (c) derive the stochastic differential equation satisfied by a geometric Brownian motion and solve it explicitly. A frequent trap is forgetting the ½ factor in the second‑order term or misidentifying the covariation of two independent Brownian motions as non‑zero.

Martingale Representation Theorem and Its Applications in Finance

Let (Ω,ℱ,(ℱ_t),ℙ) be a filtered probability space where ℱ_t = σ(W_s : s≤t) is the natural filtration of a d‑dimensional Brownian motion W, augmented by ℙ‑null sets. The martingale representation theorem states that every square‑integrable (ℱ_t)‑martingale M_t can be written as M_t = M0 + ∑i=1^d ∫0^t H_s^i dW_s^i for some predictable processes H^i satisfying 𝔼[∫0^T |H_s|2 ds] < ∞. The representation is unique up to indistinguishability. The proof uses the fact that the set of stochastic integrals of simple processes is dense in L²(Ω,ℱ_T,ℙ) and that the stochastic integral is an isometry from the space of predictable processes into the space of martingales.

In mathematical finance, the theorem underpins the completeness of the Black–Scholes model. Under the risk‑neutral measure ℚ, the discounted price process of any tradable asset is a martingale. By the representation theorem, the discounted payoff of a European claim can be expressed as a stochastic integral against the discounted stock price, which yields a replicating portfolio. The integrand H is precisely the hedging strategy (the “delta”). If the filtration is larger than the Brownian filtration (e.g., includes jumps), the representation may fail, leading to market incompleteness.

Examination questions often ask to prove the representation for a one‑dimensional Brownian motion using the Itô integral isometry and the density of simple processes, or to compute the hedging strategy for a given payoff such as a digital option. Another common exercise: show that if a martingale M has a representation with integrand H, then the quadratic variation [M]_t = ∫0^t |H_s|2 ds, and deduce that M is a continuous local martingale.

Skorokhod Embedding Theorem and Its Role in Weak Convergence

Let (X_n) be a sequence of random variables with mean zero and finite variance σ². The Skorokhod embedding theorem asserts that there exists a probability space supporting a Brownian motion B and a sequence of stopping times τ_n such that Bτ_n has the same distribution as X_n and 𝔼[τ_n] = σ². Moreover, the τ_n can be chosen so that τ_n → ∞ almost surely and the partial sum process S_n(t) = Bτ⌊nt⌋ converges in distribution to B in the Skorokhod space D[0,1]. This provides a constructive proof of Donsker’s invariance principle (the functional central limit theorem) without invoking tightness criteria directly.

Several constructions exist: the original Skorokhod embedding using the hitting time of a two‑point set, the Dubins–Gilat embedding using a martingale representation, and the Root–Rost embedding which minimizes the expected stopping time. The Root embedding uses a barrier in the (t,x) plane; the stopping time is the first exit from a region bounded by a curve. The Rost embedding uses a filling scheme based on the potential function of the target distribution. All constructions preserve the mean and variance and produce stopping times with 𝔼[τ] = Var(X).

In competitive examinations, the theorem appears in two guises: (i) a theoretical question asking to outline the Skorokhod construction for a symmetric Bernoulli variable (τ = inf{t : B_t ∈ {−1,1}}); (ii) an applied question where one must use the embedding to prove that a given sequence of random walks converges weakly to Brownian motion, by verifying the Lindeberg condition and invoking the Skorokhod representation. A common pitfall is to confuse the Skorokhod embedding (which embeds a single distribution into Brownian motion) with the Skorokhod representation theorem (which represents a weakly convergent sequence on a common probability space). The two theorems share a name but serve different purposes.

  • Confusing the ergodic decomposition with the spectral decomposition of a unitary operator; they are related but distinct concepts.
  • Assuming the Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem holds for non‑ergodic systems without conditioning on the invariant σ‑algebra.
  • Omitting the ½ factor in Itô's formula or applying the classical chain rule to stochastic integrals.
  • Treating the martingale representation theorem as valid for any filtration; it requires the filtration to be generated by a Brownian motion (or a suitable martingale).
  • Mixing up Skorokhod embedding with Skorokhod representation; the former constructs stopping times for a given law, the latter constructs a common probability space for a convergent sequence.
  • Neglecting the predictability requirement for the integrand in the Itô integral; using an adapted but non‑predictable process leads to an ill‑defined integral.
  • Forgetting that the quadratic variation of a finite‑variation process is zero, which is essential when applying Itô's formula to semimartingales with a drift component.

Stochastic Integration with Respect to Fractional Brownian Motion and the Young Integral

Fractional Brownian motion (fBm) BH with Hurst index H∈(0,1) is a centred Gaussian process with covariance 𝔼[BHtBHs]=½(|t|2H+|s|2H−|t−s|2H). For H≠½ the process is neither a martingale nor a semimartingale, so the classical Itô integral does not apply. When H>½ the sample paths have finite p-variation for any p>1/H, and the Young integral ∫0T fs dBHs can be defined pathwise for integrands f of complementary q-variation with 1/p+1/q>1. The construction uses the sewing lemma: for a partition π, the Riemann sums converge uniformly provided the integrand is sufficiently regular (e.g. Hölder continuous of order >1−H). For H<½ the paths are rougher; one must resort to rough path theory or the divergence (Skorokhod) integral from Malliavin calculus. The Young integral satisfies a chain rule without an Itô correction term, which simplifies the analysis of differential equations driven by fBm with H>½. In examinations, candidates are often asked to prove that the Young integral coincides with the Riemann–Stieltjes integral when the integrator has bounded variation, or to show that the solution map of a Young differential equation is locally Lipschitz in the p-variation topology.

Lévy Processes: Characteristic Exponents and the Lévy–Khintchine Formula

A Lévy process X=(Xt)t≥0 is a càdlàg process with stationary independent increments and X0=0. Its distribution is infinitely divisible, and the characteristic function takes the Lévy–Khintchine form 𝔼[eiξXt]=exp(−tψ(ξ)) where the characteristic exponent ψ(ξ)=−i a ξ+½ σ² ξ²+∫ℝ{0}(1−eiξx+iξx 1{|x|<1}) ν(dx). Here a∈ℝ is the drift, σ≥0 the Gaussian coefficient, and ν a Lévy measure satisfying ∫ℝ{0} min(1,x²) ν(dx)<∞. The triplet (a,σ²,ν) uniquely determines the law. The Lévy–Itô decomposition writes Xt=a t+σ Wt+∫0t∫|x|<1 x (μ−ν)(ds,dx)+∫0t∫|x|≥1 x μ(ds,dx) where μ is the Poisson random measure of jumps and W a Brownian motion. This representation underpins stochastic calculus for jump processes: the Itô formula for a C² function f reads f(Xt)−f(X0)=∫0t f'(Xs−) dXs+½∫0t f''(Xs−) d[X]sc+∑s≤t(f(Xs)−f(Xs−)−f'(Xs−)ΔXs). Examiners frequently test the ability to identify the Lévy triplet for compound Poisson, Gamma, or stable processes, and to compute the characteristic exponent of a tempered stable process.

Worked Example: Lévy Triplet of a Compound Poisson Process
Let N be a Poisson process with intensity λ>0 and let (Yk) be i.i.d. random variables with distribution μY, independent of N. Define Xt=∑k=1Nt Yk. Find the Lévy triplet (a,σ²,ν) of X.
The characteristic function of Xt is 𝔼[eiξXt]=exp(λ t (∫ℝ (eiξx−1) μY(dx))). Comparing with the Lévy–Khintchine form we read off σ²=0 (no Gaussian part). The Lévy measure is ν(dx)=λ μY(dx). The drift term a is chosen so that the compensator of small jumps matches the truncation function h(x)=x 1{|x|<1}. Hence a=−∫|x|<1 x ν(dx)=−λ ∫|x|<1 x μY(dx). The triplet is (a,0,λ μY).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Lévy–Khintchine representation, first write the generic formula, then identify each component by matching the given characteristic function or by computing the Laplace exponent. Remember that the truncation function h(x)=x 1{|x|<1} is conventional; any other bounded truncation changes the drift a but leaves σ² and ν invariant. Keep a table of common Lévy measures (compound Poisson, Gamma, α‑stable, tempered stable) for quick reference.

Optimal Stopping, Snell Envelope, and the Theory of American Options

Let (Ω,ℱ,(ℱt),ℙ) be a filtered probability space satisfying the usual conditions. An (ℱt)-stopping time τ takes values in [0,T]∪{∞}. For an adapted càdlàg payoff process (Zt) with 𝔼[supt≤T|Zt|]<∞, the optimal stopping problem is to find supτ∈𝒯 𝔼[Zτ 1{τ≤T}]. The Snell envelope (Ut) is the smallest supermartingale dominating Z; it is given by Ut=ess supτ≥t 𝔼[Zτ | ℱt]. The Doob–Meyer decomposition Ut=Mt−At with M a martingale and A a predictable increasing process yields the optimal stopping time τ* = inf{t≥0 : Ut=Zt} (with τ*=T if the set is empty). In the American option pricing context under a risk‑neutral measure ℚ, the discounted payoff Zt=e−rt(K−St)+ for a put option. The Snell envelope coincides with the option price process, and the optimal exercise boundary is the set where immediate exercise equals continuation value. Examiners often ask to prove that the Snell envelope is a supermartingale, to derive the free‑boundary problem for the American put, or to show that the optimal stopping time for a Markov payoff is the first hitting time of a closed set.

Random Measures, Poisson Point Processes, and the Laplace Functional

A random measure μ on a measurable space (E,ℰ) is a mapping ω↦μ(ω,·) such that for each A∈ℰ, μ(·,A) is a random variable. A Poisson point process (PPP) with intensity measure Λ (σ‑finite) is characterised by: (i) for disjoint A1,…,An, the counts μ(Ai) are independent Poisson(Λ(Ai)) random variables; (ii) for any A, μ(A) has Poisson(Λ(A)) distribution. The Laplace functional Lμ(f)=𝔼[exp(−∫E f dμ)] for non‑negative measurable f equals exp(−∫E (1−e−f(x)) Λ(dx)). This functional uniquely determines the law of the PPP. Campbell's formula gives 𝔼[∑x∈μ f(x)]=∫E f(x) Λ(dx) and the second moment formula involves ∫ f² dΛ + (∫ f dΛ)². The Slivnyak–Mecke theorem states that for a PPP, the Palm distribution coincides with the original law plus a point at the origin. These tools are essential for stochastic geometry (Boolean models, random graphs) and for the analysis of shot‑noise processes. Typical exam tasks: compute the Laplace functional of a homogeneous PPP on ℝd, derive the distribution of the distance to the nearest point, or apply the Mecke formula to evaluate expectations of sums over points.

Tightness Criteria for Càdlàg Processes: Aldous' Condition and the Meyer–Zheng Topology

Weak convergence of probability measures on the Skorokhod space D[0,T] requires tightness. Aldous' criterion (1978) states that a sequence (Xn) of càdlàg adapted processes is tight in D[0,T] if (i) for each η>0 there exists a compact K⊂ℝ such that supn ℙ(Xn0∉K)<η, and (ii) for every ε>0, limδ↓0 supn supτ≤T supθ≤δ ℙ(|Xnτ+θ−Xnτ|>ε)=0, where the supremum runs over all stopping times τ bounded by T. This condition is both necessary and sufficient for tightness when the limit is continuous. For processes with jumps, the Meyer–Zheng topology (the topology of convergence in measure on [0,T]) provides a compactification: every sequence of probability measures on D[0,T] has a subsequence converging in the Meyer–Zheng sense to a limit that may not be càdlàg but is measurable. The Meyer–Zheng topology is metrisable by the metric dMZ(x,y)=∫0T 1∧|x(t)−y(t)| dt. In examinations, candidates may be asked to verify Aldous' condition for a sequence of scaled random walks, to explain why the Skorokhod J1 topology is too strong for certain jump processes, or to prove that convergence in the Meyer–Zheng topology implies convergence of finite‑dimensional distributions.

  • Confusing the Young integral with the Itô integral; the former has no martingale property and no Itô correction term.
  • Forgetting that the Lévy measure ν must integrate min(1,x²); omitting this integrability condition leads to an invalid triplet.
  • Misidentifying the optimal stopping time as the first time the payoff exceeds the continuation value, rather than the first time the Snell envelope equals the payoff.
  • Applying the Laplace functional of a PPP to a non‑Poisson random measure without checking the independence of counts on disjoint sets.
  • Using the Skorokhod J1 metric when the limit process has jumps that are not matched in time; the Meyer–Zheng topology is often the correct framework.
  • Neglecting the truncation function h(x)=x 1{|x|<1} in the Lévy–Khintchine formula, which changes the drift but leaves the Lévy measure unchanged.
  • Assuming the Snell envelope is always a martingale; it is only a supermartingale, and its Doob–Meyer decomposition is essential for characterising optimal stopping.

The Four Fundamental Subspaces and Their Dimensions

Beyond the column space (which is the span of the columns of A) and the null space (the set of solutions to Ax=0), every matrix A of size m×n defines two other fundamental subspaces: the row space and the left null space. Understanding these four subspaces—Column Space C(A), Null Space N(A), Row Space C(Aᵀ), and Left Null Space N(Aᵀ)—is crucial for a complete grasp of matrix properties, solvability of linear systems, and the geometry of linear transformations.

1. Column Space C(A)

The column space of A is the span of its column vectors. It is a subspace of Rm. The system Ax=b has a solution if and only if b is in the column space of A. The dimension of the column space is called the rank of the matrix, denoted rank(A). This is equal to the number of linearly independent columns (or rows) and also the number of pivots in the row echelon form of A.

2. Null Space N(A)

The null space of A consists of all vectors x in Rn such that Ax=0. It is a subspace of Rn. The dimension of the null space is called the nullity of the matrix, denoted nullity(A). This is equal to the number of free variables in the solution to Ax=0, which is n minus the number of pivots.

3. Row Space C(Aᵀ)

The row space of A is the span of its row vectors. Equivalently, it is the column space of Aᵀ. It is a subspace of Rn. The dimension of the row space is also equal to the rank of A. This is a fundamental result: rank(A) = rank(Aᵀ). The non-zero rows in the row echelon form of A form a basis for the row space.

4. Left Null Space N(Aᵀ)

The left null space of A consists of all vectors y in Rm such that Aᵀy=0. Equivalently, it is the null space of Aᵀ. It is a subspace of Rm. The dimension of the left null space is nullity(Aᵀ), which is m minus the rank of A.

The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra: Dimensions and Orthogonal Complements

These four subspaces are not independent; they are intimately related through their dimensions and orthogonal complements. For any m×n matrix A with rank r:

  • Dimension of C(A) = r
  • Dimension of N(A) = n - r
  • Dimension of C(Aᵀ) = r
  • Dimension of N(Aᵀ) = m - r

The crucial relationships are:

  1. Rank-Nullity Theorem: For a matrix A of size m×n, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n. This states that the dimension of the row space plus the dimension of the null space equals the total number of columns.
  2. Orthogonal Complements:
    • The null space N(A) is the orthogonal complement of the row space C(Aᵀ) in Rn. This means every vector in N(A) is orthogonal to every vector in C(Aᵀ).
    • The left null space N(Aᵀ) is the orthogonal complement of the column space C(A) in Rm. This means every vector in N(Aᵀ) is orthogonal to every vector in C(A).

These relationships provide a complete picture of how a linear transformation maps vectors between spaces and what happens to the dimensions. For instance, the Rank-Nullity Theorem explains why a system Ax=b might have infinitely many solutions (if nullity(A) > 0) or no solutions (if b is not in C(A)). The orthogonal complement relationships are vital in understanding projections, least squares, and many optimization problems.

Orthogonal Bases, Projections, and the Gram-Schmidt Process

The concept of orthogonality is fundamental in linear algebra, simplifying calculations and providing geometric intuition. An orthogonal set of vectors consists of vectors where every pair is perpendicular (their dot product is zero). If, in addition, each vector has unit length, the set is orthonormal.

Orthogonal and Orthonormal Bases

A basis {v₁, v₂, ..., vₖ} for a subspace V is an orthogonal basis if vᵢ ⋅ vⱼ = 0 for all i ≠ j. If, additionally, ||vᵢ|| = 1 for all i, then it is an orthonormal basis. Orthonormal bases are particularly useful because coordinates with respect to such a basis are easy to compute: if v = c₁q₁ + ... + cₖqₖ where {q₁, ..., qₖ} is an orthonormal basis, then cᵢ = v ⋅ qᵢ.

Matrices whose columns form an orthonormal basis are called orthogonal matrices (Q). For such matrices, QᵀQ = I and Qᵀ = Q⁻¹. This property makes them ideal for transformations that preserve length and angles, such as rotations and reflections.

Orthogonal Projection onto a Subspace

Given a vector b and a subspace V, the orthogonal projection of b onto V, denoted projᵥb, is the closest vector in V to b. The error vector e = b - projᵥb is orthogonal to every vector in V. This geometric insight is the core of the Least Squares method: when Ax=b has no exact solution, we project b onto the column space of A to find the closest possible vector Ax̂, where x̂ is the least squares solution.

If V is spanned by an orthonormal basis {q₁, ..., qₖ}, the projection is simply: projᵥb = (b ⋅ q₁)q₁ + (b ⋅ q₂)q₂ + ... + (b ⋅ qₖ)qₖ

If the basis is orthogonal but not orthonormal, the formula adjusts slightly: projᵥb = [(b ⋅ v₁)/(v₁ ⋅ v₁)]v₁ + ... + [(b ⋅ vₖ)/(vₖ ⋅ vₖ)]vₖ

For a general subspace V spanned by columns of A, the projection matrix P onto C(A) is P = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ. Then projᵥb = Pb.

The Gram-Schmidt Process

The Gram-Schmidt process is an algorithm for converting any basis {v₁, v₂, ..., vₖ} for a subspace into an orthogonal basis {u₁, u₂, ..., uₖ}, and subsequently into an orthonormal basis {q₁, q₂, ..., qₖ}.

Steps:

  1. Let u₁ = v₁.
  2. For u₂, subtract the projection of v₂ onto the subspace spanned by u₁: u₂ = v₂ - projspan{u₁}(v₂) = v₂ - [(v₂ ⋅ u₁)/(u₁ ⋅ u₁)]u₁
  3. For u₃, subtract the projection of v₃ onto the subspace spanned by u₁ and u₂: u₃ = v₃ - projspan{u₁, u₂}(v₃) = v₃ - [(v₃ ⋅ u₁)/(u₁ ⋅ u₁)]u₁ - [(v₃ ⋅ u₂)/(u₂ ⋅ u₂)]u₂
  4. Continue this process for all vectors vᵢ: uᵢ = vᵢ - ∑j=1i-1 [(vᵢ ⋅ uⱼ)/(uⱼ ⋅ uⱼ)]uⱼ
  5. To obtain an orthonormal basis, normalize each orthogonal vector: qᵢ = uᵢ / ||uᵢ||

The Gram-Schmidt process is computationally intensive but conceptually vital. It underlies the QR factorization (A = QR), where Q is an orthogonal matrix and R is an upper triangular matrix. This factorization is widely used in numerical linear algebra for solving linear systems, least squares problems, and eigenvalue computations due to its numerical stability.

Applying Gram-Schmidt to find an Orthonormal Basis

Consider the basis vectors v₁ = [1, 1, 0]ᵀ and v₂ = [0, 1, 1]ᵀ for a subspace W in R³. Use the Gram-Schmidt process to find an orthonormal basis for W.

Step 1: Find the first orthogonal vector u₁.

Let u₁ = v₁ = [1, 1, 0]ᵀ.

Step 2: Find the second orthogonal vector u₂.

u₂ = v₂ - projspan{u₁}(v₂) = v₂ - [(v₂ ⋅ u₁)/(u₁ ⋅ u₁)]u₁

First, calculate the dot products:

  • v₂ ⋅ u₁ = (0)(1) + (1)(1) + (1)(0) = 1
  • u₁ ⋅ u₁ = (1)(1) + (1)(1) + (0)(0) = 2

Now, substitute these values into the formula for u₂:

u₂ = [0, 1, 1]ᵀ - (1/2)[1, 1, 0]ᵀ

u₂ = [0, 1, 1]ᵀ - [1/2, 1/2, 0]ᵀ

u₂ = [-1/2, 1/2, 1]ᵀ

So, the orthogonal basis is {u₁ = [1, 1, 0]ᵀ, u₂ = [-1/2, 1/2, 1]ᵀ}.

Step 3: Normalize the orthogonal vectors to find the orthonormal basis.

For q₁:

  • ||u₁|| = √(1² + 1² + 0²) = √2
  • q₁ = u₁ / ||u₁|| = (1/√2)[1, 1, 0]ᵀ = [1/√2, 1/√2, 0]ᵀ

For q₂:

  • ||u₂|| = √((-1/2)² + (1/2)² + 1²) = √(1/4 + 1/4 + 1) = √(1/2 + 1) = √(3/2)
  • q₂ = u₂ / ||u₂|| = (1/√(3/2))[-1/2, 1/2, 1]ᵀ = (√2/√3)[-1/2, 1/2, 1]ᵀ = [-1/√6, 1/√6, √2/√3]ᵀ

The orthonormal basis for W is {q₁ = [1/√2, 1/√2, 0]ᵀ, q₂ = [-1/√6, 1/√6, √2/√3]ᵀ}.

Mastering the Geometric Interpretation
Many advanced linear algebra problems, especially those involving projections, least squares, or orthogonal complements, become much clearer with a strong geometric intuition. Always try to visualize the vectors and subspaces involved, even if it's just in 2D or 3D. Understanding that the error vector (b - Ax̂) in least squares is orthogonal to the column space of A, or that the null space is perpendicular to the row space, can help you derive solutions or verify results without complex calculations. Draw diagrams to solidify these relationships.

Change of Basis and Similarity Transformations

In linear algebra, vectors are often represented by coordinates with respect to a chosen basis. However, the choice of basis is arbitrary, and sometimes a different basis can simplify calculations or reveal underlying properties of a linear transformation. The process of changing from one basis to another is called a change of basis, and it has profound implications for how vectors and matrices are represented.

Coordinates with Respect to a Basis

If B = {b₁, b₂, ..., bₙ} is a basis for a vector space V, any vector v in V can be uniquely written as a linear combination v = c₁b₁ + c₂b₂ + ... + cₙbₙ. The coefficients [c₁, c₂, ..., cₙ]ᵀ form the coordinate vector of v with respect to basis B, denoted [v]B.

The Change of Basis Matrix

Suppose we have two bases for Rⁿ: the standard basis E = {e₁, ..., eₙ} and an arbitrary basis B = {b₁, ..., bₙ}. To convert coordinates from basis B to the standard basis E, we form a matrix PE←B whose columns are the basis vectors b₁, ..., bₙ. Then, if [v]B is the coordinate vector of v in basis B, its standard coordinates [v]E (which is just v itself) are given by v = PE←B[v]B.

To convert coordinates from the standard basis E to basis B, we use the inverse matrix: [v]B = PB←E[v]E = (PE←B)⁻¹[v]E.

More generally, to change from an old basis B to a new basis C, the change of basis matrix PC←B is given by PC←B = (PE←C)⁻¹PE←B. Its columns are the B-basis vectors expressed in C-coordinates.

Similarity Transformations for Linear Operators

A linear transformation T: V → V can be represented by a matrix A with respect to a chosen basis B. If we change to a new basis C, the same linear transformation T will be represented by a different matrix A'. The relationship between A and A' is given by a similarity transformation.

Let A be the matrix representation of T with respect to basis B, and A' be the matrix representation of T with respect to basis C. Let P be the change of basis matrix from C to B (i.e., P = PB←C, whose columns are the vectors of basis C expressed in basis B coordinates). Then the relationship is:

A' = P⁻¹AP

This is a similarity transformation. Two matrices A and A' are said to be similar if there exists an invertible matrix P such that A' = P⁻¹AP. Similar matrices represent the same linear transformation, but in different bases. They share many important properties:

  • They have the same determinant.
  • They have the same trace (sum of diagonal elements).
  • They have the same eigenvalues.
  • They have the same characteristic polynomial.
  • They have the same rank and nullity.

The concept of similarity is central to diagonalization. When a matrix A is diagonalizable, it means it is similar to a diagonal matrix D. The diagonal entries of D are the eigenvalues of A, and the columns of the similarity matrix P are the corresponding eigenvectors. In this case, P⁻¹AP = D, which means A is similar to D. This implies that by choosing a basis of eigenvectors, the linear transformation represented by A becomes a simple scaling operation along the basis vectors, represented by the diagonal matrix D.

Understanding change of basis and similarity transformations is crucial for simplifying complex problems, especially in areas like differential equations, quantum mechanics, and numerical analysis, where choosing the right basis can dramatically reduce computational effort and provide deeper insights into the nature of the transformation.

Quadratic Forms and Positive Definite Matrices

Quadratic forms are fundamental in optimization, statistics, physics, and geometry. They generalize the concept of a squared term (like x²) to multiple variables and are closely related to symmetric matrices and eigenvalues.

What is a Quadratic Form?

A quadratic form is a polynomial where every term has a total degree of two. For a vector x = [x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ]ᵀ in Rⁿ, a quadratic form can be written as:

Q(x) = xᵀAx

where A is an n×n symmetric matrix. If A is not symmetric, we can always replace it with (A + Aᵀ)/2, which is symmetric and yields the same quadratic form. So, without loss of generality, we always assume A is symmetric when dealing with quadratic forms.

Example: For n=2, x = [x₁, x₂]ᵀ and A = [[a, b/2], [b/2, c]], then:

Q(x) = [x₁, x₂] [[a, b/2], [b/2, c]] [x₁, x₂]ᵀ = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂²

The matrix A is called the matrix of the quadratic form.

Positive Definite Matrices

A symmetric matrix A is classified based on the values of its associated quadratic form Q(x) = xᵀAx:

  1. Positive Definite (PD): Q(x) > 0 for all x ≠ 0.
    • Geometrically, the graph of Q(x) is a paraboloid opening upwards.
    • All eigenvalues of A are positive.
    • All leading principal minors (determinants of top-left submatrices) are positive.
    • All pivots (without row exchanges) are positive.
  2. Positive Semi-Definite (PSD): Q(x) ≥ 0 for all x, and Q(x) = 0 for some x ≠ 0.
    • All eigenvalues of A are non-negative, and at least one eigenvalue is zero.
    • All principal minors (not just leading) are non-negative.
  3. Negative Definite (ND): Q(x) < 0 for all x ≠ 0.
    • All eigenvalues of A are negative.
    • Leading principal minors alternate in sign: det(A₁) < 0, det(A₂) > 0, det(A₃) < 0, etc.
  4. Negative Semi-Definite (NSD): Q(x) ≤ 0 for all x, and Q(x) = 0 for some x ≠ 0.
    • All eigenvalues of A are non-positive, and at least one eigenvalue is zero.
  5. Indefinite: Q(x) takes both positive and negative values.
    • A has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Applications and Significance

  • Optimization: In multivariable calculus, the second derivative test for local extrema of a function f(x) involves the Hessian matrix (matrix of second partial derivatives). If the Hessian is positive definite at a critical point, the function has a local minimum. If it's negative definite, it's a local maximum. If indefinite, it's a saddle point.
  • Statistics: Covariance matrices are always positive semi-definite (and often positive definite if there are no perfect linear dependencies between variables). This property ensures that variances are non-negative.
  • Stability Analysis: In dynamical systems, the stability of equilibrium points often depends on whether certain matrices are positive definite.
  • Geometry: Quadratic forms define shapes like ellipses, hyperbolas, and parabolas in 2D, and ellipsoids, hyperboloids, etc., in higher dimensions. The principal axes of these shapes are given by the eigenvectors of the matrix A.

The ability to classify a symmetric matrix as positive definite (or semi-definite) is a powerful tool, providing insights into the nature of functions, the structure of data, and the behavior of systems. The criteria involving eigenvalues, pivots, and leading principal minors offer different computational paths to determine this crucial property.

Common Traps in Advanced Linear Algebra

  • Confusing Null Space and Left Null Space: Remember N(A) is in Rn (domain of A), while N(Aᵀ) is in Rm (codomain of A). They are orthogonal complements to C(Aᵀ) and C(A) respectively, not to each other.
  • Incorrectly Applying Rank-Nullity Theorem: The theorem states rank(A) + nullity(A) = n (number of columns). It's a common mistake to use 'm' (number of rows) instead of 'n'.
  • Assuming Orthogonality Implies Orthonormality: An orthogonal set has perpendicular vectors. An orthonormal set has perpendicular vectors that are also unit vectors. Normalization is the extra step.
  • Misremembering Gram-Schmidt Order: The projection of vᵢ is subtracted from vᵢ itself, and it's projected onto the subspace spanned by the *already orthogonalized* vectors u₁, ..., uᵢ₋₁, not the original v's.
  • Errors in Change of Basis Matrix Inversion: When changing from basis B to C, the matrix PC←B is (PE←C)⁻¹PE←B. Forgetting the inverse or applying it to the wrong matrix is a frequent error.
  • Confusing Similar Matrices with Congruent Matrices: Similar matrices (A' = P⁻¹AP) represent the same linear transformation in different bases. Congruent matrices (A' = PᵀAP) are relevant for quadratic forms and preserve positive definiteness, but they are not the same concept.
  • Misinterpreting Positive Definiteness Criteria: While positive eigenvalues, positive pivots, and positive leading principal minors are all equivalent conditions for a symmetric matrix to be positive definite, applying the wrong test (e.g., using leading principal minors for a non-symmetric matrix) or miscalculating them can lead to errors.

Jordan Canonical Form and Generalized Eigenvectors

When a matrix is not diagonalizable, the Jordan canonical form provides the next best structural description. Every square matrix A over an algebraically closed field (such as the complex numbers) is similar to a block diagonal matrix J composed of Jordan blocks. Each Jordan block corresponds to an eigenvalue λ and has λ on the diagonal, ones on the super‑diagonal, and zeros elsewhere. The size of the block equals the length of the longest chain of generalized eigenvectors associated with λ.

A generalized eigenvector of rank k satisfies (A − λI)kv = 0 but (A − λI)k−1v ≠ 0. Ordinary eigenvectors are the case k = 1. Chains of generalized eigenvectors are built by solving (A − λI)vi = vi−1 starting from an eigenvector v1. The number of Jordan blocks for λ equals the geometric multiplicity (dimension of the eigenspace), while the sum of their sizes equals the algebraic multiplicity.

The Jordan form is unique up to permutation of blocks. It reveals the structure of the nilpotent part of A − λI and is essential for computing functions of matrices, solving systems of linear differential equations, and analyzing the asymptotic behavior of linear dynamical systems. In practice, the Jordan form is numerically unstable; small perturbations can split a Jordan block into distinct eigenvalues. Therefore, algorithms for matrix functions often avoid explicit Jordan decomposition and use Schur or Schur‑Parlett methods instead.

Key Properties

  • Similarity invariance: J = P−1AP for some invertible P.
  • Each block Jk(λ) has minimal polynomial (x − λ)k.
  • The matrix exponential exp(Jt) is block diagonal with blocks exp(Jk(λ)t) = eλt times a polynomial in t of degree k−1.

Matrix Functions and the Exponential

For a square matrix A, a matrix function f(A) can be defined via several equivalent approaches: power series, Jordan form, Cauchy integral, or polynomial interpolation. The most important example is the matrix exponential exp(A) = Σk=0∞ Ak / k!. This series converges for all matrices and satisfies exp(A+B) = exp(A)exp(B) when A and B commute.

If A = PJP−1 is a Jordan decomposition, then f(A) = Pf(J)P−1, where f acts on each Jordan block by the formula f(Jk(λ)) = [f(λ), f'(λ), …, f(k−1)(λ)/(k−1)!] on the super‑diagonals. For the exponential, this yields the polynomial‑times‑exponential structure mentioned above.

The matrix exponential solves the linear system dx/dt = Ax with initial condition x(0) = x0 via x(t) = exp(At)x0. Stability of the zero solution is governed by the eigenvalues of A: if all eigenvalues have negative real parts, the origin is asymptotically stable; if any eigenvalue has positive real part, it is unstable. The exponential also appears in the solution of inhomogeneous systems via the variation‑of‑constants formula.

Other matrix functions include the logarithm (inverse of exponential for matrices with no eigenvalues on the negative real axis), square roots, and the sign function. These are used in control theory, model reduction, and the computation of matrix sector functions. Reliable numerical algorithms (scaling‑and‑squaring with Padé approximants for the exponential, Schur‑Parlett for general functions) are implemented in standard libraries such as LAPACK and SciPy.

Worked Example: Computing exp(At) for a 2×2 Defective Matrix
Let A = [[2, 1], [0, 2]]. Find exp(At) and use it to solve dx/dt = Ax with x(0) = [1, 0]ᵀ.
The matrix A has eigenvalue λ = 2 with algebraic multiplicity 2 but only one eigenvector, so it is a single Jordan block J = [[2, 1], [0, 2]]. Since A is already in Jordan form, P = I. For a 2×2 Jordan block J₂(λ), exp(J₂(λ)t) = eλt [[1, t], [0, 1]]. Thus exp(At) = e2t [[1, t], [0, 1]]. The solution is x(t) = exp(At)x(0) = e2t [[1, t], [0, 1]] [1, 0]ᵀ = [e2t, 0]ᵀ. This matches the direct solution of the decoupled system: dx₁/dt = 2x₁ + x₂, dx₂/dt = 2x₂ with x₂(0)=0 gives x₂(t)=0, then x₁(t)=e2t.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When asked for a matrix exponential, first check if the matrix is diagonalizable. If yes, use exp(A) = P diag(eλᵢ) P⁻¹. If not, write down the Jordan blocks; the exponential of each block is eλt times a polynomial in t whose coefficients are 1/k! on the k‑th super‑diagonal. Memorise the 2×2 and 3×3 patterns; they appear frequently in time‑limited questions.

Tensor Products and Multilinear Maps

The tensor product (Kronecker product) of matrices A (m×n) and B (p×q) is the mp×nq block matrix A ⊗ B = [aijB]. It represents the linear map on the tensor product space V ⊗ W induced by the pair of linear maps A: V → V' and B: W → W'. Key algebraic properties include bilinearity, associativity up to isomorphism, and the mixed‑product property (A ⊗ B)(C ⊗ D) = (AC) ⊗ (BD) when dimensions match.

Eigenvalues of A ⊗ B are all pairwise products λiμj where λi are eigenvalues of A and μj of B. The singular values are pairwise products of singular values. The determinant is det(A)p det(B)m, and the trace is tr(A) tr(B). These facts make the Kronecker product a powerful tool for constructing large structured matrices from small ones.
